11 U.S.C. Section 549 - Post-Petition Transfers

Plain-English guide to the trustee's power to avoid unauthorized transfers of estate property occurring after the bankruptcy filing: the general rule, the involuntary-case gap exception, the good-faith real-property exception, and the two-year statute of limitations.

Home › Avoidance Actions › Section 549 - Post-Petition Transfers

Empirical research on this section

For case-pattern analysis on how federal bankruptcy courts apply this provision, including district-level patterns and primary-source dockets, see openbankruptcyproject.org/cases/. All datasets licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

What Section 549 Does

Section 549 differs structurally from the other trustee avoidance powers. Sections 544, 547, and 548 reach transfers that occurred before the bankruptcy filing. Section 549 reaches transfers of property of the estate that occur after the filing. The provision is the back-end complement to Section 362's automatic stay: while Section 362 prohibits certain post-petition actions, Section 549 supplies the remedy for unauthorized post-petition transfers that nevertheless occur.

Once a bankruptcy petition is filed, property of the estate generally cannot be transferred without authorization from the court or as specifically permitted by the Bankruptcy Code. A debtor in possession or a Chapter 11 debtor may make certain ordinary-course transfers under Section 363(c), and other dispositions must be authorized after notice and a hearing under Section 363(b). Transfers that fail to fit any authorized channel are avoidable under Section 549.

Official citation: 11 U.S.C. § 549

Section 549(a): The General Rule

Section 549(a) authorizes the trustee to avoid a transfer of property of the estate that occurs after the commencement of the case and that is (1) authorized only under Section 303(f) or 542(c) of the Bankruptcy Code (the involuntary-case and good-faith-payment provisions), or (2) not authorized under this title or by the court. The structure is therefore one of presumption: any post-petition transfer of estate property is avoidable unless an authorization can be identified.

Common targets of Section 549 actions include:

Payments made by the debtor on pre-petition debts without court authorization

Sales of estate property outside the ordinary course without Section 363(b) approval

Foreclosure sales that proceed in violation of the automatic stay

Transfers of vehicle titles, real-property deeds, or accounts after filing

Bank-account sweeps and offsets without court approval

An unauthorized post-petition transfer is voidable rather than void, which means it remains effective until the trustee successfully avoids it. The transferee retains the property until the court enters an order requiring its return.

Section 549(b): The Involuntary-Case Gap Exception

Section 549(b) addresses the unique problem of involuntary bankruptcy cases. When creditors file an involuntary petition under Section 303, an "order for relief" does not follow immediately; instead, there is a gap period during which the alleged debtor may contest the petition. During this gap, the debtor often continues to operate and transact business. If the petition is ultimately successful and an order for relief is entered, the gap-period transfers become potentially subject to Section 549.

Section 549(b) protects gap-period transferees who acted in good faith. Specifically, the trustee may not avoid a gap-period transfer to the extent of any value, including services but not satisfaction or securing of an antecedent debt, given after the commencement of the case in exchange for the transfer, even if the transferee knew of the commencement of the case. The protection is value-for-value: the transferee keeps the transfer up to the amount of new value given but must return any excess.

The exception reflects Congress's judgment that ordinary commercial activity should be able to continue during the involuntary gap, and that parties dealing with the alleged debtor in good faith should not be penalized for transactions that could not reasonably have been suspended.

Section 549(c): The Good-Faith Real-Property Exception

Section 549(c) provides a critical exception for good-faith purchasers of real property. The trustee may not avoid a transfer of real property to a good-faith purchaser without knowledge of the commencement of the case and for present fair equivalent value, unless a copy or notice of the petition was filed in the office where conveyances of real property in the relevant county are recorded before the transfer was so far perfected that a bona fide purchaser of such property against the debtor could not acquire an interest superior to the interest of such good-faith purchaser.

The provision balances two competing concerns. On one hand, the bankruptcy estate should reach all property of the debtor as of the petition date. On the other, the real-estate market relies on the integrity of the local recording system; a buyer who searches title and pays full value should be able to take clean title without inquiring into bankruptcy filings in other jurisdictions. Section 549(c) resolves the conflict by requiring the estate to record a notice of the petition in the relevant county recording office; absent such recording, a good-faith purchaser for present fair-equivalent value takes free of the estate's claim.

A good-faith purchaser of real property for less than present fair-equivalent value receives a partial protection: a lien on the property to the extent of value given to the debtor, but the trustee may still avoid the transfer itself.

Section 549(d): The Statute of Limitations

Section 549(d) requires that an action under Section 549 be commenced before the earlier of:

Two years after the date of the transfer sought to be avoided, or

The time the case is closed or dismissed.

Section 549's statute of limitations runs from the date of each individual transfer rather than from a single anchor like the order for relief. This means that the trustee must track each post-petition transfer separately and bring suit within two years of that transfer's occurrence. For long-running cases, post-petition transfers near the beginning of the case can become time-barred even while the case remains open.

The 549(d) limitations period is significantly shorter than the 546(a) period that applies to pre-petition avoidance actions in many cases. The Supreme Court has emphasized that the case-closure deadline is jurisdictional and not subject to equitable tolling.

Interaction with the Automatic Stay

Section 549 and the automatic stay under Section 362 frequently overlap but address different remedial questions. The automatic stay is prophylactic: it bars certain actions from occurring in the first place. Section 549 is restorative: it unwinds transfers that should not have occurred. Stay violations may also generate damages under Section 362(k) for individual debtors, including punitive damages in egregious cases, providing a remedy beyond simple avoidance.

A creditor that proceeds with a foreclosure sale in violation of the stay typically faces both stay-violation liability under Section 362 and avoidance of the resulting transfer under Section 549. The two remedies are cumulative rather than alternative, and the trustee may pursue both. A bank that sweeps a deposit account post-petition similarly faces stay-violation exposure and a Section 549 avoidance claim, and the resulting recovery returns the funds to the estate with potential additional damages.

Recovery and Procedure

An action under Section 549 is an adversary proceeding under Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 7001(1). Recovery from the transferee proceeds under Section 550 on the same general framework that applies to other avoided transfers, although the good-faith-for-value defense in Section 550(b) overlaps significantly with the more specific defenses available under Section 549(b) and (c).

Section 542(a) operates as a partial parallel remedy: it requires any entity in possession, custody, or control of property of the estate to deliver such property to the trustee. Section 549 supplies the substantive avoidance theory; Section 542 supplies the corollary obligation to turn property over.

Authorized Post-Petition Transfers

Not every post-petition transfer is avoidable. Several Bankruptcy Code provisions expressly authorize transfers that the trustee cannot then avoid under Section 549. A debtor in possession under Chapter 11 has broad authority under Section 363(c)(1) to use, sell, or lease property of the estate in the ordinary course of business without notice or hearing. Outside the ordinary course, Section 363(b) permits use, sale, or lease only after notice and a hearing. Section 364 authorizes obtaining of credit, with successively higher levels of protection (and procedural hurdles) as the priority sought increases. Section 365 authorizes assumption and assignment of executory contracts.

A trustee or debtor-in-possession can also obtain court approval of an extraordinary transaction in advance through a Section 363(b) motion. Such an order, if not stayed, generally immunizes the transferee from later Section 549 attack because the transaction is authorized "by the court." Section 363(m) further protects good-faith purchasers under Section 363(b) or (c) by limiting appellate reversal even if the order is later found erroneous, provided no stay was obtained.

For Chapter 13 debtors, ordinary-course transactions during the case are typically authorized by Section 1306 and the confirmed plan. Significant non-ordinary-course transactions, including new debt above statutory thresholds and dispositions of estate property, require court authorization.

Common Litigation Scenarios

Three recurring fact patterns dominate Section 549 litigation. The first involves utility companies and other vendors that continue to apply pre-petition deposits or credits against pre-petition obligations after the filing without authorization. The second involves banks that sweep deposit accounts to satisfy pre-petition loans. The third involves vehicle and real-property liens whose holders proceed to foreclosure or repossession in violation of the stay, generating both a stay-violation claim under Section 362 and a 549 avoidance claim.

In each scenario, the analysis reduces to two questions: was the transfer authorized at the moment it occurred, and if not, does any specific Section 549 exception protect the transferee? The trustee's burden is to prove the unauthorized transfer; the transferee bears the burden on the affirmative defenses.

Section 547 - Preferential transfers

Section 548 - Fraudulent transfers

Section 550 - Recovery from transferees

## 11 USC 550 - Liability of Transferees [2026]
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/avoidance-actions/section-550-transferee-liability/

openbankruptcyproject.org
☰

11 U.S.C. Section 550 - Liability of Transferees

Plain-English guide to recovery from initial, mediate, and immediate transferees of avoided transfers: the Section 550(a) recovery framework, the Section 550(b) good-faith-for-value defense, and the Section 550(d) single-satisfaction rule.

Home › Avoidance Actions › Section 550 - Transferee Liability

Empirical research on this section

For case-pattern analysis on how federal bankruptcy courts apply this provision, including district-level patterns and primary-source dockets, see openbankruptcyproject.org/cases/. All datasets licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

What Section 550 Does

Section 550 is the recovery mechanism for the avoidance powers in Sections 544, 545, 547, 548, 549, 553(b), and 724(a). Avoidance under those sections only voids the transfer; Section 550 supplies the substantive right to recover the transferred property or its value from particular defendants. Without Section 550, the trustee would have a declaratory remedy with no enforcement teeth. With it, the trustee can pursue a chain of transferees to bring property back into the estate.

Three structural features make Section 550 unusually consequential. First, the trustee may proceed against the initial transferee even after the property has moved to subsequent transferees. Second, subsequent transferees have a good-faith-for-value defense that initial transferees do not. Third, the single-satisfaction rule limits the trustee to one full recovery in total even when multiple defendants are liable.

Official citation: 11 U.S.C. § 550

Section 550(a): Who Can Be Sued

Section 550(a) provides that, to the extent that a transfer is avoided under one of the listed sections, the trustee may recover, for the benefit of the estate, the property transferred, or, if the court so orders, the value of such property, from:

The initial transferee of such transfer or the entity for whose benefit such transfer was made.

Any immediate or mediate transferee of such initial transferee.

The trustee has the choice between recovering the property itself or its value. This choice matters when the property has changed value or has been altered after the transfer. The choice is also subject to the court's discretion under the statutory language "if the court so orders."

The "entity for whose benefit" language captures third parties that benefited indirectly from the transfer even though they were not the initial transferee. A common example is a guarantor who is released when the debtor pays the principal obligation; the guarantor is the entity for whose benefit the transfer was made and is liable under Section 550(a)(1) on the same terms as the initial transferee.

Who Is an Initial Transferee?

Identifying the initial transferee is consequential because initial transferees do not have the Section 550(b) good-faith defense. Conduits, banks acting as wire-transfer intermediaries, escrow agents, and other mere pass-through entities are typically not considered initial transferees under the dominion-and-control test articulated in the Seventh Circuit's decision in Bonded Financial Services v. European American Bank, 838 F.2d 890 (7th Cir. 1988). Under that test, a party is an initial transferee only if it has dominion and control over the funds, typically meaning it has the right to put the funds to its own use.

The dominion-and-control test has been adopted in most circuits, though the formulations and applications vary. The Eleventh Circuit applies a similar "control test" that also asks whether the recipient was a mere conduit. Some courts have adopted a "principal-agent" overlay that looks to whether the recipient acted on behalf of a principal who was the true intended beneficiary.

The Supreme Court addressed a related question in Merit Management Group v. FTI Consulting, Inc., 583 U.S. 366 (2018), holding that the Section 546(e) safe harbor for settlement payments and securities-contract transfers focuses on the overarching transfer the trustee seeks to avoid rather than on intermediate component transactions. The decision did not directly address Section 550 but reinforced the analytical approach that distinguishes the transfer-as-a-whole from individual conduit movements within the transfer.

Section 550(b): The Good-Faith-for-Value Defense

Section 550(b)(1) provides that the trustee may not recover from a mediate or immediate transferee that takes for value, including satisfaction or securing of a present or antecedent debt, in good faith, and without knowledge of the voidability of the transfer avoided. Section 550(b)(2) extends similar protection to any good-faith transferee that takes from a Section 550(b)(1) transferee.

The defense has three elements: value, good faith, and lack of knowledge of voidability. Each is hotly contested in practice.

Value: Includes satisfaction or securing of a debt, not merely cash consideration. The value need not be reasonably equivalent; even partial value supports the defense, although the recovery may be reduced.

Good faith: Generally an objective standard. A transferee that ignored obvious red flags or facts that would have led a reasonable person to investigate cannot claim good faith.

Without knowledge of voidability: The transferee need not know all facts about the prior transfer; the test is whether the transferee had knowledge sufficient to put a reasonable person on inquiry that the prior transfer was avoidable.

The defense is not available to initial transferees or to entities for whose benefit the initial transfer was made. It applies only to mediate and immediate transferees down the chain.

Section 550(b) in Securities and Finance Cases

The Section 550(b) good-faith defense plays a particularly important role in securities-fraud and Ponzi-scheme cases. When defrauded investors recover their principal and any profits from a scheme operator that later files bankruptcy, the trustee typically sues to recover both principal and profits as fraudulent transfers. Profits beyond principal are generally recoverable because the investor gave no value for them. Principal repayments are harder cases: the investor gave value at the time of the original investment, but the trustee may argue the investor knew or should have known about the underlying fraud.

The good-faith inquiry in such cases focuses on objective indicators rather than subjective good intent. Returns inconsistent with market conditions, lack of meaningful diversification, vague reporting, and inability to verify underlying holdings have all been treated as red flags that defeat good faith. The cases reflect a tension between protecting innocent investors and clawing back funds for the broader victim pool.

Section 550(c) and (d): Lien Preservation and Single Satisfaction

Section 550(c) limits recovery of preferential transfers under Section 547 when the transfer is between two non-insider creditors more than 90 days before the petition: the trustee may not recover from a transferee under such circumstances. The provision implements the policy that the one-year insider reach-back of Section 547(b)(4)(B) should not be used to recover from non-insider transferees who would not themselves have been subject to that extended reach-back.

Section 550(d) embodies the single-satisfaction rule. Once the trustee has recovered the full value of the avoided transfer, no further recovery is available even if other defendants would otherwise be liable. The trustee thus has the choice of which defendant to pursue and in what order, but once one full recovery is obtained, the others are released.

The single-satisfaction rule is important to creditors who fear cascading liability through a transfer chain. If the trustee recovers fully from the initial transferee, mediate transferees down the chain are protected from the same recovery. Conversely, if the trustee chooses to pursue a mediate transferee first and obtains full satisfaction, the initial transferee is similarly released.

Section 550(e): Improvement-of-the-Property Lien

Section 550(e) provides that a good-faith transferee from whom the trustee may recover, or any good-faith immediate or mediate transferee of such transferee, has a lien on the property recovered to secure the lesser of (1) the cost of any improvement made after the transfer, less the amount of any profit realized by such transferee from such property, or (2) any increase in the value of such property as a result of such improvement.

The provision protects good-faith transferees that have invested in the property after receiving it. Improvements include physical changes, capital expenditures, and any improvement of any property of the debtor as defined in the section. The lien attaches to the recovered property and is enforceable against the estate.

Choosing Between Property and Value

Section 550(a)'s text gives the trustee an election between recovery of "the property transferred, or, if the court so orders, the value of such property." In some cases the choice is obvious: if the transferred property has been consumed, destroyed, or sold to a protected good-faith transferee, the trustee can pursue only value. In other cases the choice has strategic consequences. If the property has appreciated since the transfer, the trustee usually prefers the property itself; if it has depreciated, the trustee usually prefers value as of the transfer date.

The "if the court so orders" clause has been interpreted to give the court significant discretion to limit the trustee's election in equity. Courts sometimes refuse value recovery when the property is readily returnable in kind, or refuse property recovery when return would disrupt third-party interests that were not before the court. The valuation date is generally the date of the transfer for purposes of calculating value recovery, though some courts apply a flexible approach that considers post-transfer events.

Section 550(f): The Statute of Limitations

Section 550(f) requires that an action under Section 550 be commenced before the earlier of one year after the avoidance of the transfer on account of which recovery is sought, or the time the case is closed or dismissed. The recovery clock runs from avoidance, which means that the trustee can avoid a transfer late in the limitations window under Section 546(a) and then have an additional year under Section 550(f) to pursue recovery.

In practice, the trustee typically combines avoidance and recovery in a single adversary complaint, so the two limitations periods rarely operate independently. The independent recovery period becomes important only when the original avoidance was pursued without joining all potential transferees.

11 U.S.C. Section 553 - Setoff

Plain-English guide to setoff preservation in bankruptcy: the mutuality requirement, the pre-petition vs. post-petition distinction, the Section 553(a)(3) 90-day improvement-in-position rule, and the administrative-hold doctrine of Citizens Bank of Maryland v. Strumpf.

Home › Avoidance Actions › Section 553 - Setoff

Empirical research on this section

For case-pattern analysis on how federal bankruptcy courts apply this provision, including district-level patterns and primary-source dockets, see openbankruptcyproject.org/cases/. All datasets licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

What Section 553 Does

Section 553 occupies an unusual position in the Bankruptcy Code. It sits in Subchapter III of Chapter 5 alongside the avoidance powers, but it is not an avoidance power. It is, instead, a preservation provision that preserves whatever right of setoff a creditor would have had under non-bankruptcy law, subject to specific bankruptcy limitations. The provision also operates as a partial avoidance mechanism through subsection (b), which permits the trustee to recover certain pre-petition setoffs that improved the creditor's position during the 90 days before filing.

Setoff is the right of an entity that owes a debt to a debtor to reduce the amount it pays the debtor by an amount the debtor owes the entity. The classic example is a bank that holds a depositor's account and is also a creditor of the depositor on a loan. Without setoff, the bank would have to pay the deposits while standing in line as a general unsecured creditor on the loan. With setoff, the bank can apply the deposits against the loan and recover dollar-for-dollar up to the amount of mutual indebtedness.

Official citation: 11 U.S.C. § 553

The Mutuality Requirement

Section 553(a) preserves a right of setoff only if the debts to be set off are "mutual." Mutuality has three traditional dimensions:

Same parties: The debts must be owed by the same parties in the same capacity. Debts owed by an individual cannot be set off against debts owed to that individual as trustee of a trust.

Same right: The debts must each be enforceable as legal obligations, not merely contingent or equitable claims.

Pre-petition both: Both debts must arise before the bankruptcy filing for setoff to be available under Section 553(a). A pre-petition debt cannot be set off against a post-petition debt under Section 553.

The mutuality requirement defeats many attempted setoffs. Triangular setoffs, in which a creditor seeks to apply a debt owed to one affiliate against a debt owed by another affiliate, generally fail for lack of mutuality. Setoffs between a debtor in one capacity and a creditor in another also fail.

Pre-Petition vs. Post-Petition Setoff

The most important structural distinction in Section 553 is between pre-petition setoff and post-petition setoff. Section 553(a) preserves only pre-petition-to-pre-petition setoffs: both debts must arise before the order for relief. Setoff of a pre-petition claim against a post-petition obligation, or of a post-petition claim against a pre-petition obligation, is generally not preserved by Section 553.

The reason is structural. Pre-petition obligations become claims against the estate; post-petition obligations of the estate are administrative or other priority obligations of the new debtor entity. Allowing cross-period setoff would let a creditor convert a general unsecured claim into a dollar-for-dollar recovery by netting it against a post-petition obligation, defeating the priority scheme of the Bankruptcy Code.

The automatic stay in Section 362(a)(7) reinforces this distinction by prohibiting any setoff against property of the estate. A creditor that wishes to exercise a Section 553-preserved setoff must obtain relief from the stay; self-help setoff after the petition violates the stay even if the underlying setoff right is otherwise preserved.

Section 553(a)(3): The 90-Day Improvement-in-Position Rule

Section 553(a) carves out three categories of setoffs that are not preserved even if mutuality and timing are satisfied. The most operationally important is Section 553(a)(3), which denies preservation of any setoff if the debt owed to the debtor by the creditor was incurred by the creditor during the 90 days before the petition date and (A) while the debtor was insolvent, and (B) for the purpose of obtaining a right of setoff against the debtor.

The provision is the setoff analogue of Section 547's preference rules. Just as a creditor cannot obtain a preferential payment during the 90 days before bankruptcy, a creditor cannot obtain a preferential setoff position by creating mutual indebtedness during that period. A creditor that, knowing the debtor is in financial distress, induces the debtor to deposit funds with the creditor in order to manufacture a setoff position will find that the position is not preserved under Section 553(a)(3).

Section 553(b) provides a related but distinct avoidance mechanism: even if the setoff position itself was not manufactured under (a)(3), the trustee may recover the amount by which the creditor's setoff position improved during the 90 days before filing. The improvement is measured by comparing the insufficiency (the amount by which the creditor's claim exceeded mutual indebtedness) at two points: 90 days before filing and on the petition date. Any reduction in insufficiency represents an improvement in position that the trustee can recover.

The Strumpf Administrative-Hold Doctrine

The Supreme Court's unanimous decision in Citizens Bank of Maryland v. Strumpf, 516 U.S. 16 (1995), resolved a circuit split about whether a bank's administrative hold on a depositor's account after the depositor files bankruptcy violates the automatic stay. The bank in Strumpf placed a temporary hold on the debtor's account while it sought relief from the stay to exercise its setoff right. The debtor argued that the hold itself was an unlawful setoff in violation of Section 362(a)(7).

The Court rejected the argument and held that an administrative hold is not a setoff because it does not actually reduce the debt the bank owes the depositor; it merely refuses to honor withdrawal requests pending court determination of the setoff right. The opinion reasoned that a bank's obligation to a depositor is a promise to pay on demand, and a refusal to honor a particular demand is not the same as a setoff that extinguishes the debt.

Strumpf has practical consequences for any creditor seeking to preserve a setoff right after the bankruptcy filing. The creditor may place an administrative freeze on the relevant account while promptly moving for stay relief. The creditor may not, however, actually apply the funds to the debt; that step requires either stay relief or court authorization. Some bankruptcy courts have policed Strumpf strictly, requiring banks to promptly file motions for relief and barring extended freezes used as leverage rather than as protective placeholders.

Citizens Bank of Maryland v. Strumpf, 516 U.S. 16 (1995): A bank's administrative hold on a deposit account pending a stay-relief motion does not violate the automatic stay or constitute a prohibited setoff.

The IRS Setoff and Government Setoff Issues

Setoff by the federal government has its own complications. The Internal Revenue Service may have multiple taxpayer relationships with the same debtor, such as owing a refund for one tax year while being owed back taxes for another. Courts generally treat the United States as a single entity for the mutuality requirement, so a debt owed to the debtor by one agency can be set off against a debt the debtor owes another. How far that treatment reaches is litigated agency by agency.

State and local governments raise harder questions because each sovereign entity is typically treated separately, and mutuality must be analyzed agency by agency. The result is a complex tapestry where the same debtor may face setoff exposure to the IRS but not to a state revenue department for an arguably related obligation.

Setoff vs. Recoupment

Section 553 governs setoff, which involves mutual but independent debts. A related doctrine called recoupment involves claims arising out of the same transaction and is not governed by Section 553. Recoupment is preserved in bankruptcy as an equitable doctrine that operates outside the Section 553 framework and is not subject to its mutuality requirements, timing rules, or improvement-in-position provisions.

The classic recoupment scenario involves an executory contract under which one party owes the other under the same contract: for example, a supplier owed payment for goods delivered who also owes warranty obligations to the same buyer. Because the claims arise from the same transaction, recoupment permits net accounting without the constraints that Section 553 imposes on setoff. Whether a given fact pattern is setoff or recoupment is often litigated, and the line between "same transaction" and "different transactions" is sometimes hard to draw.

Procedure and Burden of Proof

A creditor that wishes to exercise a Section 553-preserved setoff after the petition typically files a motion for relief from the automatic stay under Section 362(d). The motion identifies the mutual debts, demonstrates compliance with Section 553(a), and addresses any Section 553(a)(3) or (b) issues. The trustee or debtor-in-possession may respond by challenging mutuality, asserting that the creditor manufactured the setoff during the 90-day period, or showing improvement in position recoverable under (b).

The burden of proving the elements of setoff under non-bankruptcy law and the elements of preservation under Section 553(a) rests on the creditor. The trustee bears the burden on the avoidance branch under Section 553(b). A creditor that fails to seek stay relief and instead self-helps may face stay-violation damages under Section 362(k) for individual debtors, independent of the merits of the underlying setoff claim.

## Arbitration in Bankruptcy [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/bankruptcy-arbitration/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home

Alternative Dispute Resolution
Arbitration

Arbitration in Bankruptcy Proceedings

Core versus non-core analysis under Stern v. Marshall, the McMahon inherent-conflict framework, FAA preemption, and the In re Anderson / In re Belton circuit split on consumer arbitration.

The two competing federal statutes

Arbitration in bankruptcy sits at the intersection of two federal statutes with sharply different policy orientations. The Federal Arbitration Act (FAA), 9 U.S.C. Section 1 et seq., embodies a "liberal federal policy favoring arbitration agreements." The Bankruptcy Code, 11 U.S.C. Section 101 et seq., embodies an equally strong federal policy favoring the centralized resolution of disputes affecting a debtor's estate within a single forum applying uniform federal law.

When a pre-petition contract containing an arbitration clause produces a dispute that arises in or relates to a bankruptcy case, the bankruptcy court must decide whether to enforce the arbitration clause and compel arbitration of the dispute, or to retain the dispute for resolution by the bankruptcy court. The answer turns on the framework established by the Supreme Court in Shearson/American Express, Inc. v. McMahon, 482 U.S. 220 (1987), and refined by the courts of appeals in the bankruptcy context.

The McMahon framework

In McMahon, the Supreme Court held that arbitration of a statutory claim is required by the FAA unless the party opposing arbitration shows that Congress intended in another statute to preclude waiver of judicial remedies for the claim at issue. Congressional intent to preclude arbitration may be inferred from:

The text of the other statute

The legislative history

An inherent conflict between arbitration and the underlying purposes of the other statute

Applied to bankruptcy, the McMahon test asks whether enforcing an arbitration clause as to a particular dispute would create an "inherent conflict" with the underlying purposes of the Bankruptcy Code. The Bankruptcy Code does not, by its text, expressly preclude arbitration. There is no extensive legislative history on the subject. The inquiry therefore typically turns on the inherent-conflict prong - and that prong, in turn, typically turns on whether the dispute is "core" or "non-core" within the meaning of 28 U.S.C. Section 157(b).

Core versus non-core under 28 U.S.C. Section 157

Bankruptcy jurisdiction is allocated by 28 U.S.C. Section 157, which distinguishes between:

Core proceedings under Section 157(b) - matters arising under the Bankruptcy Code or arising in a case under the Code. The bankruptcy court has full statutory authority to hear and determine core proceedings and enter final orders. Section 157(b)(2) enumerates a non-exhaustive list of core matters including allowance of claims, confirmation of plans, motions to terminate the automatic stay, proceedings to determine the dischargeability of debts, and avoidance actions.

Non-core proceedings under Section 157(c) - matters that are merely "related to" a bankruptcy case. The bankruptcy court hears non-core proceedings but, absent party consent, submits proposed findings of fact and conclusions of law to the district court for de novo review.

The Stern v. Marshall constitutional overlay

The Supreme Court's decision in Stern v. Marshall, 564 U.S. 462 (2011), added a constitutional overlay to the statutory core / non-core framework. Stern held that, even where Congress has designated a matter as "core" under Section 157(b), Article III of the Constitution may forbid the bankruptcy court (a non-Article III tribunal) from entering final judgment on the matter if the claim does not stem from the bankruptcy itself and would not necessarily be resolved in the claims-allowance process. The category of "Stern claims" - statutorily core but constitutionally non-core - includes, most notably, state-law counterclaims of the estate against creditors who have not filed proofs of claim that necessarily implicate the counterclaim.

Post-Stern, the bankruptcy court analyzing an arbitration motion must consider not only the statutory core / non-core line but also the constitutional Article III line, because a "Stern claim" presents fewer reasons to deny arbitration: if Article III itself prevents the bankruptcy court from entering final judgment, the inherent-conflict rationale for refusing to compel arbitration is correspondingly weaker.

Application of McMahon to bankruptcy disputes

The courts of appeals have applied McMahon in the bankruptcy context with reasonable consistency on the framework, though with continuing disagreement on application to specific disputes. The basic framework:

Non-core disputes: The presumption of arbitrability is generally enforced. A pre-petition contract dispute between the debtor and a counterparty that arises independently of the bankruptcy filing is typically sent to arbitration if a valid arbitration clause covers the dispute. The Second Circuit's decision in MBNA America Bank, N.A. v. Hill, 436 F.3d 104 (2d Cir. 2006), is representative.

Core disputes: The bankruptcy court has discretion to refuse to compel arbitration on a showing of inherent conflict. The court typically considers the centrality of the dispute to the bankruptcy case, the impact on the orderly administration of the estate, the preclusive effect of arbitration on other claims, and whether the dispute requires interpretation of provisions of the Bankruptcy Code itself.

The In re Anderson / In re Belton circuit split on consumer arbitration

The most prominent recent disagreement among the circuits concerns the enforceability of arbitration clauses with respect to claims that a creditor violated the discharge injunction under 11 U.S.C. Section 524.

In re Anderson (Second Circuit)

In In re Anderson, 884 F.3d 382 (2d Cir. 2018), the Second Circuit held that a consumer debtor's claim that a credit-card issuer violated the discharge injunction by continuing to report a discharged debt as outstanding was not arbitrable. The court applied the McMahon framework and found an inherent conflict: the discharge injunction is a creation of the Bankruptcy Code, is enforced through the bankruptcy court's contempt power, and represents the central protection afforded the debtor by the bankruptcy system. Permitting arbitration of discharge-injunction claims would, the court reasoned, undermine the centralized federal interest in uniform enforcement of the discharge.

In re Belton (Second Circuit, related)

The Second Circuit revisited and reinforced its Anderson holding in In re Belton, 961 F.3d 612 (2d Cir. 2020), again refusing to compel arbitration of consumer claims arising from alleged credit-reporting violations of the discharge injunction. Belton emphasized the bankruptcy court's traditional and exclusive jurisdiction over discharge enforcement and the inherent conflict between arbitration and the centralized federal interest.

Contrary authority

Other circuits have been less willing to refuse arbitration of consumer claims that touch on bankruptcy issues. The Fifth Circuit in In re Henry, 944 F.3d 587 (5th Cir. 2019), enforced an arbitration clause as to an FDCPA claim against a debt collector arising from collection of a discharged debt, distinguishing between Section 524 discharge-injunction claims (potentially non-arbitrable) and Fair Debt Collection Practices Act claims (subject to arbitration). The Ninth Circuit's case law similarly takes a more permissive view of arbitration of statutory claims that touch on but are distinct from the discharge injunction itself.

The split is unresolved at the Supreme Court level. Practitioners in consumer bankruptcy disputes involving arbitration clauses must consult the controlling circuit authority, which varies materially in its willingness to refuse arbitration on inherent-conflict grounds.

FAA preemption analysis

A separate but related question is whether the Bankruptcy Code (or state-law bankruptcy-protective statutes) is preempted by the FAA to the extent of any inconsistency. The Supreme Court has held that the FAA preempts state laws that single out arbitration clauses for disfavored treatment. The bankruptcy preemption question is different: it asks whether a federal statute (the Bankruptcy Code) impliedly limits the operation of another federal statute (the FAA) as applied to particular categories of disputes.

The McMahon inherent-conflict analysis is itself the mechanism by which courts have addressed this implied-limitation question. A finding of inherent conflict is, in substance, a finding that the Bankruptcy Code impliedly displaces the FAA as to the particular dispute. Where no inherent conflict is found, the FAA controls and arbitration is compelled.

Procedural posture - the motion to compel arbitration

A party seeking to compel arbitration in a bankruptcy case typically files a motion to compel arbitration and stay or dismiss the bankruptcy-court proceeding. The motion identifies:

The arbitration clause and the contract in which it appears

The scope of the clause (which categories of disputes it covers)

The party's contention that the dispute falls within the clause

The applicable arbitration rules (AAA Commercial, JAMS, etc.)

The party's analysis under McMahon, including the core / non-core characterization and the inherent-conflict argument (or the absence of inherent conflict)

The opposing party (typically the debtor, trustee, or committee) responds with its analysis of the inherent-conflict prong, identifying the specific aspects of the dispute that implicate central bankruptcy policies. The bankruptcy court rules on the motion, typically after a hearing on the legal issues without an evidentiary record beyond the arbitration agreement itself.

Common dispute categories

Pre-petition contract claims (typically arbitrable)

The debtor's claim that a counterparty breached a pre-petition contract is typically subject to arbitration if the contract contains a valid arbitration clause covering the dispute. The claim is "related to" the bankruptcy case but does not arise under the Bankruptcy Code, and resolution does not implicate central bankruptcy policies.

Discharge-injunction violations (split)

Claims that a creditor violated the Section 524 discharge injunction by continuing to collect a discharged debt. Anderson and Belton hold these claims non-arbitrable in the Second Circuit; other circuits have reached differing results, with the split most pronounced in cases involving collateral statutory claims (FDCPA, state UDAP statutes).

Avoidance actions (generally non-arbitrable)

Preference, fraudulent-transfer, and other avoidance actions under Sections 544-550 are creations of the Bankruptcy Code. They are core proceedings, and the inherent-conflict analysis typically favors retention by the bankruptcy court. The avoidance regime depends on uniform interpretation of bankruptcy-specific concepts (insolvency, reasonably equivalent value, transfer voidable under applicable law) and is integrated with the estate-administration process.

Stay violations (non-arbitrable)

Claims under Section 362(k) for willful violations of the automatic stay turn on the application of a Bankruptcy Code provision and on remedies the Code itself creates. Most courts treat these claims as non-arbitrable on inherent-conflict grounds, parallel to the discharge-injunction analysis.

The arbitrability analysis is dispute-specific, not contract-specific. The same arbitration clause may produce different outcomes as applied to different claims arising under the same contract. A pre-petition breach-of-contract claim and a post-petition discharge-injunction claim may both fall within the clause's scope but receive different treatment under the McMahon inherent-conflict prong. Counsel should analyze each claim separately.

Related authority

Federal Criminal Statutes

Bankruptcy Crimes

Chapter 9 of Title 18 of the United States Code criminalizes a range of conduct that defrauds creditors, obstructs the bankruptcy process, or undermines the integrity of court records. These statutes are enforced by United States Attorneys' Offices, often on referral from the United States Trustee Program, the bankruptcy court, or a private party with knowledge of the offense. The five guides below explain the principal Title 18 provisions used in bankruptcy-related prosecutions.

Last modified 2026-05-22.

Home/Bankruptcy Crimes

About the federal bankruptcy-crimes regime

Federal bankruptcy crimes share a few common features: each requires proof of a specific state of mind (typically knowing or fraudulent), each carries a five-year maximum sentence (twenty years for section 1519), and each operates independently of any civil sanction the bankruptcy court may impose. A debtor, attorney, custodian, or third party can be prosecuted under these statutes whether or not the bankruptcy case itself produced a civil recovery for creditors.

The most-charged bankruptcy crime is 18 U.S.C. section 152, which contains nine subsections covering concealment of assets, false oaths, false claims, and bribery of officers of the estate. Section 157, added in 1994, broadens the scope of prosecutable bankruptcy fraud by reaching schemes to defraud accomplished through the filing of a bankruptcy case or any document in connection with one. Section 1519, enacted as part of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act in 2002, is not a bankruptcy-specific statute but applies broadly to obstruction of any matter within federal-agency jurisdiction - which includes the United States Trustee Program.

Each deep-dive below explains the statutory elements, the typical fact patterns prosecuted under the section, the available defenses, and the sentencing exposure under the United States Sentencing Guidelines.

Statute-by-statute explainers

18 U.S.C. Section 152 Concealment of AssetsThe nine-subsection workhorse of bankruptcy prosecutions: concealment of property from the trustee, false statements under oath, false claims, fee splitting, and bribery of bankruptcy officers.

18 U.S.C. Section 153 Trustee EmbezzlementEmbezzlement of estate property by a trustee, custodian, marshal, or other officer of the court, with a five-year maximum sentence per count.

18 U.S.C. Section 156 Knowing DisregardBankruptcy-petition preparer offenses: knowing disregard of the bankruptcy law or rule resulting in dismissal of the case or denial of discharge.

18 U.S.C. Section 157 Bankruptcy FraudSchemes or artifices to defraud accomplished through the filing of a petition or any document in a bankruptcy case, the broadest of the bankruptcy-fraud statutes.

18 U.S.C. Section 1519 Anti-Shredding StatuteSarbanes-Oxley provision criminalizing alteration, destruction, or falsification of records in any matter within the jurisdiction of a federal department or agency, including the United States Trustee Program. Twenty-year maximum.

Referral note: Suspected bankruptcy crimes are typically referred under 18 U.S.C. section 3057, which directs judges and trustees to report apparent violations to the local United States Attorney. Private parties may make the same referral directly to the U.S. Attorney's Office for the district in which the bankruptcy case is pending.

## 18 USC 1519 - Sarbanes-Oxley Anti-Shredding Statute [2026]

18 U.S.C. Section 1519 - Destruction, Alteration, or Falsification of Records in Federal Investigations and Bankruptcy

Doctrinal overview of the Sarbanes-Oxley anti-shredding statute: a twenty-year maximum, an "in contemplation of" reach that does not require a pending investigation, and a comparison with the bankruptcy-specific records offenses in 18 U.S.C. Section 152(8) and (9).

Home › Bankruptcy Crimes › Section 1519

What Is Section 1519?

Section 1519 of Title 18 is the anti-shredding statute enacted as Section 802 of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 in the wake of the Enron-Andersen document-destruction scandal. The statute creates a broad obstruction-of-justice offense for the knowing destruction, alteration, or falsification of records with intent to impede, obstruct, or influence a federal investigation, including investigations of cases under Title 11.

Although enacted as a securities-fraud-response statute, Section 1519's text expressly extends to bankruptcy. The statute is materially broader and more severe than the bankruptcy-specific records offenses in 18 U.S.C. § 152(8) and (9), and is increasingly an option of choice for prosecutors addressing document destruction tied to bankruptcy cases.

Official citation: 18 U.S.C. § 1519 (destruction, alteration, or falsification of records in federal investigations and bankruptcy).

Statutory Text and Elements

Section 1519 provides in full: "Whoever knowingly alters, destroys, mutilates, conceals, covers up, falsifies, or makes a false entry in any record, document, or tangible object with the intent to impede, obstruct, or influence the investigation or proper administration of any matter within the jurisdiction of any department or agency of the United States or any case filed under title 11, or in relation to or contemplation of any such matter or case, shall be fined under this title, imprisoned not more than 20 years, or both."

The elements the government must prove beyond a reasonable doubt are:

The defendant knowingly altered, destroyed, mutilated, concealed, covered up, falsified, or made a false entry in;

Any record, document, or tangible object;

With the intent to impede, obstruct, or influence;

The investigation or proper administration of any matter within the jurisdiction of a U.S. department or agency, or any case filed under Title 11;

Or in relation to or contemplation of any such matter or case.

Breadth: "Any Record, Document, or Tangible Object"

Section 1519 reaches "any record, document, or tangible object." The phrase has been the subject of significant Supreme Court attention. In Yates v. United States, 574 U.S. 528 (2015), a plurality of the Court construed "tangible object" narrowly, holding that the statute's noscitur a sociis context confines "tangible object" to objects used to record or preserve information (e.g., a hard drive) and not, in the case at hand, undersized fish that had been thrown overboard. The plurality's narrowing construction is significant for non-bankruptcy applications but does not constrict the statute's reach as applied to documentary destruction in bankruptcy cases, which falls squarely within the statute's core.

The "In Contemplation" Clause

The most consequential feature of Section 1519 in the bankruptcy context is the "in relation to or contemplation of" clause. Section 1519, unlike many obstruction statutes, does not require that an investigation or proceeding be pending at the time of the obstructive act. It is sufficient that the destruction or alteration occur in "contemplation" of a matter within federal jurisdiction or a case under Title 11.

This reach distinguishes Section 1519 from older obstruction statutes such as 18 U.S.C. § 1503 and § 1505, both of which require a pending judicial proceeding or pending agency proceeding at the time of the obstructive conduct. The Supreme Court in Arthur Andersen LLP v. United States, 544 U.S. 696 (2005), reversed a Section 1512(b) obstruction conviction on the ground that the jury instructions failed to require a sufficient nexus to a federal proceeding; Section 1519 was deliberately drafted to avoid that limitation by extending criminal liability to obstructive conduct undertaken in contemplation of a future investigation or proceeding.

For bankruptcy applications, the practical significance is that document destruction undertaken before a bankruptcy petition is filed, but in contemplation of an anticipated Title 11 case, falls within Section 1519. Section 152(8) of Title 18, by contrast, also reaches conduct "in contemplation" of a Title 11 filing, but Section 152(8) requires fraudulent intent and carries a five-year maximum, whereas Section 1519 requires only intent to obstruct and carries a twenty-year maximum.

Mens Rea

Section 1519 requires that the defendant act "knowingly" (with respect to the act of destruction, alteration, etc.) and "with the intent to impede, obstruct, or influence" the relevant matter. The statute does not require the more demanding "corruptly" mens rea that appears in 18 U.S.C. § 1512(c)(2), and it does not require the "fraudulent" intent that appears in 18 U.S.C. § 152(8). The defendant need not have known of a specific pending investigation; it is sufficient that the defendant acted in contemplation of an investigation or matter within federal jurisdiction.

Several circuits have held that Section 1519's mens rea is satisfied where the defendant subjectively believed that an investigation or proceeding was likely, even if no investigation was in fact then under way. The doctrine traces directly to the "in contemplation" clause discussed above.

Comparison with 18 U.S.C. § 152(8) and (9)

The bankruptcy-crimes regime in 18 U.S.C. § 152 includes two paragraphs that address records-related conduct, both of which overlap with Section 1519:

§ 152(8) punishes the knowing and fraudulent concealment, destruction, mutilation, falsification, or making of false entries in recorded information relating to a debtor's property or financial affairs, after the filing of a Title 11 case or in contemplation thereof. Maximum: 5 years.

§ 152(9) punishes the knowing and fraudulent withholding of recorded information from a trustee or other officer of the court entitled to its possession, after the filing of a Title 11 case. Maximum: 5 years.

The differences from Section 1519 are:

Sentence. Section 1519 carries a 20-year maximum; Section 152(8) and (9) each carry a 5-year maximum. The disparity reflects Section 1519's broader obstruction-of-justice posture compared to Section 152's bankruptcy-specific framework.

Mens rea. Section 1519 requires only intent to obstruct; Section 152(8) and (9) require fraudulent intent. The lower scienter under Section 1519 substantially eases the government's proof burden.

Scope of records. Section 1519 reaches "any record, document, or tangible object," not limited to records relating to the debtor's property or financial affairs.

Temporal reach. Both Section 1519 and Section 152(8) extend to conduct undertaken in contemplation of a Title 11 case. Section 152(9), by contrast, applies only after filing.

The two regimes are not mutually exclusive. Conduct that violates Section 152(8) or (9) frequently also violates Section 1519, and an indictment may charge both. Charging decisions reflect the comparative strengths of each statute on the particular facts and the prosecutorial strategy in the case at hand.

Penalties and Sentencing

Section 1519 carries a statutory maximum of 20 years' imprisonment, a fine under Title 18, or both. It is the most severe penalty available among the records-related federal criminal statutes. Sentencing typically proceeds under U.S.S.G. § 2J1.2 (obstruction of justice), with a base offense level of 14 and enhancements for substantial interference with the administration of justice, extensive scope, or causing or threatening physical injury.

Restitution under 18 U.S.C. § 3663A is available where the obstructive conduct caused identifiable financial loss to identifiable victims. Although Section 1519 prosecutions historically arose primarily in financial-fraud and environmental-investigation contexts, the bankruptcy clause has been invoked with growing frequency over the past decade.

Statute of Limitations

The general 5-year federal criminal limitations period of 18 U.S.C. § 3282 applies to Section 1519. Unlike Section 152(1) concealment-of-assets prosecutions, Section 1519 does not benefit from the discharge-deferral rule of 18 U.S.C. § 3284. The limitations period generally runs from the date of the obstructive act, although where the conduct is continuing, the period may run from the last act in the continuous course.

Related Provisions

18 U.S.C. § 152 - Concealment of assets; false oaths and claims; bribery (paragraphs 8 and 9 cover bankruptcy records).

18 U.S.C. § 153 - Embezzlement against estate (covers concealment and destruction of estate documents by fiduciaries).

18 U.S.C. § 157 - Bankruptcy fraud (scheme to defraud).

18 U.S.C. § 1503 - Influencing or injuring officer or juror generally.

18 U.S.C. § 1505 - Obstruction of proceedings before departments, agencies, and committees.

18 U.S.C. § 1512 - Tampering with a witness, victim, or informant (includes § 1512(c)(2), the residual obstruction provision construed by United States v. Fischer, 603 U.S. 480 (2024)).

18 U.S.C. § 1520 - Destruction of corporate audit records (companion Sarbanes-Oxley provision).

Historical Note

Section 1519 was enacted as Section 802 of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002. The drafting was motivated by the document-destruction conduct of Arthur Andersen LLP during the SEC investigation of Enron Corporation, and by the perception that existing obstruction statutes (most prominently 18 U.S.C. § 1503 and § 1505) had been read by the courts to require too narrow a temporal nexus to a pending proceeding. Section 1519's drafters expressly addressed bankruptcy by including "any case filed under title 11" alongside federal-agency matters in the protected-matter clause, recognizing that the same accounting and document-destruction conduct that had concerned Congress in the securities context arose with at least equal frequency in major bankruptcy cases. The Supreme Court's narrowing construction of "tangible object" in Yates and its restrictive reading of Section 1512(c)(2) in Fischer have not impaired Section 1519's core application to documentary destruction in bankruptcy investigations.

## 18 USC 152 - Concealment of Assets, False Oaths, and Claims; Bribery [2026]
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/bankruptcy-crimes/section-152-concealment/

openbankruptcyproject.org
☰

Home
Tools
Research
Impact
Legal Aid
About

18 U.S.C. Section 152 - Concealment of Assets; False Oaths and Claims; Bribery

Doctrinal overview of the principal federal bankruptcy-crimes statute: nine numbered offenses, fraudulent-intent mens rea, five-year maximum, and the framework that organizes most bankruptcy-fraud prosecutions in the United States.

Home › Bankruptcy Crimes › Section 152

What Is Section 152?

Section 152 of Title 18 is the central bankruptcy-crimes statute. It enumerates nine distinct offenses, each addressing a particular form of fraudulent conduct directed at the bankruptcy system. Although the section is organized as a single statute, courts and prosecutors treat each numbered subsection as a separate offense with its own elements, and an indictment routinely charges multiple subsections as separate counts arising from the same factual transaction.

Section 152 has its origins in the 1898 Bankruptcy Act and was carried into the modern federal criminal code with successive revisions in 1948, 1978, 1994, and 2005. The current structure reflects the Bankruptcy Reform Act of 1994, which broke the prior consolidated bankruptcy-fraud provision into the nine-paragraph form that appears today.

Official citation: 18 U.S.C. § 152 (concealment of assets; false oaths and claims; bribery).

The Nine Numbered Offenses

Section 152 enumerates the following nine offenses, each punishable by a fine, imprisonment for not more than 5 years, or both:

§ 152(1) - Concealment of assets. Knowingly and fraudulently concealing from a custodian, trustee, marshal, or other court officer charged with the control or custody of property, or from creditors or the United States Trustee, any property belonging to the estate of a debtor.

§ 152(2) - False oath or account. Knowingly and fraudulently making a false oath or account in or in relation to any case under Title 11.

§ 152(3) - False declaration, certificate, verification, or statement. Knowingly and fraudulently making a false declaration, certificate, verification, or statement under penalty of perjury as permitted under 28 U.S.C. § 1746 in or in relation to any case under Title 11.

§ 152(4) - False claim. Knowingly and fraudulently presenting any false claim for proof against the estate of a debtor, or using any such claim in any case under Title 11, in a personal capacity or as or through an agent, proxy, or attorney.

§ 152(5) - Receipt of property to defeat the Code. Knowingly and fraudulently receiving any material amount of property from a debtor after the filing of a case under Title 11, with intent to defeat the provisions of Title 11.

§ 152(6) - Extortion or bribery to act or refrain from acting. Knowingly and fraudulently giving, offering, receiving, or attempting to obtain any money or property, remuneration, compensation, reward, advantage, or promise thereof for acting or forbearing to act in any case under Title 11.

§ 152(7) - Fraudulent transfer or concealment in contemplation of bankruptcy. Knowingly and fraudulently transferring or concealing any of the debtor's property or the property of any other person, in contemplation of a case under Title 11 by or against the debtor, or with intent to defeat the provisions of Title 11.

§ 152(8) - Destruction or falsification of records. After the filing of a case under Title 11 or in contemplation thereof, knowingly and fraudulently concealing, destroying, mutilating, falsifying, or making a false entry in any recorded information (including books, documents, records, and papers) relating to the property or financial affairs of a debtor.

§ 152(9) - Withholding of recorded information from a trustee or officer. After the filing of a case under Title 11, knowingly and fraudulently withholding from a custodian, trustee, marshal, or other officer of the court or a United States Trustee entitled to its possession any recorded information (including books, documents, records, and papers) relating to the property or financial affairs of a debtor.

Mens Rea: "Knowingly and Fraudulently"

Every Section 152 offense requires that the conduct have been undertaken "knowingly and fraudulently." This two-part scienter element distinguishes Section 152 from mere negligent misstatements or inadvertent omissions, neither of which suffices for criminal liability.

The Tenth Circuit and other courts have generally construed "knowingly" to require awareness of the act and its general character, and "fraudulently" to require intent to deceive a court officer, the United States Trustee, or creditors. Mistakes of fact, good-faith disclosures later shown to be incorrect, and amended schedules filed to correct prior omissions are common defense vehicles; an honest, even if careless, omission does not satisfy the fraudulent-intent prong.

Because intent is rarely susceptible to direct proof, the government commonly establishes fraudulent intent through circumstantial evidence including pattern of conduct, magnitude of the omission, timing relative to the petition, false explanations, and inconsistencies between schedules and contemporaneous business records.

Penalties and Sentencing Framework

Each Section 152 offense carries a statutory maximum of 5 years' imprisonment, a fine under Title 18 (currently $250,000 for individuals and $500,000 for organizations under 18 U.S.C. § 3571), or both. Restitution under the Mandatory Victims Restitution Act of 1996 (18 U.S.C. § 3663A) is required where there is an identifiable victim and the offense involves fraud or deceit.

Sentencing in the federal system is guided by the United States Sentencing Guidelines. Bankruptcy-fraud offenses are most commonly sentenced under U.S.S.G. § 2B1.1 (theft, property destruction, and fraud), with a base offense level of 6 or 7 and a loss-table enhancement under § 2B1.1(b)(1). Additional enhancements may apply for sophisticated means, abuse of position of trust, obstruction of justice, or violation of a judicial order.

Convictions are routinely accompanied by collateral consequences including bar discipline, loss of professional license, and (for non-citizens) immigration consequences as a crime involving moral turpitude or an aggravated felony where the loss exceeds the statutory threshold.

Statute of Limitations

The general federal criminal limitations period of 5 years under 18 U.S.C. § 3282 applies to Section 152 offenses. The 1994 Bankruptcy Reform Act, however, added 18 U.S.C. § 3284, which provides that for the offense of concealment of assets, the limitations period runs from the date of the discharge or denial of discharge of the debtor, not from the date of the concealing act itself.

The practical effect of Section 3284 is to substantially extend the period during which a Section 152(1) concealment prosecution may be brought, particularly in chapter 7 cases where discharge typically issues only months after the petition, and in chapter 11 and 13 cases where discharge may not enter until years after the filing.

Prosecutorial Framework

Section 152 prosecutions are typically initiated by referral from the United States Trustee Program. Each United States Trustee field office maintains a criminal-enforcement unit that screens potential matters, prepares a referral package documenting the suspected offense, and forwards the package to the local United States Attorney's Office. The referral package customarily includes copies of relevant schedules, statements of financial affairs, 341-meeting transcripts, and supporting documentary evidence.

Other referral sources include private chapter 7 and chapter 11 trustees, creditors who develop evidence of fraud during the case, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, and the Internal Revenue Service Criminal Investigation Division where the conduct overlaps with tax offenses. The Executive Office for United States Trustees publishes annual statistics on criminal-referral volumes and outcomes in its Report to Congress, available at justice.gov/ust.

Once referred, a Section 152 matter proceeds through ordinary federal grand-jury investigation. Charging decisions are committed to the discretion of the United States Attorney's Office, in coordination with the Fraud Section of the Department of Justice Criminal Division for matters with multi-district scope or that fit within national enforcement priorities.

Related Provisions

Section 152 operates in the Chapter 9 ("Bankruptcy") cluster of Title 18, which also includes:

18 U.S.C. § 153 - Embezzlement against estate by a trustee, custodian, marshal, or other officer.

18 U.S.C. § 154 - Adverse interest and conduct of officers.

18 U.S.C. § 155 - Fee agreements in cases under Title 11 and receiverships.

18 U.S.C. § 156 - Knowing disregard of the bankruptcy law or rule by a bankruptcy petition preparer.

18 U.S.C. § 157 - Bankruptcy fraud (scheme to defraud by means of a bankruptcy case).

18 U.S.C. § 158 - Designation of United States attorneys and FBI agents to address abusive reaffirmations of debt and materially fraudulent statements.

18 U.S.C. § 1519 - Destruction, alteration, or falsification of records in federal investigations (Sarbanes-Oxley anti-shredding statute).

Conduct that violates Section 152 frequently also implicates 18 U.S.C. § 157 (which treats the bankruptcy case itself as a vehicle for a broader scheme) and, where document destruction is involved, 18 U.S.C. § 1519 (which carries a 20-year maximum and a broader scienter formulation tied to obstruction of any federal investigation).

Historical Note

The first federal bankruptcy-crimes provisions appeared in the Bankruptcy Act of 1898 and were consolidated into Title 18 of the United States Code in 1948 as part of Reviser's Note revisions. The 1978 Bankruptcy Reform Act created the modern Bankruptcy Code in Title 11, but the criminal provisions remained in Title 18, where they continue to reside. The 1994 amendments expanded coverage to include conduct directed at United States Trustees (previously, the statute spoke only of court officers and creditors) and broke the prior unitary fraud provision into the nine-paragraph framework that organizes prosecutions today.

## 18 USC 153 - Embezzlement Against Estate by Trustee or Fiduciary [2026]
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/bankruptcy-crimes/section-153-trustee-embezzlement/

openbankruptcyproject.org
☰

Home
Tools
Research
Impact
Legal Aid
About

18 U.S.C. Section 153 - Embezzlement Against Estate

Doctrinal overview of the federal embezzlement statute that reaches bankruptcy trustees, custodians, attorneys, agents, and other officers entrusted with estate property. Five-year maximum, with scope extending to debtor-in-possession personnel.

Home › Bankruptcy Crimes › Section 153

What Is Section 153?

Section 153 of Title 18 criminalizes the knowing and fraudulent appropriation, embezzlement, spending, transfer, or concealment of any property or recorded information of a bankruptcy estate by a defined class of fiduciaries. Unlike Section 152, which reaches conduct by debtors, creditors, and others external to the estate's administration, Section 153 is specifically directed at the persons charged with administering the estate.

The statute occupies a focused niche in the federal bankruptcy-crimes regime: it criminalizes the misuse of estate property by the very officers entrusted with its preservation. As a doctrinal matter, it parallels other federal embezzlement statutes that protect federally administered property funds (such as 18 U.S.C. § 656 covering bank embezzlement and 18 U.S.C. § 666 covering programs receiving federal funds), but is purpose-built for the bankruptcy context.

Official citation: 18 U.S.C. § 153 (embezzlement against estate).

Statutory Text and Elements

Section 153(a) provides: "A person described in subsection (b) who knowingly and fraudulently appropriates to the person's own use, embezzles, spends, or transfers any property or secretes or destroys any document belonging to the estate of a debtor shall be fined under this title, imprisoned not more than 5 years, or both."

The elements the government must prove beyond a reasonable doubt are:

The defendant is a person described in subsection (b) (the scope provision);

The defendant knowingly and fraudulently engaged in one of the enumerated acts (appropriation, embezzlement, spending, transfer, secreting, or destruction);

The object of the act was property or a document belonging to the estate of a debtor.

Scope: Who Is Covered Under Section 153(b)

Section 153(b) defines the class of persons subject to the statute. The covered persons include:

A trustee, custodian, marshal, attorney, or other officer of the court;

An agent, employee, or other person engaged by such an officer to perform a service with respect to the estate.

The reference to "attorney" covers counsel for trustees and counsel for the estate generally. Where the trustee retains counsel, paraprofessionals, accountants, brokers, appraisers, or other professionals under 11 U.S.C. § 327, those professionals' employees who handle estate property fall within Section 153(b)'s "agent, employee, or other person engaged by such an officer" language.

Debtor-in-Possession Personnel

In a chapter 11 case, the debtor-in-possession exercises the rights, powers, and duties of a trustee under 11 U.S.C. § 1107. Courts have recognized that officers, directors, and managing employees of a debtor-in-possession who handle estate property fall within the trustee-like fiduciary scope of Section 153(b), although the case law on this point is comparatively thin and varies by circuit.

Where a debtor proceeds under Subchapter V of chapter 11, the debtor remains in possession under 11 U.S.C. § 1184, and the Subchapter V trustee under 11 U.S.C. § 1183 takes on a more limited supervisory role. The Subchapter V trustee, like any trustee, is plainly within Section 153(b)'s scope.

Mens Rea

Section 153 requires that the conduct have been undertaken "knowingly and fraudulently," the same formulation that appears in Section 152. The defendant must have been aware that the property belonged to the estate and acted with intent to deceive or defraud. Negligent commingling, inadvertent overpayments, or mistaken classifications of property are not the criminal embezzlement contemplated by Section 153.

Specific intent is typically inferred from circumstantial evidence including the size of the diversion, the absence of contemporaneous documentation, false explanations offered to the court or United States Trustee, structuring of payments to evade detection, and any pattern of similar conduct across multiple cases.

Penalties and Restitution

A Section 153 violation is punishable by a fine under Title 18, imprisonment for not more than 5 years, or both. Restitution to the estate (and ultimately to defrauded creditors) is mandatory under 18 U.S.C. § 3663A for fraud offenses with identifiable victims.

For trustees and other officers, conviction routinely triggers removal under 11 U.S.C. § 324, disbarment from the panel of private trustees, disgorgement of fees, and state-bar discipline (including disbarment). For professionals retained under 11 U.S.C. § 327, conviction supports denial of compensation under 11 U.S.C. § 328(c) and disqualification from future appointments.

Trustees in the United States Trustee panel-trustee program must maintain a blanket bond under 11 U.S.C. § 322 and Bankruptcy Rule 2010. A Section 153 conviction typically triggers a claim against that bond, and bond surety carriers may pursue subrogation against the convicted trustee personally.

Relationship to Civil Surcharge and Removal Remedies

Criminal liability under Section 153 is distinct from civil remedies available in the bankruptcy court. The bankruptcy court may surcharge a defaulting trustee under 11 U.S.C. § 704 (chapter 7) or analogous provisions for other chapters, remove a trustee under 11 U.S.C. § 324 for cause, deny or disgorge fees under 11 U.S.C. § 326 and § 328(c), and refer matters for criminal investigation under 18 U.S.C. § 3057 (which directs bankruptcy judges who have reasonable grounds to believe a violation has occurred to report it to the appropriate United States Attorney).

The civil and criminal tracks may proceed in parallel. A trustee surcharged or removed in the bankruptcy court is not thereby insulated from criminal prosecution, and a criminal conviction is admissible in subsequent civil proceedings under the doctrine of issue preclusion as to the elements necessarily decided by the conviction.

Statute of Limitations and Procedural Posture

Section 153 prosecutions are governed by the general federal criminal limitations period of 5 years under 18 U.S.C. § 3282. Unlike Section 152(1) concealment-of-assets prosecutions, Section 153 does not benefit from the discharge-deferral rule of 18 U.S.C. § 3284, because the conduct addressed by Section 153 typically occurs in the course of administration rather than at filing.

The five-year period generally runs from the date of the embezzling act, although where the conduct constitutes a continuing offense (e.g., a continuous course of conduct in which estate funds are systematically diverted), the limitations clock may not begin until the last act in the course of conduct.

Related Provisions

18 U.S.C. § 152 - Concealment of assets; false oaths and claims; bribery (nine-paragraph framework).

18 U.S.C. § 154 - Adverse interest and conduct of officers (forbidding trustees and other officers from purchasing estate property).

18 U.S.C. § 155 - Fee agreements in cases under Title 11 and in receiverships.

18 U.S.C. § 3057 - Bankruptcy investigations (reporting duty of judges and trustees).

11 U.S.C. § 322 - Qualification of trustee (bond requirement).

11 U.S.C. § 324 - Removal of trustee or examiner.

11 U.S.C. § 326 - Limitation on compensation of trustee.

11 U.S.C. § 328 - Limitations on compensation of professional persons.

Historical Note

Section 153 originated in Section 29(b) of the Bankruptcy Act of 1898, which criminalized a more compact set of acts by trustees and other officers. The 1948 codification of Title 18 moved the provision to its present location. The 1994 Bankruptcy Reform Act updated Section 153 to align its scope with the modern Title 11 fiduciary structure, including the addition of United States Trustees to the persons-protected language and the expansion of the predicate-act list to cover modern forms of misappropriation. The structural unity of the offense - knowing, fraudulent misuse of estate property by a fiduciary - has remained constant since 1898.
