## 18 USC 156 - Knowing Disregard of Bankruptcy Law by Petition Preparer [2026]
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/bankruptcy-crimes/section-156-knowing-disregard/

openbankruptcyproject.org
☰

Home
Tools
Research
Impact
Legal Aid
About
Contact

18 U.S.C. Section 156 - Knowing Disregard of Bankruptcy Law or Rule

Doctrinal overview of the misdemeanor offense applicable to bankruptcy petition preparers who knowingly disregard the Bankruptcy Code or the Federal Rules of Bankruptcy Procedure. One-year maximum; complements the civil-enforcement framework of 11 U.S.C. Section 110.

Home › Bankruptcy Crimes › Section 156

What Is Section 156?

Section 156 of Title 18 is a misdemeanor offense added by the Bankruptcy Reform Act of 1994 as a companion to the new civil regulatory scheme for non-attorney bankruptcy petition preparers (BPPs) in 11 U.S.C. § 110. Section 156 criminalizes a bankruptcy petition preparer's knowing disregard of the Bankruptcy Code or Bankruptcy Rules where that disregard causes a case or related proceeding to be dismissed.

The statute is the only criminal provision in Title 18 directed specifically at bankruptcy petition preparers as a regulated class. It pairs with the broader civil-penalty and injunction framework of 11 U.S.C. § 110 to form a two-track BPP enforcement system: civil fines and disgorgement for routine violations, and criminal prosecution for the most serious cases.

Official citation: 18 U.S.C. § 156 (knowing disregard of bankruptcy law or rule).

Statutory Text and Elements

Section 156(a) defines "bankruptcy petition preparer" by cross-reference to 11 U.S.C. § 110, and defines "document for filing" to mean a petition or any other document prepared for filing in a case under Title 11 in connection with a case or proceeding by a person other than the debtor.

Section 156(b) provides: "If a bankruptcy case or related proceeding is dismissed because of a knowing attempt by a bankruptcy petition preparer in any manner to disregard the requirements of title 11, United States Code, or the Federal Rules of Bankruptcy Procedure, the bankruptcy petition preparer shall be fined under this title, imprisoned not more than 1 year, or both."

The elements the government must prove are:

The defendant is a bankruptcy petition preparer as defined in 11 U.S.C. § 110(a);

The defendant knowingly attempted, in any manner, to disregard the requirements of Title 11 or the Federal Rules of Bankruptcy Procedure;

A bankruptcy case or related proceeding was dismissed because of that knowing disregard.

Defining the Bankruptcy Petition Preparer

11 U.S.C. § 110(a)(1) defines a "bankruptcy petition preparer" as a person, other than an attorney for the debtor or an employee of such attorney under the direct supervision of such attorney, who prepares for compensation a document for filing. The statute deliberately excludes attorneys and their supervised employees, who are governed by Rule 9011 and the rules of professional conduct rather than by the BPP regime.

The Supreme Court in Lamie v. United States Trustee, 540 U.S. 526 (2004), and a substantial body of subsequent bankruptcy-court decisions have construed the term narrowly to exclude paralegals working directly under attorney supervision, but broadly to include "typing services," document-preparation businesses, online petition-preparation services, and others who prepare bankruptcy documents for compensation outside the attorney-supervision relationship.

The Dismissal-Causation Element

A distinctive feature of Section 156 is that the offense is not complete until a case or related proceeding has been dismissed because of the preparer's knowing disregard. The causation requirement gives the dismissal order itself an effective gatekeeping function: a Section 156 prosecution generally awaits, and is built upon, a bankruptcy-court dismissal order that identifies BPP misconduct as a cause of dismissal.

This structural feature explains why Section 156 prosecutions are relatively rare compared to civil enforcement under 11 U.S.C. § 110. Most BPP misconduct can be addressed through civil fines and disgorgement under Section 110 without ever producing a dismissal; the criminal track is reserved for the comparatively narrow set of cases where the disregard is both knowing and case-fatal.

Interplay with the Civil Regime of 11 U.S.C. § 110

11 U.S.C. § 110 imposes a layered set of civil requirements on bankruptcy petition preparers, including:

Signing every document prepared for filing and printing the preparer's name and address on it (§ 110(b)(1));

Furnishing the debtor with a copy of every document the moment it is signed (§ 110(d));

Not collecting court fees (§ 110(g));

Filing a declaration of compensation under penalty of perjury (§ 110(h));

Not using the word "legal" or any similar term in advertising (§ 110(f));

Not offering legal advice (§ 110(e)(2)).

Civil enforcement is handled by the bankruptcy court on motion of the United States Trustee, a chapter 7 trustee, or a debtor. Civil remedies include statutory fines (typically up to $500 per violation, with treble damages in some categories), disgorgement of fees, and permanent injunctions barring the preparer from acting as a BPP under § 110(j).

Section 156 supplies the criminal escalation pathway for the same regulatory subject. A preparer who has been the subject of repeated civil enforcement under § 110, who ignores court orders restricting practice, who structures business to evade BPP disclosure rules, or whose disregard is so substantial that it produces a dismissal, becomes a candidate for Section 156 prosecution. The United States Trustee Program publishes annual statistics on BPP civil enforcement, including injunction orders and disgorgement totals, in its Report to Congress.

Mens Rea: "Knowing"

Section 156 requires that the disregard have been "knowing." The statute does not require the heightened "fraudulent" intent that Sections 152 and 153 require. The lower mens rea reflects the regulatory character of Section 156 and the consumer-protection purpose of the BPP regime: the offense targets reckless or willful disregard of regulatory requirements, not specific intent to defraud.

The lower mens rea is one of the reasons the offense is a misdemeanor with only a one-year maximum. The fraudulent-intent felonies of Sections 152 and 153 are available where the conduct rises to that level; Section 156 occupies the regulatory-compliance space below.

Penalties and Sentencing

A Section 156 violation is punishable by a fine under Title 18, imprisonment for not more than 1 year, or both. Because the maximum is 1 year, the offense is a Class A misdemeanor under 18 U.S.C. § 3559(a)(6). Sentencing typically proceeds under U.S.S.G. § 2J1.7 or the residual fraud guideline at § 2B1.1, depending on the nature of the underlying disregard and the loss amount.

Conviction triggers an automatic injunction-eligibility predicate under 11 U.S.C. § 110(j) and supports debarment from future BPP activity. Restitution under 18 U.S.C. § 3663A is available where the disregard caused identifiable financial loss to the debtor or to other identifiable victims.

Related Provisions

11 U.S.C. § 110 - Penalty for persons who negligently or fraudulently prepare bankruptcy petitions (the parallel civil regime).

18 U.S.C. § 152 - Concealment of assets; false oaths and claims; bribery.

18 U.S.C. § 157 - Bankruptcy fraud (which may apply where a preparer's conduct rises to the level of a scheme).

18 U.S.C. § 158 - Designation of United States attorneys and FBI agents to address abusive reaffirmations of debt and materially fraudulent statements.

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 9009 - Forms.

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 9011 - Signing and verification of pleadings (applies to attorneys, by contrast).

Historical Note

Sections 110 and 156 were enacted together in the Bankruptcy Reform Act of 1994 to respond to concerns that non-attorney petition-preparation businesses were proliferating, often misleading consumer debtors as to the scope of the services they were providing and the legal advice the preparers were qualified to give. Congress declined to authorize licensing of non-attorney preparers but imposed disclosure and conduct rules backed by civil fines and the misdemeanor escalation of Section 156. The framework has been amended periodically since 1994 to update fine amounts and clarify scope, most notably in the Bankruptcy Abuse Prevention and Consumer Protection Act of 2005.

## 18 USC 157 - Bankruptcy Fraud (Scheme to Defraud) [2026]
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/bankruptcy-crimes/section-157-bankruptcy-fraud/

openbankruptcyproject.org
☰

Home
Tools
Research
Impact
Legal Aid
About
Contact

18 U.S.C. Section 157 - Bankruptcy Fraud

Doctrinal overview of the federal bankruptcy-fraud scheme statute: three sub-offenses, the "devised or intending to devise a scheme" framework, modeled on the mail and wire fraud statutes, and distinguished from the single-act offenses of Section 152.

Home › Bankruptcy Crimes › Section 157

What Is Section 157?

Section 157 of Title 18 is the bankruptcy-fraud-scheme statute. Added by Section 312 of the Violent Crime Control and Law Enforcement Act of 1994, it imports the mail-fraud and wire-fraud architecture ("devised or intending to devise a scheme or artifice to defraud") into the bankruptcy context. Where Section 152 punishes specific discrete acts (false oaths, concealment, false claims), Section 157 punishes the use of the bankruptcy system as a vehicle for a broader fraudulent scheme.

Section 157 is a relatively recent addition to the bankruptcy-crimes regime, but it has become a workhorse statute for prosecutions involving recurring or systemic bankruptcy abuse. Common Section 157 patterns include rent-skimming schemes built around serial filings of fractional-interest deed-transfer petitions, identity-theft bankruptcy filings used to extend automatic-stay protection over property the filer does not own, and bust-out schemes in which a debtor accumulates credit and then files to discharge it.

Official citation: 18 U.S.C. § 157 (bankruptcy fraud).

Statutory Text and the Three Sub-Offenses

Section 157 provides: "A person who, having devised or intending to devise a scheme or artifice to defraud and for the purpose of executing or concealing such a scheme or artifice or attempting to do so —

files a petition under Title 11, including a fraudulent involuntary petition under section 303 of such title;

files a document in a proceeding under Title 11; or

makes a false or fraudulent representation, claim, or promise concerning or in relation to a proceeding under Title 11, at any time before or after the filing of the petition, or in relation to a proceeding falsely asserted to be pending under such title,

shall be fined under this title, imprisoned not more than 5 years, or both."

The three sub-offenses share the same predicate scheme element but differ in the conduct that triggers liability: filing a petition (§ 157(1)), filing a document in a proceeding (§ 157(2)), or making a representation, claim, or promise (§ 157(3)). The drafters borrowed the "devised or intending to devise a scheme or artifice to defraud" framework directly from 18 U.S.C. § 1341 (mail fraud) and § 1343 (wire fraud), and federal courts construe Section 157's scheme element by reference to mail-fraud and wire-fraud case law.

The Scheme Element

Section 157's distinguishing element is the scheme. Under mail-fraud and wire-fraud doctrine imported into Section 157, a "scheme to defraud" need not be elaborate but must involve a plan or pattern that contemplates fraudulent conduct, not merely an isolated false statement. The scheme need not have succeeded; an attempt to execute or conceal the scheme satisfies the statute.

The scheme requirement explains why Section 157 prosecutions tend to involve facts with a broader temporal or transactional sweep than Section 152 prosecutions. A single false answer on Schedule B is the paradigmatic Section 152(2) or (3) offense; a coordinated multi-petition rent-skimming pattern, an organized identity-theft bankruptcy ring, or a serial-filing scheme calculated to stall foreclosure proceedings is the paradigmatic Section 157 offense.

Distinction from Section 152

Although Sections 152 and 157 frequently appear in the same indictment, the two statutes target distinct conduct:

Section 152 punishes specific enumerated acts (false oaths, concealment of assets, false claims, document destruction, etc.) regardless of whether they are part of a broader scheme. Each of the nine paragraphs is a stand-alone offense.

Section 157 punishes the use of the bankruptcy system as a vehicle for a scheme. The scheme element is essential; without it, conduct may still violate Section 152 but does not reach Section 157.

Both statutes carry a five-year maximum, and conduct that violates both may be charged as separate counts under Blockburger v. United States, 284 U.S. 299 (1932), so long as the elements differ. The Sentencing Guidelines treat both as fraud offenses under U.S.S.G. § 2B1.1 and apply the loss table similarly, but the existence of a Section 157 scheme commonly supports a sophisticated-means enhancement under § 2B1.1(b)(10).

Mens Rea

Section 157 requires that the defendant have "devised or intend[ed] to devise a scheme or artifice to defraud" and have engaged in the predicate filing or representation "for the purpose of executing or concealing such a scheme or artifice." The specific-intent requirement parallels mail-fraud and wire-fraud doctrine: the government must prove that the defendant intended to defraud, that the scheme was material, and that the defendant acted with knowledge of its fraudulent character.

Because the petition or document filing is itself the actus reus, the government need not prove that the scheme caused identifiable loss to a victim. The offense is complete when the fraudulent filing or representation is made for the purpose of executing or concealing the scheme, even if the bankruptcy court ultimately detects and prevents the fraud.

Common Section 157 Fact Patterns

The Department of Justice and the Executive Office for United States Trustees have over time identified several recurring fact patterns that drive Section 157 enforcement:

Serial filings to stall foreclosure. A debtor (or an associate) files repeated petitions, sometimes under different names or different chapters, to invoke the automatic stay of 11 U.S.C. § 362 and delay a scheduled foreclosure sale, with no genuine intention to reorganize.

Fractional-interest deed transfers. A homeowner facing foreclosure transfers a fractional interest in the property to a third party who then files a bankruptcy petition, invoking the stay over property the petitioner does not meaningfully own.

Identity-theft filings. A petition is filed in the name of a person whose identity has been stolen, often as part of a broader credit-fraud or rent-skimming scheme.

Bust-out cases. A debtor systematically incurs credit-card and other unsecured debt with no intention of repayment, then files chapter 7 to discharge the debt.

Concealed-asset schemes. A debtor coordinates with associates to transfer or hide assets in advance of filing, then files schedules omitting the assets and representations consistent with the concealment scheme.

The first three fact patterns frequently produce dual indictments under Section 157 and the mail- and wire-fraud statutes (Sections 1341 and 1343), depending on the means used to execute the scheme.

Penalties and Sentencing

Section 157 carries a statutory maximum of 5 years' imprisonment per count, a fine under Title 18, or both. Restitution under 18 U.S.C. § 3663A is mandatory where there is an identifiable victim. Sentencing typically proceeds under U.S.S.G. § 2B1.1 with loss-table enhancements, often supplemented by enhancements for sophisticated means (§ 2B1.1(b)(10)), more than ten victims or substantial financial hardship (§ 2B1.1(b)(2)), and abuse of position of trust (§ 3B1.3) where the defendant is a fiduciary.

Conviction of a Section 157 scheme offense often produces meaningfully higher sentencing exposure than a Section 152 single-act conviction on comparable underlying facts, because the loss table aggregates losses across the scheme and sophisticated-means and victim-count enhancements apply more readily to scheme conduct.

Statute of Limitations

Section 157 prosecutions are governed by the general federal criminal limitations period of 5 years under 18 U.S.C. § 3282. Unlike Section 152(1) concealment-of-assets prosecutions, Section 157 does not benefit from the discharge-deferral rule of 18 U.S.C. § 3284. The limitations period generally runs from the date of the predicate filing or representation, although where the scheme is continuing the period may run from the last act in furtherance of the scheme.

Related Provisions

18 U.S.C. § 152 - Concealment of assets; false oaths and claims; bribery (the single-act companion).

18 U.S.C. § 153 - Embezzlement against estate.

18 U.S.C. § 156 - Knowing disregard of bankruptcy law or rule by petition preparer.

18 U.S.C. § 1341 - Mail fraud (architectural source of the "scheme to defraud" formulation).

18 U.S.C. § 1343 - Wire fraud.

18 U.S.C. § 1344 - Bank fraud.

18 U.S.C. § 1349 - Attempt and conspiracy (applies to Section 1341 and 1343 but not directly to Section 157; a Section 157 conspiracy is charged under 18 U.S.C. § 371).

18 U.S.C. § 1519 - Destruction, alteration, or falsification of records in federal investigations.

Historical Note

Section 157 was enacted in 1994 in response to a perception among prosecutors that Section 152's single-act framework was poorly suited to the systemic and recurring forms of bankruptcy abuse that had become prominent in the 1980s and early 1990s, particularly serial-filing and identity-theft fact patterns. The drafters deliberately modeled the new statute on the mail-fraud and wire-fraud statutes to give prosecutors the same scheme-based architectural framework that had proved effective in those contexts. Subsequent enforcement practice has confirmed that Section 157 occupies a distinct prosecutorial niche from Section 152, with the two statutes commonly charged together when both single-act offenses and a broader scheme are present.

Bankruptcy Filing Fees (Current Federal Rates)

The federal filing fees set by the Judicial Conference are uniform across every U.S. bankruptcy court. Fee waivers and installments are available for those who qualify.

Published by the Open Bankruptcy Project. Updated 2026-05-04. Educational information only; not legal advice.

Current Filing Fees

Yes, in two ways. Chapter 7 filers under 150 percent of poverty can apply for a fee waiver (Form 103B). Anyone in any chapter can apply to pay the fee in installments (Form 103A). Both are filed with your petition; neither delays the case.

Federal bankruptcy filing fees by chapter

The fees below are set by the Judicial Conference and apply uniformly across every federal bankruptcy court.

$338Chapter 7

$313Chapter 13

$1,738Chapter 11

Chapter 7 ($338): $245 statutory fee + $78 administrative fee + $15 trustee surcharge.

Chapter 13 ($313): $235 statutory fee + $78 administrative fee.

Chapter 11 ($1,738): $1,167 statutory fee + $571 administrative fee. Subchapter V (small business) Chapter 11 has the same filing fee but reduced ongoing costs.

Chapter 12 (family farmer): $278.

Chapter 9 (municipality): $1,738.

Chapter 15 (cross-border): $1,738.

Fee Waiver

Who qualifies for a fee waiver

Chapter 7 filers can request a full waiver of the filing fee using Official Form 103B. Eligibility requires household income under 150 percent of the federal poverty line and an inability to pay in installments.

The form asks for income, expenses, dependents, and assets. The court reviews the application and either grants the waiver, denies it, or sets a hearing. Most waivers are granted on the papers without a hearing.

If denied, the court typically gives you the option to pay in installments instead. A denied waiver does not end the case; it just means you have to find a way to pay.

Installment Plan

Paying the fee over time

Anyone in any chapter can ask to pay the filing fee in installments using Official Form 103A. The standard schedule is up to four installments over 120 days.

The application is filed with your petition. The court sets the schedule; missing an installment can result in case dismissal, so do not propose a schedule you cannot meet.

Other Costs

Beyond the filing fee

Bankruptcy filing involves several smaller mandatory costs:

Pre-filing credit counseling course: ~$20-50 (required before petition).

Post-filing financial management course: ~$10-50 (required before discharge).

Schedule amendments: $32 each.

Reopening a closed case: $260 (Chapter 7), $235 (Chapter 13).

PACER access: $0.10/page (if you choose to monitor through the official portal; CourtListener is free).

FAQ

Frequently asked questions

Can I file bankruptcy without paying the filing fee?
Yes, in two ways. Chapter 7 filers under 150 percent of poverty can apply for a fee waiver (Form 103B). Anyone in any chapter can apply to pay the fee in installments (Form 103A). Both are filed with your petition; neither delays the case.

What does the filing fee actually cover?
Court administrative cost. The trustee in a no-asset Chapter 7 receives $60 of the $338 fee; the rest goes to the U.S. Trustee program and the Judiciary's general budget. The fee is set by the Judicial Conference and updated periodically.

When does the fee have to be paid?
At the time of filing. If you choose installments, you typically have 120 days to pay the full amount in up to four installments. Missing an installment can result in case dismissal.

Are there other fees besides the filing fee?
Yes. The required pre-filing credit counseling course (about $20-50 typically), the post-filing financial management course ($10-50), document copying, and amended schedule fees ($32 to amend a schedule). PACER access for monitoring the case is also pay-per-page if you use the official portal.

What if I am converting my case from one chapter to another?
Conversions have their own fees. Chapter 7 to 13 and 11 conversions cost $0 if voluntary; involuntary conversions can carry filing-fee differentials.

Are there reduced fees for service members or veterans?
Active-duty service members can receive Servicemembers Civil Relief Act protections that pause certain proceedings, but there is no general filing-fee reduction. Veterans qualify for the same fee waiver as any other low-income filer.

Next Steps

Where to go from here

After understanding the fee structure:

## Court-Annexed Bankruptcy Mediation [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/bankruptcy-mediation/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Alternative Dispute Resolution
Mediation

Court-Annexed Bankruptcy Mediation

Local rule mediation programs, mediator selection, confidentiality under Rule 8.6 of the Model Standards, and the disputes most often mediated in bankruptcy.

Statutory and rule-based authority

Bankruptcy mediation operates within a layered framework of federal authority. The Alternative Dispute Resolution Act of 1998 (28 U.S.C. Sections 651-658) directs every federal district court to authorize the use of ADR processes in civil actions, including bankruptcy adversary proceedings and contested matters. Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 9019(c) independently authorizes the bankruptcy court to require parties to participate in a settlement conference or other ADR proceeding.

The Bankruptcy Court for each district has implemented mediation by local rule or general order. The local rules typically address:

The categories of matters eligible for or required to undergo mediation

The procedure for selecting a mediator (party agreement, court appointment, or panel rotation)

Mediator qualifications, training requirements, and disclosure obligations

Confidentiality of mediation communications

Allocation of mediation fees and expenses

Reporting requirements (typically a brief report of impasse, settlement, or partial settlement, without disclosure of substantive communications)

A representative example is the Bankruptcy Court for the Southern District of New York's General Order M-452 establishing the Mediation Program. Comparable programs exist in the Bankruptcy Courts for the Districts of Delaware, the Eastern District of New York, the Central District of California, the Southern District of Texas, the Eastern District of Virginia, and most other districts with significant Chapter 11 dockets.

Mediator selection

The mediator-selection process varies by district. Common models include:

Party-agreement selection

The parties agree on a mediator from a court-maintained panel or, with court approval, from outside the panel. This model predominates in larger Chapter 11 cases where the parties are sophisticated and the disputes involve unique subject matter (mass torts, complex valuation, multi-creditor priority disputes).

Court-appointment from panel

If the parties cannot agree, the court appoints a mediator from the registered mediation panel. Panel mediators have typically satisfied training and experience requirements set by local rule (often 40 hours of mediation training plus bankruptcy or commercial litigation experience).

Mediator qualifications

The qualifications required to serve as a bankruptcy mediator vary by district. Common requirements include:

Active bar membership in good standing (typically for at least 10-15 years)

Substantial experience in bankruptcy practice, commercial litigation, or related fields

Completion of a recognized mediation training program (often 40 hours)

Continuing-education requirements (often 6-10 hours every two years)

Compliance with disclosure obligations regarding conflicts of interest

Some districts maintain separate panels for consumer bankruptcy mediation and complex Chapter 11 mediation, reflecting the different skill sets required.

Confidentiality - the Model Standards Rule 8.6 framework

The Model Standards of Conduct for Mediators, jointly issued by the American Bar Association, the American Arbitration Association, and the Association for Conflict Resolution, address mediator confidentiality at Standard V (Confidentiality). Rule 8.6 of the corresponding professional-conduct framework requires the mediator to maintain the confidentiality of all information obtained by the mediator in mediation, unless otherwise agreed to by the parties or required by applicable law.

The confidentiality framework typically operates on three layers:

Mediator confidentiality: The mediator may not disclose communications received in the course of mediation to anyone outside the mediation, including the court, except as expressly authorized by the parties or as required by law.

Party-side confidentiality: The parties typically execute a mediation agreement in which they agree not to disclose communications made during mediation in any subsequent proceeding. Many local rules incorporate this restriction directly.

Evidentiary protection: Federal Rule of Evidence 408 excludes evidence of settlement negotiations to prove or disprove the validity or amount of a disputed claim. Many districts supplement Rule 408 with a local-rule provision deeming mediation communications inadmissible and not subject to discovery.

The confidentiality framework is essential to the mediation process. Parties may speak frankly to the mediator (typically in caucus) about case weaknesses, settlement parameters, and underlying business considerations only if assured that those disclosures will not later be used against them. The framework has narrow exceptions for threats of bodily harm, ongoing or future criminal conduct, child or elder abuse, and limited circumstances where the parties expressly waive confidentiality.

Mediator confidentiality is not absolute. Most frameworks recognize exceptions for threats of imminent bodily harm, ongoing or future criminal conduct, and reports of child or elder abuse. The specific exceptions are governed by the local rule and the mediation agreement; parties and mediators should review the governing framework before relying on a particular confidentiality assumption.

The mediation process

A typical bankruptcy mediation proceeds through these stages:

Pre-mediation

The parties submit confidential mediation statements to the mediator, typically 7-14 days before the session. The statements identify the parties, summarize the dispute, identify key legal and factual issues, summarize prior settlement discussions, and outline the party's settlement position. The mediator reviews the statements and may conduct pre-mediation telephone conferences to clarify issues or address procedural matters.

Joint session

The mediation typically opens with a joint session at which the mediator describes the process, the parties make brief opening statements, and the principal disputed issues are identified. Some mediations dispense with the joint session entirely and proceed directly to caucus, particularly where the parties' relationship is sufficiently strained that joint discussion would be unproductive.

Caucus

The mediator meets separately with each party (caucus) to explore the party's interests, evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of the party's position, and develop settlement options. Information disclosed in caucus is presumptively confidential as to the other parties unless the disclosing party authorizes communication.

Settlement or impasse

If the parties reach agreement, the mediator typically facilitates drafting of a term sheet or memorandum of understanding signed at the conclusion of the mediation. The detailed settlement agreement is documented afterward. If the parties reach impasse, the mediator files a brief report indicating that the mediation concluded without settlement. The report does not disclose substantive communications.

Common mediated disputes in bankruptcy

Plan confirmation disputes

Mediation of valuation, claim treatment, and feasibility disputes in Chapter 11 plan confirmation. Particularly common where the dispute is between the debtor and the creditors' committee or between competing classes of creditors. The mediator often has substantial Chapter 11 valuation experience.

Stay-relief disputes

Mediation of motions for relief from the automatic stay, particularly where the underlying dispute is fact-intensive (adequate-protection valuation, equity cushion analysis, foreclosure history) or where the parties have an ongoing relationship that would benefit from negotiated resolution.

Fee disputes

Mediation of objections to professional-fee applications under Section 330. The mediator typically has experience as a fee examiner or as a member of a creditors' committee evaluating professional fees. Disputes commonly involve hourly rates, staffing levels, time-entry detail, and reasonableness of specific tasks.

Avoidance action mediation

Mediation of preference and fraudulent-transfer actions, particularly where the estate has filed a large number of avoidance actions and seeks an efficient resolution process. Some districts implement standing orders requiring mediation of all avoidance actions above a threshold dollar amount.

Allocation of mediation costs

The local rule typically allocates the mediator's fee equally among the principal parties, subject to court order otherwise. In Chapter 11 cases, the debtor's share is typically administrative expense of the estate; the creditor's share is borne by the creditor. In adversary proceedings, the allocation tracks the parties to the adversary. Some panel mediators serve pro bono for a limited number of hours, particularly in consumer or small-business cases.

Enforcement of mediated settlements

A mediated settlement that resolves a contested matter or adversary proceeding is enforced like any other settlement of an estate claim. If the settlement requires court approval - because it disposes of estate claims falling within Rule 9019(a) - the parties present the settlement to the court by motion. The court evaluates the settlement under the TMT Trailer factors regardless of the fact that the settlement was mediated. Mediation does not displace the substantive approval standard; it provides a procedural mechanism for arriving at the settlement that the court will then evaluate.

Related rules and authority

28 U.S.C. Section 651 et seq. - Alternative Dispute Resolution Act of 1998

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 9019(c) - Settlement conferences and ADR

Fed. R. Evid. 408 - Compromise offers and negotiations

Model Standards of Conduct for Mediators (ABA / AAA / ACR, revised 2005)

Bankruptcy court local rules - each district publishes its mediation program rules

Open Bankruptcy Project cross-references

Rule 9014 (Contested Matters)
Bankruptcy Arbitration
Rule 9011 (Sanctions)

Further reading

## BAP vs District Court Bankruptcy Appeals - 28 USC 158(c) Election [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/bap-vs-district-court-appeals/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

28 U.S.C.
Section 158(c)(1)

BAP vs District Court Appeals: The Section 158(c)(1) Election

The election between Bankruptcy Appellate Panel review and district court review of bankruptcy court orders, opt-out mechanics under Rule 8005, and the strategic considerations that drive forum choice.

Verbatim text of 28 U.S.C. Section 158(c)(1)

Subject to subsection (b), each appeal under subsection (a) shall be heard by a 3-judge panel of the bankruptcy appellate panel service established under subsection (b)(1) unless - (A) the appellant elects at the time of filing the appeal; or (B) any other party elects, not later than 30 days after service of notice of the appeal; to have such appeal heard by the district court. 28 U.S.C. Section 158(c)(1).

The structural choice

Congress created Bankruptcy Appellate Panels under 28 U.S.C. Section 158(b) to provide a specialized intermediate appellate forum for bankruptcy appeals. A BAP consists of three sitting bankruptcy judges drawn from districts within the circuit, none of whom is from the district where the appeal originated. BAPs operate only in circuits that have authorized them and only in districts that have not opted out. As of the most recent surveys, BAPs sit in the First, Sixth, Eighth, Ninth, and Tenth Circuits. The remaining circuits route all bankruptcy appeals to the district court.

Within a BAP circuit, the appellate route is not automatic. Section 158(c)(1) creates a default rule (BAP) and two opt-out mechanisms (appellant election; opposing party election within 30 days). The district may also opt out of the BAP system entirely under Section 158(b)(6), in which case all bankruptcy appeals from that district go to the district court regardless of party preference.

The opt-out mechanics under Rule 8005

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 8005 implements the Section 158(c)(1) election. The mechanics:

Appellant election - at the time of filing

The appellant must file a separate statement of election under Rule 8005(a) at the time the notice of appeal is filed. The statement must be in a separate writing, not embedded in the notice of appeal. The election is exclusively the appellant's first-shot privilege - it cannot be exercised after filing.

Other-party election - within 30 days

Any other party to the appeal may, within 30 days after service of the notice of appeal, file a statement of election under Rule 8005(b) to have the appeal heard by the district court. The 30-day window is set by Section 158(c)(1)(B) and is not extendable. Unlike the appellant's election, which is exercised by acting (filing the statement), the other-party election operates against the BAP default - inaction by the appellee preserves the BAP forum if the appellant did not opt out.

Effect of election

An effective election under either provision routes the appeal to the district court. If neither the appellant nor any other party has opted out, the appeal is heard by the BAP. The election decision is unilateral - any single party can force the appeal into district court. The BAP forum requires unanimous consent (or, more precisely, the absence of any contrary election).

Doctrinal weight of BAP decisions

A BAP is not Article III court; it is an Article I appellate body created under the bankruptcy judges' Article I status. BAP decisions are not binding on bankruptcy courts within the circuit in the way court of appeals decisions are. The circuits have divided on whether BAP decisions are binding on bankruptcy courts within the BAP's geographic reach. The Ninth Circuit has held that BAP decisions are binding on bankruptcy courts within the BAP circuit, at least until the circuit court speaks otherwise. The Eighth and Tenth Circuit BAPs have held that their decisions are persuasive but not binding on bankruptcy courts within their circuits.

District court decisions on bankruptcy appeals are similarly not binding on other bankruptcy courts within the district, although they are typically afforded considerable persuasive weight from the same judge or within the same district.

The forum choice is not binary. The further appeal from either the BAP or the district court runs to the court of appeals under 28 U.S.C. Section 158(d)(1). The court of appeals reviews the bankruptcy court's findings and conclusions directly, applying the same standards the intermediate court applied; the intermediate-court opinion does not insulate the underlying record from review.

Strategic considerations - factors favoring the BAP

Bankruptcy-specialized panel

BAP judges are sitting bankruptcy judges. Their familiarity with the Bankruptcy Code, the Federal Rules of Bankruptcy Procedure, and bankruptcy procedural practice is structurally deeper than that of a district court generalist. Cases turning on bankruptcy-specific doctrine - the operation of 11 U.S.C. Section 1129(b) cramdown, the elements of fraudulent transfer claims under Section 548, the mechanics of plan classification under Section 1122 - generally benefit from a panel that does not need to be educated on the basics.

Three-judge panel

The BAP is a three-judge body. A district court appeal is heard by a single Article III judge. The three-judge panel provides the structural benefit of collegial deliberation and reduces the risk of an idiosyncratic outcome.

Speed

BAPs in most circuits maintain shorter median dispositions than district courts, although the gap varies by circuit and by the district court's docket condition. The BAP's docket is exclusively bankruptcy appeals; a district judge's docket is dominated by civil and criminal trial work, with bankruptcy appeals competing for scheduling priority.

Strategic considerations - factors favoring the district court

Article III judge

The district judge is an Article III judge with life tenure. A party seeking adventurous statutory construction or a departure from circuit-court precedent may find a district judge more willing to engage with the merits than a panel of sitting bankruptcy judges, who may be more cautious about disturbing established doctrine.

Familiarity outside bankruptcy

Bankruptcy appeals frequently turn on issues outside the Code - the Federal Rules of Evidence, Federal Rules of Civil Procedure questions imported through FRBP Rule 7001 et seq., contract or property law from the state of the situs, statutory interpretation of non-bankruptcy federal statutes. A district judge sees those issues every day; a BAP panel sees them through the lens of bankruptcy practice.

Subsequent appellate posture

From the district court, the further appeal goes to the court of appeals on the same record. From the BAP, the further appeal also goes to the court of appeals, but the existence of an intermediate bankruptcy-specialized decision may either help or hurt depending on outcome. Where the appellant expects to lose at the intermediate level and wants the cleanest possible record for circuit review, some practitioners prefer the district court because a district judge's opinion may carry less circuit-level deference than a BAP's bankruptcy-specialized analysis.

Predictability of the assigned judge

The identity of the district judge is known on assignment. The BAP panel composition is not announced until later in the briefing cycle. Parties with a strong view about how a particular district judge will treat a particular issue may prefer the certainty.

Standards of review - the same on both tracks

Both the BAP and the district court apply the same standards of review to the bankruptcy court's order: clearly erroneous for findings of fact, de novo for conclusions of law, abuse of discretion for discretionary rulings. The choice of forum does not change the standard; it changes only the identity of the reviewer.

Briefing procedure - largely uniform

Part VIII of the Federal Rules of Bankruptcy Procedure governs both BAP and district court appeals. The notice-of-appeal deadline (14 days under Rule 8002), the record-on-appeal designation (14 days under Rule 8009), and the briefing schedule (Rule 8018) are identical. BAPs sometimes maintain supplemental local rules; the district court's local civil rules typically apply to bankruptcy appeals filed in that court except where Part VIII supersedes.

The district opt-out under Section 158(b)(6)

A district may, by majority vote of the active judges, opt out of the BAP designation for appeals arising in that district under 28 U.S.C. Section 158(b)(6). Where the district has opted out, the BAP option is unavailable regardless of the parties' preferences; all appeals are heard by the district court. The opt-out vote is durable; reversal requires another vote of the active judges.

Practical sequencing

Appellant's first move

Decide forum at the time of filing. The notice of appeal under Rule 8002 must be filed within 14 days of entry of the order being appealed; the statement of election under Rule 8005(a) accompanies that filing. Failure to file the election when filing the notice forfeits the appellant's opt-out and leaves the forum to be set by the BAP default or by an appellee election.

Appellee's counter-move

Within 30 days of service of the notice of appeal, decide whether to file a Rule 8005(b) election. If the appellant did not opt out, the appellee can still pull the appeal into the district court. The 30-day window is hard; tardy elections are without effect.

Related authority

28 U.S.C. Section 158 - Appeals from bankruptcy court

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 8005 - Election to have appeal heard by district court

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 8002 - Time for filing notice of appeal

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 8018 - Briefing schedule

## Bankruptcy Appellate Panels - Open Bankruptcy Project

Intermediate Appellate Forums

Bankruptcy Appellate Panels

A Bankruptcy Appellate Panel (BAP) is a three-judge panel of bankruptcy judges authorized by 28 U.S.C. section 158(b) to hear appeals from bankruptcy-court decisions in lieu of the district court. Five circuits currently maintain active BAPs: the First, Sixth, Eighth, Ninth, and Tenth. The remaining circuits route bankruptcy appeals directly to the district court. These guides survey each active BAP's composition, opt-out rules, jurisdiction, and procedural quirks.

Last modified 2026-05-22.

Home/Bankruptcy Appellate Panels

About the BAP system

Congress authorized BAPs in the Bankruptcy Reform Act of 1978 and refined the framework in the 1994 Bankruptcy Reform Act. A BAP exists only by judicial-council order and only if the council determines that there are insufficient judicial resources in the district courts to handle bankruptcy appeals. In circuits without a BAP, bankruptcy-court appeals proceed under 28 U.S.C. section 158(a) to the district court.

Where a BAP exists, every appeal from a bankruptcy-court final order is automatically routed to the BAP unless either party elects to have the appeal heard by the district court under 28 U.S.C. section 158(c)(1). The election must be timely - generally within 30 days of service of the notice of appeal - and is irrevocable once made. Strategic considerations for the election include the perceived expertise of the BAP (its judges hear bankruptcy appeals every day), the binding effect of its opinions within the circuit, and the procedural calendar.

BAP decisions bind the panel itself and (in most circuits) the bankruptcy courts within the circuit, but they are not binding on the district courts or on the court of appeals. Further review proceeds by appeal as of right to the court of appeals under 28 U.S.C. section 158(d)(1), or, in narrow circumstances, by direct certification to the court of appeals under section 158(d)(2).

Circuit-by-circuit guides

First Circuit BAPComposition, opt-out rules, citation conventions, and the role of the BAP in the courts of Maine, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Puerto Rico, and Rhode Island.

Sixth Circuit BAPThree-judge panels drawn from Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio, and Tennessee bankruptcy courts; opt-out timing and the relationship to district-court review.

Eighth Circuit BAPBAP composition across Arkansas, Iowa, Minnesota, Missouri, Nebraska, and North and South Dakota; binding effect within the circuit.

Ninth Circuit BAPThe oldest and most-cited BAP; opt-out election timing under Ninth Circuit Rule 8005-1, and the use of memorandum dispositions.

Tenth Circuit BAPComposition across Colorado, Kansas, New Mexico, Oklahoma, Utah, and Wyoming; opt-out mechanics and citation rules.

Election timing: The right to opt out of the BAP and proceed to the district court is governed by Bankruptcy Rule 8005 and 28 U.S.C. section 158(c)(1). Missing the deadline is irrevocable. Counsel evaluating appellate strategy should make the election decision in the first week after entry of the appealable order.

Eighth Circuit Bankruptcy Appellate Panel - Practitioner Guide 2026

First published 2026-05-22/Last modified 2026-05-22/CC-BY-4.0

Abstract

The Bankruptcy Appellate Panel for the Eighth Circuit (8th Cir. BAP) is an Article I appellate forum established by the Judicial Council of the Eighth Circuit under 28 U.S.C. § 158(b). Three-judge panels of sitting bankruptcy judges drawn from the bankruptcy courts within the circuit hear appeals from final orders of those courts when all parties consent under the election procedure of § 158(c)(1). This guide summarizes panel composition, the election and district-opt-out mechanics, the panel's appellate jurisdiction, briefing under Part VIII of the Federal Rules of Bankruptcy Procedure as supplemented by Eighth Circuit BAP local rules, and the strategic factors bearing on the choice of forum between the panel and the United States District Court.

Authorization and Geographic Coverage

The Eighth Circuit BAP was established by order of the Judicial Council of the Eighth Circuit pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 158(b)(1). The panel hears appeals arising from the bankruptcy courts of the seven states comprising the Eighth Circuit, which together include ten federal judicial districts:

Eastern District of Arkansas (E.D. Ark. Bankr.)

Western District of Arkansas (W.D. Ark. Bankr.)

Northern District of Iowa (N.D. Iowa Bankr.)

Southern District of Iowa (S.D. Iowa Bankr.)

District of Minnesota (D. Minn. Bankr.)

Eastern District of Missouri (E.D. Mo. Bankr.)

Western District of Missouri (W.D. Mo. Bankr.)

District of Nebraska (D. Neb. Bankr.)

District of North Dakota (D.N.D. Bankr.)

District of South Dakota (D.S.D. Bankr.)

The panel's clerk's office is administratively colocated with the office of the Clerk of the United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit in St. Louis. Counsel should verify the current authorization status of each constituent district through the BAP clerk's office, because districts may withdraw or modify authorization for BAP service under § 158(b)(6).

Statutory authority28 U.S.C. § 158(b), (c)

Establishing bodyJudicial Council of the Eighth Circuit

Constituent statesArkansas, Iowa, Minnesota, Missouri, Nebraska, North Dakota, South Dakota

Clerk's officeU.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit, St. Louis, Missouri

Official websitewww.ca8.uscourts.gov/bankruptcy-appellate-panel

Panel Composition

Under 28 U.S.C. § 158(b)(1)(A), bankruptcy appellate panels are composed of bankruptcy judges from districts within the circuit. The Eighth Circuit BAP draws its members from the bankruptcy benches of the constituent districts listed above. A sitting member of the panel cannot hear an appeal arising from his or her own home district under § 158(b)(5), which preserves the appearance of independent appellate review and prevents same-district peer review.

Each appeal is decided by a panel of three judges. Panels are constituted ad hoc for each appeal from the available pool of designated judges, subject to the same-district disqualification rule. The presiding judge of the BAP is designated by the Judicial Council and rotates on a defined cycle. Opinions issue per curiam or under a single authoring judge; concurrences and dissents are reported alongside the lead opinion.

The Eighth Circuit BAP maintains a substantial published body of bankruptcy appellate opinion, with decisions reported in West's Bankruptcy Reporter and available through commercial and free legal-research platforms. Several Eighth Circuit BAP opinions have been adopted by the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals on further appeal.

Election Procedure and District Opt-Out

Two consent layers govern whether an appeal proceeds to the BAP rather than to the district court. The first is district-level: under 28 U.S.C. § 158(b)(6), each judicial district within a BAP circuit may, by majority vote of its district judges, decline to authorize BAP service for appeals arising from that district. Practitioners should verify current authorization status by district through the panel's clerk's office, because authorizations can be modified by subsequent district order.

The second layer is party-level: under 28 U.S.C. § 158(c)(1), even where the district has authorized BAP service, an appeal is heard by the panel only if all parties to the appeal consent. The mechanics work as a default-and-opt-out: the appellant's filing of a notice of appeal under Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 8003 routes the appeal to the BAP unless a party files a timely statement of election to have the appeal heard by the district court instead.

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 8005 governs the election. The statement of election must be filed with the clerk of the bankruptcy court within thirty (30) days after service of the notice of appeal. If the electing party is the appellant, the election must accompany the notice of appeal. Failure to file a timely election by any party is treated as consent to BAP review.

Election is a unilateral procedural right. The statement need not state grounds; no court approval is required; and the panel cannot retain an appeal over a timely election. Counsel weighing the choice of forum should accordingly assume that a single objecting party can defeat BAP routing. Counsel for prospective appellees in cases where BAP review is strategically preferred should canvas opposing counsel informally on the election question before incurring drafting costs predicated on either forum.

Appellate Jurisdiction

The panel's subject-matter jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 158(a) extends to:

Final judgments, orders, and decrees of the bankruptcy courts under § 158(a)(1);

Interlocutory orders increasing or reducing the time fixed under 11 U.S.C. § 1121(d) for filing a plan, under § 158(a)(2); and

Other interlocutory orders, with leave of the panel, under § 158(a)(3).

Finality in bankruptcy is interpreted more pragmatically than in ordinary civil litigation. Orders resolving discrete disputes within a larger case may be final and immediately appealable even where the underlying case continues. The panel applies the Eighth Circuit's prevailing finality framework when determining whether a challenged order meets the § 158(a)(1) threshold.

Interlocutory appeals under § 158(a)(3) require a motion for leave. The panel applies a standard derived from 28 U.S.C. § 1292(b): controlling question of law, substantial ground for difference of opinion, and material advancement of the ultimate termination of the litigation. Leave is discretionary and is sparingly granted.

Briefing and Calendar

Briefing in the BAP is governed by Part VIII of the Federal Rules of Bankruptcy Procedure as supplemented by the Eighth Circuit BAP local rules. The default schedule under FRBP 8018 runs from the filing of the appeal record:

Appellant's brief: 30 days after the docketing of the appeal in the BAP

Appellee's brief: 30 days after service of the appellant's brief

Appellant's reply brief: 21 days after service of the appellee's brief (and at least 7 days before argument)

Word and page limits track FRBP 8015. The appellant's principal brief and the appellee's principal brief are each limited to 13,000 words; reply briefs are limited to 6,500 words. Certificates of compliance, jurisdictional statements, and required disclosure statements track Part VIII practice.

Oral argument is set by the panel after briefing closes. The panel may decide an appeal without argument under FRBP 8019 if the legal arguments are adequately presented in the briefs and oral argument would not significantly aid the decisional process. The Eighth Circuit BAP hears argument by video conference and at sittings convened in the circuit's principal cities (including St. Louis, Minneapolis, and Kansas City) on the panel's calendar.

Standards of Review

The panel applies the same standards of review applicable to appeals taken to the district court under 28 U.S.C. § 158(a). Findings of fact are reviewed for clear error; conclusions of law are reviewed de novo; mixed questions are reviewed under the standard appropriate to the question, with the legal component receiving de novo review. Discretionary determinations (such as approvals under 11 U.S.C. § 363, sanctions, plan confirmation in the discretionary fairness aspects of 11 U.S.C. § 1129, and most case-management rulings) are reviewed for abuse of discretion.

The panel's decisions are reviewable on further appeal to the United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit under 28 U.S.C. § 158(d)(1). The court of appeals applies the same standards to bankruptcy court rulings that the BAP applied; the BAP's intermediate decision receives no formal deference on questions of law in the further appeal.

Contrast with District-Court Appeals

An appeal to the district court under 28 U.S.C. § 158(a) is heard by a single district judge sitting as an appellate court. An appeal to the BAP is heard by a three-judge panel of sitting bankruptcy judges. Several practical differences follow:

Bench expertise. BAP judges are full-time bankruptcy judges with concentrated subject-matter exposure. District judges hear bankruptcy appeals as one part of a general civil and criminal docket. For appeals turning on contested or developing bankruptcy doctrine, the panel's specialization is often the principal substantive consideration. The Eighth Circuit covers two of the largest farm-and-agricultural-creditor markets in the country, and the BAP's bench has developed particular fluency in Chapter 12 and agricultural-secured-creditor disputes.

Panel deliberation versus single judge. Three judges reviewing the same record introduce a deliberative element that a single-judge appeal lacks. Concurrences and dissents in BAP opinions can preserve issues and shape framing for further appeal to the court of appeals.

Precedential weight. BAP decisions bind the parties to the appeal but do not bind bankruptcy courts in the circuit as a matter of formal stare decisis under the prevailing view. District-court decisions on bankruptcy appeals likewise do not formally bind other district judges or other bankruptcy judges, though both forums' decisions carry substantial persuasive weight within the circuit. Court of appeals decisions bind both forums.

Calendar and disposition time. BAP calendars tend to move on a more predictable timeline than the bankruptcy appeal queue of a busy district court, where appeals share the calendar with the district's primary civil and criminal workload. The Eighth Circuit BAP has historically maintained median disposition times that compare favorably with the bankruptcy-appeal dispositions of the circuit's larger district benches.

When the BAP Is Preferable

The following considerations tend to favor BAP review when the choice is open:

Pure or principally legal questions in core bankruptcy doctrine (avoidance, claim classification, plan confirmation standards, automatic stay scope, discharge, Chapter 13 plan modification, Chapter 12 agricultural confirmation issues) where a specialist bench is most likely to engage the issue at depth.

Appeals from non-routine procedural rulings where the panel's familiarity with bankruptcy court calendaring and motion practice produces a more textured review than a generalist district judge can ordinarily provide.

Cases where the appellate record is dense with bankruptcy-specific factual context (plan economics, claim hierarchies, fee structures) that benefits from a bench fluent in the underlying vocabulary.

Cases where panel consensus will strengthen persuasive value in any further appeal, particularly where the issue is one of first impression in the circuit.

The following considerations tend to favor district-court review:

Appeals turning principally on non-bankruptcy substantive law (state-law contract interpretation, federal tax law, securities law, ERISA, employment-discrimination cross-claims) where the district judge's broader subject-matter range is closer to the dispositive question.

Appeals with significant constitutional, Stern v. Marshall, or Article III concerns where the district court's Article III status itself is part of the analytical framing.

Strategic considerations specific to known docket conditions at the district level or to known dispositions of district judges on bankruptcy-adjacent legal questions.

Practical Filing Notes

A notice of appeal is filed in the bankruptcy court under FRBP 8003. The appeal is transmitted to the BAP by the bankruptcy clerk unless a party files a timely election to have the appeal heard by the district court instead under FRBP 8005. The thirty-day election window runs from service of the notice of appeal; counsel for appellees should calendar this date promptly because election is the single procedural decision that controls forum.

The BAP's filing fee mirrors the district-court fee schedule. Electronic filing is mandatory; the BAP uses CM/ECF infrastructure with credentials administered through the circuit clerk. Briefing extensions are routinely granted on motion for good cause, but the panel discourages serial extensions and counsel should plan for the default schedule.

Eighth Circuit BAP: www.ca8.uscourts.gov/bankruptcy-appellate-panel

U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit: www.ca8.uscourts.gov

Federal Rules of Bankruptcy Procedure (Part VIII, Appeals): uscourts.gov/rules-policies/current-rules-practice-procedure

28 U.S.C. § 158: www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/28/158

First Circuit Bankruptcy Appellate Panel - Practitioner Guide 2026

First published 2026-05-22/Last modified 2026-05-22/CC-BY-4.0

Abstract

The Bankruptcy Appellate Panel for the First Circuit (1st Cir. BAP) is an Article I appellate forum established under 28 U.S.C. § 158(b) by the Judicial Council of the First Circuit. Panels of three sitting bankruptcy judges, drawn from the bankruptcy courts within the circuit, hear appeals from final orders of those courts when all parties consent under the election procedure of § 158(c)(1). This guide summarizes panel composition, the election and opt-out mechanics, the panel's appellate jurisdiction, briefing under the BAP local rules, and the strategic factors that bear on choosing the panel over a parallel appeal to the United States District Court.

Authorization and Geographic Coverage

The First Circuit BAP was established by order of the Judicial Council of the First Circuit pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 158(b)(1), which authorizes each circuit's judicial council to establish a bankruptcy appellate panel service. The panel hears appeals arising from the bankruptcy courts of the four New England districts within the First Circuit plus the District of Puerto Rico:

District of Maine (D. Me. Bankr.)

District of Massachusetts (D. Mass. Bankr.)

District of New Hampshire (D.N.H. Bankr.)

District of Rhode Island (D.R.I. Bankr.)

District of Puerto Rico (D.P.R. Bankr.)

The Judicial Council of the First Circuit issued the order establishing BAP service, and the panel sits at the call of its presiding judge. The clerk's office for the panel is administratively colocated with the office of the Clerk of the United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit in Boston.

Statutory authority28 U.S.C. § 158(b), (c)

Establishing bodyJudicial Council of the First Circuit

Constituent districtsMaine, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Rhode Island, Puerto Rico

Clerk's officeU.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit, Boston, Massachusetts

Official websitewww.ca1.uscourts.gov/bankruptcy-appellate-panel

Panel Composition

Under 28 U.S.C. § 158(b)(1)(A), bankruptcy appellate panels are composed of bankruptcy judges from districts within the circuit. The First Circuit BAP draws its members from the bankruptcy benches of the constituent districts listed above. A sitting member of the panel cannot hear an appeal arising from his or her own home district under § 158(b)(5), which preserves the appearance of independent appellate review.

Each appeal is heard by a panel of three judges. Panels are constituted ad hoc for each appeal from the available pool of designated judges, subject to the same-district disqualification rule. The presiding judge of the BAP is typically designated by the Judicial Council and rotates on a defined cycle. Decisions issue per curiam or under the signature of an authoring judge, with concurrences and dissents identified.

Election Procedure and District Opt-Out

Two consent layers govern whether an appeal proceeds to the BAP rather than to the district court. The first is district-level: under 28 U.S.C. § 158(b)(6), each judicial district within a BAP circuit may, by majority vote of its district judges, decline to authorize BAP service for appeals arising from that district. The First Circuit's constituent districts have generally authorized BAP service, but practitioners should verify current status by district through the panel's clerk's office because authorizations can be modified by district order.

The second layer is party-level: under 28 U.S.C. § 158(c)(1), even where the district has authorized BAP service, an appeal is heard by the panel only if all parties consent. The mechanics work as a default-and-opt-out: the appellant's filing of a notice of appeal under Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 8003 routes the appeal to the BAP unless an appellee files a timely statement of election to have the appeal heard by the district court instead.

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 8005 governs the election. The statement of election must be filed with the clerk of the bankruptcy court within thirty (30) days after service of the notice of appeal (or, if the electing party is the appellant, the election must accompany the notice of appeal). Failure to file a timely election is treated as consent to BAP review. The election need not state grounds; it is a unilateral procedural right.

Any one party may force the appeal into the district court by timely electing. The right is not subject to balancing, and no court approval is required. Counsel weighing the choice of forum should accordingly assume that a single objecting party can defeat BAP routing.

Appellate Jurisdiction

The panel's subject-matter jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 158(a) extends to:

Final judgments, orders, and decrees of the bankruptcy courts under § 158(a)(1);

Interlocutory orders increasing or reducing the time fixed under 11 U.S.C. § 1121(d) for filing a plan, under § 158(a)(2); and

Other interlocutory orders, with leave of the panel, under § 158(a)(3).

Finality in bankruptcy is interpreted more pragmatically than in ordinary civil litigation. The Supreme Court has confirmed that orders resolving discrete disputes within a larger case may be final and immediately appealable even where the underlying case continues. The panel applies the prevailing finality framework of the First Circuit when determining whether a challenged order meets the § 158(a)(1) threshold.

Interlocutory appeals under § 158(a)(3) require a motion for leave. The panel applies the standard derived from 28 U.S.C. § 1292(b): controlling question of law, substantial ground for difference of opinion, and material advancement of the ultimate termination of the litigation. Leave is discretionary and is sparingly granted.

Briefing and Calendar

Briefing in the BAP is governed by Part VIII of the Federal Rules of Bankruptcy Procedure as supplemented by the First Circuit BAP local rules. The default schedule under FRBP 8018 runs from the filing of the appeal record:

Appellant's brief: 30 days after the docketing of the appeal in the BAP

Appellee's brief: 30 days after service of the appellant's brief

Appellant's reply brief: 21 days after service of the appellee's brief (and at least 7 days before argument)

Word and page limits track FRBP 8015. The appellant's principal brief and the appellee's principal brief are each limited to 13,000 words; reply briefs are limited to 6,500 words. Certificates of compliance and required disclosure statements track Part VIII practice.

Oral argument is set by the panel after briefing closes. The panel may decide an appeal without argument under FRBP 8019 if the legal arguments are adequately presented in the briefs and oral argument would not significantly aid the decisional process. Where argument is held, it is typically conducted by video conference or at the court of appeals' Boston courthouse, with sittings at other locations within the circuit on the panel's calendar.

Standards of Review

The panel applies the same standards of review applicable to appeals taken to the district court under 28 U.S.C. § 158(a). Findings of fact are reviewed for clear error; conclusions of law are reviewed de novo; mixed questions are reviewed under the standard appropriate to the question, with the legal component receiving de novo review. Discretionary determinations (such as approvals under 11 U.S.C. § 363, sanctions, and most case-management rulings) are reviewed for abuse of discretion.

The panel's decisions are reviewable on further appeal to the United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit under 28 U.S.C. § 158(d)(1). The court of appeals applies the same standards to bankruptcy court rulings that the BAP applied; the BAP's intermediate decision receives no deference on questions of law in the further appeal.

Contrast with District-Court Appeals

An appeal to the district court under 28 U.S.C. § 158(a) is heard by a single district judge sitting as an appellate court. An appeal to the BAP is heard by a three-judge panel of sitting bankruptcy judges. Several practical differences follow:

Bench expertise. BAP judges are full-time bankruptcy judges with concentrated subject-matter exposure. District judges hear bankruptcy appeals as one part of a general civil and criminal docket. For appeals turning on contested or developing bankruptcy doctrine, the panel's specialization is often the principal substantive consideration.

Panel deliberation versus single judge. Three judges reviewing the same record introduces a deliberative element that a single-judge appeal lacks. Concurrences and dissents are common in BAP decisions and can serve as signal for further-appeal positioning before the court of appeals.

Precedential weight. BAP decisions bind the parties to the appeal but do not bind bankruptcy courts in the circuit as a matter of stare decisis under the prevailing view. District-court decisions on bankruptcy appeals likewise do not formally bind other district judges or other bankruptcy judges, though both forums' decisions carry substantial persuasive weight within the circuit. Court of appeals decisions bind both forums.

Calendar and disposition time. BAP calendars tend to move on a more predictable timeline than the bankruptcy appeal queue of a busy district court, where appeals share the calendar with the district's primary civil and criminal workload. Practitioners report BAP dispositions trending faster than district-court bankruptcy appeals in most circuits, though the differential varies.

When the BAP Is Preferable

The following considerations tend to favor BAP review when the choice is open:

Pure or principally legal questions in core bankruptcy doctrine (avoidance, claim classification, plan confirmation standards, automatic stay scope, discharge) where a specialist bench is most likely to engage the issue at depth.

Appeals from non-routine procedural rulings where the panel's familiarity with bankruptcy court calendaring and motion practice produces a more textured review than a generalist district judge can ordinarily provide.

Cases where the appellate record is dense with bankruptcy-specific factual context (plan economics, claim hierarchies, fee structures) that benefits from a bench fluent in the underlying vocabulary.

Cases where consensus across the panel will strengthen persuasive value in any further appeal, particularly where the issue is one of first impression in the circuit.

The following considerations tend to favor district-court review:

Appeals turning principally on non-bankruptcy substantive law (state-law contract interpretation, federal tax law, securities law) where the district judge's broader subject-matter range is closer to the dispositive question.

Appeals with significant constitutional, jurisdictional, or Article III concerns where the district court's Article III status itself is part of the framing.

Strategic considerations specific to known docket conditions at the district level or to draw rules for assigned district judges.

Practical Filing Notes

A notice of appeal is filed in the bankruptcy court under FRBP 8003. The appeal is then transmitted to the BAP by the bankruptcy clerk unless a party files a timely election to have the appeal heard by the district court instead under FRBP 8005. The thirty-day election window runs from service of the notice of appeal; counsel for appellees should calendar this date promptly because election is the single procedural decision that controls forum.

The BAP's filing fee for an appeal mirrors the district-court fee schedule. Electronic filing is mandatory; the BAP uses the same CM/ECF infrastructure as the constituent bankruptcy courts, with credentials administered through the circuit clerk. Briefing extensions are routinely granted on motion for good cause, but the panel discourages serial extensions and counsel should plan for the default schedule.
