Ninth Circuit Bankruptcy Appellate Panel - Practitioner Guide 2026

First published 2026-05-22/Last modified 2026-05-22/CC-BY-4.0

Abstract

The Bankruptcy Appellate Panel for the Ninth Circuit (9th Cir. BAP) is the oldest and largest of the operating bankruptcy appellate panels, originally established in 1979 as a pilot program and continued in service under 28 U.S.C. § 158(b) by the Judicial Council of the Ninth Circuit. Three-judge panels of sitting bankruptcy judges drawn from the bankruptcy courts within the circuit hear appeals from final orders of those courts when all parties consent under the election procedure of § 158(c)(1). This guide summarizes panel composition, the election and district-opt-out mechanics, the panel's appellate jurisdiction, briefing under Part VIII of the Federal Rules of Bankruptcy Procedure as supplemented by Ninth Circuit BAP local rules, and the strategic factors bearing on the choice of forum between the panel and the United States District Court.

Authorization and Geographic Coverage

The Ninth Circuit BAP was authorized by the Judicial Council of the Ninth Circuit as a pilot under the predecessor BAP authorization, and is now established under 28 U.S.C. § 158(b)(1). The panel hears appeals arising from the bankruptcy courts of the nine states comprising the Ninth Circuit, which together include fifteen federal judicial districts:

District of Alaska (D. Alaska Bankr.)

District of Arizona (D. Ariz. Bankr.)

Central District of California (C.D. Cal. Bankr.)

Eastern District of California (E.D. Cal. Bankr.)

Northern District of California (N.D. Cal. Bankr.)

Southern District of California (S.D. Cal. Bankr.)

District of Hawaii (D. Haw. Bankr.)

District of Idaho (D. Idaho Bankr.)

District of Montana (D. Mont. Bankr.)

District of Nevada (D. Nev. Bankr.)

District of Oregon (D. Or. Bankr.)

Eastern District of Washington (E.D. Wash. Bankr.)

Western District of Washington (W.D. Wash. Bankr.)

District of Guam (D. Guam Bankr.)

District of the Northern Mariana Islands (D.N. Mar. I. Bankr.)

The panel's clerk's office is administratively located in Pasadena, California. Counsel should verify the current authorization status of each constituent district through the BAP clerk's office, because districts may withdraw or modify authorization for BAP service under § 158(b)(6).

Statutory authority28 U.S.C. § 158(b), (c)

Establishing bodyJudicial Council of the Ninth Circuit (pilot 1979; continued under section 158(b))

Constituent jurisdictionsAlaska, Arizona, California (4 districts), Hawaii, Idaho, Montana, Nevada, Oregon, Washington (2 districts), Guam, Northern Mariana Islands

Clerk's officePasadena, California

Official websitewww.ca9.uscourts.gov/bap

Panel Composition

Under 28 U.S.C. § 158(b)(1)(A), bankruptcy appellate panels are composed of bankruptcy judges from districts within the circuit. The Ninth Circuit BAP draws its members from the bankruptcy benches of the constituent districts listed above. A sitting member of the panel cannot hear an appeal arising from his or her own home district under § 158(b)(5), which preserves the appearance of independent appellate review and prevents same-district peer review.

Each appeal is decided by a panel of three judges. Panels are constituted ad hoc for each appeal from the available pool of designated judges, subject to the same-district disqualification rule. The presiding judge of the BAP is designated by the Judicial Council and rotates on a defined cycle. Opinions issue per curiam, by designated authoring judge, or with concurrences and dissents identified, and a significant portion are designated for publication.

The Ninth Circuit BAP maintains the most extensive published bankruptcy appellate corpus of any BAP. Its decisions are reported in West's Bankruptcy Reporter and are routinely cited within and beyond the circuit. Memorandum (unpublished) dispositions are issued for the bulk of routine appeals; published opinions are reserved for matters of broader doctrinal significance.

Election Procedure and District Opt-Out

Two consent layers govern whether an appeal proceeds to the BAP rather than to the district court. The first is district-level: under 28 U.S.C. § 158(b)(6), each judicial district within a BAP circuit may, by majority vote of its district judges, decline to authorize BAP service for appeals arising from that district. Authorization status across the Ninth Circuit's many districts has varied over time; practitioners should verify the current status for the district in which the underlying case sits before assuming BAP routing is available.

The second layer is party-level: under 28 U.S.C. § 158(c)(1), even where the district has authorized BAP service, an appeal is heard by the panel only if all parties to the appeal consent. The mechanics work as a default-and-opt-out: the appellant's filing of a notice of appeal under Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 8003 routes the appeal to the BAP unless a party files a timely statement of election to have the appeal heard by the district court instead.

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 8005 governs the election. The statement of election must be filed with the clerk of the bankruptcy court within thirty (30) days after service of the notice of appeal. If the electing party is the appellant, the election must accompany the notice of appeal. Failure to file a timely election by any party is treated as consent to BAP review.

Election is a unilateral procedural right. The statement need not state grounds; no court approval is required; and the panel cannot retain an appeal over a timely election. Counsel weighing the choice of forum should accordingly assume that a single objecting party can defeat BAP routing.

Appellate Jurisdiction

The panel's subject-matter jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 158(a) extends to:

Final judgments, orders, and decrees of the bankruptcy courts under § 158(a)(1);

Interlocutory orders increasing or reducing the time fixed under 11 U.S.C. § 1121(d) for filing a plan, under § 158(a)(2); and

Other interlocutory orders, with leave of the panel, under § 158(a)(3).

Finality in bankruptcy is interpreted more pragmatically than in ordinary civil litigation. Orders resolving discrete disputes within a larger case may be final and immediately appealable even where the underlying case continues. The panel applies the Ninth Circuit's prevailing finality framework when determining whether a challenged order meets the § 158(a)(1) threshold.

Interlocutory appeals under § 158(a)(3) require a motion for leave. The panel applies a standard derived from 28 U.S.C. § 1292(b): controlling question of law, substantial ground for difference of opinion, and material advancement of the ultimate termination of the litigation. Leave is discretionary and is sparingly granted.

Briefing and Calendar

Briefing in the BAP is governed by Part VIII of the Federal Rules of Bankruptcy Procedure as supplemented by the Ninth Circuit BAP local rules. The default schedule under FRBP 8018 runs from the filing of the appeal record:

Appellant's brief: 30 days after the docketing of the appeal in the BAP

Appellee's brief: 30 days after service of the appellant's brief

Appellant's reply brief: 21 days after service of the appellee's brief (and at least 7 days before argument)

Word and page limits track FRBP 8015. The appellant's principal brief and the appellee's principal brief are each limited to 13,000 words; reply briefs are limited to 6,500 words. Certificates of compliance, jurisdictional statements, and required disclosure statements track Part VIII practice. The Ninth Circuit BAP local rules supplement Part VIII on excerpts of record, citation format, and motion practice; counsel should consult the current local rules before assembling the appendix.

Oral argument is set by the panel after briefing closes. The panel may decide an appeal without argument under FRBP 8019 if the legal arguments are adequately presented in the briefs and oral argument would not significantly aid the decisional process. The Ninth Circuit BAP holds argument at sittings convened in major circuit cities (including Pasadena, San Francisco, Seattle, Phoenix, and Honolulu) and routinely by video conference for parties in remote districts.

Standards of Review

The panel applies the same standards of review applicable to appeals taken to the district court under 28 U.S.C. § 158(a). Findings of fact are reviewed for clear error; conclusions of law are reviewed de novo; mixed questions are reviewed under the standard appropriate to the question, with the legal component receiving de novo review. Discretionary determinations (such as approvals under 11 U.S.C. § 363, sanctions, plan confirmation in the discretionary fairness aspects of 11 U.S.C. § 1129, and most case-management rulings) are reviewed for abuse of discretion.

The panel's decisions are reviewable on further appeal to the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit under 28 U.S.C. § 158(d)(1). The court of appeals applies the same standards to bankruptcy court rulings that the BAP applied; the BAP's intermediate decision receives no formal deference on questions of law in the further appeal.

Contrast with District-Court Appeals

An appeal to the district court under 28 U.S.C. § 158(a) is heard by a single district judge sitting as an appellate court. An appeal to the BAP is heard by a three-judge panel of sitting bankruptcy judges. Several practical differences follow:

Bench expertise. BAP judges are full-time bankruptcy judges with concentrated subject-matter exposure. District judges hear bankruptcy appeals as one part of a general civil and criminal docket. For appeals turning on contested or developing bankruptcy doctrine, the panel's specialization is often the principal substantive consideration. The Ninth Circuit BAP's bench has decided more bankruptcy appeals than any other BAP, with corresponding depth across nearly every recurring doctrinal area.

Panel deliberation versus single judge. Three judges reviewing the same record introduce a deliberative element that a single-judge appeal lacks. Concurrences and dissents in BAP opinions can preserve issues and shape framing for further appeal to the court of appeals.

Precedential weight. The Ninth Circuit has held that published Ninth Circuit BAP decisions are binding precedent on bankruptcy courts within the circuit unless and until overruled by the court of appeals or the panel itself sitting en banc. This is a stronger formal precedential rule than the rule applied in most other BAP circuits. Memorandum (unpublished) dispositions are not binding precedent but are routinely cited for persuasive value within the circuit. District-court decisions on bankruptcy appeals do not formally bind other district judges or bankruptcy judges.

Calendar and disposition time. BAP calendars tend to move on a more predictable timeline than the bankruptcy appeal queue of a busy district court, where appeals share the calendar with the district's primary civil and criminal workload. The Ninth Circuit BAP has historically maintained one of the most efficient appellate calendars in the federal system for bankruptcy matters.

When the BAP Is Preferable

The following considerations tend to favor BAP review when the choice is open in the Ninth Circuit:

Pure or principally legal questions in core bankruptcy doctrine (avoidance, claim classification, plan confirmation standards, automatic stay scope, discharge, Chapter 13 plan modification) where a specialist bench is most likely to engage the issue at depth.

Appeals where binding circuit-level precedent is the desired output. Because published Ninth Circuit BAP decisions bind the circuit's bankruptcy courts, a successful BAP appeal that issues as a published opinion produces precedential value at the circuit level - a result a district-court appeal cannot replicate.

Appeals from non-routine procedural rulings where the panel's familiarity with bankruptcy court calendaring and motion practice produces a more textured review than a generalist district judge can ordinarily provide.

Cases where the appellate record is dense with bankruptcy-specific factual context (plan economics, claim hierarchies, fee structures) that benefits from a bench fluent in the underlying vocabulary.

The following considerations tend to favor district-court review:

Appeals turning principally on non-bankruptcy substantive law (state-law contract interpretation, federal tax law, securities law, ERISA) where the district judge's broader subject-matter range is closer to the dispositive question.

Appeals with significant constitutional, Stern v. Marshall, or Article III concerns where the district court's Article III status itself is part of the analytical framing.

Cases where a litigant prefers a single-judge decision-maker as a matter of litigation strategy, or wishes to avoid the binding-precedent effect of an adverse published BAP opinion.

Strategic considerations specific to known docket conditions at the district level or to known dispositions of district judges on bankruptcy-adjacent legal questions.

Practical Filing Notes

A notice of appeal is filed in the bankruptcy court under FRBP 8003. The appeal is transmitted to the BAP by the bankruptcy clerk unless a party files a timely election to have the appeal heard by the district court instead under FRBP 8005. The thirty-day election window runs from service of the notice of appeal; counsel for appellees should calendar this date promptly because election is the single procedural decision that controls forum.

The BAP's filing fee mirrors the district-court fee schedule. Electronic filing is mandatory; the BAP uses CM/ECF infrastructure with credentials administered through the circuit clerk. Briefing extensions are routinely granted on motion for good cause, but the panel discourages serial extensions and counsel should plan for the default schedule.

Official Resources

Ninth Circuit BAP: www.ca9.uscourts.gov/bap

U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit: www.ca9.uscourts.gov

Federal Rules of Bankruptcy Procedure (Part VIII, Appeals): uscourts.gov/rules-policies/current-rules-practice-procedure

28 U.S.C. § 158: www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/28/158

Sixth Circuit Bankruptcy Appellate Panel - Practitioner Guide 2026

First published 2026-05-22/Last modified 2026-05-22/CC-BY-4.0

Abstract

The Bankruptcy Appellate Panel for the Sixth Circuit (6th Cir. BAP) is an Article I appellate forum established by the Judicial Council of the Sixth Circuit under 28 U.S.C. § 158(b). Three-judge panels of sitting bankruptcy judges drawn from the bankruptcy courts within the circuit hear appeals from final orders of those courts when all parties consent under the election procedure of § 158(c)(1). This guide summarizes panel composition, the election and district-opt-out mechanics, the panel's appellate jurisdiction, briefing under Part VIII of the Federal Rules of Bankruptcy Procedure as supplemented by BAP local rules, and the strategic factors bearing on the choice of forum between the panel and the United States District Court.

Authorization and Geographic Coverage

The Sixth Circuit BAP was established by order of the Judicial Council of the Sixth Circuit pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 158(b)(1). The panel hears appeals arising from the bankruptcy courts of the four states comprising the Sixth Circuit, which together include eight federal judicial districts:

Eastern District of Kentucky (E.D. Ky. Bankr.)

Western District of Kentucky (W.D. Ky. Bankr.)

Eastern District of Michigan (E.D. Mich. Bankr.)

Western District of Michigan (W.D. Mich. Bankr.)

Northern District of Ohio (N.D. Ohio Bankr.)

Southern District of Ohio (S.D. Ohio Bankr.)

Eastern District of Tennessee (E.D. Tenn. Bankr.)

Middle District of Tennessee (M.D. Tenn. Bankr.)

Western District of Tennessee (W.D. Tenn. Bankr.)

The panel's clerk's office is administratively colocated with the office of the Clerk of the United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit in Cincinnati. Counsel should verify the current authorization status of each constituent district through the BAP clerk's office, because districts may withdraw or modify authorization for BAP service under § 158(b)(6).

Statutory authority28 U.S.C. § 158(b), (c)

Establishing bodyJudicial Council of the Sixth Circuit

Constituent statesKentucky, Michigan, Ohio, Tennessee

Clerk's officeU.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit, Cincinnati, Ohio

Official websitewww.ca6.uscourts.gov/bap

Panel Composition

Under 28 U.S.C. § 158(b)(1)(A), bankruptcy appellate panels are composed of bankruptcy judges from districts within the circuit. The Sixth Circuit BAP draws its members from the bankruptcy benches of the constituent districts listed above. A sitting member of the panel cannot hear an appeal arising from his or her own home district under § 158(b)(5), which preserves the appearance of independent appellate review and prevents same-district peer review.

Each appeal is decided by a panel of three judges. Panels are constituted ad hoc for each appeal from the available pool of designated judges, subject to the same-district disqualification rule. The presiding judge of the BAP is designated by the Judicial Council and rotates on a defined cycle. Opinions issue per curiam or under a single authoring judge; concurrences and dissents are common and are reported alongside the lead opinion.

The Sixth Circuit BAP has historically maintained one of the more substantial published bodies of bankruptcy appellate opinion in the BAP system, with decisions reported in West's Bankruptcy Reporter and broadly available through commercial and free legal-research platforms.

Election Procedure and District Opt-Out

Two consent layers govern whether an appeal proceeds to the BAP rather than to the district court. The first is district-level: under 28 U.S.C. § 158(b)(6), each judicial district within a BAP circuit may, by majority vote of its district judges, decline to authorize BAP service for appeals arising from that district. Practitioners should verify current authorization status by district through the panel's clerk's office, because authorizations can be modified by subsequent district order.

The second layer is party-level: under 28 U.S.C. § 158(c)(1), even where the district has authorized BAP service, an appeal is heard by the panel only if all parties to the appeal consent. The mechanics work as a default-and-opt-out: the appellant's filing of a notice of appeal under Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 8003 routes the appeal to the BAP unless a party files a timely statement of election to have the appeal heard by the district court instead.

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 8005 governs the election. The statement of election must be filed with the clerk of the bankruptcy court within thirty (30) days after service of the notice of appeal. If the electing party is the appellant, the election must accompany the notice of appeal. Failure to file a timely election by any party is treated as consent to BAP review.

Election is a unilateral procedural right. The statement need not state grounds; no court approval is required; and the panel cannot retain an appeal over a timely election. Counsel weighing the choice of forum should accordingly assume that a single objecting party can defeat BAP routing.

Appellate Jurisdiction

The panel's subject-matter jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 158(a) extends to:

Final judgments, orders, and decrees of the bankruptcy courts under § 158(a)(1);

Interlocutory orders increasing or reducing the time fixed under 11 U.S.C. § 1121(d) for filing a plan, under § 158(a)(2); and

Other interlocutory orders, with leave of the panel, under § 158(a)(3).

Finality in bankruptcy is interpreted more pragmatically than in ordinary civil litigation. Orders resolving discrete disputes within a larger case may be final and immediately appealable even where the underlying case continues. The panel applies the Sixth Circuit's prevailing finality framework when determining whether a challenged order meets the § 158(a)(1) threshold.

Interlocutory appeals under § 158(a)(3) require a motion for leave. The panel applies a standard derived from 28 U.S.C. § 1292(b): controlling question of law, substantial ground for difference of opinion, and material advancement of the ultimate termination of the litigation. Leave is discretionary and is sparingly granted.

Briefing and Calendar

Briefing in the BAP is governed by Part VIII of the Federal Rules of Bankruptcy Procedure as supplemented by the Sixth Circuit BAP local rules. The default schedule under FRBP 8018 runs from the filing of the appeal record:

Appellant's brief: 30 days after the docketing of the appeal in the BAP

Appellee's brief: 30 days after service of the appellant's brief

Appellant's reply brief: 21 days after service of the appellee's brief (and at least 7 days before argument)

Word and page limits track FRBP 8015. The appellant's principal brief and the appellee's principal brief are each limited to 13,000 words; reply briefs are limited to 6,500 words. Certificates of compliance, jurisdictional statements, and required disclosure statements track Part VIII practice.

Oral argument is set by the panel after briefing closes. The panel may decide an appeal without argument under FRBP 8019 if the legal arguments are adequately presented in the briefs and oral argument would not significantly aid the decisional process. The Sixth Circuit BAP hears argument by video conference and at sittings convened in the circuit's principal cities on the panel's calendar.

Standards of Review

The panel applies the same standards of review applicable to appeals taken to the district court under 28 U.S.C. § 158(a). Findings of fact are reviewed for clear error; conclusions of law are reviewed de novo; mixed questions are reviewed under the standard appropriate to the question, with the legal component receiving de novo review. Discretionary determinations (such as approvals under 11 U.S.C. § 363, sanctions, plan confirmation in the discretionary fairness aspects of 11 U.S.C. § 1129, and most case-management rulings) are reviewed for abuse of discretion.

The panel's decisions are reviewable on further appeal to the United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit under 28 U.S.C. § 158(d)(1). The court of appeals applies the same standards to bankruptcy court rulings that the BAP applied; the BAP's intermediate decision receives no formal deference on questions of law in the further appeal.

Contrast with District-Court Appeals

An appeal to the district court under 28 U.S.C. § 158(a) is heard by a single district judge sitting as an appellate court. An appeal to the BAP is heard by a three-judge panel of sitting bankruptcy judges. Several practical differences follow:

Bench expertise. BAP judges are full-time bankruptcy judges with concentrated subject-matter exposure. District judges hear bankruptcy appeals as one part of a general civil and criminal docket. For appeals turning on contested or developing bankruptcy doctrine, the panel's specialization is often the principal substantive consideration.

Panel deliberation versus single judge. Three judges reviewing the same record introduce a deliberative element that a single-judge appeal lacks. Concurrences and dissents in BAP opinions can preserve issues and shape framing for further appeal to the court of appeals.

Precedential weight. BAP decisions bind the parties to the appeal but do not bind bankruptcy courts in the circuit as a matter of formal stare decisis under the prevailing view. District-court decisions on bankruptcy appeals likewise do not formally bind other district judges or other bankruptcy judges, though both forums' decisions carry substantial persuasive weight within the circuit. Court of appeals decisions bind both forums.

Calendar and disposition time. BAP calendars tend to move on a more predictable timeline than the bankruptcy appeal queue of a busy district court, where appeals share the calendar with the district's primary civil and criminal workload. The Sixth Circuit BAP has historically maintained disposition times competitive with the circuit's district benches.

The following considerations tend to favor BAP review when the choice is open:

Pure or principally legal questions in core bankruptcy doctrine (avoidance, claim classification, plan confirmation standards, automatic stay scope, discharge, Chapter 13 plan modification) where a specialist bench is most likely to engage the issue at depth.

Appeals from non-routine procedural rulings where the panel's familiarity with bankruptcy court calendaring and motion practice produces a more textured review than a generalist district judge can ordinarily provide.

Cases where the appellate record is dense with bankruptcy-specific factual context (plan economics, claim hierarchies, fee structures) that benefits from a bench fluent in the underlying vocabulary.

Cases where panel consensus will strengthen persuasive value in any further appeal, particularly where the issue is one of first impression in the circuit.

The following considerations tend to favor district-court review:

Appeals with significant constitutional, Stern v. Marshall, or Article III concerns where the district court's Article III status itself is part of the analytical framing.

A notice of appeal is filed in the bankruptcy court under FRBP 8003. The appeal is transmitted to the BAP by the bankruptcy clerk unless a party files a timely election to have the appeal heard by the district court instead under FRBP 8005. Tenth Circuit Bankruptcy Appellate Panel - Practitioner Guide 2026

First published 2026-05-22/Last modified 2026-05-22/CC-BY-4.0

Abstract

The Bankruptcy Appellate Panel for the Tenth Circuit (10th Cir. BAP) is an Article I appellate forum established by the Judicial Council of the Tenth Circuit under 28 U.S.C. § 158(b). District of Colorado (D. Colo. Bankr.)

District of Kansas (D. Kan. Bankr.)

District of New Mexico (D.N.M. Bankr.)

Eastern District of Oklahoma (E.D. Okla. Bankr.)

Northern District of Oklahoma (N.D. Okla. Bankr.)

The following considerations tend to favor district-court review:

Appeals turning principally on non-bankruptcy substantive law (state-law contract interpretation, federal tax law, securities law, ERISA, oil-and-gas lease interpretation) where the district judge's broader subject-matter range is closer to the dispositive question.

Appeals with significant constitutional, Stern v. Marshall, or Article III concerns where the district court's Article III status itself is part of the analytical framing.

Strategic considerations specific to known docket conditions at the district level or to known dispositions of district judges on bankruptcy-adjacent legal questions.

Practical Filing Notes

A notice of appeal is filed in the bankruptcy court under FRBP 8003. The appeal is transmitted to the BAP by the bankruptcy clerk unless a party files a timely election to have the appeal heard by the district court instead under FRBP 8005. The thirty-day election window runs from service of the notice of appeal; counsel for appellees should calendar this date promptly because election is the single procedural decision that controls forum.

The BAP's filing fee mirrors the district-court fee schedule. Electronic filing is mandatory; the BAP uses CM/ECF infrastructure with credentials administered through the circuit clerk. Briefing extensions are routinely granted on motion for good cause, but the panel discourages serial extensions and counsel should plan for the default schedule.

## Second Federal Rules Committee Suggestion Submitted: 26-BK-5 on Rule 9037 SSN Exposure - Open Bankruptcy Project

Open Bankruptcy Project

Rule 9037

Home »

Suggestion 26-BK-5 Submitted

Second Federal Rules Committee suggestion submitted: 26-BK-5 on Rule 9037 SSN exposure

Published April 16, 2026  ·  Rule-Making  ·  Open Bankruptcy Project

On April 16, 2026, the Open Bankruptcy Project submitted a suggestion to the Advisory Committee on Bankruptcy Rules proposing five amendments to Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 9037. The suggestion, tracked as 26-BK-5, is OBP's second submission to the Committee; the first, 26-BK-3 on automated screening under 11 U.S.C. § 1328(f), was submitted in March and cited in the Consumer Subcommittee's April 15 agenda book.

The short version. Federal court filings are supposed to contain only the last four digits of Social Security numbers under Rule 9037(a). Empirically, that is not what happens. Using a free scan of the RECAP archive, we identified a recurring template-level exposure pattern affecting filings across multiple federal judicial districts. The five proposed amendments target the root cause (template integrity) rather than the symptom (post-hoc redaction).

What Rule 9037 requires

Rule 9037(a) limits public filings to: the last four digits of a Social Security number or taxpayer-identification number, the year of an individual's birth, a minor's initials, and the last four digits of a financial-account number. Rule 9037(h) provides a remedy on motion by a party or affected non-party to redact a non-compliant filing.

The rule places the compliance burden entirely on the filer. There is currently no automated screening at the ECF upload point, no template-integrity audit for Official Forms that contain personal-identifier fields, and no mandatory notification to affected individuals when an exposure is identified.

Where the exposure lives

The bulk of compliance gaps cluster in two places. Official Form 121 and Official Form 309E1 carry direct identifier fields; template-level misconfiguration in Form 309E1 in particular can reproduce the same exposure across every case generated from a given template. The larger category is creditor contract templates attached to proofs of claim and motions for relief from stay. When a contract template embeds the debtor's or guarantor's full SSN as a printed field, each new filing that attaches that template reproduces the identifier.

This is why the 26-BK-5 framing is template-level rather than filer-level. No individual filer is the root cause; a template generated a decade ago and never updated is.

The five proposed amendments

Auto-sealing event code. An ECF event tag at the docketing layer that automatically restricts public access to any document flagged as containing personal identifiers, until the filer redacts or the court orders otherwise.

Template-integrity audit for Official Forms. A recurring audit of Official Forms that carry personal-identifier fields (Form 121, Form 309E1, Form 309C, and others) to ensure the form templates themselves do not generate non-compliant output.

Pre-acceptance screening at the ECF upload point. A screening pass at the moment of filing that detects patterns likely to constitute Rule 9037(a) violations and returns the filing to the filer for correction before it reaches the public docket.

Non-cure provision. A codification of the existing case-law trend: redaction after public PACER publication does not remedy prior disclosure. This makes the non-cure doctrine explicit in the rule text and provides a clear basis for additional remedies (notification, sanctions) that courts presently reach through inherent authority.

Mandatory clerk notification to affected individuals. When a Rule 9037(a) violation is identified, the clerk notifies the person whose identifier was exposed. Currently notification is discretionary and uneven; this amendment makes it uniform.

Data and methodology

Unlike 26-BK-3, which was built on paid PACER data, 26-BK-5 was built entirely on the free RECAP archive maintained by the Free Law Project. The scan used a custom pattern-detection tool with extensive false-positive filtering and confidence tiering. Findings were reported in masked form only; the underlying identifiers were never extracted, stored, or transmitted. The methodology is detailed in the Rule 9037 hub page and in the case-law analysis linked below.

Using the free RECAP layer rather than paid PACER matters for replicability. The methodology can be applied by any researcher, clerk, or practitioner with a list of PDFs and a Python interpreter. It does not require institutional funding or PACER fee-exemption status.

What happens next

The suggestion has been forwarded to the Chairs and Reporters of both the Advisory Committee on Bankruptcy Rules. From there, the typical path is: discussion at the next regular committee meeting, referral to a subcommittee for drafting, circulation of proposed amendment language, public comment period, and eventual transmission to the Judicial Conference and Supreme Court for adoption.

That sequence usually takes years. The value of getting it docketed at the front end is that the empirical finding is now formally on the committee's record; later discussion will proceed from that starting point rather than from scratch.

If your SSN appears on a public filing

Don't wait for the rule amendment. A Rule 9037(h) motion is available now. The remediation workflow walks through the steps: confirm the docket location, notify the clerk, file under 9037(h), preserve a locator copy (not the identifier), and request removal from secondary republishers. The clerk notification templates provide ready-to-adapt language.

Important. If you are working through a Rule 9037(a) exposure and need a primer on the rule itself, the Rule 9037 hub covers the statute, the forms, the contract-template exposure vector, and the relevant case law. If you want the full text of 26-BK-5 as submitted to the Committee, it is the PDF linked from the public page on uscourts.gov.

## Are Bankruptcy Records Public? Yes, Under 11 USC 107(a)
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/blog/are-bankruptcy-records-public.html

Open Bankruptcy Project

Home›Blog›Are Bankruptcy Records Public?

Are Bankruptcy Records Public? Yes, Under 11 USC 107(a)

Federal bankruptcy filings are public records by statute and by Supreme Court precedent. The only narrow remedy that operates on the underlying docket is FRBP 9037(d).

Published May 18, 2026

People are often surprised to learn that the bankruptcy case they filed shows up on a Google search. The reason is structural: federal bankruptcy filings are public records by federal statute, not by editorial choice of any particular website. This post walks through the statute, the controlling Supreme Court case, what is and is not redactable, and the one procedural path that actually operates on the underlying court record.

The Statutory Rule: 11 USC 107(a)

The starting point is 11 USC 107(a). It is short and unambiguous:

"Except as provided in subsections (b) and (c) and subject to section 112, a paper filed in a case under this title and the dockets of a bankruptcy court are public records and open to examination by an entity at reasonable times without charge."

Three things follow from this. First, the default for everything filed in a bankruptcy case is public. Second, the publicness is conferred by federal statute, not by any third-party website. Third, the right of access is free at the point of use ("without charge").

The Common-Law Anchor: Nixon v. Warner Communications

The statutory rule is reinforced by a common-law right of public access to judicial records that the Supreme Court confirmed in Nixon v. Warner Communications, 435 U.S. 589 (1978). The Court held that the public has a general right "to inspect and copy public records and documents, including judicial records and documents." This common-law right operates independently of any particular statute. Even in a hypothetical world where 11 USC 107(a) did not exist, the Nixon presumption would still apply to bankruptcy filings as judicial records.

The two anchors together make bankruptcy public records doubly insulated from informal removal demands. A request to take a filing offline because it is "embarrassing" or "could affect a career" runs into both the federal statute and binding Supreme Court precedent.

What Counts as "Public" in Practice

The official source is PACER (Public Access to Court Electronic Records). PACER is the federal judiciary's electronic record system; anyone with an account can read filings on any federal bankruptcy case. PACER charges per page (currently $0.10 per page, capped at $3 per document).

Because the statutory rule makes the data public, a number of mirror archives have grown up around PACER. The largest is the CourtListener RECAP Archive, operated by the 501(c)(3) Free Law Project. RECAP republishes PACER documents for free at the point of use. The Open Bankruptcy Project is a similar mirror: a 501(c)(3) that indexes federal bankruptcy dockets so users can find their case (or a relative's case, or a creditor's case) without paying PACER fees.

None of these mirrors create the publicness. They republish what is already public by statute. Asking a mirror to remove a case but leaving the official PACER docket untouched accomplishes nothing structurally - the next pull from any mirror will re-introduce the same information from the same source.

The One Path That Operates on the Record: FRBP 9037(d)

The Federal Rules of Bankruptcy Procedure include a narrow remedy that does operate on the underlying court file. Rule 9037 governs how protected personal identifiers must appear in filings.

Subsection (a) sets the front-end rule. When filing a document in a bankruptcy case, the filer may include only:

The last four digits of a Social Security number or taxpayer-identification number.

The year of an individual's date of birth.

A minor's initials only.

The last four digits of a financial-account number.

Subsection (d) is the back-end remedy. When a document was filed without the required redactions, the court may, on motion, order the filer to redact and refile, restrict remote electronic access to the unredacted document, file a redacted version with the unredacted version filed under seal, or seal a specific document for cause shown.

What 9037(d) Does Not Do

A Rule 9037(d) motion is not a vehicle for hiding the existence of a bankruptcy filing. The case caption, the parties' names, the chapter, the filing date, the dockets, and the docket entries remain public after a successful 9037(d) motion. What changes is that protected personal identifiers (full SSN, full date of birth, account numbers, minor children's names) are removed from individual documents.

For anything beyond protected identifiers, the bar is much higher. 11 USC 107(b) permits the court to protect "trade secrets or confidential research, development, or commercial information" and to keep "scandalous or defamatory matter" out of public view. Section 107(c) addresses information that would create "undue risk of identity theft or other unlawful injury to the individual or the individual's property." Sealing under these provisions requires a specific factual showing, not a generalized concern about reputation.

Practical Takeaway

Three points stand out for anyone whose bankruptcy filing has surfaced in a Google search:

Existence of the filing is not removable. The case caption and filing date are public by federal statute and Supreme Court precedent. No mirror, court order, or removal request changes that as a structural matter.

Personal identifiers may be redactable. If full SSN, full date of birth, account numbers, or a minor child's name appears in any filed document, a FRBP 9037(d) motion can have those redacted from the official record. Mirrors will pick up the redacted version on their next pull.

Removal demands sent to mirrors do not reach PACER. The publicness lives at the federal court. Mirrors republish what PACER publishes. The procedural remedy lives at the court that holds the docket - not at any mirror.

If a bankruptcy is causing real-world harm - employment-decision discrimination, denial of credit beyond what the FCRA reporting periods would predict, identity-theft exposure - the path runs through the bankruptcy court that issued the docket, not through informal contact with a republisher. The Open Bankruptcy Project, like every other PACER mirror, follows whatever the underlying federal court orders.

Need to look up a specific case? You can search OBP's free index of federal bankruptcy filings, or read the full docket on CourtListener or PACER.

For questions about removing protected identifiers from a specific case, consult a bankruptcy attorney who can prepare a Rule 9037(d) motion in the court that holds the docket.

## Chapter 15 Cross-Border Recognition - 11 USC 1515 and 1517 [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/chapter-15-cross-border/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

11 U.S.C.
Chapter 15

Chapter 15: Cross-Border Insolvency Recognition

The Section 1515 petition for recognition of a foreign proceeding, the Section 1517 recognition factors, the foreign main / foreign nonmain distinction, and the Section 1506 public-policy exception.

The origin of Chapter 15

Chapter 15 was added to the Bankruptcy Code by the Bankruptcy Abuse Prevention and Consumer Protection Act of 2005 (BAPCPA) as the U.S. enactment of the UNCITRAL Model Law on Cross-Border Insolvency (1997). Chapter 15 replaced former Section 304 - a sparse, equitable provision authorizing limited ancillary relief in aid of foreign proceedings - with a comprehensive recognition-and-cooperation framework drawn directly from the Model Law's articles.

The Model Law's stated objectives, incorporated into 11 U.S.C. Section 1501, include: cooperation between U.S. courts and foreign courts in cross-border cases; greater legal certainty for trade and investment; fair and efficient administration of cross-border insolvencies that protects the interests of all creditors; protection and maximization of the value of the debtor's assets; and facilitation of the rescue of financially troubled businesses.

The Section 1515 petition for recognition

(a) A foreign representative applies to the court for recognition of a foreign proceeding in which the foreign representative has been appointed by filing a petition for recognition.

(b) A petition for recognition shall be accompanied by - (1) a certified copy of the decision commencing such foreign proceeding and appointing the foreign representative; (2) a certificate from the foreign court affirming the existence of such foreign proceeding and of the appointment of the foreign representative; or (3) in the absence of evidence referred to in paragraphs (1) and (2), any other evidence acceptable to the court of the existence of such foreign proceeding and of the appointment of the foreign representative. 11 U.S.C. Section 1515(a)-(b).

The petition initiates the ancillary case. It must be filed by a "foreign representative" as defined in 11 U.S.C. Section 101(24) - a person or body, including one appointed on an interim basis, authorized in a foreign proceeding to administer the reorganization or liquidation of the debtor's assets or affairs or to act as a representative of the foreign proceeding. The foreign representative is the petitioner; the U.S. debtor (if any U.S. presence exists) is not.

Section 1515(c) requires that the petition be accompanied by a statement identifying all foreign proceedings, in any jurisdiction, with respect to the debtor that are known to the foreign representative. The statement is meant to give the U.S. court the global picture before recognition is decided.

The Section 1517 recognition factors

Subject to section 1506, after notice and a hearing, an order recognizing a foreign proceeding shall be entered if - (1) such foreign proceeding for which recognition is sought is a foreign main proceeding or foreign nonmain proceeding within the meaning of section 1502; (2) the foreign representative applying for recognition is a person or body; and (3) the petition meets the requirements of section 1515. 11 U.S.C. Section 1517(a).

Recognition under Section 1517 is mandatory if the three factors are satisfied and the public-policy exception of Section 1506 does not apply. The statute uses "shall be entered," not "may be entered." This is a deliberate departure from the discretionary equitable framework of former Section 304. The U.S. court's role at the recognition stage is narrow: confirm that the foreign proceeding exists, that the foreign representative was duly appointed, and that the proceeding qualifies as foreign main or foreign nonmain under Section 1502.

The two recognition tracks - foreign main and foreign nonmain

Section 1517(b) directs the court to enter the recognition order with the proper characterization:

Foreign main proceeding

Recognized as such if it is pending in the country where the debtor has the center of its main interests ("COMI"). The presumption under 11 U.S.C. Section 1516(c) is that the debtor's registered office is the COMI in the absence of evidence to the contrary. Recognition as foreign main triggers automatic relief under Section 1520.

Foreign nonmain proceeding

Recognized as such if the foreign proceeding is pending in a country where the debtor has an "establishment" - any place of operations where the debtor carries out a nontransitory economic activity. 11 U.S.C. Section 1502(2). Recognition as foreign nonmain does not trigger Section 1520 automatic relief; available relief is limited to the discretionary relief under Section 1521.

The distinction is doctrinally load-bearing. See the foreign main versus foreign nonmain companion page for the substantive effects of the two classifications.

The Section 1506 public-policy exception

Nothing in this chapter prevents the court from refusing to take an action governed by this chapter if the action would be manifestly contrary to the public policy of the United States. 11 U.S.C. Section 1506.

Section 1506 is the only generally-applicable safety valve in the recognition framework. It is intentionally narrow. The word "manifestly" was carried over verbatim from the UNCITRAL Model Law and is meant to limit refusal to the most extreme cases - those where recognition would offend fundamental U.S. public policy in a clear and unmistakable way. The U.S. courts have applied the exception sparingly.

In In re Ephedra Products Liability Litigation, 349 B.R. 333 (S.D.N.Y. 2006), the court rejected a Section 1506 challenge to recognition of a Canadian Companies' Creditors Arrangement Act (CCAA) proceeding, holding that procedural differences between U.S. and Canadian insolvency systems - even substantial ones - do not amount to a "manifest" public-policy violation. The standard requires more than the absence of an equivalent U.S. procedure; it requires that the action sought be offensive to a fundamental U.S. interest.

The leading early-application case, In re Bear Stearns High-Grade Structured Credit Strategies Master Fund, Ltd., 374 B.R. 122 (Bankr. S.D.N.Y. 2007), aff'd, 389 B.R. 325 (S.D.N.Y. 2008), denied recognition altogether on COMI grounds - the funds had been organized in the Cayman Islands but had no economic activity there beyond the registered office - and signaled that the recognition gate, not the Section 1506 exception, is where most close calls will be resolved.

Comity, cooperation, and Section 1525

Recognition under Chapter 15 unlocks the court's authority to grant cooperation under 11 U.S.C. Section 1525 and Section 1526. The U.S. court "shall cooperate to the maximum extent possible" with foreign courts and foreign representatives, including by direct communication. The cooperation framework treats the U.S. case as ancillary to the foreign main proceeding wherever possible, with the U.S. court's role being to assist - not to displace - the foreign court's administration of the estate.

In In re SPhinX, Ltd., 351 B.R. 103 (Bankr. S.D.N.Y. 2006), aff'd, 371 B.R. 10 (S.D.N.Y. 2007), the court denied foreign-main recognition of a Cayman Islands proceeding because the COMI in fact lay elsewhere, but recognized the proceeding as foreign nonmain and granted significant discretionary cooperation. The case illustrates that the choice between foreign main and foreign nonmain is rarely the choice between recognition and rejection; it is the choice between mandatory and discretionary relief.

Relief on recognition

Recognition opens the door to three categories of relief:

Section 1519 - provisional relief between filing and recognition. Where urgently needed to protect the debtor's assets or the creditors' interests, the court may grant relief including a stay against execution against the debtor's assets in the United States and entrustment of administration of the debtor's U.S. assets to the foreign representative.

Section 1520 - automatic effects of recognition of a foreign main proceeding. Sections 361 and 362 of the Code (adequate protection and the automatic stay) apply with respect to the debtor and its U.S. property; Sections 363, 549, and 552 (use, sale, lease, and postpetition transactions) apply; and the foreign representative may operate the debtor's business.

Section 1521 - discretionary relief after recognition. Available regardless of whether the recognition is as foreign main or foreign nonmain, including extending the provisional Section 1519 relief, suspending the right to transfer assets, examining witnesses, entrusting administration to the foreign representative, and granting any additional relief that may be available to a U.S. trustee, except certain categories reserved by Section 1521(a)(7).

Foreign-proceeding doctrinal landmarks

In re Bear Stearns High-Grade Structured Credit Strategies (2007)

The Southern District of New York's denial of recognition to two Cayman-organized hedge funds because their COMI was not in the Cayman Islands. The case established that the Section 1516(c) presumption of COMI at the registered office is rebuttable and that the court must independently analyze where the debtor's center of main interests actually lies.

In re SPhinX, Ltd. (2006)

Decision adjacent to Bear Stearns denying foreign-main recognition on COMI grounds but granting foreign-nonmain recognition based on the existence of an establishment in the foreign jurisdiction. Demonstrated that the foreign-main / foreign-nonmain distinction is operative even where the registered-office presumption is rebutted.

In re Stanford International Bank Limited (2012)

The competing Antiguan and U.S. receiverships over the Stanford Ponzi-scheme assets produced extended litigation over recognition, COMI, and cooperation. The Fifth Circuit's decision in In re Stanford International Bank, Ltd., 681 F.3d 240 (5th Cir. 2012), upheld the bankruptcy court's denial of recognition to the Antiguan proceeding on the ground that the Antiguan liquidators had not carried their burden of establishing Antigua as the debtor's COMI under the totality of the circumstances.

In re ABC Learning Centres Ltd. (2013)

The Third Circuit's decision in In re ABC Learning Centres Ltd., 728 F.3d 301 (3d Cir. 2013), addressed the Section 1506 public-policy exception in the context of an Australian liquidation. The court held that the Australian receivership did not offend U.S. public policy notwithstanding procedural and substantive differences from Chapter 7, reinforcing the narrow construction of Section 1506.

Procedural framework

A Chapter 15 case is commenced by filing the Section 1515 petition in the United States Bankruptcy Court for the district where the debtor has its principal place of business or principal assets in the United States, or, in the absence of either, in any district. See 28 U.S.C. Section 1410. The Federal Rules of Bankruptcy Procedure govern the proceeding generally, with Rule 1007(a)(4) and Rule 2002(q) supplying particular Chapter 15 requirements.

Recognition is a gate, not a result. The Section 1517 order does not dispose of the case or distribute assets. It is the threshold determination that opens the door to either automatic relief (under Section 1520, for a foreign main proceeding) or discretionary relief (under Section 1521, for either type of recognized proceeding). Post-recognition, the foreign representative typically returns to court to seek the specific relief needed to administer the debtor's U.S. assets.

## Foreign Main vs Foreign Nonmain Proceeding - 11 USC 1502 COMI [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/chapter-15-foreign-main-nonmain/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

11 U.S.C.
Sections 1502, 1520, 1521

Foreign Main vs Foreign Nonmain Proceeding: COMI, Establishment, and the Effects of Recognition

The Section 1502(4) center of main interests, the Section 1502(2) establishment, and the divergent relief consequences under Sections 1520 (automatic) and 1521 (discretionary).

The statutory definitions

(4) "foreign main proceeding" means a foreign proceeding pending in the country where the debtor has the center of its main interests.

(5) "foreign nonmain proceeding" means a foreign proceeding, other than a foreign main proceeding, pending in a country where the debtor has an establishment.

(2) "establishment" means any place of operations where the debtor carries out a nontransitory economic activity. 11 U.S.C. Section 1502(2), (4), (5).

The classification is binary in operation but rests on two different geographical anchors. Foreign main proceedings are pending where the COMI lies. Foreign nonmain proceedings are pending where the debtor has an "establishment" - a fixed place of business with non-transient economic activity. A foreign proceeding that satisfies neither anchor does not qualify for recognition under Section 1517; the recognition is denied and the petition fails.

The COMI standard

"Center of main interests" is the cornerstone of the Model Law's structure and carries over into Chapter 15 unchanged. The term is not defined in the Code; courts have developed it through case law. Three reference points govern the analysis:

The Section 1516(c) presumption

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 1516(c), "[i]n the absence of evidence to the contrary, the debtor's registered office, or habitual residence in the case of an individual, is presumed to be the center of the debtor's main interests." The presumption is rebuttable. Where credible evidence challenges the registered office as the operational center of the business, the court must look beyond the formal seat to the operational reality.

Operational factors - the post-Bear Stearns framework

The Southern District of New York's decisions in In re Bear Stearns High-Grade Structured Credit Strategies Master Fund, Ltd., 374 B.R. 122 (Bankr. S.D.N.Y. 2007), aff'd, 389 B.R. 325 (S.D.N.Y. 2008), and In re SPhinX, Ltd., 351 B.R. 103 (Bankr. S.D.N.Y. 2006), articulated the now-standard factors:

The location of the debtor's headquarters and management

The location of those who actually manage the debtor (which may be headquarters of a parent or affiliated entity)

The location of the debtor's primary assets

The location of the majority of the debtor's creditors or the creditors most affected by the case

The jurisdiction whose law would apply to most disputes

The factors are not a checklist; they are inputs to a totality-of-the-circumstances analysis. Courts have rejected rigid formulas and instead asked, after weighing the factors, where the debtor's affairs are administered on a regular basis such that they are ascertainable by third parties (the creditor-cognizability test borrowed from the European Insolvency Regulation tradition).

Date of COMI determination

The Fifth Circuit's decision in In re Ran, 607 F.3d 1017 (5th Cir. 2010), held that COMI is determined as of the date of the Chapter 15 petition, not as of an earlier historical date - even where there is evidence that the debtor manipulated its location to manufacture COMI in a favorable forum on the eve of filing. Other circuits have engaged with the issue and have moved toward a similar view, recognizing that courts must guard against forum manipulation through evidence of long-term operational reality, but that the formal inquiry date is the petition date.

The establishment standard

"Establishment" carries a lower threshold than COMI. The Section 1502(2) definition - "any place of operations where the debtor carries out a nontransitory economic activity" - requires (a) a place of operations, (b) economic activity, and (c) some degree of permanence. The activity need not be the principal locus of the debtor's business; that is what distinguishes establishment from COMI.

A debtor may have multiple establishments, but only one COMI. A foreign proceeding may be recognized as foreign nonmain in multiple countries where the debtor has establishments, and the U.S. court will respect that classification provided the petitioner adduces evidence of operations beyond a registered office or a mailing address.

In In re Creative Finance Ltd., 543 B.R. 498 (Bankr. S.D.N.Y. 2016), the court denied recognition altogether - both as foreign main and as foreign nonmain - because the debtor's purported British Virgin Islands operations consisted of nothing more than a registered address. The case stands for the proposition that the establishment standard, while lower than COMI, still requires real activity.

Effects of foreign-main recognition - Section 1520

(a) Upon recognition of a foreign proceeding that is a foreign main proceeding - (1) sections 361 and 362 apply with respect to the debtor and the property of the debtor that is within the territorial jurisdiction of the United States; (2) sections 363, 549, and 552 apply to a transfer of an interest of the debtor in property that is within the territorial jurisdiction of the United States to the same extent that the sections would apply to property of an estate; (3) unless the court orders otherwise, the foreign representative may operate the debtor's business and may exercise the rights and powers of a trustee under and to the extent provided by sections 363 and 552; and (4) section 552 applies to property of the debtor that is within the territorial jurisdiction of the United States. 11 U.S.C. Section 1520(a).

Foreign-main recognition is the heavyweight outcome. It triggers automatic Code consequences that operate without further court action:

Section 362 automatic stay

The full automatic stay applies to the debtor and to the debtor's property in the United States. Creditor actions against the U.S. assets - foreclosure, repossession, judgment enforcement, setoff - are enjoined immediately upon entry of the recognition order. The stay carries the same enforcement weight (contempt; damages under Section 362(k)) as in a domestic case.

Section 363 transfer controls

Transfers of the debtor's U.S. property outside the ordinary course require court authorization. The Section 549 power to avoid unauthorized postpetition transfers applies. The Section 552 cutoff of after-acquired property security interests applies to the U.S. property.

Adequate protection - Section 361

Creditors with interests in the debtor's U.S. property may seek adequate protection under Section 361 in connection with relief from stay or use of cash collateral, drawing the U.S. statutory regime into the otherwise foreign-administered case.

Operating authority of the foreign representative

Unless the court orders otherwise, the foreign representative may operate the debtor's U.S. business and exercise the rights and powers of a trustee under Sections 363 and 552. The provision is permissive in court discretion but defaults to broad operational authority on recognition.

Effects of foreign-nonmain recognition - no Section 1520 automatic stay

Recognition as a foreign nonmain proceeding does not trigger the Section 1520 package. The automatic stay does not arise by operation of statute on recognition; transfer controls are not automatic; the foreign representative does not have default operating authority. All relief must be specifically requested and is granted at the court's discretion under Section 1521.

This is the doctrinal weight of the foreign-main / foreign-nonmain distinction. A debtor seeking the protection of the U.S. automatic stay and a foreign representative seeking the default authority to administer U.S. assets need foreign-main recognition. A debtor whose center of main interests is plainly elsewhere may still obtain useful relief through foreign-nonmain recognition, but the relief is discretionary, must be requested in detail, and is shaped by the court's view of what cooperation serves the case.

Section 1521 discretionary relief

Upon recognition of a foreign proceeding, whether main or nonmain, where necessary to effectuate the purpose of this chapter and to protect the assets of the debtor or the interests of the creditors, the court may, at the request of the foreign representative, grant any appropriate relief, including - (1) staying the commencement or continuation of an individual action or proceeding concerning the debtor's assets, rights, obligations or liabilities to the extent they have not been stayed under section 1520(a); (2) staying execution against the debtor's assets to the extent it has not been stayed under section 1520(a); (3) suspending the right to transfer, encumber or otherwise dispose of any assets of the debtor to the extent this right has not been suspended under section 1520(a); (4) providing for the examination of witnesses, the taking of evidence or the delivery of information concerning the debtor's assets, affairs, rights, obligations or liabilities; (5) entrusting the administration or realization of all or part of the debtor's assets within the territorial jurisdiction of the United States to the foreign representative or another person, including an examiner, authorized by the court; (6) extending relief granted under section 1519(a); and (7) granting any additional relief that may be available to a trustee, except for relief available under sections 522, 544, 545, 547, 548, 550, and 724(a). 11 U.S.C. Section 1521(a).

Section 1521 is the workhorse provision for foreign nonmain recognitions and for supplementary relief in foreign main recognitions. The categories of relief mirror many of the Section 1520 automatic effects, but require an affirmative motion, a finding that the relief is necessary to effectuate the chapter's purpose, and protection of creditor interests under Section 1522.

The Section 1521(a)(7) carve-out

The chapter-wide bar on using Chapter 15 to obtain U.S. avoidance powers is implemented in Section 1521(a)(7). A foreign representative cannot use Chapter 15 to bring preference actions under Section 547, fraudulent-transfer actions under Section 548, or other U.S. avoidance claims. To pursue U.S. avoidance powers, the foreign representative must commence a plenary case under another chapter (typically Chapter 11 or Chapter 7) in addition to or instead of the Chapter 15 ancillary case. The Section 1521(a)(7) line was a deliberate choice of the BAPCPA drafters and has been confirmed in cases like In re Condor Insurance Ltd., 601 F.3d 319 (5th Cir. 2010), which held that the foreign representative may sometimes pursue foreign-law avoidance theories without violating Section 1521(a)(7) - the bar runs to the specific U.S. provisions enumerated, not to the underlying concept of avoidance.

The Section 1522 protection-of-interests requirement

The court may grant relief under section 1519 or 1521, or may modify or terminate relief under subsection (c), only if the interests of the creditors and other interested entities, including the debtor, are sufficiently protected. 11 U.S.C. Section 1522(a).

Discretionary relief under Section 1519 (provisional) or Section 1521 (post-recognition) is conditioned on a finding that creditor interests are sufficiently protected. The provision lends the U.S. court ongoing supervisory authority over the operation of the relief and is the mechanism through which U.S. creditors who would be disadvantaged by deferring to the foreign administration may seek modification or termination of relief.

The interaction with plenary Chapter 7 or 11

A foreign representative may commence a plenary case under 11 U.S.C. Section 1511 upon recognition. Where a plenary case is commenced alongside the Chapter 15 case, the relief available expands dramatically - the full estate, the full panoply of avoidance powers, and the full U.S. distribution system come into play. The decision whether to file plenary in addition to ancillary is driven by the value of U.S.-based avoidance claims, the practicality of administering U.S. assets through a U.S. trustee, and the desire to obtain a U.S. discharge or restructuring effect not available through ancillary relief alone.

Comparative summary

Foreign main proceeding

COMI standard (Section 1502(4))

Registered-office presumption (Section 1516(c))

Automatic Section 362 stay on U.S. assets

Automatic Sections 363, 549, 552 controls

Default operating authority for foreign representative

Section 1521 additional discretionary relief still available

Foreign nonmain proceeding

Establishment standard (Section 1502(2))

No registered-office presumption

No automatic stay; stay obtainable under Section 1521(a)(1)-(2) on motion

No automatic Sections 363, 549, 552 controls

No default operating authority; entrustment obtainable under Section 1521(a)(5)

Section 1522 sufficient-protection requirement on all relief

Section 1521(a)(7) avoidance carve-out. Ancillary recognition does not unlock the U.S. avoidance powers under Sections 544, 545, 547, 548, 550, or 724(a). A foreign representative who needs preference recoveries or U.S. fraudulent-transfer remedies must consider filing a plenary case under Section 1511 in addition to the Chapter 15 case, or pursuing avoidance under the law of the foreign main proceeding to the extent the U.S. court will accommodate it under Section 1521(a)(7) as interpreted by In re Condor Insurance Ltd.

## Chapter 7 vs Chapter 13 Bankruptcy - Comparison Guide
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/chapter-7-vs-13/

Research Guide

Chapter 7 vs Chapter 13 Bankruptcy

Chapter 7 and Chapter 13 are the two most common consumer bankruptcy chapters in the United States. They differ in who can file, how long the case lasts, what assets are exposed, and what debts end up discharged. This page compares the two chapters factually - statutory basis, typical process, and aggregated outcomes from the Federal Judicial Center's Integrated Database.

Data updated 2026-04-21. See methodology & sources.

Written and maintained by Open Bankruptcy Project staff. Last updated 2026-09-18. Editorial policy.

Home/Chapter 7 vs 13

Statutory basis

Chapter 7 of the Bankruptcy Code (11 U.S.C. §§ 701–784) governs liquidation proceedings. A court-appointed trustee collects and liquidates non-exempt assets, distributes proceeds to creditors, and the debtor receives a discharge of most unsecured debts within about four to six months of filing.

Chapter 13 (11 U.S.C. §§ 1301–1330) governs adjustment of debts for a debtor with regular income. The debtor proposes a three- to five-year repayment plan, which the court confirms after a confirmation hearing. The discharge is entered after plan payments are completed.

11 U.S.C. § 109 sets chapter-specific eligibility: § 109(b) identifies who may be a debtor under Chapter 7; § 109(e) caps unsecured and secured debt for Chapter 13 eligibility (adjusted every three years under § 104).

Case-length and structure differences

Chapter 7 cases typically close in 3 to 6 months. Non-exempt property is liquidated by the trustee; the debtor's post-petition earnings are not part of the estate.

Chapter 13 cases run 36 or 60 months under a confirmed plan. Plan payments come from the debtor's post-petition disposable income, and the discharge enters only after all plan payments are made.

Chapter 13 cases can cure mortgage arrears over the plan period while the automatic stay (§ 362) prevents foreclosure. Chapter 7 generally cannot cure arrears.

Both chapters impose an automatic stay on filing (§ 362(a)), which halts most collection activity, civil litigation enforcement, and secured-creditor actions.

Discharge scope

The scope of the discharge is one of the most consequential differences between the two chapters. Chapter 13 discharges a slightly broader set of debts than Chapter 7, though the § 523(a) non-discharge list still applies in both.

§ 523(a) carve-outs from discharge (in both chapters): certain tax debts, domestic-support obligations, student loans absent an undue-hardship finding under the Brunner standard, debts arising from fraud or willful injury, and others.

The Chapter 13 "super-discharge" historically covered certain non-tax fraud-based debts. Post-BAPCPA (2005), § 1328(a) narrowed this, and the gap between Chapter 7 and Chapter 13 discharge scope is smaller than it once was.

§ 727(a) bars a Chapter 7 discharge altogether if the debtor has received a prior Chapter 7 discharge within 8 years, or a prior Chapter 13 discharge within 6 years in certain configurations.

§ 1328(f) imposes parallel timing bars on Chapter 13 discharges based on prior discharges.

Filing volume and chapter mix by district

The ratio of Chapter 7 to Chapter 13 filings varies significantly by district. Some districts have majority Chapter 13 filing volumes; others have majority Chapter 7. Local practice, economic conditions, and means-test eligibility drive most of the variance. The Open Bankruptcy Project publishes chapter-mix statistics for every US federal bankruptcy district.

See per-district chapter mix: browse the national district index to see what share of filings in each court are Chapter 7 vs Chapter 13 over the full FJC IDB history.

Case dispositions

The Federal Judicial Center's Integrated Database records a terminal disposition code for cases it has coded (code A: discharged; codes D–T: various dismissals; code K: converted to another chapter; plus miscellaneous closings). Disposition coverage in the IDB varies by cohort, because the IDB is a periodic snapshot rather than a continuous outcome tracker.

Chapter 13 cases face a higher dismissal risk than Chapter 7 because they require sustained plan performance over 3–5 years. Missed payments, changes in employment, and plan modifications can result in dismissal under § 1307. Chapter 13 cases that don't complete to discharge may be converted to Chapter 7 under § 1307(a) or dismissed.

Choosing between chapters

Chapter choice depends on a debtor's income, asset profile, types of debt, and goals (liquidation vs. reorganization). The means test (§ 707(b)) restricts Chapter 7 eligibility for debtors with above-median income. Debt caps under § 109(e) restrict Chapter 13 eligibility for debtors with very large secured or unsecured balances.

This page is empirical, not advisory. For a chapter-choice analysis in a specific matter, consult a licensed bankruptcy attorney admitted in the applicable district. The Open Bankruptcy Project's free discharge-eligibility screener checks § 1328(f) and § 727(a) timing bars against a user-supplied filing history.

Frequently asked questions
What is the main difference between Chapter 7 and Chapter 13?
Chapter 7 is a liquidation in which non-exempt assets are sold by a trustee and most unsecured debts are discharged within a few months. Chapter 13 is a reorganization under a three- to five-year repayment plan, with the discharge entered only after plan completion.
How long does a Chapter 7 case take?
A typical Chapter 7 case closes in approximately 3 to 6 months from filing, though no-asset cases often close sooner and cases with asset liquidation or disputes can take longer.
Can I file Chapter 7 if I have a prior bankruptcy discharge?
11 U.S.C. § 727(a)(8) bars a Chapter 7 discharge if the debtor received a prior Chapter 7 discharge within 8 years before the current petition. § 727(a)(9) addresses prior Chapter 13 discharges. The Open Bankruptcy Project's screener checks these timing bars against a supplied filing history.
What debts are not discharged in bankruptcy?
11 U.S.C. § 523(a) lists categories of non-dischargeable debts, including most tax debts, domestic-support obligations, student loans absent an undue-hardship finding, debts arising from fraud or willful injury, and others.
Can I keep my house in bankruptcy?
Chapter 13 plans can cure mortgage arrears and prevent foreclosure during the plan period. Chapter 7 does not provide a cure mechanism for mortgage arrears. Whether a home's equity is protected depends on the applicable state or federal exemption scheme.
Where can I find statistics on chapter mix by district?
The Open Bankruptcy Project publishes a free national district-level data index covering all 94 federal bankruptcy courts with filing volumes, chapter mix, and disposition statistics sourced from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database.
