## Claims Objection Procedure - Rule 3007 [2026] - Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/claims-objection-procedure/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Home/Claims Objection Procedure

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 3007
11 U.S.C. Section 502

Claims Objection Procedure

Rule 3007, the bases for objection (allowance, priority, classification), the evidentiary standard, and contested-matter mechanics.

The proof-of-claim foundation

A claim against a bankruptcy estate is asserted by filing a proof of claim on Official Form 410, as authorized by 11 U.S.C. Section 501 and governed by Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 3001. The proof of claim must identify the basis for the claim, the date the debt was incurred, the account number or other identifier, the amount, the security (if any), and the priority (if any). Rule 3001(c) requires that the proof of claim attach the writing on which the claim is founded, or - if the writing is unavailable - a statement explaining the circumstances. Rule 3001(c)(2) imposes additional itemization requirements for open-end and revolving consumer credit claims.

A properly filed proof of claim that satisfies the substantive and procedural requirements of Rule 3001 constitutes prima facie evidence of the validity and amount of the claim. Rule 3001(f). This presumption is the cornerstone of the burden-shifting framework that governs claims objections.

Section 502 - the allowance framework

11 U.S.C. Section 502(a) provides that a claim filed under Section 501 is deemed allowed unless a party-in-interest objects. Section 502(b) enumerates the substantive grounds on which a claim may be disallowed:

502(b)(1): The claim is unenforceable against the debtor and property of the debtor under any agreement or applicable law

502(b)(2): The claim is for unmatured interest

502(b)(3): The claim is for a tax assessed against the debtor's property to the extent it exceeds the property's value

502(b)(4): An insider or attorney claim that exceeds the reasonable value of services

502(b)(5): A claim for non-support obligation that is unmatured on the petition date

502(b)(6): A landlord's claim for damages from lease termination, capped under the formula

502(b)(7): An employee's claim for breach of an employment contract, similarly capped

502(b)(8): Claims for late-filed federal employment taxes

502(b)(9): Late-filed claims (subject to Rule 3002 deadlines)

Beyond Section 502(b), claims may also be subject to subordination under Section 510, recharacterization (e.g., treating a purported loan as an equity contribution), or partial disallowance for unreasonable charges. Section 502(d) provides for disallowance of any claim of an entity from which property is recoverable under specified avoidance provisions until the entity has paid the avoidable transfer back to the estate.

Rule 3007 - filing and serving the objection

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 3007 governs the form and service of a claim objection. The 2017 amendments to Rule 3007 substantially restructured the rule. The objection must be filed with the court and served on the claimant, the debtor, and the trustee. Service on the claimant is made at the address on the proof of claim, with required additional service on any address designated for service of process and on any attorney listed on the claim. The objection must be served at least 30 days before the hearing date (Rule 3007(a)(1)).

An objection must state the grounds for the objection with particularity. A bare denial that the claim is owed is generally insufficient; the objection should identify the specific Section 502(b) ground (or other ground), describe the factual or legal basis, and (if amount-only) state the amount the objector contends should be allowed.

Rule 3007(d) permits omnibus objections grouping multiple claims under specified circumstances: where the claims are filed by the same entity, where the same legal or factual basis applies, or for certain specified categories such as superseded claims or claims that have been satisfied. Omnibus objections are subject to strict limitations to protect individual claimants' procedural rights.

The burden-shifting framework

The interaction of Rule 3001(f) and Section 502(a) produces a settled burden-shifting framework:

The claimant files a proof of claim that satisfies Rule 3001's substantive and procedural requirements. The claim is prima facie valid.

The objecting party comes forward with evidence sufficient to rebut the prima facie validity. The evidence must be sufficient to demonstrate a true dispute - mere assertion of objection is insufficient.

If the objector rebuts the prima facie case, the burden of going forward shifts back to the claimant to prove the claim by a preponderance of the evidence.

The ultimate burden of persuasion remains with the claimant throughout.

The framework is summarized in In re Allegheny International, Inc., 954 F.2d 167 (3d Cir. 1992), and has been adopted by every circuit. A proof of claim that fails to satisfy Rule 3001's requirements - typically by failing to attach the underlying writing - does not lose the right to be allowed, but it loses the prima facie presumption; the claimant must then prove the claim from the start.

Contested-matter mechanics under Rule 9014

A claim objection is a contested matter under Rule 9014 unless it joins a request for relief listed in Rule 7001 (in which case an adversary proceeding is required). Rule 9014 incorporates many adversary-proceeding rules into contested matters by reference, including most discovery rules. The court may direct that additional adversary-proceeding rules apply.

The contested-matter procedural skeleton:

Objection filed and served (Rule 3007)

Response (typically filed before the hearing date; local rules vary)

Pre-trial discovery as permitted by Rule 9014 and the court's scheduling order

Hearing on the objection

Order allowing, disallowing, modifying, or reducing the claim

If the objection raises a complex factual dispute or seeks affirmative relief (such as a determination of the validity, priority, or extent of a lien under Rule 7001(2), or an injunction under Rule 7001(7)), the objection must be re-filed or supplemented as an adversary complaint.

Claim transfer and standing

A claim may be transferred under Rule 3001(e). The transferee files a notice of transfer with the court, which serves notice on the transferor. After the unobjected window expires, the transferee is substituted as the holder of the claim. The debtor's standing to object to a claim is well-settled in cases in which the debtor has a pecuniary interest in the allowance of the claim (e.g., a solvent estate, a Chapter 11 case in which the debtor remains in possession, or a Chapter 13 case where the plan funds claim allowances).

Common objection theories

The most frequently asserted objection theories in consumer cases include:

Insufficient documentation under Rule 3001(c)

The proof of claim lacks the writing on which the claim is based, or - in an open-end consumer credit claim - lacks the statement of account history, contract attachment, or other Rule 3001(c)(3) information. The objection rebuts the prima facie presumption and forces the claimant to come forward with documentary proof. Many objections of this type are resolved by amendment of the proof of claim.

Statute of limitations

The claim is barred under state law because the limitations period had run before the petition date. Section 502(b)(1) makes a claim disallowable to the extent it is unenforceable under applicable law, which includes time-bar defenses available to the debtor outside bankruptcy.

Improperly claimed priority

The claimant has asserted priority status under Section 507 to which it is not entitled - for example, classifying a general unsecured claim as a Section 507(a)(8) tax priority, or treating a non-domestic-support obligation as a Section 507(a)(1) priority. The objection challenges classification rather than allowance; the claim may still be allowed at general unsecured status.

Improperly claimed secured status

The claimant has asserted secured status under Section 506 to which it is not entitled - for example, claiming a lien that was never recorded, was released, or is subordinate to a senior lien that consumes the available collateral value. A motion to determine the secured status of the claim under Rule 3012 may be combined with the claim objection.

Claim previously satisfied

The claim was paid before the petition date or has been satisfied by foreclosure on the collateral or by setoff. The objection identifies the satisfaction and produces supporting evidence.

Claim allowance and Section 1325 (Chapter 13)

In Chapter 13, claim allowance is the foundation of plan distributions. A confirmed Chapter 13 plan binds creditors regardless of the amounts ultimately allowed; the plan typically estimates allowed amounts and provides for adjustment as claims are allowed or disallowed. The claim-objection process runs in parallel with plan distributions, with disbursements being held in escrow or adjusted as objections are resolved.

The proof of claim's prima facie validity is the default; the objector must come forward with rebuttal evidence. A claim objection that does not present evidence sufficient to rebut the prima facie validity is subject to denial without further proceedings. Conversely, a proof of claim that fails to comply with Rule 3001's documentation requirements loses the prima facie presumption and must be proven on the merits.

District Practice Guides

Bankruptcy Court Local Rules

The federal Bankruptcy Code and the Federal Rules of Bankruptcy Procedure apply nationwide, but every U.S. bankruptcy court also maintains a set of local rules, general orders, and standing orders that govern day-to-day practice. Local rules cover everything from chambers procedures and required form documents to motion calendars, ECF filing conventions, and judge-specific preferences.

Last modified 2026-05-22.

Home/Court Rules

About the bankruptcy court system

Bankruptcy cases are heard in the United States Bankruptcy Courts, which are units of the U.S. District Courts established under 28 U.S.C. § 151. There are 94 federal judicial districts and a corresponding bankruptcy court for each. Bankruptcy judges serve fourteen-year terms under 28 U.S.C. § 152 and may be designated to hear cases anywhere within their circuit.

Although the Bankruptcy Code and Federal Rules of Bankruptcy Procedure supply the substantive framework, each bankruptcy court issues its own local rules under Bankruptcy Rule 9029. Local rules typically cover ECF filing conventions, chambers copies, hearing calendars, mediation programs, fee application formatting, presumptive procedures for cash collateral and DIP financing, and Chapter 13 plan-form standards. Many districts also adopt judge-specific standing orders that vary within the same courthouse.

The guides below summarize the local procedural landscape for six high-volume districts. They are intended as orientation for practitioners and pro se filers unfamiliar with a district, not as substitutes for the official local rules text published on each court's own website.

District guides

Central District of California (C.D. Cal.)Five-division consumer-heavy district with extensive local form requirements and a robust mediation program.

District of Kansas (D. Kan.)Statewide single-district court with Topeka, Wichita, and Kansas City divisions and uniform Chapter 13 plan form.

Northern District of Illinois (N.D. Ill.)Chicago-based commercial-heavy district with detailed cash-collateral and complex-case procedures.

Southern District of New York (S.D.N.Y.)Manhattan-based mega-case venue with extensive complex-case orders and committee practice rules.

Southern District of Texas (S.D. Tex.)Houston-based district known for the complex-case panel and accelerated confirmation procedures.

Western District of Missouri (W.D. Mo.)Kansas City and Springfield divisions, with a model uniform Chapter 13 plan and active Subchapter V practice.

Verify before filing: Local rules change frequently. Confirm current text on each court's official website before relying on procedural details summarized in these guides.

## U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the Central District of California - Local Rules Guide 2026 | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/court-rules/cdcal-bankruptcy/

Open Bankruptcy Project

Home/Court Rules/Central District of California

U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the Central District of California - Local Rules Guide 2026

First published 2026-05-22/Last modified 2026-05-22/CC-BY-4.0

Abstract

The United States Bankruptcy Court for the Central District of California (Bankr. C.D. Cal.) is the largest bankruptcy court in the United States by case volume. The district encompasses the bulk of the Los Angeles metropolitan area and the Inland Empire. The court's local rules are codified as the Local Bankruptcy Rules for the Central District of California (LBR 1001-1 through LBR 9075-1) and are unusually detailed in their integration with mandatory court-approved form orders. This guide summarizes the local-rule features that most often diverge from federal default practice.

Court Identification and Coverage

The Central District of California comprises Los Angeles, Orange, Riverside, San Bernardino, Santa Barbara, San Luis Obispo, and Ventura counties. The bankruptcy court maintains five divisional offices:

Los Angeles Division - Edward R. Roybal Federal Building and U.S. Courthouse, 255 East Temple Street, Los Angeles, CA 90012.

Santa Ana Division - Ronald Reagan Federal Building, 411 West Fourth Street, Santa Ana, CA 92701.

San Fernando Valley Division - 21041 Burbank Boulevard, Woodland Hills, CA 91367.

Riverside Division - 3420 Twelfth Street, Riverside, CA 92501.

Northern Division - 1415 State Street, Santa Barbara, CA 93101.

Bankruptcy judges are Article I judges appointed under 28 U.S.C. § 152 to fourteen-year terms by the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit. The court's chief-judge designation and full judicial roster are published on its website.

Official court websitewww.cacb.uscourts.gov

CM/ECF electronic filingecf.cacb.uscourts.gov

Local rulesPublished on court website under "Local Bankruptcy Rules"

CircuitNinth Circuit (Bankruptcy Appellate Panel jurisdiction)

RegionU.S. Trustee Region 16

Local Rule Numbering Scheme

The court uses the standard four-digit scheme keyed to the Federal Rules of Bankruptcy Procedure, with court-approved form orders identified by an "F" prefix. Representative rules:

LBR 1002-1 - commencement of case (with mandatory case-cover sheet)

LBR 2014-1 - employment of professionals

LBR 2016-1 - compensation of professionals

LBR 2090-1 - attorneys; admission to practice

LBR 2091-1 - withdrawal of attorney

LBR 9013-1 - motions and applications

LBR 9013-3 - notice of motion - mandatory form requirement

LBR 9037-1 - redaction and restriction of public access

The district is distinctive in maintaining a comprehensive set of court-approved mandatory and optional forms (the "F" forms), many of which counsel must use in lieu of attorney-drafted versions. Most motions, notices, and proposed orders in routine matters must use the form prescribed by the court.

Attorney Admission: LBR 2090-1

LBR 2090-1 governs attorney admission to practice before the court. The rule provides:

Standing admission. An attorney admitted to practice in the United States District Court for the Central District of California is automatically admitted to practice in the bankruptcy court.

Pro hac vice admission. An attorney admitted to practice and in good standing in another United States court may apply for pro hac vice admission in a particular case under C.D. Cal. L.R. 83-2.1 (district court rule), through a sponsoring attorney of record.

The court requires each attorney appearing in a case to maintain an individual CM/ECF login. The sponsoring attorney in a pro hac vice admission remains responsible for compliance with local rules.

Motion Practice and Hearings

LBR 9013-1 prescribes the form and content of motions; LBR 9013-3 imposes a mandatory notice-of-motion form requirement. The district is unusually rigorous in enforcing form compliance: a noncompliant motion may be denied or set aside even where the substance of the relief sought is unobjectionable.

Hearings are scheduled on the assigned judge's calendar. Each judge publishes self-calendaring rules and posted hearing dates; counsel select an available date and notice the motion accordingly. Negative-notice procedures are common for routine matters. Default notice period is 21 days under FRBP 9014, modified by particular rules and judge-specific procedures.

The court was an early and aggressive adopter of remote-appearance technology. Most non-evidentiary hearings are conducted by Zoom or telephone; in-person attendance is required only when the assigned judge directs it. Evidentiary hearings and contested confirmation hearings are typically conducted in person at the appropriate divisional courthouse.

The Court-Approved Form System

The C.D. Cal. mandatory-form system is the district's most distinctive procedural feature. Court-approved forms are designated with an "F" prefix (e.g., F 9013-1.1.MOTION) and are posted on the court's website. Counsel must use:

Mandatory forms for filings where the local rules specifically require the court-approved form (e.g., motions for relief from stay, motions to extend time, certain notices).

Optional forms where the court provides a form that counsel may use but is not required to use, typically for routine matters.

The mandatory-form regime substantially reduces the variance in motion-practice content across the district. It also imposes a significant initial training cost for counsel new to practice in the district. The forms catalogue is updated periodically; counsel should download the current version from the court's website rather than reusing prior-case templates.

Withdrawal of Attorney: LBR 2091-1

LBR 2091-1 governs withdrawal of an attorney's appearance. The rule requires:

A motion served on the client and on all parties who have entered an appearance.

Compliance with the court-approved mandatory form for withdrawal notices and motions.

Court order before withdrawal becomes effective.

For artificial-entity clients (corporations, LLCs, partnerships), substitution of successor counsel before withdrawal is granted, consistent with the federal common-law rule that artificial entities cannot proceed pro se.

The rule applies to the individual attorney's appearance. A firm's employment under 11 U.S.C. § 327, where applicable, is separately governed and separately terminable by order modifying or vacating the employment order.

Fee Disclosure and Compensation

LBR 2014-1 supplements FRBP 2014 by requiring a verified statement disclosing all connections to parties in interest, the debtor, the United States Trustee, and any person employed in the office of the United States Trustee. Compensation applications under LBR 2016-1 must comply with U.S. Trustee guidelines and the court-approved mandatory form for fee applications. The court enforces fee-application formatting requirements strictly; noncompliant applications may be set aside.

FRBP 2016(b) supplemental-disclosure obligations apply with full force. The "Rights and Responsibilities" agreement is required in Chapter 13 cases between debtor and debtor's counsel, governing the scope of services and fees.

Electronic Filing (CM/ECF)

All documents must be filed electronically through CM/ECF except those specifically excluded by standing order. The court's electronic filing system is at ecf.cacb.uscourts.gov. Document size is capped at the court's published ECF limit per upload. Filings must comply with FRBP 9037 redaction requirements, supplemented by LBR 9037-1 procedures for restricted public access.

General Orders

The court maintains a catalogue of General Orders covering recurring procedural matters and case-administration issues. Active categories include:

General Orders governing electronic filing and remote-appearance procedures

General Orders implementing Chapter 13 administration and the Rights and Responsibilities agreement

General Orders adopting and updating the mandatory court-approved forms

General Orders implementing Federal Rule changes at the district level

Judge-specific procedures posted on the court's website

The complete list of General Orders and judge-specific procedures is on the court's website. Counsel should consult the current catalogue before relying on any federal default procedure.

Practical Impact for Counsel

Three features of C.D. Cal. bankruptcy practice most often surprise counsel from other districts:

Mandatory form compliance is dispositive. The court's mandatory-form regime is rigorously enforced. Substantively correct motions filed on noncompliant forms can be denied or set aside, regardless of the merits. Counsel must obtain and use the current "F" forms from the court website for every filing where a mandatory form exists.

Each judge's self-calendaring procedures vary. The court does not centrally assign hearing dates. Counsel select an available date from the assigned judge's posted calendar and notice the motion for that date. The judge-specific calendar conventions and self-calendaring rules are essential reading at the outset of any case.

Ninth Circuit Bankruptcy Appellate Panel review available. Unlike many circuits, the Ninth Circuit maintains a Bankruptcy Appellate Panel. Appeals from the C.D. Cal. bankruptcy court may be taken either to the Ninth Circuit BAP or to the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California under 28 U.S.C. § 158(c). The choice is made by election under the rules; the appellee may consent or opt out.

Official Resources

Court website: www.cacb.uscourts.gov

CM/ECF login: ecf.cacb.uscourts.gov

Local rules and court-approved forms: Posted on the court website under "Local Bankruptcy Rules" and "Forms"

U.S. Trustee Region 16: www.justice.gov/ust-regions-r16

District court: www.cacd.uscourts.gov (C.D. Cal. L.R. 83-2.1 attorney admission)

Ninth Circuit Bankruptcy Appellate Panel: www.ca9.uscourts.gov/bap/

Local rules, court-approved forms, general orders, and judge-specific procedures are updated periodically; counsel should consult the current versions on the court's website before relying on any procedural statement here.

U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the District of Kansas - Local Rules Guide 2026

First published 2026-05-22/Last modified 2026-05-22/CC-BY-4.0

Abstract

The United States Bankruptcy Court for the District of Kansas (D. Kan. Bankr.) sits as a unit of the United States District Court for the District of Kansas under 28 U.S.C. § 151. Its local bankruptcy rules are codified in a four-digit scheme keyed to the Federal Rules of Bankruptcy Procedure (D. Kan. Bankr. L.R. 1001.1 through 9037.1) and supplemented by standing orders posted on the court's website. This guide summarizes the local-rule features that most often diverge from federal default practice in the district.

Court Identification and Coverage

The District of Kansas is a single-district federal jurisdiction encompassing the entire State of Kansas (105 counties). The bankruptcy court maintains divisional offices at:

Topeka - Frank Carlson Federal Building, 444 SE Quincy, Topeka, KS 66683. Principal courthouse and clerk's office for the central and northeastern divisions.

Kansas City, Kansas - Robert J. Dole United States Courthouse, 500 State Avenue, Kansas City, KS 66101. Serves the Wyandotte and Johnson County metropolitan area.

Wichita - U.S. Courthouse, 401 N. Market Street, Wichita, KS 67202. Serves south-central Kansas.

The court is staffed by Article I bankruptcy judges appointed under 28 U.S.C. § 152 to fourteen-year terms by the United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit. The current chief-judge designation and full judicial roster are published on the court's website.

Official court websitewww.ksb.uscourts.gov

CM/ECF electronic filingecf.ksb.uscourts.gov

Local rulesPublished on the court website under "Local Rules & Standing Orders"

CircuitTenth Circuit (no Bankruptcy Appellate Panel - appeals to U.S. District Court)

RegionU.S. Trustee Region 20

Local Rule Numbering Scheme

The District of Kansas uses the four-digit scheme keyed to the Federal Rules of Bankruptcy Procedure, with a period rather than a hyphen separating the federal-rule digits from the subsection number. Representative rules:

D. Kan. Bankr. L.R. 1007.1 - schedules, statements, and lists

D. Kan. Bankr. L.R. 2014.1 - employment of professionals

D. Kan. Bankr. L.R. 2016.1 - compensation of professionals

D. Kan. Bankr. L.R. 9010.1 - representation, entry and withdrawal of appearance

D. Kan. Bankr. L.R. 9013.1 - motion practice

D. Kan. Bankr. L.R. 9037.1 - redaction and restriction of public access

A small set of legacy three-digit numbers persists for general administrative provisions. Where a federal rule has no local counterpart, the federal rule controls.

Attorney Admission and Bar Status

Practice in the D. Kan. Bankruptcy Court requires admission to the bar of the United States District Court for the District of Kansas. Admission rules are governed by D. Kan. Rule 83.5 of the district court's local rules. Standing admission is open to attorneys licensed and in good standing with the Supreme Court of Kansas, with reciprocal admission available to out-of-state attorneys subject to the conditions in Rule 83.5. Pro hac vice admission is available on motion of local counsel of record, who must remain available throughout the engagement.

Each attorney filing electronically must maintain an individual CM/ECF account. Shared logins are prohibited and may result in administrative discipline.

Motion Practice and Hearings

Local Rule 9013.1 supplements Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 9013 by requiring motions to state with particularity the grounds for the relief requested and to be accompanied by a proposed order. The District of Kansas has historically used a "Notice of Opportunity for Hearing" mechanism that combines the motion and notice into a single filing for matters that may be granted without hearing absent objection.

The standard objection period for negative-notice matters is twenty-one (21) days under FRBP 9014, with shorter periods authorized for specific categories by standing order. The court permits telephonic and video appearance for non-evidentiary hearings; contested evidentiary hearings are typically conducted in person at the appropriate divisional courthouse.

Chapter 13 cases are heard on calendar at the divisional courthouses according to a regular rotation. The court has approved a uniform Chapter 13 plan form and a uniform confirmation order form, both posted on the website. Counsel filing a non-standard plan must explain the deviation in the body of the plan or in a separate motion.

Withdrawal of Appearance: D. Kan. Bankr. L.R. 9010.1

The District of Kansas combines its representation, entry, and withdrawal provisions in a single local rule, D. Kan. Bankr. L.R. 9010.1. The withdrawal provisions impose three operative requirements that parallel the practice in most federal bankruptcy courts:

Withdrawal of a counsel of record requires leave of court, granted on motion.

The motion must be served on the client and on all parties who have entered an appearance.

Where the client is a corporation, partnership, limited liability company, or other artificial entity, the order granting withdrawal will typically be conditioned on the entry of successor counsel, because such entities cannot proceed pro se in federal court.

The successor-counsel requirement traces to the federal common-law rule that artificial entities must appear through licensed counsel. See Rowland v. California Men's Colony, 506 U.S. 194 (1993). The same successor-counsel posture applies to debtors in possession in Chapter 11 and Subchapter V cases.

Withdrawal under L.R. 9010.1 operates at the level of the individual attorney's appearance. It does not, standing alone, terminate a firm's employment as a professional person under 11 U.S.C. § 327; that authorization runs to the firm under the order of employment and is terminated only by a separate order modifying or vacating the employment order.

Employment of Professionals and Fee Disclosure

D. Kan. Bankr. L.R. 2014.1 supplements FRBP 2014 by requiring that applications to employ professional persons under 11 U.S.C. § 327 include a verified statement of all connections to parties in interest, the debtor, the United States Trustee, and any person employed in the office of the United States Trustee. Supplemental disclosures are mandatory upon any change in circumstances.

Compensation applications under L.R. 2016.1 must comply with United States Trustee guidelines and must itemize time entries with sufficient particularity to permit independent review. Fee applications in Chapter 11 and Subchapter V cases are routinely set for hearing.

Under FRBP 2016(b), debtor's counsel in any case must file a statement disclosing compensation paid or agreed to be paid in connection with the case and must file a supplemental statement within 14 days of any subsequent payment or agreement not previously disclosed. The District of Kansas enforces the supplemental-disclosure obligation strictly across all chapters.

Electronic Filing (CM/ECF)

All documents must be filed electronically through CM/ECF except documents specifically excluded by standing order (sealed documents, oversized exhibits, and certain pro se filings). The court's electronic filing system is at ecf.ksb.uscourts.gov. Document size is capped at the court's published ECF limit per upload. Filings must comply with FRBP 9037 redaction requirements; the court will restrict public access to filings that contain unredacted personal identifiers pending remediation.

Standing Orders and General Orders

The District of Kansas Bankruptcy Court maintains a catalogue of standing and general orders covering recurring procedural questions. Active categories include:

Standing orders adopting the uniform Chapter 13 plan form and uniform confirmation order

Standing orders governing telephonic and video appearance procedures

Standing orders authorizing negative-notice treatment for specified motion categories

Standing orders implementing fee-disclosure procedures and U.S. Trustee compensation guidelines

General orders implementing changes to the Bankruptcy Code and Federal Rules at the district level

The complete list and full text of currently effective standing orders is on the court's website. Counsel should review the current catalogue before relying on any default federal procedure, because a standing order may have altered the default.

Practical Impact for Counsel

Three features of District of Kansas bankruptcy practice most often surprise counsel from other districts:

Withdrawal requires leave of court and successor counsel for entities. The L.R. 9010.1 framework requires court order on noticed motion; in cases involving corporate, LLC, or partnership debtors, successor counsel must be in place before withdrawal will be granted. The corporate pro se bar is rigorously applied, and an entity debtor left without counsel can face conversion or dismissal.

Section 327 employment is firm-level, distinct from individual appearance. An employment order entered under 11 U.S.C. § 327 names a firm. Departure of the lead individual attorney from the firm does not terminate the firm's authorization to render compensable services to the estate. Conversely, an individual attorney whose appearance is on the docket but whose firm has not been employed under § 327 is not authorized to bill the estate.

No Tenth Circuit Bankruptcy Appellate Panel. Unlike the Eighth, Ninth, and First Circuits, the Tenth Circuit does not maintain a bankruptcy appellate panel. Bankruptcy appeals are taken to the United States District Court for the District of Kansas under 28 U.S.C. § 158(a), with further review available in the Tenth Circuit Court of Appeals.

Official Resources

Court website: www.ksb.uscourts.gov

CM/ECF login: ecf.ksb.uscourts.gov

Local rules (PDF): Posted on the court website under "Local Rules & Standing Orders"

U.S. Trustee Region 20: www.justice.gov/ust-regions-r20

District court: www.ksd.uscourts.gov (D. Kan. Rule 83.5 attorney admission)

Tenth Circuit Court of Appeals: www.ca10.uscourts.gov

This page provides general information about the local procedures of the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the District of Kansas as of the last-modified date. It is not legal advice. Local rules and standing orders are updated periodically; counsel should consult the current versions on the court's website before relying on any procedural statement here.

U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the Northern District of Illinois - Local Rules Guide 2026

First published 2026-05-22/Last modified 2026-05-22/CC-BY-4.0

Abstract

The United States Bankruptcy Court for the Northern District of Illinois (Bankr. N.D. Ill.) sits as a unit of the United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois under 28 U.S.C. § 151. The court is among the largest-volume bankruptcy filing venues in the United States. Its local rules are codified as the Local Bankruptcy Rules for the Northern District of Illinois (L.R. 1001-1 through 9075-1) and are supplemented by an extensive collection of standing orders and judge-specific procedures. This guide summarizes the local-rule features that most often diverge from federal default practice in the district.

Court Identification and Coverage

The Northern District of Illinois comprises 18 counties in the northern third of Illinois, including the Chicago metropolitan area. The bankruptcy court maintains divisional offices at:

Chicago (Eastern Division) - Everett McKinley Dirksen United States Courthouse, 219 South Dearborn Street, Chicago, IL 60604. Principal courthouse and clerk's office for the bulk of the district's bankruptcy filings.

Rockford (Western Division) - Stanley J. Roszkowski United States Courthouse, 327 South Church Street, Rockford, IL 61101. Serves the western counties of the district.

Bankruptcy judges are Article I judges appointed under 28 U.S.C. § 152 to fourteen-year terms by the United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit. The court's chief-judge designation and full judicial roster are published on the court's website.

Official court websitewww.ilnb.uscourts.gov

CM/ECF electronic filingecf.ilnb.uscourts.gov

Local rulesPublished on the court website under "Procedures > Local Rules"

CircuitSeventh Circuit (no Bankruptcy Appellate Panel - appeals to U.S. District Court)

RegionU.S. Trustee Region 11

Local Rule Numbering Scheme

The court uses the standard four-digit scheme keyed to the Federal Rules of Bankruptcy Procedure:

L.R. 1007-1 - schedules, statements, and lists

L.R. 2014-1 - employment of professionals

L.R. 2016-1 - compensation of professionals

L.R. 2091-1 - withdrawal of appearance

L.R. 3015-1 - Chapter 13 plans

L.R. 9013-1 - motion practice generally

L.R. 9037-1 - redaction and restriction of public access

Attorney Admission

Practice before the Bankr. N.D. Ill. requires admission to the bar of the United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois (general bar) or trial bar admission for certain proceedings. The district court's general bar admission rules are at N.D. Ill. L.R. 83.10 and following. The bankruptcy court accepts as standing admission an attorney's good-standing admission to the general bar of the district court. Pro hac vice admission is available on motion of local counsel of record, who remains responsible for compliance with local rules throughout the engagement.

Each attorney filing electronically must obtain an individual CM/ECF login from the clerk's office. Shared logins are prohibited.

Motion Practice and Hearings

L.R. 9013-1 prescribes the form and notice requirements for motions, including the standard notice and hearing procedures used across the district. Most motions are noticed for hearing on the assigned judge's calendar with a notice period derived from FRBP 2002 and any judge-specific procedure. Routine matters such as motions for relief from stay, motions to extend the deadline for objections to discharge, and unopposed extensions of bar dates are commonly resolved on negative notice.

Each judge of the Bankr. N.D. Ill. publishes chambers procedures setting out the judge's preferences for proposed orders, hearing setup, and emergency motion practice. The judge-specific procedures are posted on the court's website and frequently update; counsel should review them at the outset of each new case.

Hearings may be held in person, by telephone, or by video, depending on the assigned judge and the nature of the matter. Evidentiary hearings and contested confirmation hearings are typically conducted in person at the appropriate divisional courthouse.

Withdrawal of Appearance: L.R. 2091-1

L.R. 2091-1 governs withdrawal of an attorney's appearance. The rule requires:

A motion served on the client and on all parties who have entered an appearance in the case.

Court approval before the withdrawal becomes effective.

In cases where the client is a corporation, LLC, partnership, or other artificial entity, substitution of successor counsel before withdrawal is granted, consistent with the federal common-law rule that artificial entities cannot proceed pro se.

The rule applies to the individual attorney's appearance. A firm's employment under 11 U.S.C. § 327, where applicable, is governed by the order of employment and is separately terminable.

Employment of Professionals and Fee Disclosure

L.R. 2014-1 supplements FRBP 2014 by requiring a verified statement disclosing all connections to parties in interest, the debtor, the United States Trustee, and any person employed in the office of the United States Trustee. The court enforces strictly the supplemental-disclosure obligation when circumstances change.

Compensation applications under L.R. 2016-1 must comply with the U.S. Trustee's compensation guidelines and itemize time entries with sufficient particularity to permit independent review. The court routinely sets fee applications for hearing in Chapter 11 and Subchapter V cases regardless of whether objections have been filed.

FRBP 2016(b) requires debtor's counsel to file a statement disclosing compensation paid or agreed to be paid in connection with the case and to file a supplemental statement within 14 days of any subsequent payment or agreement not previously disclosed. The district enforces the supplemental-disclosure obligation strictly across all chapters.

Chapter 13 Practice: L.R. 3015-1 and the Model Plan

The Bankr. N.D. Ill. handles one of the largest Chapter 13 dockets in the country. L.R. 3015-1 governs Chapter 13 plan practice and is supplemented by the court's model Chapter 13 plan form, which counsel filing in the district are expected to use absent good cause. Specific Chapter 13 trustees serve the Eastern and Western Divisions, and each trustee's office maintains its own administrative procedures consistent with the local rules.

The model plan format simplifies confirmation of routine plans by standardizing the placement of plan-specific elections, treatment of secured claims, and treatment of priority claims. Deviation from the model plan must be flagged in the body of the plan and explained on the record.

Electronic Filing (CM/ECF)

All documents must be filed electronically through CM/ECF except those specifically excluded by standing order or judge-specific procedure. The court's CM/ECF system is at ecf.ilnb.uscourts.gov. Document size is capped at the court's published ECF limit per upload. Filings must comply with FRBP 9037 redaction requirements; L.R. 9037-1 supplements with district-specific procedures for restricting public access and sealing.

Standing Orders and General Orders

The court maintains an extensive collection of standing and administrative orders. Active categories include:

Administrative Orders governing electronic filing and CM/ECF use

Standing orders implementing the Chapter 13 model plan and confirmation procedures

Standing orders addressing case-management procedures during exigent circumstances

Standing orders implementing Federal Rule changes at the district level

Judge-specific procedures published on the court's website that supplement generic local-rule procedures

The complete list of standing and administrative orders is posted on the court's website. Counsel should consult the current catalogue before relying on any federal default procedure.

Practical Impact for Counsel

Three features of N.D. Ill. bankruptcy practice most often surprise counsel from other districts:

Judge-specific procedures vary substantially. Each judge publishes chambers procedures with material differences in motion practice, proposed-order format, and emergency-motion handling. Counsel should treat the judge's published procedures as binding alongside the local rules.

The Chapter 13 model plan is the default expectation. Counsel filing in the Eastern Division should anticipate using the model plan form unless there is a documented reason to deviate. The Chapter 13 trustees enforce the model-plan expectation through their confirmation review process.

Two-division court with shared CM/ECF. The Chicago and Rockford divisions operate on a unified CM/ECF system but with different judge assignments and somewhat different scheduling practices. Counsel should confirm the assigned judge's division-specific schedule when planning hearings.

CM/ECF login: ecf.ilnb.uscourts.gov

Local rules (PDF): Posted on the court website under "Procedures > Local Rules"

U.S. Trustee Region 11: www.justice.gov/ust-regions-r11

District court: www.ilnd.uscourts.gov (N.D. Ill. L.R. 83.10 attorney admission)

Seventh Circuit Court of Appeals: www.ca7.uscourts.gov

U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the Southern District of New York - Local Rules Guide 2026

First published 2026-05-22/Last modified 2026-05-22/CC-BY-4.0

Abstract

The United States Bankruptcy Court for the Southern District of New York (Bankr. S.D.N.Y.) is one of the busiest and most procedurally sophisticated bankruptcy courts in the United States, with a long-standing concentration of large Chapter 11 reorganizations and cross-border insolvency proceedings under Chapter 15. The court's local rules are codified as the Local Bankruptcy Rules for the Southern District of New York (S.D.N.Y. L.B.R. 1001-1 through 9077-1) and are supplemented by an extensive body of general orders and judge-specific case management procedures. This guide summarizes the local-rule features that most often diverge from federal default practice.

Court Identification and Coverage

The Southern District of New York comprises the New York counties of New York (Manhattan), Bronx, Westchester, Rockland, Putnam, Orange, Dutchess, and Sullivan. The bankruptcy court maintains divisional offices at:

Manhattan - Alexander Hamilton U.S. Custom House, One Bowling Green, New York, NY 10004. Principal courthouse and the venue for most large Chapter 11 filings.

White Plains - 300 Quarropas Street, White Plains, NY 10601. Serves Westchester and the lower Hudson Valley.

Poughkeepsie - 355 Main Street, Poughkeepsie, NY 12601. Serves the mid-Hudson Valley.

The court is staffed by Article I bankruptcy judges appointed under 28 U.S.C. § 152 by the United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit. The chief-judge designation and complete judicial roster are published on the court's website.

Official court websitewww.nysb.uscourts.gov

CM/ECF electronic filingecf.nysb.uscourts.gov

Local rulesPosted on court website under "Court Information > Local Rules"

CircuitSecond Circuit (no Bankruptcy Appellate Panel - appeals to U.S. District Court for S.D.N.Y.)

RegionU.S. Trustee Region 2

Local Rule Numbering Scheme

The court uses the standard four-digit scheme keyed to the Federal Rules of Bankruptcy Procedure:

L.B.R. 1007-2 - affidavit pursuant to local rule (the "First Day" affidavit standard in Chapter 11)

L.B.R. 2014-1 - employment of professionals

L.B.R. 2016-1 - compensation of professional persons

L.B.R. 2016-2 - U.S. Trustee guidelines and fee committee procedures (in larger cases)

L.B.R. 2090-1 - attorneys; admission to practice

L.B.R. 9013-1 - motions, applications, objections, responses

L.B.R. 9037-1 - redaction and restriction of public access

Attorney Admission: L.B.R. 2090-1

Local Bankruptcy Rule 2090-1 governs attorney admission to practice before the court. The rule provides two categories of admission:

Standing admission. An attorney admitted to practice in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York is automatically admitted to practice in the bankruptcy court.

Pro hac vice admission. An attorney admitted to practice and in good standing in another United States court (district court, court of appeals, or state court of last resort) may be admitted to practice in a particular case on motion filed by an attorney of record under L.B.R. 9077-1.

The court requires that each attorney appearing in a case maintain an individual CM/ECF login. Pro hac vice admission requires the sponsoring attorney to remain available for service and responsible for compliance with local rules.

Motion Practice and Hearings

L.B.R. 9013-1 prescribes the form and content of motions and objections, including:

Required components: notice of motion, motion or application, supporting affidavit or declaration, memorandum of law (in any motion involving disputed questions of law), and a proposed order.

A standard notice period of 14 days for hearings on motions (subject to particular rule modifications and to FRBP 2002 notice requirements).

Specific requirements for "First Day" pleadings in Chapter 11, including the L.B.R. 1007-2 affidavit by an officer of the debtor.

Judge-specific chambers procedures published on the court's website that supplement (and in some respects override) generic motion-practice procedures.

Hearings in large Chapter 11 cases are typically scheduled as omnibus hearing dates set by the court in the initial case management order. Routine matters proceed on negative notice when properly noticed under FRBP 2002 and the applicable judge's procedures. Telephonic and video appearance is available for non-evidentiary hearings.

Complex Chapter 11 Procedures

The Bankr. S.D.N.Y. has developed extensive procedures for "complex" or "mega" Chapter 11 cases that are routinely incorporated through initial case-management and procedural orders. Common features include:

Omnibus hearing dates fixed in advance for the duration of the case.

Approval of streamlined notice and service procedures, often through a court-approved claims and noticing agent.

"First Day" relief packages addressing cash management, employee compensation, taxes, utilities, and critical vendor payments.

Fee committees or fee examiners appointed under standing or case-specific orders to review professional compensation applications in cases over a designated threshold.

Case-specific protective orders governing discovery and confidential information.

These procedures are not codified as local rules but are routinely entered through orders that have over time hardened into a recognized "S.D.N.Y. complex case protocol." Counsel should review the assigned judge's chambers procedures and recent large-case orders to understand the protocol's current contours.

Fee Disclosure and Compensation Procedures

L.B.R. 2016-1 supplements FRBP 2016 by prescribing the form and content of compensation applications. Applications must comply with the U.S. Trustee's compensation guidelines and, in large cases, with the local "Fee Committee Order" if one has been entered. The S.D.N.Y. court is one of the leading users of fee examiners and fee committees, and counsel filing in a complex case should anticipate independent review of monthly and interim compensation requests.

FRBP 2016(b) supplemental-disclosure obligations apply with full force; the court enforces strictly the obligation to disclose any change in compensation arrangements within 14 days of the change.

Electronic Filing (CM/ECF)

All documents must be filed electronically through CM/ECF except those specifically excluded by general order or judge-specific procedure. The court's electronic filing system is at ecf.nysb.uscourts.gov. Document size is capped at the court's published ECF limit per upload; oversized exhibits must be filed in compliant segments. Filings must comply with FRBP 9037 redaction requirements, and L.B.R. 9037-1 supplements the federal rule with district-specific procedures for sealing and restricting public access.

General Orders

The court maintains an extensive catalogue of General Orders ranging from M-100-series administrative orders to more recent M-500-series substantive orders. Notable categories include:

General Orders governing electronic filing requirements and CM/ECF user obligations

General Orders implementing fee guidelines and fee-committee procedures

General Orders on Chapter 13 administration and uniform plan provisions

General Orders implementing Federal Rule changes at the district level

Case-management procedures adopted as default approaches in complex cases

The complete catalogue is posted on the court's website. Counsel should consult the current catalogue and the assigned judge's chambers procedures before relying on any federal default procedure.

Practical Impact for Counsel

Three features of S.D.N.Y. practice most often surprise counsel from other districts:

The L.B.R. 1007-2 affidavit is mandatory in Chapter 11. Every Chapter 11 case filed in the district requires an affidavit by a debtor representative on the first day setting forth the structure of the debtor's businesses, the circumstances leading to the filing, and the relief sought on a first-day basis. The affidavit's content and structure are prescribed in detail by L.B.R. 1007-2.

Judge-specific chambers procedures matter as much as the local rules. Each judge of the S.D.N.Y. publishes chambers procedures that supplement (and sometimes modify) generic local-rule procedures, including specific requirements for proposed orders, hearing requests, and motion-practice format. Counsel should review the assigned judge's procedures at the outset of any case.

Fee committees and fee examiners are common in large cases. Unlike many districts where U.S. Trustee review is the principal compensation check, S.D.N.Y. large cases routinely include an independent fee committee or fee examiner empowered to review and negotiate fee applications. Counsel should plan for the additional review layer and the associated time and cost.

Official Resources

Court website: www.nysb.uscourts.gov

CM/ECF login: ecf.nysb.uscourts.gov

Local rules (PDF): Posted on the court website under "Court Information > Local Rules"

U.S. Trustee Region 2: www.justice.gov/ust-regions-r2

District court: www.nysd.uscourts.gov (attorney admission)

Second Circuit Court of Appeals: www.ca2.uscourts.gov

U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the Southern District of Texas - Local Rules Guide 2026

First published 2026-05-22/Last modified 2026-05-22/CC-BY-4.0

Abstract

The United States Bankruptcy Court for the Southern District of Texas (Bankr. S.D. Tex.) became one of the leading venues for large Chapter 11 cases in the United States over the past decade. The court's Complex Chapter 11 Procedures and the Houston Division's specialized complex-case panel attract energy, healthcare, and retail debtors from across the country. The local rules are codified as the Bankruptcy Local Rules for the Southern District of Texas (BLR 1001-1 through BLR 9077-1) and are supplemented by General Orders and the published Complex Chapter 11 Procedures. This guide summarizes the local-rule features that most often diverge from federal default practice.

Court Identification and Coverage

The Southern District of Texas comprises 43 counties in southeast Texas, including the Houston, Galveston, Brownsville, Corpus Christi, McAllen, and Laredo metropolitan areas. The bankruptcy court maintains divisional offices at:

Houston Division - 515 Rusk Avenue, Houston, TX 77002. Principal courthouse and venue for the bulk of the district's complex Chapter 11 filings.

Corpus Christi Division - 1133 N. Shoreline Boulevard, Corpus Christi, TX 78401.

Brownsville Division - 600 East Harrison Street, Brownsville, TX 78520.

McAllen Division - 1701 W. Business Highway 83, McAllen, TX 78501.

Galveston Division - 601 Rosenberg Street, Galveston, TX 77550.

Laredo Division - 1300 Victoria Street, Laredo, TX 78040.

Bankruptcy judges are Article I judges appointed under 28 U.S.C. § 152 to fourteen-year terms by the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit. The court's chief-judge designation and judicial roster are published on its website.

Official court websitewww.txs.uscourts.gov/bankruptcy

CM/ECF electronic filingecf.txsb.uscourts.gov

Local rulesPublished on court website under "Bankruptcy Local Rules"

CircuitFifth Circuit (no Bankruptcy Appellate Panel - appeals to U.S. District Court)

RegionU.S. Trustee Region 7

Local Rule Numbering Scheme

The court uses the four-digit scheme keyed to the Federal Rules of Bankruptcy Procedure, designated "BLR":

BLR 1007-1 - schedules, statements, and lists

BLR 2014-1 - employment of professionals

BLR 2016-1 - compensation of professionals

BLR 2090-1 - attorneys; admission to practice

BLR 2091-1 - withdrawal of appearance

BLR 9013-1 - motion practice

BLR 9037-1 - redaction and restriction of public access

The court's Complex Chapter 11 Procedures are not codified as numbered local rules but operate as a standing operating framework adopted in case-management orders issued at the outset of qualifying cases.

Attorney Admission: BLR 2090-1

BLR 2090-1 governs attorney admission to practice. The rule provides:

Standing admission. An attorney admitted to practice in the United States District Court for the Southern District of Texas is automatically admitted to practice in the bankruptcy court.

Pro hac vice admission. An attorney admitted to practice and in good standing in another United States court may apply for pro hac vice admission in a particular case through a sponsoring local counsel of record, under the district court's pro hac vice rules.

Each attorney must maintain an individual CM/ECF login. Sponsoring local counsel in a pro hac vice admission remains responsible for compliance with local rules throughout the engagement.

Motion Practice and Hearings

BLR 9013-1 prescribes the form and content of motions. Motions must state with particularity the grounds for relief, attach a proposed order, and be set for hearing on the assigned judge's calendar with notice consistent with FRBP 2002. Many routine matters proceed on negative notice when properly noticed; the court's procedural orders identify specific motion categories eligible for negative-notice treatment.

The Houston Division is unusually flexible with hearing scheduling, particularly in complex Chapter 11 cases, where omnibus hearing dates are typically set in advance and "first day" relief is heard on an expedited basis. Telephonic and video appearance is available for non-evidentiary hearings; contested evidentiary hearings and confirmation hearings are typically in person.

Complex Chapter 11 Procedures

The Bankr. S.D. Tex. is one of the leading venues in the country for large Chapter 11 cases. The court's published Procedures for Complex Chapter 11 Cases (the "Complex Case Procedures") govern qualifying cases. A case qualifies as "complex" if it meets the criteria set forth in the Complex Case Procedures (typically, debt above a threshold, public securities, or other indicia of complexity). On qualification:

The case is assigned to a judge from the court's designated complex-case panel.

An initial case-management order is entered incorporating omnibus hearing dates, streamlined notice procedures, and modified motion-practice requirements.

The case typically uses an approved claims and noticing agent.

"First day" relief - cash management, employee compensation, taxes, utilities, critical vendors - is heard on an expedited basis.

Fee committees or fee examiners may be appointed for independent compensation review.

The Houston Division panel of judges experienced in complex Chapter 11 reorganizations has been a principal draw for large filings. The Complex Case Procedures are posted on the court's website and are periodically updated.

Withdrawal of Appearance: BLR 2091-1

BLR 2091-1 governs withdrawal of an attorney's appearance. The rule requires:

A motion served on the client and on all parties who have entered an appearance.

Court order before the withdrawal becomes effective.

In cases where the client is an artificial entity (corporation, LLC, partnership), substitution of successor counsel before withdrawal is granted, consistent with the federal common-law rule that artificial entities cannot proceed pro se.

The rule applies to the individual attorney's appearance. A firm's employment under 11 U.S.C. § 327, where applicable, is separately governed by the order of employment and is separately terminable by order modifying or vacating the employment order.

Fee Disclosure and Compensation

BLR 2014-1 supplements FRBP 2014 by requiring a verified statement disclosing all connections to parties in interest, the debtor, the United States Trustee, and any person employed in the office of the United States Trustee. The court applies the disclosure obligation strictly and expects supplemental disclosures upon any change.

Compensation applications under BLR 2016-1 must comply with the U.S. Trustee's compensation guidelines and itemize time entries with sufficient particularity to permit independent review. In complex Chapter 11 cases, compensation procedures often include a fee committee or fee examiner under the initial case-management order. The court enforces the U.S. Trustee's billing guidelines and any case-specific compensation procedures alike.

FRBP 2016(b) supplemental-disclosure obligations apply with full force across all chapters; the court enforces strictly the obligation to disclose any subsequent compensation arrangement within 14 days.

Electronic Filing (CM/ECF)

All documents must be filed electronically through CM/ECF except those specifically excluded by general order. The court's electronic filing system is at ecf.txsb.uscourts.gov. Document size is capped at the court's published ECF limit per upload. Filings must comply with FRBP 9037 redaction requirements; BLR 9037-1 supplements with district-specific procedures for restricting public access and sealing.

General Orders

The court maintains a catalogue of General Orders addressing recurring procedural matters and case-administration issues. Active categories include:

General Orders adopting and updating the Complex Chapter 11 Procedures

General Orders governing electronic filing and CM/ECF use

General Orders implementing Chapter 13 administration

General Orders implementing Federal Rule changes at the district level

Judge-specific case-management orders that serve as the operative framework in complex cases

The complete catalogue is on the court's website. Counsel should consult both the current General Orders and the assigned judge's recent case-management orders before relying on any federal default procedure.

Practical Impact for Counsel

Three features of S.D. Tex. bankruptcy practice most often surprise counsel from other districts:

The Complex Case Procedures dominate large-case practice. The published procedures, supplemented by initial case-management orders, materially modify routine motion-practice requirements, notice periods, and hearing-calendar mechanics in qualifying cases. Counsel filing in a complex case should treat the Complex Case Procedures as the operative procedural framework alongside the BLRs.

Houston Division concentration of complex-case judges. The court's complex-case panel sits primarily in Houston. Counsel filing complex cases in other divisions should anticipate the possibility of transfer or coordinated case management with the Houston complex-case judges.

Fifth Circuit has no Bankruptcy Appellate Panel. Bankruptcy appeals are taken to the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Texas under 28 U.S.C. § 158(a), with further review available in the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals. There is no BAP option.

Official Resources

Court website: www.txs.uscourts.gov/bankruptcy

CM/ECF login: ecf.txsb.uscourts.gov

Local rules and Complex Case Procedures: Posted on the court website

U.S. Trustee Region 7: www.justice.gov/ust-regions-r7

District court: www.txs.uscourts.gov (attorney admission)

Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals: www.ca5.uscourts.gov

U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the Western District of Missouri - Local Rules Guide 2026

First published 2026-05-22/Last modified 2026-05-22/CC-BY-4.0

Abstract

The United States Bankruptcy Court for the Western District of Missouri (W.D. Mo. Bankr.) sits as a unit of the United States District Court for the Western District of Missouri under 28 U.S.C. § 151. Its local rules are codified in a four-digit numbering scheme derived from the Federal Rules of Bankruptcy Procedure (LBR 1001-1 through LBR 9037-1) and supplemented by a body of standing orders and general orders. This guide summarizes the rules that most often diverge from federal default practice for attorneys appearing in the district.

Court Identification and Coverage

The Western District of Missouri encompasses 66 counties spanning roughly the western half of the State of Missouri, including the Kansas City metropolitan area, Springfield, St. Joseph, Joplin, and Jefferson City. The bankruptcy court maintains divisional offices in:

Kansas City (Western Division) - 400 East 9th Street, Kansas City, MO 64106. Principal courthouse and clerk's office.

Springfield (Southern Division) - 222 North John Q. Hammons Parkway, Springfield, MO 65806.

St. Joseph (St. Joseph Division) - hearings held periodically at the federal courthouse in St. Joseph.

Jefferson City (Central Division) - hearings held periodically at the federal courthouse in Jefferson City.

The court is staffed by Article I bankruptcy judges appointed under 28 U.S.C. § 152 to fourteen-year terms by the United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit. The official roster of sitting judges and current chief-judge designation is published on the court's website.

Official court websitewww.mow.uscourts.gov/bankruptcy

CM/ECF electronic filingecf.mowb.uscourts.gov

Local rules (consolidated)Published on the court website under "Rules & Procedures"

CircuitEighth Circuit (Bankruptcy Appellate Panel jurisdiction)

RegionU.S. Trustee Region 13

Local Rule Numbering Scheme

The court adopts the four-digit numbering scheme recommended by the Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts. The first four digits track the relevant Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure; the suffix denotes the local subsection. For example:

LBR 1007-1 - lists, schedules, statements and other documents (tracks FRBP 1007)

LBR 2016-1 - debtor's attorney's fee agreement in Chapter 7 cases (tracks FRBP 2016)

LBR 2016-3 - fee agreements in Chapter 11 and 12 cases; applications for compensation in general (tracks FRBP 2016)

LBR 2019-1 - attorneys: withdrawal and substitution (formerly LBR 2091-1; renumbered in the Local Rules adopted January 5, 2026)

LBR 3007-1 - objections to claims (tracks FRBP 3007)

LBR 9013-1 - motion practice (tracks FRBP 9013)

Where a federal rule has no local counterpart, the federal rule governs without supplementation. Local rules supplement but cannot override the Federal Rules of Bankruptcy Procedure or the Bankruptcy Code.

Attorney Admission and Bar Status

Practice before the W.D. Mo. Bankruptcy Court requires admission to the bar of the United States District Court for the Western District of Missouri. The district's general bar admission rules are found at W.D. Mo. L.R. 83.5. Standing admission is open to attorneys licensed and in good standing with the Supreme Court of Missouri (or any other state bar, subject to reciprocal practice rules). Out-of-district attorneys may seek pro hac vice admission on motion of a local counsel of record, who remains responsible for compliance with local rules throughout the engagement.

The bankruptcy court does not maintain a separate bankruptcy-specific bar; admission to the district court bar carries with it the right to appear in bankruptcy proceedings. Each attorney filing electronically must obtain an individual CM/ECF login from the clerk's office; shared logins are prohibited.

Motion Practice and Hearings

Most contested motions in the district are heard on the chambers calendar of the assigned bankruptcy judge. Local Rule 9013-1 requires that motions state with particularity the grounds for the relief requested, attach a proposed order, and be accompanied by a notice of opportunity to object where the relief is of a kind that may be granted without hearing absent objection. The court's standard notice period for negative-notice motions is twenty-one (21) days, consistent with FRBP 9013 and 9014.

The court has issued standing orders authorizing routine matters - most cash collateral stipulations, agreed extensions of bar dates, and certain claim-objection categories - to be heard on negative notice. Counsel should consult the court's posted procedural orders for the current list of matters that may proceed on negative notice in a given case type.

Telephonic and video appearances are available for most non-evidentiary hearings under the court's continuing standing orders adopted during the public-health emergency and retained as ordinary practice. Evidentiary hearings and contested confirmation hearings are typically conducted in person at the courthouse, subject to the assigned judge's preferences.

Withdrawal and Substitution: LBR 2019-1 (formerly 2091-1)

The local rule on attorney withdrawal is among the district's most consequential for ongoing case staffing. In the Local Rules adopted January 5, 2026, the court renumbered the withdrawal rule from LBR 2091-1 to LBR 2019-1 (Attorneys – Withdrawal and Substitution); citations to 2091-1 in filings predating that adoption refer to the same rule. The operative subsection, W.D. Mo. Bankr. L.R. 2019-1(A), provides:

An attorney of record may withdraw only by Court permission, by an order entered after service of notice of withdrawal on the client, other counsel of record, the trustee, if any, and the United States Trustee. An order will not be entered until new counsel enters an appearance, except for good cause.

Three operative features control. First, withdrawal is by Court permission, not unilateral notice. Second, notice of withdrawal must be served on the client, other counsel of record, the trustee (if any), and the United States Trustee. Third, the order will not be entered until successor counsel appears, except on a showing of good cause — a condition that carries particular weight where the client cannot proceed pro se (corporate, LLC, partnership debtors and similar artificial entities). Rule 2019-1(B) separately permits substitution by notice where new counsel is employed in the same law firm as the attorney of record.

This rule operates at the level of the individual attorney's appearance. Where a law firm represents the debtor under an employment order entered pursuant to 11 U.S.C. § 327, the firm's authorization to render compensable services to the estate is separately governed by the § 327 order and is not terminated by an individual attorney's withdrawal of appearance.

Employment of Professionals and Fee Disclosure

The Local Rules adopted January 5, 2026 contain no local counterpart to Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 2014; applications to employ professional persons under 11 U.S.C. § 327 are governed by the federal rule directly, which requires a verified statement disclosing all connections with the debtor, creditors, any other party in interest, their respective attorneys and accountants, the United States Trustee, and any person employed in the office of the United States Trustee. Supplemental disclosure practice follows the federal rule and case law.

Fee agreements and compensation are addressed by chapter-specific local rules: LBR 2016-1 (debtor's attorney's fee agreements in Chapter 7 cases), LBR 2016-2 (debtor's attorney's fee agreements and allowance of compensation in Chapter 13 cases), and LBR 2016-3 (fee agreements in Chapter 11 and Chapter 12 cases, and applications for compensation in general). Counsel should consult the rule matching the case chapter rather than assuming a single district-wide compensation rule.

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 2016(b) requires debtor's counsel in any case to file a statement disclosing compensation paid or agreed to be paid by or on behalf of the debtor for services rendered in contemplation of or in connection with the case, and to file a supplemental statement within 14 days of any payment or agreement not previously disclosed. The W.D. Mo. court enforces the supplemental-disclosure obligation strictly.

Electronic Filing (CM/ECF)

All documents must be filed electronically through the court's CM/ECF system except for documents specifically excluded by standing order (typically: documents under seal, paper exhibits exceeding ECF size limits, and pro se filings by debtors without electronic-filing privileges). The court's CM/ECF system is accessible at ecf.mowb.uscourts.gov.

Document size is capped at the court's posted ECF limit per upload. Large exhibits must be split into compliant segments and filed as separate docket entries. Filings must comply with Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 9037 redaction requirements; the court will, on motion or sua sponte, restrict access to filings containing unredacted personal identifiers pending remediation.

Standing Orders and General Orders

The court issues standing orders to address recurring procedural matters and general orders for case-administration purposes that apply across all cases in the district. Categories of standing orders presently in force include:

Standing orders authorizing negative-notice procedures for specified categories of motions

Standing orders governing telephonic and video appearance procedures

Standing orders addressing the form and content of confirmation orders in Chapter 13 cases

Standing orders adopting form documents (chapter 13 plan, model orders) for use across the district

General orders implementing changes to the Bankruptcy Code or Federal Rules at the district level

The complete list of standing orders is maintained on the court's website. Counsel should consult the current list before deviating from any default federal procedure, because a standing order may have modified the default in ways that affect notice periods, form requirements, or hearing-calendar placement.

Practical Impact for Counsel

Three features of W.D. Mo. practice most often surprise attorneys whose primary experience is in other districts:

Withdrawal cannot be unilateral. The LBR 2019-1 (formerly 2091-1) requirement that withdrawal be by court order after notice to the client, other counsel of record, the trustee, and the United States Trustee, with successor counsel required except for good cause, is stricter than the practice in some districts that permit substitution of counsel by stipulation. Counsel intending to terminate a representation should plan for the motion-and-order timeline and identify successor counsel early.

Section 327 employment is firm-level. An employment order entered under 11 U.S.C. § 327 runs to the firm named in the application, not to any individual attorney within the firm. Departure of the originally-named lead attorney does not, without more, terminate the firm's authority to render compensable services. This is a feature of federal bankruptcy law rather than W.D. Mo. local rule, but the district enforces the distinction consistently.

Negative-notice scope is broader than default federal practice. The court's standing orders authorize negative-notice treatment for a broader range of motions than counsel may expect. The 21-day default notice period under FRBP 9014 applies where no shorter or longer period is fixed by standing order; counsel should verify the applicable notice period from the current standing-order list rather than assuming the federal default.

Official Resources

Court website: www.mow.uscourts.gov/bankruptcy

CM/ECF login: ecf.mowb.uscourts.gov

Local rules (PDF, consolidated): Posted on the court website under "Rules & Procedures"

U.S. Trustee Region 13: www.justice.gov/ust-regions-r13

Eighth Circuit Bankruptcy Appellate Panel: www.ca8.uscourts.gov/bankruptcy-appellate-panel

District court: www.mow.uscourts.gov (W.D. Mo. L.R. 83.5 attorney admission)
