## Cramdown Mechanics Under Section 1129(b) - Chapter 11 [2026] - Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/cramdown-mechanics/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Home/Cramdown Mechanics

11 U.S.C. Section 1129(b)
Chapter 11
Cramdown

Cramdown Mechanics Under Section 1129(b)

The fair-and-equitable test for secured, unsecured, and equity classes; the absolute priority rule; the three sub-paths of Section 1129(b)(2)(A) for secured cramdown; and the new-value corollary after LaSalle.

What cramdown does

Cramdown is the mechanism by which a Chapter 11 plan can be confirmed over the dissent of one or more classes of creditors or interest holders. Without cramdown, Section 1129(a)(8) would require every impaired class to accept the plan; in practice no large case could be confirmed because at least one impaired class almost always dissents. 11 U.S.C. Section 1129(b) permits confirmation despite dissent if two conditions are met: at least one impaired class has accepted the plan (the impaired-accepting-class requirement, sometimes called the "consenting class" requirement, derived from Section 1129(a)(10)), and the plan is "fair and equitable" and "does not discriminate unfairly" with respect to each dissenting impaired class.

The phrase "fair and equitable" is a term of art with class-specific content. Section 1129(b)(2) supplies a non-exhaustive definition for three categories - secured claims, unsecured claims, and interests - and the case law has refined what each category requires.

The unfair-discrimination prong

The "does not discriminate unfairly" prong of Section 1129(b)(1) is distinct from "fair and equitable" but is often discussed alongside it. The prong compares treatment among classes of similar priority. A plan that pays one class of unsecured creditors 80 cents on the dollar while paying another class of equal-priority unsecured creditors 5 cents on the dollar must justify the disparity by reference to a legitimate basis - typically a difference in the legal nature of the claims (for example, a tort claim versus a trade claim) or a contribution the favored class is making to the reorganization.

Courts use various tests to evaluate unfair discrimination. Some apply a four-factor inquiry asking whether there is a reasonable basis for the discrimination, whether the debtor cannot confirm without it, whether the discrimination is proposed in good faith, and whether the degree of discrimination is proportional. Others apply a rebuttable presumption against discrimination where the disparity in treatment exceeds defined thresholds. The doctrine is unsettled and litigated heavily in cases involving separately classified trade claims, indemnity claims, and similarly situated bondholder pools.

Fair and equitable - secured classes: the three sub-paths

Section 1129(b)(2)(A) prescribes three sub-paths by which a plan can be fair and equitable with respect to a dissenting secured class. The drafter must pick one; the sub-paths are not freely interchangeable. The Supreme Court confirmed in RadLAX Gateway Hotel, LLC v. Amalgamated Bank, 566 U.S. 639 (2012), that the specific governs the general - a plan involving a sale of collateral must use the sale-specific sub-path and cannot relabel the transaction to escape its requirements.

Sub-path (i): retention of lien plus deferred cash payments

The class retains its lien on the collateral, and each holder receives deferred cash payments totaling at least the allowed amount of the secured claim with a present value, as of the effective date of the plan, equal to at least the value of the collateral. The present-value requirement is the cramdown-interest-rate problem analyzed in Till v. SCS Credit Corp., 541 U.S. 465 (2004), where a plurality of the Supreme Court endorsed a "formula" approach starting from the prime rate and adjusting upward for the risk of nonpayment. The Court's footnote 14 reserved the question whether an "efficient market" rate should govern in Chapter 11 - a reservation that has divided the circuits in the years since.

If the secured class has elected under Section 1111(b)(2), sub-path (i) is modified: the aggregate face amount of the payments must equal the entire allowed claim, while the present value need only equal the collateral value. The election thus adds a face-amount floor on top of the present-value floor.

Sub-path (ii): sale free and clear with credit-bid right

The collateral is sold free and clear of the lien under Section 363(k), with the secured creditor's right to credit-bid preserved, and the lien attaches to the proceeds. The credit-bid right - the right to bid the face amount of the secured claim rather than cash - is the secured creditor's structural protection against undervaluation by the auction process. The creditor whose collateral is being auctioned can always outbid an undervalued cash bid by bidding the full allowed claim amount, taking the collateral itself if no third party will pay fair value.

The credit-bid right may be capped "for cause" under Section 363(k), but the cause must be substantial. Lower-court rulings have capped credit bids where the secured creditor's lien is subject to a bona fide dispute, where the credit bid would chill the auction in ways that would impair recovery, or where the creditor has engaged in inequitable conduct. Routine cramdown sales preserve the credit bid at face value.

Sub-path (iii): indubitable equivalent

The class receives the "indubitable equivalent" of its secured claim. This is the catch-all path, drawn from Judge Learned Hand's 1935 opinion in In re Murel Holding Corp., 75 F.2d 941 (2d Cir. 1935). The indubitable-equivalent standard requires that the substitute consideration both compensate the creditor for the present value of its claim and assure the creditor of the safety of its principal. The doctrine is analyzed in depth in the indubitable-equivalent deep dive. After RadLAX, sub-path (iii) cannot be used as a workaround to strip the credit-bid right that sub-path (ii) provides; sales of collateral must go through sub-path (ii).

Fair and equitable - unsecured classes: the absolute priority rule

Section 1129(b)(2)(B) defines fair and equitable for a dissenting class of unsecured claims. The class must either receive property of a value, as of the effective date, equal to the allowed amount of its claims, or - if it receives less - no junior class may receive or retain any property "on account of" its junior claim or interest. This second branch is the absolute priority rule.

The absolute priority rule embeds the bankruptcy ordering of claims into plan confirmation. Equity holders cannot retain their shares if the unsecured class is being paid less than in full and dissents. The rule was a fixture of equity-receivership practice long before the 1978 Bankruptcy Code, traceable through Northern Pacific Railway Co. v. Boyd, 228 U.S. 482 (1913), and carried forward into Chapter X of the 1898 Act and then into Chapter 11.

The new-value corollary

The new-value corollary is the most contested doctrine in modern cramdown law. The corollary holds that equity holders who contribute new value - cash or property - to a reorganization may retain their interests over a dissenting unsecured class, on the theory that their retention is "on account of" the new contribution rather than "on account of" their pre-petition ownership.

The Supreme Court declined to decide whether the new-value corollary survived the 1978 Code in Norwest Bank Worthington v. Ahlers, 485 U.S. 197 (1988). It returned to the doctrine in Bank of America Nat'l Trust & Sav. Ass'n v. 203 N. LaSalle St. P'ship, 526 U.S. 434 (1999), and held that an exclusive new-value plan - one in which the debtor-equity holders proposed to retain their interests in exchange for a new contribution without exposing the opportunity to competing bids - violated the absolute priority rule. The Court emphasized that retaining equity through an uncompeted-for option constituted retention "on account of" the prior interest because the option itself had value that the equity holders received only because of their ownership position.

After LaSalle, a new-value plan must either expose the equity opportunity to the market through a competing-bid mechanism (such as a Section 363 auction) or allow other interested parties to propose a competing plan during the period the debtor proposes new-value retention. The Court did not formally adopt the new-value corollary; it left open the possibility that a properly market-tested new-value contribution might satisfy the absolute priority rule. Lower courts have generally accepted that a market-tested new-value plan can confirm, though the doctrine remains formally unresolved at the Supreme Court level.

Fair and equitable - equity classes

Section 1129(b)(2)(C) defines fair and equitable for a dissenting class of interests. The class must either receive property equal to the greatest of the allowed amount of any fixed liquidation preference, any fixed redemption price, or the value of the interest - or no class junior may receive or retain anything on account of its interest. The provision matters most in cases with preferred-stock classes or multi-tier equity capital structures, where the priorities among equity tranches mirror the priorities among debt tranches.

In single-tier-equity cases (the typical small-business Chapter 11), Section 1129(b)(2)(C) collapses into the practical question whether the equity class receives anything. If the equity class receives nothing and is therefore deemed to reject under Section 1126(g), the plan need not provide for its retention at all and the absolute priority rule is satisfied vacuously.

The impaired-accepting-class requirement

Section 1129(a)(10) requires that, if any class of claims is impaired under the plan, at least one impaired class of claims (other than insiders) must accept the plan. The requirement is jurisdictional in the sense that a plan without an accepting impaired class cannot be confirmed even if every other element of Section 1129 is satisfied.

The requirement constrains class-designation gerrymandering. A debtor cannot create an artificial impaired class - for example, by impairing a single trade claim by a token amount - solely to manufacture an accepting class. Courts evaluating manufactured-acceptance challenges look to whether the impairment is "real" and whether the classification serves legitimate plan purposes, with significant variance among the circuits. The Eighth Circuit's analysis in In re Windsor on the River Associates, 7 F.3d 127 (8th Cir. 1993), held that artificial impairment violates the good-faith requirement of Section 1129(a)(3). Other circuits have read the impaired-accepting-class requirement narrowly, accepting any real impairment as sufficient.

The valuation problem at the heart of cramdown

Every cramdown sub-path turns on a valuation question. Secured-class cramdown under sub-path (i) requires valuing the collateral to set the present-value floor. Unsecured-class cramdown under the absolute priority rule requires valuing the reorganized enterprise to determine whether the unsecured class is in fact being paid less than in full. The indubitable-equivalent sub-path requires valuing whatever substitute consideration is being offered.

Valuation in Chapter 11 is litigated through dueling expert reports, with debtors typically pressing low collateral values and high enterprise values (to satisfy unsecured creditors with smaller stakes while limiting secured cramdown payments) and creditors pressing the opposite. Courts apply weighted-average-cost-of-capital and discounted-cash-flow methodologies for going concerns, comparable-sales and capitalization-rate analyses for real estate, and orderly-liquidation-value or replacement-cost analyses for equipment. The valuation date is generally the effective date of the plan, which adds a forecasting dimension to disputes confirmed shortly before plan effectiveness.

Sequencing under Section 1129(b). Cramdown is conditional, not automatic. The plan proponent must first satisfy every requirement of Section 1129(a) except (a)(8) (universal class acceptance). The proponent must then prove (1) at least one impaired class accepted, (2) the plan does not discriminate unfairly against dissenting classes, and (3) the plan is fair and equitable as to each dissenting class under the class-specific tests of Section 1129(b)(2). Failure on any element defeats confirmation; the debtor's remedy is amendment and re-solicitation or dismissal.

Practice Area Primers

Cross-Discipline Interaction Primers

Bankruptcy is a federal forum that intersects with nearly every other area of substantive law. A bankruptcy filing can reshape a divorce-court support order, change the treatment of a wage-and-hour claim, alter the rights of an indenture trustee, suspend tax-collection enforcement, and bring trust assets into the property-of-the-estate analysis. These primers map the most common interaction points.

Last modified 2026-05-22.

Home/Cross-Discipline

Why cross-discipline interactions matter

A bankruptcy petition does not merely consolidate financial claims. It triggers an automatic stay under 11 U.S.C. § 362, creates a bankruptcy estate under § 541, and overrides much of the procedural posture established in other forums. Practitioners who work in adjacent disciplines often encounter bankruptcy as an interruption to their primary matter without understanding how the Bankruptcy Code reorders priority, claim treatment, and enforcement.

The primers below are written for non-bankruptcy practitioners and informed pro se litigants. Each surveys the principal Code sections, exclusions, exceptions, and procedural touchpoints where the bankruptcy system collides with another body of law. None substitutes for case-specific advice from counsel admitted in the relevant district.

Practice-area primers

Bankruptcy and EmploymentTreatment of wage claims, WARN Act liability, employee benefit plans, executory employment contracts, and section 503(b) priority for post-petition wages.

Bankruptcy and Family LawDomestic-support obligations under sections 101(14A) and 523(a)(5), property settlements under section 523(a)(15), and stay exceptions for family-court proceedings.

Bankruptcy and SecuritiesSEC standing, section 1145 exemption from registration, indenture trustee claims, securities litigation stay practice, and subordination under section 510(b).

Bankruptcy and TaxPriority of tax claims under section 507(a)(8), dischargeability under section 523(a)(1), automatic-stay carve-outs for tax assessment, and section 505 determination procedure.

Bankruptcy and Trust LawSpendthrift trust treatment under section 541(c)(2), self-settled trust attacks, beneficial-interest valuation, and trustee duties when a beneficiary files.

For practitioners outside bankruptcy: The Bankruptcy Code reorders most priority and enforcement positions established in other forums. Reading the relevant primer before responding to a notice of bankruptcy filing usually prevents the most common procedural errors.

Bankruptcy and Employment — Interaction Primer 2026

First published 2026-05-22/Version 0.1.0/CC-BY-4.0/status: draft

Abstract

Bankruptcy law sits at the boundary of employment law in three principal registers. First, the filing of a petition halts wage garnishments and other collection activity directed at the debtor's earnings under the automatic stay of 11 U.S.C. § 362(a)(2). Second, the treatment of post-petition earnings differs sharply between Chapter 7 (where they are excluded from the estate) and Chapter 13 (where they are property of the estate). Third, employer-sponsored retirement assets receive substantial protection: ERISA-qualified pension benefits are excluded from the estate under § 541(c)(2) as construed in Patterson v. Shumate, 504 U.S. 753 (1992), while non-ERISA individual retirement accounts and Roth IRAs are exempt under § 522(d)(12) and § 522(n), subject to a statutory cap.

This primer summarizes the principal interaction points between the Bankruptcy Code, the Employee Retirement Income Security Act, the Internal Revenue Code's retirement-account provisions, and federal and state wage-protection law.

Wage Garnishment and the Automatic Stay

Section 362(a)(2) prohibits "the enforcement, against the debtor or against property of the estate, of a judgment obtained before the commencement of the case under this title." Wage-garnishment writs are post-judgment enforcement mechanisms, and they fall squarely within the prohibition. Section 362(a)(6) independently bars "any act to collect, assess, or recover a claim against the debtor that arose before the commencement of the case." A garnishment-in-progress must terminate upon notice of the petition; the employer must cease withholding under the garnishment writ, and any funds withheld but not yet remitted should be returned to the debtor or otherwise dealt with as the bankruptcy court directs.

Garnishments for domestic support obligations are an exception. Section 362(b)(2)(C) permits "the withholding of income that is property of the estate or property of the debtor for payment of a domestic support obligation under a judicial or administrative order or a statute." Child-support and alimony withholdings continue uninterrupted.

An employer's failure to halt a non-exempt garnishment after notice of the petition can expose the employer to liability for violation of the stay under § 362(k), which authorizes "actual damages, including costs and attorneys' fees, and, in appropriate circumstances, punitive damages" for willful stay violations. The case-law has developed a practical-knowledge standard: notice received by the payroll department or by an officer authorized to act on garnishment matters is generally sufficient.

Post-Petition Earnings: Chapter 7 vs. Chapter 13

The treatment of post-petition earnings is one of the sharpest doctrinal divides in consumer bankruptcy.

Chapter 7

Section 541(a)(6) excludes from property of the estate "earnings from services performed by an individual debtor after the commencement of the case." The exclusion is foundational to the fresh-start policy of Chapter 7: the debtor's post-petition labor income belongs to the debtor and is not available to creditors. The Chapter 7 trustee's reach is limited to property that existed as of the petition date (including pre-petition accrued wages not yet paid) and to certain proceeds and after-acquired property captured by other § 541 subsections.

Chapter 13

Section 1306(a)(2) sweeps in "earnings from services performed by the debtor after the commencement of the case but before the case is closed, dismissed, or converted to a case under chapter 7." Chapter 13 thus extends the estate to include three to five years of post-petition wages, which are used to fund the plan payments to creditors. The interaction with § 541(a)(6) is governed by § 1306, which expressly supersedes the Chapter 7 exclusion for the duration of the Chapter 13 case.

The Supreme Court addressed the disposition of post-petition earnings upon conversion of a Chapter 13 case to Chapter 7 in Harris v. Viegelahn, 575 U.S. 510 (2015), holding that undistributed Chapter 13 plan payments revert to the debtor on conversion. Funds in the hands of the Chapter 13 trustee at the moment of conversion are not transferred to the Chapter 7 estate; they are returned to the debtor for the debtor's use.

Severance and Bonus Payments

The line between excluded post-petition earnings and included pre-petition property can be subtle. Severance pay attributable to pre-petition employment is generally property of the estate even if paid after filing; severance attributable to post-petition continuation of employment is not. Performance bonuses that are earned through a mix of pre- and post-petition services typically require pro-ration. The standard inquiry is into the consideration that gave rise to the payment, not into the date of the check.

ERISA-Qualified Retirement Plans and Patterson v. Shumate

Section 541(c)(2) of the Bankruptcy Code provides that "a restriction on the transfer of a beneficial interest of the debtor in a trust that is enforceable under applicable nonbankruptcy law is enforceable in a case under this title." The Supreme Court in Patterson v. Shumate, 504 U.S. 753 (1992), unanimously held that the anti-alienation provision of the Employee Retirement Income Security Act, codified at 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(1) and 26 U.S.C. § 401(a)(13), constitutes "applicable nonbankruptcy law" within the meaning of § 541(c)(2).

The practical result is that the debtor's beneficial interest in an ERISA-qualified pension plan, 401(k) plan, profit-sharing plan, or defined-benefit plan is excluded from the estate altogether. It does not enter the estate, and the trustee has no claim on it. The exclusion is not subject to a dollar cap. A debtor with a multi-million-dollar 401(k) balance keeps the entire account through Chapter 7, provided the plan is ERISA-qualified and the anti-alienation provision is enforceable.

The qualification matters. Plans that fail ERISA's qualification requirements — for example, top-hat plans for executives, certain church plans that have opted out, certain governmental plans — do not enjoy the § 541(c)(2) shelter. They may nonetheless be exempt under § 522(d)(12) or under analogous state-law exemptions, but they enter the estate first and must be claimed as exempt to be retained.

Non-ERISA IRAs and the Section 522(n) Cap

Individual retirement accounts under IRC §§ 408 and 408A (traditional IRAs and Roth IRAs) are not ERISA-qualified. They are not excluded from the estate under § 541(c)(2). Instead, they are exempt under § 522(d)(12), subject to the dollar cap in § 522(n).

Section 522(n) was added by BAPCPA in 2005 and caps the exemption of "amounts attributable to individual retirement accounts described in section 408 or 408A of the Internal Revenue Code" at a statutory amount that adjusts triennially under § 104. The cap does not apply to rollovers from ERISA-qualified plans into IRAs; those rolled-over amounts remain fully exempt. The cap also does not apply to SEP-IRAs and SIMPLE IRAs to the extent they constitute employer-sponsored plans subject to ERISA-like treatment.

The interplay creates a planning consideration. A debtor contemplating bankruptcy who has accumulated IRA assets approaching the cap should consider whether to consolidate ERISA-rollover IRAs separately from contributory IRAs, since the rollover portion retains its fully-exempt character. Documentation of rollover origin matters for the post-petition exemption defense.

The Supreme Court addressed a separate IRA-related question in Clark v. Rameker, 573 U.S. 122 (2014), holding that inherited IRAs are not "retirement funds" within the meaning of the § 522(d)(12) exemption. An IRA inherited from a non-spouse decedent is not a retirement vehicle for the inheritor; it is a transferred asset subject to mandatory distribution rules under IRC § 401(a)(9). The inherited IRA enters the estate and is not exempt under federal law.

Wage Priority Under Section 507(a)(4)

When the debtor is an employer rather than an employee, employment-law considerations enter the bankruptcy estate from the other side. Section 507(a)(4) confers fourth-priority status on unsecured claims for "wages, salaries, or commissions, including vacation, severance, and sick leave pay" earned by an individual within 180 days before the petition or before cessation of the debtor's business, whichever is earlier, subject to a statutory cap per individual employee that adjusts under § 104.

Section 507(a)(5) confers fifth-priority status on unsecured contributions to employee benefit plans arising from services rendered within the same 180-day window, again subject to a statutory cap.

In Chapter 11, the WARN Act (29 U.S.C. §§ 2101–2109) interacts with priority treatment. WARN claims for the 60-day notice period typically receive priority treatment for the post-petition portion (as administrative expense) and fourth-priority treatment for the pre-petition portion that falls within the § 507(a)(4) window. The case-law has split on the precise characterization, particularly for closures effected immediately upon filing.

First-Day Wage Orders in Chapter 11

In Chapter 11 cases of operating businesses, a typical first-day motion is a "wage motion" requesting authority to pay pre-petition wages, salaries, commissions, and benefits to employees in the ordinary course. The motion is supported by the "necessity of payment" doctrine and by the § 507(a)(4) priority status of the underlying claims. Courts routinely grant the motion to preserve workforce stability and to comply with state wage-payment laws that may impose personal liability on corporate officers for non-payment of accrued wages.

The order typically caps the amount payable per employee at the § 507(a)(4) priority cap, on the rationale that any amount above the cap is a general unsecured claim and should await the plan process. Some districts have local guidelines or standing orders that prescribe the form of relief.

## Bankruptcy and Family Law - Interaction Primer 2026 - Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/cross-discipline/bankruptcy-and-family-law/

Open Bankruptcy Project

HomeAboutResearchMethodologyCitationsPressContact

Home/Cross-Discipline/Bankruptcy and Family Law

Bankruptcy and Family Law — Interaction Primer 2026

First published 2026-05-22/Version 0.1.0/CC-BY-4.0/status: draft

Abstract

Family law obligations occupy a privileged position in bankruptcy. Domestic support obligations — alimony, maintenance, and child support — are first-priority unsecured claims under 11 U.S.C. § 507(a)(1) and are never dischargeable under any chapter. Non-support divorce-decree obligations (typically property settlements and hold-harmless agreements) are non-dischargeable in Chapter 7 and Chapter 11 cases of individual debtors under § 523(a)(15), though historically dischargeable in Chapter 13. The automatic stay yields to specified family proceedings under § 362(b)(2). State equitable-distribution rights interact with the bankruptcy estate in subtle and consequential ways.

This primer summarizes the principal interaction points between the Bankruptcy Code and state family law. It is general information and does not constitute legal advice in any jurisdiction.

The Domestic Support Obligation

The 2005 BAPCPA amendments introduced the unified concept of the "domestic support obligation" (DSO) and gave it elevated status throughout the Code. Section 101(14A) defines a DSO as a debt that (i) is owed to or recoverable by a spouse, former spouse, child of the debtor, that child's parent, legal guardian, or responsible relative, or a governmental unit; (ii) is "in the nature of alimony, maintenance, or support" without regard to whether the underlying instrument labels it as such; (iii) is established by a separation agreement, divorce decree, property settlement, court order, or determination of a governmental unit; and (iv) has not been assigned to a non-governmental entity (except for collection purposes).

The "in the nature of" language is operative. The bankruptcy court is not bound by the label affixed by the state divorce court; it conducts a federal-law inquiry into the actual function of the obligation. Standard factors examined by the courts include the language of the decree, the parties' relative financial positions at the time of the decree, whether the obligation terminates on death or remarriage, whether it varies with the recipient's needs, and whether it provides for present support or for a long-term division of marital property.

Non-Dischargeability of DSO Under Section 523(a)(5)

Section 523(a)(5) excepts from discharge any debt "for a domestic support obligation." The exception applies in every chapter and is one of the few exceptions that applies without an adversary proceeding: a DSO survives discharge automatically, and the creditor need not file a § 523 complaint to preserve the claim. Sections 727(b), 1141(d)(2), 1192(2), 1228(a)(2), and 1328(a)(2) each cross-reference § 523(a)(5) and confirm the across-the-board treatment.

The non-dischargeability of DSO is doctrinally tied to public policy: support obligations exist to protect dependents whose welfare cannot be left to the vagaries of bankruptcy distribution. The Supreme Court's pre-Code decision in Wetmore v. Markoe, 196 U.S. 68 (1904), held that alimony obligations were not provable debts under the prior bankruptcy statute precisely because they served a continuing protective function. The principle persists, recodified.

Priority of DSO Claims Under Section 507(a)(1)

Section 507(a)(1) confers first-priority status on allowed unsecured DSO claims, ahead of administrative expenses. Subsection (a)(1)(A) treats claims owed directly to a spouse, former spouse, or child as first priority; subsection (a)(1)(B) treats claims that have been assigned to a governmental unit or that are owed directly to a governmental unit as a closely-following first-priority sub-class, but still ahead of administrative expenses.

The practical consequence in a Chapter 7 case is that DSO arrears are paid first from any liquidation proceeds available for unsecured creditors. In Chapter 11 and Chapter 13, full payment of priority DSO claims through the plan is required as a precondition to confirmation under §§ 1129(a)(9)(B), 1322(a)(2), and 1322(a)(4) (special treatment for assigned support claims).

Section 1325(a)(8) further requires, as a precondition to Chapter 13 plan confirmation, that the debtor be current on post-petition DSO obligations that became due after filing. Section 1328(a) conditions Chapter 13 discharge on certification by the debtor that all DSO obligations — both pre-petition arrears handled through the plan and post-petition payments — have been paid.

Section 523(a)(15) and Non-Support Divorce-Decree Obligations

Not every obligation arising from a divorce is a DSO. Property-equalization payments, debt-allocation provisions, hold-harmless agreements, and attorney's-fee awards that are not "in the nature of" support fall outside § 523(a)(5). Before 2005, such non-support obligations were dischargeable in Chapter 7 unless the creditor brought a § 523(a)(15) action and proved one of two statutory factors (inability to pay or balance-of-equities).

BAPCPA simplified the framework. Section 523(a)(15) now excepts from discharge any debt "to a spouse, former spouse, or child of the debtor and not of the kind described in paragraph (5) that is incurred by the debtor in the course of a divorce or separation or in connection with a separation agreement, divorce decree or other order of a court of record, or a determination made in accordance with State or territorial law by a governmental unit." The pre-BAPCPA defenses are gone in Chapter 7 and Chapter 11 cases.

Section 523(a)(15) is not cross-referenced in § 1328(a)(2). The omission means that § 523(a)(15) obligations remain dischargeable in a Chapter 13 case that proceeds to full-payment discharge under § 1328(a). Chapter 13 thus retains its historical role as a relief mechanism for debtors burdened by non-support divorce-decree obligations, although DSO arrears remain non-dischargeable in Chapter 13 under § 523(a)(5).

The distinction between § 523(a)(5) and § 523(a)(15) accordingly remains consequential in Chapter 13 even after BAPCPA. The same factual inquiry into the function of the obligation determines the outcome.

The Automatic Stay and Family Court Proceedings

Section 362(a) imposes the automatic stay on most actions to collect pre-petition claims against the debtor. Section 362(b)(2) carves out specific family-court activities. As amended by BAPCPA, the stay does not bar:

The commencement or continuation of a civil action or proceeding "for the establishment of paternity" (§ 362(b)(2)(A)(i));

The establishment or modification of an order for domestic support obligations (§ 362(b)(2)(A)(ii));

Proceedings concerning child custody or visitation (§ 362(b)(2)(A)(iii));

Proceedings for the dissolution of a marriage, except to the extent that the proceeding seeks to determine the division of property that is property of the estate (§ 362(b)(2)(A)(iv));

Proceedings regarding domestic violence (§ 362(b)(2)(A)(v));

The collection of a DSO from property that is not property of the estate (§ 362(b)(2)(B));

The withholding of income that is property of the estate or of the debtor for payment of a DSO (§ 362(b)(2)(C)); and

The reporting of overdue support to a credit reporting agency (§ 362(b)(2)(E)).

The carve-outs reflect a policy judgment that ongoing family-law functions should not be disrupted by the debtor's bankruptcy. The principal stay-protected zone within a pending dissolution proceeding is the division of estate property: the family court may issue the divorce decree and may resolve custody and support, but it may not finally partition assets that, as of the petition date, are property of the bankruptcy estate.

Equitable Distribution and the Bankruptcy Estate

In a marital-property regime — whether common-law equitable distribution or community property — the non-debtor spouse holds some form of pre-existing interest in marital assets at the moment of the petition. The exact nature of that interest is a question of state law, and its bankruptcy treatment depends on whether it rises to the level of a "legal or equitable interest" recognizable under § 541(a)(1) or whether it is merely an inchoate claim that ripens only on the entry of a divorce decree.

In community-property jurisdictions, § 541(a)(2) brings into the estate all interests of the debtor and the debtor's spouse in community property that is (a) under the sole, equal, or joint management and control of the debtor, or (b) liable for an allowable claim against the debtor. The non-debtor spouse's community interest is thus drawn into the federal proceeding.

In equitable-distribution jurisdictions, the analysis turns on whether state law treats the non-debtor spouse's pre-decree interest as a present property right or as a contingent right that crystallizes only with the decree. The circuits have divided on the question, with most decisions favoring estate inclusion where state law confers a present marital-property interest.

The timing interplay matters. If the dissolution decree is entered pre-petition, the property division is generally a fait accompli, subject to attack under § 547 (preference) or § 548 (fraudulent transfer) only in narrow circumstances. If the petition precedes the decree, the bankruptcy court generally controls disposition of estate property, and the family court must proceed within the boundaries that § 362(b)(2)(A)(iv) draws.

Exemptions and the Non-Debtor Spouse

Several federal exemption provisions under § 522(d) and many state exemption schemes contain doubling provisions or joint-filing enhancements that allow married debtors filing jointly under § 302 to claim larger exemptions than either spouse could claim individually. The homestead exemption is the most frequently doubled item, and it is governed by § 522(d)(1) under federal exemptions or by the state-law analog under § 522(b)(3) where the state has opted out of the federal scheme.

Joint filing under § 302 is permitted only for spouses; it creates a single jointly-administered estate and does not require consolidation, though courts may order consolidation in appropriate cases. A jointly-filed petition triggers an automatic stay applicable to both spouses and to property in which either holds an interest.

## Bankruptcy and Securities - Interaction Primer 2026 - Open Bankruptcy Project

Bankruptcy and Securities — Interaction Primer 2026

First published 2026-05-22/Version 0.1.0/CC-BY-4.0/status: draft

Abstract

The intersection of bankruptcy law and federal securities law is dominated by a handful of recurring questions. When a Chapter 11 plan distributes new securities of the reorganized debtor to claim and interest holders, 11 U.S.C. § 1145 supplies a federal registration exemption that displaces the Securities Act of 1933 registration requirement and preempts most state blue sky registration. The Securities and Exchange Commission has statutory standing to appear and be heard in Chapter 11 cases under § 1109(a). Securities-fraud claims against the debtor are non-dischargeable for individual debtors under § 523(a)(19), added by Sarbanes-Oxley. Registered investment companies and stockbrokers are barred from filing Chapter 11 and instead receive specialized liquidation regimes under Subchapter III and the Securities Investor Protection Act.

This primer summarizes those interactions. It is general information and does not constitute legal advice.

The Section 1145 Plan-Securities Exemption

Section 1145(a)(1) of the Bankruptcy Code provides that the registration requirements of Section 5 of the Securities Act of 1933 do not apply to "the offer or sale under a plan of a security of the debtor, of an affiliate participating in a joint plan with the debtor, or of a successor to the debtor under the plan" if the offer or sale is "in exchange for a claim against, an interest in, or a claim for an administrative expense in the case concerning, the debtor or such affiliate" or is principally in such exchange and partly for cash or property.

The exemption is automatic and self-executing. No application to the Securities and Exchange Commission, no filing of a Form S-1 or other registration statement, and no quiet period are required. The reorganization court's confirmation order is treated as the functional equivalent of registration for securities-law purposes. Section 1145(a)(2) extends the exemption to subsequent transfers by entities other than "underwriters" as defined in § 1145(b).

The underwriter definition in § 1145(b) is narrower than the Securities Act definition. It encompasses (i) those who purchase claims against the debtor or interests with a view to distribution, (ii) those who offer to sell securities offered under the plan for holders, (iii) those who offer to buy securities offered under the plan from holders if the offer to buy is with a view to distribution, and (iv) issuers and any "person directly or indirectly controlling or controlled by, or under direct or indirect common control with," the issuer. Resales by non-underwriters are exempt from registration under § 1145(a)(2); resales by § 1145(b) underwriters are not, and instead require registration or compliance with another exemption (most commonly Rule 144).

Limits of the Exemption

The § 1145 exemption is limited in three principal respects. First, it covers only securities of the debtor, an affiliate participating in a joint plan, or a successor to the debtor; securities of unaffiliated third parties (for example, securities of a sponsor or financial partner that are bundled into a plan distribution) are not exempt and require independent registration or another exemption such as Section 4(a)(2) or Rule 506.

Second, the exemption applies only when the securities are issued in exchange for claims or interests; cash sales to new investors for additional capital are not within § 1145(a)(1) and typically rely on the § 1145(a)(3) provision for "portfolio sales" by the reorganized debtor of unused authorized securities, or on a private placement under Section 4(a)(2) of the Securities Act.

Third, the antifraud provisions of the federal securities laws — principally Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder — apply with full force to plan-issued securities. The § 1145 exemption is from registration, not from disclosure-based liability. The disclosure statement approved under § 1125 is the principal vehicle for satisfying the antifraud regime in the plan-confirmation context.

Blue Sky Law Interplay

Section 1145(a)(2) provides that "the offer of a security through any warrant, option, right to subscribe, or conversion privilege that was sold in the manner specified in paragraph (1) of this subsection, or the sale of a security upon the exercise of such a warrant, option, right, or privilege" is exempt. Section 1145(d) preempts state blue sky registration: a security issued under a Chapter 11 plan that qualifies for the § 1145 federal exemption is also exempt from state securities-act registration requirements.

The state-law preemption operates by virtue of the Supremacy Clause and the Code's express federal-exemption framework. State antifraud provisions are generally not preempted; only registration and qualification requirements are displaced. State securities administrators retain enforcement authority over fraudulent conduct in connection with plan-issued securities.

The interaction with the National Securities Markets Improvement Act of 1996 (NSMIA) is layered. NSMIA generally preempts state blue sky registration for "covered securities," a class that includes securities listed on national exchanges and certain other categories. Plan-issued securities that would not qualify as NSMIA-covered securities still receive state-law exemption through § 1145(d) directly.

SEC Participation in Chapter 11 Cases

Section 1109(a) provides that "the Securities and Exchange Commission may raise and may appear and be heard on any issue in a case under this chapter, but the Securities and Exchange Commission may not appeal from any judgment, order, or decree entered in the case." The provision recognizes the SEC's institutional interest in the protection of public investors and gives it a standing right to participate in Chapter 11 cases without proving party-in-interest status under § 1109(b).

The SEC's principal interventions in Chapter 11 practice address (i) the adequacy of disclosure statements under § 1125 where the debtor's securities are or will be publicly traded, (ii) the propriety of plan provisions that release non-debtor third parties from securities-fraud liability, (iii) plan provisions that exculpate or release officers and directors with potential securities-law exposure, and (iv) the appointment of an equity committee where existing equity may have a meaningful interest.

The disclosure-statement role overlaps but does not coincide with the antifraud regime. Section 1125 imposes a federal "adequate information" standard; the SEC may comment on whether the disclosure statement satisfies that standard with reference to the investor-protection considerations that animate the federal securities laws generally.

Non-Dischargeability of Securities-Fraud Claims Under Section 523(a)(19)

Section 523(a)(19) was added by the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 in response to corporate-fraud scandals of the early 2000s. The subsection excepts from individual discharge any debt that is:

"(A) for the violation of any of the Federal securities laws (as that term is defined in section 3(a)(47) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934), any of the State securities laws, or any regulation or order issued under such Federal or State securities laws; or (B) for common law fraud, deceit, or manipulation in connection with the purchase or sale of any security; and (C) that results, before, on, or after the date on which the petition was filed, from (i) any judgment, order, consent order, or decree entered in any Federal or State judicial or administrative proceeding; (ii) any settlement agreement entered into by the debtor; or (iii) any court or administrative order for any damages, fine, penalty, citation, restitutionary payment, disgorgement payment, attorney fee, cost, or other payment owed by the debtor."

Two features of § 523(a)(19) distinguish it from other fraud-based non-dischargeability provisions. First, the predicate adjudication may occur "before, on, or after the date on which the petition was filed." A securities-fraud judgment entered post-petition is captured if the underlying conduct predates filing; the temporal asymmetry of ordinary fraud-discharge provisions does not apply.

Second, the provision sweeps both federal and state securities laws, and also reaches common-law fraud "in connection with the purchase or sale of any security." The "in connection with" language tracks Rule 10b-5 jurisprudence and is broadly construed.

The interaction with Chapter 11 corporate debtors is different. Section 1141(d)(6)(A) makes § 523(a)(2)(B) and (a)(19) claims against corporate debtors non-dischargeable in Chapter 11 to the extent owed to "a domestic governmental unit, or owed to a person as the result of an action filed under subchapter III of chapter 37 of title 31 [the False Claims Act] or any similar State statute." Private securities-fraud claims against corporate debtors remain subject to discharge under § 1141(d); only the carved-out governmental and qui tam categories survive.

Stockbrokers, Commodity Brokers, and Subchapter III

Section 109 of the Bankruptcy Code disqualifies certain securities-industry entities from filing in conventional chapters and channels them into specialized regimes. Section 109(b)(2) bars a "stockbroker" from Chapter 7 commercial liquidation in favor of Subchapter III of Chapter 7 (§§ 741–753), which provides for the orderly liquidation of stockbroker estates with special protection for customer property. Section 109(d) bars stockbrokers from Chapter 11 altogether.

Commodity brokers receive parallel treatment under Subchapter IV (§§ 761–767). Both subchapters give customer claims priority over general creditor claims with respect to "customer property" as statutorily defined, and both establish trustee duties oriented toward returning customer assets rather than maximizing distributions to general creditors.

The Securities Investor Protection Act of 1970 (SIPA), codified at 15 U.S.C. §§ 78aaa et seq., establishes a parallel liquidation regime for SIPC-member broker-dealers, administered by the Securities Investor Protection Corporation. A SIPA liquidation is initiated in federal district court and then transferred to bankruptcy court; the bankruptcy court applies SIPA-modified Bankruptcy Code provisions. Customer claims up to specified statutory limits receive SIPC insurance protection, paid from the SIPC fund.

Section 109(b)(2) also bars "domestic insurance companies" and "domestic banks" from Chapter 7, channeling them respectively into state insurance-receivership regimes and federal bank-receivership under the FDIC. Registered investment companies (mutual funds, closed-end funds) under the Investment Company Act of 1940 are not categorically barred from Chapter 11, but their reorganization is constrained by the Investment Company Act's substantive requirements, and the SEC's involvement under § 1109(a) is correspondingly more intensive.

Subordination of Securities-Damage Claims

Section 510(b) subordinates "a claim arising from rescission of a purchase or sale of a security of the debtor or of an affiliate of the debtor, for damages arising from the purchase or sale of such a security, or for reimbursement or contribution allowed under section 502 on account of such a claim" to all other claims and interests in the same class as the security, except that if the security is common stock, such claims have the same priority as common stock.

The provision implements a structural priority judgment: investors who suffered securities-fraud damages in connection with the purchase of a debtor's stock or bonds take their place in the capital structure at the level of the security they purchased, not at the senior-creditor level. The doctrine traces to the recognition that securities-fraud claimants assumed the equity-like risk associated with the security and should not be elevated above other holders of similar-class instruments.

The Supreme Court has not directly addressed § 510(b)'s scope. The leading court-of-appeals interpretation is the Third Circuit's analysis in In re Telegroup, Inc., 281 F.3d 133 (3d Cir. 2002), holding that the provision reaches any claim that "arises from" the purchase or sale of a security, including claims for breach of contract related to stock issuance and claims for fraud in connection with stock-based compensation arrangements.

Bankruptcy and Tax — Interaction Primer 2026

First published 2026-05-22/Version 0.1.0/CC-BY-4.0/status: draft

Abstract

Bankruptcy law and federal tax law overlap at almost every stage of a case. Federal income tax claims occupy a privileged position in the priority scheme under 11 U.S.C. § 507(a)(8) and are non-dischargeable in many circumstances under § 523(a)(1). Confirmation of a Chapter 11 or Chapter 12 plan can trigger a federal stamp-tax exemption under § 1146(a). Cancellation of indebtedness in bankruptcy is excluded from gross income under Internal Revenue Code § 108(a)(1)(A), but at the cost of tax-attribute reduction under § 108(b). Tax refunds attributable to pre-petition periods are property of the estate under § 541(a) and may be turned over to the trustee.

This primer summarizes the principal points at which the Bankruptcy Code interacts with the Internal Revenue Code and with state taxing authorities. It is general information for a non-specialist audience and does not constitute legal or tax advice.

Section 1146 Stamp-Tax Exemption on Plan Transfers

Section 1146(a) of the Bankruptcy Code provides that "the issuance, transfer, or exchange of a security, or the making or delivery of an instrument of transfer under a plan confirmed under section 1129 of this title, may not be taxed under any law imposing a stamp tax or similar tax." The exemption applies to deed-recording taxes, mortgage-recording taxes, and analogous transfer levies that state and local jurisdictions impose on the transfer of real property and other instruments.

The Supreme Court construed the temporal reach of the exemption in Florida Department of Revenue v. Piccadilly Cafeterias, Inc., 554 U.S. 33 (2008), holding that § 1146(a) applies only to transfers that occur after the plan is confirmed, not to pre-confirmation transfers. Pre-confirmation sales under § 363(b), whether or not later folded into a plan, are not within the exemption. The exemption's scope is narrow but useful: it can save the estate significant sums in real-estate-heavy reorganizations, and the savings flow through to creditor recoveries.

Practitioners structuring a Chapter 11 plan that contemplates real-property transfers should attend to the timing question. The transfer must occur "under a plan confirmed under section 1129" and the instrument of transfer must be tied to the confirmed plan, not to an earlier sale order.

Cancellation of Debt Income and IRC Section 108

Outside of bankruptcy, the discharge of indebtedness is generally a taxable event. Internal Revenue Code § 61(a)(11) includes "income from discharge of indebtedness" in gross income. A debtor who settles a $100,000 loan for $20,000 ordinarily recognizes $80,000 of cancellation-of-debt (COD) income.

IRC § 108(a)(1)(A) carves out a bankruptcy exclusion: COD income is excluded from gross income if the discharge "occurs in a title 11 case." A title 11 case means a case under the Bankruptcy Code in which the taxpayer is under the jurisdiction of the court and the discharge is granted by the court or is pursuant to a plan approved by the court. The exclusion applies to discharge in Chapter 7, 11, 12, and 13.

The exclusion is not free. IRC § 108(b) requires the debtor to reduce specified tax attributes by the amount of excluded COD income, in the following order: (1) net operating losses; (2) general business credits; (3) minimum tax credits; (4) capital loss carryovers; (5) basis in property; (6) passive activity loss and credit carryovers; and (7) foreign tax credit carryovers. The reduction is made as of the first day of the taxable year following the discharge year. The debtor may elect under § 108(b)(5) to apply the reduction first against property basis.

The interplay matters most acutely in Chapter 11 reorganizations of solvent businesses with substantial NOLs. The bankruptcy discharge protects the debtor from current taxation on the COD but consumes the very NOLs that would otherwise shelter future operating income. Tax counsel and bankruptcy counsel must coordinate plan design to optimize attribute preservation.

Dischargeability of Tax Debts: Sections 523(a)(1) and (a)(7)

The Bankruptcy Code does not extend the discharge to all tax claims. Section 523(a)(1) carves out three principal categories of non-dischargeable tax debt for individual debtors:

§ 523(a)(1)(A): Taxes of the kind and for the periods specified in § 507(a)(3) or § 507(a)(8), whether or not a claim is filed or allowed. This sweep captures most recent income taxes, withholding taxes, and employment taxes within statutorily-defined lookback periods.

§ 523(a)(1)(B): Taxes for which a required return (or equivalent report or notice) was not filed or was filed late and within two years before the petition date. This is the "late-filed return" exception, which has generated substantial circuit-level litigation over what counts as a "return."

§ 523(a)(1)(C): Taxes with respect to which the debtor "made a fraudulent return or willfully attempted in any manner to evade or defeat such tax." Civil tax fraud findings transfer into the bankruptcy court for purposes of this exception.

Section 523(a)(7) addresses penalty claims. It excepts from discharge any debt "to the extent such debt is for a fine, penalty, or forfeiture payable to and for the benefit of a governmental unit, and is not compensation for actual pecuniary loss." The provision contains a safe harbor for tax penalties relating to a tax that is itself dischargeable and that was assessed more than three years before the petition; such penalties are dischargeable even if the predicate tax is non-dischargeable for other reasons. Interest tracks the underlying tax: dischargeable if the tax is dischargeable, non-dischargeable otherwise.

Practitioners should run a tax-dischargeability analysis on every individual case with material tax liability before filing. The three-year, two-year, and 240-day lookback periods under § 507(a)(8) interact with tolling provisions under § 507(a)(8) flush language and the Internal Revenue Code's statute-of-limitations rules.

Priority of Tax Claims Under Section 507

Section 507(a)(8) confers eighth-priority status on a defined set of unsecured tax claims of governmental units. The eighth priority is junior to administrative expenses, wage claims, contributions to employee benefit plans, and certain other categories, but is senior to general unsecured claims. The principal sub-categories include:

Income or gross-receipts taxes for a taxable year ending on or before the petition date, for which a return was last due within three years of the petition;

Property taxes incurred before the commencement of the case and last payable without penalty within one year before the petition;

Trust-fund taxes (the employer's share of withholding) that the debtor was required to collect or withhold;

Employment taxes on wages, salaries, or commissions earned within three years of the petition;

Excise taxes on specified transactions within the same general lookback windows; and

Customs duties within applicable lookback periods.

In Chapter 13, § 1322(a)(2) requires the plan to provide for the full payment of all priority claims unless the holder agrees to different treatment. Eighth-priority tax claims must therefore be paid in full over the plan term. In Chapter 11, § 1129(a)(9)(C) requires deferred cash payments equal to the present value of priority tax claims over a period not exceeding five years from the petition date.

Secured tax claims (typically tax liens recorded before the petition) ride outside the § 507 priority scheme and are addressed under the secured-claim provisions of §§ 506 and 1129(b). The interaction between recorded tax liens and the debtor's exemptions, particularly under state homestead law, is a recurring source of complexity in consumer cases.

Tax Refunds as Property of the Estate

Section 541(a)(1) defines property of the estate to include "all legal or equitable interests of the debtor in property as of the commencement of the case." Pre-petition tax refunds, including refunds of taxes withheld during the year of filing for the pre-petition portion of that year, are property of the estate.

In Segal v. Rochelle, 382 U.S. 375 (1966), decided under the Bankruptcy Act of 1898, the Supreme Court held that a tax-loss-carryback refund was property of the estate even though the right to the refund did not mature until after filing. The principle carried forward into the Bankruptcy Code through the broad § 541(a)(1) definition and the Supreme Court's general directive in United States v. Whiting Pools, Inc., 462 U.S. 198 (1983), that the estate's reach is to be construed broadly.

For individual debtors, the practical result is that the Chapter 7 trustee may demand turnover of the pre-petition portion of any tax refund received for the year of filing. The portion is typically computed pro rata by reference to the petition date within the tax year. The debtor may exempt some portion of the refund under federal or state exemption schemes (a wildcard exemption is the most common shelter), but any unexempted portion belongs to the estate.

In Chapter 13, tax refunds are generally treated as disposable income subject to the plan; many courts and districts have local rules or standing orders requiring debtors to turn over tax refunds above a threshold each year of the plan.

The Automatic Stay and Tax Collection Activity

The automatic stay of § 362(a) halts most tax-collection activity by the IRS and state taxing authorities upon the petition. Levies, garnishments, lien recordings, and collection-due-process proceedings are stayed. Section 362(b)(9) carves out a limited set of permissible activities: the issuance of a notice of tax deficiency, an audit, a demand for tax returns, and the assessment of any tax. The IRS may continue to determine and assess tax liability during the case; it simply cannot collect outside the bankruptcy process.

Section 505(a) confers concurrent jurisdiction on the bankruptcy court to determine the amount or legality of any tax. The debtor or the trustee may invoke § 505 to litigate disputed pre-petition tax liability in bankruptcy court rather than in the Tax Court or in a federal district court refund suit. The choice has strategic implications for evidence, discovery, and appellate review.

## Bankruptcy and Trust Law - Interaction Primer 2026 - Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/cross-discipline/bankruptcy-and-trust-law/

Open Bankruptcy Project

Bankruptcy and Trust Law — Interaction Primer 2026

First published 2026-05-22/Version 0.1.0/CC-BY-4.0/status: draft

Abstract

The intersection of bankruptcy and trust law is governed by a single doctrinal lever: 11 U.S.C. § 541(c)(2). That provision incorporates by reference state-law transfer restrictions on beneficial interests in trusts, making spendthrift protection enforceable in bankruptcy where it is enforceable outside bankruptcy. A traditional third-party-settled spendthrift trust shields the beneficiary-debtor's interest from the estate. A self-settled trust generally does not: most states' trust law denies spendthrift effect against the settlor's own creditors, and most jurisdictions' fraudulent-transfer statutes provide additional avenues of attack. The Bankruptcy Code's principal weapon against asset-protection trusts is § 548(e), enacted by BAPCPA, which extends the fraudulent-transfer reach to a ten-year lookback for self-settled trusts and similar devices.

This primer summarizes the principal interaction points. It is general information and is not legal or estate-planning advice.

Spendthrift Trusts and Section 541(c)(2)

The traditional spendthrift trust is a third-party-settled trust in which the settlor (a parent, grandparent, or other donor) provides for distributions to one or more beneficiaries, subject to an express transfer restriction that prevents the beneficiary from voluntarily assigning, and creditors from involuntarily reaching, the beneficial interest. The restriction is enforceable under the law of nearly every state, codified in the Uniform Trust Code at § 502 and in the Restatement (Third) of Trusts at § 58.

Section 541(c)(2) of the Bankruptcy Code provides that "a restriction on the transfer of a beneficial interest of the debtor in a trust that is enforceable under applicable nonbankruptcy law is enforceable in a case under this title." The text incorporates state spendthrift law by reference. If a state would recognize the transfer restriction outside bankruptcy, the bankruptcy court will recognize it within bankruptcy. The beneficiary-debtor's interest in the trust does not enter the estate; the trustee in bankruptcy takes nothing with respect to the trust.

The Supreme Court in Patterson v. Shumate, 504 U.S. 753 (1992), addressed § 541(c)(2) in the context of ERISA-qualified pension plans and held that "applicable nonbankruptcy law" includes federal law as well as state law. The reasoning extends across the trust-law landscape: any enforceable transfer restriction — whether grounded in a state spendthrift statute, a federal pension provision, or another body of nonbankruptcy law — will shield the beneficial interest from the estate.

The protection is limited to the beneficial interest itself, not to distributions actually made. Once a distribution is paid to the beneficiary, the funds lose their trust character and become the beneficiary's general property, subject to ordinary creditor remedies and (post-petition) to ordinary estate-property analysis. A pre-petition distribution that the beneficiary holds at the petition date is property of the estate; a post-petition distribution in a Chapter 7 case is generally not property of the estate, though it may be reachable in Chapter 13 under § 1306.

Self-Settled Trusts: The Traditional Rule

The traditional rule, embodied in the Restatement (Second) of Trusts § 156 and the Restatement (Third) of Trusts § 58(2), is that a settlor cannot place property in trust for the settlor's own benefit and shield it from the settlor's creditors. The rationale is straightforward: the settlor cannot, by self-declaration, secure for itself the use of property while denying creditors access to it. The doctrine is sometimes summarized as "what the settlor gives, the settlor's creditors can reach."

The Uniform Trust Code § 505(a) preserves the traditional rule in default form: "during the lifetime of the settlor, the property of a revocable trust is subject to claims of the settlor's creditors," and "with respect to an irrevocable trust, a creditor or assignee of the settlor may reach the maximum amount that can be distributed to or for the settlor's benefit."

In bankruptcy, the application of state self-settled-trust law through § 541(c)(2) generally results in the inclusion of self-settled trust property in the estate to the extent the settlor-debtor is a beneficiary. The state-law transfer restriction is unenforceable against the settlor's own creditors, so it does not qualify under § 541(c)(2) as an "enforceable" restriction.

Domestic Asset-Protection Trusts

A minority of states — including, among others, Alaska, Delaware, Nevada, South Dakota, and Wyoming — have enacted domestic asset-protection trust (DAPT) statutes that purport to validate self-settled spendthrift trusts and to shield trust property from the settlor's creditors after specified statutory lookback periods. The statutes vary in their specifics: the lookback period for creditor reach typically ranges from two to four years, the categories of exempt creditors (alimony, child support, pre-existing torts) vary, and the procedural requirements for trust formation differ.

The bankruptcy analysis of DAPTs has been complicated by two distinct issues. First, conflict-of-laws: a settlor domiciled outside the DAPT state who creates a DAPT under the favorable state's law may face the argument that the settlor's domiciliary state's traditional rule governs, particularly where the settlor's creditors are also outside the DAPT state. Some bankruptcy courts have applied the settlor's domiciliary state's law and denied protection.

Second, § 548(e). Enacted by BAPCPA, this provision extends the fraudulent-transfer lookback to ten years for transfers to a "self-settled trust or similar device" if the debtor is a beneficiary, the transfer was made with actual intent to hinder, delay, or defraud a creditor, and the debtor is the settlor of the trust. The ten-year window is substantially longer than the ordinary two-year § 548(a) period and longer than any DAPT statute's lookback. The provision is structured as a federal overlay that operates independently of state validation of the trust form.

Irrevocable Life Insurance Trusts and Other Third-Party Irrevocable Trusts

An irrevocable life insurance trust (ILIT) is a third-party irrevocable trust commonly used in estate planning to hold a life insurance policy outside the insured's gross estate for federal estate-tax purposes. The insured contributes annual premium payments to the trust, the trustee uses those contributions to pay the policy premium, and the trust holds the death benefit on the insured's death for distribution to designated beneficiaries.

From a bankruptcy perspective, the ILIT raises two distinct questions. First, if the insured-settlor files bankruptcy during life: the insured is not a beneficiary of the ILIT (the structure is designed to keep the insured outside the beneficial class for estate-tax reasons), so the ILIT corpus is not property of the insured's estate under § 541. The insured retains no interest that the trustee in bankruptcy can reach. Annual premium contributions to the trust may, however, be attacked as fraudulent transfers under § 548 or under state-law equivalents through § 544(b), depending on the contribution dates and the settlor's solvency at the time of each contribution.

Second, if a beneficiary files bankruptcy: the spendthrift analysis of § 541(c)(2) governs. A well-drafted ILIT will contain transfer restrictions that satisfy the applicable state spendthrift statute; the beneficiary-debtor's interest will then be excluded from the estate. Distributions actually received pre-petition and held at the petition date enter the estate by ordinary operation; post-petition distributions are governed by the chapter-specific analysis.

Other third-party irrevocable trusts — testamentary trusts created by a parent's will, inter vivos trusts created by a grandparent, dynasty trusts — receive the same treatment. The beneficiary's interest is sheltered by § 541(c)(2) so long as the trust contains an enforceable transfer restriction; distributions are addressed under ordinary estate-property rules.

Fraudulent Transfer Recovery Under Section 548

Section 548 is the principal federal fraudulent-transfer provision and the principal weapon against asset-protection strategies that depend on pre-petition transfers from the debtor to trusts or other holding vehicles. Two branches of § 548 are operative:

Section 548(a)(1)(A) — actual fraud. The trustee may avoid any transfer made within two years before the petition if the transfer was made "with actual intent to hinder, delay, or defraud" any creditor. The intent standard is satisfied by direct or circumstantial evidence and is frequently proven through the "badges of fraud" doctrine: insider status of the transferee, retention of possession by the transferor, secrecy of the transfer, pending or threatened litigation against the transferor at the time of the transfer, transfer of substantially all the transferor's assets, absconding by the transferor, removal or concealment of assets, lack of reasonably equivalent value, and insolvency at the time of or shortly after the transfer.

Section 548(a)(1)(B) — constructive fraud. The trustee may avoid any transfer made within two years before the petition if the debtor received less than reasonably equivalent value in exchange and was insolvent on the date of the transfer or became insolvent as a result, was engaged in business with unreasonably small capital, or intended to incur debts beyond the ability to pay as they matured. No intent element is required; the constructive-fraud branch operates on objective criteria.

Section 548(e) — ten-year self-settled trust reach. This subsection, enacted by BAPCPA, provides a separate ten-year lookback for transfers made to self-settled trusts or similar devices where (i) the transfer was made within ten years before the petition, (ii) the transfer was made to a self-settled trust or similar device, (iii) the transfer was by the debtor, (iv) the debtor is a beneficiary, and (v) the debtor made the transfer with actual intent to hinder, delay, or defraud any entity to which the debtor was or became indebted on or after the date of the transfer.

Section 544(b) supplements § 548 by allowing the trustee to invoke any applicable state fraudulent-transfer statute (typically the Uniform Voidable Transactions Act, the successor to the Uniform Fraudulent Transfer Act) through any actual unsecured creditor in existence at the petition date. Many state UVTA enactments provide a four-year lookback, longer than § 548's general two-year window, with extensions for actual-fraud claims discovered late.

Strong-Arm Powers and Trust Distributions

Section 544(a), the strong-arm clause, gives the trustee the rights and powers of a hypothetical judicial lien creditor, a hypothetical execution creditor, and (with respect to real property) a hypothetical bona fide purchaser, all as of the petition date. The strong-arm powers can interact with trust law in two principal contexts.

First, a beneficiary's interest in a trust that is recorded or otherwise of record may be reachable by the strong-arm trustee to the extent that an actual judicial lien creditor of the beneficiary could reach it under state law. This is the analytical step that defeats the strong-arm clause where the trust contains an enforceable spendthrift provision: an actual judicial lien creditor could not reach the beneficial interest, so the hypothetical-lien trustee cannot reach it either.

Second, mandatory distributions due to the beneficiary as of the petition date may be reachable as accrued but unpaid distributions, even where the trust as a whole is spendthrift-protected. The right to a fixed and currently-due distribution is a present property right that survives spendthrift protection in most jurisdictions; the executor of that right enters the estate.

## Debt Dischargeability in Bankruptcy - Reference Guide

Research Guide

Which Debts Are Discharged in Bankruptcy

Bankruptcy discharges most debts, but not all. Section 523(a) of the Bankruptcy Code lists the statutory exceptions to discharge. This page collects the most common categories - taxes, student loans, support obligations, fraud-based debts, and others - with pointers to the controlling statutory language and leading case law.

Data updated 2026-04-21. See methodology & sources.

Written and maintained by Open Bankruptcy Project staff. Last updated 2026-09-18. Editorial policy.

Home/Debt Relief

Debts generally discharged

Most unsecured consumer debts are discharged in both Chapter 7 and Chapter 13. Typical examples include credit card balances, medical bills, personal loans, signature lines of credit, older utility bills, and deficiency judgments on repossessed collateral. Secured debts are handled differently - the personal in personam liability is discharged, but the lien remains on the property unless avoided or surrendered.

Taxes - § 523(a)(1)

Most federal, state, and local income tax debts are non-dischargeable if they fall within specific categories: recent tax years (roughly the three most recent), taxes for which no return was filed, taxes for which a return was filed late within two years of filing, and taxes for which a fraudulent return was filed. Older income tax debts that fail the non-dischargeability test under § 523(a)(1) can be discharged.

Student loans - § 523(a)(8)

Educational loans and certain educational benefit overpayments are non-dischargeable absent a finding that excepting them from discharge would impose an "undue hardship" on the debtor and the debtor's dependents. The Brunner test, used by most circuits, requires: (1) the debtor cannot maintain a minimal standard of living if forced to repay; (2) additional circumstances indicate this state is likely to persist; (3) the debtor has made good-faith efforts to repay.

Domestic support obligations - § 523(a)(5) and § 523(a)(15)

Alimony, child support, and other domestic support obligations are non-dischargeable in both chapters. Property-settlement obligations owed to a former spouse or child are non-dischargeable in Chapter 7 under § 523(a)(15), but Chapter 13 historically permitted discharge of § 523(a)(15) obligations - post-BAPCPA, that distinction narrowed.

Fraud and related exceptions - § 523(a)(2), (4), (6)

§ 523(a)(2): debts for money, property, services, or an extension of credit obtained by false pretenses, a false representation, or actual fraud. Includes both general fraud and debts incurred by use of a false financial statement.

§ 523(a)(4): debts for fraud or defalcation while acting in a fiduciary capacity, embezzlement, or larceny.

§ 523(a)(6): debts for willful and malicious injury to another person or property. Intent requirement is narrow - the creditor must show intent to cause the injury, not just intent to do the act.

Other common non-dischargeable categories

Fines, penalties, and restitution payable to a governmental unit - § 523(a)(7)

Debts for death or personal injury caused by a debtor operating a motor vehicle, vessel, or aircraft while intoxicated - § 523(a)(9)

Debts not listed in the petition (with limited exceptions) - § 523(a)(3)

Debts listed in a prior bankruptcy case in which discharge was denied, waived, or revoked - § 523(a)(10)

Certain condominium/HOA post-petition assessments - § 523(a)(16)

Court-ordered civil restitution or criminal restitution - § 523(a)(13)

Certain governmental-benefit overpayments and educational loan guarantor claims

Chapter 7 vs Chapter 13 discharge scope

Chapter 13 historically provided a slightly broader "super-discharge," discharging some debts that would survive Chapter 7. Post-BAPCPA (2005), the categories subject to the super-discharge narrowed substantially. A few differences remain - most notably, certain property-settlement-type marital debts under § 523(a)(15) are treated differently, and certain late-paid taxes are treated differently in Chapter 13.

Frequently asked questions
Can tax debts be discharged in bankruptcy?
Most recent income tax debts are non-dischargeable under § 523(a)(1), but older income tax debts that meet all dischargeability criteria (including timely-filed returns and sufficient age) can be discharged. Tax debts for which no return was filed, or for which a fraudulent return was filed, are non-dischargeable regardless of age.
Are student loans dischargeable?
§ 523(a)(8) makes student loans non-dischargeable absent a finding of "undue hardship." Most circuits apply the Brunner test: inability to maintain a minimal standard of living, persistence of the inability, and good-faith repayment efforts.
Does bankruptcy discharge child support?
No. Domestic support obligations under § 523(a)(5) - alimony, child support, and maintenance - are non-dischargeable in every chapter.
Can fraud-based debts be discharged?
§ 523(a)(2), (4), and (6) exclude from discharge debts for money obtained by fraud, fiduciary defalcation, embezzlement, larceny, and willful-and-malicious injury. These categories require creditor adversary proceedings to establish the non-dischargeability.
What debts are typically discharged in Chapter 7?
Most unsecured consumer debts: credit card balances, medical bills, signature loans, older utility bills, and deficiency judgments. Secured debt personal liability is also discharged, though liens remain on property until the collateral is surrendered or the lien is otherwise addressed.
