## Statement of Financial Affairs (Form 107) Anatomy [2026] - Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/forms-anatomy/sofa-form-107/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Home/Forms Anatomy/SOFA - Form 107

Official Form 107
Statement of Financial Affairs

Statement of Financial Affairs (Form 107)

The 24-question anatomy: 2-year versus 6-year lookback windows, insider payments, gifts, losses, pre-filing transfers, and property held for others.

What the SOFA is for

The Statement of Financial Affairs - SOFA - is the disclosure document that places the debtor's pre-petition financial behavior on the public record. Official Form 107 (individual debtors) is organized around 24 numbered questions covering specific historical categories. Unlike the schedules, which capture the debtor's position as of the petition date, the SOFA captures the debtor's transactional history during defined lookback windows ranging from one to six years. The SOFA is the principal evidentiary basis for trustee avoidance actions under Section 547 (preferences), Section 548 (fraudulent transfers), and Section 544(b) (state-law avoidance).

The SOFA is signed under penalty of perjury. A materially false SOFA answer can support objection to discharge under Section 727(a)(4) in Chapter 7 and criminal referral under 18 U.S.C. Section 152. The form is short relative to the schedules, but each question functions as a tripwire for downstream avoidance and discharge consequences.

Lookback windows

SOFA questions use distinct lookback windows. The window matters; misapplying it produces over-inclusion (a trustee inquiry into items not actually required) or under-inclusion (a false answer).

Current year and prior 2 years - income from employment (Q1) and other sources (Q2).

90 days pre-petition - payments to non-insider creditors aggregating $600 or more (Q6, under the consumer-case threshold; the threshold is $8,575 for primarily-business cases under the April 1, 2025 Section 104 adjustment).

1 year pre-petition - payments to insiders (Q3) and benefits to insiders (Q4); legal actions filed by or against (Q9); foreclosures and repossessions (Q11); gifts above per-recipient thresholds (Q12); losses to fire/theft/casualty (Q13).

2 years pre-petition - prior bankruptcy filings (Q22 of older form versions; current version includes via separate disclosure); financial-account closures (Q20); safe deposit boxes (Q21); storage units (Q23).

2 years pre-petition - transfers other than ordinary course (Q18).

10 years pre-petition - transfers to self-settled trusts and similar devices (Q19) - the asset-protection-trust lookback added by BAPCPA.

6 years pre-petition - certain business-related disclosures for self-employed debtors.

Question 3 - payments to insiders

SOFA Question 3 asks whether, within the year before filing, the debtor made any payments or transfers to or for the benefit of an insider. "Insider" is defined at Section 101(31) and includes, for an individual debtor: relatives of the debtor; general partners of the debtor; partnerships in which the debtor is a general partner; corporations of which the debtor is a director, officer, or person in control; and others. The "relative" category reaches grandparents through grandchildren, in-laws, and step-relations.

The disclosure is the trustee's roadmap to insider-preference recovery. Under Section 547(b)(4)(B), the preference look-back for insiders extends to one year, not 90 days. A repayment of a personal loan to a parent or sibling within the year - even one that would not be avoidable as to a non-insider - is recoverable as a preference. Disclosure on SOFA Q3 places the transfer on the record and lets the trustee evaluate avoidance. Concealment exposes the debtor to denial of discharge under Section 727 and the transfer remains recoverable for a longer window under Section 544(b) via state-law fraudulent transfer reach-back.

Question 12 - gifts

SOFA Question 12 asks about gifts within the year preceding filing. The threshold for individual debtors is $600 to any single recipient (with separate disclosure of charitable contributions). A series of gifts to the same person aggregating above the threshold should be disclosed; a single gift above the threshold should be disclosed. Holiday gifts to children, contributions to family members in need, and donations of property to family or friends all potentially fall within the question. The disclosure is read in connection with Section 548's two-year fraudulent-transfer reach (a gift is by definition a transfer "for less than reasonably equivalent value") and may also support a constructive-fraudulent-transfer recovery if the debtor was insolvent at the time.

Question 9 - losses

SOFA Question 9 (in current form numbering) asks about losses from fire, theft, other casualty, or gambling during the year before filing. The disclosure has two principal consequences. First, it surfaces insurance recovery rights - the debtor's claim against an insurer for an unpaid loss is a chose in action that is property of the estate under Section 541(a)(1) and should also be listed on Schedule A/B. Second, it surfaces gambling-loss patterns that may bear on dischargeability under Section 523(a)(2)(C) presumptions for luxury goods and cash advances or, more rarely, on discharge under Section 727(a)(3) for inadequate financial records.

Questions 18 and 19 - pre-filing transfers

SOFA Question 18 asks about transfers of property within two years before filing, other than property transferred in the ordinary course of business or financial affairs. The "ordinary course" carve-out is narrow: routine bill payments, deposits to savings accounts in the debtor's own name, and similar transactions are ordinary; a transfer of real estate, the sale of a vehicle, the gift of a substantial asset, or the transfer of an account to another person's name is not.

The disclosure feeds the trustee's Section 548 fraudulent-transfer analysis. Section 548 reaches transfers made within two years before filing that were made with actual intent to hinder, delay, or defraud (actual fraud) or that were constructively fraudulent (transfer for less than reasonably equivalent value while insolvent). Section 544(b), invoking applicable state law, often extends the reach-back to four years or longer.

SOFA Question 19 asks about transfers to a self-settled trust or similar device of which the debtor is a beneficiary, within the ten years before filing. The ten-year window was added by BAPCPA at Section 548(e), targeting offshore and domestic asset-protection trusts. The question's reach is broader than the trust-only language suggests; counsel should evaluate whether any asset-protection structure created during the decade before filing falls within the disclosure obligation.

Question 23 - property held for others

SOFA Question 23 asks whether the debtor holds any property in trust or as a bailee for someone else. The disclosure is important because such property is typically not property of the estate - the debtor holds only legal title, not equitable interest. Examples include: tools or equipment held for a customer pending pickup; deposits held by the debtor for clients; property held by the debtor as a fiduciary under a court order or contract; property held by the debtor as a custodian under the Uniform Transfers to Minors Act for a minor child.

Failure to disclose property held for others creates two problems. First, the asset may appear in the debtor's records (bank statements, possession) without explanation, drawing trustee suspicion. Second, if the trustee administers the property as if it belonged to the estate, the rightful owner has a claim against the estate and possibly against the debtor for breach of fiduciary duty.

Question 6 - payments to creditors (90-day window)

SOFA Question 6 asks about payments within the 90 days before filing on debts to non-insider creditors that aggregate $600 or more to any one creditor (consumer cases; higher threshold for primarily-business cases). The disclosure is the principal source for the trustee's Section 547(b) preference analysis. A payment to an unsecured creditor on antecedent debt within the 90-day window, while the debtor was insolvent, may be recoverable as a preference if it allowed the creditor to receive more than the creditor would have received in a hypothetical Chapter 7 distribution.

Several preference defenses are available to the recipient creditor under Section 547(c), including the contemporaneous-exchange-for-new-value defense, the ordinary-course-of-business defense, and the subsequent-new-value defense. The disclosure on Q6 puts the payment in front of the trustee; whether the trustee actually pursues recovery turns on the available defenses and on the dollars at issue.

Common errors

Misapplying the lookback windows - reporting only 90 days of insider payments when Q3 asks for one year.

Treating "ordinary course" too broadly in Q18 to omit real-estate transfers and substantial gifts as if they were routine.

Omitting Q3 payments to relatives on the theory that family members are not "creditors." The question reaches all payments to insiders, not only creditor payments.

Failing to disclose property held for others under Q23, then having the trustee discover the property without context.

Omitting Q9 losses when an insurance claim is pending, thereby concealing what is also a Schedule A/B chose in action.

The SOFA is the historical companion to the schedules. The schedules capture the petition-date snapshot. The SOFA captures the pre-petition film. Trustees compare the two; concealment of pre-petition transactional history is the most common basis for objection to discharge under Section 727 and for criminal referral under 18 U.S.C. Section 152.

Related authority

11 U.S.C. Section 547 - Preferences

11 U.S.C. Section 548 - Fraudulent transfers and obligations

11 U.S.C. Section 544(b) - State-law avoidance by reach-back

11 U.S.C. Section 727(a) - Discharge denial grounds (Chapter 7)

11 U.S.C. Section 101(31) - Definition of insider

## Statement of Intention (Form 108) Anatomy [2026] - Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/forms-anatomy/statement-of-intention-form-108/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Home/Forms Anatomy/Statement of Intention - Form 108

Official Form 108
11 U.S.C. Section 521(a)(2)

Statement of Intention (Form 108)

The Section 521(a)(2) reaffirm-redeem-surrender election, the 30-day filing deadline, the 45-day performance deadline, and the Section 521(d) ipso facto stripping consequences of failure.

What the Statement of Intention is for

The Statement of Intention is the Chapter 7 individual debtor's election regarding secured personal property and personal-property leases. The form is required only in Chapter 7 cases (not Chapter 13, where the plan handles secured-property treatment) and only for individual debtors. Its statutory basis is 11 U.S.C. Section 521(a)(2), which requires the debtor to file a statement of intention with respect to property securing consumer debts and personal-property leases, and to perform that intention within the statutory window.

The election is binary-plus-one. For each secured consumer-debt item of personal property and each personal-property lease, the debtor must elect to (a) retain and reaffirm - sign a reaffirmation agreement under Section 524(c) to remain personally liable on the debt; (b) retain and redeem - pay the secured creditor a lump-sum equal to the property's fair market value under Section 722; or (c) surrender - turn the property over to the secured creditor. A fourth historical option, "retain without reaffirmation" (the so-called "ride-through"), was abrogated by BAPCPA in 2005, with surviving relevance only in a narrow band of circuit-specific doctrine.

The 30-day filing deadline

Section 521(a)(2)(A) requires the debtor to file the Statement of Intention within 30 days after the petition date or by the date of the first meeting of creditors (the 341 meeting), whichever is earlier. The 30-day clock runs from filing; the 341 meeting is typically scheduled 21 to 50 days after filing depending on the district. In most cases the 30-day deadline binds.

The Statement of Intention is one of several documents whose filing deadline is anchored to the petition date or the 341 meeting under Section 521(a). The filing deadline is procedural and can be extended for cause shown, but extensions are not freely granted in routine cases. The trustee's review at the 341 meeting will check whether the Statement of Intention has been filed and whether the elections on it match the secured-debt entries on Schedule D.

The 45-day performance deadline

Section 521(a)(6) requires the individual debtor to perform the stated intention within 45 days after the first 341 meeting. "Perform" means: enter into the reaffirmation agreement (if reaffirming), redeem the property by lump-sum payment (if redeeming), or deliver the property to the secured creditor (if surrendering). The 45-day clock runs from the date of the first 341 meeting, not the petition date. The two deadlines together set up a sequential timeline: file within 30 days of petition (or by 341 meeting if earlier), perform within 45 days of 341 meeting.

For an unexpired personal-property lease, Section 365(p)(2) provides a parallel mechanism: the lease is deemed rejected if the trustee does not assume within 60 days of the order for relief, and the debtor may then enter into a written assumption agreement with the lessor.

The reaffirm-redeem-surrender election in detail

Reaffirm

Reaffirmation under Section 524(c) is a contract between the debtor and the creditor in which the debtor agrees to remain personally liable on a debt that would otherwise be discharged. The reaffirmation agreement must be filed with the court before discharge, must include the disclosures required by Section 524(k), and must (in most cases) include attorney certification that the agreement does not impose an undue hardship or, where the debtor is not represented by counsel, court approval after a hearing. The debtor has a 60-day window after the agreement is filed (or before discharge, whichever is later) to rescind under Section 524(c)(4).

Reaffirmation is the most legally serious of the three elections because it survives the discharge - the debt remains collectible after the case closes. The benefit to the debtor is the retention of property and the continuation of the original contract terms. The risk is that a default after discharge becomes a non-discharged judgment-vulnerable obligation.

Redeem

Redemption under Section 722 permits the individual Chapter 7 debtor to pay the secured creditor a lump-sum equal to the allowed secured claim - which is the amount of the debt up to the property's fair market value - and take the property free of the lien. Redemption is available only for tangible personal property intended primarily for personal, family, or household use, and only for property exempted under Section 522 or abandoned by the trustee. The lump-sum requirement means redemption is practically available only when the debtor has access to cash (sometimes via a redemption financing company) or where the property's value is small.

The principal advantage is the cram-down effect: a $20,000 auto loan secured by a $12,000 vehicle becomes a $12,000 payment, with the $8,000 unsecured deficiency discharged. The disadvantage is that the entire $12,000 must be paid at once, not over time.

Surrender

Surrender is the election to turn the collateral over to the secured creditor. The debtor's personal liability is discharged in the bankruptcy; the secured creditor's deficiency claim is unsecured and dischargeable. Surrender is the default election when the property is worth less than the debt, when the debtor cannot afford to keep current on the payments, or when the property is no longer needed.

The act of surrendering does not relieve the debtor of the obligation to actually deliver the property. Where the debtor surrenders on Form 108 but then opposes the secured creditor's recovery (for example, by contesting a state-court replevin action or by failing to make the property available), most circuits hold that the debtor is bound by the surrender election and may be sanctioned for inconsistent conduct. See In re Failla, 838 F.3d 1170 (11th Cir. 2016), and parallel authority in other circuits.

The vanished "ride-through" option

Before BAPCPA, several circuits permitted Chapter 7 debtors to retain personal-property collateral without reaffirming and without redeeming by simply remaining current on the secured debt - the so-called "ride-through" option. The lender, having no reaffirmed promise, could not pursue a deficiency post-discharge, but could repossess if the debtor defaulted; the in-personam discharge made repayment voluntary as a practical matter.

BAPCPA added Section 521(a)(6) and Section 362(h) to abrogate ride-through for personal property. Under Section 521(a)(6), if the debtor fails to perform the intention within 45 days of the first 341 meeting, the automatic stay terminates as to the property under Section 362(h) and the property ceases to be property of the estate. Under Section 521(d), any ipso facto clause in the underlying contract (a clause making bankruptcy itself a default) becomes enforceable. The combined effect is that ride-through is no longer reliably available; the lender can either insist on reaffirmation or repossess.

A narrow residue of ride-through has survived in a handful of circuits for debtors who are current on the debt at the petition date and remain current thereafter, under the theory that the lender's pre-default repossession rights are limited by state-law foreclosure restrictions even if Section 521(d) lifts the bankruptcy-specific protections. The doctrine is district-by-district.

Section 521(d): the ipso facto stripping consequence

Section 521(d) is the doctrinal teeth behind BAPCPA's elimination of ride-through. The section provides that if the debtor fails to perform the stated intention within the 45-day window, the protections of Section 365(e)(1) (anti-ipso-facto in executory contracts and leases) and Section 541(c)(1) (anti-ipso-facto in property of the estate) do not apply. In ordinary language: an ipso facto clause that would otherwise be unenforceable becomes enforceable. The contract can be terminated on the basis of the bankruptcy filing itself, even if the debtor is otherwise current.

The consequence for a non-compliant debtor is a creditor freed from anti-ipso-facto protections, with full state-law remedies for default and repossession. The 45-day window is therefore not a soft deadline - it is the boundary between continued contractual protection and lender-friendly default treatment.

Real property is not on Form 108

Form 108 addresses personal property securing consumer debt and personal-property leases. Real property is not on the Statement of Intention. The treatment of real property securing consumer debt (typically the debtor's home) in a Chapter 7 case is governed by Section 521(a) general disclosure requirements, by the automatic stay and any motion for relief from stay, and by the lender's foreclosure rights under non-bankruptcy law. A Chapter 7 individual who wishes to retain a home subject to a mortgage must continue to make mortgage payments to avoid post-discharge foreclosure; reaffirmation of a residential mortgage is permissible but uncommon because the in-rem mortgage survives discharge whether or not reaffirmed and the debtor's personal liability can usually be discharged without losing the home so long as payments continue.

Form 108 is short and the deadlines are unforgiving. Thirty days to file, forty-five days from the 341 meeting to perform. Section 521(d) is the BAPCPA-enacted consequence for missing either: ipso facto protections vanish and the lender's state-law remedies are unencumbered by bankruptcy.

Official Bankruptcy Forms Reference

Bankruptcy Forms Reference

The Official Bankruptcy Forms are the standardized petition, schedule, statement, and notice forms used in every federal bankruptcy case. They are promulgated by the Judicial Conference of the United States and published by the Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts. These reference pages cover fifteen forms, with links to the official current PDFs on uscourts.gov.

Last modified 2026-09-20.

Home/Forms

About the Official Bankruptcy Forms

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 9009 requires that the Official Forms prescribed by the Judicial Conference be used without alteration except as permitted by the rules or by the forms themselves. The forms are renumbered with a "B" prefix and a three-digit identifier. The current Official Forms architecture was adopted as part of the 2015 forms modernization project and consolidated the older varied-letter scheme into a unified numerical system.

Individual debtors typically file Form B101 as the voluntary petition, the B106 series of schedules, the B107 Statement of Financial Affairs, the B108 Statement of Intention if Chapter 7, the B121 SSN statement, and one of the B122 means-test forms. The bankruptcy clerk subsequently issues the B309 series notice scheduling the section 341 meeting of creditors. Non-individual entities use the parallel non-individual forms (B201B, B106Sum-Nonindividual, B202, etc.).

All Official Forms are available without charge from the U.S. Courts website. The pages below describe each form's purpose, structure, common pitfalls, and the consequences of error or omission. They do not replace the form instructions published by the Administrative Office.

Form reference pages

Form B101 - Voluntary Petition for IndividualsThe petition that initiates a voluntary case for an individual debtor; demographic, chapter election, debt-type, and prior-case disclosures.

Form B103A - Application to Pay the Filing Fee in InstallmentsThe individual's application to pay the filing fee in up to four installments within 120 days under Rule 1006(b).

Form B103B - Application to Have the Chapter 7 Filing Fee WaivedThe Chapter 7 fee waiver application under 28 U.S.C. Section 1930(f) for filers below 150% of the poverty guideline who cannot pay in installments.

Form B106 - Individual Bankruptcy Schedules A/B through JThe asset, liability, executory contract, codebtor, income, and expense schedules together with the summary and declaration.

Form B107 - Statement of Financial Affairs for IndividualsIncome history, payments to creditors, lawsuits, transfers, closed accounts, business interests, and other prepetition financial activity.

Form B108 - Statement of Intention for Chapter 7The debtor's section 521(a)(2) election to retain, redeem, reaffirm, or surrender each item of property securing a consumer debt.

Form B113 - Chapter 13 PlanThe national Chapter 13 plan form, required unless the district has adopted a local plan form under Rule 3015.1.

Form B121 - Statement About Your Social Security NumbersThe non-public statement filed with the petition that supplies the full SSN to the court for case-administration purposes under Rule 1007(f).

Form B122A-1 - Chapter 7 Statement of Current Monthly IncomeThe first step of the means test used to determine whether the section 707(b) presumption of abuse applies to an individual Chapter 7 case.

Form B122A-2 - Chapter 7 Means Test CalculationThe second means-test form, filed when current monthly income on Form B122A-1 is above the state median.

Form B122B - Chapter 11 Statement of Your Current Monthly IncomeThe current-monthly-income calculation required for individual Chapter 11 debtors to assist with applicable disposable-income analysis.

Form B122C-1 - Chapter 13 Statement of CMI and Commitment PeriodThe Chapter 13 current-monthly-income statement that determines the three- or five-year applicable commitment period.

Form B201A - Section 342(b) Notice to Individual DebtorsThe pre-filing notice required by section 342(b) describing the chapters and the consequences of selecting each.

Form B309A - Notice of Chapter 7 Case (No Proof of Claim Required)The clerk's notice to creditors of the filing, the 341 meeting date, and the dischargeability and discharge-objection deadlines.

Form B423 - Certification About a Financial Management Course (abrogated)Abrogated effective December 1, 2024. Debtors now file the course provider's certificate under Rule 1007(b)(7).

Use current forms: The Official Forms are updated periodically. Always download the current version from the U.S. Courts forms site before filing.

## Form B101 - Voluntary Petition for Individuals Filing for Bankruptcy [2026] - Bankruptcy Forms Reference
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/forms/b101-voluntary-petition/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Home > Forms > B101 Voluntary Petition

Official Bankruptcy Form
B101

Form B101: Voluntary Petition for Individuals Filing for Bankruptcy

The opening document of an individual bankruptcy case, with required variants B101A (Initial Statement About Eviction Judgment) and B101B (Statement About Payment of Eviction Judgment).

Download Official Form 101 (PDF, uscourts.gov)

Current version: effective June 22, 2024, from uscourts.gov. Official form page.

Your court may also require local forms. Check your bankruptcy court's website before filing.

Purpose and statutory authority

Official Form B101 is the Voluntary Petition that an individual files to commence a case under 11 U.S.C. Section 301. The filing of the petition is the act that creates the bankruptcy estate under 11 U.S.C. Section 541 and triggers the automatic stay under 11 U.S.C. Section 362. The form is promulgated under the rulemaking authority of 28 U.S.C. Section 2075 and the Federal Rules of Bankruptcy Procedure, and is prescribed by the Judicial Conference of the United States.

The petition is the legal instrument that asks the bankruptcy court to grant relief under a specified chapter of Title 11. By signing the petition, the debtor declares under penalty of perjury that the information is true and correct and acknowledges receipt of the required disclosures under 11 U.S.C. Section 342(b).

Who must file Form B101

Form B101 is used by individuals (including a married couple filing a joint petition) seeking relief under Chapter 7, Chapter 11, Chapter 12, or Chapter 13. A non-individual debtor (corporation, partnership, limited liability company) uses Form B201 instead. The form is filed in the United States Bankruptcy Court for the judicial district where the individual has had a domicile, residence, principal place of business, or principal assets for the longer portion of the 180 days preceding filing, per 28 U.S.C. Section 1408.

Eligibility to file under a particular chapter is governed by 11 U.S.C. Section 109. Among other requirements, an individual debtor must have received a credit-counseling briefing from an approved nonprofit budget and credit-counseling agency within the 180 days before filing, per Section 109(h). The petition includes a certification of that briefing.

Key sections of Form B101

Part 1 - Identification

Debtor's legal name, any other names used in the prior eight years, last four digits of the Social Security number (full SSN goes on the non-public Form B121), Employer Identification Number, addresses, and the district where the case is being filed.

Part 2 - Chapter election

The debtor checks the chapter under which relief is sought: 7, 11 (with Subchapter V election option for small business cases under Section 1182), 12, or 13.

Part 3 - Prior cases

List of all bankruptcy cases filed by the debtor or any spouse, business, or affiliate within the last eight years. This data feeds the analysis of discharge bars under Section 727(a)(8)/(9) and Section 1328(f).

Parts 4-9 - Property, debts, statistics

Summary of nature of debts (primarily consumer or business), estimated asset and liability ranges, estimated number of creditors, estimated funds available for unsecured creditors, and the credit-counseling certification.

Required variants B101A and B101B

Form B101A (Initial Statement About an Eviction Judgment Against You) is filed with the petition if a landlord has obtained a judgment for possession against the debtor. It implements the limited stay carve-out in 11 U.S.C. Section 362(b)(22) and (l). The debtor must also deposit any rent that would become due within 30 days post-petition with the clerk of court. Form B101B (Statement About Payment of an Eviction Judgment) is then filed within 30 days to certify cure.

Filing context and deadlines

Form B101 is the document whose filing commences the case. Several other documents must accompany the petition or be filed within statutory windows after filing under Fed. R. Bankr. P. 1007:

Form B121 (Statement About Your Social Security Numbers) - with the petition

Form B106 series (Schedules A/B through J) - within 14 days, extendable for cause

Form B107 (Statement of Financial Affairs) - within 14 days

Form B108 (Statement of Intention, Chapter 7 only) - within 30 days post-petition or by the meeting of creditors, whichever is earlier

Form B122A-1 / B122B / B122C-1 (Means Test forms) - with the petition or within 14 days

Credit-counseling certificate (separate from the petition certification) - with the petition

Payment-advice copies covering the 60 days pre-petition - within 14 days, per Section 521(a)(1)(B)(iv)

Filing fee: $338 for Chapter 7, $1,738 for Chapter 11 (including Subchapter V: a $1,167 filing fee plus the $571 administrative fee), $278 for Chapter 12, $313 for Chapter 13 (as of 2026). The debtor may apply to pay the Chapter 7 fee in installments under Fed. R. Bankr. P. 1006(b), or to waive the Chapter 7 fee under 28 U.S.C. Section 1930(f) if household income is below 150% of the federal poverty guideline.

Common pitfalls

Inaccurate venue under 28 U.S.C. Section 1408. An individual who recently moved must look back across the full 180-day pre-filing window and file in the district where the longer portion was spent, not the district of current residence.

Omitted prior cases in Part 3. The eight-year look-back includes joint filings, dismissed cases, cases of related business entities, and cases of a current or former spouse. Omission can produce a Section 727(a)(4) false-oath issue or trigger automatic-stay limitations under Section 362(c)(3) or (c)(4).

Missing or stale credit-counseling certificate. The briefing must be within the 180 days before filing. Filings without a valid certificate are subject to dismissal under Section 109(h) and Fed. R. Bankr. P. 1007(b)(3).

Wrong chapter election. Individuals with primarily consumer debt face the means-test gatekeeping in Section 707(b); the chapter selected on the petition must be consistent with the means-test result on Form B122A or B122C.

Joint petition without joint eligibility. Only spouses may file a joint petition under Section 302; same-sex married couples qualify, but unmarried partners do not.

Failure to file B101A when eviction judgment exists. Omission of B101A and the corresponding deposit forfeits the limited stay extension that Section 362(l) makes available, and the landlord may proceed with the writ of possession.

Where to obtain the official current version

Always use the current official form. Official Bankruptcy Forms are revised periodically. The current version is available free at the Administrative Office of the United States Courts forms library: uscourts.gov/forms-rules/forms/bankruptcy-forms. The direct link for Form B101 and its instructions is at uscourts.gov/forms/individual-debtors/voluntary-petition-individuals-filing-bankruptcy.

## Form B106 - Individual Bankruptcy Schedules A/B through J [2026] - Bankruptcy Forms Reference
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/forms/b106-schedules/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Home > Forms > B106 Schedules

Official Bankruptcy Form
B106 Series

Form B106: Individual Bankruptcy Schedules A/B through J

The complete inventory of an individual debtor's assets, liabilities, executory contracts, income, and expenses, signed under penalty of perjury.

Download Official Form 106Sum (PDF, uscourts.gov)
Download Official Form 106A/B (PDF, uscourts.gov)
Download Official Form 106C (PDF, uscourts.gov)
Download Official Form 106D (PDF, uscourts.gov)
Download Official Form 106E/F (PDF, uscourts.gov)
Download Official Form 106G (PDF, uscourts.gov)
Download Official Form 106H (PDF, uscourts.gov)
Download Official Form 106I (PDF, uscourts.gov)
Download Official Form 106J (PDF, uscourts.gov)
Download Official Form 106J-2 (PDF, uscourts.gov)
Download Official Form 106Dec (PDF, uscourts.gov)

Current versions, from uscourts.gov: Schedule C updated April 1, 2025 (effective April 1, 2022); the Summary, Schedules A/B, D, E/F, G, H, I, J, J-2, and the Declaration are each effective December 1, 2015. Official forms library.

Your court may also require local forms. Check your bankruptcy court's website before filing.

Purpose and statutory authority

The B106 series implements the individual debtor's statutory duty under 11 U.S.C. Section 521(a)(1)(B) to file a list of creditors and a schedule of assets and liabilities, a schedule of current income and current expenditures, a statement of the debtor's financial affairs, and copies of any payment advices. The schedules are the principal documentary record of what the bankruptcy estate contains, what the debtor owes, and what the debtor claims as exempt from administration.

The forms are promulgated under 28 U.S.C. Section 2075. Schedules are signed under penalty of perjury, which gives false-oath consequences under Section 727(a)(4) for Chapter 7 cases and under 18 U.S.C. Section 152 as a federal criminal matter.

Who must file

Every individual debtor (whether under Chapter 7, 11, 12, or 13) must file the B106 series. Joint debtors file one set of schedules covering both spouses' property and obligations, with column markings to indicate which spouse holds each item. Non-individual debtors use the B206 series instead.

Schedule-by-schedule walkthrough

B106Summary

Cover summary aggregating totals from each underlying schedule. Includes statistical summary of certain liabilities required for individual cases under Section 159 reporting.

B106A/B - Property

All real property (Part 1) and personal property (Parts 2-7), valued at fair market replacement value. Includes vehicles, household goods, electronics, collectibles, cash and bank accounts, financial assets, business interests, claims and causes of action, and any other interest of value.

B106C - Exemptions

Property the debtor claims as exempt from the estate. Debtor elects either the federal exemptions of 11 U.S.C. Section 522(d) or the applicable state exemptions, subject to opt-out states. Each item must reference the specific statutory subsection and the dollar amount claimed.

B106D - Secured creditors

All creditors holding claims secured by property, with description of collateral, amount of claim, value of collateral, and unsecured deficiency if any.

B106E/F - Unsecured creditors

Part 1 lists priority unsecured claims under Section 507(a) (domestic support, tax claims, wage claims, etc.). Part 2 lists general (non-priority) unsecured claims, with check boxes for contingent, unliquidated, and disputed status.

B106G - Executory contracts and unexpired leases

All ongoing contracts and leases (residential lease, vehicle lease, service contracts, etc.) that may be assumed or rejected under Section 365.

B106H - Codebtors

Individuals or entities also liable on any debts listed, including non-filing spouses, business partners, and guarantors. Important for codebtor stay analysis under Section 1301 in Chapter 13.

B106I and B106J - Income and expenses

Schedule I reports current monthly income from all sources for each spouse, and Schedule J reports current monthly expenses. The difference is the monthly net income that funds Chapter 13 plan payments or is examined in Chapter 7 abuse analysis under Section 707(b)(3).

Declaration

Form B106Dec (Declaration About an Individual Debtor's Schedules) is signed under penalty of perjury by each debtor and acknowledges that the information in the schedules is true and correct to the best of the debtor's knowledge.

Filing context and deadlines

Schedules must be filed with the petition or within 14 days thereafter, per Fed. R. Bankr. P. 1007(c). The court may extend the deadline on motion for cause. Amendments to schedules are permitted as of right before the case is closed, per Fed. R. Bankr. P. 1009(a). An amendment must be served on the trustee and any affected creditor, and a notice that the schedules have been amended is sent to all creditors when the amendment adds a creditor.

Common pitfalls

Undisclosed causes of action are a primary false-oath risk. Pending or potential lawsuits, employment-discrimination claims, personal-injury claims, and any other contingent claim the debtor holds against a third party are property of the estate under Section 541. Omission from Schedule A/B can produce judicial-estoppel preclusion in the later litigation in addition to false-oath exposure.

Undervaluing personal property. Replacement value, not garage-sale value, is the standard. Aggregate "household goods $500" with no itemization invites a Rule 2004 examination.

Missing the codebtor on a joint loan. A non-filing spouse on a vehicle loan must appear on Schedule H. Omission can produce automatic-stay issues for the codebtor in Chapter 13 cases.

Citing the wrong exemption authority. States that opt out of the federal scheme require state citations only; mixing federal and state citations on Schedule C is reversible on objection.

Schedule J expenses that do not match Form B122 means-test deductions. Discrepancies invite trustee scrutiny on both means-test compliance and plan-feasibility analysis.

Failure to amend after the meeting of creditors. Information that surfaces at the Section 341 meeting (an additional bank account, a missed creditor, a non-disclosed transfer) creates an obligation to amend promptly.

Related rules and forms

11 U.S.C. Section 521 - Debtor's duties

11 U.S.C. Section 522 - Exemptions

11 U.S.C. Section 541 - Property of the estate

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 1007 - Lists, schedules, and statements

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 1009 - Amendments

Form B101 - Voluntary Petition

Form B107 - Statement of Financial Affairs

Where to obtain the official current version

Current versions are maintained at the Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts. Individual schedules are posted at uscourts.gov/forms-rules/forms/bankruptcy-forms. The individual-debtor category page links each B106 sub-form, the declaration, and the summary form.

## Form B107 - Statement of Financial Affairs for Individuals [2026] - Bankruptcy Forms Reference
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/forms/b107-sofa/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Home > Forms > B107 Statement of Financial Affairs

Official Bankruptcy Form
B107

Form B107: Statement of Financial Affairs for Individuals

The narrative companion to the schedules: pre-petition history of payments, transfers, lawsuits, income, and financial accounts.

Download Official Form 107 (PDF, uscourts.gov)

Current version: updated April 1, 2025 (effective April 1, 2022), from uscourts.gov. Official form page.

Your court may also require local forms. Check your bankruptcy court's website before filing.

Purpose and statutory authority

Official Form B107 (Statement of Financial Affairs, often called the SOFA) implements 11 U.S.C. Section 521(a)(1)(B)(iii)'s requirement that the debtor file a "statement of the debtor's financial affairs." Where the B106 schedules photograph the debtor's situation as of the petition date, the SOFA traces the debtor's pre-petition financial activity, transfers, payments to creditors and insiders, lawsuits, repossessions, gifts, losses, and account activity. The SOFA is the primary source document the trustee uses to evaluate preferences, fraudulent transfers, undisclosed assets, and pre-petition planning.

The form is promulgated under 28 U.S.C. Section 2075 and signed under penalty of perjury, with false-oath consequences under Section 727(a)(4) and criminal exposure under 18 U.S.C. Section 152.

Who must file

Every individual debtor in Chapter 7, 11, 12, or 13 files Form B107. Joint debtors file one SOFA covering both spouses. Non-individual debtors file Form B207 instead.

The numbered inquiries

Parts 1-2: Income and payments

Lifetime employment income for the current and two prior calendar years, and other income sources. Payments to any creditor totaling $600+ within 90 days pre-petition (or $8,575 aggregate to a single non-consumer-debt creditor under Section 547(c)(9), as adjusted April 1, 2025).

Part 3: Insider transactions

All payments and transfers to or for the benefit of insiders (relatives, business affiliates, general partners) within one year pre-petition. This window matches Section 547(b)(4)(B) preference reach-back.

Parts 4-5: Legal actions and repossessions

All lawsuits, court actions, administrative proceedings, garnishments, attachments, and repossessions within one year pre-petition.

Parts 6-7: Charitable contributions and losses

Gifts and charitable contributions exceeding $600 within two years, and losses from theft, fire, casualty, or gambling within one year.

Parts 8-9: Professionals and other transfers

Payments to debt counseling agencies, bankruptcy attorneys, or other professionals consulted about debt or bankruptcy in the year pre-petition. Other transfers of property within two years (ten years for self-settled trusts under Section 548(e)).

Parts 10-13: Financial accounts and safe deposits

Bank accounts closed in the year pre-petition, safe deposit boxes used, setoffs by financial institutions, and property held for others.

Parts 14-17: Environmental, businesses, addresses, taxes

Environmental information (only if applicable), connection to any business within four years, prior addresses within three years (relevant to venue and exemption-state determination under Section 522(b)(3)), and personally identifiable customer information held.

Signature page

Declaration under penalty of perjury by each debtor and (if applicable) by a bankruptcy petition preparer under Section 110.

Filing context and deadlines

Form B107 is due with the petition or within 14 days after the petition is filed, per Fed. R. Bankr. P. 1007(c). Amendments are permitted under Fed. R. Bankr. P. 1009(a) at any time before the case is closed. The SOFA is reviewed line-by-line at the meeting of creditors under Section 341(a), where the trustee asks the debtor to confirm the answers under oath.

Common pitfalls

Part 3 insider payments are the most-litigated omission. Payments to a parent, sibling, or business affiliate within the one-year window must be disclosed even if the payment was a small loan repayment or rent. Trustees frequently pursue Section 547(b) and Section 548 actions seeded by Part 3 entries; omission can produce a Section 727(a)(4) false-oath denial of discharge.

Underreporting Part 1 income. Year-to-date income must be reconciled to W-2s, 1099s, and any K-1 distributions. Unreported business income from a side gig is a frequent meeting-of-creditors flag.

Part 4 garnishments not listed. A wage garnishment within 90 days that captured more than $600 is both a Part 4 entry and a potential Section 547(b) preference recovery for the trustee.

Part 9 attorney payment misalignment. The amount disclosed on the SOFA must match the disclosure on Form B2030 (Disclosure of Compensation of Attorney) and the actual fee paid; discrepancies are reviewed under Section 329.

Part 8 prior addresses incomplete. The two-year "domicile" lookback governs which state's exemptions apply under Section 522(b)(3)(A); missing addresses can foreclose the intended exemption election.

Part 18 connection to business omitted. Any sole proprietorship, partnership interest, or 5%+ interest in any corporation within four years pre-petition must be disclosed.

Related rules and forms

11 U.S.C. Section 547 - Preferences

11 U.S.C. Section 548 - Fraudulent transfers

11 U.S.C. Section 727 - Discharge in Chapter 7

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 1007 - Lists, schedules, and statements

Form B101 - Voluntary Petition

Form B106 series - Schedules

Where to obtain the official current version

The current SOFA is at the U.S. Courts forms library. See uscourts.gov/forms-rules/forms/bankruptcy-forms under the individual-debtor category. The form is revised periodically and dollar thresholds in Part 2 and Part 6 are adjusted on the three-year cycle of 11 U.S.C. Section 104.

## Form B108 - Statement of Intention for Individuals Filing Under Chapter 7 [2026] - Bankruptcy Forms Reference
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/forms/b108-statement-intention/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Home > Forms > B108 Statement of Intention

Official Bankruptcy Form
B108

Form B108: Statement of Intention for Individuals Filing Under Chapter 7

The debtor's election to reaffirm, redeem, surrender, or assume on each item of secured collateral and each leased personal property.

Download Official Form 108 (PDF, uscourts.gov)

Current version: effective December 1, 2015, from uscourts.gov. Official form page.

Your court may also require local forms. Check your bankruptcy court's website before filing.

Purpose and statutory authority

Official Form B108 implements 11 U.S.C. Section 521(a)(2), which requires an individual Chapter 7 debtor whose schedules include debts secured by property of the estate to file a statement of intention specifying how the debtor will treat each secured debt. The form also captures the debtor's intentions on personal-property leases under Section 365(p).

The intention statement is not itself a binding agreement. It is a declaration of plan: the debtor commits to perform the elected option within the post-petition windows set by Section 521(a)(2)(B) and Section 362(h).

Who must file

Every individual Chapter 7 debtor with scheduled secured debt or scheduled personal-property leases. Chapter 11, 12, and 13 debtors do not file Form B108; their treatment of secured debt and leases is handled through the plan and through Section 365 motions.

The four options for each secured debt

Reaffirm

Sign a reaffirmation agreement under Section 524(c) excepting the personal liability on the debt from discharge. Court approval is required if the debtor is not represented by counsel; if represented, counsel's certification under Section 524(c)(3) is required.

Redeem

Pay the secured creditor the allowed secured claim amount in a single lump sum under Section 722. Available only for tangible personal property primarily for personal, family, or household use that is exempt or has been abandoned.

Surrender

Give the property back to the secured creditor. The discharge eliminates personal liability on any deficiency.

Other (rare)

The form contains an "Other" line. Strategies sometimes shown here (such as "ride-through" or "pay and retain") have been substantially curtailed by Section 521(a)(6) and Section 362(h) for cases in courts that do not recognize them.

Personal-property leases

For each scheduled lease of personal property, the debtor elects to assume under Section 365(p)(2) or to reject (vehicle leases are the most common example). Assumption requires the debtor to notify the lessor in writing; the lessor may set conditions for assumption consistent with the underlying lease.

Deadlines

File Form B108: within 30 days after the date of filing the petition, or by the date of the meeting of creditors under Section 341(a), whichever is earlier (Section 521(a)(2)(A)).

Perform the election: within 30 days after the first date set for the meeting of creditors (Section 521(a)(2)(B)).

Section 362(h) deadline: if the debtor does not timely file the statement, or does not timely perform, the automatic stay terminates as to the collateral and the property is no longer property of the estate (Section 362(h)(1)).

Consequences of inaction

Section 362(h) is self-executing. If the statement of intention is not filed within the statutory window, or the elected action is not performed within 30 days of the first meeting of creditors, the automatic stay terminates as to the collateral and the property leaves the estate. The trustee may file a motion under Section 362(h)(2) to find that the property is of consequential value or benefit to the estate to keep the stay in place.

For personal-property leases, failure to timely assume under Section 365(p) is treated as rejection, and the lessor may proceed under state law to recover the property.

Common pitfalls

Reaffirmation without the means. A reaffirmation that creates a presumption of undue hardship under Section 524(m) requires court approval; the debtor's Schedule J must show ability to pay.

"Retain and pay" with no court approval. Outside of the few circuits that historically allowed ride-through, a debtor who keeps collateral without reaffirming, redeeming, or curing through plan provisions risks Section 362(h) termination and post-discharge repossession.

Failure to update on amended schedules. If a creditor or collateral is added by amendment, the statement of intention must be amended within 30 days of the amendment under Fed. R. Bankr. P. 1019(1)(B) principles.

Lease assumption without lessor cooperation. The lessor may decline assumption or may condition it on cure of arrears; the debtor cannot force assumption unilaterally.

Related rules and forms

11 U.S.C. Section 521(a)(2), (a)(6)

11 U.S.C. Section 362(h) - Automatic-stay termination

11 U.S.C. Section 524(c), (m) - Reaffirmation

11 U.S.C. Section 722 - Redemption

11 U.S.C. Section 365(p) - Lease assumption by individual

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 1007(b)(2)

Form B240A (Reaffirmation Agreement) and Form B240A/B ALT

Where to obtain the official current version

The form library is at uscourts.gov. See uscourts.gov/forms-rules/forms/bankruptcy-forms under the individual-debtor category.

Form B106 (Schedules)

## Form B121 - Statement About Your Social Security Numbers [2026] - Bankruptcy Forms Reference
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/forms/b121-ssn-statement/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Home > Forms > B121 Statement About Your Social Security Numbers

Official Bankruptcy Form
B121

Form B121: Statement About Your Social Security Numbers

The non-public form that carries the debtor's full SSN or ITIN, used by the court for identity verification and creditor notice while keeping the number off the public docket.

Download Official Form 121 (PDF, uscourts.gov)

Current version: effective December 1, 2015, from uscourts.gov. Official form page.

Your court may also require local forms. Check your bankruptcy court's website before filing.

Purpose and statutory authority

Official Form B121 is the means by which an individual debtor provides the court with the debtor's full Social Security Number (or Individual Taxpayer Identification Number, or statement that no SSN/ITIN has been issued). The form supports identity verification by the trustee, accurate creditor notice, and credit-bureau reporting of the bankruptcy filing. It is treated as a non-public record under Fed. R. Bankr. P. 1007(f) and is not posted to the public docket on PACER.

The form coordinates with Fed. R. Bankr. P. 9037(a), which limits public filings to the last four digits of any SSN or ITIN. Only the last four digits appear on Form B101 and other publicly-filed documents; the full number is captured here.

Who must file

Every individual debtor. Joint debtors file a single B121 listing both spouses' full numbers. A debtor with no SSN and no ITIN checks the corresponding box and provides any other government-issued identification information available.

What the form requires

Each debtor's legal name as it appears on the petition

Each debtor's full Social Security Number or full ITIN

If no SSN or ITIN, an attestation to that fact

Signature(s) of debtor(s) under penalty of perjury

Filing context and handling

Form B121 is filed with the petition under Fed. R. Bankr. P. 1007(b)(7) and 1007(c). It is delivered to the clerk in physical or sealed-electronic form. The court uses it (a) to verify the debtor's identity at the meeting of creditors under Section 341(a) and Fed. R. Bankr. P. 4002(b)(1)(A) (where the trustee compares the number to the debtor's government-issued photo identification), and (b) to populate the notices that the Bankruptcy Noticing Center sends to creditors and to the major consumer reporting agencies.

The form is not docketed publicly. Trustees and the court access it under court-supervised conditions; it is not available through ordinary PACER queries.

Coordination with Rule 9037

Form B121 is the safe place for full SSNs in a bankruptcy case. All other public filings, including Form B101 (Voluntary Petition), Form B309 (Notice of Bankruptcy Case), Form B410 (Proof of Claim), and any attachment such as a contract or loan agreement, must be redacted to the last four digits of SSN/ITIN under Fed. R. Bankr. P. 9037(a). The two forms are designed to operate together: full number on B121, last four digits everywhere public.

Common pitfalls

Wrong number on B121. A typo prevents creditor matching and may require an amended B121 plus a notice to creditors who received the wrong number. Fed. R. Bankr. P. 1009(a) permits amendment as of right.

SSN appearing in full on other filings. Even though Form B121 is non-public, a filer who attaches a loan contract showing the full SSN to a proof of claim or motion has created a Rule 9037 exposure independent of B121.

Joint petition with only one SSN listed. Both spouses' full numbers must appear when a joint petition is filed.

Mismatch with government ID at Section 341 meeting. The trustee verifies the number against the debtor's photo ID; a discrepancy can adjourn the meeting and trigger a Rule 4002 examination.

Related rules and forms

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 1007(b)(7), (f) - Required statement and non-public treatment

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 9037 - Privacy protection for filings made with the court

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 4002(b)(1) - Documentation of identity at the meeting of creditors

Form B101 - Voluntary Petition (public, last four digits only)

Rule 9037 reference page

Where to obtain the official current version

See uscourts.gov/forms-rules/forms/bankruptcy-forms under the individual-debtor category. The form is short and changes infrequently.

Form B106 (Schedules)
Form B201A (342(b) Notice)

## Form B122A-1 - Chapter 7 Statement of Current Monthly Income [2026] - Bankruptcy Forms Reference
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/forms/b122a-1-means-test-ch7/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Home > Forms > B122A-1 Chapter 7 Statement of Current Monthly Income

Official Bankruptcy Form
B122A-1

Form B122A-1: Chapter 7 Statement of Your Current Monthly Income

The means-test entry point: compute current monthly income, annualize, and compare to the state median to determine whether Form B122A-2 must also be filed.

Download Official Form 122A-1 (PDF, uscourts.gov)
Download Official Form 122A-1Supp (PDF, uscourts.gov)

Current versions, from uscourts.gov: Form 122A-1 effective December 1, 2019; Form 122A-1Supp effective December 1, 2015. Official form page. Filers whose income is above the state median also file Form 122A-2.

Your court may also require local forms. Check your bankruptcy court's website before filing.

Purpose and statutory authority

Official Form B122A-1 implements the income-side calculation of the Chapter 7 means test under 11 U.S.C. Section 707(b)(2) and the definition of "current monthly income" in Section 101(10A). The form computes the debtor's average monthly income from all sources during the six full calendar months preceding the filing month, annualizes the figure, and compares it to the median family income for the debtor's household size in the debtor's state of residence (as published by the United States Trustee Program).

Where annualized current monthly income is at or below the state median, the means-test inquiry is satisfied at the income step. Where it exceeds the state median, the debtor must also file Form B122A-2 (Means Test Calculation) to compute allowable expense deductions and the resulting disposable-income figure that drives the presumption of abuse under Section 707(b)(2)(A).

Who must file

Every individual Chapter 7 debtor with primarily consumer debts. A debtor whose debts are primarily non-consumer (e.g., business debts exceed consumer debts in dollar amount) is exempt from the means test under Section 707(b)(1) but still files B122A-1 with the non-consumer-debt exclusion box checked. Disabled veterans who incurred their indebtedness primarily during active duty also have a statutory exclusion at Section 707(b)(2)(D).

How current monthly income is computed

Average gross income from all sources received in the six full calendar months immediately preceding the calendar month in which the petition is filed

Includes wages, salary, business income, rental income, interest, dividends, pension and retirement income, unemployment compensation (with a Section 101(10A)(B) carve-out for benefits received under the Social Security Act)

Includes regular contributions from any source for household expenses, including from a non-filing spouse or other household member

Excludes Social Security Act benefits, victims-of-war-crimes payments, victims-of-terrorism payments, and similar statutory exclusions

Marital adjustment

For a married debtor not filing jointly, the non-filing spouse's income is reported as part of household current monthly income, then adjusted on Line 13 to back out amounts not regularly contributed to household expenses of the debtor or the debtor's dependents.

Median-income comparison

The form references the United States Trustee Program's means-testing data tables, which publish state median family income by household size and update twice yearly (typically May 1 and November 1). The applicable table is determined by the petition date.

Filing context and deadlines

Form B122A-1 is filed with the petition or within 14 days after the petition date, per Fed. R. Bankr. P. 1007(b)(4) and (c). If the income computation produces an above-median result, Form B122A-2 is due on the same schedule. The United States Trustee files a Statement of Presumed Abuse under Section 704(b)(1) within 10 days of the meeting of creditors when warranted.

Common pitfalls

The six-month CMI period is fixed by statute; it does not end on the petition date. It ends on the last day of the calendar month preceding the petition month. A petition filed June 10 uses December through May income; a petition filed June 30 uses the same period. Filers sometimes shift the petition date by a few days to capture a more favorable six-month average.

Including or excluding bonus and overtime incorrectly. Bonus and overtime received during the CMI window are CMI even if irregular; the proper place to argue that they will not recur is Form B122A-2's "additional expense or income adjustments" or in a Section 707(b)(2)(B) special-circumstances showing.

Household size errors. The household size for median comparison is not always the "number of people living in the home." Courts use different approaches (income-tax dependent test, IRS dependency test, economic-unit test). The chosen method should be consistent with Schedule J and the local approach.

Misclassifying non-consumer debt. A bright-line dollar test compares scheduled consumer debts to scheduled non-consumer debts; misclassification of debt category on the schedules ripples into the B122A-1 non-consumer exclusion box.

Using stale median figures. The applicable median table is the one in effect on the petition date. A petition filed close to a USTP table update should be checked against the date-of-filing table.

Related rules and forms

11 U.S.C. Section 101(10A) - Definition of current monthly income

11 U.S.C. Section 707(b) - Dismissal of Chapter 7 case for abuse

11 U.S.C. Section 704(b) - U.S. Trustee statement of presumed abuse

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 1007(b)(4)

Form B122A-2 - Chapter 7 Means Test Calculation

Form B122A-1 Supp - Statement of Exemption from Presumption of Abuse Under Section 707(b)(2)

Where to obtain the official current version

See uscourts.gov/forms-rules/forms/bankruptcy-forms under "Means Test Forms." Median income and expense tables are at justice.gov/ust/means-testing.

Official Bankruptcy Form
B122B

Form B122B: Chapter 11 Statement of Your Current Monthly Income

Income computation for an individual Chapter 11 debtor, feeding the projected-disposable-income confirmation requirement of Section 1129(a)(15).

Who uses this form: an individual debtor in a Chapter 11 case, other than under Subchapter V, files Form 122B under Fed. R. Bankr. P. 1007(b)(5). Chapter 7 filers use Form 122A-1 and Chapter 13 filers use Form 122C-1.

Purpose and statutory authority

Official Form B122B captures current monthly income for an individual Chapter 11 debtor. The form supports the projected-disposable-income test for confirmation of an individual Chapter 11 plan under 11 U.S.C. Section 1129(a)(15), which (where an unsecured creditor objects) requires that the plan either pay the unsecured claim in full or commit projected disposable income (as defined by reference to Section 1325(b)(2)) over a five-year period.

The "B" in B122B reflects its position in the means-test family: B122A series for Chapter 7, B122B for Chapter 11, B122C series for Chapter 13. All three use the same Section 101(10A) definition of current monthly income but apply it to different confirmation and abuse-screening machinery.

Who must file

Every individual debtor in Chapter 11, including individual debtors who elect to be treated under Subchapter V of Chapter 11 (Section 1182). Non-individual Chapter 11 debtors (corporations, LLCs, partnerships) do not file Form B122B because Section 1129(a)(15) applies only to individuals.

Note: although the form's archival reference sometimes uses the phrase "non-individual" loosely (because the form is the income statement on the "B" track distinct from the "A" individual-Chapter-7 track and the "C" individual-Chapter-13 track), in practice Form B122B is the individual-Chapter-11 instrument. Non-individual Chapter 11 debtors are not subject to the personal-debtor means-test family.

How current monthly income is computed

The computation tracks Form B122A-1 closely:

Gross income from all sources averaged across the six full calendar months preceding the petition month

Includes wages, salary, business income, rental income, interest and dividends, pension and retirement income, regular household contributions from any source

Excludes Social Security Act benefits and the other categorical exclusions of Section 101(10A)(B)

Joint debtor income is combined; non-filing spousal income flows through the marital-adjustment line

Relationship to Section 1129(a)(15)

Form B122B is the income-side input to the Section 1129(a)(15) calculation, which is triggered only if the holder of an allowed unsecured claim objects to confirmation. Where triggered, the debtor must show either (A) that the plan pays the allowed unsecured claim in full as of the effective date, or (B) that the value of property to be distributed under the plan over the longer of five years or the plan term is not less than the debtor's projected disposable income.

"Projected disposable income" in this context borrows the Chapter 13 definition in Section 1325(b)(2): current monthly income minus amounts reasonably necessary for the debtor's and dependents' maintenance and support, charitable contributions up to 15% of gross income, and business-operations expenses where applicable.

Filing context and deadlines

Form B122B is filed with the petition or within 14 days under Fed. R. Bankr. P. 1007(b)(6) and (c). Confirmation is generally not earlier than the Section 1125 disclosure-statement process for traditional Chapter 11 cases, or the Section 1188 status-conference timeline for Subchapter V cases. The Form B122B figures inform the plan-feasibility and projected-disposable-income showings at confirmation.

Common pitfalls

Treating B122B as a presumption-of-abuse form. Unlike Chapter 7's Section 707(b)(2) machinery, Chapter 11 does not use the means-test result to dismiss the case for presumed abuse. The B122B output is a confirmation-stage input, not a screening filter.

Inconsistency with the operating-business projections. An individual Chapter 11 debtor running a small business (often the Subchapter V context) presents projected income via Form B122B and via the plan exhibits; consistency between the six-month historical CMI and the prospective projections is examined at confirmation.

Stale figures at confirmation. Where confirmation occurs months after filing, courts have sometimes required an updated Form B122B or supplemental projection if the underlying income has materially changed.

Misapplied Social Security exclusion. The exclusion is for benefits under the Social Security Act; private disability and pension income generally is not excluded.

Related rules and forms

11 U.S.C. Section 101(10A) - Current monthly income

11 U.S.C. Section 1129(a)(15) - Individual Chapter 11 confirmation

11 U.S.C. Section 1325(b) - Projected disposable income (borrowed reference)

11 U.S.C. Section 1182 - Subchapter V definitions

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 1007(b)(6)

Where to obtain the official current version

See uscourts.gov/forms-rules/forms/bankruptcy-forms under "Means Test Forms." Income exclusion definitions track the United States Trustee Program guidance at justice.gov/ust/means-testing.

## Form B122C-1 - Chapter 13 Statement of Current Monthly Income and Calculation of Commitment Period [2026] - Bankruptcy Forms Reference
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/forms/b122c-1-ch13-calculation/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Home > Forms > B122C-1 Chapter 13 Statement of Current Monthly Income and Commitment Period

Official Bankruptcy Form
B122C-1

Form B122C-1: Chapter 13 Statement of Current Monthly Income and Calculation of Commitment Period

The income side of Chapter 13 confirmation analysis: compute CMI, compare to the state median, and set the 3-year or 5-year applicable commitment period.

Download Official Form 122C-1 (PDF, uscourts.gov)

Current version: effective October 1, 2019, from uscourts.gov. Official form page.

Your court may also require local forms. Check your bankruptcy court's website before filing.

Purpose and statutory authority

Official Form B122C-1 implements the income computation for a Chapter 13 debtor under 11 U.S.C. Section 1325(b) and the definition of "current monthly income" at Section 101(10A). The form computes annualized CMI, compares to the state median family income for the household size, and determines the "applicable commitment period" of either three years (below-median) or five years (at- or above-median) under Section 1325(b)(4).

Where the debtor is at or above the state median, the debtor must also file Form B122C-2 (Calculation of Your Disposable Income), which applies the Section 707(b)(2)-style expense deductions to produce the projected disposable income figure the plan must commit if an unsecured creditor or the trustee objects under Section 1325(b)(1)(B).

Who must file

Every individual debtor in Chapter 13. Joint debtors file one combined B122C-1 covering household income.

How current monthly income is computed

Gross income from all sources averaged across the six full calendar months preceding the petition month

Includes wages, salary, business income, rental income, interest, dividends, pension and retirement income, and regular household contributions

Excludes benefits received under the Social Security Act, victims-of-war-crimes payments, victims-of-terrorism payments, and the other Section 101(10A)(B) exclusions

Non-filing spouse income is included as household income, with a marital-adjustment line for amounts not regularly contributed

Applicable commitment period

Below-median: 3 years

If annualized CMI is below the applicable state median family income for the debtor's household size, the applicable commitment period under Section 1325(b)(4)(A)(i) is three years. The plan may run longer for cause approved by the court but cannot exceed five years.

At- or above-median: 5 years

If annualized CMI equals or exceeds the applicable state median, the commitment period is five years under Section 1325(b)(4)(A)(ii). The five-year cap is absolute under Section 1322(d)(1).

Median-income comparison

The form references the United States Trustee Program's median family income tables at justice.gov/ust/means-testing. The applicable table is the one in effect on the petition date; USTP updates tables on the May 1 / November 1 cycle.

Filing context and deadlines

Form B122C-1 is filed with the petition or within 14 days under Fed. R. Bankr. P. 1007(b)(6) and (c). If above-median, Form B122C-2 is due on the same schedule. The confirmation hearing under Section 1324 is held not earlier than 20 days nor later than 45 days after the meeting of creditors, per Section 1324(b); the disposable-income analysis is the principal substantive confirmation issue raised by the trustee and unsecured creditors.

Common pitfalls

The applicable commitment period is a "temporal" floor, not just a "value" floor. Even where the debtor has zero projected disposable income, the Supreme Court's analysis in Hamilton v. Lanning and circuit-level treatment generally requires that the plan extend over the full applicable commitment period (3 or 5 years) unless the unsecured class is paid in full.

Household-size mismatch with Schedule J. A debtor who claims one household size on B122C-1 and a different size on Schedule J invites trustee scrutiny on both filings.

Non-recurring income included without explanation. Large one-time bonuses or settlement proceeds received in the six-month window can push a below-median debtor above the median; supplemental B122C-1 amendments or special-circumstances showings under Section 707(b)(2)(B) (incorporated by Section 1325) may be needed.

Stale median tables. A petition filed within days of a USTP table update should be checked against the date-of-filing table.

Self-employed business income. Business income is reported on B122C-1 net of ordinary and necessary operating expenses (not gross receipts); Schedule I-style gross-revenue figures may not match.

Related rules and forms

11 U.S.C. Section 101(10A) - Current monthly income

11 U.S.C. Section 1322(d) - Plan duration

11 U.S.C. Section 1325(b) - Disposable income; applicable commitment period

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 1007(b)(6)

Form B122C-2 - Chapter 13 Calculation of Your Disposable Income

Where to obtain the official current version

See uscourts.gov/forms-rules/forms/bankruptcy-forms under "Means Test Forms." Median income and IRS-derived expense tables are at justice.gov/ust/means-testing.

Form B106 (Schedules)
Form B122A-1 (Ch. 7)
Form B122B (Ch. 11)
Section 1328 Discharge

## Form B201A - Notice Required by 11 U.S.C. Section 342(b) for Individuals Filing for Bankruptcy [2026] - Bankruptcy Forms Reference
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/forms/b201-individual-notice/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Home > Forms > B201A Section 342(b) Notice for Individuals

Official Bankruptcy Form
B201A

Form B201A: Notice Required by 11 U.S.C. Section 342(b) for Individuals Filing for Bankruptcy

The mandatory written notice that must be given to a consumer debtor before the petition is filed, summarizing the chapters and the consequences of bankruptcy.

Download Form 2010, the Section 342(b) Notice (PDF, uscourts.gov)

uscourts.gov lists this notice as Director's Form B 2010, derived from Form 201A. Current version: effective December 1, 2020, from uscourts.gov. Official form page.

Your court may also require local forms. Check your bankruptcy court's website before filing.

Purpose and statutory authority

Official Form B201A is the standardized written notice that 11 U.S.C. Section 342(b) requires a clerk of court (and, when an attorney is involved, the attorney) to give to an individual consumer debtor before a petition is filed. The notice describes the four chapters under which an individual may file, summarizes the services available from credit-counseling agencies, advises about debt-relief-agency disclosures, and warns about bankruptcy crimes under 18 U.S.C. Section 152 and related provisions.

The notice is one of two consumer-protection disclosures the 2005 Bankruptcy Abuse Prevention and Consumer Protection Act added at filing. The companion is Form B2030 (Disclosure of Compensation of Attorney for Debtor) under Section 329.

Who must give and receive the notice

The clerk of the bankruptcy court must give the notice to any individual whose debts are primarily consumer debts under Section 342(b). When the debtor is represented by an attorney, the attorney also delivers the notice as part of the pre-filing intake. The debtor's receipt of the notice is confirmed on the petition itself (Form B101, Part 5), where the debtor signs an acknowledgment.

What the notice contains

Chapter 7 - Liquidation

Explanation of the liquidation process, eligibility under the means test, the trustee's role, and the discharge.

Chapter 13 - Adjustment of debts

Plain-English description of the 3- to 5-year plan structure, the role of the standing trustee, and the eligibility limits under Section 109(e).

Chapter 11 - Reorganization

Short description of the reorganization process, with note that individuals may proceed under Chapter 11 (including Subchapter V where eligible).

Chapter 12 - Family farmer or fisherman

Short description of the specialized adjustment process available to family farmers and family fishermen with regular annual income meeting the Section 101(18)/(19A) thresholds.

Additional content

Statement that bankruptcy is a serious step with long-term consequences

Notice of credit-counseling and debtor-education requirements under Section 109(h) and Section 727(a)(11) / 1328(g)

Notice of bankruptcy-crime exposure for false statements, concealment of assets, and similar conduct

Notice of debt-relief-agency status and disclosure obligations under Sections 526-528 (if applicable to the assisting professional)

Notice of the right to file pro se

Filing context and deadlines

Section 342(b) requires the notice to be given before the petition is filed. The debtor's receipt acknowledgment appears on the petition. Fed. R. Bankr. P. 1007(b)(3) also requires the debtor to file a certificate from an approved credit-counseling agency under Section 521(b)(1); that is a separate document from the 342(b) notice but is closely associated in the consumer-debtor intake workflow.

Common pitfalls

Stale notice version. Form B201A has been revised since 2005 to reflect statutory amendments. Using an out-of-date version (for example, one that omits the Subchapter V reference or uses superseded dollar thresholds) is the principal compliance problem at filing.

Notice not given pre-filing. Where the debtor is represented, the attorney's intake checklist should document delivery of B201A before petition signature.

Acknowledgment box on B101 left unchecked. An incomplete acknowledgment on the petition produces a clerk's deficiency notice and may delay docketing.

Wrong notice used for non-consumer-debt debtor. Section 342(b) by its terms covers an individual whose debts are primarily consumer debts. Many practitioners still deliver the notice to a debtor with primarily non-consumer debts to support a clean record.

Related rules and forms

11 U.S.C. Section 342(b) - Notice to consumer debtors

11 U.S.C. Section 109(h) - Credit counseling

11 U.S.C. Sections 526-528 - Debt relief agency provisions

18 U.S.C. Section 152 - Concealment of assets; false oaths and claims; bribery

Form B101 - Voluntary Petition

Form B2030 - Disclosure of Compensation of Attorney for Debtor

Where to obtain the official current version

See uscourts.gov/forms-rules/forms/bankruptcy-forms under "Director's Procedural Forms." Note that the official numbering family for the 342(b) notice is the 200-series and the variant for individuals is B201A; B201B is reserved for non-individual notices where applicable.

Form B106 (Schedules)
Form B107 (SOFA)
