## Form B309A - Notice of Chapter 7 Bankruptcy Case (No Proof of Claim Required) [2026] - Bankruptcy Forms Reference
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/forms/b309a-meeting-creditors/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Home > Forms > B309A Notice of Chapter 7 Bankruptcy Case

Official Bankruptcy Form
B309A

Form B309A: Notice of Chapter 7 Bankruptcy Case (No Proof of Claim Required)

The court-issued notice that goes to every scheduled creditor in a Chapter 7 no-asset case, setting the meeting of creditors and announcing that no proofs of claim are required at this time.

Who uses this form: the bankruptcy clerk generally completes Form 309A and sends it to creditors, according to the official Form 309 instructions. A debtor does not fill it out or file it.

Purpose and statutory authority

Official Form B309A is the standardized "Notice of Chapter 7 Bankruptcy Case" issued by the clerk of the bankruptcy court in a Chapter 7 case where the trustee's preliminary determination is that the case has no assets available for distribution to unsecured creditors. The notice implements 11 U.S.C. Section 342(a)'s requirement that creditors receive notice of the case and key deadlines, and Fed. R. Bankr. P. 2002(a)'s 21-day-minimum notice for the meeting of creditors and related deadlines.

The "A" variant in the 309 family is the no-asset Chapter 7 notice. The 309 family includes Form B309B (Chapter 7 asset case, proof-of-claim deadline included), B309C (Chapter 11 non-individual), B309D (Chapter 11 individual), B309E1/E2 (Chapter 11 Subchapter V), B309F1/F2 (Chapter 11 non-Subchapter V), B309G (Chapter 12), B309H (Chapter 13), and B309I (Chapter 13 with asset deadline).

Who issues and who receives

The clerk of the bankruptcy court (through the Bankruptcy Noticing Center) issues Form B309A. It is mailed to every creditor and party in interest listed on the debtor's creditor matrix, to the debtor, to the Chapter 7 trustee, and to the United States Trustee. Service is typically by U.S. mail; creditors may opt in to electronic noticing through the BNC.

Key information on the notice

Case identification

Case number, district, debtor name(s) and aliases, debtor address(es), last four digits of SSN/ITIN under Rule 9037(a), filing date, and chapter.

Trustee and meeting

Name and contact information for the appointed Chapter 7 trustee, date/time/location (or virtual access information) for the Section 341 meeting of creditors.

Discharge-objection deadline

Deadline for filing a complaint objecting to discharge under Section 727 or to determine the dischargeability of a debt under Section 523(c): 60 days after the first date set for the meeting of creditors, per Fed. R. Bankr. P. 4004(a) and 4007(c).

Exemption-objection deadline

Deadline for objections to claims of exemption under Fed. R. Bankr. P. 4003(b): 30 days after the conclusion of the meeting of creditors.

Automatic-stay notice

Statement that the filing of the bankruptcy case operates as an automatic stay under Section 362(a) prohibiting most collection efforts against the debtor and property of the estate.

No-asset claim language

Statement that the trustee believes there will be no property available for distribution from the estate, and that creditors therefore should not file a proof of claim at this time. If assets are later identified, a subsequent notice (Form B309B or equivalent) will set a bar date.

Filing context and timing

The notice issues shortly after the petition is filed and the trustee is appointed. The meeting of creditors must be held not less than 21 nor more than 40 days after the order for relief under Section 341(a) and Fed. R. Bankr. P. 2003(a). The notice therefore typically goes out within the first 7-14 days post-petition.

Common pitfalls

"No proof of claim required" is conditional. If the trustee later identifies assets, the court issues a separate "Notice of Possible Dividend" or a B309B-style notice setting a bar date. Creditors should monitor the docket for case-status changes; the no-asset notice is not a permanent disposition.

Missing creditor on the matrix. A creditor not listed on the debtor's creditor matrix does not receive the notice and may not be bound by the discharge for the listed-creditor purposes of Section 523(a)(3).

Stale address. Creditors with an address change should ensure the bankruptcy clerk has the current address on file, particularly for credit-card or medical-debt creditors whose servicers may relocate.

Confusing B309A with B309B. If you receive a B309B (asset case) or a follow-on Notice of Possible Dividend, the proof-of-claim deadline applies and missing it can foreclose distribution.

Discharge-objection deadlines run from the first-set meeting date. Continuances of the meeting of creditors do not extend the 60-day discharge-objection deadline unless an extension is timely sought under Fed. R. Bankr. P. 4004(b) or 4007(c).

Related rules and forms

11 U.S.C. Section 341 - Meetings of creditors

11 U.S.C. Section 342 - Notice

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 2002 - Notices to creditors

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 2003 - Meeting of creditors

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 4004 - Grant or denial of discharge

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 4007 - Dischargeability complaints

Form B309B - Notice of Chapter 7 Bankruptcy Case (proof of claim required)

Form B410 - Proof of Claim

Where to obtain the official current version

See uscourts.gov/forms-rules/forms/bankruptcy-forms under "Director's Procedural Forms" / "Notice forms." Note that the Form 309 family includes variants for every chapter and a Subchapter V split (E1/E2); using the wrong variant for the case chapter is a common clerk's-office issue corrected by re-noticing.

Form B121 (SSN)
Rule 9037 (Redaction)

## Form 103A: Pay the Bankruptcy Filing Fee in Installments [Free PDF] - Bankruptcy Forms Reference
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/forms/b103a-filing-fee-installments/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Home > Forms > 103A Pay Filing Fee in Installments

Official Bankruptcy Form
103A

Official Form 103A: Application for Individuals to Pay the Filing Fee in Installments

The form an individual files with the petition to ask the court for permission to pay the bankruptcy filing fee in up to four payments instead of all at once.

Download Official Form 103A (PDF, uscourts.gov)

Current version: effective December 1, 2015 (form marked 12/15), from uscourts.gov. Official form page.

Your court may also require local forms. Check your bankruptcy court's website before filing.

What Form 103A is

Official Form 103A is an application to pay the bankruptcy filing fee in installments. Under Fed. R. Bankr. P. 1006(b)(1), the clerk must accept an individual's voluntary petition for filing, even if no part of the fee is paid, when the petition comes with a completed and signed Form 103A.

The form has two parts. Part 1 is the proposed payment timetable. Part 2 is the signature, where the filer states that they cannot pay the full fee at once. The form also includes a proposed order that the court may use, change, or replace with its own.

Who files it

Individuals file Form 103A. Line 1 of the form covers Chapter 7, 11, 12, and 13 cases. The official instructions state that the form is not meant for a filer who can afford to pay the full fee at filing. A Chapter 7 filer who cannot pay the fee at all, even in installments, may qualify to ask for a waiver on Official Form 103B.

When it is filed

The official instructions list Form 103A among the documents filed on the date the case is opened, alongside the petition, when the filer cannot pay the entire fee.

The payment limits in Rule 1006

No more than four installments. The court designates the number of installments, which may not exceed four, along with the amount and date of each.

120 days. All payments must be made within 120 days after the petition is filed.

Extension up to 180 days. The court may extend the time for an installment for cause, but the last one must be paid within 180 days after filing.

Court decides the timetable. Before the meeting of creditors, the court may order payment of the whole fee or set installments. The form states that if the court approves the application, the court will set the final payment timetable.

Filing fee amounts

The "entire fee" the installments must add up to depends on the chapter. These totals match the fees printed in the official instructions:

Chapter 7: $338

$245 filing fee under 28 U.S.C. Section 1930(a)(1)(A), plus the $78 administrative fee and the $15 trustee fee set by the Judicial Conference's miscellaneous fee schedule.

Chapter 13: $313

$235 filing fee under 28 U.S.C. Section 1930(a)(1)(B), plus the $78 administrative fee.

Chapter 12: $278

$200 filing fee under 28 U.S.C. Section 1930(a)(5), plus the $78 administrative fee.

Chapter 11: $1,738

$1,167 filing fee under 28 U.S.C. Section 1930(a)(3), plus the $571 administrative fee.

What attaches to it

If a bankruptcy petition preparer helped complete the form, the instructions call for the preparer's Notice, Declaration, and Signature (Official Form 119) to be included.

The last page of the form is the court's order approving installment payments, which the court fills in.

Common problems the form and rule point to

Proposed payments that do not add up. The form states that the total must equal the entire fee for the chapter checked on line 1.

A timetable outside the rule. More than four installments, or a final payment later than 120 days after filing, falls outside Rule 1006(b)(2) unless the court extends it.

An unsigned or incomplete application. Rule 1006(b)(1) requires a completed and signed application for the clerk to accept a petition without the fee.

Paying others first. Until the fee is paid in full, Rule 1006(b)(3) bars further payment to an attorney or anyone else who provides services in connection with the case.

A missed installment. The form warns that if a payment is not made when due, the case may be dismissed. It also states that debts will not be discharged until the entire fee is paid.

Related forms and pages

Form 103B (Fee Waiver)
Form 101 (Petition)
Bankruptcy Filing Fees
All Forms

Frequently asked questions

How many installments can the bankruptcy filing fee be split into?
Under Fed. R. Bankr. P. 1006(b)(2), the court may allow no more than four installments, and all payments must be made within 120 days after the petition is filed. For cause, the court may extend an installment, but the last one must be paid within 180 days after filing.
Can debts be discharged before the filing fee is paid?
Official Form 103A states that debts will not be discharged until the entire filing fee is paid.
Where is the official Form 103A?
The current Official Form 103A, effective December 1, 2015, is free on uscourts.gov. This page links directly to that PDF.

Sources

## Bankruptcy Fee Waiver Form 103B: Application to Waive the Chapter 7 Filing Fee [Free PDF] - Bankruptcy Forms Reference
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/forms/b103b-chapter-7-fee-waiver/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Home > Forms > 103B Chapter 7 Fee Waiver

Official Bankruptcy Form
103B

Official Form 103B: Application to Have the Chapter 7 Filing Fee Waived

The form an individual files with a Chapter 7 petition to ask the court to waive the filing fee entirely.

Download Official Form 103B (PDF, uscourts.gov)

Current version: effective December 1, 2015 (form marked 12/15), from uscourts.gov. Official form page.

Your court may also require local forms. Check your bankruptcy court's website before filing.

What Form 103B is

Official Form 103B is an application asking the bankruptcy court to waive the Chapter 7 filing fee. The authority for the waiver is 28 U.S.C. Section 1930(f)(1), which lets the court waive the fee in a Chapter 7 case for an individual. Under Fed. R. Bankr. P. 1006(c), the clerk must accept an individual's voluntary Chapter 7 petition when it comes with a completed and signed Form 103B.

The Chapter 7 fee is $338: a $245 filing fee under Section 1930(a)(1)(A), plus the $78 administrative fee and the $15 trustee fee from the Judicial Conference's miscellaneous fee schedule.

Who qualifies

The official instructions say that for the fee to be waived, all of these statements must be true:

The case is filed under Chapter 7.

The filer is an individual.

The total combined monthly income for the filer's family is less than 150% of the official poverty guideline last published by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services.

The filer cannot afford to pay the fee in installments.

Section 1930(f)(1) states the same two tests: income less than 150 percent of the poverty line for a family of that size, and inability to pay the fee in installments. The instructions point to uscourts.gov bankruptcy case policies for more on the guidelines. The form defines "family" as the filer, a spouse, and dependents, and the instructions note that family may differ from the "household" used on Schedules I and J.

A filer under Chapter 11, 12, or 13, or a filer who can pay in installments, would look at Official Form 103A for installment payments instead.

What the form asks

Part 1: family size, the family's average monthly net income, any non-cash government assistance, expected income changes, and why the fee cannot be paid in installments within 120 days.

Part 2: average monthly expenses and who else helps pay them.

Part 3: property, including cash, accounts, a home, other real estate, vehicles, and money owed to the filer. A filer who has already completed Schedule A/B attaches copies and skips to Part 4.

Part 4: payments made or promised to anyone for help with the bankruptcy, and any bankruptcy filed in the last 8 years.

Part 5: a signature under penalty of perjury declaring that the filer cannot afford the fee in full or in installments.

When it is filed and what attaches

The official instructions list Form 103B among the documents filed on the date the case is opened, for a Chapter 7 filer who meets the waiver criteria. Attachments the form and instructions mention:

Copies of Schedule A/B, if already completed (form, Part 3).

The bankruptcy petition preparer's Notice, Declaration, and Signature (Official Form 119), if a preparer helped.

What the court can decide

According to the instructions, after reviewing the application the court may waive the fee, set a hearing, or require the fee to be paid in installments or in full. The order printed at the end of the form shows three outcomes:

Granted. The order states that the court may still order the fee paid later if developments in the case show the waiver was unwarranted.

Denied. The court sets payment terms. The order states that the debtor may propose a different timetable, and may use Form 103A to do so.

Scheduled for hearing. The order states that if the debtor does not appear, the court may deny the application.

Common problems the form and statute point to

Wrong chapter. Section 1930(f)(1) and the form title limit this waiver to Chapter 7.

Income at or above the limit. The test is income less than 150% of the poverty guideline for the family's size.

No explanation on line 5. The form asks why the fee cannot be paid in installments within 120 days.

Missing the hearing. The order form states that the court may deny the application if the debtor does not appear.

An unsigned application. Rule 1006(c) requires a completed and signed application.

Related forms and pages

Form 103A (Installments)
How a Fee Waiver Request Works
Form 106 (Schedules)
All Forms

Frequently asked questions

Who qualifies for a Chapter 7 bankruptcy fee waiver?
Under 28 U.S.C. Section 1930(f)(1) and the official instructions, the filer must be an individual filing under Chapter 7, the family's total combined monthly income must be less than 150% of the official poverty guideline for the family's size, and the filer must be unable to pay the fee in installments.
Can Form 103B waive the Chapter 13 filing fee?
No. Form 103B and Section 1930(f)(1) cover the Chapter 7 filing fee. For other chapters, Official Form 103A is the application to pay the fee in installments.
What happens if the fee waiver is denied?
The order on Form 103B states that the court sets payment terms, and the debtor may propose a different timetable, for example on Official Form 103A.

## Official Form 113 Chapter 13 Plan [Free PDF] and When a Local Plan Form Applies - Bankruptcy Forms Reference
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/forms/b113-chapter-13-plan/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Home > Forms > 113 Chapter 13 Plan

Official Bankruptcy Form
113
Chapter 13

Official Form 113: Chapter 13 Plan

The national form for a Chapter 13 repayment plan. A district may instead require its own single local plan form under Rule 3015.1.

Download Official Form 113 (PDF, uscourts.gov)

Current version: effective December 1, 2017 (form marked 12/17), from uscourts.gov. Official form page.

Your court may also require local forms. Check your bankruptcy court's website before filing.

Check for a local plan form first. Under Fed. R. Bankr. P. 3015(c)(1), a Chapter 13 debtor must use Form 113 unless the court has adopted a local form under Rule 3015.1. Rule 3015.1 allows a district to require a single local form instead of Form 113. The bankruptcy court's website shows whether a local plan form is in use.

What Form 113 is

Official Form 113 is the plan a Chapter 13 debtor proposes for paying creditors over time. The committee note describes it as the required plan form in all Chapter 13 cases, except where Rule 3015(c) permits a local form. The form itself warns debtors that an option appearing on the form does not mean it is appropriate in a given case or permitted in a given district, and that plans that do not comply with local rules and judicial rulings may not be confirmable.

What a local plan form must contain

Rule 3015.1 sets requirements for any local form used in place of Form 113. Among them, the local form must:

be adopted for the district after public notice and an opportunity for comment;

number and label each paragraph in boldface with a heading;

open with a paragraph where the debtor indicates whether the plan contains a nonstandard provision, limits a secured claim based on collateral value, or avoids a security interest or lien;

contain separate paragraphs on curing and maintaining home loan payments, domestic support obligations, claims described in the final paragraph of Section 1325(a), and surrender of property; and

end with a place for nonstandard provisions and a certification by the debtor's attorney, or by an unrepresented debtor, that there are no other nonstandard provisions.

When the plan is due

Under Rule 3015(b)(1), the plan is filed with the petition or within 14 days after the petition is filed. The time may not be extended except for cause and on notice as the court orders.

Under Rule 3015(b)(2), if a case is converted to Chapter 13, the plan is due within 14 days after conversion.

How Form 113 is organized

Part 1: Notices

Warnings to debtors and creditors, and three check boxes stating whether the plan limits a secured claim, avoids a lien or security interest, or includes nonstandard provisions.

Part 2: Plan Payments and Length

Regular payments to the trustee, how they are made, and treatment of income tax refunds.

Parts 3 to 5: Claims

Secured claims (Part 3), fees and priority claims (Part 4), and nonpriority unsecured claims (Part 5).

Parts 6 to 9

Executory contracts and unexpired leases (Part 6), vesting of estate property (Part 7), nonstandard plan provisions (Part 8), and signatures (Part 9).

Nonstandard provisions

Rule 3015(c)(2) defines a nonstandard provision as one that is not included in the form or deviates from it. With either Form 113 or a local form, a nonstandard provision is effective only if it is placed in the section designated for nonstandard provisions. Part 1 of Form 113 adds that if an item is checked "Not Included," or if both boxes are checked, the provision will be ineffective if set out later in the plan.

Service and objections

Under Rule 3015(d), if the plan was not included with the notice of the confirmation hearing, the debtor must serve the plan on the trustee and creditors when it is filed.

Under Rule 3015(f)(1), unless the court orders otherwise, an objection to confirmation must be filed and served at least 7 days before the confirmation hearing.

Common problems the rules and form point to

Using Form 113 where a local form is required. Rule 3015(c)(1) makes Form 113 the default only when the court has not adopted a local form.

A nonstandard provision in the wrong place. Outside Part 8, or without the matching Part 1 box, it is not effective.

A late plan. The 14-day period in Rule 3015(b) is extended only for cause and on notice.

An unserved plan. Rule 3015(d) requires service when the plan did not go out with the confirmation-hearing notice.

An altered form. Rule 9009(a) requires Official Forms to be used without alteration except as the rules, the form, or the national instructions allow.

Related forms and pages

Form 122C-1 (Ch. 13 Income)
Chapter 13 Guide
Plan Modification
All Forms

Frequently asked questions

Do all Chapter 13 debtors use Official Form 113?
Not in every district. Under Fed. R. Bankr. P. 3015(c)(1), the debtor must use Form 113 unless the court has adopted a local form under Rule 3015.1, which allows a district to require a single local plan form instead.
When must a Chapter 13 plan be filed?
Under Rule 3015(b)(1), with the petition or within 14 days after the petition is filed. In a case converted to Chapter 13, within 14 days after conversion.
What is a nonstandard provision in a Chapter 13 plan?
Rule 3015(c)(2) defines it as a provision not included in the form or that deviates from it. It is effective only if placed in the section of the form designated for nonstandard provisions.

## Form 122A-2: Chapter 7 Means Test Calculation [Free PDF, April 2025 Version] - Bankruptcy Forms Reference
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/forms/b122a-2-means-test-calculation/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Home > Forms > 122A-2 Chapter 7 Means Test Calculation

Official Bankruptcy Form
122A-2
Means Test

Official Form 122A-2: Chapter 7 Means Test Calculation

The second means-test form, filed by a Chapter 7 debtor whose current monthly income on Form 122A-1 is above the state median for the household size.

Download Official Form 122A-2 (PDF, uscourts.gov)

Current version: updated April 1, 2025 (form marked 04/25; effective April 1, 2022), from uscourts.gov. Official form page.

Your court may also require local forms. Check your bankruptcy court's website before filing.

What Form 122A-2 is

Official Form 122A-2 carries out the calculation often called the means test. The official instructions describe it as reducing income by living expenses and payments on certain debts, which leaves an amount available to pay other debts. If that amount is high enough, a presumption of abuse arises under Section 707(b) of the Bankruptcy Code.

The form starts from the filer's completed Official Form 122A-1. Line 1 copies total current monthly income from line 11 of that form.

Who must file it

Under Fed. R. Bankr. P. 1007(b)(4), an individual Chapter 7 debtor files Form 122A-1, and files Form 122A-2 only if current monthly income exceeds the median family income for the debtor's state and household size. The rule does not apply when Section 707(b)(2)(D) applies. The instructions explain that a filer covered by an exemption on Form 122A-1Supp (for example, debts that are not primarily consumer debts, or certain military service) completes only the verification on Form 122A-1.

The instructions also state that a filer under Chapter 11, 12, or 13 does not fill out the Chapter 7 means-test forms. Chapter 13 filers use Forms 122C-1 and 122C-2.

When it is due

Rule 1007(c)(1) requires the documents in Rule 1007(b)(4), which include Form 122A-2, to be filed with the petition or within 14 days after it is filed. The court may extend the time on motion and for cause under Rule 1007(c)(7).

How the form is organized

Part 1: Determine Your Adjusted Income. Starts from Form 122A-1 and allows a subtraction for any part of a non-filing spouse's income not regularly used for the household.

Part 2: Calculate Your Deductions from Your Income. Living expenses, secured debt payments, priority claims, and other allowed deductions.

Part 3: Determine Whether There Is a Presumption of Abuse. Compares the result to the thresholds printed on the form.

Part 4: Give Details About Special Circumstances. Where the filer may describe special circumstances that justify added expenses or income adjustments. The form states that the case trustee must also get documentation.

Part 5: Sign Below. A declaration under penalty of perjury.

Several lines need figures from outside the form. The instructions direct filers to justice.gov/ust/means-testing for lines 6 through 15, 30, and 36. The dollar thresholds in Part 3 carry a note on the form that they are subject to adjustment on April 1, 2028, and every 3 years after that.

What a presumption of abuse means

The official instructions state that a presumption of abuse does not mean the filer is actually trying to abuse the bankruptcy system. It means the filer is presumed to have enough income that Chapter 7 relief should not be granted. The instructions add that the presumption may be overcome by showing special circumstances, and that a filer who cannot get Chapter 7 relief may be eligible under another chapter. They also note that, depending on the result, the U.S. trustee, bankruptcy administrator, or creditors can file a motion to dismiss under Section 707(b).

Common problems the form and instructions point to

Starting without Form 122A-1. The form states that a completed Form 122A-1 is needed to fill it out.

An outdated version. The current form was updated April 1, 2025, and its thresholds change on the schedule printed on the form.

Missing outside figures. Lines that depend on the U.S. Trustee Program's means-testing data cannot be completed from the form alone.

Special circumstances without support. Part 4 states that documentation goes to the case trustee.

No signature. Part 5 is a declaration under penalty of perjury.

Related forms and pages

Form 122A-1 (Income)
Means Test Calculator
Presumption of Abuse
All Forms

Frequently asked questions

Who has to fill out Form 122A-2?
Under Fed. R. Bankr. P. 1007(b)(4), an individual Chapter 7 debtor files Form 122A-2 when current monthly income on Form 122A-1 exceeds the median family income for the debtor's state and household size, unless Section 707(b)(2)(D) applies.
When is Form 122A-2 due?
Rule 1007(c)(1) requires it with the petition or within 14 days after the petition is filed. The court may extend the time on motion and for cause.
Does a presumption of abuse mean the filer did something wrong?
No. The official instructions state that a presumption of abuse does not mean the filer is actually trying to abuse the bankruptcy system, and that it may be overcome by showing special circumstances.

## Form 423 Financial Management Course Certification: Abrogated in 2024, What Is Filed Now - Bankruptcy Forms Reference
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/forms/b423-financial-management-course/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Home > Forms > 423 Financial Management Course (Abrogated)

Official Bankruptcy Form
423
Abrogated

Official Form 423: Certification About a Financial Management Course (Abrogated)

Form 423 was discontinued effective December 1, 2024. Debtors now file the course provider's certificate of completion, unless the provider has already notified the court.

Download Official Form 423 Abrogation Notice (PDF, uscourts.gov)

Status: abrogated effective December 1, 2024, per uscourts.gov. There is no current version of Form 423 to fill out. Official form page.

Your court may also require local forms. Check your bankruptcy court's website before filing.

Form 423 is no longer used

The uscourts.gov forms library lists Official Form 423 as abrogated effective December 1, 2024. The official notice states that the form, which was used to document completion of a required course on personal financial management, was discontinued on that date.

What is filed instead

The notice explains that an individual debtor who has completed the course now files the certificate of course completion issued by the approved provider (often called a Certificate of Debtor Education), if the provider has not already notified the court. The rule behind this is Fed. R. Bankr. P. 1007(b)(7), which requires the provider's certificate unless:

an approved provider has notified the court that the debtor completed the course after filing the petition, or

the debtor is not required to complete a course as a condition of discharge.

Who the requirement covers

Rule 1007(b)(7) applies to an individual debtor in a Chapter 7 or Chapter 13 case, and in a Chapter 11 case in which Section 1141(d)(3) applies.

Deadlines under Rule 1007(c)(4)

Unless the court extends the time, the certificate is due:

Chapter 7: within 60 days after the first date set for the meeting of creditors under Section 341.

Chapter 11 or Chapter 13: no later than the date the last payment is made under the plan, or the date a motion for a discharge is filed under Section 1141(d)(5)(B) or Section 1328(b).

Why the course matters to the discharge

In Chapter 7, 11 U.S.C. Section 727(a)(11) lists failure to complete the personal financial management course after filing as a ground for denying the discharge. In Chapter 13, 11 U.S.C. Section 1328(g)(1) states that the court shall not grant a discharge unless the debtor completed the course after filing. Both sections have exceptions for a person described in Section 109(h)(4) and for districts where the U.S. trustee or bankruptcy administrator determines that approved courses are not adequate.

Common problems

Filing the old form. Form 423 was abrogated effective December 1, 2024. The rule now calls for the provider's certificate.

Taking the course before filing. Rule 1007(b)(7), Section 727(a)(11), and Section 1328(g)(1) all refer to a course completed after the petition is filed.

Missing the deadline. The Chapter 7 deadline runs from the first date set for the meeting of creditors, not from the date of the meeting that actually takes place.

Assuming the provider filed it. The exception applies only when an approved provider has notified the court.

Related forms and pages

Form 101 (Petition)
Section 111 Credit Counseling
Form 309A (341 Notice)
All Forms

Frequently asked questions

Is Official Form 423 still used?
No. uscourts.gov lists Official Form 423 as abrogated effective December 1, 2024.
What is filed instead of Form 423?
Under Fed. R. Bankr. P. 1007(b)(7), the debtor files the certificate of course completion issued by the approved provider, unless the provider has notified the court that the debtor completed the course after filing, or the debtor is not required to complete one.
When is the financial management course certificate due?
Under Rule 1007(c)(4), in Chapter 7 it is due within 60 days after the first date set for the meeting of creditors. In Chapter 11 or 13 it is due no later than the date of the last plan payment or the date a motion for a discharge is filed under Section 1141(d)(5)(B) or 1328(b). The court may extend the time.

## Hearing Preparation - Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/hearing-prep/

Open Bankruptcy Project

Mission
Cases
Research
RECAP
About
Contact

Procedural Walkthroughs

Hearing Preparation

Bankruptcy court hearings range from the highly informal 341 meeting (no judge, no formal evidence) to multi-day evidentiary trials in adversary proceedings. Knowing the rules of engagement before the hearing is the single biggest determinant of outcome. These five hearing-preparation guides walk through what to expect, what to bring, what to wear, and how to plan testimony for the most common bankruptcy hearings.

Last modified 2026-05-22.

Home/Hearing Preparation

About bankruptcy hearings generally

Bankruptcy hearings fall into three procedural categories. Section 341 meetings are conducted by the trustee, not the judge, and serve a fact-gathering function akin to a deposition under oath. Contested-matter hearings (motion practice under Bankruptcy Rule 9014) are conducted by the bankruptcy judge on the motion calendar, often without live testimony, and apply a relaxed version of the rules of evidence. Adversary-proceeding hearings (Part VII of the Bankruptcy Rules) are conducted under the full Federal Rules of Civil Procedure and Federal Rules of Evidence as modified by the Bankruptcy Rules.

Preparation differs accordingly. A 341 meeting requires the debtor to bring photo ID, Social Security verification, and original of any documents the trustee has requested; testimony is in narrative form and is rarely combative. A contested matter calendar hearing usually involves attorney argument on a fully-briefed motion; live witnesses are unusual outside a few categories such as relief-from-stay hearings where valuation is disputed. An adversary trial follows the same format as a federal civil trial including pre-trial conferences, motions in limine, exhibit lists, and witness preparation.

The deep-dives below walk through each hearing type, the typical scheduling cadence, the documents to bring, the typical questions and arguments, and the post-hearing follow-up. They are pitched at the level of a debtor or creditor counsel preparing for a first hearing in an unfamiliar matter, not at the practitioner already steeped in the local culture of a given court.

Hearing-prep guides

341 Meeting of CreditorsThe trustee-conducted meeting of creditors required by section 341, the standard trustee question script under the Handbook for Chapter 7 Trustees, document requirements, and how to handle creditor questioning.

Confirmation HearingPreparation for the chapter 11, chapter 12, chapter 13, or Subchapter V confirmation hearing including objection consolidation, declarant preparation, and the confirmation-order presentation.

Relief from Stay HearingThe 30-day fast-track hearing under section 362(e), valuation evidence for the equity-cushion analysis, and the typical evidentiary posture for an unopposed versus contested motion.

Dischargeability HearingTrial preparation for a section 523 dischargeability adversary proceeding, including the burden of proof, common section 523(a)(2), (4), and (6) trial themes, and the use of summary-judgment motions.

Fee Application HearingDefending a section 330 fee application against UST or party-in-interest objections, the lodestar presentation, the documentation of unusual time entries, and the no-look-fee alternative in chapter 13.

Calendar etiquette: Most bankruptcy courts publish their tentative rulings on contested matters the day before the hearing. Counsel should check the court's website or PACER for tentatives and notify the courtroom deputy whether the matter will be submitted on the tentative or argued. Failure to appear when the matter is set for argument can result in adverse rulings.

Disclaimer: Educational content published by the Open Bankruptcy Project, a 501(c)(3) public charity (EIN 41-5159631). Not legal advice. For representation in a specific matter, contact a licensed attorney admitted to practice in the relevant district.

## 341 Meeting of Creditors Preparation - What the Trustee Asks [2026] - Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/hearing-prep/341-meeting-preparation/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Home/Hearing Prep/341 Meeting Preparation

11 U.S.C. Section 341
Hearing Preparation

341 Meeting of Creditors Preparation

What the trustee asks, what to bring, what to wear, and the common pitfalls that turn a routine examination into a continued meeting or a Rule 2004 expansion.

What the 341 meeting is

The meeting of creditors is the proceeding mandated by 11 U.S.C. Section 341 at which the debtor appears under oath and is examined about the petition, schedules, statement of financial affairs, and the debtor's financial condition generally. The examiner is the case trustee in Chapter 7, Chapter 12, and Chapter 13 cases; in Chapter 11 cases the United States Trustee or a designee conducts the meeting. The bankruptcy judge does not attend and does not preside; the statute expressly forbids judicial participation in the meeting of creditors. The meeting is not a hearing in the courtroom sense - it is a recorded examination, typically held at a United States Trustee meeting room, a federal building hearing room, or (increasingly) by video or telephone conference under standing orders that survived the temporary remote-meeting authority of the pandemic period.

The proceeding is governed procedurally by Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 2003, which sets the timing window (no fewer than 21 nor more than 40 days after the petition date in Chapter 7 and 13; 21 to 50 days in Chapter 11; modified for small business and Subchapter V cases) and requires that the meeting be recorded.

Identification - the threshold requirement

The debtor must present, before the meeting begins, original (not photocopied) government-issued photo identification and an original document evidencing the Social Security number. The acceptable forms are specified by the United States Trustee Program in its handbook. Photo identification commonly accepted: a current driver's license, a state identification card, a U.S. passport, a permanent resident card, a current military identification, or a current passport from another country. Social Security number evidence commonly accepted: an original Social Security card, a current W-2, a recent payroll stub showing the full SSN, an IRS Form 1099, or an IRS transcript.

A debtor who appears without the required identification will not be examined. The meeting will be continued and the debtor must reappear. Repeated continuance for identification failure can prompt dismissal of the case. This is the most common preventable failure at the meeting; it is also the most embarrassing one.

Documents to bring

Beyond identification, prepare the following:

A copy of the petition, schedules, and statement of financial affairs as filed

The two most recent pay statements from each employment source (or self-employment income summary)

The most recent federal income tax return (and, in many districts, the two most recent)

The most recent statements for every deposit account, retirement account, and brokerage account listed on the schedules

Mortgage statements and vehicle loan statements showing principal balance, monthly payment, and any arrearage

Domestic support order, divorce decree, or property settlement agreement if any support obligations exist

Evidence of insurance on real property and vehicles

For self-employed debtors, profit-and-loss statements for the months between the most recent tax return and the petition date

Many trustees also send a pre-meeting letter listing district-specific documents. Read the letter; bring everything it asks for. A trustee who has to repeat document requests at the meeting will often continue the meeting rather than proceed with gaps, which delays the discharge.

The standard examination

The United States Trustee Program publishes required questions that every trustee must ask. The list is short and predictable:

State your full name and address for the record.

Did you sign the petition, schedules, statements, and related documents, and is the signature your own?

Did you read the petition, schedules, statements, and related documents before signing?

Are you personally familiar with the information contained in the petition, schedules, and statements?

To the best of your knowledge, is the information contained in the petition, schedules, and statements true and correct?

Are there any errors or omissions to bring to the trustee's attention?

Are all of your assets identified on the schedules?

Are all of your creditors listed on the schedules?

Have you previously filed bankruptcy? (If yes, identify the case number, court, and chapter.)

What is the address of your current employer?

Is the copy of your most recent tax return that you provided to the trustee a true copy?

Do you have a domestic support obligation? (If yes, the trustee will ask further questions about the obligee and the amount.)

Have you made any payments to creditors (other than ordinary course) or to insiders within the look-back period?

Have you transferred any property (other than in the ordinary course) within the look-back period?

Beyond these, the trustee may ask anything relevant to the administration of the estate. Common follow-ups: the source and use of unusual deposits in bank statements; the basis of vehicle valuations; the existence of personal-injury claims, inheritance expectancies, or tax refunds; the relationship of any insider transferees; and the disposition of recently-closed accounts.

Common pitfalls

Volunteering information

Answer the question asked. Do not narrate; do not explain motivation; do not editorialize. A long answer creates additional examination paths and additional opportunities to contradict the schedules. "Yes," "No," "I don't know," and "I don't remember" are complete answers when accurate.

Guessing

The debtor is under oath. A guess that turns out to be wrong is a false oath. If the answer is not known with confidence, say so. The trustee will accept "I don't know" and move on; the trustee will not accept a confident answer that later proves false.

Inconsistency with the schedules

If the meeting answer differs from what the schedules say, the trustee will ask which is correct. The correct response is rarely to disavow the schedules on the spot; the schedules are the sworn document. If an error exists, the trustee will direct the debtor to file amended schedules. Do not contradict the schedules without first identifying the contradiction as an error that will be amended.

Missing or untimely tax returns

11 U.S.C. Section 521(e)(2) requires the debtor to deliver to the trustee a copy of the most recent federal tax return at least 7 days before the meeting. Failure can cause dismissal under Section 521(e)(2)(B). The deadline is not waivable by the trustee informally; if missed, file a motion for extension promptly.

Cash on hand and unusual deposits

Recent large cash withdrawals or deposits are visible on bank statements and will be questioned. Prepare a one-line explanation for each transaction over the trustee's customary threshold (typically $1,000 - $2,500). "I cashed my paycheck" is acceptable when documented; "I don't recall" is not, when the amount is significant.

Conduct expectations

Dress neatly and conservatively. Business casual is appropriate; courtroom attire is not required but signals seriousness. Arrive 30 minutes early. Silence the phone. Address the trustee as "Trustee [last name]" or "Ms./Mr. [last name]." Do not interrupt; let the question finish before answering. If a creditor attends and asks a question, the trustee will allow it within the scope of the meeting; the same answer-the-question-asked discipline applies.

The meeting is recorded. Anything said becomes part of the record and can be used in subsequent adversary proceedings, in motions to dismiss for cause, in objections to discharge under Section 727, and in dischargeability complaints under Section 523. Treat the answers accordingly.

After the meeting

The trustee will state on the record whether the meeting is concluded or continued. A concluded meeting starts the clock for objections: 60 days from the conclusion for nondischargeability complaints under Section 523(a)(2), (4), and (6), and for objections to discharge under Section 727; 30 days for objections to exemptions under Rule 4003(b). A continued meeting does not start those clocks until the meeting is actually concluded. If the trustee announced an amendment requirement or a document request, deliver the items before the continuance date; failure to do so commonly results in a motion to dismiss for unreasonable delay.

The 341 meeting is short and procedural in most cases. The median Chapter 7 consumer meeting runs 4 to 8 minutes. Preparation is what produces a short meeting; the debtor who knows the schedules, brings the documents, and answers narrowly gets through the examination quickly. The debtor who does not is the one who comes back.

Related statutes and authority

11 U.S.C. Section 343 - Examination of the debtor

11 U.S.C. Section 521 - Debtor's duties

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 2003 - Meeting of creditors

## Plan Confirmation Hearing Preparation - Chapters 11, 12, 13 [2026] - Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/hearing-prep/confirmation-hearing-preparation/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Home/Hearing Prep/Confirmation Hearing Preparation

11 U.S.C. Sections 1129 / 1225 / 1325
Confirmation

Plan Confirmation Hearing Preparation

The evidentiary record, feasibility testimony, valuation evidence, and objection handling that determine whether a plan is confirmed under Chapters 11, 12, or 13.

What confirmation is

Plan confirmation is the court's adjudication that a proposed reorganization or repayment plan satisfies the statutory requirements for that chapter and may bind creditors. The applicable provisions are 11 U.S.C. Section 1129 for Chapter 11, Section 1225 for Chapter 12, and Section 1325 for Chapter 13. Subchapter V of Chapter 11 imports the Section 1129 framework with substantial modifications under Section 1191. The confirmation hearing is an evidentiary proceeding. The proponent of the plan bears the burden of proving each confirmation requirement; objecting parties bear the burden on affirmative defenses (such as the absolute priority rule challenge or a good-faith objection grounded in non-financial facts).

The structure of the hearing

The hearing typically proceeds in three phases:

Procedural rulings. The court takes up any pending motions in limine, evidentiary objections, and procedural disputes (disclosure statement adequacy in Chapter 11 cases where deferred, ballot tabulation disputes, late-filed objections). The court may make preliminary findings about the contested or uncontested status of each requirement.

Proponent's case-in-chief. The plan proponent presents testimony and documentary evidence on the contested confirmation requirements. In most consumer Chapter 13 cases the proponent's case is brief and largely documentary; in Chapter 11 cases it commonly involves multiple witnesses including a financial advisor, a valuation expert, and an officer of the debtor.

Objectors' case and rebuttal. Objecting creditors present their evidence on the contested issues. The proponent may put on rebuttal. Closing argument follows; the court may rule from the bench or take the matter under advisement.

The core confirmation requirements

Best interests of creditors test

Each impaired class must receive at least as much under the plan as it would receive in a hypothetical Chapter 7 liquidation as of the effective date. Section 1129(a)(7), Section 1225(a)(4), Section 1325(a)(4). The test is performed creditor by creditor for each impaired class; it requires a liquidation analysis. The proponent's liquidation analysis must value each asset at its forced-sale value (not going-concern value), subtract administrative expenses of a hypothetical Chapter 7, distribute through the priority waterfall, and identify the recovery percentage to each class. The chief vulnerabilities of liquidation analyses: overstatement of administrative expenses, understatement of unencumbered asset values, omission of preference and fraudulent-transfer recoveries that would inure to a Chapter 7 trustee.

Feasibility

The plan must be feasible: not likely to be followed by liquidation or further financial reorganization, except as proposed in the plan itself. Section 1129(a)(11), Section 1225(a)(6), Section 1325(a)(6). Feasibility is the requirement most frequently litigated in contested cases. The proponent must offer evidence (commonly through a projection witness) of sufficient cash flow to make the plan payments. The projections must be supported, not asserted. Standard impeachment of feasibility projections: comparison to historical performance, reasonableness of growth assumptions, treatment of expense items historically present but omitted prospectively, sensitivity to identified risks (commodity prices, customer concentration, regulatory exposures), and the existence of a reasonable downside scenario.

Good faith

The plan must be proposed in good faith and not by any means forbidden by law. Section 1129(a)(3), Section 1225(a)(3), Section 1325(a)(3). Good-faith objections typically involve allegations that the plan is principally a litigation-defeat device, that classification of claims was gerrymandered to assemble an accepting impaired class, that the debtor's pre-petition conduct (concealment, transfers, dischargeability-evading behavior) infects the plan, or - in Chapter 13 - that the proposed payment percentage is unreasonably low relative to ability.

Acceptance / cramdown

Each impaired class must accept the plan, or the plan must satisfy cramdown requirements. Section 1129(a)(8) and (b); Section 1325(a)(5) and (b). Acceptance of a class of claims requires acceptances from creditors holding at least two-thirds in amount and more than one-half in number of allowed claims voting. Cramdown over a non-accepting class requires fair-and-equitable treatment, which in turn requires either payment-in-full of the secured claim with present-value interest (the indubitable-equivalent or replacement-lien test) or compliance with the absolute priority rule for unsecured classes.

Disposable income (Chapter 13)

An above-median Chapter 13 debtor must commit projected disposable income for five years; a below-median debtor for three years (extendable to five for cause). Section 1325(b). The disposable-income calculation is mechanical for above-median debtors (Form 122C calculation) and discretionary for below-median debtors (Schedules I and J). Objecting trustees commonly contest the household-size determination, the validity of claimed expenses, and the categorization of secured-debt deductions.

Evidentiary record - what to put on

Anticipate the requirements at issue and assemble the record accordingly. In a Chapter 13 contested confirmation, the typical record includes: the debtor's testimony in support of Schedules I/J and the disposable-income calculation; documentation of post-petition income (pay statements or business records); documentation of post-petition expenses where contested; appraisals or valuation testimony for any contested secured-claim valuation; and (where 910-day or 1-year claim valuation is at issue) documentation of vehicle or collateral condition.

In Chapter 11 contested confirmation, the typical record adds: a financial-advisor witness for the projections and feasibility; a valuation witness for the going-concern or liquidation analyses; an officer of the debtor for the business narrative and for any management-continuity testimony required for absolute-priority compliance; counsel testimony or stipulation on solicitation compliance; and the ballot tabulation report.

Objection handling

Objections to confirmation must be filed before the hearing per the court's confirmation scheduling order. Late objections are commonly disallowed; an objecting party should preserve the objection by filing even an unverified placeholder before the deadline if the substance is still developing. At the hearing, address each filed objection systematically. The proponent's preparation should include a written objection-response chart (every objection, the proponent's position, the evidence supporting the position, the witness through whom the evidence is offered). Objecting parties should be prepared to identify (a) the specific statutory requirement allegedly violated, (b) the factual basis, and (c) the evidence to be offered.

Valuation evidence

Valuation disputes drive many contested confirmations - secured-claim bifurcation under Section 506(a), best-interests asset valuation, going-concern enterprise valuation. The court will weigh competing expert testimony. The recurring impeachment categories: methodology mismatch (comparable-sales versus income-approach versus cost-approach for the asset class), comparable inappropriateness, discount-rate selection, treatment of one-time items in normalized cash flow, and the appraiser's prior testimony in similar matters. A valuation that survives cross-examination is one that selects the right methodology for the asset, applies the methodology consistently, and discloses assumptions.

Subchapter V differences

Subchapter V (small business debtors electing under Section 1182) confirms under Section 1191. If all impaired classes accept, confirmation is consensual under Section 1191(a). If an impaired class rejects, the debtor may seek cramdown under Section 1191(b), which dispenses with the absolute priority rule and substitutes a projected-disposable-income test similar to Chapter 13: the plan must commit projected disposable income for three to five years to unsecured creditors. The Subchapter V trustee plays a facilitative role, attends the hearing, and may take a position on confirmation.

Confirmation hearings reward preparation that the plan, the disclosure statement, and the ballots cannot themselves accomplish. The contested issues at confirmation are not legal interpretations of the statute - they are factual disputes about projections, valuations, and good faith. The party that arrives with the better-supported factual record usually prevails.

Related statutes and authority

11 U.S.C. Section 1129 - Confirmation of plan (Chapter 11)

11 U.S.C. Section 1225 - Confirmation of plan (Chapter 12)

11 U.S.C. Section 1325 - Confirmation of plan (Chapter 13)

11 U.S.C. Section 1191 - Confirmation of plan (Subchapter V)

11 U.S.C. Section 506(a) - Determination of secured status

Till v. SCS Credit Corp., 541 U.S. 465 (2004) - Present-value interest rate for cramdown

Bank of America v. 203 N. LaSalle Street Partnership, 526 U.S. 434 (1999) - Absolute priority and new value

## Dischargeability Hearing Preparation - Section 523 Adversary Proceedings [2026] - Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/hearing-prep/dischargeability-hearing-preparation/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Home/Hearing Prep/Dischargeability Hearing Preparation

11 U.S.C. Section 523
Adversary Proceeding

Dischargeability Hearing Preparation

Section 523 adversary proceeding mechanics, the 60-day complaint deadline, evidence preservation, summary judgment versus trial, and the differing burdens that govern each subsection of nondischargeable debt.

What a dischargeability proceeding is

A dischargeability proceeding is an adversary proceeding (a discrete civil action within the bankruptcy case) seeking a judgment that a particular debt is excepted from discharge under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a). The proceeding is governed by the adversary-proceeding rules in Part VII of the Federal Rules of Bankruptcy Procedure, which incorporate most of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure. It is separate from the underlying bankruptcy case in docket structure (new adversary number assigned), but proceeds before the same bankruptcy judge.

The proceeding does not relitigate the underlying debt. The amount and existence of the debt are commonly the subject of a prior judgment or established by stipulation; the dischargeability proceeding adjudicates whether that debt falls within a Section 523(a) exception. Where the underlying debt is itself unliquidated, the bankruptcy court has jurisdiction to adjudicate both liability and nondischargeability in the same proceeding.

The 60-day deadline

The complaint to determine dischargeability of a debt under Section 523(a)(2), (4), or (6) must be filed not later than 60 days after the first date set for the meeting of creditors. Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 4007(c). The deadline is jurisdictional in many circuits and is not subject to equitable tolling absent unusual circumstances. The court may extend the deadline only on motion filed before its expiration. Creditors who learn of the bankruptcy after the deadline have a separate right under Section 523(a)(3) - the unscheduled-debt exception - that does not depend on a timely complaint.

Other Section 523 categories - notably (a)(1) tax debts, (a)(5) and (a)(15) domestic obligations, (a)(7) governmental fines, (a)(8) student loans, and (a)(9) drunk-driving liability - are nondischargeable by operation of law and may be the subject of a complaint at any time during or after the bankruptcy case. The 60-day deadline applies only to the three subsections that require a complaint to render the debt nondischargeable: (a)(2) fraud, (a)(4) embezzlement / fiduciary defalcation, and (a)(6) willful and malicious injury.

The complaint - elements and pleading

The complaint must plead facts establishing each element of the asserted Section 523(a) subsection. Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 9(b)'s particularity requirement, incorporated by Bankruptcy Rule 7009, applies to fraud-based claims (Sections 523(a)(2)(A) and (B), and to the extent based on fraud, 523(a)(4)). Boilerplate fraud allegations are routinely dismissed; the complaint must identify the specific representation, when made, by whom, to whom, the falsity, the scienter, the reliance, and the damages.

The elements of the most-litigated subsections:

Section 523(a)(2)(A) - false pretenses, false representation, or actual fraud. A misrepresentation made by the debtor with intent to deceive, on which the creditor justifiably relied, and which caused damages. The Supreme Court's decision in Husky International Electronics, Inc. v. Ritz, 578 U.S. 355 (2016), extended "actual fraud" to include fraudulent-transfer schemes that do not involve a misrepresentation to the creditor.

Section 523(a)(2)(B) - false written financial statements. A written statement respecting the debtor's financial condition, materially false, made with intent to deceive, on which the creditor reasonably relied. The "respecting the debtor's financial condition" language was narrowed by Lamar, Archer & Cofrin, LLP v. Appling, 584 U.S. 709 (2018), holding that the phrase covers oral statements about a single asset, removing them from the writing requirement.

Section 523(a)(4) - fraud or defalcation while acting in a fiduciary capacity, embezzlement, or larceny. The fiduciary capacity must be a technical trust or express trust, not a general fiduciary duty. The Supreme Court in Bullock v. BankChampaign, N.A., 569 U.S. 267 (2013), held that "defalcation" requires a culpable state of mind involving knowledge of, or gross recklessness as to, the improper nature of the relevant fiduciary behavior.

Section 523(a)(6) - willful and malicious injury. Kawaauhau v. Geiger, 523 U.S. 57 (1998), held that "willful" requires a deliberate or intentional injury, not merely a deliberate act that produces injury. Recklessness or negligence does not suffice.

The plaintiff's burden on each element is preponderance of the evidence (Grogan v. Garner, 498 U.S. 279 (1991)), notwithstanding the higher clear-and-convincing standard often required for common-law fraud in nonbankruptcy courts.

Evidence preservation

The plaintiff's preservation obligations begin pre-complaint. The complaint should be drafted from a documentary base, not from allegations to be later supported. Common preservation issues:

Original communications. Emails, text messages, recorded calls, and contemporaneous notes establishing the alleged misrepresentation. If the underlying business or banking relationship is closed, records may be subpoena-only and subject to retention-limit destruction.

Loan or extension-of-credit application documents. For Section 523(a)(2)(B), the actual written statement and any contemporaneous lender notes documenting reliance and the materiality of the false items.

Transaction records. For Section 523(a)(4) defalcation or embezzlement claims, the trust or fiduciary records, ledgers, and bank statements covering the period of alleged misconduct.

Prior litigation record. If a state-court judgment exists, the trial transcript, exhibits, and findings of fact may have issue-preclusive effect under collateral-estoppel doctrine, depending on the issues actually litigated and necessary to the judgment.

Defendants face parallel preservation issues. Spoliation sanctions in adversary proceedings track Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 37(e); destruction of relevant evidence after the duty to preserve attached can support adverse-inference instructions or, in extreme cases, default judgment.

Summary judgment

Section 523 adversary proceedings are summary-judgment-eligible under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 56, incorporated by Bankruptcy Rule 7056. Summary judgment is commonly sought where:

The plaintiff invokes collateral estoppel from a prior state-court judgment that necessarily decided the elements of the Section 523(a) exception. The classic example: a state-court jury verdict for fraud, where the elements decided substantially overlap with Section 523(a)(2)(A). The bankruptcy court applies the issue-preclusion law of the state that rendered the judgment.

The defendant moves on a limitations or threshold defense (untimely complaint under Rule 4007(c), failure to plead with Rule 9(b) particularity, failure to allege a required element).

The dispositive issue is documentary and not credibility-dependent (the written representation was true, no reasonable jury could find scienter on the documentary record, the alleged trust was not a technical trust).

Where summary judgment is denied because credibility is at issue (intent, reliance, knowledge), the matter proceeds to bench trial. Section 523 proceedings are tried to the bankruptcy judge without a jury; jury-trial rights do not generally attach to dischargeability determinations.

Trial preparation

Trial of a Section 523 proceeding is typically one to three days. The plaintiff's case-in-chief usually comprises (a) the underlying transaction documents; (b) the plaintiff's testimony or representative testimony on reliance and damages; (c) the debtor as an adverse witness on intent, knowledge, and motive; and (d) any third-party witnesses to the misrepresentation or to the misconduct. The defendant's case typically comprises (a) explanatory testimony on intent and knowledge; (b) any third-party witnesses corroborating the debtor's account; and (c) rebuttal evidence on damages or on the asserted preclusion. Each side's cross-examination chiefly attacks scienter and reliance, where the evidence is most often documentary-light and credibility-driven.

Pretrial submissions in adversary proceedings commonly include: a joint statement of stipulated facts; exhibit lists with objections; witness lists; deposition designations; and trial briefs identifying the contested legal issues. Local rules vary widely on form and timing; consult the case scheduling order and the judge's chambers procedures.

Discovery

Discovery in adversary proceedings is governed by Bankruptcy Rules 7026 through 7037, which incorporate the federal civil discovery rules with adaptations. Initial disclosures under Rule 26(a) are required unless local practice or the scheduling order modifies. Discovery in dischargeability proceedings often focuses on (a) the debtor's contemporaneous records (financial statements, accounting records, communications) at the time of the alleged misrepresentation or misconduct; (b) the plaintiff's reliance documentation (underwriting files, decision memoranda); and (c) third-party records bearing on solvency, intent, or the transaction. Subpoenas to former employers, banks, accountants, and counterparties are routine.

Dischargeability trials reward early preparation. The discovery window is short (often four to six months in standard scheduling orders), the documentary record must usually be assembled before the complaint is filed to ensure compliance with Rule 9(b), and the 60-day complaint deadline is unforgiving. Creditors who wait until after the 341 meeting to evaluate a Section 523 claim frequently miss the window.

Related statutes and authority

Grogan v. Garner, 498 U.S. 279 (1991) - Preponderance burden in dischargeability

Bullock v. BankChampaign, N.A., 569 U.S. 267 (2013) - Defalcation mental state

Husky International Electronics, Inc. v. Ritz, 578 U.S. 355 (2016) - "Actual fraud" without misrepresentation

Lamar, Archer & Cofrin, LLP v. Appling, 584 U.S. 709 (2018) - Oral statement about a single asset

## Fee Application Hearing Preparation - Rule 2016(a) Documentation [2026] - Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/hearing-prep/fee-application-hearing-preparation/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Home/Hearing Prep/Fee Application Hearing Preparation

11 U.S.C. Section 330
Rule 2016

Fee Application Hearing Preparation

The Rule 2016(a) documentation requirements, lodestar reconstruction, objection categories, and the court's independent review authority that govern compensation of bankruptcy professionals.

What the fee application process is

A fee application is the procedural vehicle by which an estate-employed professional - debtor's counsel, trustee's counsel, official committee counsel, financial advisor, accountant, appraiser, or other professional retained under 11 U.S.C. Section 327 or analogous provisions - seeks court approval of compensation to be paid from estate funds. The statutory authority is 11 U.S.C. Section 330; the procedural framework is Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 2016 and corresponding local rules; substantive guidance comes from the U.S. Trustee's Guidelines for Reviewing Applications for Compensation.

Compensation in bankruptcy is fundamentally different from compensation in nonbankruptcy practice. The court must approve every dollar paid from estate funds, including fees the professional and the client have agreed upon by engagement letter. The retainer paid pre-petition is also subject to court review under Rule 2016(b) disclosure. A professional who receives or applies estate funds without court approval is exposed to disgorgement.

Rule 2016(a) supporting documentation

Rule 2016(a) requires that a fee application contain "a detailed statement of (1) the services rendered, time expended and expenses incurred, and (2) the amounts requested." In practice, this requires:

Contemporaneous time records in tenths-of-an-hour increments, listing for each entry the date of service, the timekeeper, the time billed, the billing rate, the dollar amount, and a narrative description of the task sufficient to permit independent review of reasonableness and necessity. Reconstructed time records (those prepared after the fact) are heavily disfavored and, in many districts, will be disallowed entirely.

Timekeeper biographies and rates. The application should identify each timekeeper, the timekeeper's role (partner, associate, paralegal), the timekeeper's hourly rate, and a brief biography establishing the rate's reasonableness in the relevant market.

Project or matter categorization. The U.S. Trustee Guidelines require segregation of time into project categories (case administration, asset analysis, litigation, plan confirmation, fee applications, etc.) with a summary by project category. Lump time entries that fail to permit project allocation are commonly reduced.

Expense detail. Reimbursable expenses must be itemized. Photocopy charges above actual cost, secretarial overtime, in-office meals, and overhead items billed as expenses are routinely disallowed.

Narrative summary of services. A description of what was accomplished in the application period, the benefit to the estate, and the relationship of the services to the case's progress.

Connection statement. Disclosure of any change in connection or compensation status since the original Section 327 application or prior fee application.

The lodestar method

The dominant compensation methodology in bankruptcy is the lodestar: hours reasonably expended multiplied by a reasonable hourly rate. The Section 330(a)(3) factors the court considers include (a) the time spent, (b) the rates charged, (c) whether the services were necessary to the administration of, or beneficial at the time at which the service was rendered toward the completion of, the case, (d) whether the services were performed within a reasonable amount of time commensurate with the complexity, importance, and nature of the problem, (e) the demonstrated skill and experience of the professional, and (f) whether the compensation is reasonable based on the customary compensation charged by comparably skilled practitioners in cases other than bankruptcy.

The Supreme Court in Baker Botts L.L.P. v. ASARCO LLC, 576 U.S. 121 (2015), held that Section 330 does not authorize compensation for time spent defending a fee application against an objection. Time spent preparing the application is compensable; time spent defending it is not. The distinction is implemented in many districts through a "fee defense" disallowance at the post-application stage.

Lodestar reconstruction

Where contemporaneous records are inadequate or missing, reconstruction is sometimes attempted. Reconstruction is not a substitute for contemporaneous records; courts treat reconstructed time with skepticism. Acceptable reconstruction supplementation typically requires (a) corroborating documentary evidence (calendars, email metadata, court filings, deposition transcripts) that anchor the time entries to specific activities on specific dates, and (b) an explanation of why contemporaneous records are unavailable. A professional whose entire fee application is reconstructed from billing memory will not be paid in most courts.

Objection categories

The principal categories of fee objection - whether raised by the U.S. Trustee, a creditor, a creditors' committee, or sua sponte by the court - are:

Vagueness

Time entries that do not permit the reviewer to determine what was done. "Research" without identifying the topic; "review correspondence" without identifying the correspondence; "conference with co-counsel" without identifying the subject. The remedy is reduction or disallowance of the specific entries.

Block billing

Single time entries combining multiple discrete tasks without segregation, preventing reasonableness review of any individual component. Many local rules and U.S. Trustee guidelines impose presumptive percentage reductions on block-billed entries (commonly 10% to 30%).

Overstaffing

Multiple professionals at a single deposition, hearing, or conference where the case's complexity does not justify the duplication; multiple partners on tasks suitable for an associate; partner time on tasks suitable for a paralegal. The U.S. Trustee routinely objects to "associate-shadowed-by-partner" hearing appearances absent a specific justification.

Excessive time

Hours billed disproportionate to the task. Six hours to draft a routine motion to extend a deadline; twenty hours to research an issue on which the firm has prior memoranda; multi-day "review of the file" without identification of specific deliverables. Reviewers compare hours billed to the work product produced.

Clerical or secretarial tasks

Time spent on filing, scheduling, calendaring, copying, organizing files, and other tasks that are properly overhead rather than professional services. Such time is routinely disallowed regardless of the timekeeper's seniority.

Non-bankruptcy work

Time on matters not properly the subject of estate compensation - personal matters of the principals, prepetition collection of pre-engagement fees, non-bankruptcy litigation funded by the estate without prior court approval.

Lack of benefit

Services that did not produce a benefit to the estate. The Supreme Court in Lamie v. United States Trustee, 540 U.S. 526 (2004), confirmed that Section 330(a)(1) limits compensation in Chapter 7 cases to the trustee and to professionals employed under Section 327; debtor's counsel in Chapter 7 is compensated through the retainer, not from estate funds.

Excessive rates

Rates above the prevailing market for the relevant locality and practice area. The U.S. Trustee may submit rate-survey data; objections at this level are less common but do occur, particularly where lead counsel imports out-of-market rates without a corresponding showing of necessity.

Sua sponte review

The bankruptcy court has independent authority and obligation to review fee applications even if no objection is filed. In re Busy Beaver Building Centers, Inc., 19 F.3d 833 (3d Cir. 1994), articulates the standard adopted in most circuits: the court is the gatekeeper of estate compensation and may reduce fees on its own motion. The court may direct the applicant to provide additional documentation, may set the matter for hearing, and may enter an order reducing the requested compensation with findings supporting the reduction.

In some districts the court refers fee applications to a special examiner or to a fee committee for an initial review; the court then enters an order based on the report. The applicant typically has an opportunity to respond before the order is entered.

Hearing preparation

Contested fee applications are bench-tried on the documentary record supplemented by limited live testimony. The applicant should prepare:

A response brief that addresses each objection category-by-category, identifying for each contested entry either a defense or a withdrawal/reduction.

A revised summary of fees, presenting the requested amount net of any voluntarily reduced entries, so the court has a clear bottom-line figure.

A timekeeper available to testify briefly about the contested entries and to explain the necessity and benefit, if the court requests.

Comparable-case data (other approved fee applications in similar matters) if rates or aggregate fees are challenged.

The objecting party should prepare a chart identifying each contested entry by date, timekeeper, amount, and objection basis, with citations to the supporting authority. A general objection ("the fees are excessive") without specific entry-level analysis is commonly overruled; the court will not undertake line-by-line review without prompts.

Interim and final applications

Section 331 authorizes interim fee applications no more frequently than 120 days, although shorter intervals may be approved by court order in large or complex cases. Interim applications are interlocutory; the court retains authority to reconsider interim awards in connection with the final application. A final fee application is filed at case closure or upon completion of the engagement; the court's final order is appealable as a final order.

Fee application preparation begins at engagement, not at filing. The contemporaneous-records discipline, the timekeeper rate justification, the project-category structure, and the connection-disclosure obligations all start on day one. A fee application built from clean records billed in real time and to category survives most objections; one assembled from billing memory does not.

Related statutes and authority

11 U.S.C. Section 330 - Compensation of officers

11 U.S.C. Section 331 - Interim compensation

In re Busy Beaver Building Centers, Inc., 19 F.3d 833 (3d Cir. 1994) - Court's sua sponte review duty

Open Bankruptcy Project cross-references

Identifying Professional Conduct Concerns
