## KRPC 1.1 / MRPC 4-1.1 - Competence [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/krpc-1-1/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Rule of Professional Conduct
KRPC 1.1 / MRPC 4-1.1

KRPC 1.1 / MRPC 4-1.1: Competence

Legal knowledge, skill, thoroughness, and preparation reasonably necessary for the representation.

Verbatim text of KRPC 1.1 (Kansas)

A lawyer shall provide competent representation to a client. Competent representation requires the legal knowledge, skill, thoroughness and preparation reasonably necessary for the representation. Kan. Sup. Ct. R. 226, KRPC 1.1.

Missouri Rule 4-1.1

Missouri Rule 4-1.1 is substantively identical to KRPC 1.1 and tracks ABA Model Rule 1.1. Both states adopt the four-element formulation: knowledge, skill, thoroughness, and preparation. The Comment to Model Rule 1.1, which Kansas and Missouri have largely adopted, fills in the operative content of each element.

The four elements of competence

Legal knowledge

The lawyer must know the law applicable to the representation. The Comment recognizes that a lawyer need not have special training or prior experience to handle a matter; competence may be acquired through study or association with a lawyer of established competence. But the lawyer must actually have, or actually acquire, the knowledge before undertaking the action. A lawyer who files pleadings in a substantive area without the required underlying knowledge satisfies neither the knowledge nor the preparation requirement.

Skill

Skill is the practical ability to apply knowledge to client matters. The relevant skills vary by practice area. In transactional work, skill includes the ability to draft, negotiate, and structure agreements. In litigation, skill includes pleading, motion practice, discovery, examination of witnesses, and argument. A lawyer holding out for matters that require litigation skill must actually have, or acquire, that skill.

Thoroughness

Thoroughness is the discipline of complete attention to the matter. It encompasses identifying all relevant facts, all applicable law, and all reasonable courses of action. A lawyer who treats a matter as routine when the facts demonstrate non-routine elements has not provided thorough representation.

Preparation

Preparation is the work performed in advance of the lawyer's action - the legal research, factual investigation, document review, and procedural compliance that must precede competent execution. The duty of preparation scales with the complexity and stakes of the matter; it is calibrated to "reasonably necessary," not to any fixed standard.

Comment 8 - Maintaining competence (technological competence)

Comment 8 to Model Rule 1.1, adopted in substance by Kansas and Missouri, states that to maintain the requisite knowledge and skill a lawyer should keep abreast of changes in the law and its practice, including the benefits and risks associated with relevant technology. This is the source of the now-widely-recognized "duty of technological competence." A lawyer practicing in a field where electronic case management, electronic filing, electronic service, or electronic discovery is standard must be reasonably competent in the relevant technology.

Duty of technological competence. A majority of jurisdictions now expressly recognize a duty of technological competence flowing from Comment 8 to Rule 1.1. A lawyer who does not understand the relevant electronic systems - including electronic filing, electronic service, electronic discovery, and increasingly the use and limits of artificial intelligence tools - cannot rely on technological unfamiliarity to defeat competence claims.

Calibration to the matter

The rule does not require that every lawyer be competent in every field. It requires competence in the matters the lawyer undertakes. A lawyer with general practice experience may undertake a specialized matter, but must achieve competence before action - whether by study, by association with a competent lawyer, or by declining the matter. A lawyer who undertakes a matter beyond the lawyer's competence, without taking the steps competence requires, violates the rule regardless of the outcome.

Emergency exception

The Comment recognizes a narrow exception for emergencies. In situations in which referral or consultation is impractical and immediate action is required, a lawyer may give advice or assistance in a matter in which the lawyer does not have the skill ordinarily required where doing so is in the client's interest. The emergency exception does not extend beyond the emergency and does not justify continued representation in a matter beyond the lawyer's competence.

Common procedural posture

Substantive area outside ordinary practice

A lawyer is asked to handle a matter in a substantive area outside the lawyer's ordinary practice. The lawyer must either (a) acquire the necessary knowledge through study or consultation before undertaking the matter, (b) associate with a lawyer of established competence in the area, or (c) decline the representation. Taking the matter without doing one of these things is a competence violation independent of outcome.

Insufficient preparation for hearing or filing

A lawyer attends a hearing or files a paper without the preparation reasonably necessary for the matter - inadequate factual investigation, incomplete legal research, or failure to identify applicable procedural requirements. This is a thoroughness-and-preparation violation under Rule 1.1, often paired with diligence concerns under Rule 1.3 and candor concerns under Rule 3.3 where the filing contains factual or legal errors.

Relationship to other rules

Rule 1.1 sets the floor for the substantive quality of representation. Other rules build on it:

Rule 1.3 (Diligence) - Even competent representation can fall short if it is not pursued with reasonable diligence; the two rules are typically analyzed together.

Rule 1.4 (Communication) - Competent representation includes communicating with the client at the level required by Rule 1.4.

Rule 1.5 (Fees) - The reasonableness of fees under Rule 1.5 is partly a function of whether the work performed was competent.

Rule 3.1 (Meritorious Claims) - A lawyer who has not done the work to determine whether a claim has a basis in law and fact has not provided competent representation and is also at risk under Rule 3.1.

Practical impact

Competence is the foundational professional duty. Two consequences recur in disciplinary practice:

Unfamiliarity is not a defense. A lawyer who took on a matter without the requisite competence is responsible for the consequences. The rule does not protect lawyers who hold out for work beyond their actual competence.

Competence is matter-specific. The fact that a lawyer is competent in some matters does not establish competence in any particular new matter. Each undertaking requires the knowledge, skill, thoroughness, and preparation reasonably necessary for it.

Related authority

Kansas Rules of Professional Conduct - Kansas Supreme Court Rules

Missouri Rules of Professional Conduct - Missouri Supreme Court Rule 4

## KRPC 1.10 / MRPC 4-1.10 - Imputation of Conflicts of Interest [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/krpc-1-10/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Rule of Professional Conduct
KRPC 1.10 / MRPC 4-1.10

KRPC 1.10 / MRPC 4-1.10: Imputation of Conflicts of Interest

Screening protocols, lateral-mobility safe harbors, and the consent framework that preserves matters when lawyers change firms.

What Rule 1.10 affirmatively does

Rule 1.10 is the rule that defines the conflict-of-interest perimeter at the firm level. It identifies when one lawyer's conflict is imputed to the firm, but it does so within an architecture that includes a personal-interest carve-out, a screening safe harbor for lateral lawyers, a consent pathway for clients of the firm and prior firms, and a clean re-entry once a conflicted lawyer leaves. The rule lets firms grow through lateral hiring and lets lawyers move between firms without freezing the firms or stranding the clients.

Verbatim text of KRPC 1.10 (Kansas, abbreviated)

(a) While lawyers are associated in a firm, none of them shall knowingly represent a client when any one of them practicing alone would be prohibited from doing so by Rule 1.7 or 1.9, unless the prohibition is based on a personal interest of the prohibited lawyer and does not present a significant risk of materially limiting the representation of the client by the remaining lawyers in the firm.

(b) When a lawyer has terminated an association with a firm, the firm is not prohibited from thereafter representing a person with interests materially adverse to those of a client represented by the formerly associated lawyer and not currently represented by the firm, unless: (1) the matter is the same or substantially related to that in which the formerly associated lawyer represented the client; and (2) any lawyer remaining in the firm has information protected by Rules 1.6 and 1.9(c) that is material to the matter.

(c) A disqualification prescribed by this rule may be waived by the affected client under the conditions stated in Rule 1.7. Kan. Sup. Ct. R. 226, KRPC 1.10.

Missouri Rule 4-1.10

Missouri Rule 4-1.10 tracks ABA Model Rule 1.10 and adopts the same imputation default, the personal-interest carve-out, the post-departure rule, and the consent pathway. The screening framework for laterals has developed somewhat differently across jurisdictions; both Kansas and Missouri permit screening in specific contexts described below.

1.10(a) - The imputation default and the personal-interest carve-out

The default rule is firm-wide imputation: a conflict that would disqualify one lawyer under Rule 1.7 or 1.9 disqualifies all lawyers associated in the same firm. The default reflects the firm-as-unit conception of practice - clients engage the firm, confidences are shared within the firm, and the firm's incentives are unified.

The default has a built-in carve-out. If the prohibition is based on a personal interest of one lawyer - and that personal interest does not present a significant risk of materially limiting the representation by the remaining lawyers - the conflict is not imputed. A personal political belief, a personal financial entanglement that does not implicate the matter, or a personal social relationship that does not affect judgment are typical examples. The carve-out is structural: it keeps the firm available for matters that one lawyer cannot personally take.

1.10(b) - The clean re-entry rule after a lawyer leaves

When a lawyer leaves a firm, the firm is not categorically disqualified from accepting work adverse to that lawyer's former clients. Disqualification attaches only if two conditions both hold: (1) the matter is the same or substantially related to the matter in which the departed lawyer represented the client, and (2) any remaining lawyer in the firm has Rule 1.6 or 1.9(c) protected information material to the matter.

The architecture is enabling for the firm. When a lawyer moves on and takes the client matter with the lawyer, the firm reverts to a clean position with respect to that client unless the firm retains material confidential information through one of its remaining lawyers.

The screening safe harbor for laterals

The most operationally important development in Rule 1.10 is the screening safe harbor for lawyers moving from one firm to another. ABA Model Rule 1.10(a)(2) provides that imputation does not extend to a lateral lawyer's prior-firm conflicts if the disqualified lawyer is timely screened from any participation in the matter and apportioned no part of the fee, written notice is promptly given to the former client, and a certification of compliance is provided on the former client's request.

Kansas and Missouri have adopted versions of the screening safe harbor with conditions appropriate to each state. The effective elements of a screen are well-developed:

Elements of an effective screen

Timely imposition - at the moment of hire or earlier

Written prohibition of the lateral lawyer's access to files

Physical or electronic isolation from the matter

Apportionment of zero fee from the matter to the lateral lawyer

Firm-wide notice of the screen to all attorneys and staff

Documentation of the screen

Written screen memorandum signed by the lateral and by firm management

Written notice to the former client identifying the screened lawyer and the steps taken

Acknowledgement on the firm's conflict-check system that the matter is screened

Certification of compliance available on the former client's request

Screening enables lateral mobility. The screening safe harbor lets firms hire experienced lawyers without acquiring every conflict from every prior engagement. Lawyers can move between firms without abandoning their careers when they have touched matters at a prior firm.

1.10(c) - The consent pathway

Any disqualification under Rule 1.10 may be waived by the affected client under the same conditions as Rule 1.7. This is the second affirmative pathway - even where screening is unavailable or insufficient, the client whose interests the rule protects can consent. Informed consent confirmed in writing under 1.7(b)(4) reopens the matter to the firm.

Common procedural posture

Lateral arrival

A firm hires a lateral lawyer. The firm runs a conflict check that surfaces three matters where the lateral previously represented clients now adverse to the firm's existing clients. For each matter, the firm evaluates whether the lateral has material confidential information; if so, the firm imposes a written screen, gives written notice to the former clients, and certifies compliance. Where information is not material, no screen is needed. Where the lateral was the responsible attorney and retains substantial knowledge of the matter, the firm typically combines screening with client consent.

Lawyer departure

A lawyer leaves the firm and takes a client matter. The firm assesses whether any remaining lawyer in the firm has Rule 1.6 or 1.9(c) information material to that matter. If not, the firm is free under 1.10(b) to accept new work adverse to the former client. If so, the firm declines or seeks consent under 1.10(c).

Firm-management measures contemplated by 5.1(a)

Rule 5.1(a) requires firms to maintain measures that give reasonable assurance of compliance with the rules. For Rule 1.10, those measures typically include:

A conflict-checking system that captures every new engagement and every lateral arrival

Written protocols for the imposition of screens

Standard-form notice letters to former clients of laterals

Periodic audits of active screens

Training for partners and associates on identifying screening triggers

Continuing nature of the analysis

Imputation is not a one-time intake check. A matter that was conflict-free at the intake can become conflicted as new parties are added, as the firm hires new lawyers, or as existing engagements expand in scope. The conflict-checking system must run continuously to capture these changes.

Related rules and authority

Rule 1.7 - Concurrent conflicts; the source rule for imputation in current-client situations

Rule 1.9 - Former clients; the source rule for imputation in former-client situations

Rule 1.6 - Confidentiality of information; the predicate for the post-departure analysis under 1.10(b)

Rule 1.18 - Prospective clients; companion screening framework

Rule 5.1 - Supervisory responsibility; conflict screening is a typical firm-management measure

Practical impact

Rule 1.10 is the rule that determines whether a firm can accept a matter or accept a lateral lawyer. Three takeaways recur:

The personal-interest carve-out is broader than firms sometimes realize. Many one-lawyer conflicts do not need to be imputed if they do not present a significant risk of materially limiting the representation by remaining lawyers.

Screening is a deliberate process. An effective screen is documented, timed at hire, and audited; an undocumented informal practice is not a screen.

Client consent reopens the matter. The 1.10(c) consent pathway is available even where the screening safe harbor is not.

Related authority

## KRPC 1.15 / MRPC 4-1.15 - Safekeeping Property + IOLTA [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/krpc-1-15/

Open Bankruptcy Project

Rule of Professional Conduct
KRPC 1.15 / MRPC 4-1.15

KRPC 1.15 / MRPC 4-1.15: Safekeeping Property and the IOLTA Program

The trust-account architecture, the prompt-notice and prompt-delivery duties, the recordkeeping framework, and the IOLTA program structure.

What Rule 1.15 affirmatively does

Rule 1.15 is the architecture for handling other people's money. It tells the lawyer how to set up the trust account, how to keep client and third-party property separate from the lawyer's own, how to notify the owner when funds arrive, how to deliver funds when due, and how to maintain records that demonstrate compliance. Paired with each jurisdiction's IOLTA framework, the rule also supplies a public-interest funding source for legal-aid programs without imposing a cost on individual clients. The rule is the structural backbone of client-property handling and the access-to-justice funding mechanism the bar maintains.

Verbatim text of KRPC 1.15 (Kansas, abbreviated)

(a) A lawyer shall hold property of clients or third persons that is in a lawyer's possession in connection with a representation separate from the lawyer's own property. Funds shall be kept in a separate account maintained in the state where the lawyer's office is situated, or elsewhere with the consent of the client or third person. Other property shall be identified as such and appropriately safeguarded. Complete records of such account funds and other property shall be kept by the lawyer and shall be preserved for a period of five years after termination of the representation.

(b) Upon receiving funds or other property in which a client or third person has an interest, a lawyer shall promptly notify the client or third person. Except as stated in this rule or otherwise permitted by law or by agreement with the client, a lawyer shall promptly deliver to the client or third person any funds or other property that the client or third person is entitled to receive and, upon request by the client or third person, shall promptly render a full accounting regarding such property.

(c) When in the course of representation a lawyer is in possession of property in which both the lawyer and another person claim interests, the property shall be kept separate by the lawyer until there is an accounting and severance of their interest. If a dispute arises concerning their respective interests, the portion in dispute shall be kept separate by the lawyer until the dispute is resolved.

(d) [Recordkeeping requirements - separate ledger for each client, monthly reconciliation, preservation of records.] Kan. Sup. Ct. R. 226, KRPC 1.15.

Missouri Rule 4-1.15

Missouri Rule 4-1.15 tracks ABA Model Rule 1.15 with state-specific provisions for the Missouri Lawyers' Fund for Client Protection and detailed trust-account recordkeeping requirements. Both jurisdictions require participation in the IOLTA program for funds that cannot earn net interest for the client.

1.15(a) - The separate-account architecture

The first structural requirement is separation. Client funds and third-party funds held in connection with a representation must be kept in a separate account from the lawyer's own funds. Other property (documents, securities, tangible items) must be identified and appropriately safeguarded.

The separate account is typically a state-chartered or federally-insured bank account in the state where the lawyer's office is located, designated by name as an attorney trust account. The account is the lawyer's account in title but the clients' funds in substance. Cleared, identifiable client funds flow through the trust account; the lawyer's earned fees and operating funds flow through a separate business account.

1.15(b) - Prompt notice and prompt delivery

When a lawyer receives funds in which a client or third person has an interest, two duties trigger at the moment of receipt:

Prompt notice. The lawyer must promptly notify the client or third person that the funds have been received. The notice supplies the information the owner needs to monitor the account.

Prompt delivery. The lawyer must promptly deliver the funds the client or third person is entitled to receive, and on request render a full accounting.

The "promptly" standard is functional: it means as soon as is reasonable under the circumstances, taking account of the time required to clear deposits, identify net amounts after deductions, and confirm the owner's instructions.

1.15(c) - The dispute-segregation rule

When the lawyer is in possession of property in which both the lawyer and another person claim interests - for example, a settlement that includes both the client's recovery and the lawyer's contingent fee - the property is held separately until an accounting and severance. If a dispute arises about the respective interests, the disputed portion is held separately until the dispute is resolved. The undisputed portion is delivered promptly.

1.15(d) - The recordkeeping framework

Subdivision (d) supplies the records the lawyer must maintain. The framework varies slightly by jurisdiction but the core elements are constant:

Account-level records

Bank statements for the trust account

Canceled checks or images

Deposit slips with itemization of each deposit

Wire transfer records

Monthly reconciliations

Client-level records

Separate ledger for each client whose funds pass through the trust account

Running balance for each client

Identification of each transaction by date, source/payee, and purpose

Documentation of every disbursement

Settlement statements for contingent-fee matters

The records must be preserved for five years (Kansas) or as specified by Missouri rule after the termination of each representation.

The IOLTA program structure

IOLTA - Interest on Lawyers' Trust Accounts - is the program by which interest earned on pooled client funds that are too small or too short-term to earn net interest for any individual client is remitted to a state-administered fund that supports legal aid and access-to-justice programs.

IOLTA solves a coordination problem. Many client deposits are too small to justify the administrative cost of a separate interest-bearing account for each client. Before IOLTA, the interest these funds generated was either lost or accrued to the bank. IOLTA pools the interest from many such accounts and channels it to legal-services programs that serve clients who could not otherwise afford counsel.

Kansas IOLTA

The Kansas IOLTA program is administered through the Kansas Bar Foundation. Trust funds that cannot earn net interest for an individual client are deposited in IOLTA accounts at participating financial institutions; the interest is remitted to the Foundation and distributed in grants to programs that provide civil legal services to low-income Kansans.

Missouri IOLTA

The Missouri Lawyer Trust Account Foundation administers the Missouri IOLTA program. The structure parallels the Kansas program: pooled interest from IOLTA-eligible trust funds is remitted to the Foundation and distributed as grants to legal-services providers across the state.

Client-specific vs. IOLTA

The threshold question for each deposit is whether the funds can practicably earn net interest for the individual client. If yes - usually because the amount is large enough or the holding period long enough - the funds are placed in a separate interest-bearing account designated for that client. If not, the funds go into the firm's IOLTA account.

The shape of a compliant trust-account practice

Account setup. Trust account opened at a participating financial institution; account titled to identify it as a trust account; IOLTA designation registered with the state administrator where required.

Deposit discipline. Every deposit recorded in the corresponding client ledger before or contemporaneously with the deposit; source identified.

Disbursement discipline. No disbursement that would overdraw the client's individual ledger balance, even if the trust account as a whole has sufficient funds; each disbursement documented by purpose.

Monthly reconciliation. The bank balance, the book balance, and the sum of client ledger balances all reconcile to the same figure each month.

Annual review. An annual review of trust-account practices, including verification that earned fees have been timely transferred out and that no funds have remained dormant.

Common procedural posture

Settlement deposit

A settlement check arrives. The lawyer deposits it to the trust account. Prompt notice is given to the client. After clearance, the lawyer prepares a settlement statement that shows gross recovery, contingent fee under 1.5(c), expenses deducted, and net to the client. The client's share is delivered promptly; the fee is transferred to the firm's operating account; the expense reimbursements are paid.

Advance fee deposit

A new client pays an advance fee for work not yet performed. The unearned portion is held in the trust account. As work is performed, the lawyer invoices and transfers earned amounts to the firm's operating account, documenting each transfer in the client ledger. If the representation ends with unearned funds remaining, the funds are refunded under Rule 1.16(d).

Continuing nature of the duty

Rule 1.15 imposes continuing obligations: the separate-account requirement runs throughout the representation, the records must be preserved beyond termination, and the IOLTA participation is an ongoing program enrollment rather than a one-time election. The recordkeeping discipline of monthly reconciliation is the principal operational habit that demonstrates compliance.

Related rules and authority

Rule 1.4 - Communication; prompt notice under 1.15(b) is the property-handling instance of the 1.4 duty

Rule 1.5 - Fees; settlement statements under 1.5(c) are typically prepared from trust-account records

Rule 1.16 - Termination; unearned fees in trust are refunded on termination

Rule 5.1 - Supervisory responsibility; trust-account oversight is a typical firm-management measure

Rule 5.3 - Supervision of nonlawyers; bookkeeping staff who maintain trust records

Practical impact

Rule 1.15 is the rule that audits the firm most directly. Three takeaways recur:

Separation is the engine. The simplest and most important act is keeping client funds in a separate account from the firm's funds, every day.

Reconciliation prevents shortfalls. Monthly reconciliation catches errors before they become disciplinary matters.

IOLTA is a public-interest contribution. Participation in IOLTA channels otherwise-stranded interest into legal-services funding without imposing cost on any individual client.

Related authority

ABA Model Rule 1.15 - model rule with comment

Kansas IOLTA - Kansas Bar Foundation IOLTA program

Missouri IOLTA - Missouri Lawyer Trust Account Foundation

Kansas Rules of Professional Conduct - Kansas Supreme Court Rules

Missouri Rules of Professional Conduct - Missouri Supreme Court Rule 4

KRPC 1.5 (Fees)
KRPC 1.16 (Termination)

## KRPC 1.16 / MRPC 4-1.16 - Declining or Terminating Representation [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/krpc-1-16/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Rule of Professional Conduct
KRPC 1.16 / MRPC 4-1.16

KRPC 1.16 / MRPC 4-1.16: Declining or Terminating Representation

Mandatory withdrawal, permissive withdrawal, and the lawyer's duties on termination including file production.

Verbatim text of KRPC 1.16 (Kansas)

(a) Except as stated in paragraph (c), a lawyer shall not represent a client or, where representation has commenced, shall withdraw from the representation of a client if:

(1) the representation will result in violation of the rules of professional conduct or other law;

(2) the lawyer's physical or mental condition materially impairs the lawyer's ability to represent the client; or

(3) the lawyer is discharged.

(b) Except as stated in paragraph (c), a lawyer may withdraw from representing a client if:

(1) withdrawal can be accomplished without material adverse effect on the interests of the client;

(2) the client persists in a course of action involving the lawyer's services that the lawyer reasonably believes is criminal or fraudulent;

(3) the client has used the lawyer's services to perpetrate a crime or fraud;

(4) a client insists upon pursuing an objective that the lawyer considers repugnant or with which the lawyer has a fundamental disagreement;

(5) the client fails substantially to fulfill an obligation to the lawyer regarding the lawyer's services and has been given reasonable warning that the lawyer will withdraw unless the obligation is fulfilled;

(6) the representation will result in an unreasonable financial burden on the lawyer or has been rendered unreasonably difficult by the client; or

(7) other good cause for withdrawal exists.

(c) A lawyer must comply with applicable law requiring notice to or permission of a tribunal when terminating a representation. When ordered to do so by a tribunal, a lawyer shall continue representation notwithstanding good cause for terminating the representation.

(d) Upon termination of representation, a lawyer shall take steps to the extent reasonably practicable to protect a client's interests, such as giving reasonable notice to the client, allowing time for employment of other counsel, surrendering papers and property to which the client is entitled and refunding any advance payment of fee or expense that has not been earned or incurred. The lawyer may retain papers relating to the client to the extent permitted by other law. Kan. Sup. Ct. R. 226, KRPC 1.16.

Missouri Rule 4-1.16

Missouri Rule 4-1.16 is substantively identical to KRPC 1.16. Both rules follow ABA Model Rule 1.16, which establishes the same four-part structure: mandatory withdrawal grounds in subdivision (a), permissive withdrawal grounds in subdivision (b), tribunal-permission requirement in subdivision (c), and termination duties in subdivision (d).

Mandatory withdrawal under 1.16(a)

Subdivision (a) identifies three circumstances in which withdrawal is mandatory rather than discretionary:

1.16(a)(1) - Continued representation will result in violation of the rules of professional conduct or other law. The classic example is an unwaivable conflict of interest under Rule 1.7 that becomes apparent mid-representation.

1.16(a)(2) - The lawyer's physical or mental condition materially impairs the ability to represent the client.

1.16(a)(3) - The lawyer is discharged by the client. A client may discharge a lawyer at any time, with or without cause, subject only to the lawyer's right to be heard on a withdrawal motion in any matter where tribunal permission is required.

Permissive withdrawal under 1.16(b)

Subdivision (b) identifies seven circumstances in which withdrawal is permitted but not required. The first - withdrawal without material adverse effect on the client's interests - operates as a general permission to withdraw when no harm results. The remaining six identify specific circumstances:

Client persists in criminal or fraudulent course of action using lawyer's services - 1.16(b)(2)

Client has used lawyer's services to perpetrate crime or fraud - 1.16(b)(3)

Client insists on objective the lawyer considers repugnant or fundamentally disagrees with - 1.16(b)(4)

Client fails to fulfill obligation to lawyer (typically fees) after reasonable warning - 1.16(b)(5)

Representation creates unreasonable financial burden or has been rendered unreasonably difficult by client - 1.16(b)(6)

Other good cause - 1.16(b)(7)

Tribunal permission under 1.16(c)

When the representation is before a tribunal that requires notice or permission for termination, the lawyer must comply with that requirement. In federal bankruptcy court, the local rule governing withdrawal applies (see Rule 9010 and discussion of local rules). When ordered by a tribunal to continue representation notwithstanding good cause for termination, the lawyer must do so. The tribunal's order overrides the otherwise-permissive (or even mandatory) grounds for withdrawal, with limited exceptions where continuation would itself violate the rules of professional conduct.

The 1.16(d) termination duties

Subdivision (d) is the operative endpoint of any representation. Upon termination - whether by client discharge, by lawyer-initiated withdrawal, or by completion of the matter - the lawyer must take reasonable steps to protect the client's interests. The enumerated steps include:

Reasonable notice to the client

The client must be informed of the termination and its consequences. Where the termination is lawyer-initiated, this includes informing the client of the basis (to the extent ethically permitted) and the steps the client must take to protect the client's interests.

Time for employment of other counsel

The withdrawing lawyer must allow time for the client to obtain successor counsel. In matters with pending deadlines or hearings, "reasonable time" is a function of those deadlines; a withdrawal motion filed on the eve of a hearing without the client having a meaningful opportunity to obtain new counsel is generally not consistent with the rule.

Surrender of papers and property

The lawyer must surrender to the client all papers and property to which the client is entitled. This is the "client file" obligation. The scope of the client file is broad in most jurisdictions and includes all materials provided by the client to the lawyer, all materials the lawyer prepared for the client's purposes, and all materials received from third parties in the course of the representation. Where a lawyer has a duty to produce the client file, the entire file generally must be produced; selective production may itself be both a 1.16(d) violation and grounds for malpractice exposure.

Refund of unearned fees or expenses

Advance payments of fees or expenses that have not been earned or incurred must be refunded. The substantive question of what has been "earned" is governed by the engagement agreement and applicable fee-shifting authority; in bankruptcy matters, Section 329(b) provides an independent federal mechanism for evaluating reasonableness of fees paid.

The "entire file" standard. Where the rule requires production of the client file, the entire file is generally required. Partial production of selected portions, with retention of materials the lawyer prefers not to produce, has been treated by reviewing authority as a violation of the rule independent of any underlying defect in the representation itself.

Permitted retention of papers

The last sentence of subdivision (d) preserves any right the lawyer has under other law to retain papers - typically an attorney's lien for unpaid fees. The scope of any such lien is governed by state law and varies materially by jurisdiction. Most jurisdictions either (a) do not permit retention of materials whose retention would prejudice the client's substantive position in pending proceedings, or (b) permit retention only as to materials prepared at the lawyer's expense and not yet paid for, while requiring production of materials provided by the client or essential to ongoing matters.

Common procedural posture

Client discharge in active bankruptcy case

The client emails the lawyer instructing the lawyer to cease work. Rule 1.16(a)(3) makes withdrawal mandatory. The lawyer files a withdrawal motion under the local rule (Rule 9010 framework), provides notice to the client and all parties entitled to notice, and on entry of an order granting withdrawal complies with Rule 1.16(d) - including surrender of the client file and refund of any unearned advance fees.

Lawyer-initiated withdrawal for fees

The client has fallen significantly behind on fee obligations. The lawyer provides reasonable warning that withdrawal will be sought unless the obligation is addressed. If the obligation is not addressed, the lawyer may move to withdraw under 1.16(b)(5). The motion must satisfy the local-rule timing and notice requirements; tribunal permission under 1.16(c) is required before the representation is procedurally terminated.

Related rules and authority

Rule 1.3 - Diligence in carrying out the representation

Rule 1.4 - Communication with the client

Rule 1.5 - Fees and the reasonableness standard

Rule 1.7 / 1.9 - Conflicts of interest, frequent basis for mandatory withdrawal under 1.16(a)(1)

Rule 8.4(d) - Conduct prejudicial to administration of justice; failure to produce the file may rise to 8.4(d)

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 9010 - Local-rule withdrawal procedure in federal bankruptcy court

Practical impact

Rule 1.16(d) is the most-litigated subdivision of the rule because it sets a continuing duty that runs from termination forward. The duty does not extinguish at the moment of termination; it continues until the client has received reasonable notice, has had time to obtain successor counsel, has received the file, and has received any refund due. A representation can be procedurally terminated by court order while the 1.16(d) duties remain unperformed; the procedural endpoint does not discharge the substantive duties.

Related authority

ABA Model Rule 1.16 - model rule with comment

Kansas Rules of Professional Conduct - Kansas Supreme Court Rules

Missouri Rules of Professional Conduct - Missouri Supreme Court Rule 4

Open Bankruptcy Project cross-references

KRPC 1.4 (Communication)
KRPC 3.3 (Candor)
KRPC 5.1 (Supervision)
KRPC 8.3 (Reporting)
KRPC 8.4 (Misconduct)
Rule 9010 (Representation)
Rule 2016 (Compensation)
Section 329 Guide

## KRPC 1.17 / MRPC 4-1.17 - Sale of Law Practice [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/krpc-1-17/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Rule of Professional Conduct
KRPC 1.17 / MRPC 4-1.17

KRPC 1.17 / MRPC 4-1.17: Sale of Law Practice

The four conditions enabling practice transition, the client-continuity architecture, and the seller-plus-buyer-plus-transition framework.

Verbatim text of KRPC 1.17 (Kansas)

A lawyer or law firm may sell or purchase a law practice, or an area of law practice, including good will, if the following conditions are satisfied:

(a) The seller ceases to engage in the private practice of law, or in the area of practice that has been sold, from an office that is within the geographic area in which the practice has been conducted;

(b) The entire practice, or the entire area of practice, is sold to one or more lawyers or law firms;

(c) The seller gives written notice to each of the seller's clients regarding:

(1) the proposed sale;

(2) the client's right to retain other counsel or to take possession of the file; and

(3) the fact that the client's consent to the transfer of the client's files will be presumed if the client does not take any action or does not otherwise object within ninety (90) days of receipt of the notice; and

(d) The fees charged clients shall not be increased by reason of the sale. Kan. Sup. Ct. R. 226, KRPC 1.17.

Missouri Rule 4-1.17

Missouri Rule 4-1.17 is substantively parallel and tracks ABA Model Rule 1.17. The rule's purpose, articulated in Comment [1], is to permit the sale of a practice so that retiring or transitioning lawyers can realize the value they have built, while protecting clients with a structured transition architecture.

The four conditions 1.17 enables for practice transition

Rule 1.17 operates as a permission structure. By satisfying four conditions, a lawyer or firm acquires a clean path to transfer a practice that would otherwise be encumbered by the personal nature of the lawyer-client relationship. The four conditions function as enabling architecture rather than as a list of restrictions.

(a) Seller cessation

The seller ceases the private practice (or the area of practice sold) from an office within the geographic area in which the practice has been conducted. The condition ensures the transferred clients are actually transferring, not merely being marketed to a different firm letterhead.

(b) Entire-practice or entire-area scope

The sale must cover the entire practice, or the entire area of practice. Selective transfer of valuable matters while retaining others is not permitted. The condition prevents cherry-picking that would leave behind the matters least attractive to a buyer.

(c) Client-notice framework

Written notice to each affected client, identifying the proposed sale, the right to retain other counsel or take possession of the file, and the 90-day passive-consent window. Notice is the client's mechanism for accepting, redirecting, or terminating the transition.

(d) Fee maintenance

Fees charged to existing clients may not be increased by reason of the sale. The condition prevents the transaction from being financed by client overcharge. The client cannot be made worse off as a price-payer by the change in attorney.

Client-continuity architecture

The four conditions together form the client-continuity architecture. The architecture's central insight is that clients do not transfer automatically with the sale of a practice; the lawyer-client relationship is personal, and the rules of professional conduct do not permit the client to be treated as transferable property. Rule 1.17 substitutes a structured-consent mechanism for ordinary commercial conveyance.

The mechanism has three moving parts:

Written notice initiates the transition and creates a documentary record of what each client was told

Affirmative options - the right to retain other counsel or take possession of the file - preserve client autonomy

The 90-day passive-consent window establishes a default that permits orderly transition without requiring affirmative client action for every file

The 90-day window is structural: it gives the client a meaningful opportunity to evaluate the transition, while preventing the practice from being permanently encumbered by clients who do not respond. The Comment to Model Rule 1.17 emphasizes that the notice should be clear enough to make the choice meaningful, including identification of the buyer and information sufficient for the client to assess the substitution.

Seller, buyer, and transition framework

The rule allocates responsibilities across three roles - seller, buyer, and transition - each with its own competence and continuity obligations.

Seller obligations

Cease the practice (or area) from within the geographic area, satisfying condition (a)

Sell the entire practice or area, satisfying condition (b)

Issue the written notice to every affected client, satisfying condition (c)

Refrain from raising fees by reason of the sale, satisfying condition (d)

Continue to honor confidentiality under Rule 1.6 through and beyond the transition

Buyer obligations

Accept the practice or area in its entirety, including matters that may be less commercially attractive

Honor existing client expectations, including fee structures, through condition (d)

Apply competent representation under Rule 1.1 to each acquired matter, including matters in unfamiliar substantive areas (which may require declining or referring particular matters rather than acquiring incompetence)

Conduct conflicts analysis under Rule 1.7 and Rule 1.9 against the existing client roster of the acquiring firm

Transition-period architecture

The 90-day notice window is itself a transition period. During the window:

Active matters require diligence under Rule 1.3 regardless of whether the file ultimately transfers; deadlines do not pause for the notice window

Communication under Rule 1.4 continues with the responsible lawyer - the seller before transfer, the buyer after, or the file's new lawyer if the client elects to retain other counsel

If the client elects to take possession of the file or retain different counsel, the file-handling duty under Rule 1.16(d) applies; the file is returned to the client or transmitted to successor counsel

Confidentiality under Rule 1.6 governs the information flow throughout, including what the buyer may review during due diligence

Jurisdiction continuity and geographic scope

Condition (a) requires cessation from an office "within the geographic area in which the practice has been conducted." The geographic-scope language preserves the client-protection purpose: a seller who continues practicing in the same area would frustrate the structured-transition mechanism by remaining available as the client's lawyer of habit. The geographic scope is calibrated to the practice's actual market.

Jurisdiction continuity also matters for the buyer. A buyer admitted in a different jurisdiction must address admission status before acquiring matters that require local practice. The interaction with Rule 5.5 on unauthorized practice and with Rule 8.5 on disciplinary authority must be analyzed at the front end of the transaction.

The "good will" recognition

The rule's permission to include "good will" in the sale was a significant addition. Earlier versions of the professional conduct rules either prohibited the sale of a practice altogether or permitted only the sale of tangible assets. The current rule recognizes that the value of an established practice - the relationships, the referral network, the reputation - is real and may be transferred for value, subject to the four conditions. The good-will recognition is what makes the rule operationally useful; without it, the practical incentive to comply with the four conditions would be limited.

Relationship to Rule 1.16 (Termination)

A sale under Rule 1.17 effects a termination of the seller's representation of clients who elect to retain other counsel or take possession of their files, and a transition of representation to the buyer for clients who passively consent. The file-return and orderly-transition duties under Rule 1.16(d) apply to the non-transferring clients. Rule 1.17 is best understood as a structured-1.16 procedure for a whole practice, with the notice framework providing the client-protection architecture that ordinary 1.16 termination would otherwise require client-by-client.

Relationship to Rules 1.6, 1.7, and 1.9

Confidentiality under Rule 1.6 governs what the buyer may learn during due diligence. Conflicts analysis under Rule 1.7 and Rule 1.9 must be conducted by the buyer against its existing client roster before the transition is complete; matters that would create a conflict cannot simply be acquired through the 1.17 framework. The interaction is structural: the four conditions of 1.17 do not relieve any other rule's requirements.

Related rules and authority

Rule 1.1 - Competence; buyer competence in acquired areas

Rule 1.6 - Confidentiality; due-diligence and file-transfer information flow

Rule 1.7 - Current-client conflicts; buyer-side analysis

Rule 1.16 - Termination; file-return duties for non-transferring clients

Rule 5.5 - Unauthorized practice; jurisdiction continuity

Rule 8.5 - Disciplinary authority; cross-jurisdictional transactions

Practical impact

Rule 1.17 enables what would otherwise be impossible - the orderly transfer of a law practice for value - by substituting structured client-protection architecture for ordinary commercial conveyance. The four conditions, taken together, allow retiring or transitioning lawyers to realize the value they have built while preserving the client's autonomy and continuity of representation. The rule rewards practices that operate with the kind of file organization, client communication, and fee discipline that make the 1.17 conditions naturally satisfiable; practices that have not invested in those infrastructures find the conditions harder to meet at the moment of transition.

Related authority

ABA Model Rule 1.17 - model rule with comment

Kansas Rules of Professional Conduct - Kansas Supreme Court Rules

Missouri Rules of Professional Conduct - Missouri Supreme Court Rule 4

Open Bankruptcy Project cross-references

KRPC 1.3 (Diligence)
KRPC 1.4 (Communication)
KRPC 1.7 (Conflicts)
KRPC 1.16 (Termination)
KRPC 5.5 (Unauthorized practice)
KRPC 8.5 (Disciplinary authority)

## KRPC 1.18 / MRPC 4-1.18 - Duties to Prospective Client [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/krpc-1-18/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Rule of Professional Conduct
KRPC 1.18 / MRPC 4-1.18

KRPC 1.18 / MRPC 4-1.18: Duties to Prospective Client

The consultation duty, the limited-information protection, and the screening + consent safe harbors that preserve continued representation.

What Rule 1.18 affirmatively does

Rule 1.18 is the rule that structures the threshold lawyer-client encounter - the consultation that may or may not become an engagement. The rule recognizes that prospective clients share information during these consultations, and it both protects that information and provides three pathways by which a firm can continue to represent existing or new matters notwithstanding a prospective-client consultation. The rule is enabling for prospective clients (they can speak candidly) and for firms (they have a structured pathway to remain available for adverse work where appropriate).

Verbatim text of KRPC 1.18 (Kansas)

(a) A person who consults with a lawyer about the possibility of forming a client-lawyer relationship with respect to a matter is a prospective client.

(b) Even when no client-lawyer relationship ensues, a lawyer who has learned information from a prospective client shall not use or reveal that information, except as Rule 1.9 would permit with respect to information of a former client.

(c) A lawyer subject to paragraph (b) shall not represent a client with interests materially adverse to those of a prospective client in the same or a substantially related matter if the lawyer received information from the prospective client that could be significantly harmful to that person in the matter, except as provided in paragraph (d). If a lawyer is disqualified from representation under this paragraph, no lawyer in a firm with which that lawyer is associated may knowingly undertake or continue representation in such a matter, except as provided in paragraph (d).

(d) When the lawyer has received disqualifying information as defined in paragraph (c), representation is permissible if:

(1) both the affected client and the prospective client have given informed consent, confirmed in writing; or

(2) the lawyer who received the information took reasonable measures to avoid exposure to more disqualifying information than was reasonably necessary to determine whether to represent the prospective client; and

(i) the disqualified lawyer is timely screened from any participation in the matter and is apportioned no part of the fee therefrom; and

(ii) written notice is promptly given to the prospective client. Kan. Sup. Ct. R. 226, KRPC 1.18.

Missouri Rule 4-1.18

Missouri Rule 4-1.18 tracks ABA Model Rule 1.18 and adopts the same four-paragraph architecture: definition of prospective client, the information-use restriction, the conflict rule with the "significantly harmful" threshold, and the two safe-harbor pathways.

1.18(a) - Who is a prospective client

A prospective client is a person who consults with a lawyer about the possibility of forming a client-lawyer relationship with respect to a matter. The definition contemplates a deliberate, bidirectional inquiry: the prospective client is exploring engagement, and the lawyer is providing information that bears on whether engagement is feasible. Unsolicited communications from members of the public who broadcast their situation without consultation - for example, mass emails sent to multiple lawyers without invitation - generally do not create a prospective-client relationship.

The Comment to Model Rule 1.18 notes that a person who provides information to a lawyer in response to advertising that merely describes the lawyer's services may be a prospective client; a person who provides information unilaterally to a lawyer who has not invited it generally is not.

1.18(b) - The information-use restriction

Even when no client-lawyer relationship ensues, the lawyer who learned information from a prospective client shall not use or reveal that information except as Rule 1.9 would permit with respect to former-client information. This is the structural protection that lets the prospective client speak candidly during the consultation. The information may be used or revealed only in the limited ways Rule 1.9 permits for former-client information - principally when the information has become generally known.

1.18(c) - The conflict and the "significantly harmful" threshold

Subdivision (c) supplies a narrower disqualification standard than Rule 1.9. A lawyer who received information from a prospective client may not represent a client with interests materially adverse to the prospective client in the same or a substantially related matter if the information could be significantly harmful to the prospective client in the matter.

Three elements all must be present for disqualification under 1.18(c): (1) material adversity between the prospective client's interests and the proposed new client's interests, (2) substantial relationship between the matter discussed and the proposed new matter, and (3) information received that could be significantly harmful in the new matter.

The "significantly harmful" threshold matters. Information that is publicly available, or that is general background about a matter, or that does not bear on the strategy or vulnerabilities of the prospective client in the specific matter, generally is not "significantly harmful." The rule does not categorically foreclose representation based on any contact; it foreclosures based on contact that conveyed strategically meaningful information.

1.18(d) - The two safe-harbor pathways for continued representation

When 1.18(c) would otherwise disqualify, subdivision (d) supplies two affirmative pathways by which the firm can continue to take the adverse matter.

Pathway 1: Informed consent in writing from both

Both the affected client and the prospective client give informed consent, confirmed in writing. This is the bilateral-consent pathway. Where the prospective client retains the disqualifying-information protection but is willing to release it - perhaps because the matter the firm wishes to take is sufficiently distant from the prospective consultation - the consent pathway opens the matter.

Pathway 2: Limited information + screening + notice

This is the operational pathway most firms rely on. It has three integrated components:

Limited-information measure

The lawyer who received the information took reasonable measures to avoid exposure to more disqualifying information than was reasonably necessary to determine whether to represent the prospective client. The lawyer's intake protocol should ask enough to evaluate the engagement and stop before extracting strategic detail.

Timely screen + no fee

The lawyer who received the information is timely screened from any participation in the matter and apportioned no part of the fee. The screen elements mirror the lateral-screening elements under Rule 1.10.

Prompt written notice

Written notice is promptly given to the prospective client. The notice identifies the screened lawyer, the screen's existence, and the matter the firm is undertaking.

Documentation

The screen is documented in writing, the limited-information measures are recorded in the intake file, and the notice to the prospective client is preserved.

The shape of an effective intake protocol

A 1.18-aware intake protocol typically includes:

A scripted opening that identifies what information the lawyer needs to determine whether to take the matter

Conflict-check questions asked before substantive consultation begins

A signal to stop the inquiry when conflict-check returns a hit until the conflict is resolved

A written consultation memorandum that records what was discussed in summary terms, kept separately from substantive engagement files

A "thanks but no" letter for prospective clients the firm declines, confirming that the consultation did not become an engagement

Common procedural posture

Initial consultation that does not become an engagement

A prospective client meets with a lawyer to discuss a possible commercial dispute. The firm declines the engagement (for any reason - fee, scope, capacity). Later, the prospective client's adversary asks the firm to represent it in the same matter. The firm runs a 1.18 analysis: was significantly harmful information conveyed in the consultation? If yes, the firm must satisfy one of the two 1.18(d) pathways before taking the adverse matter. If no, the firm may take the matter without further analysis.

Consultation that surfaces a conflict before substantive discussion

The intake intake protocol catches a conflict in the first five minutes of the consultation. The lawyer pauses the substantive discussion, explains the conflict, and offers to refer the prospective client to other counsel. Because limited-information measures were observed, the firm preserves the option to continue representing the existing client; if the prospective client subsequently becomes an adversary's client, the screening + notice pathway under 1.18(d)(2) is available.

Relationship to other conflict rules

Rule 1.7 - Current-client conflicts; analytically distinct because 1.18 applies before an engagement exists

Rule 1.9 - Former-client conflicts; the rule whose treatment of "information" 1.18(b) incorporates

Rule 1.10 - Imputation; 1.18(c) explicitly extends imputation to firm members, but 1.18(d) provides the screening exception that 1.10 does not always provide for current/former conflicts

Continuing nature of the duty

The information-use restriction under 1.18(b) continues indefinitely - the prospective client whose consultation did not become an engagement nevertheless retains the protection of the information shared in the consultation. The duty to evaluate adverse matters under 1.18(c) attaches whenever the firm contemplates new work that touches the matter discussed in the prior consultation.

Related rules and authority

Rule 1.7 - Current-client conflicts

Rule 1.9 - Former-client duties; the basis for 1.18(b)'s information-use restriction

Rule 1.10 - Imputation; companion screening framework

Rule 1.4 - Communication; the channel through which informed consent under 1.18(d)(1) is obtained

Rule 5.1 - Supervisory responsibility; intake screening is a firm-management measure

Practical impact

Rule 1.18 is the rule firms operationalize through intake protocols. Three takeaways recur:

Limited-information intake is the engine. The 1.18(d)(2) safe harbor is available only when the intake protocol limits the information received to what was reasonably necessary.

Documentation preserves the safe harbor. The screening, the fee apportionment, the written notice, and the consultation memo together demonstrate compliance.

Consent reopens the matter. Where the screening safe harbor is unavailable or insufficient, the 1.18(d)(1) bilateral-consent pathway remains.

Related authority

ABA Model Rule 1.18 - model rule with comment

Kansas Rules of Professional Conduct - Kansas Supreme Court Rules

Missouri Rules of Professional Conduct - Missouri Supreme Court Rule 4

KRPC 1.9 (Former Clients)

## KRPC 1.2 / MRPC 4-1.2 - Scope of Representation and Allocation of Authority [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/krpc-1-2/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Rule of Professional Conduct
KRPC 1.2 / MRPC 4-1.2

KRPC 1.2 / MRPC 4-1.2: Scope of Representation and Allocation of Authority Between Client and Lawyer

The decision allocation Rule 1.2 structures, the limited-scope framework it authorizes, and the counseling boundary it draws.

What Rule 1.2 affirmatively does

Rule 1.2 is the architecture of decision-making in the lawyer-client relationship. It allocates authority between the two participants so that each knows which decisions belong to whom, it expressly authorizes representation of a limited scope so that clients who cannot afford full representation can still obtain meaningful legal help, and it gives the lawyer broad latitude to counsel a client on the legal consequences of any contemplated course of conduct, including conduct of doubtful legality. The rule is structural and enabling rather than restrictive: it tells the lawyer what the lawyer is empowered to do at the client's direction and within the scope agreed upon.

Verbatim text of KRPC 1.2 (Kansas)

(a) A lawyer shall abide by a client's decisions concerning the objectives of representation and, as required by Rule 1.4, shall consult with the client as to the means by which they are to be pursued. A lawyer may take such action on behalf of the client as is impliedly authorized to carry out the representation. A lawyer shall abide by a client's decision whether to settle a matter. In a criminal case, the lawyer shall abide by the client's decision, after consultation with the lawyer, as to a plea to be entered, whether to waive jury trial and whether the client will testify.

(b) A lawyer's representation of a client, including representation by appointment, does not constitute an endorsement of the client's political, economic, social or moral views or activities.

(c) A lawyer may limit the scope of the representation if the limitation is reasonable under the circumstances and the client gives informed consent.

(d) A lawyer shall not counsel a client to engage, or assist a client, in conduct that the lawyer knows is criminal or fraudulent, but a lawyer may discuss the legal consequences of any proposed course of conduct with a client and may counsel or assist a client to make a good faith effort to determine the validity, scope, meaning or application of the law. Kan. Sup. Ct. R. 226, KRPC 1.2.

Missouri Rule 4-1.2

Missouri Rule 4-1.2 is substantively parallel to KRPC 1.2 and tracks ABA Model Rule 1.2. Both rules structure four affirmative architectures: (1) client authority over objectives, (2) lawyer authority over means in consultation with the client, (3) a limited-scope option available with informed consent, and (4) a broad counseling latitude that includes good-faith challenges to the law.

1.2(a) - The decision-allocation architecture

Subdivision (a) divides decisions into three working categories. The first category - decisions the client controls - includes the objectives of the representation, the decision whether to settle, and in a criminal matter the plea, the jury trial waiver, and whether the client will testify. These are decisions that allocate the client's substantive rights and personal exposures, and the rule reserves them to the person whose rights and exposures they are.

The second category - the means by which objectives are pursued - is shared. The lawyer brings professional judgment about strategy, tactics, and the choice among lawful methods; the client brings substantive interests and the contextual knowledge of what the client can accept. Rule 1.4 requires the lawyer to consult with the client on means. The shared architecture recognizes that strategic choices implicate both professional craft and client interest.

The third category - actions impliedly authorized to carry out the representation - lets the lawyer act efficiently on the client's behalf without separate authorization for every step. Filing a routine motion, sending a standard discovery request, agreeing to a customary scheduling extension - these proceed under implied authority once the representation is established.

1.2(b) - The non-endorsement principle

Subdivision (b) provides that representation of a client does not constitute the lawyer's endorsement of the client's views or activities. This is a load-bearing structural feature: it enables lawyers to take on clients whose views differ from the lawyer's own, and it lets appointed counsel serve clients in matters where the lawyer would otherwise face attribution of the client's positions. The principle protects the availability of counsel to controversial clients and to clients whose causes are unpopular.

1.2(c) - The limited-scope framework

Subdivision (c) authorizes limited-scope representation: a lawyer may agree to represent a client for a defined slice of a matter rather than the whole. The two conditions are (1) the limitation must be reasonable under the circumstances, and (2) the client must give informed consent.

Limited-scope (or "unbundled") representation expands access. The framework lets clients who cannot afford full representation purchase the legal services that matter most: drafting a single brief, appearing at a single hearing, ghostwriting pleadings for a pro se litigant, providing strategic consultation without entering an appearance. Many courts have adopted local rules that recognize the limited-scope appearance.

The bankruptcy-court wrinkle: a limited appearance is not always available

Rule 1.2(c) authorizes limited-scope representation as a matter of professional ethics. Whether a lawyer can make a limited entry of appearance in a given court is a separate, procedural question governed by that court's own rules, not by Rule 1.2(c). The two do not always line up.

In bankruptcy, the availability of a limited appearance varies by district, and many courts do not offer a clean one. A number of bankruptcy courts treat any entry of appearance as a general appearance: once counsel appears for a debtor, counsel is counsel of record and can step away only by a motion to withdraw granted by leave of court. In that setting, "appear for a single motion or hearing, then exit" is not a self-executing option, even though Rule 1.2(c) permits the underlying limited engagement. The constraint is sharpest for entity debtors (corporations and LLCs), which cannot proceed pro se at all and therefore cannot fill the gaps between limited tasks themselves.

The practical consequences for someone seeking unbundled help in a bankruptcy case:

Behind-the-scenes help is the most portable. Drafting, ghostwriting, and strategic consultation under 1.2(c) do not require an entry of appearance, so they remain available across districts, subject to any local disclosure rule for prepared filings.

Anything filed or argued in court is heavier than it looks. If you need a lawyer to actually sign, file, or appear, expect a full entry of appearance followed by a separate motion to withdraw, not a one-time cameo. Budget and consent accordingly.

Check the local rules first. Some bankruptcy courts have express limited-appearance provisions; many do not, and most require leave of court to withdraw once counsel has appeared. Confirm your district's appearance and withdrawal rules before assuming a limited appearance is on the table.

The reasonableness condition

A limitation is reasonable when the slice the lawyer agrees to handle can meaningfully be handled separately and when the lawyer can perform that slice competently. A limitation is not reasonable if it would deprive the client of effective representation - for example, agreeing to draft a complaint without preserving any pre-suit defenses the lawyer should have investigated.

The informed-consent condition

Informed consent means the client understands what is included, what is excluded, what risks attend the exclusions, and what alternatives exist. The lawyer must communicate the basis of the limitation clearly enough that a reasonable client can decide whether to accept it. Written confirmation is best practice in Kansas and is required in some Missouri contexts where fee structure intersects with scope.

1.2(d) - The counseling boundary and what it preserves

Subdivision (d) draws a single boundary - the lawyer may not counsel or assist a client in conduct the lawyer knows to be criminal or fraudulent - and then expressly preserves the lawyer's broad latitude on the affirmative side of that boundary.

What 1.2(d) preserves is substantial:

Discussion of legal consequences. The lawyer may discuss the legal consequences of any proposed course of conduct with the client. The client may be considering an action of doubtful legality; the lawyer is permitted - indeed, often obligated under Rule 1.4 - to lay out what the law says about it.

Good-faith challenges to the law. The lawyer may counsel or assist a client in a good faith effort to determine the validity, scope, meaning, or application of the law. This includes test-case litigation, declaratory-judgment actions, and structured noncompliance designed to obtain judicial review.

Counseling on lawful workarounds. If a client's first-instinct course of conduct would be unlawful, the lawyer may counsel the client on lawful alternatives that achieve similar objectives.

The shape of an effective engagement letter

Objectives section

Names the decisions reserved to the client under 1.2(a): the scope of relief sought, the disposition decision, and (in criminal matters) plea, jury waiver, and testimony. Confirms that the lawyer will consult with the client on means under Rule 1.4.

Scope section

If the engagement is limited under 1.2(c), the scope section names what is included and what is excluded, identifies the risks of the exclusions, and confirms the client's informed consent. If the engagement is full-scope, the section says so and notes the milestones at which scope can be revisited.

Continuing nature of the allocation

The decisions reserved to the client under 1.2(a) remain reserved throughout the representation. A client's objectives can change; the client's decision whether to settle is the client's decision at the time the offer is on the table, not a decision delegated at the engagement's outset. The lawyer's consultation duty under Rule 1.4 runs continuously and supplies the information on which the client exercises 1.2(a) authority.

Related rules and authority

Rule 1.1 - Competence; required for any agreed scope

Rule 1.3 - Diligence within the agreed scope

Rule 1.4 - Communication; supplies the information the client uses to exercise 1.2(a) authority

Rule 1.5 - Fees; intersects with scope at the engagement-letter stage

Rule 1.7 - Conflict of interest analysis informed by scope

Rule 1.16 - Declining or terminating representation when scope cannot be performed

Practical impact

Rule 1.2 is the rule lawyers consult first when shaping an engagement and last when a dispute arises about what the engagement covered. Two takeaways recur:

Clarity at the front end is the engine of the rule. A clear allocation of decisions, a clear definition of scope, and a clear written engagement letter are the operational forms in which the rule does its work.

The rule expands access to counsel. The limited-scope framework in 1.2(c) is the principal tool by which the profession answers the access-to-justice question. Lawyers who use 1.2(c) effectively serve clients who would otherwise proceed pro se.

Related authority

ABA Model Rule 1.2 - model rule with comment

Kansas Rules of Professional Conduct - Kansas Supreme Court Rules

Missouri Rules of Professional Conduct - Missouri Supreme Court Rule 4

## KRPC 1.3 / MRPC 4-1.3 - Diligence [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/krpc-1-3/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Rule of Professional Conduct
KRPC 1.3 / MRPC 4-1.3

KRPC 1.3 / MRPC 4-1.3: Diligence

Reasonable diligence, promptness, and the duty to carry matters through to completion.

Verbatim text of KRPC 1.3 (Kansas)

A lawyer shall act with reasonable diligence and promptness in representing a client. Kan. Sup. Ct. R. 226, KRPC 1.3.

Missouri Rule 4-1.3

Missouri Rule 4-1.3 is substantively identical to KRPC 1.3 and tracks ABA Model Rule 1.3. The rule itself is a single sentence; the operative content is supplied by the Comment, which Kansas and Missouri have largely adopted.

"Reasonable diligence"

Diligence is the application of attention and effort to the client's matter at a level commensurate with what the matter requires. Comment 1 to Model Rule 1.3 explains that a lawyer should pursue a matter on behalf of a client despite opposition, obstruction, or personal inconvenience, and must take whatever lawful and ethical measures are required to vindicate the client's cause. The standard is "reasonable," not maximal; the rule does not require heroic effort, but it does require effort proportionate to the matter.

Comment 1 also recognizes the lawyer's autonomy in the choice of means. A lawyer is not bound to press for every advantage that might be realized for a client. The lawyer has professional discretion in determining the means by which a matter should be pursued. But the discretion is bounded by the lawyer's duty of competent and zealous representation; "discretion" does not encompass inaction on the matter.

"Promptness"

Promptness is the temporal dimension of diligence. Comment 3 emphasizes that perhaps no professional shortcoming is more widely resented than procrastination. Even when a client's interests are not affected in substance, unreasonable delay can cause the client needless anxiety and undermine confidence in the lawyer's trustworthiness. The duty of promptness applies to:

Returning client communications within a reasonable time

Filing documents required by deadlines (statutory, rule-based, or court-ordered)

Taking action on opportunities that have a time-limited window

Pursuing the matter to its conclusion rather than allowing it to stall

Carrying the matter through to completion

Comment 4 establishes that unless the relationship is terminated as provided in Rule 1.16, a lawyer should carry through to conclusion all matters undertaken for a client. If a lawyer's employment is limited to a specific matter, the relationship terminates when the matter has been resolved. If a lawyer has served a client over a substantial period in a variety of matters, the client sometimes may assume that the lawyer will continue to serve on a continuing basis unless the lawyer gives notice of withdrawal.

Ambiguity about whether the representation continues is itself a problem. Comment 4 advises that doubt about whether a client-lawyer relationship still exists should be clarified by the lawyer, preferably in writing, so that the client will not mistakenly suppose the lawyer is looking after the client's affairs when the lawyer has ceased to do so. Where a representation has effectively ended without formal closure, the duty of diligence interacts with the duty of communication under Rule 1.4 and the termination duties under Rule 1.16.

Workload management - Comment 2

Comment 2 addresses the lawyer's professional discretion in managing workload. A lawyer's workload must be controlled so that each matter can be handled competently. A lawyer who takes on more work than the lawyer can competently and diligently perform - whether through underestimation of the work required or through accepting too many matters - has not satisfied the rule by performing diligently on some matters and neglecting others. The duty of diligence runs to each client.

The interaction with Rule 1.1 (Competence)

Rules 1.1 and 1.3 are conceptually distinct but operationally paired. Competence concerns the quality of the lawyer's work; diligence concerns its timing and consistency. A lawyer can be competent but not diligent (capable but inattentive). A lawyer can be diligent but not competent (attentive but unprepared). Both rules must be satisfied for representation to meet the basic professional standard.

Common procedural posture

Missed deadline

A statutory deadline, court-ordered deadline, or rule-based deadline passes without action by the lawyer. Unless the lawyer can establish that the inaction was the product of a reasonable strategic decision communicated to and approved by the client under Rule 1.4, the missed deadline is a diligence violation. Depending on the consequence to the client, the violation may also generate exposure under malpractice principles independent of the disciplinary rules.

Stalled matter with no client communication

A matter sits without action for an extended period and the client is not advised of the status. This implicates both Rule 1.3 (failure to pursue the matter with reasonable diligence) and Rule 1.4 (failure to keep the client reasonably informed). Where the inaction has caused the client to lose substantive rights, the diligence violation is the underlying conduct and the communication failure compounds it.

Diligence in the bankruptcy context

Bankruptcy practice is characterized by short deadlines (proof-of-claim bar dates, objection-to-discharge deadlines, plan-confirmation timelines) and intersecting jurisdictional triggers (automatic stay, plan effective dates). Diligence in this context routinely requires both calendar discipline and active attention to docket events. A lawyer who relies on the client to identify deadlines, or who treats incoming docket notifications as background noise, is at risk under Rule 1.3 even before any substantive harm results.

Relationship to other rules

Rule 1.1 (Competence) - The qualitative companion; the two rules are typically analyzed together.

Rule 1.4 (Communication) - Diligence in the matter usually requires communication with the client; failures of one frequently track failures of the other.

Rule 1.16 (Withdrawal) - When the lawyer is unable to satisfy diligence obligations because of workload, the answer is not silent inaction but withdrawal subject to the termination duties of Rule 1.16(d).

Rule 3.2 (Expediting Litigation) - The litigation analog; a lawyer must make reasonable efforts to expedite litigation consistent with the interests of the client.

Practical impact

Diligence is the most-cited duty in lawyer-discipline matters because its violation is often visible from a docket or calendar without requiring analysis of substance. Two patterns recur:

Procrastination as professional misconduct. The rule treats delay not as a soft failure but as an enumerated professional duty violation. The Comment's reference to procrastination as a shortcoming that is "widely resented" is a direct signal that delay is a disciplinable matter.

Workload is the lawyer's problem. Overcommitment is not a defense to diligence violations. The lawyer must control the workload to meet diligence obligations to every client; the alternative is to decline matters under Rule 1.16(a) or to withdraw if commitments cannot be met.

Related authority

ABA Model Rule 1.3 - model rule with comment

Kansas Rules of Professional Conduct - Kansas Supreme Court Rules

Missouri Rules of Professional Conduct - Missouri Supreme Court Rule 4

KRPC 1.4 (Communication)
KRPC 1.16 (Termination)
KRPC 3.1 (Meritorious Claims)
KRPC 5.1 (Supervision)
KRPC 8.4 (Misconduct)
