## KRPC 1.4 / MRPC 4-1.4 - Communication with Clients [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/krpc-1-4/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Rule of Professional Conduct
KRPC 1.4 / MRPC 4-1.4

KRPC 1.4 / MRPC 4-1.4: Communication with Clients

The lawyer's duty to keep the client reasonably informed and to respond to reasonable requests for information.

Verbatim text of KRPC 1.4 (Kansas)

(a) A lawyer shall:

(1) promptly inform the client of any decision or circumstance with respect to which the client's informed consent is required by these rules;

(2) reasonably consult with the client about the means by which the client's objectives are to be accomplished;

(3) keep the client reasonably informed about the status of the matter;

(4) promptly comply with reasonable requests for information; and

(5) consult with the client about any relevant limitation on the lawyer's conduct when the lawyer knows that the client expects assistance not permitted by the Rules of Professional Conduct or other law.

(b) A lawyer shall explain a matter to the extent reasonably necessary to permit the client to make informed decisions regarding the representation. Kan. Sup. Ct. R. 226, KRPC 1.4.

Verbatim text of MRPC 4-1.4 (Missouri)

(a) A lawyer shall:

(1) promptly inform the client of any decision or circumstance with respect to which Rule 4-1.0(e) requires the client's informed consent;

(2) reasonably consult with the client about the means by which the client's objectives are to be accomplished;

(3) keep the client reasonably informed about the status of the matter;

(4) promptly comply with reasonable requests for information; and

(5) consult with the client about any relevant limitation on the lawyer's conduct when the lawyer knows that the client expects assistance not permitted by the Rules of Professional Conduct or other law.

(b) A lawyer shall explain a matter to the extent reasonably necessary to permit the client to make informed decisions regarding the representation. Mo. Sup. Ct. R. 4-1.4.

The structure of the duty

Kansas Rule of Professional Conduct 1.4 and Missouri Rule of Professional Conduct 4-1.4 are substantively identical and track the language of ABA Model Rule 1.4. The rule operates in two complementary parts: subdivision (a) sets five specific affirmative obligations of the lawyer; subdivision (b) requires the lawyer to explain matters to the extent reasonably necessary to permit the client to make informed decisions about the representation.

The animating principle is that a client cannot exercise the client's own decision-making authority over the representation - authority allocated to the client by Rule 1.2 - without information sufficient to do so. Rule 1.4 is the mechanism that ensures the flow of information adequate to that allocation of authority.

The five obligations of subdivision (a)

1. Informed consent on required decisions

The lawyer must promptly inform the client of any decision or circumstance for which the client's informed consent is required by the rules. Informed consent under Rule 1.0 requires the lawyer to communicate adequate information and explanation about the material risks of and reasonably available alternatives to the proposed course of conduct. This obligation arises in connection with conflicts of interest under Rules 1.7 and 1.9, settlement decisions under Rule 1.2(a), entry of pleas in criminal matters, waiver of jury trial, and similar decisions reserved to the client.

2. Reasonable consultation on means

The lawyer must reasonably consult with the client about the means by which the client's objectives are to be accomplished. The allocation of authority between lawyer and client in Rule 1.2 reserves objectives to the client and gives the lawyer professional discretion over means. Rule 1.4(a)(2) qualifies that allocation: even on matters within the lawyer's professional discretion, the lawyer must consult with the client on the means selected.

3. Keeping the client reasonably informed

The lawyer must keep the client reasonably informed about the status of the matter. The duty is affirmative; it does not depend on the client asking. The frequency and depth of status updates appropriate to "reasonably informed" depend on the complexity of the matter and the client's reasonable expectations. A litigation matter with pending hearings, court-ordered deadlines, or settlement discussions typically requires more frequent communication than a transactional matter in an inactive phase.

4. Promptly comply with reasonable requests for information

The lawyer must promptly comply with reasonable requests for information. The standard is reasonableness in both the request and the response. A request for routine status information should be answered promptly. A request for documentation, copies of filings, or substantive analysis should be answered within a reasonable time, scaled to the complexity of the request and the demands of other client matters.

5. Consultation on limitations on conduct

When the lawyer knows that the client expects assistance not permitted by the rules or by other law, the lawyer must consult with the client about the limitation. A client requesting a course of conduct the lawyer cannot ethically perform is entitled to be told why and what alternatives are available.

Subdivision (b) - explanation sufficient for informed decisions

Rule 1.4(b) imposes a separate obligation: the lawyer must explain matters to the extent reasonably necessary to permit the client to make informed decisions about the representation. The text imposes an obligation calibrated to the client's decision-making, not to the lawyer's perception of what the client needs to know. The Comment to Model Rule 1.4 notes that adequacy of explanation must take account of the client's sophistication; a sophisticated client may need less explanation than an unsophisticated one to reach an informed decision.

Failure to communicate in the bankruptcy context

Bankruptcy representations are frequently the subject of Rule 1.4 complaints because the procedural pace of a bankruptcy case generates frequent decision points - meeting-of-creditors dates, deadlines to file proofs of claim, deadlines to object to discharge, plan-confirmation hearings, motions for relief from stay - each of which requires communication for the client to make informed decisions. Common Rule 1.4 patterns include:

Failure to inform a debtor of an upcoming Section 341 meeting

Failure to forward a relief-from-stay motion to the debtor for substantive response

Failure to inform a client of a settlement offer received from a creditor or trustee

Unanswered communications from the client over weeks or months without explanation

Delivery of the case file or specific documents in response to a request being deferred without an articulated reason

The duty does not turn on whether the matter is going well. A lawyer cannot suspend Rule 1.4 communication on the theory that there is nothing new to report; if a hearing is approaching, the client must be informed of it. Equally, a lawyer cannot defer answering a reasonable inquiry from a client on the theory that the answer is unfavorable.

Common procedural posture

Client request for status

The client emails the attorney requesting an update on a pending matter. The lawyer's obligation under Rule 1.4(a)(4) is to respond promptly. A delay of several weeks without acknowledgment is generally inadequate under any reasonableness standard. A short acknowledgment with a substantive response promised by a specific date is generally adequate; failure to follow up by the promised date may itself be a separate violation.

Material development in the case

A trustee issues a notice of intent to abandon property, a creditor files a relief-from-stay motion, or the court enters an order requiring a response. Rule 1.4(a)(3) requires the lawyer to inform the client of the development; Rule 1.4(b) requires sufficient explanation that the client can make any decisions reserved to the client.

Relationship to other rules

Rule 1.2 - Allocates objectives to the client and means to the lawyer; Rule 1.4 is the communication mechanism that makes Rule 1.2 operational.

Rule 1.3 - Requires diligence in carrying out the representation. Sustained communication failure often co-occurs with diligence failures.

Rule 1.16(d) - On termination of representation, the lawyer must take reasonable steps to protect the client's interests, including surrendering the file. See KRPC 1.16 / MRPC 4-1.16.

Rule 8.4(d) - Conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice. Repeated communication failure that prevents the client from making informed decisions may rise to a Rule 8.4(d) violation in addition to a Rule 1.4 violation.

Related authority

ABA Model Rule 1.4 - model rule with comment

Kansas Rules of Professional Conduct - Kansas Supreme Court Rules

Missouri Rules of Professional Conduct - Missouri Supreme Court Rule 4

KRPC 3.3 (Candor)
KRPC 5.1 (Supervision)
KRPC 8.3 (Reporting)
KRPC 8.4 (Misconduct)
Rule 9010 (Representation)

## KRPC 1.5 / MRPC 4-1.5 - Fees [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/krpc-1-5/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Rule of Professional Conduct
KRPC 1.5 / MRPC 4-1.5

KRPC 1.5 / MRPC 4-1.5: Fees

The fee architecture the rule permits: reasonable-fee factors, contingent-fee structure, fee-sharing between firms, and the written-agreement requirement.

What Rule 1.5 affirmatively does

Rule 1.5 is the architecture of attorney compensation. It identifies the factors that make a fee reasonable, expressly authorizes contingent fees in matters where the recovery makes contingency workable, permits two unrelated firms to share a fee on a single matter under defined conditions, and requires that the basis or rate of the fee be communicated to the client in writing in the contexts where written confirmation matters most. The rule is enabling: it tells the bar what fee structures are permitted and how to deploy them.

Verbatim text of KRPC 1.5 (Kansas, abbreviated)

(a) A lawyer's fee shall be reasonable. The factors to be considered in determining the reasonableness of a fee include the following: (1) the time and labor required, the novelty and difficulty of the questions involved, and the skill requisite to perform the legal service properly; (2) the likelihood, if apparent to the client, that the acceptance of the particular employment will preclude other employment by the lawyer; (3) the fee customarily charged in the locality for similar legal services; (4) the amount involved and the results obtained; (5) the time limitations imposed by the client or by the circumstances; (6) the nature and length of the professional relationship with the client; (7) the experience, reputation, and ability of the lawyer or lawyers performing the services; and (8) whether the fee is fixed or contingent.

(b) When the lawyer has not regularly represented the client, the basis or rate of the fee shall be communicated to the client, preferably in writing, before or within a reasonable time after commencing the representation.

(c) A fee may be contingent on the outcome of the matter for which the service is rendered, except in a matter in which a contingent fee is prohibited by paragraph (d) or other law. A contingent fee agreement shall be in writing and shall state the method by which the fee is to be determined, including the percentage or percentages that shall accrue to the lawyer in the event of settlement, trial or appeal, litigation and other expenses to be deducted from the recovery, and whether such expenses are to be deducted before or after the contingent fee is calculated.

(e) A division of fee between lawyers who are not in the same firm may be made only if: (1) the division is in proportion to the services performed by each lawyer or each lawyer assumes joint responsibility for the representation; (2) the client is advised of and does not object to the participation of all the lawyers involved; and (3) the total fee is reasonable. Kan. Sup. Ct. R. 226, KRPC 1.5.

Missouri Rule 4-1.5

Missouri Rule 4-1.5 tracks ABA Model Rule 1.5 and adopts the same eight reasonableness factors, the same contingent-fee structure, and the same fee-sharing conditions. Missouri imposes additional written-disclosure requirements at the contingent-fee end of the spectrum.

1.5(a) - The eight reasonableness factors

Subdivision (a) supplies the eight-factor test that determines whether a fee is reasonable. The factors are not weighted; they are read together as a holistic measure of reasonableness in context.

Labor-side factors

Time and labor required (factor 1), the novelty and difficulty of the questions involved (factor 1), the skill required (factor 1), and the time limitations imposed (factor 5). These measure what the work cost the lawyer to perform.

Market-side factors

Customary fee in the locality (factor 3), the amount involved and results obtained (factor 4), and the experience and reputation of the lawyer (factor 7). These measure what the work was worth in the market.

Relationship factors

Nature and length of the professional relationship (factor 6) and the preclusion of other employment (factor 2). These measure the opportunity cost of the engagement and the depth of the lawyer-client relationship.

Structure factor

Whether the fee is fixed or contingent (factor 8). A contingent fee that compensates for the risk of nonrecovery may reasonably exceed an hourly fee that the lawyer would have charged for the same work.

1.5(b) - Communication of the basis or rate

When a lawyer has not regularly represented the client, the basis or rate of the fee must be communicated to the client - preferably in writing in Kansas and required in writing for contingent fees in both jurisdictions - before or within a reasonable time after commencing the representation. The communication describes how the fee will be calculated: hourly rate plus expenses, flat fee for a defined scope, contingent percentage, or some combination.

1.5(c) - The contingent-fee structure

Subdivision (c) expressly authorizes contingent fees in any matter where contingency is not specifically prohibited. The contingent-fee architecture has four required components in the written agreement:

Method of calculation. The agreement must state how the fee is calculated - typically as a percentage of recovery.

Percentages at each stage. If the percentage varies by settlement, trial, or appeal, each percentage must be stated.

Litigation and other expenses. The expenses to be deducted from the recovery must be identified.

Order of operations. The agreement must state whether expenses are deducted before or after the contingent fee is calculated - a distinction that meaningfully changes the client's net recovery.

The contingent fee expands access. Contingency makes representation available to clients who could not pay an hourly rate. The structure aligns the lawyer's compensation with the client's recovery and shifts the risk of nonrecovery to the lawyer. Rule 1.5(c) does not cap the percentage; it requires that the percentage and structure be in writing and that the total fee remain reasonable under the 1.5(a) factors.

Settlement statement at conclusion

Upon conclusion of a contingent-fee matter, the lawyer must provide the client with a written statement showing the outcome, the remittance to the client, the method of determination, and the expenses deducted.

1.5(d) - Matters where contingency is not used

Contingent fees are not used in two specific categories: domestic relations matters where the fee is contingent on securing a divorce or on the amount of alimony or support, and criminal-defense matters. The carve-outs exist to keep the fee structure from interfering with substantive outcomes in matters where contingency would distort the lawyer's incentives.

1.5(e) - Fee sharing between firms

Two unrelated firms may share a single fee on a matter when three conditions are met:

Proportional division or joint responsibility. Either each lawyer's share matches the services that lawyer performed, or each lawyer assumes joint responsibility for the representation.

Client notice without objection. The client is advised of the participation of all lawyers involved and does not object.

Total fee reasonable. The aggregate fee, after splitting, satisfies the 1.5(a) reasonableness factors.

The architecture allows specialty referrals - a generalist refers a complex matter to a specialty firm and remains involved enough to assume joint responsibility - while preserving the client's right to know about and consent to the arrangement.

The engagement-letter checklist

Basis or rate. Hourly rate, flat fee, or contingent percentage.

Scope. What the fee covers, by reference to Rule 1.2.

Expenses. What costs the client pays separately, and whether expenses are deducted before or after a contingent fee is calculated.

Billing rhythm. When the client receives bills and what level of detail they contain.

Modifications. How a change in fee structure will be handled - by amendment with the client's signed consent.

Termination. What happens to the unearned portion of a flat fee or retainer upon termination under Rule 1.16(d).

Continuing nature of the duty

The reasonableness of a fee is evaluated at the time the work is done and again at the time the fee is collected. A fee that was reasonable at the engagement's outset can drift toward unreasonableness if the matter expands and the lawyer does not communicate the change. Rule 1.4's communication duty supplies the running update that keeps Rule 1.5 reasonableness intact.

Related rules and authority

Rule 1.1 - Competence; the floor that a reasonable fee assumes

Rule 1.2 - Scope of representation; defines what the fee covers

Rule 1.4 - Communication; keeps the fee picture current with the client

Rule 1.15 - Safekeeping property; unearned portions of advance payments belong in trust

Rule 1.16 - Termination; unearned fees are refunded

Practical impact

Rule 1.5 is the rule clients consult when they question a bill and the rule lawyers consult when they design a fee structure. Three takeaways recur:

Written agreements are the engine. A written engagement letter that satisfies 1.5(b) prevents most fee disputes before they begin.

The eight factors operate as a holistic test. No single factor is decisive; reasonableness is the aggregate impression.

Contingency expands access. Subdivision (c) is one of the principal access-to-justice mechanisms in the rules of professional conduct.

Related authority

ABA Model Rule 1.5 - model rule with comment

Kansas Rules of Professional Conduct - Kansas Supreme Court Rules

Missouri Rules of Professional Conduct - Missouri Supreme Court Rule 4

## KRPC 1.7 / MRPC 4-1.7 - Conflict of Interest: Current Clients [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/krpc-1-7/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Rule of Professional Conduct
KRPC 1.7 / MRPC 4-1.7

KRPC 1.7 / MRPC 4-1.7: Conflict of Interest - Current Clients

The conditions under which concurrent representation may continue with informed consent in writing.

What Rule 1.7 affirmatively does

Rule 1.7 is the rule that tells a lawyer when, and on what terms, the lawyer may represent more than one client at the same time whose interests are not aligned. The rule identifies two patterns of concurrent conflict, then states four conditions that, when all met, permit the representation to go forward. The rule is enabling: it gives lawyers and clients a structured pathway to keep representation in place where it would otherwise have to end, and where the clients themselves prefer that it continue.

Verbatim text of KRPC 1.7 (Kansas)

(a) Except as provided in paragraph (b), a lawyer shall not represent a client if the representation involves a concurrent conflict of interest. A concurrent conflict of interest exists if:

(1) the representation of one client will be directly adverse to another client; or

(2) there is a significant risk that the representation of one or more clients will be materially limited by the lawyer's responsibilities to another client, a former client or a third person or by a personal interest of the lawyer.

(b) Notwithstanding the existence of a concurrent conflict of interest under paragraph (a), a lawyer may represent a client if:

(1) the lawyer reasonably believes that the lawyer will be able to provide competent and diligent representation to each affected client;

(2) the representation is not prohibited by law;

(3) the representation does not involve the assertion of a claim by one client against another client represented by the lawyer in the same litigation or other proceeding before a tribunal; and

(4) each affected client gives informed consent, confirmed in writing. Kan. Sup. Ct. R. 226, KRPC 1.7.

Missouri Rule 4-1.7

Missouri Rule 4-1.7 tracks ABA Model Rule 1.7 and adopts the same two-pattern definition and the same four-condition waiver framework. Both jurisdictions require that informed consent be confirmed in writing.

1.7(a) - The two patterns of concurrent conflict

Pattern one: direct adversity (1.7(a)(1))

Direct adversity exists when the lawyer would represent one current client in a matter against another current client - even an unrelated matter. Suing a current client in a matter unrelated to the work the firm is doing for that client is directly adverse. The rule treats direct adversity as a conflict because the lawyer's duty of loyalty to each client cannot be reconciled in the moment of representation against the other.

Pattern two: material limitation (1.7(a)(2))

Material limitation exists when there is a significant risk that the lawyer's representation of one client will be materially limited by the lawyer's responsibilities to another current client, a former client, a third person, or a personal interest. The material-limitation pattern is broader than direct adversity and reaches situations where the representation can proceed in form but the lawyer's judgment, advocacy, or candor would be measurably constrained by the competing responsibility or interest.

1.7(b) - The four conditions for representation to go forward

Subdivision (b) supplies the waiver framework. When all four conditions are satisfied, representation may proceed despite the concurrent conflict identified in (a).

Condition 1: Reasonable belief of competent representation

The lawyer must reasonably believe that the lawyer can provide competent and diligent representation to each affected client. This is an objective test - what a reasonable lawyer in the circumstances would believe. The condition is not satisfied by the lawyer's subjective optimism; it requires a basis in the structure of the engagement and the lawyer's capacity.

Condition 2: Not prohibited by law

The representation must not be prohibited by other law. Certain client combinations are foreclosed by statute or court rule regardless of consent - for example, some government-employment contexts and some banking-regulatory contexts.

Condition 3: No same-tribunal cross-claims

The representation must not involve one client asserting a claim against another client represented by the lawyer in the same litigation or other proceeding before a tribunal. This is a categorical prohibition: a lawyer may not represent both plaintiff and defendant in the same case even with consent.

Condition 4: Informed consent in writing

Each affected client must give informed consent, confirmed in writing. Informed consent requires the lawyer to communicate adequate information about the material risks of and reasonably available alternatives to the conflicted representation. Confirmation in writing closes the loop and supplies the documentary record.

The shape of effective informed consent

Informed consent that satisfies 1.7(b)(4) typically describes:

The identity of the other client whose interests are involved

The matter or matters in which the conflict arises

The material risks the conflict presents to the consenting client - including the risk of constrained advocacy and the risk of confidentiality limits

The reasonably available alternatives to the conflicted representation - including engagement of separate counsel

The implications for confidential information shared with the lawyer

The right of the client to revoke consent prospectively

Informed consent is a process, not a signature. The Comment to Model Rule 1.7 emphasizes that the lawyer's communication of material risks must be sufficient to permit the client to make an informed decision. A boilerplate consent form that does not describe the specific risks of the specific conflict does not satisfy the standard.

Advance conflict waivers

Subdivision (b)(4) accommodates advance waivers - consents given at the engagement's outset that cover conflicts that may arise later. The effectiveness of an advance waiver depends on the extent to which the client appreciated the material risks at the time of consent. A waiver from a sophisticated client represented by independent counsel that identifies the categories of conflicts in advance is more likely to be effective than a one-sentence waiver from an unsophisticated client.

Common procedural posture

Two clients in unrelated matters

A firm represents Client A in a real-estate transaction and is asked to represent Client B in an employment matter against Client A. The representation of B is directly adverse to A under 1.7(a)(1). Representation may go forward under 1.7(b) only if the firm reasonably believes it can serve both clients competently and diligently, and both clients give informed consent confirmed in writing.

Joint representation of co-parties

Two co-defendants ask one lawyer to represent both. The representation poses a material-limitation risk under 1.7(a)(2) because positions that benefit one defendant may disadvantage the other. The lawyer evaluates whether the co-defendants' interests are sufficiently aligned to permit competent representation of both. If so, joint representation can proceed with informed consent that addresses the specific risks - including loss of attorney-client privilege between the joint clients in any later dispute between them.

Continuing duty to monitor

A conflict analysis at intake is necessary but not sufficient. Rule 1.7 imposes a continuing duty: if circumstances change such that a new conflict arises or a previously waived conflict becomes more burdensome than the consent contemplated, the lawyer must re-evaluate and, if appropriate, seek fresh consent. The duty to monitor is structurally linked to the firm-management measures contemplated by Rule 5.1(a) - effective conflict screening is an ongoing function.

Related rules and authority

Rule 1.1 - Competence; the floor that 1.7(b)(1) reasonable belief presupposes

Rule 1.4 - Communication; the channel through which informed consent is obtained

Rule 1.9 - Duties to former clients; the symmetric rule on the other side of the engagement timeline

Rule 1.10 - Imputation of conflicts; extends 1.7 analysis to all lawyers in a firm

Rule 1.18 - Duties to prospective clients; conflicts can attach from a consultation that did not become an engagement

Rule 5.1 - Supervisory responsibility; firm-management measures include conflict-screening

Practical impact

Rule 1.7 is the rule firms operationalize through conflict-checking systems. Two takeaways recur:

Early identification preserves options. A conflict identified at intake is often waivable; a conflict identified after substantive work has begun may not be.

Written consent is the durable record. The writing required by 1.7(b)(4) supplies the proof that the conflict was disclosed and consented to. Oral consent without written confirmation is not sufficient under the rule.

Related authority

ABA Model Rule 1.7 - model rule with comment

Kansas Rules of Professional Conduct - Kansas Supreme Court Rules

Missouri Rules of Professional Conduct - Missouri Supreme Court Rule 4

KRPC 1.4 (Communication)

KRPC 1.10 (Imputation)

## KRPC 1.9 / MRPC 4-1.9 - Duties to Former Clients [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/krpc-1-9/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Rule of Professional Conduct
KRPC 1.9 / MRPC 4-1.9

KRPC 1.9 / MRPC 4-1.9: Duties to Former Clients

Substantial-relationship analysis, the prohibition on adverse use of former-client confidences, and the consent gate.

Verbatim text of KRPC 1.9 (Kansas)

(a) A lawyer who has formerly represented a client in a matter shall not thereafter represent another person in the same or a substantially related matter in which that person's interests are materially adverse to the interests of the former client unless the former client gives informed consent, confirmed in writing.

(b) A lawyer shall not knowingly represent a person in the same or a substantially related matter in which a firm with which the lawyer formerly was associated had previously represented a client:

(1) whose interests are materially adverse to that person; and

(2) about whom the lawyer had acquired information protected by Rules 1.6 and 1.9(c) that is material to the matter; unless the former client gives informed consent, confirmed in writing.

(c) A lawyer who has formerly represented a client in a matter or whose present or former firm has formerly represented a client in a matter shall not thereafter:

(1) use information relating to the representation to the disadvantage of the former client except as these Rules would permit or require with respect to a client, or when the information has become generally known; or

(2) reveal information relating to the representation except as these Rules would permit or require with respect to a client. Kan. Sup. Ct. R. 226, KRPC 1.9.

Missouri Rule 4-1.9

Missouri Rule 4-1.9 is substantively identical to KRPC 1.9 and tracks ABA Model Rule 1.9. The rule operates in three subdivisions: (a) governs successive representation by the same lawyer; (b) governs migration of lawyers between firms; (c) governs the continuing duty regarding former-client information regardless of representation status.

1.9(a) - The substantial-relationship test

A lawyer who formerly represented a client may not represent a new client in the same or a substantially related matter where the new client's interests are materially adverse to the former client, absent informed consent confirmed in writing. The operative inquiries:

Was the matter the same?

Identity of matter is the simplest case. The same litigation, the same transaction, the same project - all qualify.

Was the matter substantially related?

Comment 3 to Model Rule 1.9 identifies the "substantial relationship" inquiry as turning on whether the matters involve the same transaction or legal dispute, or whether there is otherwise a substantial risk that confidential factual information that would normally have been obtained in the prior representation would materially advance the new client's position in the subsequent matter. The analysis is generally factual rather than strictly procedural; matters can be substantially related even where the legal theories or causes of action differ.

Are the interests materially adverse?

Direct opposition in litigation, transactional adversity, or adverse positioning in negotiation all qualify. Adversity in the sense of "different but not opposed" - for example, two clients with parallel but not conflicting interests - typically does not trigger Rule 1.9.

1.9(b) - Migrating-lawyer rule

When a lawyer moves between firms, the new firm cannot represent persons in matters where (1) the lawyer's prior firm represented a now-adverse client in the same or substantially related matter, and (2) the migrating lawyer acquired material confidential information at the prior firm. Both conditions must be met: representation alone at the prior firm is not enough if the migrating lawyer was not personally exposed to material confidential information.

1.9(c) - Continuing duty regarding former-client information

The duty to protect former-client information continues regardless of whether a subsequent representation is undertaken. Subdivision (c) prohibits:

(c)(1) Using information relating to the prior representation to the disadvantage of the former client, except as the rules would permit with respect to a current client, or when the information has become generally known

(c)(2) Revealing such information except as the rules would permit or require with respect to a current client

The "generally known" exception in (c)(1) is narrow. Information is not generally known merely because it is contained in publicly available court filings; the standard typically requires that the information be known in the relevant community such that further dissemination by the lawyer adds nothing material.

The duty under 1.9(c) is permanent. Unlike the substantial-relationship test in 1.9(a), which conditions disqualification on the new matter being substantially related, the confidentiality duty in 1.9(c) attaches to former-client information and continues indefinitely. A lawyer who later opposes a former client in an unrelated matter still cannot use or reveal information from the prior representation to the former client's disadvantage.

Relationship to confidentiality under Rule 1.6

Rule 1.6 imposes the confidentiality duty regarding current clients; Rule 1.9(c) extends that duty to former clients. The substantive scope of protected information is the same: "information relating to the representation" is broader than attorney-client privileged communications and includes any information the lawyer learned in the course of representing the client, regardless of source.

Consent gate

The substantial-relationship and migrating-lawyer bars in subdivisions (a) and (b) are subject to the same consent mechanism: informed consent of the former client, confirmed in writing. "Informed consent" under Rule 1.0 requires that the former client be adequately informed of the material risks and reasonable alternatives. "Confirmed in writing" requires either a writing signed by the client or a writing transmitted by the lawyer to the client memorializing the consent.

The confidentiality duty under (c), by contrast, is not subject to a consent-cures analysis in the same way; revelation or adverse use is permitted only as the rules would permit for a current client. The general permission structure of Rule 1.6 (including narrow exceptions for crime/fraud prevention or rectification, defense of the lawyer in proceedings, etc.) governs.

Imputation under Rule 1.10

A conflict held by an individual lawyer is generally imputed to the lawyer's firm under Rule 1.10. The screening exception applies in some former-client contexts, but only when its specific conditions are met. The interaction of Rules 1.9 and 1.10 is the source of most firm-level former-client disqualification analysis.

Common procedural posture

New matter against a former client

The firm is approached to represent a new client against an entity that the firm formerly represented. The Rule 1.9(a) substantial-relationship inquiry runs: was the prior matter the same as or substantially related to the new matter? If yes and the interests are materially adverse, the firm must either decline or obtain informed consent from the former client confirmed in writing.

Lateral hire from a firm that previously opposed

A firm hires a lateral lawyer from a firm that previously represented a current-firm adversary. Rule 1.9(b) runs: did the lateral lawyer personally acquire material confidential information about the former client at the prior firm? If yes and the matters are substantially related, the new firm is conflicted as to the migrating lawyer, with screening under Rule 1.10 potentially available depending on the jurisdiction's specific rule.

Relationship to other rules

Rule 1.6 (Confidentiality) - Governs the substantive scope of information protected; Rule 1.9(c) extends the duty to former clients.

Rule 1.7 (Current-Client Conflicts) - The concurrent analog; Rule 1.7 governs current clients and Rule 1.9 governs former clients.

Rule 1.10 (Imputation) - Imputation of individual conflicts to the firm.

Rule 1.16 (Termination) - Mandatory withdrawal under 1.16(a)(1) if continued representation would violate Rule 1.9.

Rule 1.0 (Definitions) - Definitions of "informed consent," "writing," and "confirmed in writing."

Practical impact

Rule 1.9 is the framework for disqualification motions brought by former clients. Two patterns recur:

Substantial relationship is a low bar. Courts and reviewing authorities generally apply the substantial-relationship test in favor of the former client. Where there is reasonable doubt about whether prior-representation information could be material in the new matter, the doubt typically runs in favor of disqualification.

The continuing duty under (c) is independent. A lawyer can satisfy the substantial-relationship analysis in (a) - because the matters are not substantially related - but still violate (c) by using or revealing former-client information adversely.

Related authority

ABA Model Rule 1.9 - model rule with comment

Kansas Rules of Professional Conduct - Kansas Supreme Court Rules

Missouri Rules of Professional Conduct - Missouri Supreme Court Rule 4

KRPC 1.16 (Termination)
KRPC 1.4 (Communication)
KRPC 5.1 (Supervision)
KRPC 8.4 (Misconduct)

## KRPC 2.1 / MRPC 4-2.1 - Advisor [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/krpc-2-1/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Rule of Professional Conduct
KRPC 2.1 / MRPC 4-2.1

KRPC 2.1 / MRPC 4-2.1: Advisor

The advisor role architecture: independent professional judgment, candid counsel, and the permitted scope of non-legal considerations.

Verbatim text of KRPC 2.1 (Kansas)

In representing a client, a lawyer shall exercise independent professional judgment and render candid advice. In rendering advice, a lawyer may refer not only to law but to other considerations such as moral, economic, social and political factors, that may be relevant to the client's situation. Kan. Sup. Ct. R. 226, KRPC 2.1.

Missouri Rule 4-2.1

Missouri Rule 4-2.1 is substantively identical and tracks ABA Model Rule 2.1. The rule is structurally affirmative: it establishes what the advisor role looks like rather than enumerating what it forbids. Two operative duties, each cast in active voice, frame the rule: the lawyer shall exercise independent professional judgment, and the lawyer shall render candid advice. A third clause expands the permitted scope of advice: the lawyer may refer to non-legal considerations relevant to the client's situation.

The advisor role 2.1 establishes

Rule 2.1 distinguishes the advisor role from the advocate role and supplies the operational content of advisor practice. As an advisor, the lawyer is helping the client understand legal rights and obligations, evaluate options, and decide what to do. The two duties and the one permission together constitute the advisor-role architecture.

Independent professional judgment

The judgment offered to the client must be the lawyer's own, formed through the lawyer's professional analysis, free of distortion by the lawyer's own interests, by the interests of third parties, or by reluctance to deliver advice the client may not want to hear. The independence is structural; it is the condition that makes the advice worth obtaining.

Candid advice

The advice delivered must be candid - direct, complete, and unvarnished by the lawyer's discomfort with the conclusion. Comment [1] to the rule notes that a client may be entitled to straightforward advice expressing the lawyer's honest assessment, even when the assessment is unwelcome.

Independent professional judgment as professional infrastructure

Independence under 2.1 is more than the absence of disqualifying conflicts; it is the affirmative formation of the lawyer's own judgment as the basis for advice. The infrastructural reading requires:

Adequate analysis of the legal question - sufficient research, factual investigation, and consideration of alternatives to support a real professional opinion

Insulation from influences that would distort the judgment - third-party payers, business referral sources, and the lawyer's own interest in particular outcomes

Resistance to client pressure for the advice the client wants to hear; the advisor role would collapse if the lawyer simply mirrored back the client's preferred conclusion

Acknowledgement of uncertainty where the law or facts do not support a confident position; manufactured certainty is not professional judgment

Comment [1] frames the duty in these terms: legal advice often involves unpleasant facts and alternatives that a client may be disinclined to confront. In presenting advice, a lawyer endeavors to sustain the client's morale and may put advice in as acceptable a form as honesty permits. However, a lawyer should not be deterred from giving candid advice by the prospect that the advice will be unpalatable to the client.

The permitted scope of candid counsel - non-legal considerations

The second sentence of Rule 2.1 expands the advisor's range. In rendering advice, a lawyer may refer not only to law but to other considerations - moral, economic, social, and political factors - that may be relevant to the client's situation. The clause is permissive ("may refer"), not mandatory, and it is calibrated to what is "relevant to the client's situation."

The permission is significant because it positions the advisor as a counselor rather than a narrow legal-question-answering function. A client deciding whether to bring a lawsuit, structure a transaction, or accept a settlement is rarely choosing among options on legal grounds alone. The advisor role contemplates that the lawyer may bring the full range of considerations to bear, while respecting that the decision belongs to the client.

Moral considerations

Comment [2] addresses the moral dimension directly: advice couched in narrowly legal terms may be of little value to a client, especially where practical considerations such as cost or effects on other people are predominant. Purely technical legal advice can therefore be inadequate. The advisor is permitted to acknowledge the moral dimension where it bears on the client's actual situation.

Economic, social, and political considerations

The economic dimension is often inseparable from the legal one - a client deciding whether to litigate is also deciding how to allocate capital and attention. The social and political dimensions become relevant where the client's reputation, relationships, or public standing are affected by the legal choice. The advisor's permitted scope under 2.1 makes it appropriate to surface these dimensions as part of candid counsel.

Advisor versus advocate - the role distinction

Rule 2.1 occupies the "Counselor" section of the rules of professional conduct, sitting alongside Rules 2.3 (evaluation for use by third persons) and 2.4 (lawyer serving as third-party neutral). The placement signals that the advisor role is structurally distinct from the advocate role addressed in Article 3 of the rules.

Advisor (Article 2)

The lawyer is helping the client understand and decide. Independent judgment and candid advice are the operative qualities. The audience is the client.

Advocate (Article 3)

The lawyer is asserting the client's position before a tribunal or in negotiation with adverse parties. Diligent advocacy bounded by candor toward the tribunal under Rule 3.3 is the operative quality. The audience is external.

The same lawyer in the same matter regularly shifts between roles. The advisor-advocate distinction does not mean the lawyer cannot do both; it means the lawyer should be aware of which role is operative at a given moment, because the operative qualities differ. A lawyer who delivers advocate-style framing to the client - presenting only the favorable case - has not satisfied the advisor duty.

When to volunteer advice

Comment [5] addresses when a lawyer is expected to initiate advice that the client has not requested. In general, a lawyer is not expected to give advice until asked by the client. However, when a lawyer knows that a client proposes a course of action likely to result in substantial adverse legal consequences to the client, the lawyer's duty under Rule 1.4 may require that the lawyer offer advice if the client's course of action is related to the representation. The advisor duty under 2.1 reinforces the communication duty under Rule 1.4: candid advice volunteered at the moment it would be useful is part of the advisor role.

Counsel-to-counsel referral

Comment [4] notes that matters that go beyond strictly legal questions may also be in the domain of another profession. Where consultation with a professional in another field is itself something a competent lawyer would recommend, the lawyer should make such a recommendation. The advisor role is not the role of universal expert; it includes the judgment to identify when other professional input would serve the client and to surface that need as part of candid advice.

The architecture in summary

Rule 2.1 establishes a three-part advisor architecture: (1) independent professional judgment formed through the lawyer's own analysis; (2) candid advice delivered without distortion by the lawyer's discomfort with the conclusion; (3) permitted scope that extends to moral, economic, social, and political considerations relevant to the client's situation. The architecture is what makes the advisor relationship valuable to a client deciding what to do.

Relationship to Rule 1.4 (Communication)

Rule 2.1 is in close dialogue with Rule 1.4. Communication under 1.4 governs what the lawyer must tell the client about the status, scope, and material developments of the representation; the advisor role under 2.1 governs the quality of the substantive advice the lawyer delivers within that communication. The two rules work together: candid advice rendered with independent judgment is one of the most important things 1.4 communication conveys.

Relationship to Rule 1.2 (Scope of Representation)

Rule 1.2 allocates decision-making authority between lawyer and client. The advisor role under 2.1 supplies the substantive input that makes the client's allocated decisions meaningful. A client who is to decide the objectives of the representation under 1.2(a) needs the candid, independent advice under 2.1 to decide well.

Relationship to Rule 1.7 (Conflicts)

Independent professional judgment under 2.1 presupposes the absence of disqualifying conflicts under Rule 1.7. The conflicts framework protects independence at the structural level (by precluding the representation entirely or requiring informed consent); the 2.1 duty operates within the cleared space.

Related rules and authority

Rule 1.2 - Scope of representation; allocates decisions between lawyer and client

Rule 1.4 - Communication; the channel through which 2.1 advice reaches the client

Rule 1.7 - Conflicts; the structural protection for independence

Rule 2.3 - Evaluation for use by third persons

Rule 2.4 - Lawyer serving as third-party neutral

Rule 3.3 - Candor toward the tribunal; the advocate-role companion

Practical impact

Rule 2.1 is the rule that makes the lawyer's advice valuable. The architecture - independence + candor + permitted breadth of considerations - is what distinguishes professional advice from agreement, from sales pitch, and from narrow legal-question answering. A practice organized around the 2.1 architecture treats every advice moment as an opportunity to deliver something the client could not otherwise obtain: the lawyer's own honest assessment of the client's actual situation across the dimensions that matter.

Related authority

ABA Model Rule 2.1 - model rule with comment

Kansas Rules of Professional Conduct - Kansas Supreme Court Rules

Missouri Rules of Professional Conduct - Missouri Supreme Court Rule 4

Open Bankruptcy Project cross-references

KRPC 1.7 (Conflicts)
KRPC 3.3 (Candor)
KRPC 1.3 (Diligence)

## KRPC 3.1 / MRPC 4-3.1 - Meritorious Claims and Contentions [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/krpc-3-1/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Rule of Professional Conduct
KRPC 3.1 / MRPC 4-3.1

KRPC 3.1 / MRPC 4-3.1: Meritorious Claims and Contentions

The good-faith litigation architecture - basis in law or fact, room for good-faith arguments to extend or change the law, and the constitutional carve-out for criminal defense.

Good-faith litigation architecture that 3.1 protects

Rule 3.1 is best read as an architecture for legitimate advocacy. It defines the floor at which advocacy enjoys full protection: any claim or defense with a non-frivolous basis in existing law and the facts, or any claim or defense that rests on a good-faith argument for an extension, modification, or reversal of existing law. The rule is permissive at its core - it preserves the lawyer's freedom to advance every meritorious position and every novel position that is honestly grounded in research and reflection.

The rule's affirmative function appears throughout published authority: it identifies what advocacy is protected, what theories are open to counsel, and what room exists for argument that the prevailing rule should change. Courts and bar authorities have repeatedly emphasized that 3.1 is not designed to penalize bold theory or unsettled questions - it is designed to give those theories a stable home so long as they are honestly held and minimally supported.

Verbatim text of KRPC 3.1 (Kansas)

A lawyer shall not bring or defend a proceeding, or assert or controvert an issue therein, unless there is a basis in law and fact for doing so that is not frivolous, which includes a good-faith argument for an extension, modification or reversal of existing law. A lawyer for the defendant in a criminal proceeding, or the respondent in a proceeding that could result in incarceration, may nevertheless so defend the proceeding as to require that every element of the case be established. Kan. Sup. Ct. R. 226, KRPC 3.1.

Missouri Rule 4-3.1

Missouri Rule 4-3.1 is substantively identical to KRPC 3.1 and tracks ABA Model Rule 3.1. Both rules cast the duty in terms of what advocacy is permitted, with the negative formulation (no frivolous claims) serving only to mark the outer edge of the protected zone.

The non-frivolous-basis standard, read affirmatively

Counsel may bring or defend any proceeding for which there is a non-frivolous basis in law and fact. That single sentence opens a wide field. A claim is non-frivolous when a reasonable lawyer, after such inquiry as is reasonable under the circumstances, could conclude that the claim has at least colorable support. The standard does not require certainty of success; it does not require freedom from doubt; it does not require that the claim be the strongest claim available.

The Comment to Model Rule 3.1 emphasizes that the filing of an action or defense is not frivolous merely because the facts have not first been fully substantiated, or because the lawyer expects to develop vital evidence only by discovery. Counsel may file based on the information available at filing, then develop the evidentiary record through the discovery tools the court system provides for that purpose. The rule respects the reality that civil litigation is in part an information-gathering exercise.

Good-faith argument for an extension, modification, or reversal

The second clause of the rule is the engine of legal development. Every published change in doctrine - every overruled precedent, every recognized cause of action, every newly limited defense - began as a good-faith argument that the existing rule should change. Rule 3.1 protects that argument explicitly.

To qualify, the argument must be (a) made in good faith and (b) directed at extending existing law (applying a principle to a new context), modifying existing law (refining the rule's contours), or reversing existing law (overturning a precedent the lawyer believes is wrongly decided). Each of these is an affirmatively protected mode of advocacy. The Comment notes that the lawyer's belief need not be objectively certain; the belief must be honestly held and grounded in some recognized methodology of legal reasoning.

Practical implications:

Cases of first impression are protected. Where no on-point authority exists, counsel may proceed on principled extension from analogous authority.

Circuit splits create space. Where authority is divided, the choice to advance the position adopted by some courts and rejected by others is not frivolous.

Doctrinal evolution is contemplated. Arguments that an older rule should yield to a newer principle, or that statutory interpretation should be updated, are within the protected zone.

The criminal-defense carve-out under 3.1

The rule's final sentence creates a specific zone of expanded protection for criminal-defense counsel and respondents in proceedings that could result in incarceration. Defense counsel may require that every element of the case be established by the government, irrespective of counsel's personal assessment of the defendant's guilt. This is not a side note - it is a constitutional accommodation embedded in the rule.

The carve-out reflects the structural premise of the adversary criminal system: the government bears the burden, and the defendant's right to require proof of every element is part of the due-process architecture. Defense counsel honors that architecture by holding the government to its proof, and Rule 3.1 makes clear that doing so is not a violation of the meritorious-claim duty even where counsel privately doubts the strength of the defense.

Affirmative read-out. Rule 3.1 should be understood as protecting four categories of advocacy: (1) claims and defenses with conventional support in law and fact; (2) claims and defenses with colorable support pending discovery; (3) good-faith arguments to extend, modify, or reverse existing law; and (4) the full defense of any criminal or incarceration-eligible respondent. These four categories cover the substantial majority of advocacy that counsel will ever undertake.

Common procedural posture

Filing on incomplete evidence

Counsel files a complaint based on information known at intake plus reasonable inferences, with the understanding that discovery will refine the factual record. Under 3.1 and its Comment, this is protected. The duty is to have a reasonable basis at filing, not to have completed the discovery the case is designed to develop.

Advancing a novel constitutional theory

Counsel raises a constitutional argument that no controlling court has accepted. Under the good-faith-argument clause, the theory is protected so long as it is honestly grounded in recognized legal reasoning and the lawyer holds the position in good faith. Doctrinal evolution depends on exactly this kind of advocacy.

Reasonable inquiry as the gatekeeping concept

The Comment ties the non-frivolous-basis standard to "such inquiry into the facts and law as is reasonable under the circumstances." Reasonable inquiry is the operational gatekeeper between the protected zone and the very narrow zone the rule excludes. The depth of inquiry expected scales with the stakes of the matter, the time available before filing, and the access counsel has to the relevant facts and authorities.

An emergency filing on a temporary restraining order does not require the same depth of pre-filing investigation as a complex commercial complaint filed under no time pressure. The rule is calibrated to context, and the Comment expressly recognizes that pre-filing investigation may be limited where the circumstances justify limitation.

Relationship to Rule 11 / Rule 9011

Rule 3.1 is the professional-responsibility analog to Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 11 and Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 9011. Each operates as a check on filings without basis, and each preserves the same affirmative zone for good-faith argument. A filing that satisfies Rule 9011's certification requirements - that it is not being presented for an improper purpose, that the legal contentions are warranted by existing law or by a non-frivolous argument for changing the law, that the factual contentions have evidentiary support or are likely to have such support after discovery - will ordinarily satisfy Rule 3.1 as well.

Related rules and authority

Rule 3.3 - Candor toward the tribunal; supplies the affirmative duty as to legal authority and factual representations

Rule 11 / Rule 9011 - Federal certification of filings; substantially parallel standard

Rule 3.4 - Fairness to opposing party and counsel

Rule 8.4 - Misconduct; severe frivolous-claim conduct may also implicate 8.4(d)

Practical impact

The most important practical consequence of Rule 3.1 is the breadth of the protected zone. The rule does not require counsel to be right; it requires counsel to have a non-frivolous basis or a good-faith argument. Aggressive theory, novel theory, theory inviting doctrinal change, and full defense in criminal matters all sit comfortably within the affirmative architecture the rule establishes.

Aggressive does not equal frivolous. Vigorous advocacy that pushes the boundaries of existing doctrine is protected so long as the push is grounded.

Losing does not equal frivolous. The outcome of a case is not the measure of whether the case was meritorious to bring or defend at the time of filing.

The criminal-defense carve-out is absolute as to elements. Defense counsel may always require proof of every element of the prosecution's case.

Related authority

ABA Model Rule 3.1 - model rule with comment

Kansas Rules of Professional Conduct - Kansas Supreme Court Rules

Missouri Rules of Professional Conduct - Missouri Supreme Court Rule 4

KRPC 3.4 (Fairness)
KRPC 3.5 (Tribunal)
KRPC 3.6 (Publicity)

## KRPC 3.2 / MRPC 4-3.2 - Expediting Litigation [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/krpc-3-2/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Rule of Professional Conduct
KRPC 3.2 / MRPC 4-3.2

KRPC 3.2 / MRPC 4-3.2: Expediting Litigation

The reasonable-expediting framework - efforts to advance litigation consistent with the client's legitimate interests and with the court's interest in efficient adjudication.

Reasonable expediting framework that 3.2 establishes

Rule 3.2 establishes a framework for moving litigation forward at a reasonable pace. Counsel's duty is affirmative: take reasonable steps to expedite litigation consistent with the legitimate interests of the client. The rule recognizes that litigation serves the parties and the public best when adjudication is timely; it places counsel in the role of a steward of judicial efficiency alongside being an advocate.

The framework operates by reference to two anchor concepts. The first is reasonableness, measured by what counsel of ordinary diligence would do in similar circumstances. The second is the legitimate interest of the client, which includes the client's interest in thorough preparation, in adequate investigation, in considered strategy, and in not being rushed into decisions of substance.

Verbatim text of KRPC 3.2 (Kansas)

A lawyer shall make reasonable efforts to expedite litigation consistent with the interests of the client. Kan. Sup. Ct. R. 226, KRPC 3.2.

Missouri Rule 4-3.2

Missouri Rule 4-3.2 is substantively identical to KRPC 3.2 and tracks ABA Model Rule 3.2. The Comment to Model Rule 3.2 articulates the affirmative framing: dilatory practices bring the administration of justice into disrepute, and the question of whether a delay is justified must be evaluated by reference to legitimate purposes - not by reference to whether the delay serves the lawyer's or the client's tactical advantage.

The "reasonable efforts" standard

"Reasonable efforts" is the operative phrase. It is calibrated to context. Reasonable efforts in a complex multi-district litigation differ from reasonable efforts in a small-claim collection. Reasonable efforts during a discovery-heavy phase differ from reasonable efforts on the eve of trial. The rule does not require maximum effort at every moment; it requires effort proportionate to the matter, the procedural posture, and the resources of the parties and the court.

What counts as a reasonable effort to expedite:

Meeting court-ordered deadlines and scheduling-order milestones

Responding to discovery within the time the rules and orders permit

Conferring in good faith on scheduling, on extensions, and on stipulations that narrow disputes

Identifying issues that can be resolved on the papers and presenting them for prompt adjudication

Communicating with opposing counsel about anticipated motions, anticipated witnesses, and anticipated needs for the court's attention

Consistency with the client's legitimate interests

The rule's qualifier - "consistent with the interests of the client" - protects counsel's ability to take the time genuinely required to serve the client. A client has a legitimate interest in being fully prepared, in not being subjected to half-formed motions, and in having counsel pursue every theory that might bear on the outcome. The rule does not require sacrifice of any of those interests in the name of speed.

The qualifier also marks the distinction between justified time-taking and unjustified delay. Time spent on substantive investigation, on legal research, on conferring with the client about strategy, on coordinating expert witnesses, on preparing dispositive motions - all of this is time the rule contemplates and protects. The Comment to Model Rule 3.2 is explicit: "realizing financial or other benefit from otherwise improper delay in litigation is not a legitimate interest of the client." Time taken for legitimate reasons is not delay in the relevant sense.

What the rule does not require

The expediting duty is not a duty to capitulate. It does not require counsel to drop colorable defenses to move a case faster. It does not require counsel to waive procedural protections that exist to give parties time to respond. It does not require counsel to forgo motions that, if granted, would dispose of the matter entirely. The Comment to Model Rule 3.2 emphasizes that the rule's question is whether a competent lawyer acting in good faith would regard the course of action as having some substantial purpose other than delay.

Affirmative read-out. Rule 3.2 protects the lawyer who works diligently to advance a case while preserving every legitimate step in the case's natural progression. It is a rule about pace, not a rule about scope; it does not require counsel to do less for the client, only that counsel do it within a reasonable timeframe.

The judicial-efficiency dimension

The Comment to Model Rule 3.2 frames the rule as serving the administration of justice. Courts have limited capacity; dockets must move; parties and witnesses have lives that proceed alongside litigation. Counsel who makes reasonable efforts to expedite contributes to a court system that can serve all litigants. This systemic dimension is the affirmative purpose of the rule, and it is the dimension most often invoked in disciplinary decisions.

The rule operates alongside court-imposed scheduling regimes - case-management orders, scheduling orders under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 16, status conference requirements, and similar mechanisms. The lawyer who actively engages with these mechanisms - proposing realistic schedules, honoring deadlines, requesting extensions only when genuinely needed and well in advance - operates in the affirmative zone of the rule.

Common procedural posture

Discovery-period diligence

Counsel serves discovery requests promptly after the start of the discovery period, responds to received discovery within the time the rules permit, and confers in good faith on disputes before motion practice. This is the heart of 3.2 in operation - active engagement with the procedural calendar in a way that respects both the client's interest in thorough preparation and the court's interest in moving the case.

Stipulating to undisputed facts

Counsel agrees to a written stipulation of undisputed facts, narrowing the issues that need to be tried. The stipulation reflects the affirmative spirit of 3.2: it preserves the client's position on contested matters while clearing uncontested matters from the court's attention. Counsel may do so without conceding any disputed point.

Extensions and continuances

Rule 3.2 does not bar extensions or continuances. It contemplates them. Counsel may request additional time when additional time is needed - for additional discovery, for additional briefing, for accommodating witnesses, for resolving outstanding procedural issues. The rule simply requires that the request be grounded in a legitimate purpose connected to the matter, not in tactical advantage divorced from the matter's progress.

Best practices commonly observed in bar guidance:

Request continuances early when the need becomes apparent, rather than at the last moment

State the basis for the continuance plainly in the motion

Confer with opposing counsel on the request before filing

Propose a specific new date or timeframe rather than leaving the matter open-ended

Relationship to other rules

Rule 3.2 sits within the litigation-conduct cluster (Rules 3.1 through 3.9). It interacts with several adjacent rules:

Rule 1.3 - Diligence; the duty of diligence to the client overlaps substantially with the expediting duty to the court

Rule 3.1 - Meritorious claims; counsel may not delay through frivolous motions or repeated reassertion of rejected positions

Rule 3.4 - Fairness to opposing party and counsel; 3.4(d) addresses obstruction in discovery, which often overlaps with 3.2 concerns

Rule 8.4 - Misconduct; severe and unjustified delay may also implicate 8.4(d) (conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice)

Practical impact

Rule 3.2 is most often invoked as one element of broader patterns rather than as a stand-alone violation. The lawyer who consistently meets deadlines, responds to discovery, and engages with court schedules does not encounter the rule as a barrier; the rule operates in the background as a check on the rare attorney whose conduct draws the court's attention as a pattern of unjustified delay.

Diligent practice satisfies the rule. Counsel who runs a careful, well-managed docket complies with 3.2 as a matter of routine.

Justified time-taking is protected. The rule's qualifier (consistent with client interests) protects the time needed for thorough advocacy.

The systemic dimension matters. Counsel's pace bears on the courts and on other parties; the affirmative duty runs to that broader interest as well as to the immediate matter.

Related authority

ABA Model Rule 3.2 - model rule with comment

Kansas Rules of Professional Conduct - Kansas Supreme Court Rules

Missouri Rules of Professional Conduct - Missouri Supreme Court Rule 4

## KRPC 3.3 / MRPC 4-3.3 - Candor Toward the Tribunal [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/krpc-3-3/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Rule of Professional Conduct
KRPC 3.3 / MRPC 4-3.3

KRPC 3.3 / MRPC 4-3.3: Candor Toward the Tribunal

False statements of fact and law, the duty to correct, the scope of "tribunal," and the limit on confidentiality where candor is at stake.

Verbatim text of KRPC 3.3 (Kansas)

(a) A lawyer shall not knowingly:

(1) make a false statement of fact or law to a tribunal or fail to correct a false statement of material fact or law previously made to the tribunal by the lawyer;

(2) fail to disclose to the tribunal legal authority in the controlling jurisdiction known to the lawyer to be directly adverse to the position of the client and not disclosed by opposing counsel; or

(3) offer evidence that the lawyer knows to be false. If a lawyer, the lawyer's client, or a witness called by the lawyer, has offered material evidence and the lawyer comes to know of its falsity, the lawyer shall take reasonable remedial measures, including, if necessary, disclosure to the tribunal. A lawyer may refuse to offer evidence, other than the testimony of a defendant in a criminal matter, that the lawyer reasonably believes is false.

(b) A lawyer who represents a client in an adjudicative proceeding and who knows that a person intends to engage, is engaging or has engaged in criminal or fraudulent conduct related to the proceeding shall take reasonable remedial measures, including, if necessary, disclosure to the tribunal.

(c) The duties stated in paragraphs (a) and (b) continue to the conclusion of the proceeding, and apply even if compliance requires disclosure of information otherwise protected by Rule 1.6.

(d) In an ex parte proceeding, a lawyer shall inform the tribunal of all material facts known to the lawyer that will enable the tribunal to make an informed decision, whether or not the facts are adverse. Kan. Sup. Ct. R. 226, KRPC 3.3.

Missouri Rule 4-3.3

Missouri Rule 4-3.3 is substantively identical to KRPC 3.3 and tracks ABA Model Rule 3.3. Both rules organize the candor duty into four subdivisions: prohibited conduct in subdivision (a), remedial obligation in adjudicative proceedings in subdivision (b), duration and override of confidentiality in subdivision (c), and the heightened ex parte duty in subdivision (d).

3.3(a)(1) - False statements of fact or law

A lawyer shall not knowingly make a false statement of fact or law to a tribunal. The prohibition reaches both affirmative misstatements and failure to correct a prior misstatement of material fact or law made by the lawyer. The "knowingly" standard means actual knowledge, which may be inferred from circumstances. Constructive knowledge - what a reasonable lawyer should have known - is not by itself sufficient under the rule, though it may be relevant under Rule 8.4(c) or under Rule 9011 in federal practice.

"False statement of fact"

The category includes affirmative factual assertions in pleadings, motions, briefs, oral argument, evidentiary submissions, and other communications with the tribunal. The standard is objective falsity, not subjective belief. A statement that is literally true but materially misleading in context may be a false statement under the rule.

"False statement of law"

The category includes legal contentions known to be unsupported. The classic example is an assertion that controlling authority stands for a proposition it does not stand for. The standard is knowledge; a good-faith argument for extension or modification of existing law is not a false statement of law, but mischaracterization of existing authority is.

3.3(a)(2) - Disclosure of directly adverse authority

A lawyer shall not fail to disclose to the tribunal legal authority in the controlling jurisdiction known to the lawyer to be directly adverse to the position of the client and not disclosed by opposing counsel. The duty is conditioned on three factors: (a) the authority must be in the controlling jurisdiction, (b) it must be directly adverse to the client's position, and (c) opposing counsel has not disclosed it. The rule does not require disclosure of merely unfavorable authority or of authority that distinguishes the client's case; the threshold is "directly adverse."

3.3(a)(3) - False evidence

The lawyer shall not offer evidence the lawyer knows to be false. If material evidence has been offered and the lawyer comes to know of its falsity, the lawyer must take reasonable remedial measures, including if necessary disclosure to the tribunal. The duty applies regardless of who offered the evidence - the lawyer, the lawyer's client, or a witness called by the lawyer. The rule preserves a lawyer's discretion to refuse to offer evidence (other than a criminal defendant's testimony) the lawyer reasonably believes - rather than knows - to be false.

The duty to correct

The duty to correct - embedded in 3.3(a)(1) and articulated again in 3.3(a)(3) and 3.3(b) - is the operative continuing duty under the rule. A prior statement, evidence, or position discovered after submission to be false generates a remedial obligation. The lawyer's first option is typically to persuade the client (or witness) to withdraw or correct the offending material. If that is unsuccessful, "reasonable remedial measures" may include withdrawal of the affected pleading, motion, or evidence and, where necessary, disclosure to the tribunal.

The remedial duty overrides Rule 1.6. Subdivision (c) provides that the duties in subdivisions (a) and (b) apply even if compliance requires disclosure of information otherwise protected by Rule 1.6 (confidentiality of information). The candor duty is one of the limited circumstances in which a lawyer must disclose information that confidentiality would otherwise protect.

Duration of the duty

The duties under subdivisions (a) and (b) continue to the conclusion of the proceeding. The Comment to Model Rule 3.3 defines conclusion of the proceeding as a final judgment in the matter, including the expiration or final disposition of any appeal. The duty does not extinguish at the conclusion of a particular hearing or the entry of a particular order.

3.3(d) - The ex parte duty

In an ex parte proceeding, the lawyer's duty expands beyond the prohibitions of subdivisions (a) and (b). The lawyer must inform the tribunal of all material facts known to the lawyer that will enable the tribunal to make an informed decision, "whether or not the facts are adverse." The ordinary adversarial process - in which opposing counsel surfaces adverse facts - is absent in an ex parte proceeding, and the rule fills that gap by making the lawyer responsible for the completeness of the factual record.

The scope of "tribunal"

"Tribunal" is defined in Rule 1.0 to mean a court, an arbitrator in a binding arbitration proceeding, or a legislative body, administrative agency, or other body acting in an adjudicative capacity. In the bankruptcy context, the bankruptcy court is plainly a tribunal. The United States Trustee, when reviewing fee applications or conducting investigations, is generally treated as a tribunal where the relevant activity is adjudicative; the analysis is fact-specific. Statements made in court filings - whether the matter is contested or unopposed - are statements to the tribunal.

Common procedural posture

Filing with incorrect date

A motion is filed reciting a particular date for a transaction. The lawyer later discovers the date was incorrect. Rule 3.3(a)(1) requires the lawyer to correct the prior statement; this is typically accomplished by an amended filing or a notice to the court. The duty is not satisfied by simply leaving the incorrect filing on the record.

Adverse Tenth Circuit authority not cited

A brief in the District of Kansas relies on out-of-circuit authority while not citing controlling Tenth Circuit authority directly adverse to the client's position. If opposing counsel has not disclosed the adverse authority, Rule 3.3(a)(2) requires the lawyer to disclose it.

Relationship to Rule 9011

In federal bankruptcy practice, Rule 3.3 operates in parallel with Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 9011. A filing that lacks evidentiary support violates Rule 9011(b)(3); a filing containing a knowingly false statement of fact violates both Rule 9011(b)(3) and KRPC 3.3(a)(1). The two regimes are independent and a violation of one may be redressable under the other. Federal Rule 9011 sanctions can be sought through the safe-harbor motion procedure; KRPC 3.3 violations are addressed by the state disciplinary authority on referral.

Related rules and authority

Rule 1.0(m) - Definition of "tribunal"

Rule 1.2(d) - Lawyer shall not counsel or assist client in conduct lawyer knows is criminal or fraudulent

Rule 1.6 - Confidentiality of information; subject to 3.3(c) override

Rule 8.4(c) - Dishonesty, fraud, deceit, misrepresentation

Rule 8.3 - Duty to report serious misconduct

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 9011 - Signature, representations, sanctions

Related authority

ABA Model Rule 3.3 - model rule with comment

Kansas Rules of Professional Conduct - Kansas Supreme Court Rules

Missouri Rules of Professional Conduct - Missouri Supreme Court Rule 4
