## KRPC 3.4 / MRPC 4-3.4 - Fairness to Opposing Party and Counsel [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/krpc-3-4/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Rule of Professional Conduct
KRPC 3.4 / MRPC 4-3.4

KRPC 3.4 / MRPC 4-3.4: Fairness to Opposing Party and Counsel

Permitted evidence handling, the witness-contact framework, the structured rules of discovery participation, and the framework for references to inadmissible matter.

Permitted evidence and witness handling that 3.4 establishes

Rule 3.4 is a structured charter for the lawyer's interaction with evidence, witnesses, and opposing counsel. Read affirmatively, the rule confirms what counsel may do at every step: gather and preserve evidence within the scope of legitimate inquiry, contact witnesses and pay statutorily authorized fees, participate fully in discovery within the framework the rules establish, and make references at trial that fall within the scope of admissible matter or matter that the lawyer reasonably believes will be admitted.

The rule operates as a fairness architecture - a description of how the adversary process is supposed to run when both sides are working within its framework. The narrow set of conduct the rule places outside the framework exists to keep that architecture intact; the much broader zone of permitted conduct is what the rule, in practice, protects.

Verbatim text of KRPC 3.4 (Kansas)

A lawyer shall not:

(a) unlawfully obstruct another party's access to evidence or unlawfully alter, destroy or conceal a document or other material having potential evidentiary value. A lawyer shall not counsel or assist another person to do any such act;

(b) falsify evidence, counsel or assist a witness to testify falsely, or offer an inducement to a witness that is prohibited by law;

(c) knowingly disobey an obligation under the rules of a tribunal except for an open refusal based on an assertion that no valid obligation exists;

(d) in pretrial procedure, make a frivolous discovery request or fail to make reasonably diligent effort to comply with a legally proper discovery request by an opposing party;

(e) in trial, allude to any matter that the lawyer does not reasonably believe is relevant or that will not be supported by admissible evidence, assert personal knowledge of facts in issue except when testifying as a witness, or state a personal opinion as to the justness of a cause, the credibility of a witness, the culpability of a civil litigant or the guilt or innocence of an accused;

(f) request a person other than a client to refrain from voluntarily giving relevant information to another party unless: (1) the person is a relative or an employee or other agent of a client; and (2) the lawyer reasonably believes that the person's interests will not be adversely affected by refraining from giving such information. Kan. Sup. Ct. R. 226, KRPC 3.4.

Missouri Rule 4-3.4

Missouri Rule 4-3.4 is substantively identical to KRPC 3.4 and tracks ABA Model Rule 3.4. The structure is the same: subdivisions (a) through (f) each carve a small zone of unfair conduct out of a much larger zone of permitted advocacy.

Evidence-handling permissions

Counsel may gather, organize, preserve, and present evidence on the client's behalf. The rule confirms two affirmative parameters of that work:

Lawful preservation. Counsel may take custody of documents and tangible items having potential evidentiary value and preserve them in the ordinary course of the representation. Maintaining a litigation hold, organizing client documents for production, and securing physical items for forensic examination are all within the protected zone.

Lawful access. Counsel may use every method the rules of procedure provide for gathering evidence - requests for production, subpoenas, depositions, requests for admission, third-party document subpoenas, and the like. None of these are obstructive; they are the access mechanisms the system provides.

The narrow zone subdivision (a) places outside the protected sphere is "unlawful" obstruction, alteration, destruction, or concealment - that is, conduct contrary to law, court order, or rule of procedure. The qualifier "unlawful" carries weight; routine evidence handling is plainly not what the rule reaches.

Witness contact framework

Counsel may contact witnesses, interview them, ask them to attend deposition or trial, and pay them lawful witness fees and reasonable expenses. The rule's Comment makes the affirmative framework explicit:

Reasonable compensation for time. Counsel may pay a witness reasonable compensation for time lost in attending or testifying, and reasonable expenses incurred

Expert-witness compensation. Counsel may pay an expert witness a reasonable fee for the expert's professional services

Voluntary interviews. Counsel may seek voluntary interviews with witnesses (subject to Rule 4.2's no-contact rule for represented persons)

The rule places outside the protected zone only payments that operate as inducements to testify in a particular way - that is, payment contingent on content of testimony, or payment beyond what statute permits.

Witness-availability framework under 3.4(f)

Subdivision (f) addresses requests that a person refrain from voluntarily giving information to another party. The default rule is that counsel may not make such requests of non-clients, but the rule expressly permits the request in a defined zone: the person is a relative, employee, or other agent of the client, AND counsel reasonably believes the person's interests will not be adversely affected. This is an affirmative carve-in: within the defined zone, counsel may give such advice on a routine basis as part of representing the organizational or family-related client.

Discovery participation framework under 3.4(d)

Subdivision (d) addresses pretrial procedure and operates on two parallel duties: do not make a frivolous discovery request, and make reasonably diligent effort to comply with a legally proper discovery request. The affirmative content of both duties is broad. Counsel may serve any discovery request grounded in a legitimate theory of the case, and counsel may interpose any objection the rules of procedure provide. The rule simply requires that requests not be frivolous and that responses not be obstructive.

What the rule plainly permits:

Asserting privileges (attorney-client, work product, joint-defense, common-interest, statutory privileges)

Objecting on grounds of relevance, proportionality, burden, or scope

Seeking protective orders or in-camera review where appropriate

Negotiating discovery scope and timing with opposing counsel

Producing documents subject to confidentiality designations under a stipulated order

Affirmative read-out. Rule 3.4 is a fairness architecture, not a set of traps. The vast majority of evidence handling, witness contact, and discovery participation falls inside the protected zone. The rule's prohibitions exist to keep the architecture intact for everyone.

Tribunal-obligation framework under 3.4(c)

Subdivision (c) prohibits knowing disobedience of a tribunal's rules, but expressly preserves the lawyer's ability to make an open refusal based on an assertion that no valid obligation exists. This is a deliberate design choice: it protects counsel's ability to challenge the validity of an order or rule through appropriate channels - by direct appeal, by mandamus, by interlocutory application - so long as the challenge is made openly rather than through covert non-compliance. Counsel may, for example, refuse to comply with an order counsel believes to be unconstitutional and seek prompt review.

Trial-reference framework under 3.4(e)

Subdivision (e) governs counsel's references at trial. Its affirmative content: counsel may allude to any matter the lawyer reasonably believes is relevant and will be supported by admissible evidence. The standard turns on the lawyer's reasonable belief; certainty is not required. Counsel may preview anticipated evidence in opening statement, may reference exhibits before they are formally admitted (subject to the court's procedures), and may make arguments about the inferences the evidence supports.

The rule also addresses three specific categories of restriction at trial:

Assertion of personal knowledge of facts in issue (permitted only when the lawyer testifies as a witness - see Rule 3.7)

Statement of personal opinion on the justness of a cause

Statement of personal opinion on the credibility of a witness, the culpability of a civil litigant, or the guilt or innocence of an accused

The affirmative space: counsel may argue every inference the evidence supports, may marshal the evidence in any rhetorical structure, and may urge the fact-finder to reach any conclusion the evidence permits. The rule constrains personal-opinion vouching; it does not constrain argument.

Common procedural posture

Litigation hold and document preservation

Counsel issues a litigation hold to the client, organizes preservation of relevant documents, and oversees production through document-by-document privilege review. The entire process is within the protected zone of 3.4(a). Routine preservation and privilege screening are precisely what the rule contemplates.

Expert witness retention

Counsel retains an expert, agrees to a reasonable fee for the expert's professional services and time spent testifying, and prepares the expert through customary expert-witness preparation. The arrangement is plainly within 3.4's permitted framework. The rule prohibits inducement to testify in a particular way; it does not prohibit reasonable compensation for the expert's professional work.

Relationship to other rules

Rule 3.3 - Candor toward the tribunal; partial overlap on falsification of evidence

Rule 3.5 - Impartiality and decorum of the tribunal

Rule 4.4 - Respect for rights of third persons; aligned values

Rule 8.4(c) - Conduct involving dishonesty or fraud; reaches some 3.4(a)-(b) violations

Practical impact

Rule 3.4 is the workhorse of day-to-day litigation conduct. Counsel who follows the rules of procedure, asserts colorable objections, preserves documents under reasonable holds, pays expert witnesses customary fees, and argues the inferences the evidence supports operates entirely within the protected zone. The rule's prohibitions reach a narrow class of conduct - knowing destruction, falsification, contingent witness inducement, frivolous discovery practice - that is far outside ordinary practice.

Related authority

ABA Model Rule 3.4 - model rule with comment

Kansas Rules of Professional Conduct - Kansas Supreme Court Rules

Missouri Rules of Professional Conduct - Missouri Supreme Court Rule 4

KRPC 3.2 (Expediting)
KRPC 3.3 (Candor)
KRPC 3.5 (Tribunal)
KRPC 3.6 (Publicity)

## KRPC 3.5 / MRPC 4-3.5 - Impartiality and Decorum of the Tribunal [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/krpc-3-5/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Rule of Professional Conduct
KRPC 3.5 / MRPC 4-3.5

KRPC 3.5 / MRPC 4-3.5: Impartiality and Decorum of the Tribunal

Tribunal-interaction protocols - when ex parte contact is authorized, the juror-contact framework before and after discharge, and decorum during proceedings.

Tribunal-interaction protocols that 3.5 permits

Rule 3.5 is a protocol document for the lawyer's interaction with judges, jurors, and the tribunal generally. Read affirmatively, it identifies the channels through which counsel may properly contact a judicial officer, the conditions under which contact with jurors and prospective jurors is appropriate (including the substantially expanded contact authorized after discharge), and the standards of decorum that protect both the lawyer's effective advocacy and the tribunal's authority.

The rule operates as an authorization regime. When counsel follows the protocols - notice to opposing counsel, contact through the clerk, conduct within the rules of the tribunal - the resulting interaction is fully protected. The rule's narrow prohibitions exist to define the protocols, not to restrict the substantial communication the rules of procedure and judicial administration make available.

Verbatim text of KRPC 3.5 (Kansas)

A lawyer shall not:

(a) seek to influence a judge, juror, prospective juror or other official by means prohibited by law;

(b) communicate ex parte with such a person during the proceeding unless authorized to do so by law or court order;

(c) communicate with a juror or prospective juror after discharge of the jury if: (1) the communication is prohibited by law or court order; (2) the juror has made known to the lawyer a desire not to communicate; or (3) the communication involves misrepresentation, coercion, duress or harassment; or

(d) engage in conduct intended to disrupt a tribunal. Kan. Sup. Ct. R. 226, KRPC 3.5.

Missouri Rule 4-3.5

Missouri Rule 4-3.5 is substantively identical to KRPC 3.5 and tracks ABA Model Rule 3.5. The structure is the same: subdivision (a) reaches improper influence; subdivision (b) addresses ex parte contact during the proceeding (with the affirmative carve-in for contact authorized by law or court order); subdivision (c) governs post-discharge juror contact (preserving the substantial zone of permitted contact); subdivision (d) addresses tribunal disruption.

Judicial-contact framework under 3.5(b)

The ex parte prohibition in subdivision (b) is bounded by two important authorization clauses: contact "authorized by law" and contact authorized "by court order." Together they cover a substantial set of permitted interactions that counsel routinely engages in:

Emergency ex parte motions. Temporary restraining orders, ex parte seizure orders, and similar emergency relief are obtained through ex parte applications expressly authorized by procedural rules.

In camera review. When counsel submits material for the court's review outside the presence of opposing parties, the contact is authorized by the order directing the review.

Routine scheduling contact through the clerk. Most jurisdictions permit (and many require) counsel to coordinate scheduling with the court's clerk or judicial assistant.

Ministerial inquiries. Questions about the status of an order, the location of a filed paper, or local procedure are generally treated as authorized ministerial contact.

Settlement conferences with the judge. Where a court holds settlement conferences ex parte by design, the contact is authorized by the court's procedure.

The Comment to Model Rule 3.5 expressly recognizes that procedural rules and statutes authorize many forms of ex parte contact, and that the lawyer's duty is to operate within the authorized channels - notifying opposing counsel when notification is required, providing on-the-record submissions when required, and following the procedural framework the contact rests upon.

Improper-influence framework under 3.5(a)

Subdivision (a) prohibits seeking to influence a judge, juror, prospective juror, or other official "by means prohibited by law." The affirmative content is significant: every means of influence that is not prohibited by law remains available - oral argument, written briefing, evidentiary presentation, requests for clarification, motions for reconsideration, and every other procedural tool the system provides. Counsel's job is to influence the tribunal through these legitimate means; the rule simply requires that the means be legitimate.

Juror-contact framework

The rule addresses three temporal phases of juror contact:

Before the jury is empaneled (voir dire)

Voir dire is the structured opportunity counsel has to communicate with prospective jurors. The rule does not restrict the substance of voir dire questioning beyond the limits the tribunal imposes; counsel may explore prospective jurors' backgrounds, experiences, and views to the extent the court permits.

During the proceeding

Counsel may not communicate ex parte with sitting jurors during the proceeding, but again the limitation is one of channel rather than substance. Communication through the court's questions and instructions, written submissions of proposed jury instructions, and arguments in open court are all means by which counsel properly communicates with the jury during the proceeding.

After discharge of the jury

Subdivision (c) preserves a substantial zone of permitted post-discharge contact. Counsel may communicate with discharged jurors so long as the communication is not prohibited by law or court order, the juror has not indicated a desire not to communicate, and the communication does not involve misrepresentation, coercion, duress, or harassment. Permitted post-discharge contact includes:

Conversations to understand the jury's reasoning that may inform appellate review or future advocacy

Discussions about the presentation of evidence to inform future trial practice

Research into juror experience for academic or improvement purposes

Identification of grounds for new trial or motion-for-judgment-as-a-matter-of-law where appropriate

Affirmative read-out. The post-discharge juror-contact zone is substantial. Counsel who approaches discharged jurors respectfully, with prior court awareness where local practice requires it, and who honors any expressed wish not to talk, operates within the protected zone the rule preserves.

Decorum framework under 3.5(d)

Subdivision (d) addresses conduct "intended to disrupt a tribunal." The standard is intent-based. Vigorous argument, persistent objection, repeated motions for reconsideration, and forceful cross-examination are not "intended to disrupt" - they are intended to advocate. The Comment to Model Rule 3.5 makes the distinction explicit: the rule does not require the lawyer to be passive in the face of an adverse ruling or to abandon advocacy techniques because they are uncomfortable for the tribunal. Disruption is the deliberate impairment of the tribunal's functioning, not the inconvenience of zealous advocacy.

The Comment also recognizes that counsel may stand by an objection, may insist on the right to be heard, and may make a record for appellate review even over the tribunal's resistance. These are decorous activities in the relevant sense.

Common procedural posture

Emergency TRO application

Counsel files an application for a temporary restraining order on grounds requiring ex parte relief. The proceeding is authorized by Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 65(b) and analogous state rules. The ex parte presentation, including any in-camera disclosure of confidential material, is within the affirmative zone of 3.5(b).

Post-trial juror interview

After a verdict, counsel reaches out to a discharged juror to understand the jury's deliberations. The juror agrees to speak. No court order forbids the conversation, no rule of the jurisdiction prohibits it, and counsel conducts the interview with civility and without coercion. The conversation falls within the post-discharge zone 3.5(c) preserves.

Relationship to other rules

Rule 3.3 - Candor toward the tribunal; the lawyer's duty in any tribunal contact

Rule 3.5(c) - Read in conjunction with local rules on post-trial juror contact (many federal districts have local rules requiring leave of court)

Rule 4.4 - Respect for rights of third persons; harassment limitation parallels 3.5(c)(3)

Rule 8.4(d) - Conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice; severe disruption may also implicate

Judicial codes of conduct - The judge's parallel ethical regime governs the judge's side of any contact

Practical impact

The lawyer who follows the established protocols - notifying opposing counsel when contact requires notice, going through the clerk for scheduling, presenting emergency motions through the procedures the rules authorize, conducting voir dire within the court's framework, conducting post-discharge juror contact respectfully - operates entirely within the zone 3.5 protects. The rule's prohibitions reach a narrow set of conduct (improper influence, unauthorized contact, juror harassment, deliberate tribunal disruption) that is far outside ordinary practice.

Related authority

ABA Model Rule 3.5 - model rule with comment

Kansas Rules of Professional Conduct - Kansas Supreme Court Rules

Missouri Rules of Professional Conduct - Missouri Supreme Court Rule 4

## KRPC 3.6 / MRPC 4-3.6 - Trial Publicity [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/krpc-3-6/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Rule of Professional Conduct
KRPC 3.6 / MRPC 4-3.6

KRPC 3.6 / MRPC 4-3.6: Trial Publicity

Public-statement safe harbors, the right-to-reply framework, the substantial-likelihood-of-material-prejudice standard, and the Gentile First Amendment architecture.

Public-statement safe harbors that 3.6 protects

Rule 3.6 is best read as a public-statement architecture. It identifies what counsel may say to the public, to the press, and through other channels of mass dissemination at every stage of a matter. The rule names categories of statements that are categorically safe harbors, preserves an affirmative right to reply to publicity initiated by others, and applies the constitutional standard of "substantial likelihood of material prejudice" articulated by the Supreme Court of the United States in Gentile v. State Bar of Nevada, 501 U.S. 1030 (1991).

The rule's affirmative content is broad: routine case-status statements, descriptions of the claim and defenses, information already on the public record, statements warning of imminent danger, and reply statements protecting the client from prejudicial publicity initiated by others. These categories cover the substantial majority of statements counsel makes about pending matters.

Verbatim text of KRPC 3.6 (Kansas)

(a) A lawyer who is participating or has participated in the investigation or litigation of a matter shall not make an extrajudicial statement that the lawyer knows or reasonably should know will be disseminated by means of public communication and will have a substantial likelihood of materially prejudicing an adjudicative proceeding in the matter.

(b) Notwithstanding paragraph (a), a lawyer may state:

(1) the claim, offense or defense involved and, except when prohibited by law, the identity of the persons involved;

(2) information contained in a public record;

(3) that an investigation of a matter is in progress;

(4) the scheduling or result of any step in litigation;

(5) a request for assistance in obtaining evidence and information necessary thereto;

(6) a warning of danger concerning the behavior of a person involved, when there is reason to believe that there exists the likelihood of substantial harm to an individual or to the public interest; and

(7) in a criminal case, in addition to (1) through (6): (i) the identity, residence, occupation and family status of the accused; (ii) if the accused has not been apprehended, information necessary to aid in apprehension of that person; (iii) the fact, time and place of arrest; and (iv) the identity of investigating and arresting officers or agencies and the length of the investigation.

(c) Notwithstanding paragraph (a), a lawyer may make a statement that a reasonable lawyer would believe is required to protect a client from the substantial undue prejudicial effect of recent publicity not initiated by the lawyer or the lawyer's client. A statement made pursuant to this paragraph shall be limited to such information as is necessary to mitigate the recent adverse publicity. Kan. Sup. Ct. R. 226, KRPC 3.6.

Missouri Rule 4-3.6

Missouri Rule 4-3.6 is substantively identical to KRPC 3.6 and tracks ABA Model Rule 3.6. Both rules incorporate the Gentile framework as the constitutional baseline.

The seven categorical safe harbors of 3.6(b)

Subdivision (b) catalogs the categories of statements that are categorically protected. These are not "exceptions" to a rule that otherwise forbids speech; they are an affirmative description of the speech that is plainly safe. They include:

Claim, offense, defense, and identity of parties. Counsel may describe what the case is about and (subject to applicable confidentiality law) who is involved.

Information contained in a public record. Anything on the public docket - filed papers, court orders, transcripts - may be quoted or summarized without further limitation.

That an investigation is in progress. Counsel may confirm that a matter is under investigation.

Scheduling or result of any step in litigation. Hearing dates, motion outcomes, trial scheduling - all may be described.

Request for assistance in obtaining evidence. A public call for witnesses, documents, or information falls within the safe harbor.

Warning of danger. Where there is reason to believe substantial harm threatens, counsel may publicly warn.

Criminal-case identifying and apprehension information. Six specific categories of identifying and procedural information about criminal defendants and arrests.

The right-to-reply framework under 3.6(c)

Subdivision (c) is the affirmative right to reply. It preserves counsel's ability to defend the client from publicity counsel did not initiate. Three operative conditions:

A reasonable lawyer must believe the reply is required to protect the client

The publicity being responded to must be recent and not initiated by the lawyer or client

The reply must be limited to information necessary to mitigate the adverse publicity

The right-to-reply framework recognizes that publicity often flows in only one direction - from prosecutors, from opposing parties, from media reports based on partial information, or from public officials with their own platforms. Counsel for the affected client retains the affirmative ability to respond, and that response is part of the rule's protected zone.

The Gentile framework

The Supreme Court's decision in Gentile v. State Bar of Nevada, 501 U.S. 1030 (1991), supplies the constitutional architecture for Rule 3.6. The Court held that a State may regulate lawyer speech about pending cases under a "substantial likelihood of material prejudice" standard - a standard the Court found constitutionally adequate as applied to lawyers because of the lawyer's role in the administration of justice. At the same time, the Court emphasized that the rule must give clear notice of what is permitted, and that vague safe-harbor provisions may not satisfy due process.

Several propositions follow from Gentile and from the cases applying it:

The constitutional standard is "substantial likelihood of material prejudice," not "any possibility of prejudice"

The safe harbors of subdivision (b) and the right-of-reply of subdivision (c) must be applied with sufficient clarity to give counsel fair notice of what is permitted

The First Amendment interest at stake includes the lawyer's interest in speaking, the client's interest in having an advocate publicly, and the public's interest in information about matters of public concern

Restrictions on lawyer speech must be narrowly tailored to the State's interest in fair trials

Affirmative read-out. Counsel who restricts public statements to the seven categorical safe harbors, or who responds to publicity initiated by others within the right-of-reply framework, operates inside the protected zone the rule preserves. The constitutional standard sets the outer perimeter; the safe harbors describe the safe interior; the right of reply describes the protective response.

The substantial-likelihood-of-material-prejudice standard

The general prohibition in subdivision (a) reaches only extrajudicial statements that (i) the lawyer knows or reasonably should know will be disseminated by public communication and (ii) will have a substantial likelihood of materially prejudicing an adjudicative proceeding. Three operative components:

Knowledge or reasonable awareness of dissemination. Private statements, statements to other lawyers in the matter, and statements not reasonably expected to be publicly disseminated are not reached.

Substantial likelihood. The standard is not "any possibility" but "substantial likelihood" - a heightened threshold the Supreme Court endorsed in Gentile.

Material prejudice to an adjudicative proceeding. The prejudice must be to the proceeding itself, not generalized public concern.

Common procedural posture

Press conference at filing

Counsel files a civil complaint and holds a press conference describing the claim, the parties, the relief sought, the hearing schedule, and the filing date. Each of these falls squarely within subdivisions (b)(1) and (b)(4). The press conference is fully within the protected zone.

Reply to adverse press release

An opposing party issues a press release characterizing counsel's client unfavorably. Counsel makes a public statement, limited to factual correction, describing what the public record shows. The statement is within the right-of-reply zone subdivision (c) protects.

Public-record statements as a primary safe harbor

Subdivision (b)(2) - statements of information contained in a public record - is in practice the broadest of the safe harbors. Every filed paper, every docket entry, every court order, every transcript of a public proceeding, every public regulatory filing constitutes a public record for this purpose. Counsel may summarize, quote, link to, or otherwise convey public-record information freely. The Comment to Model Rule 3.6 emphasizes that the public has a legitimate interest in this information and that counsel has a corresponding ability to convey it.

Relationship to other rules

Rule 3.3 - Candor toward the tribunal; statements made in court are governed by 3.3 rather than 3.6

Rule 3.4 - Fairness to opposing party; 3.4(e) governs in-court references to inadmissible matter

Rule 3.8(f) (prosecutors) - Special restrictions on prosecutor extrajudicial statements

Rule 1.6 - Confidentiality; public statements must respect client-information limits

Rule 8.4 - Misconduct; dishonest public statements may implicate 8.4(c)

Practical impact

The lawyer who restricts public statements to the seven categorical safe harbors and the right-of-reply framework operates within a wide protected zone. Most counsel will find that the cases they handle and the statements they wish to make fall comfortably inside the safe harbors. The constitutional standard articulated in Gentile ensures that the rule cannot be applied in a vague or expansive manner that would chill protected speech.

Related authority

Gentile v. State Bar of Nevada, 501 U.S. 1030 (1991) - constitutional framework for lawyer trial-publicity speech

ABA Model Rule 3.6 - model rule with comment

Kansas Rules of Professional Conduct - Kansas Supreme Court Rules

Missouri Rules of Professional Conduct - Missouri Supreme Court Rule 4

KRPC 3.3 (Candor)

## KRPC 3.7 / MRPC 4-3.7 - Lawyer as Witness [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/krpc-3-7/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Rule of Professional Conduct
KRPC 3.7 / MRPC 4-3.7

KRPC 3.7 / MRPC 4-3.7: Lawyer as Witness

The advocate-witness exceptions - uncontested matter, value of legal services rendered, and substantial hardship - and the firm-imputation analysis under 3.7(b).

Advocate-witness exceptions that 3.7 permits

Rule 3.7 governs the relatively narrow situation in which a lawyer is likely to be a necessary witness at a trial in which the lawyer also serves as advocate. The rule is best read as a description of when the dual role is affirmatively permitted. Three express exceptions allow the same lawyer to continue as trial advocate, and a separate firm-imputation provision in subdivision (b) preserves the firm's ability to serve as advocate even when one of its lawyers will testify.

The combined structure preserves the client's freedom to retain (and keep) chosen counsel in a wide range of cases. The default rule that an advocate-witness should not try the case is more limited than is commonly understood; the three exceptions and the firm-imputation framework reach a substantial share of the cases in which the question arises.

Verbatim text of KRPC 3.7 (Kansas)

(a) A lawyer shall not act as advocate at a trial in which the lawyer is likely to be a necessary witness unless:

(1) the testimony relates to an uncontested issue;

(2) the testimony relates to the nature and value of legal services rendered in the case; or

(3) disqualification of the lawyer would work substantial hardship on the client.

(b) A lawyer may act as advocate in a trial in which another lawyer in the lawyer's firm is likely to be called as a witness unless precluded from doing so by Rule 1.7 or Rule 1.9. Kan. Sup. Ct. R. 226, KRPC 3.7.

Missouri Rule 4-3.7

Missouri Rule 4-3.7 is substantively identical to KRPC 3.7 and tracks ABA Model Rule 3.7. The structure is the same: subdivision (a)'s three exceptions, and subdivision (b)'s firm-imputation rule keyed only to the conflict-of-interest provisions.

The "necessary witness" threshold

Subdivision (a) applies only when the lawyer is "likely to be a necessary witness." Both elements matter:

Likely. A theoretical possibility that the lawyer might be called is not enough. The lawyer's testimony must be reasonably likely.

Necessary. The testimony must be necessary - meaning it cannot reasonably be obtained from another source. If another witness can provide the same testimony, the lawyer is not a necessary witness.

The "necessary witness" threshold often resolves the question without reaching the three exceptions. If documents, third-party witnesses, or other lawyers can establish the same point, the lawyer is not a necessary witness and the rule does not bar continued advocacy.

Exception 1: Uncontested issue

Subdivision (a)(1) permits the advocate-witness role when the testimony relates to an uncontested issue. Uncontested testimony - foundational background, authentication of routine documents, undisputed events on the procedural record - does not raise the concerns that motivate the general rule, because the jury is not asked to weigh the lawyer's credibility against contrary testimony. The exception is broad enough to cover most procedural and foundational testimony lawyers commonly give.

Exception 2: Value of legal services

Subdivision (a)(2) preserves the lawyer's ability to testify on the nature and value of legal services rendered in the case. This exception is especially important in fee-shifting contexts (attorney-fee awards under statute, fee applications in bankruptcy, sanction proceedings, contract-based fee provisions), where the lawyer is uniquely positioned to describe the work performed and its reasonable value. The Comment to Model Rule 3.7 specifically identifies this exception as a recognition that the lawyer is often the most qualified witness on the lawyer's own work.

Exception 3: Substantial hardship on the client

Subdivision (a)(3) permits the dual role when disqualification of the lawyer would work substantial hardship on the client. The Comment identifies factors relevant to substantial hardship:

The lawyer's distinctive familiarity with the case (developed expertise that another lawyer could not readily replicate)

The cost of bringing replacement counsel up to speed

The complexity of the matter and the stage at which the witness issue is identified

The availability of qualified replacement counsel and the time available to retain them

The client's choice and the disruption to the attorney-client relationship

Hardship is evaluated from the client's perspective, with weight given to the client's autonomy in selecting counsel. The exception is not narrow - it covers a substantial set of cases where late-emerging witness issues, distinctive lawyer expertise, or client choice would make disqualification disproportionate.

Affirmative read-out. Rule 3.7 permits the advocate-witness role in three substantial categories: (1) testimony on uncontested issues; (2) testimony on the value of the lawyer's own services; and (3) cases where disqualification would substantially harm the client. Combined with the "necessary witness" threshold, the rule reserves disqualification for the narrow class of cases in which a contested factual issue genuinely requires the lawyer's own testimony with no substantial hardship to the client.

Firm-imputation analysis under 3.7(b)

Subdivision (b) is the most important affirmative provision of the rule for firm practice. It provides that a lawyer may act as advocate in a trial in which another lawyer in the same firm is likely to be called as a witness, unless precluded by Rule 1.7 (concurrent conflicts) or Rule 1.9 (former-client conflicts). The default position is permission, not disqualification.

This is a deliberate narrowing of the older "imputation" rule that would have disqualified the entire firm. The current rule reflects the conclusion that the concerns driving 3.7(a) - jury confusion about whether the lawyer is testifying or arguing, conflict between the advocate's role and the witness's oath, possible adverse effect on the firm's representation - are substantially mitigated when different lawyers fill the two roles. The firm-imputation framework asks only the conflict-of-interest question (does the witness lawyer's testimony create a 1.7 or 1.9 conflict?), not the advocate-witness question.

Common procedural posture

Fee application after representation

Counsel files a fee application in a bankruptcy proceeding and testifies at a fee hearing about the nature and value of services rendered. The testimony falls squarely within subdivision (a)(2). The lawyer may continue as advocate without restriction.

Late-emerging witness issue in complex matter

Three weeks before trial in a complex commercial case, a fact emerges making the lead lawyer a potential witness on a contested issue. Counsel has been intimately involved in two years of case development; retaining and educating replacement trial counsel would cost the client substantial time and expense. Subdivision (a)(3)'s substantial-hardship exception is available.

The role of the tribunal

The Comment to Model Rule 3.7 notes that the tribunal has a strong interest in fair proceedings and may, in appropriate circumstances, raise the advocate-witness question on its own. The rule does not require the lawyer to wait for a motion to disqualify; counsel may evaluate the question proactively at the time the witness issue is identified, and may seek tribunal guidance where appropriate. The court's evaluation generally tracks the same factors the rule identifies.

Pretrial vs. trial advocacy

The rule's prohibition is keyed to acting as advocate "at a trial." Pretrial advocacy - discovery, motion practice, settlement, depositions - is not within the rule's scope, even when the lawyer is likely to be a necessary witness at trial. This is a substantial preservation of the lawyer's role: counsel who will need to step aside for trial may still conduct the case through every pretrial phase.

Relationship to other rules

Rule 1.7 - Conflict of interest with current clients; the gating question for firm-imputation under 3.7(b)

Rule 1.9 - Conflict of interest with former clients; the other gating question for 3.7(b)

Rule 3.4(e) - Trial reference rule; restricts personal-opinion vouching outside testimony

Rule 3.3 - Candor toward the tribunal; applies to the lawyer's testimony as it does to any witness

Practical impact

Rule 3.7 should be read with attention to the breadth of its affirmative content. The combined effect of the "necessary witness" threshold, the three exceptions, the firm-imputation rule, and the pretrial-only scope is that disqualification is the outcome only in a narrow class of cases: trials in which the lawyer is likely to be a necessary witness on a contested issue, where another firm lawyer could not serve as advocate (because of a 1.7 or 1.9 conflict), where the testimony is not within the value-of-services exception, and where substantial hardship to the client cannot be shown. That intersection is small.

Related authority

ABA Model Rule 3.7 - model rule with comment

Kansas Rules of Professional Conduct - Kansas Supreme Court Rules

Missouri Rules of Professional Conduct - Missouri Supreme Court Rule 4

## KRPC 4.4 / MRPC 4-4.4 - Respect for Rights of Third Persons [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/krpc-4-4/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Rule of Professional Conduct
KRPC 4.4 / MRPC 4-4.4

KRPC 4.4 / MRPC 4-4.4: Respect for Rights of Third Persons

The lawyer's duties to non-clients during the course of representation, including the substantial-purpose limitation on means and the inadvertent-document procedure.

Verbatim text of KRPC 4.4 (Kansas)

(a) In representing a client, a lawyer shall not use means that have no substantial purpose other than to embarrass, delay, or burden a third person, or use methods of obtaining evidence that violate the legal rights of such a person.

(b) A lawyer who receives a document or electronically stored information relating to the representation of the lawyer's client and knows or reasonably should know that the document or electronically stored information was inadvertently sent shall promptly notify the sender. Kan. Sup. Ct. R. 226, KRPC 4.4.

Missouri Rule 4-4.4

Missouri Rule 4-4.4 is substantively parallel to KRPC 4.4 and tracks ABA Model Rule 4.4. The rule frames the lawyer's relationship to non-clients during the course of representation. Subdivision (a) calibrates the lawyer's choice of means by reference to substantial purpose and to the legal rights of third persons. Subdivision (b) establishes a specific procedure for handling inadvertently transmitted documents and electronic information.

The structural premise

The Comment to Model Rule 4.4 frames the rule's premise: the duty of zealous representation to one's client operates within a framework that respects the legal rights of others. The rule does not catalog all of those rights - it directs the lawyer outward to the substantive law that defines them and provides a professional-conduct anchor for compliance.

The rule is structured permissively rather than as a general standard of civility. Lawyers may pursue vigorous representation - including conduct that incidentally burdens or inconveniences third persons - so long as that conduct has a substantial purpose tied to the representation and the methods used to obtain evidence stay within the bounds the law sets for the rights of others.

4.4(a) - The substantial-purpose framework

Subdivision (a) operates as a means-calibration rule. It contains two distinct provisions:

The "no substantial purpose" branch

The first branch directs that the lawyer shall not use means that have "no substantial purpose other than to embarrass, delay, or burden a third person." The framing is in the negative, but its operational effect is to identify a permitted zone. Conduct that has any substantial purpose tied to the representation - obtaining relevant evidence, advancing a legal position, protecting a client right, satisfying a procedural requirement - is within the rule even where it incidentally burdens a third person. The prohibition applies only where the lawyer's means have no purpose other than to impose burden, delay, or embarrassment.

The "substantial" qualifier is significant. Marginal or pretextual purposes do not satisfy the standard. The substantial-purpose inquiry is objective: would a reasonable lawyer perceive a legitimate purpose for the means employed, beyond the imposition of burden?

The "legal rights" branch

The second branch directs that the lawyer shall not use methods of obtaining evidence that violate the legal rights of third persons. The provision incorporates the body of substantive law that defines third-person rights in evidence-gathering contexts - privacy statutes, anti-eavesdropping laws, computer-access statutes, statutes governing recording of communications, rules governing access to medical and financial records, and analogous bodies of law. The professional-conduct dimension overlays the substantive law: methods that violate the underlying law are also a violation of 4.4(a).

By inverse, the rule recognizes that methods of evidence gathering authorized by law - formal discovery, public-record requests, properly noticed subpoenas, interviews conducted with informed consent, observation of public conduct - are within the rule's permission, even where the resulting evidence is unfavorable to or causes inconvenience to the third person.

4.4(b) - The inadvertent-document procedure

Subdivision (b) addresses the specific situation of a document or electronically stored information that a lawyer receives and that the lawyer knows or reasonably should know was inadvertently sent. The rule establishes a single procedural obligation: prompt notification of the sender.

The triggering conditions

Receipt of a document or ESI relating to the representation. The rule applies to materials the receiving lawyer comes into possession of through the conduct of the representation - email transmissions, file productions, fax communications, electronic file transfers, and analogous channels.

Knowledge or constructive knowledge of inadvertence. The lawyer must know, or reasonably should know, that the transmission was inadvertent. Constructive knowledge can arise from indicia on the face of the transmission (an obviously misdirected email, a privilege-log entry mistakenly included in a production, an attached file that does not match the body of the message) or from the surrounding circumstances.

The required action

The action the rule requires is prompt notification of the sender. The rule does not, in its text, address what the receiving lawyer must do with the materials themselves - whether to return, sequester, delete, or read - and leaves those questions to substantive law and to the lawyer's professional judgment in light of the duties owed to the receiving lawyer's own client. The Comment to Model Rule 4.4 notes that the rule's text addresses only the notification obligation; broader questions of return, use, or disqualification are governed by other law and by the lawyer's evaluation of countervailing duties.

The "reasonably should know" element is objective. Subdivision (b)'s notification duty attaches where the inadvertence is reasonably apparent, even if the receiving lawyer has not in fact recognized it. A document that is obviously misdirected, or a production that obviously includes materials the producing party intended to withhold, triggers the duty regardless of the receiving lawyer's subjective state of mind.

The "no substantial purpose" inquiry in practice

The substantial-purpose analysis under 4.4(a) considers conduct in light of its connection to the representation. Several categories of conduct routinely satisfy the substantial-purpose test:

Discovery requests tied to the issues in the case. A document request, deposition notice, or subpoena that seeks evidence relevant to a claim or defense has a substantial purpose tied to the representation, even where compliance imposes burden on a third party. Proportionality and other discovery-rule limits operate independently of Rule 4.4.

Subpoenas for records held by third parties. Records subpoenas issued through proper procedural channels have a substantial purpose where the records are relevant to the matter.

Witness interviews. Interviewing a witness who has information relevant to the matter has a substantial purpose, conducted within the bounds of Rule 4.2 (represented persons) and Rule 4.3 (unrepresented persons).

Public-record requests. Requests to government agencies under public-records statutes have a substantial purpose when the records bear on the matter.

Common procedural contexts

Inadvertent disclosure in document production

A producing party transmits a large document production that, on review, contains materials marked privileged on the producing party's privilege log. The receiving lawyer's reasonable review reveals the discrepancy. Subdivision (b) requires prompt notification of the sender. The receiving lawyer then evaluates the producing party's clawback procedure under the applicable procedural rules and the standing order in the case, and acts in accordance with those external frameworks while satisfying the rule's notification requirement.

Subpoena to a non-party records custodian

A lawyer issues a properly noticed subpoena to a third-party records custodian (medical provider, bank, employer) for records relevant to the client's claims or defenses. The subpoena imposes compliance burden on the custodian. The substantial-purpose inquiry under 4.4(a) is satisfied by the relevance of the records to the matter; the legal-rights inquiry is satisfied by the use of an authorized procedural channel (the subpoena) issued in conformity with the applicable rule, with any privacy-statute requirements satisfied separately.

Relationship to evidence-gathering and discovery rules

Rule 4.4 operates alongside the body of substantive and procedural law governing evidence gathering. The lawyer's professional-conduct compliance with 4.4(a) is assessed against the backdrop of the procedural rules that authorize particular methods (formal discovery rules, subpoena procedures, third-party records procedures) and the substantive rules that limit them (privilege, privacy statutes, anti-eavesdropping statutes). Conformity with the operative substantive and procedural framework is the typical path to compliance with 4.4(a)'s legal-rights branch.

Related rules and authority

Rule 4.1 - Truthfulness in statements to others; the broader candor framework for non-client communications

Rule 4.2 - Communication with persons represented by counsel

Rule 4.3 - Dealing with unrepresented persons

Rule 3.4 - Fairness to opposing party and counsel

Rule 1.6 - Confidentiality; relevant to the receiving lawyer's duties to the receiving lawyer's own client when handling inadvertent transmissions

Practical impact

Rule 4.4 carries several recurring practical consequences:

Substantial purpose is the affirmative key. Lawyers conducting vigorous representation are within the rule so long as the means employed have a substantial purpose tied to the representation. The rule does not require minimization of all burden to third persons; it requires that burden not be the sole or principal purpose.

Methods of evidence gathering are bounded by external law. The "legal rights" branch of 4.4(a) directs lawyers to the substantive law governing the rights of third persons in evidence-gathering contexts. Compliance with the operative substantive framework is the typical path to compliance with the rule.

Inadvertent-document handling is procedurally specific. Subdivision (b) imposes a discrete notification obligation when the conditions are met. Questions of return, use, or disqualification are governed by other law.

Related authority

ABA Model Rule 4.4 - model rule with comment

Kansas Rules of Professional Conduct - Kansas Supreme Court Rules

Missouri Rules of Professional Conduct - Missouri Supreme Court Rule 4

Open Bankruptcy Project cross-references

KRPC 3.3 (Candor)
KRPC 3.4 (Fairness)
KRPC 3.5 (Tribunal Decorum)
KRPC 5.1 (Supervision)
KRPC 8.4 (Misconduct)

## KRPC 5.1 / MRPC 4-5.1 - Responsibilities of Partners and Supervisory Lawyers [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/krpc-5-1/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Rule of Professional Conduct
KRPC 5.1 / MRPC 4-5.1

KRPC 5.1 / MRPC 4-5.1: Responsibilities of Partners, Managers, and Supervisory Lawyers

Firm-management duty, supervisory duty, and ratification by knowledge or silence.

Verbatim text of KRPC 5.1 (Kansas)

(a) A partner in a law firm, and a lawyer who individually or together with other lawyers possesses comparable managerial authority in a law firm, shall make reasonable efforts to ensure that the firm has in effect measures giving reasonable assurance that all lawyers in the firm conform to the Rules of Professional Conduct.

(b) A lawyer having direct supervisory authority over another lawyer shall make reasonable efforts to ensure that the other lawyer conforms to the Rules of Professional Conduct.

(c) A lawyer shall be responsible for another lawyer's violation of the Rules of Professional Conduct if:

(1) the lawyer orders or, with knowledge of the specific conduct, ratifies the conduct involved; or

(2) the lawyer is a partner or has comparable managerial authority in the law firm in which the other lawyer practices, or has direct supervisory authority over the other lawyer, and knows of the conduct at a time when its consequences can be avoided or mitigated but fails to take reasonable remedial action. Kan. Sup. Ct. R. 226, KRPC 5.1.

Missouri Rule 4-5.1

Missouri Rule 4-5.1 is substantively identical to KRPC 5.1 and tracks ABA Model Rule 5.1. The rule operates in three concentric layers: firm-management duty in subdivision (a), direct-supervisory duty in subdivision (b), and individual responsibility for another lawyer's violation in subdivision (c).

5.1(a) - Firm-management duty

Every partner in a law firm and every lawyer with comparable managerial authority must make reasonable efforts to ensure that the firm has measures in effect giving reasonable assurance that all lawyers in the firm conform to the rules of professional conduct. The duty is firm-wide and structural; it is not satisfied by personal compliance alone.

The Comment to Model Rule 5.1 identifies the kinds of measures contemplated, which scale with the size and complexity of the firm:

Policies and procedures designed to detect and resolve conflicts of interest

Accounting practices for trust accounts

Procedures for identifying dates by which actions must be taken in pending matters

Education of subordinate lawyers in the rules of professional conduct

Provision for adequate supervision of inexperienced lawyers

The standard is "reasonable efforts" - what is reasonable in a small firm differs from what is reasonable in a large firm, and what is reasonable in a firm with a uniform practice differs from what is reasonable in a firm with multiple practice areas.

5.1(b) - Direct supervisory duty

A lawyer having direct supervisory authority over another lawyer must make reasonable efforts to ensure that the supervised lawyer conforms to the rules. The duty is individual rather than firm-wide; it attaches to the supervisory relationship rather than to firm-management status. A senior associate supervising the work of a junior associate has a 5.1(b) duty even if neither is a partner.

The "reasonable efforts" standard in 5.1(b) is calibrated to the nature of the supervisory relationship. The supervising lawyer is generally responsible for reviewing the supervised lawyer's work product, providing guidance on ethical questions, and intervening when ethical concerns arise. The duty does not require the supervising lawyer to review every action taken by every supervised lawyer in real time; it requires reasonable supervision under the circumstances.

5.1(c) - Individual responsibility for another lawyer's violation

Subdivision (c) imposes personal responsibility for another lawyer's violation in two circumstances:

5.1(c)(1) - Order or ratification

The lawyer orders the conduct, or with knowledge of the specific conduct ratifies it. "Ratifies" reaches both express ratification (approval after the fact) and implicit ratification (acceptance of the conduct's results). The standard is knowledge of the specific conduct, not knowledge of conduct in general; a partner who is aware that subordinate lawyers in the firm sometimes take certain actions does not, by that general awareness, ratify any specific action.

5.1(c)(2) - Knowledge in time to avoid or mitigate

The lawyer has managerial or direct supervisory authority over the violating lawyer, and knows of the conduct at a time when its consequences can be avoided or mitigated, and fails to take reasonable remedial action. This is the "knew and did nothing" branch of the rule. It requires both (a) actual knowledge of the conduct and (b) a temporal window in which remedial action could have made a difference.

"Ratification by silence" is the colloquial label for 5.1(c)(2). A managing partner or direct supervisor who learns of a subordinate's violation while there is still time to correct it, and who takes no action, is personally responsible for the violation under the rule. The supervisor's silence in the face of known violation operates as a separate violation.

Common procedural posture

Discovered conflict mid-representation

An associate discovers a conflict of interest that should have been identified at intake. The associate reports to the supervising partner. Under 5.1(b), the partner must take reasonable steps to ensure the firm withdraws or obtains informed consent as required by Rule 1.7. Failure to act on the disclosure - by silence, by deferral, or by directing the associate to ignore the conflict - exposes the partner to 5.1(c)(2) responsibility.

Inaccurate factual statement in a brief

A supervising lawyer reviews an associate's brief and discovers a factual statement the lawyer knows to be inaccurate. Rule 3.3(a)(1) requires correction. If the supervising lawyer signs the brief or permits it to be filed without correction, the supervisor is personally exposed under both 3.3(a)(1) and 5.1(c)(1). If the brief is filed without the supervisor's pre-filing review but the supervisor later learns of the inaccuracy while the matter is still pending, 5.1(c)(2) attaches if no remedial action is taken.

Continuing nature of the duty

Subdivisions (a) and (b) impose continuing duties; they are not satisfied by one-time effort. A firm-management policy adopted at firm formation and never updated does not satisfy 5.1(a) as the firm grows, changes practice areas, or experiences personnel turnover. A supervisory relationship establishes a 5.1(b) duty that runs for the duration of the relationship.

Relationship to Rule 5.3

Rule 5.1 governs supervision of lawyers; Rule 5.3 governs supervision of nonlawyer assistants. The two rules are structurally parallel: both impose firm-management duties on partners and managerial authorities, supervisory duties on direct supervisors, and individual responsibility for violations committed with knowledge or under direction. A complete analysis of supervisory responsibility in a firm with both lawyer and nonlawyer staff typically requires application of both rules in tandem.

Relationship to Rule 5.2

Rule 5.2 governs the responsibilities of the subordinate lawyer. Rule 5.2(a) provides that a lawyer is bound by the rules notwithstanding direction of a supervisor, but Rule 5.2(b) provides a subordinate lawyer is not violating the rules by acting in accordance with a supervisory lawyer's reasonable resolution of an arguable question of professional duty. The interaction with Rule 5.1: a supervisor's "reasonable resolution" of an arguable question gives the subordinate cover under 5.2(b); a supervisor's direction to engage in clearly unethical conduct does not relieve the subordinate of 5.2(a) responsibility and does not insulate the supervisor under 5.1(c).

Related rules and authority

Rule 1.4 - Communication with the client; firm-management may include procedures for ensuring 1.4 compliance

Rule 1.7 / 1.9 - Conflicts of interest; conflict screening is a typical 5.1(a) measure

Rule 3.3 - Candor toward the tribunal; supervisor exposure on improperly filed papers

Rule 5.2 - Subordinate lawyer responsibilities

Rule 5.3 - Supervision of nonlawyer assistants

Rule 8.3 - Reporting professional misconduct; supervisor knowledge may trigger 8.3 obligations

Rule 8.4(a) - Violation through the acts of another

Practical impact

Rule 5.1 is the structural backbone of firm-level professional responsibility. Two consequences recur in published disciplinary decisions:

The "I didn't know" defense fails when the conduct was knowable. Subdivision (a) is a duty to maintain measures that would have produced knowledge. A managing partner cannot rely on subjective lack of awareness if the firm lacked the reasonable measures the rule requires.

Awareness without action is itself a violation. Subdivision (c)(2) treats silence in the face of known violation as a separate violation. The duty to act when learning of subordinate misconduct is independent of, and in addition to, any duty under Rule 8.3 to report.

Related authority

ABA Model Rule 5.1 - model rule with comment

Kansas Rules of Professional Conduct - Kansas Supreme Court Rules

Missouri Rules of Professional Conduct - Missouri Supreme Court Rule 4

Open Bankruptcy Project cross-references

KRPC 1.4 (Communication)
KRPC 1.16 (Termination)
KRPC 3.3 (Candor)
KRPC 8.3 (Reporting)
KRPC 8.4 (Misconduct)
Rule 9011 (Sanctions)

## KRPC 5.3 / MRPC 4-5.3 - Responsibilities Regarding Non-Lawyer Assistants [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/krpc-5-3/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Rule of Professional Conduct
KRPC 5.3 / MRPC 4-5.3

KRPC 5.3 / MRPC 4-5.3: Responsibilities Regarding Non-Lawyer Assistants

Firm-management duty, direct supervisory duty, and individual responsibility for the work of paralegals, legal secretaries, and other non-lawyer staff.

Verbatim text of KRPC 5.3 (Kansas)

With respect to a nonlawyer employed or retained by or associated with a lawyer:

(a) a partner, and a lawyer who individually or together with other lawyers possesses comparable managerial authority in a law firm shall make reasonable efforts to ensure that the firm has in effect measures giving reasonable assurance that the person's conduct is compatible with the professional obligations of the lawyer;

(b) a lawyer having direct supervisory authority over the nonlawyer shall make reasonable efforts to ensure that the person's conduct is compatible with the professional obligations of the lawyer; and

(c) a lawyer shall be responsible for conduct of such a person that would be a violation of the Rules of Professional Conduct if engaged in by a lawyer if:

(1) the lawyer orders or, with the knowledge of the specific conduct, ratifies the conduct involved; or

(2) the lawyer is a partner or has comparable managerial authority in the law firm in which the person is employed, or has direct supervisory authority over the person, and knows of the conduct at a time when its consequences can be avoided or mitigated but fails to take reasonable remedial action. Kan. Sup. Ct. R. 226, KRPC 5.3.

Missouri Rule 4-5.3

Missouri Rule 4-5.3 is substantively identical to KRPC 5.3 and tracks ABA Model Rule 5.3. The rule applies whether the non-lawyer is an employee of the firm (paralegal, legal secretary, investigator on staff) or is retained on a contract basis (outside investigator, freelance paralegal, contract document-review staff, third-party vendor providing services that substitute for or augment lawyer work). The three-part structure parallels Rule 5.1 for supervised lawyers: firm-management duty, direct supervisory duty, and individual responsibility for conduct.

5.3(a) - Firm-management duty

Every partner and every lawyer with comparable managerial authority in the firm must make reasonable efforts to ensure that the firm maintains measures giving reasonable assurance that the conduct of each non-lawyer in or associated with the firm is compatible with the professional obligations of the lawyers themselves. The duty is structural and firm-wide; it is not satisfied by the personal compliance of any individual lawyer.

The Comment to Model Rule 5.3 identifies categories of measures that scale with the size and practice profile of the firm:

Written policies governing the role and scope of work of non-lawyer assistants in each practice area

Training programs that orient non-lawyer staff to confidentiality, conflicts, file-management, and tribunal-related obligations of the lawyers they assist

Procedures for review of work product prepared by non-lawyer staff before it leaves the firm or is filed with a tribunal

Conflict-checking protocols that include matters worked on by non-lawyer staff

Supervision protocols for outside vendors and contract staff whose work product is delivered to clients or filed on the firm's behalf

The standard is "reasonable efforts." What is reasonable in a sole-practitioner office with one legal secretary differs from what is reasonable in a multi-office firm with a paralegal staff measured in dozens and an array of outside vendors. The duty scales with the complexity of the operation.

5.3(b) - Direct supervisory duty

A lawyer with direct supervisory authority over a non-lawyer assistant must make reasonable efforts to ensure that the assistant's conduct is compatible with the professional obligations of the lawyer. The duty attaches to the supervisory relationship itself - the lawyer assigning work, reviewing output, or directing the assistant's day-to-day activities holds the duty regardless of partnership status.

The reasonable-efforts standard in 5.3(b) is calibrated to the specific tasks delegated. A lawyer who delegates routine document preparation to a paralegal owes a different intensity of supervision than a lawyer who delegates client communication, fact-gathering interviews, or post-filing follow-up. The greater the consequence of the delegated task for the client's interests or for compliance with the rules, the more searching the supervision the lawyer must provide.

5.3(c) - Individual responsibility for non-lawyer conduct

Subdivision (c) imposes personal responsibility on a lawyer when a non-lawyer engages in conduct that would itself violate the Rules of Professional Conduct if engaged in by a lawyer. The responsibility attaches in two circumstances:

5.3(c)(1) - Order or ratification

The lawyer orders the conduct, or with knowledge of the specific conduct ratifies it. Ratification reaches both express approval after the fact and implicit acceptance of the conduct's results. The knowledge standard is "specific conduct," not generalized awareness; a lawyer's general knowledge that staff occasionally take certain actions does not, without more, ratify any particular action.

5.3(c)(2) - Knowledge in time to avoid or mitigate

The lawyer holds managerial authority in the firm or direct supervisory authority over the non-lawyer, learns of the conduct at a time when its consequences can be avoided or mitigated, and fails to take reasonable remedial action. This is the "knew and did nothing" branch of the rule. It requires both actual knowledge of the conduct and a temporal window in which remedial action could have made a difference. Knowledge acquired after the consequences have crystallized does not, by itself, trigger 5.3(c)(2); it may, however, trigger other duties (file-correction obligations, disclosure to affected parties, or reporting obligations under separate rules).

Ratification by silence applies to non-lawyer conduct as well as lawyer conduct. A managing partner or direct supervisor who learns of conduct by a non-lawyer assistant that would be a rule violation if engaged in by a lawyer, while there is still time to correct or mitigate the conduct, is personally responsible under 5.3(c)(2) if no remedial action is taken. The supervisor's silence operates as a discrete violation independent of the underlying conduct.

Practical implications for paralegals, legal secretaries, and contract staff

Several categories of non-lawyer conduct recur in published ethics opinions and disciplinary decisions as supervision-sensitive:

Client communication

Paralegals and legal secretaries frequently transmit communications to clients and to opposing parties. Communications attributable to the firm carry the lawyer's professional obligations. The supervising lawyer is responsible for ensuring that communications transmitted by staff (a) accurately reflect the matter's status, (b) do not include legal advice the assistant is not authorized to give, and (c) preserve confidentiality as required by Rule 1.6.

File management and document production

File assembly, scanning, indexing, and production are routinely delegated to non-lawyer staff. The supervising lawyer is responsible for ensuring that the production satisfies the lawyer's obligations under Rule 1.16(d) (surrender of papers to which the client is entitled) and that documents produced or filed do not contain information that should have been redacted under Fed. R. Bankr. P. 9037 or analogous privacy rules.

Marketing and solicitation

Communications soliciting prospective clients, posted online or transmitted directly, are governed by Rules 7.1 through 7.3 regardless of whether the communication is composed by the lawyer or by non-lawyer staff. The supervising lawyer is responsible for ensuring that staff-generated marketing complies with those rules.

Court-related interactions

Filings, calendaring, and procedural follow-up are commonly delegated. The supervising lawyer remains personally responsible under Rule 3.3 for the accuracy of representations made to a tribunal, regardless of which individual at the firm typed or filed the document.

Scope of permitted non-lawyer activity

The Rules of Professional Conduct do not themselves define the boundary between work that may be performed by non-lawyer staff and work that may not. The scope of permitted non-lawyer activity is defined by state regulation outside the Rules of Professional Conduct - principally state statutes and Supreme Court rules governing the practice of law and any regulatory regimes for legal-services providers. Readers should consult published state regulations and authoritative state-bar guidance for the operative boundaries in any given jurisdiction.

Rule 5.3 operates within whatever boundary the state has drawn. Where state law permits a non-lawyer to perform a particular task under lawyer supervision, the supervising lawyer must perform that supervision in conformity with 5.3. Where state law does not permit a non-lawyer to perform a task at all, the rule provides an additional layer of supervisory accountability if the conduct nonetheless occurs.

Common procedural posture

Paralegal-assembled production package

A paralegal assembles a file-production package in response to a client's request for the client's file under Rule 1.16(d). The supervising lawyer's 5.3(b) duty includes ensuring that the package includes the materials the rule requires and that the paralegal has not, in good faith but in error, omitted material categories. Where the lawyer reviews the package before transmission, deficiencies are identified and corrected. Where the lawyer does not review the package and learns later that material was omitted, the 5.3(c)(2) question is whether the lawyer learned in time to supplement and whether reasonable remedial action followed.

Contract document-review vendor

A firm retains a contract vendor to perform first-pass document review on a large production. The 5.3(a) duty requires the firm to maintain conflict-checking and confidentiality protocols that cover the vendor. The 5.3(b) duty requires the lawyer overseeing the engagement to provide adequate instruction on responsiveness criteria, privilege screening, and chain-of-custody protocols. Vendor conduct that would violate Rule 1.6 (confidentiality) if engaged in by a lawyer is the firm's responsibility under 5.3(c) to the extent the conditions of subdivision (c)(1) or (c)(2) are met.

Relationship to Rule 5.1

Rule 5.1 governs supervision of lawyers; Rule 5.3 governs supervision of non-lawyer assistants. The two rules are structurally parallel: both impose firm-management duties on partners and managerial authorities, supervisory duties on direct supervisors, and individual responsibility for violations committed with knowledge or under direction. In a firm with both lawyer and non-lawyer staff, a complete analysis of supervisory responsibility typically requires application of both rules in tandem. See KRPC 5.1.

Relationship to Rule 8.4(a)

Rule 8.4(a) makes it professional misconduct for a lawyer to violate the rules through the acts of another. The interaction with Rule 5.3 is direct: where a non-lawyer acts at the lawyer's direction in a way that, if performed by the lawyer, would violate a rule, the lawyer is responsible under 8.4(a) as well as under 5.3(c)(1). The two rules operate concurrently rather than as alternatives.

Continuing nature of the duty

Subdivisions (a) and (b) impose continuing duties. A staffing structure adopted at firm formation and never revisited does not satisfy 5.3(a) as the firm grows, takes on new practice areas, or adds new categories of vendor relationships. A supervisory relationship establishes a 5.3(b) duty that runs for the duration of the relationship and adjusts in intensity as the scope of delegation changes.

Related rules and authority

Rule 1.4 - Communication with the client; staff-transmitted communications are within the lawyer's responsibility

Rule 1.6 - Confidentiality; firm measures under 5.3(a) typically include staff confidentiality protocols

Rule 1.16(d) - Termination duties; file production is a high-frequency 5.3(b) supervision context

Rule 3.3 - Candor toward the tribunal; staff-prepared filings remain the supervising lawyer's responsibility

Rule 5.1 - Supervision of lawyers; structural parallel

Rule 7.1 - 7.3 - Communications about the lawyer's services; staff-generated marketing

Rule 8.4(a) - Violation through the acts of another

Practical impact

Rule 5.3 carries two recurring practical consequences:

Delegation does not delegate the rule. A lawyer who delegates a task to a non-lawyer assistant retains the professional obligations the rules attach to that task. Subdivision (a) requires firm-level measures, subdivision (b) requires individual supervision, and subdivision (c) attaches individual responsibility where the supervision fails.

Awareness without action is a discrete violation. Subdivision (c)(2) treats supervisor silence in the face of known conduct as itself violative when the supervisor learns in time to avoid or mitigate consequences. The duty to act runs independently of any duty to report under other rules.

Related authority
