KRPC 5.4 / MRPC 4-5.4

KRPC 5.4: The Professional-Independence Architecture

The compensation, ownership, and third-party-payor framework that preserves a lawyer's independent professional judgment.

Verbatim text of KRPC 5.4 (Kansas)

(a) A lawyer or law firm shall not share legal fees with a nonlawyer, except that:

(1) an agreement by a lawyer with the lawyer's firm, partner, or associate may provide for the payment of money, over a reasonable period of time after the lawyer's death, to the lawyer's estate or to one or more specified persons;

(2) a lawyer who undertakes to complete unfinished legal business of a deceased lawyer may pay to the estate of the deceased lawyer that proportion of the total compensation which fairly represents the services rendered by the deceased lawyer;

(3) a lawyer or law firm may include nonlawyer employees in a compensation or retirement plan, even though the plan is based in whole or in part on a profit-sharing arrangement; and

(4) a lawyer may share court-awarded legal fees with a nonprofit organization that employed, retained or recommended employment of the lawyer in the matter.

(b) A lawyer shall not form a partnership with a nonlawyer if any of the activities of the partnership consist of the practice of law.

(c) A lawyer shall not permit a person who recommends, employs, or pays the lawyer to render legal services for another to direct or regulate the lawyer's professional judgment in rendering such legal services.

(d) A lawyer shall not practice with or in the form of a professional corporation or association authorized to practice law for a profit, if:

(1) a nonlawyer owns any interest therein, except that a fiduciary representative of the estate of a lawyer may hold the stock or interest of the lawyer for a reasonable time during administration;

(2) a nonlawyer is a corporate director or officer thereof; or

(3) a nonlawyer has the right to direct or control the professional judgment of a lawyer. Kan. Sup. Ct. R. 226, KRPC 5.4.

Missouri Rule 4-5.4

Missouri Rule 4-5.4 is substantively identical to KRPC 5.4 and tracks ABA Model Rule 5.4. Both jurisdictions adopt the architecture in four operative subdivisions: (a) the fee architecture, (b) the partnership-form architecture, (c) the third-party-payor architecture, and (d) the practice-entity ownership architecture.

The professional-independence architecture 5.4 establishes

Rule 5.4 exists to protect three client-facing interests that ride together: the client's interest in confidential communication, the client's interest in undivided loyalty, and the client's interest in legal advice driven by professional judgment rather than by the financial interest of a non-client. Each subdivision is a structural support beam for that protective architecture.

The Comment to the Model Rule articulates the design purpose directly: the provisions express traditional limitations on sharing fees and on practice forms, and these limitations are to protect the lawyer's professional independence of judgment. Subdivision (a) handles the compensation surface. Subdivision (b) handles the entity-formation surface where a lawyer and a nonlawyer might enter business together. Subdivision (c) handles the bill-paying surface where someone other than the client funds the representation. Subdivision (d) handles the ongoing-entity surface where ownership, governance, or control of a law-practice entity is at issue. Each surface, treated structurally, removes a different vector through which a nonlawyer could acquire leverage over a lawyer's advice.

Permitted nonlawyer-employee compensation structures under 5.4(a)

The compensation architecture under 5.4(a) is fully compatible with the realities of a modern law-firm payroll. Nonlawyer employees - paralegals, legal assistants, investigators, IT staff, office administrators, marketing professionals, billing clerks - are routinely and properly compensated out of the firm's legal-fee revenue. The rule's structure preserves this in several specific ways:

Salary and wages funded from law-firm earnings. The Comment confirms that the rule does not prohibit payment of salary or wages to nonlawyer employees out of legal-fee revenue. The firm's revenue funds the firm's payroll in the ordinary course; the rule's "fee-sharing" concept reaches dispositional arrangements that confer a share of a particular legal fee, not the routine payment of employee compensation.

Estate-of-deceased-lawyer payments under 5.4(a)(1). A firm may agree, in advance, that money will be paid over a reasonable period after a lawyer's death to the deceased lawyer's estate or to specified beneficiaries. This permits practical succession planning and orderly transition arrangements.

Completion-of-unfinished-business payments under 5.4(a)(2). When a successor lawyer completes unfinished matters of a deceased lawyer, the successor may pay to the deceased lawyer's estate the proportion of total compensation fairly representing the services the deceased lawyer rendered. The architecture preserves the orderly winding-down of pending matters.

Nonlawyer profit-sharing and retirement plans under 5.4(a)(3). Nonlawyer employees may participate in compensation or retirement plans even when those plans are based in whole or in part on a profit-sharing arrangement. The rule explicitly authorizes nonlawyer participation in the firm's economic upside through plan structures.

These four categories together describe a wide compensation envelope. The architecture's structural concern is not the existence of payments to nonlawyers from legal-fee revenue, but rather the existence of arrangements that would give a nonlawyer a financial stake in a particular matter such that the nonlawyer's interest could influence professional judgment.

Permitted fee-sharing exceptions under 5.4(a)

Beyond the employment-compensation envelope, subdivision (a) preserves specific fee-sharing carve-outs that serve identifiable policy interests:

5.4(a)(4) - Court-awarded fees shared with a nonprofit. A lawyer may share court-awarded legal fees with a nonprofit organization that employed, retained, or recommended employment of the lawyer in the matter. The carve-out preserves the funding model that supports public-interest representation: a nonprofit referrer or employer may receive a share of statutory or court-awarded fees, enabling sustainable provision of representation in fee-shifting matters.

Estate succession (a)(1). Already described above; categorically permitted by the rule architecture.

Completion of a deceased lawyer's matters (a)(2). Already described above; the architecture preserves continuity of representation.

Retirement and profit-sharing plans for nonlawyer employees (a)(3). Already described above; the architecture preserves competitive employee-benefit structures.

The drafting choice to enumerate exceptions rather than to articulate a general "no influence" standard produces predictability: a firm administrator structuring a retirement plan, an executor of a deceased lawyer's estate, or a public-interest organization negotiating a fee-recoupment arrangement can read the rule and identify exactly which structure is preserved.

The practice-entity ownership framework under 5.4(b) and 5.4(d)

Subdivisions (b) and (d) together establish the entity-ownership architecture that maintains lawyer control over law-practice entities in jurisdictions that have adopted the Model Rule structure:

5.4(b) - Partnership architecture. A lawyer does not form a partnership with a nonlawyer if any of the activities of the partnership consist of the practice of law. The architecture preserves the practice-of-law partnership as a lawyer-only structure in jurisdictions that follow the Model Rule.

5.4(d)(1) - Ownership interest architecture. A lawyer does not practice with or in the form of a for-profit professional corporation or association authorized to practice law if a nonlawyer owns any interest in it, with the limited exception that a fiduciary representative of a deceased lawyer's estate may hold the deceased lawyer's stock or interest for a reasonable time during administration.

5.4(d)(2) - Governance architecture. A nonlawyer may not be a corporate director or officer of the practice entity. The architecture extends beyond ownership to governance: even if a nonlawyer holds no equity interest, the nonlawyer may not occupy a director or officer seat in the entity.

5.4(d)(3) - Control architecture. A nonlawyer may not have the right to direct or control the professional judgment of a lawyer. This is the doctrinal anchor of the whole subdivision: every other element exists to keep this control architecture intact.

The cumulative design is that, in jurisdictions following the Model Rule structure, the practice-of-law entity is owned, governed, and directionally controlled by lawyers. Revenue-extraction by non-client outside investors is held out of the form, which preserves the lawyer's professional judgment as the operative input to client advice.

The director/officer/employee structure 5.4(d) permits and protects

Subdivision (d) is sometimes described as a closed-form restriction; it is more accurate to describe it as an architecture that preserves a specific functional layering. The architecture permits and actively protects:

Lawyer professional corporations. The professional-corporation form (PA, PC, LLC, PLLC, depending on jurisdiction) is the standard form for law practice and is fully compatible with 5.4(d). All owners are lawyers; all directors and officers are lawyers; the entity holds malpractice insurance, owns the lease, employs the staff, and contracts in the entity's name.

Nonlawyer professional staff in operational roles. The entity employs a wide range of nonlawyer professionals - chief operating officers, chief financial officers, chief technology officers, chief marketing officers, paralegals, legal nurse consultants, investigators, IT staff. None of these roles requires director or officer status; all of these roles can be staffed at high seniority and high compensation without any tension with 5.4(d).

Lawyer-managed multi-disciplinary teams. A litigation team can be a lawyer-led group that includes paralegals, investigators, e-discovery technologists, jury consultants, forensic accountants, and trial-prep specialists. The architecture preserves a lawyer at the apex of professional-judgment decisions while permitting deeply integrated multi-disciplinary teams underneath.

Counsel relationships across organizations. A lawyer may be employed by a nonprofit, a corporation, a government agency, or any other organization. The 5.4(d) ownership architecture limits the form of the law-practice entity itself; it does not limit the universe of organizations that may employ a lawyer in a counsel role.

How alternative-business-structures (ABS) jurisdictions handle the same architecture differently

Several jurisdictions have adopted variations on the Model Rule architecture that permit alternative business structures - law-practice entities in which nonlawyer participation, ownership, or governance is permitted under regulated frameworks. The comparative landscape is descriptive, not normative:

Arizona. Effective 2021, the Arizona Supreme Court eliminated its analogue to 5.4 and created the Alternative Business Structure framework, permitting nonlawyer ownership of law firms subject to a state-administered licensure regime. The framework requires an ABS to be approved and supervised by the state; nonlawyer participation is gated through regulatory licensure rather than through professional-conduct prohibition.

Utah. Beginning 2020, Utah established a regulatory sandbox under the Office of Legal Services Innovation. Sandbox participants may include entities with nonlawyer ownership or that combine legal and nonlegal services, again subject to a state-administered approval and supervision regime.

England and Wales. The Legal Services Act 2007 established the Alternative Business Structure framework administered through the Solicitors Regulation Authority and other approved regulators. Nonlawyer ownership has been permitted in licensed bodies for more than a decade.

The comparative point is not which architecture is preferable but rather that the underlying professional-independence goal is portable across multiple regulatory designs. In ABS jurisdictions, the independence-protection function is shifted from a single rule of professional conduct to a layered regulatory regime that includes entity-level licensure, supervision, and prohibitions against directing a lawyer's professional judgment in any particular matter. Kansas and Missouri have, to date, retained the Model Rule architecture in 5.4; understanding the comparative landscape clarifies that the operative concern is independence of professional judgment, however that protection is structurally implemented.

The 5.4(c) third-party-payor architecture

Subdivision (c) addresses a common and entirely legitimate arrangement: a person or entity other than the client pays the lawyer to render services for the client. Third-party-payor arrangements arise across the practice landscape - insurance defense, employer-paid representation, parent-paid representation for an adult child, organization-paid representation for a member or employee, trust-paid representation for a beneficiary, and many others.

The architecture under 5.4(c) preserves these arrangements while protecting the lawyer's professional judgment. The lawyer does not permit the payor to direct or regulate the lawyer's professional judgment in rendering services to the client. The structural features that 5.4(c) protects:

The client is the client. Even where a third party pays, the lawyer's representation runs to the client, not to the payor. Professional duties of loyalty, communication, and confidentiality run to the client.

Independent judgment over strategic decisions. Decisions about case strategy, settlement evaluation, motion practice, and witness selection rest on the lawyer's professional judgment exercised on behalf of the client, not on the payor's preferences about cost or outcome.

Settlement authority rests with the client. Settlement decisions are reserved to the client under Rule 1.2(a). The payor's interest in resolving the matter at a particular cost cannot be permitted to override the client's settlement authority.

Confidentiality is preserved. Communications between the lawyer and the client remain confidential under Rule 1.6. The payor's interest in monitoring the representation cannot be permitted to compromise the client-lawyer confidential relationship.

The architecture interlocks with Rule 1.8(f), which conditions third-party payment on client informed consent, no interference with the lawyer-client relationship, and protection of confidential information. Read together, 5.4(c) and 1.8(f) create a complete framework: 1.8(f) governs the entry into the arrangement, and 5.4(c) governs its ongoing operation.

Cross-references that work with 5.4

Rule 5.4 sits in a network of related rules that together implement the professional-independence design:

Rule 1.7 - Conflicts of interest. A third-party-payor arrangement can create a 1.7 material-limitation conflict if there is a significant risk that the lawyer's representation will be limited by responsibilities to the payor; conflict analysis under 1.7 runs in parallel with the 5.4(c) independence analysis.

Rule 1.8(f) - Third-party payment. Conditions the entry into any third-party-payor arrangement: client gives informed consent, there is no interference with the lawyer's independence of professional judgment or with the client-lawyer relationship, and confidential information is protected as required by Rule 1.6.

Rule 1.16 - Declining or terminating representation. When an arrangement that initially satisfies 5.4(c) and 1.8(f) breaks down - for instance, when the payor attempts to direct the representation in a manner inconsistent with the client's interests - the lawyer's options include withdrawal under 1.16 and, in some cases, mandatory withdrawal if continued representation would result in a rule violation.

Rule 1.6 - Confidentiality. Information relating to the representation remains confidential regardless of who pays the bill; 5.4(c) prevents the payor from acquiring control over confidential information by paying for the representation.

Rule 5.1 and Rule 5.3 - Supervision. Firm-management measures under 5.1 typically include protocols for identifying and documenting third-party-payor arrangements at intake; nonlawyer-supervision measures under 5.3 typically include protocols ensuring that nonlawyer staff understand the architecture of the client-lawyer relationship even where a payor is involved.

Rule 2.1 - Advisor role. The lawyer exercises independent professional judgment and renders candid advice; 5.4 protects the structural conditions under which this is possible.

Related authority

Kansas Rules of Professional Conduct - Kansas Supreme Court Rules

ABA Model Rule 1.8(f) - third-party payment provision

## KRPC 5.5 / MRPC 4-5.5 - Jurisdictional Scope of Law Practice [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/krpc-5-5/

Open Bankruptcy Project

Rule of Professional Conduct
KRPC 5.5 / MRPC 4-5.5

KRPC 5.5 / MRPC 4-5.5: Jurisdictional Scope of Law Practice

Where a lawyer may practice and under what conditions, including temporary-practice safe harbors and federal and in-house exceptions.

Verbatim text of KRPC 5.5 (Kansas)

(a) A lawyer shall not practice law in a jurisdiction in violation of the regulation of the legal profession in that jurisdiction, or assist another in doing so.

(b) A lawyer who is not admitted to practice in this jurisdiction shall not:

(1) except as authorized by these Rules or other law, establish an office or other systematic and continuous presence in this jurisdiction for the practice of law; or

(2) hold out to the public or otherwise represent that the lawyer is admitted to practice law in this jurisdiction.

(c) A lawyer admitted in another United States jurisdiction, and not disbarred or suspended from practice in any jurisdiction, may provide legal services on a temporary basis in this jurisdiction that:

(1) are undertaken in association with a lawyer who is admitted to practice in this jurisdiction and who actively participates in the matter;

(2) are in or reasonably related to a pending or potential proceeding before a tribunal in this or another jurisdiction, if the lawyer, or a person the lawyer is assisting, is authorized by law or order to appear in such proceeding or reasonably expects to be so authorized;

(3) are in or reasonably related to a pending or potential arbitration, mediation, or other alternative dispute resolution proceeding in this or another jurisdiction, if the services arise out of or are reasonably related to the lawyer's practice in a jurisdiction in which the lawyer is admitted to practice and are not services for which the forum requires pro hac vice admission; or

(4) are not within paragraphs (c)(2) or (c)(3) and arise out of or are reasonably related to the lawyer's practice in a jurisdiction in which the lawyer is admitted to practice.

(d) A lawyer admitted in another United States jurisdiction, and not disbarred or suspended from practice in any jurisdiction, may provide legal services in this jurisdiction that:

(1) are provided to the lawyer's employer or its organizational affiliates and are not services for which the forum requires pro hac vice admission; or

(2) are services that the lawyer is authorized to provide by federal law or other law of this jurisdiction. Kan. Sup. Ct. R. 226, KRPC 5.5.

Missouri Rule 4-5.5

Missouri Rule 4-5.5 is substantively identical to KRPC 5.5 and tracks ABA Model Rule 5.5. The rule frames where a lawyer may practice (within jurisdictions of admission), the conditions under which a lawyer may engage in temporary practice in jurisdictions other than those of admission (the four safe harbors of subdivision (c)), and two structural exceptions for in-house and federal-law work (subdivision (d)).

5.5(a) - Jurisdictional anchor

Subdivision (a) establishes the baseline principle: a lawyer must conform to the regulation of the legal profession in any jurisdiction in which the lawyer practices, and must not assist another in conduct that would violate that jurisdiction's regulation. The rule directs the reader outward to the regulatory authority of each jurisdiction - the admissions regime, the licensure rules, and any related regulatory provisions of that jurisdiction's Supreme Court or equivalent regulatory body define what activity falls inside or outside the regulated profession. Rule 5.5(a) imports those external definitions and makes conformity with them a professional-conduct obligation.

5.5(b) - Systematic presence and holding out

Subdivision (b) addresses two specific situations for lawyers not admitted in the jurisdiction:

5.5(b)(1) - A lawyer not admitted in the jurisdiction may not, except as authorized by the rules or other law, establish an office or other systematic and continuous presence in the jurisdiction for the practice of law. The key qualifiers are "systematic" and "continuous." Episodic activity that fits within a 5.5(c) safe harbor does not establish a systematic presence; opening an office, listing the jurisdiction in firm marketing as a place of practice, or holding regular intake meetings in the jurisdiction generally does.

5.5(b)(2) - A lawyer not admitted in the jurisdiction may not hold out to the public or otherwise represent that the lawyer is admitted there. The duty extends to firm websites, letterhead, marketing materials, social-media profiles, and oral representations. Where a lawyer is admitted in one jurisdiction and licensed only there, materials that imply broader admission misstate the lawyer's authority to practice in the additional jurisdictions named.

5.5(c) - Temporary-practice safe harbors

Subdivision (c) is the rule's affirmative permission provision. It permits a lawyer admitted in another United States jurisdiction (and not disbarred or suspended anywhere) to provide legal services on a temporary basis in the host jurisdiction in four enumerated categories.

5.5(c)(1) - Association with locally admitted counsel

Services undertaken in association with a lawyer admitted in the host jurisdiction who actively participates in the matter. "Actively participates" requires substantive involvement, not nominal sponsorship. Co-counsel arrangements in which the locally admitted lawyer engages with the substance of the matter satisfy the standard; arrangements in which the local lawyer's role is limited to lending a name to a filing generally do not.

5.5(c)(2) - Pending or potential tribunal proceedings

Services in or reasonably related to a pending or potential proceeding before a tribunal in the host jurisdiction or another jurisdiction, where the lawyer or the person the lawyer is assisting is authorized by law or order to appear, or reasonably expects to be so authorized. This safe harbor includes the activity surrounding pro hac vice admission - investigation, fact-gathering, witness interviews, and motion preparation undertaken in reasonable expectation of admission.

5.5(c)(3) - Pending or potential ADR proceedings

Services in or reasonably related to a pending or potential arbitration, mediation, or other alternative-dispute-resolution proceeding, where the services arise out of or are reasonably related to the lawyer's practice in a jurisdiction in which the lawyer is admitted, and the forum does not require pro hac vice admission. The "arise out of or are reasonably related to" standard ties the host-jurisdiction work to the lawyer's home-jurisdiction practice.

5.5(c)(4) - General reasonable-relation safe harbor

Services that do not fall within (c)(2) or (c)(3) but that arise out of or are reasonably related to the lawyer's practice in a jurisdiction of admission. This is the broadest of the four safe harbors and the principal vehicle for transactional and counseling work that crosses jurisdictional lines. The "reasonably related" test is generally satisfied where the host-jurisdiction work is an extension of an established client relationship, involves the law of the lawyer's home jurisdiction, or involves a body of federal law in which the lawyer routinely practices.

"Temporary" is qualitative, not durational. The Comment to Model Rule 5.5 emphasizes that "temporary" is not defined by a numerical limit on days or matters; services that are recurring or extended may still be temporary if they do not amount to a systematic or continuous presence under 5.5(b)(1). The factors include the duration of the engagement, the number of matters in the host jurisdiction, the existence of an office or persistent advertising in the host jurisdiction, and whether the lawyer's host-jurisdiction work is incidental to or central to the lawyer's overall practice.

5.5(d) - In-house and federal-law exceptions

Subdivision (d) authorizes two ongoing (not temporary) categories of practice by a lawyer admitted in another United States jurisdiction:

5.5(d)(1) - In-house counsel

Services provided to the lawyer's employer or its organizational affiliates, where the forum does not require pro hac vice admission. This permits a lawyer admitted in one state to serve as in-house counsel in another state, providing advice to the employer and its affiliates. The exception does not permit the in-house lawyer to provide services to third parties or to appear in proceedings for which the forum requires admission or pro hac vice authorization.

5.5(d)(2) - Federal law and other authorizing law

Services the lawyer is authorized to provide by federal law or by other law of the host jurisdiction. The federal-law branch covers practice before federal agencies and courts under federal admission regimes - federal trademark and patent practice, immigration practice before agencies that authorize practitioners by federal credential, practice before federal courts that maintain their own admission rolls (subject to those courts' admission requirements), and similar federally authorized work. The state-law branch covers any host-jurisdiction statute or rule that affirmatively authorizes practice by lawyers admitted elsewhere - for example, a host-jurisdiction rule permitting limited-scope appearances by out-of-state lawyers in specific matter categories.

Cross-border counsel relationships

Several configurations recur in cross-border legal services and shape the application of Rule 5.5:

Federal-court practice in the lawyer's state of physical residence

A lawyer admitted in State A who maintains an office in State B and whose practice is principally before federal courts in State B operates within a combination of 5.5(b), 5.5(c)(4), and 5.5(d)(2). Federal-court practice is governed by the admission rules of the relevant federal court. The state Rule 5.5 inquiry centers on whether the lawyer's office and practice in State B include legal services governed by State B's body of state law and, if so, whether those services fit within a safe harbor or another authorization.

Co-counsel on a matter pending in the host jurisdiction

A lawyer admitted in State A serves as co-counsel on a matter pending in a State B court alongside a lawyer admitted in State B. The 5.5(c)(1) safe harbor applies if the State B lawyer actively participates. If the State A lawyer also seeks to appear in court, the lawyer obtains pro hac vice admission under State B's rules; pre-admission activity falls within 5.5(c)(2) as work in reasonable expectation of authorization.

The "regulation of the legal profession" reference

Subdivision (a) imports each jurisdiction's external regulatory framework. The scope of activity that the regulatory framework reserves to admitted lawyers, the contours of any exceptions for legal-services entities or limited-license practitioners, and the categories of cross-jurisdiction practice the framework authorizes are matters of state regulation outside the Rules of Professional Conduct. Readers should consult published state regulations and authoritative state-bar guidance for the operative framework in any given jurisdiction.

Rule 5.5 operates within whatever framework the state has adopted. Where a state's framework grants a particular category of authority to practice, the rule recognizes that authority. Where the framework does not, the rule provides a professional-conduct anchor for conformity to the framework's boundaries.

Continuing nature of the inquiry

The conditions of 5.5(c) and 5.5(d) are not satisfied once and then disregarded; they must continue to be satisfied throughout the period of host-jurisdiction work. A safe-harbor engagement that begins as a single matter and grows into a recurring practice may at some point cross from temporary into systematic and continuous under 5.5(b)(1). The Comment to Model Rule 5.5 notes that the inquiry should be revisited as the scope of host-jurisdiction work evolves.

Related rules and authority

Rule 7.1 - Communications about the lawyer's services; representations of admission and practice scope

Rule 7.5 - Firm names and letterheads; how multi-jurisdiction firms identify the jurisdictions of admission of their lawyers

Rule 8.5 - Disciplinary authority and choice of law in cross-border matters

Rule 5.1 - Supervisory responsibility, including over lawyers operating in multiple jurisdictions

Rule 5.3 - Supervisory responsibility regarding non-lawyer assistants whose work may be performed across jurisdictions

Practical impact

Rule 5.5 is the principal anchor for cross-jurisdiction legal services. Several themes recur:

The rule is structurally permissive. Subdivisions (c) and (d) define the conditions under which cross-jurisdiction work is affirmatively authorized. Lawyers and firms operating across jurisdictions should structure engagements to fit within one of the safe harbors or exceptions.

Marketing and online presence implicate 5.5(b)(2). Firm websites, attorney bios, and social-media profiles that list jurisdictions of practice are subject to the holding-out limitation. Listings should accurately reflect each lawyer's jurisdictions of admission, and any cross-jurisdiction practice listed should be tied to the relevant safe harbor or exception.

Active participation matters under 5.5(c)(1). Where the safe harbor depends on association with locally admitted counsel, the active-participation requirement looks to substance. Co-counsel arrangements that involve nominal sponsorship without engagement do not satisfy the rule's terms.

## KRPC 5.6: The Client-Choice + Lawyer-Mobility Architecture [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/krpc-5-6/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Rule of Professional Conduct
KRPC 5.6 / MRPC 4-5.6

KRPC 5.6: The Client-Choice + Lawyer-Mobility Architecture

The rule architecture that preserves a client's right to choose counsel and a lawyer's right to move, with a retirement-arrangement safe harbor and a settlement-restriction limit.

Verbatim text of KRPC 5.6 (Kansas)

A lawyer shall not participate in offering or making:

(a) a partnership, shareholders, operating, employment, or other similar type of agreement that restricts the right of a lawyer to practice after termination of the relationship, except an agreement concerning benefits upon retirement; or

(b) an agreement in which a restriction on the lawyer's right to practice is part of the settlement of a client controversy. Kan. Sup. Ct. R. 226, KRPC 5.6.

Missouri Rule 4-5.6

Missouri Rule 4-5.6 is substantively identical to KRPC 5.6 and tracks ABA Model Rule 5.6. The rule operates as a two-part architectural commitment: subdivision (a) preserves lawyer mobility against firm-side restraints, and subdivision (b) preserves future client access against litigation-side restraints. A defined retirement-arrangement carve-out lives inside subdivision (a).

1. The client-autonomy architecture 5.6 establishes

Rule 5.6 is most usefully read as a client-protective rule that happens to operate through restrictions on lawyer-to-lawyer and lawyer-to-litigant agreements. The protected interest is not the lawyer's freedom of contract; it is the client's freedom to choose counsel of the client's preference. The Comment to Model Rule 5.6 makes the linkage explicit: an agreement restricting the right of a lawyer to practice "not only limits their professional autonomy but also limits the freedom of clients to choose a lawyer."

The architecture works in three interlocking pieces. First, by forbidding agreements that restrict a lawyer's practice after departing a firm, subdivision (a) ensures that when a firm reorganizes, a partner retires, or an associate moves, the client base of that firm or that lawyer remains free to follow whichever lawyer they choose. Second, by forbidding settlement provisions that restrict a lawyer's future practice, subdivision (b) ensures that the litigation system cannot be used to purchase the elimination of effective counsel from a future field of representation. Third, by defining a single specific safe harbor for retirement-benefit arrangements, the rule signals that the architectural commitment to mobility is the default and any departure from it must fit a defined exception.

The downstream effect is that the rule preserves a competitive market for legal services in which the binding choice of counsel sits with the client. The client-choice priority is the through-line that connects subdivision (a) and subdivision (b); both subdivisions are addressed to lawyers, but both are designed to keep an option open for someone who is not a party to the agreement at all - the client, or the future client, who will need counsel later.

2. The retirement-arrangement safe harbor under 5.6(a)

Subdivision (a) contains a single defined exception: "an agreement concerning benefits upon retirement." A partnership agreement, shareholders agreement, operating agreement, or employment agreement may condition the payment of retirement benefits on the retired lawyer's agreement not to compete for some period or in some geographic area. The carve-out exists because retirement-benefit funding requires predictability: a firm that is funding retirement obligations from ongoing revenue has a legitimate interest in not having those obligations matched by an immediate departure of clients with the retiring lawyer.

The safe harbor is bounded in important ways:

The restriction must be tied to retirement benefits, not to all forms of departure. A "retirement" provision that operates whenever a lawyer leaves the firm, regardless of age, length of service, or actual retirement from practice, is not within the carve-out. Courts and bar opinions have consistently treated the question as one of substance over label.

The restriction must be reasonable in scope. Although the rule does not on its face impose a reasonableness limit, the Comment and a substantial body of state authority treat duration and geographic scope as relevant to whether the agreement is genuinely "concerning benefits upon retirement" or is functioning as a general non-compete.

The carve-out does not authorize restrictions on representation of specific clients. A retirement agreement that bars the retiring lawyer from representing identified former clients of the firm runs into the client-choice principle that animates the rule even within the safe harbor.

The architecturally significant feature of the carve-out is that it exists at all. By creating one defined exception, the rule signals that the prohibition is not absolute but also is not balanceable against generalized firm-interest arguments. Firms that want to restrict departing-lawyer practice for reasons other than retirement-benefit funding must do so without participating in any agreement of the kind 5.6(a) forbids.

3. The settlement-restriction limit under 5.6(b)

Subdivision (b) addresses a different problem with the same client-choice rationale. In some litigation contexts, particularly mass-tort and high-stakes commercial disputes, a defendant may have a strong interest in preventing plaintiffs' counsel from representing future plaintiffs against the same defendant. Subdivision (b) forecloses any settlement that incorporates such a restriction.

The rule operates against the lawyer on both sides of the table. A defendant's lawyer who "offers" such a settlement violates the rule; a plaintiff's lawyer who "makes" such an agreement violates the rule. The mutual application is structural - the rule is not protecting either side's lawyer from the other, it is protecting people not in the room, namely the future clients who will need counsel knowledgeable about the defendant's conduct.

The Comment to Model Rule 5.6 explains the rationale: "Paragraph (b) prohibits a lawyer from agreeing not to represent other persons in connection with settling a claim on behalf of a client. This provision involves an unacceptable bargain: the public interest in lawyers who are available to represent clients is sold for the private interest of the litigants in the settlement."

State bar opinions interpreting analogues to 5.6(b) have consistently reached the same outcomes on a recurring set of fact patterns:

An agreement that the settling plaintiffs' lawyer will not represent any other person against the same defendant is prohibited.

An agreement that the settling plaintiffs' lawyer will return or destroy litigation work product, when the practical effect would be to prevent representation of future clients, is treated as a 5.6(b) restriction.

An agreement that the settling lawyer will refer future inquiries to the defendant or to specific counsel is treated as a 5.6(b) restriction when its effect is to deflect representation.

An agreement that the settling lawyer will be hired by the defendant as a consultant in a manner that creates conflicts foreclosing future representation is treated as a 5.6(b) workaround.

The pattern of bar opinions reflects the architectural commitment: the rule prohibits the substance, not the form, of restrictions on future representation arrived at through settlement.

4. Other permitted arrangements that work within 5.6's architecture

The architecture leaves room for several categories of agreement that do not impair the protected mobility:

Limited-time covenants protecting trade secrets and proprietary information

A departing lawyer's obligations with respect to firm trade secrets, client lists treated as confidential business information, and proprietary firm processes are governed by state trade-secret and contract law and are not displaced by Rule 5.6. The line between a trade-secret protection and a practice restriction is fact-specific; agreements that operate functionally as practice restrictions but are labeled as trade-secret protections receive substance-over-form treatment.

Non-solicitation and notice provisions

Provisions requiring a departing lawyer to give notice to the firm before departure, to participate in an orderly transition, or to refrain from soliciting firm employees are generally treated as outside the 5.6 prohibition because they do not restrict the lawyer's practice. Provisions that restrict client solicitation come closer to the 5.6 line and are evaluated by their practical effect on client choice.

Of-counsel and contract arrangements

Of-counsel relationships, contract-lawyer engagements, and similar non-partnership arrangements may include reasonable provisions about the relationship's termination without running into 5.6 if those provisions do not restrict the lawyer's right to practice after termination.

Comparative jurisdictional treatments

State enforcement of 5.6 varies in detail. Some jurisdictions have read the retirement carve-out narrowly; others have permitted reasonable financial disincentives (forfeiture of certain benefits) on departing lawyers while drawing the line at outright practice restrictions. The architectural commitment is uniform across jurisdictions following the Model Rule; the marginal cases differ.

5. The interaction between 5.6 and partnership/employment law generally

Rule 5.6 establishes the floor of the architecture, not the ceiling. State contract law, state non-compete statutes, and federal employment law all overlay the rule. The relationship works in several directions:

State non-compete enforceability is downstream of 5.6 in legal-services contexts. Even in jurisdictions that broadly enforce non-competes in commercial settings, lawyer non-competes that would otherwise be enforceable as a matter of contract law are unenforceable to the extent they conflict with 5.6.

Federal employment law does not generally displace 5.6. The rule is an ethics-discipline rule and applies to the lawyer's conduct in offering or making the agreement, independent of whether the agreement is otherwise lawful as an employment contract.

State variation operates at the margins. States differ in their treatment of forfeiture-for-competition provisions, in their definition of "retirement," and in their approach to settlement-related practice restrictions. The architectural commitment to client choice and lawyer mobility is uniform; the boundary cases are not.

The rule is a discipline rule, not just a contract-validity rule. A lawyer who participates in offering or making a prohibited agreement can be subject to discipline even if the agreement itself is unenforceable as a matter of contract law and even if no client is in fact deprived of preferred counsel.

The architecture preserves the floor in a way that does not preempt legitimate firm-economic interests, employer interests, or settlement structures - it forecloses only those structures that would conflict with the client-choice and lawyer-mobility commitments.

6. Cross-references that work with 5.6

Rule 1.7 - Concurrent conflicts

The interaction with Rule 1.7 is structural. When a lawyer moves between firms, the conflict analysis under 1.7 (and the imputation analysis under 1.10) determines whether the lawyer can represent particular clients at the new firm. Rule 5.6 ensures that those conflict analyses are conducted in real disputes about real clients, not foreclosed in advance by a contractual restriction on practice.

Rule 1.10 - Imputation

Rule 1.10 governs how conflicts move with lawyers between firms. The interaction with 5.6 is that 1.10 supplies the substantive doctrine for evaluating any post-move conflict, while 5.6 ensures that the move itself is not contractually foreclosed. Together, the two rules create a system in which lawyers can move and clients can choose, with conflicts addressed case by case.

Rule 5.4 - Professional independence

Rule 5.4 protects professional independence from non-lawyer ownership and control. Rule 5.6 protects professional independence from contractual restraints on practice. The two rules together define a substantive commitment that the lawyer's professional judgment, and the client's choice of lawyer, are not subject to outside structural constraints.

Rule 1.16 - Termination

When a lawyer-client relationship terminates, Rule 1.16 governs the lawyer's duties on withdrawal. Rule 5.6 ensures that the lawyer's future ability to practice is not contractually restricted in a way that would limit the client's downstream choice of counsel. The two rules together address the front end (termination duties) and the back end (future-practice freedom) of the same departure event.

Practical impact

Rule 5.6 is one of the small set of ethics rules whose primary effect is to keep options open for non-parties. Three recurring features deserve emphasis:

The protected interest is the client's, not the lawyer's. Lawyer mobility is the mechanism; client choice is the goal. Reading the rule as a lawyer-protective rule misses the architecture.

The retirement-benefits carve-out is narrow and defined. It is not a general balancing test; it is a single exception for one defined kind of arrangement, and substance-over-form review governs whether any given agreement fits it.

Substance, not form, governs settlement-restriction analysis. Provisions that operate as future-practice restrictions are treated as 5.6(b) violations regardless of how they are labeled - work-product return, consulting arrangements, referral obligations, and similar mechanisms have all been treated as 5.6(b) workarounds when their effect is to restrict representation of future clients.

Kansas Rules of Professional Conduct - Kansas Supreme Court Rules

Missouri Rules of Professional Conduct - Missouri Supreme Court Rule 4

## KRPC 6.1 / MRPC 4-6.1 - Voluntary Pro Bono Public Service [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/krpc-6-1/

Open Bankruptcy Project

Rule of Professional Conduct
KRPC 6.1 / MRPC 4-6.1

KRPC 6.1 / MRPC 4-6.1: Voluntary Pro Bono Public Service

The aspirational fifty-hour goal, the affirmative menu of qualifying service, and the financial-contribution alternative.

Verbatim text of KRPC 6.1 (Kansas)

A lawyer should render public interest legal service. A lawyer may discharge this responsibility by providing professional services at no fee or a reduced fee to persons of limited means or to public service or charitable groups or organizations, by service in activities for improving the law, the legal system or the legal profession, and by financial support for organizations that provide legal services to persons of limited means. Kan. Sup. Ct. R. 226, KRPC 6.1.

Missouri Rule 4-6.1

Missouri Rule 4-6.1 articulates the same aspirational expectation in language closely tracking ABA Model Rule 6.1. The Model Rule sets an explicit numerical aspiration of at least fifty hours of pro bono public service per year, and both Kansas and Missouri have adopted the substance of that framework through the rule, its comments, and accompanying bar guidance.

What 6.1 affirmatively does

Rule 6.1 is the only rule of professional conduct that articulates an affirmative public-service expectation as a feature of the lawyer's role rather than as a constraint on conduct. The architecture has four components:

It identifies voluntary pro bono service as a professional responsibility of every lawyer, regardless of practice setting, seniority, or specialty.

It supplies an aspirational numerical target (fifty hours per year under the Model Rule formulation) so that the expectation is concrete rather than abstract.

It enumerates a menu of qualifying activities broad enough that lawyers in every practice setting can identify a fit.

It recognizes a financial-contribution alternative for lawyers whose practice circumstances make direct service impracticable.

The fifty-hour aspiration

The Model Rule formulation, on which the Kansas and Missouri rules draw, expresses the aspiration as at least fifty hours of pro bono public service per year. The fifty-hour figure is a target, not a mandate; failure to reach it is not a basis for discipline. The point of the numerical target is to translate a general expectation into a planning unit a lawyer can build into an annual schedule.

The fifty-hour figure scales to roughly one hour per week of working time, an interval most full-time practitioners can accommodate without restructuring their practice. The Model Rule comment notes that lawyers who cannot meet the target in a given year because of unusual practice demands are expected to make up the shortfall in subsequent years, sustaining the expectation as a multi-year average rather than a strict annual count.

The qualifying-activity menu

Rule 6.1 enumerates several categories of service that qualify, designed so that every lawyer can identify activities compatible with the lawyer's existing practice. The categories sort into three groups:

Direct legal services to persons of limited means

The principal category contemplates legal representation of persons of limited means at no fee or at a substantially reduced fee. Persons of limited means include individuals whose household income is at or below a level qualifying for legal aid in their jurisdiction, and individuals whose income, though above the legal-aid eligibility threshold, makes retention of paid counsel for the matter at hand impracticable. Representation through a legal aid organization, a court-annexed clinic, a bar association referral panel, or a direct lawyer-client relationship all qualify; the rule does not require any particular institutional channel.

Services to public-service organizations and charitable groups

Service to charitable, religious, civic, community, governmental, and educational organizations qualifies when the matter is in furtherance of the organization's mission and the organization either could not afford counsel or where payment would significantly deplete the organization's resources. Examples include forming a nonprofit corporation for a community service organization, advising a religious congregation on a real-estate transaction, drafting bylaws for a neighborhood association, providing employment-law guidance to a small charity, and similar matters where the beneficiary is the organization's public-service mission rather than a fee-paying client.

Activities for improving the law, the legal system, or the legal profession

A third category covers law-reform work, bar-association activity, judicial-system service, continuing legal education delivery to other lawyers, and similar activities whose beneficiary is the legal system rather than an individual client. Serving on a bar committee evaluating rule changes, drafting a model statute for a state agency, teaching a CLE course at no fee, and writing a treatise chapter or rule-related article all qualify.

Structure of the financial-contribution alternative

Rule 6.1 explicitly recognizes that financial support of organizations that deliver legal services to persons of limited means is a permitted means of discharging the public-service responsibility. The financial-contribution alternative is structurally important for several reasons:

It permits lawyers in highly specialized practices (where individual representation would not produce useful pro bono leverage) to support the same outcome through funding.

It permits lawyers whose calendars are temporarily compressed to maintain participation without reducing the quality of service delivered to clients.

It recognizes that legal-aid organizations and similar service providers depend on a funding base distinct from direct lawyer hours, and that funding is itself a service the bar provides to the public.

The Model Rule comment treats the financial-contribution alternative as fully compatible with the spirit of the rule when the lawyer's contribution is meaningful relative to the lawyer's resources. The dollar amount associated with the alternative is sometimes expressed as the equivalent of the lawyer's billing rate multiplied by the fifty-hour target, though no formal conversion is required.

Reduced-fee services framework

Rule 6.1 contemplates not only no-fee service but also substantially reduced-fee service, and the comment indicates that representation at a fee substantially below the lawyer's customary rate can satisfy the rule when the reduction is set with reference to the client's ability to pay rather than the matter's complexity. This is structurally important in three ways:

It permits a lawyer to undertake a moderately complex matter for a client of limited means at a fee the client can afford, without converting the matter into a fully pro bono engagement.

It permits a lawyer to develop a sliding-fee practice in which a portion of matters are billed at customary rates and a portion are billed at sub-customary rates calibrated to client circumstances.

It signals that the public-service responsibility extends to fee design as well as fee waiver, and that a lawyer who structures fees to make representation accessible is acting within the rule's purpose.

Two practice-setting patterns

Solo and small-firm practice

For solo and small-firm lawyers, the fifty-hour target is often most efficiently met through direct representation in matters substantively related to the lawyer's paying practice. A consumer-bankruptcy practitioner who handles two no-fee Chapter 7 filings per year contributes roughly the equivalent of the target in efficient, high-quality service. The substantive overlap between paid and pro bono work produces high marginal hourly value because the lawyer's existing infrastructure (forms, software, support staff, court familiarity) carries the pro bono matter at low incremental cost.

Large-firm and specialized practice

For lawyers in highly specialized practices with limited overlap to the matters typically handled through legal-aid channels, the target is often met through a combination of direct service in specialized clinics (transactional pro bono, immigration, veterans benefits, expungement) and financial contribution to legal-services organizations. Many large firms maintain pro bono coordinators whose role is to surface matters that match the firm's practice mix, so that lawyers can fulfill the responsibility through work substantively related to their daily practice.

Voluntary character and aspirational status

Rule 6.1 is aspirational, not mandatory. The rule's recurring verbs are "should" rather than "shall." A lawyer who does not meet the fifty-hour target in a given year is not subject to discipline under the rule. The rule's force comes from its articulation of a professional norm and from the bar's collective expectation that members participate in public service as a feature of the profession's role.

Several jurisdictions have considered (and a small number have adopted) mandatory pro bono requirements, but the Kansas and Missouri rules retain the aspirational character of the Model Rule. The aspirational character has two practical consequences. First, the rule operates through professional culture and bar-association programming rather than through disciplinary enforcement. Second, the rule's reach is broader than a mandatory rule could be: because no penalty attaches to falling short, the rule can ask for more (fifty hours per year is a substantial commitment) without provoking the political resistance a mandate would generate.

Reporting frameworks

Many states have adopted voluntary or mandatory annual pro bono reporting, in which lawyers indicate at registration or renewal whether they performed pro bono service in the prior year and the approximate hours. Reporting frameworks do not convert the substantive rule into a mandate but provide aggregate visibility to the bench, the bar, and the public on the profession's overall participation rate. Kansas and Missouri lawyers should consult current bar guidance for the reporting practice in effect in each state.

Relationship to organized programs

The rule contemplates that pro bono service will commonly be delivered through organized programs, and other rules of professional conduct accommodate that delivery mode. Rule 6.5 relaxes conflict-checking standards for short-term limited legal services delivered through nonprofit or court-annexed programs, removing the principal practical barrier to clinic, hotline, and pro bono day participation. Rule 6.2 articulates the limited circumstances in which a lawyer may decline a court-appointed representation, framing court-appointed service as a presumptive obligation rather than an opt-in.

Related rules and authority

Rule 6.2 - Accepting appointments

Rule 6.3 - Membership in legal services organizations

Rule 6.5 - Nonprofit and court-annexed limited legal services programs

Rule 1.2(c) - Limited scope of representation

Rule 1.5 - Fees; the reduced-fee framework

Practical impact

Rule 6.1 functions as the constitutional charter of the profession's public-service role. Two recurring observations:

The aspiration is workable. Fifty hours per year is roughly one hour per week, and the qualifying-activity menu is broad enough that lawyers in every practice setting can identify a fit. The most common reason for shortfall is not the volume of the target but the absence of planning; lawyers who treat the target as a calendar item generally meet it.

The financial-contribution alternative is genuine. Where direct service is impracticable, contribution to a legal-services organization advances the same end the rule serves and is recognized by the rule as a coordinate means of compliance.

Related authority

ABA Model Rule 6.1 - model rule with comment

Kansas Rules of Professional Conduct - Kansas Supreme Court Rules

Missouri Rules of Professional Conduct - Missouri Supreme Court Rule 4

KRPC 1.4 (Communication)
KRPC 1.5 (Fees)

Specific questions about pro bono service planning or program participation should be evaluated by qualified counsel or by the lawyer's state bar pro bono coordinator. Last modified 2026-05-22.

## KRPC 6.2 / MRPC 4-6.2 - Accepting Appointments [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/krpc-6-2/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Rule of Professional Conduct
KRPC 6.2 / MRPC 4-6.2

KRPC 6.2 / MRPC 4-6.2: Accepting Appointments

The professional baseline of accepting tribunal appointments and the three categories of good cause that authorize a lawyer to seek to avoid an appointment.

Verbatim text of KRPC 6.2 (Kansas)

A lawyer shall not seek to avoid appointment by a tribunal to represent a person except for good cause, such as:

(a) representing the client is likely to result in violation of the Rules of Professional Conduct or other law;

(b) representing the client is likely to result in an unreasonable financial burden on the lawyer; or

(c) the client or the cause is so repugnant to the lawyer as to be likely to impair the client-lawyer relationship or the lawyer's ability to represent the client. Kan. Sup. Ct. R. 226, KRPC 6.2.

Missouri Rule 4-6.2

Missouri Rule 4-6.2 is substantively parallel to KRPC 6.2 and tracks ABA Model Rule 6.2. The rule frames the professional baseline of acceptance of tribunal appointments and identifies the categories of good cause that authorize a lawyer to seek to avoid a particular appointment.

The structural premise

The Comment to Model Rule 6.2 frames the underlying premise: legal representation is the principal mechanism through which the rights and interests of persons before tribunals are protected, and the responsibility to provide that representation is shared across the lawyers of the bar. Tribunal-appointment systems - whether under federal indigent-defense statutes, state public-defender systems, court-appointed-counsel rosters in civil matters, or court-appointed guardian-ad-litem arrangements - operate by distributing appointments among the lawyers eligible to receive them. The rule operates as the professional-conduct anchor for that distributive system.

The rule's affirmative orientation is that acceptance of appointment is the baseline professional posture. Lawyers in good standing whose practice profile makes them eligible for appointment under the operative appointment regime accept appointments as a routine incident of practice. The rule then identifies the categories of good cause that authorize departure from the baseline.

The "good cause" framework

The rule is structured as a baseline plus enumerated categories. The baseline directs that a lawyer shall not seek to avoid an appointment "except for good cause." The enumerated categories that follow - subdivisions (a), (b), and (c) - are introduced by "such as," indicating that they are illustrative rather than exhaustive. Each enumerated category, however, articulates a distinct ground recognized by the rule itself; other grounds may qualify as good cause where they are analogous in character and weight.

6.2(a) - Rule or law violation

The first enumerated ground for good cause is that the representation is likely to result in a violation of the Rules of Professional Conduct or other law. The category is the broadest of the three and encompasses several recurring fact patterns:

Conflict of interest under Rules 1.7 or 1.9. Where the appointment would place the lawyer in a position that violates the current-client or former-client conflict rules, the lawyer's representation would be precluded by those rules, and good cause is established for purposes of 6.2(a).

Lack of competence under Rule 1.1. Where the matter requires expertise the lawyer does not possess and cannot reasonably acquire within the time frame of the representation, accepting the appointment would risk a Rule 1.1 violation. The Comment to Model Rule 6.2 notes that mere unfamiliarity with the subject matter does not establish good cause if the lawyer can become competent within reasonable time and effort; the category is reserved for situations in which competence cannot be achieved.

Jurisdictional limitations under Rule 5.5. Where the appointment would require practice in a jurisdiction in which the lawyer is not authorized to practice and no safe harbor applies, good cause is established.

Other-law constraints. Where another body of law (federal court admission rules, state-licensure requirements for particular matter categories, specialized-practice authorization regimes) precludes the lawyer's participation, that external constraint qualifies under 6.2(a).

6.2(b) - Unreasonable financial burden

The second enumerated ground for good cause is that the representation is likely to result in an unreasonable financial burden on the lawyer. The category recognizes that appointed representation is often compensated below market rates - or, in some appointment regimes, on a pro bono or modest-honorarium basis - and that there is a point at which the financial impact of a particular appointment exceeds the baseline burden the lawyer accepts as part of the shared appointment system.

The standard is "unreasonable," not merely "burdensome." The Comment to Model Rule 6.2 frames the inquiry by reference to the magnitude of the financial impact on the lawyer's practice (a single substantial matter at compensation well below the lawyer's typical engagement may qualify; a routine appointment at standard appointment-roster compensation typically does not), the lawyer's overall appointment load (a lawyer who has recently completed several appointments may have a stronger case than a lawyer who has received few), and the resources of the lawyer or firm relative to the demands of the matter (a sole practitioner's response to a complex appointment differs from a large firm's).

6.2(c) - Impairing repugnance

The third enumerated ground for good cause is that the client or the cause is so repugnant to the lawyer as to be likely to impair the client-lawyer relationship or the lawyer's ability to represent the client. The category recognizes that effective representation depends on the lawyer's ability to advocate competently for the client's interests and that there is a threshold of personal disagreement beyond which that ability is materially impaired.

The standard incorporates two important qualifiers:

"So repugnant." The repugnance must be substantial. Ordinary distaste for a particular cause or client does not establish good cause; the rule contemplates a strong reaction that rises above the lawyer's normal range of acceptable representations.

"Likely to impair." The repugnance must be likely to impair the relationship or the representation. The inquiry is forward-looking and tied to the probable effect on the representation, not to the lawyer's preferences as such.

The Comment to Model Rule 6.2 emphasizes that representation of an unpopular client or cause is generally not by itself good cause under (c). The professional ethos the rule articulates is that lawyers regularly represent persons and causes that draw public criticism, and that doing so is part of the function the bar performs. Subdivision (c) is reserved for the narrower category in which the lawyer's personal reaction to the client or cause is so strong as to actually impair the representation.

The three categories are illustrative. The rule's "such as" phrasing recognizes that good cause may also be established by grounds not specifically enumerated. The illustrations provide guidance on the character and weight required; analogous grounds (e.g., severe illness, a non-conflict personal relationship to a witness or party of a kind that materially affects the lawyer's capacity) may qualify under the same standard.

The character of the appointment regime

The procedural framework through which appointments are made and through which a lawyer raises good cause is defined by the operative appointment regime rather than by Rule 6.2. Federal criminal appointments under the Criminal Justice Act, state public-defender systems, court-appointed counsel under bankruptcy provisions, court-appointed guardian-ad-litem regimes, and civil-appointment systems each have their own procedures for assignment, conflict-checking, and motion practice on appointment-avoidance grounds. Rule 6.2 provides the professional-conduct anchor for the lawyer's compliance with the operative regime's procedures.

Common procedural contexts

Conflict-based motion to be relieved

A lawyer receives an appointment in a matter that, on conflict check, reveals a current-client conflict under Rule 1.7. The lawyer promptly notifies the appointing tribunal under the operative procedure and moves to be relieved. The 6.2(a) ground (likely rule violation) is established by the conflict, and the tribunal's procedure provides the channel for substitution. The lawyer's professional-conduct posture under 6.2 is satisfied by raising the ground through the appropriate procedure rather than by declining the appointment unilaterally.

Capacity-based application for relief

A lawyer carrying a heavy appointment load receives a further appointment that, by virtue of its complexity and the lawyer's existing commitments, would constitute an unreasonable financial burden under 6.2(b). The lawyer applies to the appointing authority for relief on that ground, providing documentation of current load and the new matter's projected demands. The appointing authority evaluates the application under the operative regime's standards.

Relationship to the broader pro bono and access framework

Rule 6.2 sits within a larger framework that encourages voluntary pro bono service (addressed by Rule 6.1) and that authorizes a range of structured limited-services activities (addressed by Rules 6.3 and 6.5). The rule operates at the intersection of those voluntary frameworks and the formal appointment system: where appointment occurs through a tribunal under an operative appointment regime, Rule 6.2 governs the lawyer's professional-conduct response. Voluntary pro bono and structured limited-services activities are governed by their own respective rules and do not implicate the appointment-avoidance question that Rule 6.2 addresses.

Related rules and authority

Rule 1.1 - Competence; the standard the lawyer must meet in any accepted representation

Rule 1.7 - Conflict of interest with current clients

Rule 1.9 - Conflict with former clients

Rule 1.16 - Declining or terminating representation; the broader framework for non-acceptance

Rule 6.1 - Voluntary pro bono publico service

Rule 6.3 - Membership in legal services organization

Rule 6.5 - Nonprofit and court-annexed limited legal services programs

Practical impact

Rule 6.2 carries several recurring practical consequences:

Acceptance is the baseline. Lawyers eligible for appointment under an operative appointment regime accept appointments as a routine incident of practice. The rule recognizes the appointment system as a function the bar shares.

Good cause runs through enumerated and analogous grounds. The three enumerated grounds - rule or law violation, unreasonable financial burden, impairing repugnance - articulate the character and weight the rule contemplates. Analogous grounds may qualify where they meet the same standard.

The procedural channel is provided by the operative appointment regime. Good cause is raised through the tribunal's procedure for appointment review. The rule's professional-conduct standard runs alongside that procedure.

Related authority

ABA Model Rule 6.2 - model rule with comment

Kansas Rules of Professional Conduct - Kansas Supreme Court Rules

Missouri Rules of Professional Conduct - Missouri Supreme Court Rule 4

## KRPC 6.3 / MRPC 4-6.3 - Membership in Legal Services Organization [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
