KRPC 6.3 / MRPC 4-6.3

KRPC 6.3 / MRPC 4-6.3: Membership in Legal Services Organization

A lawyer's authorized participation as director, officer, or member of a legal services organization that serves persons other than the lawyer's clients, subject to two protective conditions.

Verbatim text of KRPC 6.3 (Kansas)

A lawyer may serve as a director, officer or member of a legal services organization, apart from the law firm in which the lawyer practices, notwithstanding that the organization serves persons having interests adverse to a client of the lawyer. The lawyer shall not knowingly participate in a decision or action of the organization:

(a) if participating in the decision or action would be incompatible with the lawyer's obligations to a client under Rule 1.7; or

(b) where the decision or action could have a material adverse effect on the representation of a client of the organization whose interests are adverse to a client of the lawyer. Kan. Sup. Ct. R. 226, KRPC 6.3.

Missouri Rule 4-6.3

Missouri Rule 4-6.3 is substantively parallel to KRPC 6.3 and tracks ABA Model Rule 6.3. The rule operates as an affirmative authorization for lawyer participation in the governance of legal services organizations, even where those organizations serve persons whose interests are adverse to the lawyer's clients. The authorization is then qualified by two narrowly defined protective conditions.

The structural premise

The Comment to Model Rule 6.3 frames the rule's purpose: legal services organizations - civil legal aid, public-interest legal centers, indigent-defense entities, court-affiliated legal services programs, bar-sponsored access-to-justice initiatives - depend on the participation of practicing lawyers in their governance and operations. The contributions practicing lawyers bring include subject-matter expertise, bar-network connections, fundraising capacity, and the credibility that comes with active practice. Without their participation, the organizations cannot operate effectively.

At the same time, the lawyers most useful to such organizations are typically engaged in active practice, in which they represent clients whose interests will sometimes be adverse to those of the persons the organization serves. The rule resolves the tension by authorizing the participation as the default and then articulating the discrete circumstances in which the lawyer's role on the organization must be limited.

The affirmative grant

The rule's opening sentence is the affirmative grant: a lawyer may serve as director, officer, or member of a legal services organization, apart from the law firm in which the lawyer practices, notwithstanding that the organization serves persons having interests adverse to the lawyer's clients. Several features of the grant warrant attention:

"May serve." The grant is permissive. The rule does not require lawyer participation; it authorizes it.

"Director, officer, or member." The grant covers the full range of governance and membership roles - board service, executive committee positions, officer roles, advisory roles, and general organizational membership.

"Apart from the law firm." The grant addresses participation in organizations separate from the lawyer's firm. The provision distinguishes organizational governance from in-firm practice.

"Notwithstanding that the organization serves persons having interests adverse to a client of the lawyer." The grant explicitly authorizes participation even where the organization's client base includes interests adverse to the lawyer's clients. The rule recognizes that this is the norm rather than the exception in active practice.

The two protective conditions

The grant is qualified by two protective conditions that limit what the lawyer may do within the organization. The conditions are narrowly drawn and operate at the level of specific decisions or actions, not at the level of overall participation. The lawyer remains a director, officer, or member; the conditions identify the discrete decisions in which the lawyer does not participate.

6.3(a) - Compatibility with Rule 1.7 obligations

The lawyer shall not knowingly participate in a decision or action of the organization if participating would be incompatible with the lawyer's obligations to a client under Rule 1.7. The condition imports the current-client conflict framework. The compatibility inquiry asks whether the lawyer's vote, recommendation, or other contribution to the decision would place the lawyer in conflict with the duties owed to a current client.

Compatibility is evaluated decision by decision. A board member who has a Rule 1.7 conflict with respect to a particular matter the board is considering recuses from that matter; the same member may participate in other matters in which no such conflict exists. The condition operates as a discrete-decision recusal rule, not as a categorical disqualification from board service.

6.3(b) - Material adverse effect on organizational clients

The lawyer shall not knowingly participate in a decision or action that could have a material adverse effect on the representation of an organizational client whose interests are adverse to a client of the lawyer. The condition extends the protective framework to the organization's clients: even where the lawyer's participation would not violate Rule 1.7 vis-a-vis the lawyer's own client, the lawyer abstains from decisions that would materially adversely affect the organization's representation of a person whose interests are adverse to the lawyer's client.

The "could have a material adverse effect" standard is forward-looking and probabilistic. The decision need not be certain to produce the effect; the standard is whether the effect is a material adverse possibility. The "material" qualifier excludes trivial or speculative effects.

Recusal is from the decision, not from the organization. The two conditions operate as discrete-decision recusal requirements. A lawyer who recuses from particular decisions because of (a) or (b) remains an active director, officer, or member of the organization with respect to all other matters within the organization's work. The structural feature is preservation of broad participation with narrow recusal in protected categories.

The "apart from the law firm" framing

The grant authorizes participation in organizations "apart from the law firm." The framing distinguishes the lawyer's role on the legal services organization from the lawyer's practice within the firm. The organization is its own institutional entity, governed by its own board, employing its own staff, and representing its own client base. The lawyer's role within the organization is governed by the organization's bylaws and policies, with Rule 6.3 supplying the professional-conduct anchor on the lawyer-conduct side.

Several practical features follow from this framing:

The organization's representations of its own clients are governed by the organization's own conflict-checking procedures and counsel-assignment practices. Those representations do not, by virtue of the lawyer's board membership, become representations by the lawyer or the lawyer's firm.

The lawyer's board role does not, by itself, give the lawyer's firm access to confidential information about the organization's clients. The organization's confidentiality framework operates independently.

The organization may handle its own conflict-checking with respect to board members by procedures that exclude board members from particular matter assignments or that segregate matter information from board-level decisions.

Common organizational structures

Civil legal aid board service

A lawyer in private practice serves on the board of a civil legal aid organization that provides representation to low-income individuals in landlord-tenant, consumer, family, and bankruptcy matters. The lawyer's firm represents landlords, consumer lenders, and creditors in some of these categories. Rule 6.3 authorizes the board service. The lawyer recuses from board decisions that bear directly on a particular matter in which the organization is opposing the lawyer's firm (e.g., a strategic decision about a categorical litigation campaign that would affect a pending firm matter), and otherwise participates fully in the organization's governance.

Pro bono coordinating organization

A lawyer serves as an officer of a bar-sponsored pro bono coordinating organization that places matters with volunteer lawyers across multiple practice areas. The lawyer's organizational role - recruiting volunteers, setting program priorities, fundraising - is broadly authorized by Rule 6.3 and rarely implicates either (a) or (b). The organization's individual-matter decisions are made by program staff and the volunteer lawyers who accept placements, not by the officer-lawyer.

Recordkeeping at the organization level

While Rule 6.3 itself does not impose recordkeeping requirements, organizations with active board members in private practice commonly maintain procedures that document compliance with the rule's protective conditions:

Conflict-disclosure forms that board members complete at intake and update periodically

Pre-meeting conflict-checking against the organization's matter docket

Recusal records noting which board members abstained from which decisions, with the recusal ground identified

Information-barrier procedures separating board-level discussion from matter-level case information when warranted

These procedures support both the individual lawyer's compliance with Rule 6.3 and the organization's institutional governance.

Relationship to other rules

Rule 1.7 - Conflict of interest with current clients; imported by 6.3(a)

Rule 1.6 - Confidentiality; relevant where organizational information might bear on a firm matter or vice versa

Rule 1.10 - Imputed disqualification; relevant in evaluating whether the lawyer's organizational role affects the firm's conflict analysis

Rule 6.5 - Nonprofit and court-annexed limited legal services programs; the related framework for the lawyer's direct service through such programs

Continuing nature of the inquiry

The compatibility analysis under 6.3(a) and the material-adverse-effect analysis under 6.3(b) are not one-time inquiries. They are conducted with respect to each decision the organization addresses in which the lawyer's participation is contemplated. A lawyer with a continuing board role re-evaluates each board agenda for items implicating the conditions and recuses as appropriate.

Practical impact

Rule 6.3 carries several recurring practical consequences:

Participation is the affirmative default. The rule's grant is permissive and broad. Lawyers in private practice may participate fully in the governance of legal services organizations even where their firm's client base produces some overlap with the organization's client base.

Recusal is matter-specific. The two protective conditions operate at the decision level, not at the membership level. A lawyer with a 6.3(a) or 6.3(b) issue on a particular matter recuses from that matter and continues in the role generally.

The organization and the lawyer's firm remain institutionally separate. The "apart from the law firm" framing preserves the organization's institutional independence. The organization handles its own representations through its own conflict-checking and counsel-assignment procedures.

Related authority

ABA Model Rule 6.3 - model rule with comment

Kansas Rules of Professional Conduct - Kansas Supreme Court Rules

Missouri Rules of Professional Conduct - Missouri Supreme Court Rule 4

KRPC 1.9 (Former Clients)
KRPC 6.2 (Appointments)
KRPC 6.5 (Limited Services Programs)

## KRPC 6.5 / MRPC 4-6.5 - Nonprofit and Court-Annexed Limited Legal Services Programs [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/krpc-6-5/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Rule of Professional Conduct
KRPC 6.5 / MRPC 4-6.5

KRPC 6.5 / MRPC 4-6.5: Nonprofit and Court-Annexed Limited Legal Services Programs

An affirmative framework for short-term limited legal services delivered through nonprofit and court-annexed programs, with modified conflict-of-interest rules tailored to the practice.

Verbatim text of KRPC 6.5 (Kansas)

(a) A lawyer who, under the auspices of a program sponsored by a nonprofit organization or court, provides short-term limited legal services to a client without expectation by either the lawyer or the client that the lawyer will provide continuing representation in the matter:

(1) is subject to Rules 1.7 and 1.9(a) only if the lawyer knows that the representation of the client involves a conflict of interest; and

(2) is subject to Rule 1.10 only if the lawyer knows that another lawyer associated with the lawyer in a law firm is disqualified by Rule 1.7 or 1.9(a) with respect to the matter.

(b) Except as provided in paragraph (a)(2), Rule 1.10 is inapplicable to a representation governed by this Rule. Kan. Sup. Ct. R. 226, KRPC 6.5.

Missouri Rule 4-6.5

Missouri Rule 4-6.5 is substantively parallel to KRPC 6.5 and tracks ABA Model Rule 6.5. The rule provides an affirmative framework that authorizes short-term limited legal services through nonprofit and court-annexed programs and modifies the conflict-of-interest rules to make that practice feasible.

The structural premise

The Comment to Model Rule 6.5 frames the rule's purpose: legal-services programs that provide short-term assistance - drop-in advice clinics, courthouse self-help kiosks, telephone-hotline programs, bar-sponsored brief-advice events - meet a substantial access-to-justice need. Persons facing legal problems often benefit substantially from a brief consultation with a lawyer even where ongoing representation is neither contemplated nor feasible. Without a tailored framework, however, the conflict-of-interest rules designed for full representation would make this category of practice impractical: a volunteer lawyer at a drop-in clinic cannot run a full firm-wide conflict check against each client who walks through the door for a fifteen-minute consultation.

Rule 6.5 resolves the impracticality by establishing a tailored conflict-of-interest framework for this discrete practice category. Within the framework's conditions, lawyers may provide short-term limited legal services without the full conflict-check apparatus that ordinary representation requires.

The framework's threshold conditions

The rule's modified conflict framework applies to representations that satisfy three threshold conditions. Where any condition is not met, the ordinary conflict-of-interest rules apply.

Auspices of a nonprofit or court program

The services must be provided "under the auspices of a program sponsored by a nonprofit organization or court." The auspices requirement ensures that the lawyer is operating within an institutional framework with its own intake, screening, and follow-up processes. The institutional framework is what allows the modified conflict regime to function: the program, rather than the individual volunteer lawyer, holds the structural responsibility for matter management and post-encounter handoff. Eligible auspices include bar-sponsored pro bono clinics, court-affiliated self-help centers, civil legal aid drop-in programs, and analogous structured initiatives.

Short-term and limited

The services must be "short-term limited legal services." The Comment to Model Rule 6.5 frames this as a single discrete encounter - typically a single meeting or telephone consultation - rather than continuing representation. The duration is qualitative rather than measured by a numerical limit. Services that are properly understood as brief advice or limited assistance fall within the framework; services that develop into ongoing representation move outside the framework and into the ordinary conflict regime.

No expectation of continuing representation

Neither the lawyer nor the client expects the lawyer to provide continuing representation in the matter. The mutual-expectation condition operates as the structural distinction between a Rule 6.5 encounter and ordinary representation. The lawyer's role is bounded at the outset to the short-term limited service. Where the client's matter requires continuing work, the program's protocols typically include referral mechanisms - to a staff lawyer, to a private-bar referral service, or to another resource - and the volunteer lawyer's role concludes at the referral.

The modified conflict regime

Within the threshold conditions, Rule 6.5 modifies the application of the ordinary conflict-of-interest rules in three respects.

6.5(a)(1) - Knowledge-based application of Rules 1.7 and 1.9(a)

Rules 1.7 (current-client conflict) and 1.9(a) (former-client conflict) apply only where the lawyer knows that the representation involves a conflict of interest. The ordinary "should know" standard is replaced by an actual-knowledge standard. The Comment to Model Rule 6.5 frames the modification as a recognition that the time-compressed nature of short-term services does not permit comprehensive conflict screening. A volunteer lawyer who proceeds in good faith without conducting a firm-wide conflict check is within the rule even if a comprehensive check would have revealed an issue, provided the lawyer does not in fact know of a conflict.

6.5(a)(2) - Knowledge-based imputation

Rule 1.10 (imputed disqualification) applies only where the volunteer lawyer knows that another lawyer in the firm is disqualified under Rule 1.7 or 1.9(a) with respect to the matter. The ordinary firm-wide imputation regime - in which a conflict held by any firm lawyer disqualifies all firm lawyers - is replaced by an actual-knowledge standard. The volunteer lawyer is not charged with constructive knowledge of every firm-wide conflict; the volunteer lawyer is subject to imputation only where the volunteer lawyer actually knows of the colleague's disqualification.

6.5(b) - Inapplicability of Rule 1.10 outside the knowledge channel

Except as provided in (a)(2), Rule 1.10 is inapplicable to a representation governed by Rule 6.5. The provision insulates the volunteer lawyer's firm from broader imputation effects flowing from the short-term encounter. The matter the volunteer lawyer handles does not, by virtue of the brief consultation, become a firm-wide matter subject to ordinary imputation in subsequent firm work.

The framework rests on the auspices of the program. The modified conflict regime is available because the program supplies the institutional structure - intake, screening, follow-up, and referral - that would otherwise have to be supplied by full firm-conflict procedures. The framework operates within structured programs; it is not a free-standing modification of the conflict rules for any short-term encounter.

Common program structures

Courthouse self-help clinic

A court-annexed self-help center hosts a weekly drop-in clinic at which volunteer lawyers provide brief advice to self-represented litigants on civil matters. Each consultation is bounded - typically twenty to thirty minutes - with no continuing-representation expectation. The clinic's intake form documents the matter category and confirms the limited-services framing. Volunteer lawyers provide advice within the Rule 6.5 framework, with referrals provided by the clinic for matters requiring ongoing representation.

Nonprofit bankruptcy brief-advice program

A nonprofit organization sponsors a periodic brief-advice program at which volunteer lawyers meet with prospective debtors for a one-time consultation on bankruptcy options. The program supplies intake forms, eligibility screening, and referral protocols for clients who proceed to file. The volunteer lawyer's role concludes at the end of the consultation; the conflict modifications of Rule 6.5 apply to the encounter, and ongoing representation, if any, is handled separately through the lawyer's regular engagement procedures.

The interaction with ongoing representation

A consultation that begins within the Rule 6.5 framework may, at the lawyer's and client's mutual election, transition into ongoing representation. The transition moves the matter outside the Rule 6.5 framework and into the ordinary engagement framework, with the full conflict-of-interest rules applying from the point of transition forward. The Rule 6.5 modifications do not carry over into the ongoing representation; that representation is structured and governed like any other.

The transition is typically marked by a separate engagement document, completion of the firm's ordinary conflict-checking process, and formal acceptance of the matter under the firm's intake procedures. Until the transition occurs, the encounter remains within the Rule 6.5 framework.

The role of program intake and referral processes

Program intake and referral processes are structural complements to Rule 6.5. The program's processes typically address:

Confirmation of the limited-services framing with the client at intake

Brief categorical screening for obvious conflicts that the program can identify from intake information

Information barriers between the volunteer lawyer's encounter and other program activities

Referral protocols for clients whose matters require continuing representation

Documentation of the encounter sufficient to permit a follow-up referral lawyer to step in without re-creating intake

These processes do not appear in the text of Rule 6.5, but they are the institutional infrastructure that supports the rule's operation.

Relationship to other rules

Rule 1.7 - Conflict with current clients; applies only with actual knowledge under 6.5(a)(1)

Rule 1.9 - Conflict with former clients; subdivision (a) applies only with actual knowledge under 6.5(a)(1)

Rule 1.10 - Imputed disqualification; modified under 6.5(a)(2) and largely inapplicable under 6.5(b)

Rule 1.2(c) - Limited-scope representation; the underlying authorization for limited services to which Rule 6.5 adds the conflict-rule modifications

Rule 6.1 - Voluntary pro bono publico service; the broader pro bono framework

Rule 6.3 - Membership in legal services organization; the governance-side framework

Continuing nature of the framework's threshold conditions

The three threshold conditions are continuously evaluated through the encounter. A consultation that begins within the framework but that develops into something materially different - because the lawyer agrees to continuing representation, because the program's auspices end mid-encounter, or because the limited-services framing is otherwise abandoned - moves outside the framework when the precipitating change occurs. The lawyer's evaluation of the framework's applicability is anchored to the encounter as actually conducted, not to its initial design.

Practical impact

Rule 6.5 carries several recurring practical consequences:

The rule is an affirmative authorization. The modified conflict regime makes structured short-term services feasible at scale. The rule's design is to enable rather than to restrict.

Knowledge is the operative standard. Under 6.5(a)(1) and 6.5(a)(2), the ordinary conflict-screening obligations are replaced by an actual-knowledge standard. Volunteer lawyers acting in good faith without comprehensive firm-wide checking are within the rule provided they do not in fact know of a conflict.

The framework depends on program structure. The auspices requirement is structural. Lawyers providing services outside a sponsoring program operate under the ordinary conflict rules; the modified regime is available only within structured programs.

Related authority

ABA Model Rule 6.5 - model rule with comment

Kansas Rules of Professional Conduct - Kansas Supreme Court Rules

Missouri Rules of Professional Conduct - Missouri Supreme Court Rule 4

KRPC 1.9 (Former Clients)
KRPC 6.2 (Appointments)
KRPC 6.3 (Legal Services Org)

## KRPC 7.1 / MRPC 4-7.1 - Communications Concerning a Lawyer's Services [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/krpc-7-1/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Rule of Professional Conduct
KRPC 7.1 / MRPC 4-7.1

KRPC 7.1 / MRPC 4-7.1: Communications Concerning a Lawyer's Services

The architecture of permitted communications: truthful content, non-misleading framing, and the conditions for informative messaging.

Verbatim text of KRPC 7.1 (Kansas)

A lawyer shall not make a false or misleading communication about the lawyer or the lawyer's services. A communication is false or misleading if it contains a material misrepresentation of fact or law, or omits a fact necessary to make the statement considered as a whole not materially misleading. Kan. Sup. Ct. R. 226, KRPC 7.1.

Missouri Rule 4-7.1

Missouri Rule 4-7.1 articulates the same standard with elaborating sub-parts addressing comparison claims, results, and specialty designations. Both rules track ABA Model Rule 7.1, the foundational rule of the 7-series and the only rule in the series that applies to all communications concerning lawyer services, regardless of medium or audience.

What 7.1 affirmatively permits

Rule 7.1 is the constitutional charter of lawyer communications. It begins from the premise that lawyers may communicate about their services and structures that communication around a single standard: the communication must be truthful and must not be misleading. Within that standard, the rule permits a wide range of informative content:

Identification of the lawyer and firm, including name, address, telephone, email, and website

Description of areas of practice, including the matters typically handled and the types of clients typically served

Bar admissions and academic credentials, including law school, graduation date, and jurisdictions of admission

Professional honors and memberships, including bar leadership roles and bona fide professional recognitions

Languages spoken by the lawyer or by staff who routinely interact with clients

Fee structure, including hourly rates, flat fees for defined matters, contingent-fee terms, and consultation policies

Office hours, locations, and accessibility information for clients with disabilities, language preferences, or scheduling constraints

Each of these categories is informative content the rule treats as presumptively permitted, subject to the single overarching standard of truthful, non-misleading framing.

Structure of the permitted communication standard

The 7.1 standard operates in two pieces:

Truthful as to facts and law

The communication must not contain a material misrepresentation of fact or law. A misrepresentation is "material" if it bears on the recipient's decision-making process about whether to engage the lawyer or how to evaluate the lawyer's services. Errors of detail that do not bear on a reasonable recipient's decision are not material. A statement that the firm was founded in 1985 when the actual founding year was 1984 is unlikely to be material; a statement that the firm has handled "thousands of cases" when the actual number is in the dozens is material because the order-of-magnitude misstatement bears directly on the recipient's evaluation of experience.

Non-misleading as to the whole

The communication must not omit a fact necessary to make the statement considered as a whole not materially misleading. The omission branch is structurally distinct from the affirmative-misrepresentation branch: a communication can be technically accurate sentence-by-sentence but misleading as a whole because of what it leaves out. The standard asks whether a reasonable recipient, considering the communication as it appears in the medium and context where it is delivered, would form a misleading impression.

The "considered as a whole" standard means context and emphasis matter. A footnote disclaimer set in small type at the bottom of an advertisement may not cure a misleading headline; the test is whether the reasonable recipient, reading the communication the way it is actually delivered, takes away an accurate impression.

Conditions for results-related communications

Statements about case results (verdicts, settlements, recoveries, win rates) are permitted under Rule 7.1 when the statement is truthful and accompanied by such context as is necessary to avoid creating an unjustified expectation. The Comment to Model Rule 7.1 identifies the kinds of context the rule contemplates:

That results depend on the facts of each case

That the result described was achieved in a matter with facts particular to that matter

That the result described is not a guarantee or prediction of results in other matters

A truthful statement of a past result, accompanied by clear and conspicuous context of the kind described, is a permitted communication. The same statement without context can be misleading if it leaves the reasonable recipient with an unjustified expectation about likely outcomes in the recipient's own matter.

Conditions for comparison communications

Statements comparing the lawyer's services with the services of other lawyers are permitted when the comparison can be factually substantiated. The standard does not bar comparison; it requires that comparison claims rest on objective, verifiable facts rather than on subjective superlatives.

Verifiable comparisons: A statement that the lawyer has tried more cases of a particular type in a particular court than any other lawyer in the past five years is permitted if the count can be substantiated through court records.

Substantiated rankings: A statement that the lawyer is listed in a bona fide independent ranking publication (one that uses transparent methodology and is not pay-to-play) is permitted if accurately characterized.

Subjective superlatives: Claims such as "the best lawyer in town" or "the most experienced bankruptcy practitioner in the state" without verifiable substantiation are not permitted because they are inherently unverifiable comparative assertions.

Conditions for testimonial and endorsement content

Client testimonials and third-party endorsements are permitted under Rule 7.1 when handled within the truthful, non-misleading framework. The structural conditions are:

The testimonial accurately represents the client's actual experience

The testimonial does not create an unjustified expectation as to results in other matters

Compensation to the speaker, if any, is disclosed

The testimonial does not contain content that would itself violate Rule 7.1 if stated by the lawyer (e.g., misleading comparison or results-based claims)

The Comment to Model Rule 7.1 specifically notes that the rule does not categorically prohibit testimonials but requires the same truthful, non-misleading standard applicable to all 7.1 communications. Many jurisdictions also require an explicit context statement accompanying testimonials about case results, paralleling the results-related context requirement.

Specialty and certification designations

Rule 7.1 (and parallel provisions in Rule 7.4 in some jurisdictions) governs statements about specialization. The framework is:

Practice-area descriptions are permitted: A lawyer may state that the lawyer's practice is "limited to" or "concentrated in" a particular field. This is not a specialty certification; it is a description of the lawyer's practice scope.

Certification by an accredited organization is permitted: A lawyer who is certified as a specialist by an organization accredited by the state bar (or by the ABA in some jurisdictions) may state the certification, identifying the certifying organization.

"Specialist" as a bare claim is generally not permitted: A lawyer who is not certified may not call themselves a "specialist" in a field without context, because the term carries an implication of formal credentialing not supported by the bare claim.

Two pattern situations

Practice-area webpage

A firm webpage describing the firm's consumer bankruptcy practice is a paradigmatic 7.1 communication. The page may identify the lawyers, list bar admissions and academic credentials, describe the types of bankruptcy matters handled, identify the courts in which the firm appears, describe the firm's typical fee structure, and provide contact information. Each item is informative content within the rule. The page must not omit material facts (for example, if the firm only handles Chapter 7 and not Chapter 13, the description should not imply broader scope). Past results, if included, require the contextual statements described above.

Directory profile

A lawyer profile in an online directory (state bar lawyer-finder, commercial legal directory, etc.) is a 7.1 communication and is governed by the same standard. The profile may state areas of practice, year admitted, languages, fee policy, and similar information. If the directory's structure invites the lawyer to claim a rating, badge, or "top" designation, the lawyer should ensure that the underlying claim is verifiable and that any context statements required by the directory's terms are accurately presented.

Continuing-accuracy obligation

Communications under 7.1 carry a continuing-accuracy expectation. A statement that was accurate when made may become inaccurate over time as the lawyer's practice changes, bar memberships lapse, certifications expire, or fee policies change. A lawyer who maintains a website, directory profile, or other persistent communication is expected to keep the content current; the persistence of a once-true but now-inaccurate statement can itself become misleading under the rule's "considered as a whole" standard.

Related rules and authority

Rule 7.2 - Advertising; the medium-specific elaboration of 7.1

Rule 7.3 - Direct contact with prospective clients

Rule 7.4 - Communication of fields of practice and specialization

Rule 7.5 - Firm names and letterheads (in jurisdictions retaining a separate rule)

Rule 8.4(c) - Conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation (the general rule of which 7.1 is the communication-specific corollary)

Practical impact

Rule 7.1 is the umbrella rule under which all lawyer communications operate. Two recurring observations:

The standard is broad and the latitude is wide. Within the truthful, non-misleading framework, lawyers may communicate a great deal of informative content about their services, qualifications, fee structures, and availability. The rule does not bar informative communication; it conditions it.

Omissions matter as much as affirmative misstatements. The "considered as a whole" standard reaches communications that are technically accurate but leave a misleading impression. A lawyer designing a communication should consider not only whether each sentence is true but whether the overall takeaway corresponds to reality.

## KRPC 7.2 / MRPC 4-7.2 - Advertising [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project

Rule of Professional Conduct
KRPC 7.2 / MRPC 4-7.2

KRPC 7.2 / MRPC 4-7.2: Advertising

The architecture of permitted advertising media, the structured exceptions for payment connected to recommendations, and the name-and-address attribution requirement.

Verbatim text of KRPC 7.2 (Kansas)

(a) Subject to the requirements of Rules 7.1 and 7.3, a lawyer may advertise services through written, recorded or electronic communication, including public media.

(b) A lawyer shall not give anything of value to a person for recommending the lawyer's services except that a lawyer may

(1) pay the reasonable costs of advertisements or communications permitted by this Rule;

(2) pay the usual charges of a legal service plan or a not-for-profit or qualified lawyer referral service;

(3) pay for a law practice in accordance with Rule 1.17; and

(4) refer clients to another lawyer or a nonlawyer professional pursuant to an agreement not otherwise prohibited under these Rules that provides for the other person to refer clients or customers to the lawyer, if (i) the reciprocal referral agreement is not exclusive, and (ii) the client is informed of the existence and nature of the agreement.

(c) Any communication made pursuant to this Rule shall include the name and office address of at least one lawyer or law firm responsible for its content. Kan. Sup. Ct. R. 226, KRPC 7.2.

Missouri Rule 4-7.2

Missouri Rule 4-7.2 follows the same structure, with detailed elaboration in subdivisions addressing specific media and disclosure requirements. Both rules track ABA Model Rule 7.2. The 2018 Model Rule revisions reorganized parts of the former 7.2 framework; jurisdictional adoptions vary in detail. Practitioners should consult the current Kansas and Missouri text and any state bar guidance for current-form requirements.

What 7.2 enables

Rule 7.2 is the affirmative authorization for lawyer advertising. Read with Rule 7.1, it establishes that lawyers may advertise their services across any medium of communication, subject to the truthful, non-misleading standard of 7.1 and the direct-contact constraints of 7.3. The rule's architecture has three pillars:

Subdivision (a) authorizes advertising through written, recorded, or electronic communication, including public media. The medium-neutral phrasing is deliberate; the rule does not bar any particular advertising medium.

Subdivision (b) states the general restriction on payment to third parties for recommending lawyer services, then enumerates the exceptions that structure how such payment may permissibly occur.

Subdivision (c) imposes the attribution requirement: every 7.2 communication must include the name and office address of at least one lawyer or law firm responsible for its content.

Structure of the permitted advertising media

The medium-neutral authorization in 7.2(a) covers, without limitation:

Print: newspaper advertising, magazine advertising, brochures, directory listings, mailers

Broadcast: television commercials, radio spots, podcast sponsorships

Outdoor: billboards, transit advertising, bus stop displays

Internet and digital: firm websites, blog posts, social-media profiles and posts, online video, search-engine advertising, display advertising, sponsored content

Telephone directory: yellow-pages listings, online directory profiles

Office and signage: building signage, office collateral, presentation materials

Each medium is permitted; each is subject to the 7.1 truthful, non-misleading standard, the 7.3 limits on direct solicitation, and the 7.2(c) name-and-address attribution. The medium-neutral framing was a deliberate Model Rule choice intended to avoid having the rule become obsolete with each new technology.

Payment for recommendations: the structured exceptions

Subdivision (b) states a general restriction on giving anything of value to a person for recommending the lawyer's services, and then enumerates four exceptions that structure how value may permissibly flow in connection with recommendations. Each exception is itself a permitted commercial arrangement; together they form the affirmative payment architecture.

(b)(1) - Paying for advertising

The lawyer may pay the reasonable costs of advertisements or communications permitted by the rule. This exception covers all paid advertising: print, broadcast, digital, outdoor, sponsored content, search-engine advertising, and any other paid placement. Payment to an advertising vendor for placement of the lawyer's ad is permitted because the payment is for the advertising service, not for a recommendation.

(b)(2) - Lawyer referral services and legal service plans

The lawyer may pay the usual charges of a legal service plan or a not-for-profit or qualified lawyer referral service. A qualified lawyer referral service is one that meets the criteria of the state bar or other authority empowered to qualify such services. The exception affirmatively authorizes participation in:

Bar-sponsored lawyer referral services that route inquiries to participating member lawyers

Legal service plans (group legal plans, employer-sponsored legal benefits, prepaid plans) in which the lawyer participates as a panel member

Not-for-profit referral services operated by community organizations, legal-aid affiliates, or similar entities

The exception is structured around the institutional character of the referring entity, not around the absence of payment; participating lawyers commonly pay membership fees, per-referral fees, or percentage-based participation costs, and these payments are within the exception.

(b)(3) - Sale of a law practice

The lawyer may pay for a law practice in accordance with Rule 1.17. This exception accommodates the transfer of a practice from a retiring or relocating lawyer to a purchasing lawyer, where the purchase price reflects in part the value of the practice's existing client relationships. Rule 1.17 imposes detailed conditions on practice sales (sale of an entire area of practice, notice to clients, fee limits) that operate as the substantive framework within which 7.2(b)(3) applies.

(b)(4) - Reciprocal referral arrangements

The lawyer may enter a reciprocal referral arrangement with another lawyer or with a nonlawyer professional, subject to two conditions: the agreement must not be exclusive, and the client must be informed of the existence and nature of the agreement. The exception affirmatively authorizes:

Lawyer-to-lawyer reciprocal referral relationships across complementary practice areas (e.g., a business litigation practice and a transactional tax practice)

Lawyer-to-nonlawyer reciprocal referrals with related professionals (e.g., a bankruptcy practice and a credit counselor, a personal-injury practice and a medical provider, an estate-planning practice and a financial planner)

The non-exclusivity condition ensures the arrangement does not foreclose the participants from working with other professionals; the disclosure condition ensures the client knows the structural relationship behind the recommendation.

Reading (b) as architecture

The four (b) exceptions are not loopholes; they are the framework. The (b) structure recognizes four legitimate commercial channels through which value flows in connection with lawyer marketing, and authorizes each on its own terms. Paying an advertising vendor is permitted because the payment is for advertising. Paying a qualified referral service is permitted because the service operates within a regulated framework. Paying for a practice is permitted because Rule 1.17 supplies the substantive guardrails. Reciprocal referrals are permitted on the non-exclusive, disclosed terms the rule specifies. Each is a designed commercial structure, not an exception to a default prohibition.

The name-and-address attribution requirement

Subdivision (c) requires every communication made pursuant to the rule to include the name and office address of at least one lawyer or law firm responsible for its content. The attribution requirement performs three functions:

Accountability: A recipient who has a question, a concern, or a complaint can identify the lawyer responsible for the communication.

Regulatory traceability: A disciplinary authority reviewing a communication can identify the lawyer responsible for ensuring 7.1 and 7.2 compliance.

Anti-deception baseline: The requirement that the communication identify a real lawyer at a real address prevents the use of anonymous or untraceable marketing channels for lawyer services.

The requirement is satisfied by including the lawyer or firm name and the office street address. A website URL or email address alone does not satisfy the requirement; a physical office address must appear. The requirement is satisfied if the address is for any office of the firm (a multi-office firm may use a single principal-office address).

Two pattern situations

Digital advertising campaign

A firm running a search-engine advertising campaign for a consumer practice area is engaged in 7.2 advertising. Each ad must comply with 7.1 (truthful, non-misleading content), must not constitute prohibited direct contact under 7.3, must include the firm name and office address (typically through the linked landing page, which itself qualifies as the communication for attribution purposes), and may permissibly involve payment to the advertising platform under 7.2(b)(1). Reciprocal referral arrangements with credit-counseling services or other related professionals operate under 7.2(b)(4), with disclosure to the referred client.

Bar referral panel participation

A lawyer who joins a state bar lawyer referral panel is paying for participation in a qualified lawyer referral service. The participation fee, the per-referral fee, and any percentage charge taken by the bar from successful matches are all within 7.2(b)(2). The bar's published guidance typically describes how the program qualifies as a "lawyer referral service" under the rule, and conscientious participation requires reviewing that guidance and maintaining membership in good standing.

Special-purpose communications

The rule applies to communications that promote the lawyer's services; it does not generally reach internal client communications, communications to other lawyers about co-counsel arrangements, court filings, and similar non-marketing speech. Statements made in the course of representing a client (such as a press statement issued in connection with active litigation) are generally governed by Rules 3.6 and 3.8, not by Rule 7.2, though where the statement crosses into promotion of the lawyer's services it can become subject to 7.2 as well.

Related rules and authority

Rule 7.1 - Communications concerning a lawyer's services (the substantive content standard)

Rule 7.3 - Direct contact with prospective clients (the solicitation framework)

Rule 7.4 - Communication of fields of practice and specialization

Rule 1.17 - Sale of law practice (operating framework for 7.2(b)(3))

Rule 5.4 - Professional independence of a lawyer (governs fee-sharing constraints that interact with referral arrangements)

Practical impact

Rule 7.2 enables lawyer advertising as a settled feature of legal-services markets. Two recurring observations:

The medium is open; the substance is regulated. A lawyer may advertise in any medium subject to the 7.1 content standard. The rule does not require pre-approval, does not restrict the medium, and does not require a particular format for the ad itself.

Payment exceptions structure the commercial environment. The four (b) exceptions are the framework within which paid marketing, panel participation, practice transitions, and reciprocal referrals operate. Each is a recognized commercial channel that the rule explicitly authorizes on its specified terms.

Related authority

ABA Model Rule 7.2 - model rule with comment

Kansas Rules of Professional Conduct - Kansas Supreme Court Rules

Missouri Rules of Professional Conduct - Missouri Supreme Court Rule 4

KRPC 7.3 (Direct Contact)
KRPC 7.4 (Fields of Practice)
KRPC 1.5 (Fees)
KRPC 5.4 (Independence)
KRPC 8.4 (Misconduct)

## KRPC 7.3 / MRPC 4-7.3 - Direct Contact with Prospective Clients [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/krpc-7-3/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Rule of Professional Conduct
KRPC 7.3 / MRPC 4-7.3

KRPC 7.3 / MRPC 4-7.3: Direct Contact with Prospective Clients

The compliant channels for direct outreach: written and recorded communication, prior-relationship and institutional exceptions, and labeling conventions.

Verbatim text of KRPC 7.3 (Kansas)

(a) A lawyer shall not by in-person, live telephone or real-time electronic contact solicit professional employment from a prospective client when a significant motive for the lawyer's doing so is the lawyer's pecuniary gain, unless the person contacted: (1) is a lawyer; or (2) has a family, close personal, or prior professional relationship with the lawyer.

(b) A lawyer shall not solicit professional employment from a prospective client by written, recorded or electronic communication or by in-person, telephone or real-time electronic contact even when not otherwise prohibited by paragraph (a), if: (1) the prospective client has made known to the lawyer a desire not to be solicited by the lawyer; or (2) the solicitation involves coercion, duress or harassment.

(c) Every written, recorded or electronic communication from a lawyer soliciting professional employment from a prospective client known to be in need of legal services in a particular matter shall include the words "Advertising Material" on the outside envelope, if any, and at the beginning and ending of any recorded or electronic communication, unless the recipient of the communication is a person specified in paragraphs (a)(1) or (a)(2).

(d) Notwithstanding the prohibitions in paragraph (a), a lawyer may participate with a prepaid or group legal service plan operated by an organization not owned or directed by the lawyer that uses in-person or telephone contact to solicit memberships or subscriptions for the plan from persons who are not known to need legal services in a particular matter covered by the plan. Kan. Sup. Ct. R. 226, KRPC 7.3.

Missouri Rule 4-7.3

Missouri Rule 4-7.3 follows the same architecture with detailed Missouri-specific elaboration on written-communication labeling and the institutional exceptions. Both rules track ABA Model Rule 7.3. The 2018 revisions to the Model Rule reorganized terminology; jurisdictional adoptions vary.

The affirmative architecture: what 7.3 permits

Rule 7.3 is best read by inverting the conventional summary. The rule permits a broad universe of direct contact with prospective clients and identifies a narrow set of channels that carry heightened risk of overreach. Understanding the affirmative architecture clarifies what the rule actually does:

Written communication is broadly permitted. A lawyer may send a letter, an email, a postcard, a brochure, or other written material to a prospective client, subject to the labeling requirement in subdivision (c) and the consent-and-coercion limits in subdivision (b). Written communication is the rule's primary affirmative channel because the recipient can review and discard at the recipient's pace, without the pressure of a live interaction.

Recorded communication is broadly permitted. A recorded voicemail, an audio or video message, or a similar non-live recorded contact is permitted on the same terms as written communication.

Electronic non-real-time communication is broadly permitted. Email, asynchronous chat, and similar electronic channels that do not involve real-time live interaction are permitted on the same terms.

Live contact with specified categories is permitted. In-person, telephone, and real-time electronic contact is permitted with lawyers, with family members, with persons in a close personal relationship with the lawyer, and with persons with a prior professional relationship.

Group and prepaid plan outreach is permitted. Subdivision (d) explicitly authorizes lawyer participation with prepaid or group legal service plans operated by entities not owned or directed by the lawyer, including plans whose marketing involves direct contact with prospective plan members.

The narrow zone: live, pecuniary-motivated solicitation of strangers

The rule's central restriction in subdivision (a) reaches a specifically defined zone: in-person, live telephone, or real-time electronic contact, where a significant motive is pecuniary gain, with persons who do not fall within the lawyer-relationship, family, close-personal, or prior-professional-relationship categories. Each element is necessary:

Live interaction: The rule's concern is the live-interaction pressure of in-person, real-time telephone, or real-time electronic contact. Written, recorded, and asynchronous electronic contact is not live and is not within (a).

Pecuniary motive: The rule applies where a significant motive is pecuniary gain. Contact motivated by genuine pro bono interest, public-service intent, or non-pecuniary professional concern is outside (a).

Stranger recipient: The rule applies to persons outside the enumerated relationship categories. Contact with lawyers, family, close personal contacts, and prior-professional-relationship contacts is outside (a).

Conditions for written, recorded, and electronic communication

Written, recorded, and electronic communication is permitted as a direct-outreach channel and is subject to two structural conditions:

The labeling convention

Communications directed to a prospective client known to be in need of legal services in a particular matter must include the words "Advertising Material" on the outside envelope (for mailed materials) and at the beginning and ending of recorded or electronic communications. The labeling requirement:

Signals to the recipient that the material is solicitation rather than personal correspondence

Permits the recipient to discard the communication unopened if not interested

Creates a clear regulatory marker that distinguishes the communication from non-solicitation contact

The labeling requirement does not apply to communications with the four enumerated relationship categories (lawyers, family, close personal, prior professional), reflecting the rule's judgment that the heightened-context value of the label is not needed within those relationships.

Consent and non-harassment

Subdivision (b) imposes two cross-cutting limits that apply to written, recorded, electronic, and live contact alike:

Communication must cease if the prospective client has indicated a desire not to be solicited by the lawyer.

Communication must not involve coercion, duress, or harassment regardless of channel.

These limits are channel-neutral baselines; they apply whether the communication is a single letter or a sustained outreach campaign.

The relationship exceptions to live contact

Subdivision (a)'s carve-outs identify four categories where live contact is permitted because the existing relationship supplies the contextual protection the rule otherwise relies on the medium to provide:

Lawyer-to-lawyer contact

A lawyer may directly contact another lawyer to discuss potential representation, co-counsel arrangements, referrals, or specialty consultations. The lawyer recipient possesses the training to evaluate the proposal without protection from live-interaction pressure.

Family and close personal relationships

A lawyer may directly contact a family member or a person in a close personal relationship to offer representation. The existing personal relationship supplies the contextual familiarity that makes the live contact appropriate.

Prior professional relationships

A lawyer may directly contact a person with whom the lawyer has a prior professional relationship. This category includes former clients, persons the lawyer has previously represented in unrelated matters, persons who have consulted the lawyer in a professional capacity (even where no formal representation followed), and similar pre-existing professional ties. The exception affirmatively enables continuity of relationship: a former client who later faces a new matter can be contacted by the lawyer who previously represented them.

Institutional channels: prepaid and group legal service plans

Subdivision (d) is the affirmative authorization for lawyer participation with prepaid and group legal service plans. The structural elements:

The plan must be operated by an organization not owned or directed by the lawyer (the plan must be an independent organizational structure, not a marketing wrapper for the lawyer's practice).

The plan may use in-person or telephone contact to solicit memberships or subscriptions.

The contact must be for plan enrollment, not for representation in a particular matter the prospective member is known to need.

The exception affirmatively enables a substantial category of legal-services delivery: employer-sponsored group plans, union legal benefits, organization-affiliated plans, prepaid consumer plans, and similar arrangements that make routine legal services available to broad populations through a subscription model.

Court-appointed and lawyer-referral routing

Direct contact in connection with court appointments and lawyer-referral-service routing operates outside the (a) restriction in practice, because contact through those channels is initiated by the appointing or referring entity rather than by the lawyer's direct solicitation. A lawyer who accepts a court appointment to represent an indigent defendant, or who receives a referral through a qualified bar referral service, and who then contacts the new client to initiate representation, is not making the kind of "in-person solicitation" the rule addresses; the lawyer is making contact with a client whose engagement was initiated by an institutional process.

Two pattern situations

Mailing to public-record contacts

A lawyer who learns from public records that a person is facing a particular legal situation (e.g., a court filing, a property action, a published notice) and who wishes to offer representation may send a written communication. The communication must comply with Rule 7.1's truthful, non-misleading standard, must include the "Advertising Material" label on the envelope and (if relevant) in the communication, must comply with the consent-and-non-harassment limits of 7.3(b), and must include the name-and-address attribution of Rule 7.2(c). The written-mailing channel is the rule's principal affirmative pathway for outreach to identified prospects.

Reconnection with former client

A lawyer who represented a client in a closed matter and who later wishes to offer representation in a new matter is squarely within the prior-professional-relationship exception. The lawyer may telephone, email, or meet the former client to discuss the new matter without 7.3(a) restriction. The (b) consent-and-non-harassment limits still apply, and the lawyer must respect any prior request by the client not to be contacted.

The role of the labeling convention

The "Advertising Material" label is the structural counterpart to the asynchronous channel. Written, recorded, and electronic communications are broadly permitted in part because the recipient retains control over the interaction. The label reinforces that control by giving the recipient an immediate signal to evaluate, accept, or discard the communication. The label converts the communication into a clearly identified outreach the recipient can engage with on the recipient's own terms.

Online forms and inbound solicitation

Rule 7.3 governs lawyer-initiated direct contact with prospective clients. It does not generally reach inbound contact: a prospective client who completes a contact form on the lawyer's website, sends an email inquiry, calls the lawyer's office, or initiates a chat with the firm's website chat function is the initiating party, and the lawyer's responsive communication is not "solicitation" within the rule. The rule's concern is the live-interaction pressure of lawyer-initiated stranger outreach, not the lawyer's response to prospective-client inquiry.

Related rules and authority

Rule 7.1 - Communications concerning a lawyer's services (the content standard)

Rule 7.2 - Advertising (the medium-and-attribution framework)

Rule 7.4 - Communication of fields of practice and specialization

Rule 4.2 - Communication with persons represented by counsel (governs contact with represented parties, including prospective clients already represented)

Rule 4.3 - Dealing with unrepresented persons

Practical impact

Rule 7.3 has often been described in terms of what it prohibits; read carefully it is better understood by what it permits. Two recurring observations:

Written, recorded, and electronic outreach is broadly available. Lawyers may engage in substantial direct outreach to prospective clients through asynchronous channels, subject to truthful content, attribution, and the "Advertising Material" labeling convention. The rule does not restrict the volume or reach of properly labeled written outreach.

The relationship and institutional exceptions enable continuity and access. The prior-professional-relationship exception preserves continuity of representation across matters; the prepaid and group plan authorization opens access for populations served through subscription models; the court-appointment and qualified-referral pathways operate outside the (a) restriction in practice.

Related authority

ABA Model Rule 7.3 - model rule with comment

Kansas Rules of Professional Conduct - Kansas Supreme Court Rules

Missouri Rules of Professional Conduct - Missouri Supreme Court Rule 4

KRPC 7.2 (Advertising)
KRPC 7.4 (Fields of Practice)
KRPC 6.1 (Pro Bono)
KRPC 6.5 (Limited Services)

## KRPC 7.4 / MRPC 4-7.4 - Communication of Fields of Practice and Specialization [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/krpc-7-4/

Open Bankruptcy Project

Rule of Professional Conduct
KRPC 7.4 / MRPC 4-7.4

KRPC 7.4 / MRPC 4-7.4: Communication of Fields of Practice and Specialization

An affirmative framework authorizing lawyers to communicate the fields of law in which they practice, with specific provisions for patent, admiralty, and certified-specialist designations.

Verbatim text of KRPC 7.4 (Kansas)

(a) A lawyer may communicate the fact that the lawyer does or does not practice in particular fields of law.

(b) A lawyer admitted to engage in patent practice before the United States Patent and Trademark Office may use the designation "Patent Attorney" or a substantially similar designation.

(c) A lawyer engaged in Admiralty practice may use the designation "Admiralty," "Proctor in Admiralty" or a substantially similar designation.

(d) A lawyer shall not state or imply that a lawyer is certified as a specialist in a particular field of law, unless:

(1) the lawyer has been certified as a specialist by an organization that has been approved by an appropriate state authority or that has been accredited by the American Bar Association; and

(2) the name of the certifying organization is clearly identified in the communication. Kan. Sup. Ct. R. 226, KRPC 7.4.

Missouri Rule 4-7.4

Missouri Rule 4-7.4 is substantively parallel to KRPC 7.4 and tracks the ABA Model Rule framework. The rule operates as an affirmative authorization for lawyer communication of fields of practice, with two specific designations recognized for federally regulated practice categories (patent and admiralty) and a specific condition for use of a "certified specialist" designation.

The affirmative framework

The rule is organized as an affirmative authorization. Subdivision (a) opens with the general permission: a lawyer may communicate that the lawyer does or does not practice in particular fields. The provision authorizes a broad range of communications:

Website pages identifying the firm's practice areas

Attorney biographies listing the fields in which the lawyer practices

Letterhead and business cards identifying practice fields

Directory listings categorizing the lawyer by practice area

Marketing materials describing the firm's substantive areas of work

Statements by the lawyer in client and prospective-client communications about the fields the lawyer handles

The rule's affirmative grant under (a) does not require certification or any specific credential beyond the lawyer's licensure. Communications under (a) are simply descriptive of the lawyer's practice fields and are permitted as such.

7.4(b) - Patent designation

A lawyer admitted to practice before the United States Patent and Trademark Office may use the designation "Patent Attorney" or a substantially similar designation. The provision recognizes the distinctive federally regulated practice category. Patent practice is governed by a federal admission regime maintained by the USPTO; admission requires satisfaction of the agency's scientific or technical training requirements and passage of the agency's examination. A lawyer admitted under that regime is authorized by Rule 7.4(b) to communicate the admission through the designation "Patent Attorney."

The "substantially similar designation" language permits variants such as "Patent Practitioner," "Registered Patent Attorney," and "USPTO-Registered Patent Attorney." The variants must accurately reflect the lawyer's actual USPTO registration; designations that overstate or misstate the registration fall outside the rule's grant.

7.4(c) - Admiralty designation

A lawyer engaged in Admiralty practice may use the designation "Admiralty," "Proctor in Admiralty," or a substantially similar designation. The provision preserves a historical practice category for which traditional designations have long been recognized. Admiralty practice is the field of law governing maritime matters - vessel ownership, marine cargo, marine personal injury, maritime liens, and related matters within the federal admiralty jurisdiction. The designation supports informed selection of counsel for matters falling within the field.

7.4(d) - The "certified specialist" framework

Subdivision (d) addresses use of the "certified specialist" designation. The provision is the rule's most specific element and reflects a deliberate balancing: the rule recognizes the value of credential-based identification for consumers but conditions use of the credential language on two structural elements that ensure the credential is meaningful.

7.4(d)(1) - Approved or accredited certifying organization

The lawyer must have been certified by an organization that has been (a) approved by an appropriate state authority or (b) accredited by the American Bar Association. The condition channels the certifying activity through institutional review. State authorities and the ABA's accreditation framework evaluate certifying organizations for their certification standards, examination integrity, continuing-education requirements, and overall credibility. A "certified specialist" designation under (d)(1) thus carries with it the institutional vouching of the approving or accrediting authority.

7.4(d)(2) - Clear identification of the certifying organization

The name of the certifying organization must be clearly identified in the communication. The condition ensures that the recipient of the communication can evaluate the credential's source. A reference to "certified specialist in [field]" without identification of the certifying organization does not satisfy the condition; the communication must include the organization's name in a manner the recipient can readily perceive.

Subdivision (a) and subdivision (d) are different categories. The general practice-field communication permitted by 7.4(a) does not require certification and is broadly authorized. The "certified specialist" designation under 7.4(d) is a credential statement and is conditioned on the two structural elements of (d)(1) and (d)(2). Lawyers may communicate their fields of practice under (a) without any reference to specialization; the (d) framework applies when the lawyer wishes to use the credential-specific language.

The relationship to Rule 7.1

Rule 7.4 operates within the broader framework of Rule 7.1, which governs communications about the lawyer's services and prohibits false or misleading communications. The two rules work in tandem:

Rule 7.4(a) authorizes practice-field communication; Rule 7.1 requires that the communication not be false or misleading. A lawyer's listing of a practice field under (a) is within the rule when the lawyer actually practices in the field.

Rules 7.4(b) and (c) authorize specific designations; Rule 7.1 requires the designations to accurately reflect the lawyer's qualifications. The "Patent Attorney" designation under (b) presumes actual USPTO admission; an "Admiralty" designation under (c) presumes actual engagement in the field.

Rule 7.4(d) conditions the "certified specialist" designation on the two structural elements; Rule 7.1 requires that the certification statement, including the identifying information for the certifying organization, be accurate.

The institutional review framework for certifying organizations

The "approved by an appropriate state authority" prong of 7.4(d)(1) refers to the state-level approval frameworks that many jurisdictions maintain for certifying organizations. State approval processes typically evaluate:

The certifying organization's substantive standards for certification (years of practice, examination requirements, peer review, continuing-legal-education obligations)

The certifying organization's procedures for examination administration and grading

The certifying organization's recertification requirements ensuring continued competence

The certifying organization's governance and conflict-management structures

The "accredited by the American Bar Association" prong refers to the ABA's national accreditation framework for specialty certification programs, which performs analogous evaluations on a national scale. Either approval channel satisfies the condition of (d)(1).

Common practice-area communications

Firm website practice-area listing

A firm's website includes a "Practice Areas" page listing the substantive fields the firm handles - corporate transactions, commercial litigation, employment law, bankruptcy, family law. The listing is a 7.4(a) communication; the firm communicates the fields in which its lawyers practice. The listing is within the rule when the firm actually maintains substantive practice in each listed field. No certification is required, and no "specialist" language is used.

Attorney biography with credential reference

An attorney biography on a firm website identifies the lawyer's primary practice fields and includes a reference to a credential held by the lawyer (for example, a state-approved certification in family law, with the certifying organization clearly named). The practice-field references are governed by 7.4(a); the credential reference is governed by 7.4(d) and includes the certifying-organization identification that (d)(2) requires.

Cross-jurisdiction considerations

Lawyers practicing across jurisdictions communicate their practice fields in materials that may be viewed from any jurisdiction. The Rule 7.4 framework operates alongside the jurisdictional-scope considerations under Rule 5.5 and the bar-admission representations under Rule 7.1: a multi-jurisdiction practice description identifies the fields in which the lawyer practices, the jurisdictions in which the lawyer is admitted, and (where applicable) the certifying organizations that have credentialed the lawyer's specialty designations. Each component of the communication is governed by the applicable rule provisions.

Continuing nature of the inquiry

Communications under Rule 7.4 are subject to ongoing accuracy obligations. A practice-field listing remains within 7.4(a) so long as the lawyer continues to practice in the field; a designation under (b) or (c) remains accurate so long as the lawyer maintains the underlying status (USPTO registration or active admiralty practice); a "certified specialist" designation under (d) remains within the rule so long as the certification remains in good standing and the certifying organization remains approved or accredited. Materials are updated to reflect changes in any of these statuses.

Relationship to other rules

Rule 7.1 - Communications about the lawyer's services; the general accuracy framework that overlays Rule 7.4

Rule 7.2 - Communications about legal services (advertising); the related provision governing the channels through which communications are made

Rule 7.5 - Firm names and letterheads; relevant where the practice-field communication appears on firm-identifying materials

Rule 5.5 - Jurisdictional scope; practice-field communications include implicit representations about the jurisdictions in which the lawyer practices

Rule 1.1 - Competence; the underlying obligation to provide competent representation in the fields the lawyer holds out as practicing

Practical impact

Rule 7.4 carries several recurring practical consequences:

Practice-field communication is broadly authorized. Lawyers and firms communicate the fields in which they practice through the customary channels - websites, biographies, marketing materials, directory listings - within the framework of 7.4(a) and Rule 7.1's accuracy overlay.

Specific designations have specific bases. The "Patent Attorney" and "Admiralty" designations are tied to defined practice categories with established federal or specialized frameworks. Use of these designations under (b) and (c) presumes the underlying qualifications.

"Certified specialist" requires institutional vouching. The (d) framework conditions the credential designation on certification by an approved or accredited organization and on clear identification of the certifying organization. The two elements ensure that the designation carries substantive content for the recipient.

Related authority

ABA Model Rules on Communications About the Lawyer's Services - model rules with comments

Kansas Rules of Professional Conduct - Kansas Supreme Court Rules

Missouri Rules of Professional Conduct - Missouri Supreme Court Rule 4

KRPC 5.5 (Jurisdictional Scope)
KRPC 5.1 (Supervision)
KRPC 5.3 (Non-Lawyer Supervision)

## KRPC 8.3 / MRPC 4-8.3 - Reporting Professional Misconduct [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project

Open Bankruptcy Project
