11 U.S.C. Section 1325(b)
Form 122C-1
Form 122C-2

Form 122C: Chapter 13 Disposable Income and the Applicable Commitment Period

The Section 1325(b)(2) disposable-income definition, the Section 1325(b)(4) commitment period split, and the Supreme Court's forward-looking adjustment in Hamilton v. Lanning.

What the Form 122C series does

Official Form 122C-1, Statement of Your Current Monthly Income and Calculation of Commitment Period, and Official Form 122C-2, Chapter 13 Calculation of Your Disposable Income, are the Chapter 13 analogues to the Chapter 7 Form 122A series. They serve two related but distinct functions in Chapter 13.

First, Form 122C-1 calculates current monthly income on the same statutory basis as Form 122A-1 and compares the annualized figure to the applicable state median family income. The result of this comparison sets the applicable commitment period: three years for a below-median debtor, five years for an above-median debtor, under 11 U.S.C. Section 1325(b)(4).

Second, for above-median debtors only, Form 122C-2 computes monthly disposable income through a deduction schedule that closely parallels Form 122A-2. The output figure feeds into the confirmation requirement at Section 1325(b)(1)(B): an above-median debtor's plan must provide that the monthly disposable income computed by the form will be applied to make payments to unsecured creditors over the applicable commitment period.

The statutory architecture of Section 1325(b)

Section 1325(b)(1) sets the disposable-income confirmation requirement: a plan over the objection of the trustee or any unsecured creditor cannot be confirmed unless it either pays unsecured claims in full or provides that all of the debtor's "projected disposable income" received during the applicable commitment period will be applied to make payments to unsecured creditors. The two operative phrases are "projected disposable income" and "applicable commitment period."

Section 1325(b)(2) defines "disposable income" as current monthly income (with the same Section 101(10A) source rules) less amounts reasonably necessary to be expended for maintenance or support of the debtor and dependents, for charitable contributions up to 15 percent of gross income, and for the continuation, preservation, and operation of a business if the debtor operates one. Section 1325(b)(3) then provides the bridge to the IRS-Standards regime: for above-median debtors, "amounts reasonably necessary to be expended" are determined by reference to the means-test deduction schedule at Section 707(b)(2)(A) and (B), the same schedule used on Form 122A-2.

For below-median debtors, the "reasonably necessary" determination is performed under the discretion of the bankruptcy court without reference to the IRS Standards; below-median debtors complete only Form 122C-1 and report their actual budget on Schedules I and J for confirmation purposes.

The applicable commitment period

Section 1325(b)(4) bifurcates the plan duration based on the state median income comparison performed on Form 122C-1. A debtor whose annualized current monthly income is at or below the applicable state median family income for the debtor's household size has an applicable commitment period of three years. A debtor whose income is above median has a five-year period.

The five-year period for above-median debtors is a confirmation requirement, not a debtor preference. An above-median debtor cannot propose a three-year plan over creditor or trustee objection; the plan must extend through the full sixty months unless unsecured claims are paid in full. The Supreme Court has held that the commitment period is a "temporal" requirement and not merely a "monetary" minimum, meaning that the debtor cannot satisfy the commitment-period requirement by front-loading payments and concluding early.

A practical consequence of the bifurcation is that an above-median debtor whose monthly disposable income is small but positive still faces a five-year commitment with that small monthly amount applied to unsecured creditors. The cumulative payout to unsecured creditors over five years can be substantial even from a small monthly figure, and unsecured creditors who receive distributions in such cases benefit from the commitment period extension.

Form 122C-1 - the entry-point form

Form 122C-1 mirrors Form 122A-1 in structure. The same six-month look-back applies. The same source categories (gross wages, business income, rental income, interest and dividends, pension income, unemployment compensation, third-party contributions to household expenses, and other income) are enumerated. The same statutory exclusions apply: Social Security Act benefits, war-crime and terrorism victim payments, earned income credit, and certain veterans benefits paid for service-connected disability. The same state median income tables are referenced.

The differences from Form 122A-1 are formal rather than substantive. Form 122C-1 includes the commitment-period determination as its terminal output; Form 122A-1 does not. The disposable-income calculation is in a separate companion form for Chapter 13 (Form 122C-2); for Chapter 7 it is in Form 122A-2.

Form 122C-2 - the deduction schedule

For above-median debtors, Form 122C-2 implements the Section 1325(b)(3) reasonably-necessary calculation through the same four-family deduction structure that appears on Form 122A-2:

IRS National Standards for food, clothing, personal care, household supplies, miscellaneous, and out-of-pocket healthcare.

IRS Local Standards for housing (non-mortgage and mortgage-or-rent components) and transportation (operating and ownership components), with the latter subject to Ransom v. FIA Card Services, N.A., 562 U.S. 61 (2011), in the same manner as Form 122A-2.

Other Necessary Expenses from the closed enumeration (taxes, mandatory payroll deductions, term life insurance, court-ordered support, childcare, healthcare premiums and expenses beyond the standard allowance, telecommunications, and limited education expenses).

Deductions for secured and priority debts, calculated as the average monthly amount due over 60 months following the petition date.

The Chapter 13 administrative-expense allowance that appears on Form 122A-2 does not appear on Form 122C-2; the debtor is in fact filing under Chapter 13, and actual trustee fees and other plan-administration costs are paid through the plan rather than treated as a means-test deduction.

The marital adjustment is available on Form 122C-2 for a married debtor who files individually, on the same terms as on Form 122A-2.

Hamilton v. Lanning and the forward-looking adjustment

The Supreme Court resolved a deep circuit split on the meaning of "projected disposable income" in Hamilton v. Lanning, 560 U.S. 505 (2010). The question was whether the "projected" qualifier in Section 1325(b)(1)(B) permits a bankruptcy court to depart from the mechanical Form 122C-2 figure when the debtor's actual income or expenses at the time of confirmation will predictably differ from the six-month historical look-back captured by the form.

The Court rejected a strictly mechanical reading. Justice Alito's opinion held that "projected disposable income" generally takes the Form 122C-2 disposable-income figure as a starting point, but the court may consider "known or virtually certain" changes to the debtor's income or expenses going forward. The mechanical figure is the presumptive output; the forward-looking adjustment is the exception, justified when the historical look-back captures income that the debtor will not in fact have during the commitment period (a debtor who lost a high-paying job before petition) or expenses that the debtor will not in fact incur (a debtor whose dependent child reaches majority during the plan, terminating childcare expenses).

The Court summarized the holding as follows: "When a bankruptcy court calculates a debtor's projected disposable income, the court may account for changes in the debtor's income or expenses that are known or virtually certain at the time of confirmation." The doctrine has been applied in numerous reported decisions, generally to debtor benefit when historical income was unusually high or to creditor benefit when historical income was unusually low.

The companion holding in Hall v. United States

A related Supreme Court decision, Hall v. United States, 566 U.S. 506 (2012), addressed the treatment of post-petition tax claims arising from a Chapter 13 debtor's sale of farm property under Section 1222(a)(2)(A). The Court held that the post-petition tax was not "incurred by the estate" within the meaning of Section 503(b)(B) and was therefore not subject to discharge as an administrative expense. Although Hall is not a means-test case, it bears on the operation of Chapter 13 in the agricultural context that Section 1222 was enacted to address.

Disposable income for below-median debtors

A below-median Chapter 13 debtor does not use Form 122C-2 for the disposable-income calculation. The "reasonably necessary" determination is performed under the court's general discretion under Section 1325(b)(2), informed by Schedules I (Income) and J (Expenses) that the debtor files with the petition. Schedules I and J reflect actual current income and projected actual expenses rather than the historical six-month average; they are forward-looking by their nature.

The discretionary regime gives below-median debtors substantially more flexibility than above-median debtors. A below-median debtor's monthly expenses on Schedule J can reflect actual rent, actual utility costs, actual food expenses, and actual recurring costs, even where those exceed the IRS Local Standards. The trustee may object that particular expenses are unreasonable, but the court evaluates the objection without reference to a fixed table.

Voluntary contributions and reasonable necessity

Section 1325(b)(2) expressly identifies charitable contributions of up to 15 percent of gross income as reasonably necessary. The text was added by the Religious Liberty and Charitable Donation Protection Act of 1998 and predates BAPCPA; the BAPCPA-era jurisprudence has integrated the provision with the Section 707(b)(2) deduction schedule for above-median debtors. Charitable contributions are unique among voluntary contributions in receiving express statutory protection.

Voluntary retirement contributions present a different question. Section 541(b)(7) excludes from the estate certain retirement contributions, and bankruptcy courts have divided on whether such excluded contributions also escape the "disposable income" computation. The majority view permits a reasonable level of ongoing retirement contributions as a Schedule J expense for below-median debtors and as an Other Necessary Expense or special-circumstances item for above-median debtors, though the case law remains unsettled.

Confirmation and the disposable-income objection

The disposable-income requirement is enforced at confirmation. The trustee or any unsecured creditor may object to a plan that fails to commit projected disposable income to unsecured creditors. A debtor whose Form 122C-2 produces a positive disposable-income figure may avoid the objection by paying the figure to unsecured creditors, by paying unsecured claims in full, or by demonstrating through a Hamilton-type forward-looking adjustment that the actual projected figure is lower than the mechanical output.

A debtor whose Form 122C-2 produces a negative or zero disposable-income figure satisfies Section 1325(b)(1)(B) on its face, but the plan must still satisfy the best-interests-of-creditors test at Section 1325(a)(4), which requires that unsecured creditors receive at least as much through the plan as they would receive in a hypothetical Chapter 7 liquidation. The two requirements operate independently.

Form 122C is the same statute viewed from a different angle. The disposable-income figure that triggers presumption of abuse in Chapter 7 (Form 122A-2 output multiplied by 60) is essentially the same figure that fixes the unsecured-creditor payment obligation in Chapter 13 (Form 122C-2 output multiplied by the applicable commitment period). A debtor with substantial disposable income faces conversion or dismissal in Chapter 7 and a higher unsecured-creditor distribution in Chapter 13. The means test integrates the two chapters by design.

Related statutes and authority

Frequently asked questions
What is the applicable commitment period?
Under section 1325(b)(4), a debtor whose annualized current monthly income is at or below the applicable state median has a three-year commitment period; a debtor above the median has a five-year period. Form 122C-1 performs the comparison.
Do below-median debtors complete Form 122C-2?
No. A below-median Chapter 13 debtor does not use Form 122C-2 for the disposable-income calculation. What is reasonably necessary is determined under section 1325(b)(2) with the court's general discretion, informed by Schedules I and J.
How does Form 122C-1 differ from Form 122A-1?
It mirrors it: the same six-month look-back and the same income categories. The difference is what the result does. In Chapter 7 the comparison drives a presumption of abuse; in Chapter 13 it sets the commitment period and decides whether Form 122C-2 applies.
What did Hamilton v. Lanning decide?
In Hamilton v. Lanning, 560 U.S. 505 (2010), the Supreme Court held that projected disposable income under section 1325(b)(1)(B) permits a forward-looking adjustment where changes in the debtor's income or expenses are known or virtually certain at confirmation, rather than a purely mechanical multiplication of the look-back figure.
Are charitable contributions a reasonably necessary expense?
Section 1325(b)(2) expressly treats charitable contributions of up to 15 percent of gross income as reasonably necessary, language added by the Religious Liberty and Charitable Donation Protection Act of 1998.
Who can object to a plan on disposable-income grounds?
The trustee or any unsecured creditor, at confirmation. Over such an objection, a plan cannot be confirmed unless it pays unsecured claims in full or commits all of the debtor's projected disposable income for the applicable commitment period.

## Rebutting the Presumption of Abuse - Section 707(b)(2)(B) Special Circumstances Deep Dive [2026] - Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/means-test-deep-dives/presumed-abuse-rebuttal/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Home/Means Test Deep Dives/Rebutting the Presumption of Abuse

11 U.S.C. Section 707(b)(2)(B)
11 U.S.C. Section 707(b)(3)
Special Circumstances

Rebutting the Presumption of Abuse: Section 707(b)(2)(B) Special Circumstances

The itemization and documentation framework for overcoming a Form 122A-2 presumption, and the Section 707(b)(3) totality-of-circumstances test that operates when the presumption is rebutted or never arose.

The two-track abuse inquiry

The Bankruptcy Code provides two paths to a finding of abuse under 11 U.S.C. Section 707(b). The first is the mechanical presumption at Section 707(b)(2), triggered when an above-median debtor's monthly disposable income (computed on Form 122A-2) exceeds the statutory threshold when multiplied by 60. The second is the discretionary totality-of-circumstances inquiry at Section 707(b)(3), which applies in two scenarios: when the presumption is overcome by a Section 707(b)(2)(B) special-circumstances showing, and when the presumption never arose because the debtor was below median or because above-median deductions reduced disposable income below the threshold.

This page treats both tracks. The presumption rebuttal under Section 707(b)(2)(B) is the gateway concern for above-median debtors whose Form 122A-2 produces a presumption-triggering figure. The Section 707(b)(3) totality test is the residual concern for all consumer debtors after the presumption framework concludes.

Section 707(b)(2)(B) - the statutory text

Section 707(b)(2)(B)(i) provides that the presumption "may only be rebutted by demonstrating special circumstances, such as a serious medical condition or a call or order to active duty in the Armed Forces, to the extent such special circumstances . . . justify additional expenses or adjustments of current monthly income for which there is no reasonable alternative."

Section 707(b)(2)(B)(ii) imposes four procedural requirements on the debtor invoking the rebuttal: (1) itemize each additional expense or income adjustment; (2) provide documentation for such expense or adjustment; (3) provide a detailed explanation of the special circumstances making the expenses or adjustments necessary and reasonable; and (4) attest under oath to the accuracy of the information.

Section 707(b)(2)(B)(iv) sets the arithmetic test for successful rebuttal: the special-circumstances additional expenses or income adjustments must reduce monthly disposable income by an amount sufficient to bring 60-month disposable income below the statutory threshold. A debtor whose itemized special-circumstances showing is documented and sworn but whose re-computed disposable income still exceeds the threshold has not rebutted the presumption.

The In re Pageau itemization standard

The leading reported decision on the rigor of the itemization and documentation requirement is In re Pageau, 383 B.R. 221 (Bankr. D.N.H. 2008). The court held that the special-circumstances showing must identify each additional expense with specificity, document the expense with supporting records, and articulate why the expense is necessary and why no reasonable alternative exists. A generalized claim of financial hardship is insufficient; the debtor must walk the court through each line item.

The Pageau standard requires the debtor to address four elements for each claimed special-circumstances expense or adjustment:

Itemization. The expense must be identified with line-item particularity (not "medical bills" but a schedule listing each provider, date, and amount).

Documentation. Supporting records (billing statements, insurance Explanation of Benefits, prescription receipts, military orders, school enrollment confirmations, etc.) must be produced.

Necessity. The debtor must articulate why the expense is necessary - typically, why it is essential to the debtor's or a dependent's health, welfare, or ability to produce income.

No reasonable alternative. The debtor must explain why a lower-cost option does not exist, why an existing benefit (insurance, employer subsidy, government program) does not cover the cost, and why the expense cannot be eliminated.

Several subsequent decisions have elaborated the no-reasonable-alternative requirement. A debtor cannot establish special circumstances by reference to a chosen lifestyle commitment; the absence of alternatives must be objective rather than preferential. A debtor's voluntary commitment to a particular school for a child, when public alternatives exist at no additional cost, has been held insufficient. A debtor's medically necessary specialty treatment, when no lower-cost treatment is available, has been held sufficient.

The statutory examples and their boundaries

The statute identifies two examples of special circumstances: "a serious medical condition" and "a call or order to active duty in the Armed Forces." The use of the word "such as" indicates the examples are illustrative rather than exhaustive. Courts have nonetheless treated the statutory examples as setting a tone that limits the universe of qualifying circumstances.

Serious medical condition. A condition that produces ongoing out-of-pocket medical expenses substantially beyond the National Standards healthcare allowance qualifies. Reported decisions have credited chronic-disease management costs, specialty pharmaceutical costs not covered by insurance, durable medical equipment, and home-health-aide costs. A condition that has produced only past expenses (without ongoing burden) is typically not credited because the special-circumstances rebuttal is forward-looking; the debtor must show that the additional expense will continue during the relevant period.

Active duty. Military activation that materially increases the debtor's expenses (multiple-residence costs, separation-driven childcare, equipment costs not reimbursed) or reduces income (a debtor whose civilian salary exceeds military pay) can qualify. The disabled-veteran and reservist exemptions at Section 707(b)(2)(D) provide an independent escape from the presumption framework for qualifying military debtors and are often the preferred mechanism for that population.

Beyond the statutory examples, reported decisions have credited under the special-circumstances framework: care obligations for a non-dependent family member with disability; commuting costs for an employment that has no local alternative; foreign-tax obligations for a debtor with overseas income; and education costs imposed by a custody decree.

What does not qualify as special circumstances

The reported decisions are consistent on what falls outside the special-circumstances framework. The following claimed adjustments have been rejected:

Lifestyle preferences. Charitable giving (beyond the 15-percent Section 1325(b)(2)(A) allowance available in Chapter 13), country-club dues, vacation expenses, and discretionary recreation do not qualify.

Voluntary retirement contributions in Chapter 7. Most courts hold that ongoing 401(k) contributions are not special circumstances in the Chapter 7 means test, though the question is more contested in Chapter 13.

Unsecured-debt service. Payments on credit cards, personal loans from family members, and student loans do not qualify; the means test treats these as the very obligations from which Chapter 7 would discharge the debtor.

Anticipated but uncommitted future expenses. An expectation that a child may attend private school in the future or that a medical condition may worsen does not qualify; the framework requires present and continuing expenses with documented basis.

Garden-variety overspending. A debtor whose monthly outflows exceed the IRS Standards in ordinary categories (food, clothing, recreation) cannot characterize the excess as special circumstances; the IRS Standards are the statutory allowance for these categories.

Income-side adjustments

The special-circumstances framework is not limited to additional-expense itemization. Section 707(b)(2)(B)(i) permits "adjustments of current monthly income." A debtor whose six-month look-back captured income that has terminated (a debtor who lost a high-paying job in the look-back's final month, for example) may seek to reduce the CMI input through a documented showing.

Reported decisions have accepted income-side adjustments where the look-back captures: a one-time bonus or severance payment unlikely to recur; rental income from property since sold; business income from operations since terminated; or wages from a job since lost through no fault of the debtor. The adjustment is mathematically equivalent to subtracting the no-longer-existing income from the CMI base; the procedural requirement (itemization, documentation, attestation, sworn explanation) is identical to the expense-side analysis.

Procedural mechanics

The debtor invoking special circumstances files an itemized statement either as a section of Form 122A-2 or as a supplemental attachment to it. The trustee may then file a motion under Section 707(b) seeking dismissal or conversion, and the special-circumstances showing becomes the centerpiece of the contested hearing. The burden of persuasion on rebuttal rests on the debtor.

The Federal Rules of Bankruptcy Procedure govern the timing of trustee motions and debtor responses. Under Rule 1017(e), a Section 707(b) motion based on the means test must be filed within 60 days after the first date set for the meeting of creditors, although the court may extend this deadline. A debtor anticipating a Section 707(b)(2) presumption motion should prepare the special-circumstances showing for filing concurrently with Form 122A-2.

The Section 707(b)(3) totality-of-circumstances backup test

Section 707(b)(3) provides that even if the presumption does not arise or has been rebutted, the court may still consider whether granting Chapter 7 relief would be an abuse "considering . . . (A) whether the debtor filed the petition in bad faith; or (B) the totality of the circumstances . . . of the debtor's financial situation demonstrates abuse."

The Section 707(b)(3) inquiry is discretionary and fact-intensive. It captures cases that satisfy the mechanical means test but that nonetheless present circumstances suggesting Chapter 7 is inappropriate. The leading pre-BAPCPA decision articulating the framework is In re Krohn, 886 F.2d 123 (6th Cir. 1989), which identified factors the court should consider: whether the debtor enjoys a stable source of future income; whether the debtor has the capacity to repay a substantial portion of debt out of future earnings; whether the petition was filed in response to sudden illness, calamity, disability, or unemployment; whether the schedules and Statement of Affairs misrepresent material facts; whether the proposed family budget is excessive or unreasonable; and whether the debtor's lifestyle is consistent with the claimed inability to pay.

Although Krohn predates BAPCPA, its factor analysis has been carried forward in post-BAPCPA Section 707(b)(3) jurisprudence. Many circuits and bankruptcy courts have cited the Krohn factors approvingly in totality-of-circumstances analyses, with adaptation to reflect the BAPCPA-era distinction between Section 707(b)(2) presumption analysis and Section 707(b)(3) totality analysis.

Ransom v. FIA Card Services in the rebuttal context

The Supreme Court's decision in Ransom v. FIA Card Services, N.A., 562 U.S. 61 (2011), is most often cited for its holding on the vehicle ownership allowance, but the decision also articulates a methodological principle relevant to the rebuttal framework. The Court emphasized that the means-test deduction schedule must be applied as Congress drafted it, even when a particular debtor's circumstances appear to call for a different result. The methodological holding is in tension with a broad reading of special circumstances: if Congress intended the IRS Standards to control, then judicially crafted exceptions for particular debtors' circumstances erode the statutory design.

The practical effect of Ransom on the rebuttal framework is to reinforce the narrow construction of "special circumstances" already established by Pageau and similar decisions. A debtor who argues that her circumstances are special because the IRS Standards produce an unfair result in her case is essentially arguing for a judicial revision of the statute, which Ransom forecloses. The rebuttal succeeds only where the debtor identifies a particularized expense or income adjustment that the standard schedule cannot accommodate and that no reasonable alternative would obviate.

In re Egebjerg and ongoing 401(k) loan repayments

A frequently cited decision on the boundary between ordinary expenses and special circumstances is In re Egebjerg, 574 F.3d 1045 (9th Cir. 2009). The Ninth Circuit held that monthly repayments of a 401(k) loan are not deductible as a Section 707(b)(2) "Other Necessary Expense" because the repayment is not paid to a third party in the ordinary sense; the debtor is essentially repaying himself. The court also rejected the debtor's special-circumstances argument, holding that the existence of a voluntary loan from one's own retirement account does not, without more, constitute special circumstances. The decision is the leading authority for the proposition that voluntary financial commitments to oneself or to favored creditors do not rebut the presumption.

The rebuttal is procedural, but the standard is substantive. Form 122A-2 invites the debtor to itemize special circumstances in a designated section. Filling out the section is the procedural step; succeeding on the substantive standard requires line-item documentation, articulated necessity, demonstrated absence of reasonable alternative, and an arithmetic showing that the additional expense or income adjustment brings disposable income below the threshold. A debtor whose Form 122A-2 output exceeds the threshold by a large margin faces a correspondingly large rebuttal burden.

Bad-faith filing under Section 707(b)(3)(A)

Section 707(b)(3)(A) captures bad-faith filings as an independent abuse category. Bad faith is established by conduct demonstrating that the debtor seeks Chapter 7 relief for a purpose inconsistent with the statute's design: pre-petition asset transfers to insulate property from creditors, concealment of income or assets, repeated filings to thwart enforcement actions, and similar conduct. Bad faith may also be inferred from the timing of the filing relative to anticipated wage increases, expected inheritance, or other near-term financial improvements that the debtor seeks to enjoy free of the discharged debt.

A bad-faith finding produces dismissal regardless of the means-test mathematics. A debtor whose Form 122A-2 output is below the presumption threshold but whose pre-petition conduct evidences bad faith may face dismissal under Section 707(b)(3)(A); the means test is not a safe harbor against bad-faith review.

Strategic implications for above-median debtors

An above-median debtor whose initial Form 122A-2 produces a presumption-triggering figure has three substantive options: rebut under Section 707(b)(2)(B) through documented special circumstances; convert to Chapter 13, where the disposable-income figure becomes the unsecured-creditor payment obligation rather than a dismissal trigger; or face dismissal of the Chapter 7 case. The choice depends on the debtor's circumstances. A debtor with substantial special-circumstances expenses can pursue rebuttal; a debtor with a stable disposable income can convert to a Chapter 13 plan funded by the disposable-income figure; a debtor with neither faces the structural conclusion that Chapter 7 relief is not the appropriate procedural vehicle.

Frequently asked questions
What counts as special circumstances under section 707(b)(2)(B)?
The statute names two examples, a serious medical condition and a call or order to active duty in the Armed Forces, and the words "such as" make them illustrative rather than exhaustive. The circumstances must justify additional expenses or adjustments of current monthly income for which there is no reasonable alternative.
What must a debtor file to rebut the presumption?
An itemized statement of each additional expense or income adjustment, with documentation, attested under oath, filed as part of Form 122A-2 or as a supplemental attachment. Under In re Pageau, 383 B.R. 221 (Bankr. D.N.H. 2008), the showing must identify each item, document it, and explain why there is no reasonable alternative.
Can a change in income be a special circumstance?
Yes. Section 707(b)(2)(B)(i) permits adjustments of current monthly income, so a debtor whose six-month look-back captured income that has since terminated can present the change as a special circumstance with documentation.
What has been rejected as a special circumstance?
The reported decisions consistently reject adjustments that reflect ordinary living expenses or voluntary financial choices rather than circumstances beyond the debtor's control. In re Egebjerg, 574 F.3d 1045 (9th Cir. 2009), held that monthly repayments of a 401(k) loan are not deductible as a special circumstance.
What is the section 707(b)(3) totality test?
A backup inquiry. Even where the presumption does not arise or has been rebutted, the court may still find abuse under section 707(b)(3) if the petition was filed in bad faith or if the totality of the debtor's financial circumstances demonstrates abuse.
What are the options when Form 122A-2 triggers the presumption?
Rebut it under section 707(b)(2)(B) with documented special circumstances, or convert to Chapter 13, where the same disposable-income figure funds a plan instead of barring relief. Which path fits depends on facts this page cannot see.

## Means Test Mechanics - Section 707(b) Calculation Deep Dive [2026] - Open Bankruptcy Project

Open Bankruptcy Project

Tools

Home/Means Test Mechanics

11 U.S.C. Section 707(b)
Means Test

Means Test Mechanics: How Section 707(b) Actually Calculates

Current monthly income, IRS national and local expense standards, the presumption of abuse formula, and the regional cost-of-living variables that drive outcomes.

What the means test is and is not

The means test is the eligibility filter enacted by the Bankruptcy Abuse Prevention and Consumer Protection Act of 2005 (BAPCPA) and codified at 11 U.S.C. Section 707(b). Its function is to identify above-median-income individual consumer debtors whose Chapter 7 filings should be presumed abusive of the bankruptcy process. The test does not adjudicate the merits of a filing; it produces a numerical output that determines which procedural posture (Chapter 7 with no presumption, Chapter 7 with presumption rebuttable for special circumstances, or conversion or dismissal) applies.

The means test applies only to individual debtors whose debts are primarily consumer debts. A debtor whose debts are primarily business debts is exempt from the means test entirely, regardless of income. Whether debts are primarily consumer depends on dollar-weighted classification, not on the count of accounts. The threshold question, often dispositive, is whether mortgage debt incurred to acquire a personal residence counts as consumer debt; circuits diverge.

Step one - current monthly income (CMI)

Current monthly income is defined at 11 U.S.C. Section 101(10A) as the average monthly income from all sources received by the debtor during the six-month period ending on the last day of the calendar month immediately preceding the petition date. The definition is mechanical and backward-looking. A debtor who lost employment in the month of filing still includes prior-period wages in CMI; a debtor whose income spiked during the look-back excludes nothing.

CMI is the average of the six pre-petition calendar months. Sources included are gross wages, salary, tips, bonuses, overtime, commissions; income from operation of a business, profession, or farm; interest, dividends, and royalties; rental income; pension and retirement income; unemployment compensation (excluded only if the debtor opts the foreign-source exclusion for benefits received under the Social Security Act); regular contributions to the household from non-debtors; and amounts paid by a third party for the debtor's household expenses. Social Security benefits are expressly excluded by statute. Tax refunds are not CMI; they reflect prior-period income already counted as wages.

The CMI annualized (multiplied by twelve) is then compared to the applicable state median family income for a household of the debtor's size. The state median figures are published by the U.S. Census Bureau and updated by the U.S. Trustee Program. A debtor at or below median exits the means test at this point; no further calculation is required and there is no presumption of abuse.

Step two - the above-median calculation

An above-median debtor proceeds to the disposable-income calculation. Allowed deductions from CMI are organized into three categories: (1) IRS National Standards for food, clothing, household supplies, personal care, and miscellaneous; (2) IRS Local Standards for housing (broken into a non-mortgage component and a mortgage-or-rent component, both county-specific) and transportation (broken into ownership costs and operating costs, also locality-specific); and (3) Other Necessary Expenses, which include taxes, mandatory payroll deductions, term life insurance, court-ordered support payments, childcare, healthcare not covered by insurance, telecommunications service, and education expenses for an employment-required course or for a child under age eighteen.

The IRS Standards are not optional and not negotiable. They are fixed national or local figures published by the Internal Revenue Service for use in the Service's own collection-financial-standards program. The bankruptcy use is a borrowing of that schedule; courts have rejected challenges to the IRS Standards as the wrong measure of necessary expenses, observing that Congress incorporated them by reference and that judicial substitution of a different schedule would defeat the statutory design.

Above-median debtors also deduct (a) average monthly payments on secured debts coming due within 60 months following the petition date, calculated as the total of the next 60 months' contractual payments divided by 60; (b) priority debt obligations divided by 60; (c) the projected administrative expenses of a Chapter 13 plan, capped at the U.S. Trustee's published percentage; and (d) certain other categorical expenses identified at Section 707(b)(2)(A)(ii) through (iv).

Step three - the presumption

The output of step two is monthly disposable income. The presumption of abuse arises if monthly disposable income, multiplied by 60, is (a) at least $16,675 (the 2024-2025 indexed dollar amount; the figure is adjusted triennially under Section 104), or (b) at least $10,000 and at least 25 percent of the debtor's nonpriority unsecured debt. A debtor whose 60-month disposable income falls below both thresholds is not presumed abusive; one above either threshold is presumed abusive. The dollar thresholds are not policy guidelines; they are statutory bright lines.

The presumption is rebuttable only by demonstration of special circumstances that justify additional expenses or income adjustments and produce a re-computed disposable income below the threshold. Section 707(b)(2)(B) identifies "a serious medical condition or a call or order to active duty in the Armed Forces" as illustrative; courts have read the category narrowly, requiring the debtor to itemize each additional expense and to provide documentation. Unanticipated future expenses, ordinary lifestyle preferences, and discretionary obligations are not special circumstances.

The role of regional cost-of-living

BAPCPA delegates the calibration of necessary expenses to the IRS Standards, which are themselves county-specific for housing and transportation. The practical effect is a substantial geographic dispersion in means-test outcomes for debtors with otherwise identical income and household profiles. A household earning the same gross income in a high-cost coastal metropolitan area and in a low-cost interior county will produce different disposable-income outputs because their local housing and transportation allowances differ.

The transportation operating-cost figure is regional rather than county-specific; the ownership-cost figure depends on the number of vehicles owned (capped at two for a married household). A debtor without an auto loan or lease still receives the operating-cost allowance for any vehicle owned; courts have divided on whether the ownership-cost allowance is available to a debtor whose vehicle is paid off. The Supreme Court resolved the question for Chapter 13 purposes in Ransom v. FIA Card Services, N.A., 562 U.S. 61 (2011), holding the ownership allowance unavailable to a debtor with no current loan or lease obligation; the holding is generally applied in Chapter 7 means-test analysis as well.

Special income exclusions

Beyond the Social Security exclusion, CMI also excludes:

Payments to victims of war crimes or crimes against humanity

Payments to victims of international terrorism or domestic terrorism, on account of their status as victims

Reimbursement to certain debtors under the National Guard and Reservists Debt Relief Act for service-related period income (when applicable)

Disability benefits paid under a private long-term disability policy are CMI; only Social Security disability benefits are excluded. Veterans' benefits are excluded only if paid for a service-connected disability. The line items matter; a misclassification on the Form 122A-1 can flip a below-median debtor into above-median territory.

Household size

Household size determines which state median figure applies, which IRS National Standard tier applies, and (in some districts) which local-standard tier applies. Districts split on the proper measure: the "heads on beds" approach counts every person who shares the debtor's residence; the "income tax dependents" approach counts only persons the debtor could claim as dependents under the Internal Revenue Code; the "economic unit" approach asks whether the additional person contributes to or draws from the household economy. The choice can determine whether the debtor is above- or below-median.

Form 122A and the official forms

The means test is implemented through Official Forms 122A-1 (Statement of Your Current Monthly Income), 122A-1Supp (Statement of Exemption from Presumption of Abuse), and 122A-2 (Chapter 7 Means Test Calculation). The Administrative Office of the United States Courts updates the forms periodically. The forms are reproduced at the United States Courts website. Errors on the forms - particularly in CMI computation, household size, or allowed-expense documentation - are the most common source of trustee objection in Chapter 7 cases of above-median debtors.

The means test is mechanical, but the inputs are contestable. The arithmetic of Section 707(b) is fixed; the determinations of household size, source classification of income, special-circumstances expense allowance, and primarily-consumer-debt characterization are not. Most contested means-test outcomes turn on input determinations, not on the formula.

Research Guide

The Chapter 7 Means Test

The Chapter 7 means test under 11 U.S.C. § 707(b) screens higher-income debtors out of Chapter 7 liquidation and into Chapter 13 repayment plans. This page explains the two-step calculation, the Official Forms involved, where the median-income figures come from, and how the presumption of abuse operates.

Data updated 2026-04-21. See methodology & sources.

Written and maintained by Open Bankruptcy Project staff. Last updated 2026-09-17. Editorial policy.

Home/Means Test

Try the tool: the Chapter 7 Means Test Calculator compares your annualized income to your state's median for your household size, using the official April 2026 UST figures. Runs entirely in your browser.

Where the means test came from

The means test was added to the Bankruptcy Code by the Bankruptcy Abuse Prevention and Consumer Protection Act (BAPCPA) of 2005. Congress enacted the test to restrict Chapter 7 relief for debtors presumed to have the means to pay a meaningful portion of their debts in a Chapter 13 plan.

The test has two stages: first, comparison of the debtor's current monthly income to the applicable state median; and second, if income exceeds median, a deduction-based calculation that generates a presumption of abuse if monthly disposable income exceeds specified thresholds.

Current monthly income

Section 101(10A) defines "current monthly income" (CMI) as the average monthly income the debtor received during the six-month period ending on the last day of the calendar month before the petition date. CMI includes nearly all sources - wages, business income, rental income, interest, and most regular household contributions - with limited statutory exclusions (Social Security, certain military payments, victim-of-crime payments).

Median-income comparison

The debtor's annualized CMI is compared to the applicable state's median family income for a household of the same size, as published by the US Census Bureau and adjusted by the US Trustee Program. If CMI falls at or below median, the means test is completed on Official Form 122A-1 and the debtor qualifies for Chapter 7 without further calculation.

Where the numbers come from: median-income figures and IRS-based expense allowances are published at justice.gov/ust/means-testing. The US Trustee Program updates the figures approximately every six months.

Form 122A-2 deduction calculation

Above-median debtors complete Form 122A-2, which subtracts allowable expenses from CMI to arrive at monthly disposable income over 60 months. Categories of allowed deductions include IRS-derived national and local standards for food, housing, and transportation; actual deductions for secured debt payments over the next 60 months; priority debt; and certain additional expenses documented by the debtor.

The presumption of abuse

§ 707(b)(2) establishes a presumption of abuse if monthly disposable income multiplied by 60 exceeds the greater of 25% of non-priority unsecured claims or a statutory floor amount (adjusted periodically under § 104). A triggered presumption results in dismissal or conversion to Chapter 13, subject to rebuttal by the debtor for special circumstances.

If the means test shows no presumption of abuse, the Chapter 7 case proceeds.

If the presumption is triggered, the US Trustee or any party in interest may move to dismiss or convert under § 707(b).

Special-circumstances rebuttal under § 707(b)(2)(B) requires documented unavoidable expenses or reduced income not otherwise accounted for.

Debtors whose debts are primarily non-consumer (business) are exempt from § 707(b).

Post-BAPCPA empirical observations

Published research on BAPCPA's effects has found that the means test did shift some filings from Chapter 7 to Chapter 13, while also imposing substantial compliance costs. The Federal Judicial Center's Integrated Database shows filing volume in both chapters has moved with broader economic cycles in ways not easily separable from the test's effect.

The national district index publishes chapter-mix ratios for every US federal bankruptcy district, which lets readers compare post-BAPCPA chapter distributions across jurisdictions.

Frequently asked questions
What is the Chapter 7 means test?
The means test is a two-step calculation under 11 U.S.C. § 707(b) that screens Chapter 7 eligibility. Step one compares the debtor's current monthly income to the applicable state median. Step two, if needed, calculates monthly disposable income and creates a presumption of abuse if the disposable-income threshold is exceeded.
What is "current monthly income" for the means test?
11 U.S.C. § 101(10A) defines CMI as the debtor's average monthly income over the six-month period ending the last day of the calendar month before the petition. It includes nearly all sources of income, with specific statutory exclusions.
Where do the median-income numbers come from?
The US Trustee Program publishes median-income figures at justice.gov/ust/means-testing based on US Census Bureau data. The figures are updated approximately every six months.
Am I required to take the means test?
Every Chapter 7 consumer debtor must complete Form 122A-1, and above-median debtors must complete Form 122A-2. Debtors whose debts are primarily non-consumer are exempt from § 707(b) presumption-of-abuse analysis.
What happens if the presumption of abuse is triggered?
The US Trustee or any party in interest may move to dismiss the case or convert it to Chapter 13 under § 707(b). The debtor may rebut the presumption by showing special circumstances under § 707(b)(2)(B).

at openbankruptcyproject.org/cases/ and is intended to support
empirical research, public-records access, and educational use by debtors, attorneys,
researchers, journalists, and the general public.

The index is built from the RECAP Archive,
maintained by the Free Law Project, and every case
record links to CourtListener
as the primary source. Users who want to view a docket, pull a filing, or verify a case
detail are routed to CourtListener, where the underlying records live.

Scope: Metadata Only

The index contains metadata only - case number, case caption, chapter, and date filed --
organized by federal bankruptcy district. The Open Bankruptcy Project does not reproduce
docket PDFs, filing text, or document content of any kind. All primary-source access,
including full dockets and individual filings, is handled through CourtListener. This
design keeps the index lightweight, keeps attribution clean, and keeps traffic flowing
to the canonical primary-source host.

What the index is: a navigation and research layer on top of the RECAP
Archive. Browse by district, see case-level metadata, click through to CourtListener for
anything deeper.

What the index is not: a mirror of docket PDFs, an e-filing system, or a
replacement for PACER or CourtListener.

Purpose and Use

Federal bankruptcy data is public, but it is not always easy to navigate at the district
level or across districts. The national case index is designed to lower the cost of three
specific activities: empirical research on filing patterns across districts, public-records
access for non-specialist users who do not want to create a PACER account for a single
lookup, and educational use in law-school clinics and civics classrooms.

The dataset is published under a Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International
license and is marked up with schema.org/Dataset
structured data so that search engines, academic aggregators, and research tools can
discover and cite it.

How to Browse

The hub page at openbankruptcyproject.org/cases/ lets users enter by
district. From the district view, each case links out to its CourtListener docket page
for primary-source access. The scope is uniform across all 94 districts; the index does
not favor, highlight, or single out any district as a focus of investigation.

Data Sources and Attribution

The national case index is built from, and depends entirely on, the following upstream
infrastructure, which is credited here in accordance with the CC BY-SA 4.0 license:

Free Law Project - https://free.law/.
A 501(c)(3) nonprofit that builds and maintains open legal infrastructure, including
CourtListener and the RECAP Archive.

RECAP Archive - https://www.courtlistener.com/recap/.
A public archive of federal court filings contributed by PACER users through the RECAP
browser extension. The archive is the upstream source of the case records indexed here.

CourtListener - https://www.courtlistener.com/.
The primary-source host for every case record in the index. Each case link in the
index resolves to its CourtListener docket page.

The Open Bankruptcy Project is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit and is independent of the Free Law
Project. We are grateful to the Free Law Project and its contributors for the open
infrastructure that makes this kind of research possible.

Title 18 Companion Statutes

Obstruction Statutes

Bankruptcy fraud rarely travels alone. The same conduct that violates 18 U.S.C. section 152 or 18 U.S.C. section 157 will often also implicate one or more of the general federal obstruction statutes - sections 1001, 1503, 1505, and 1623 - which reach false statements and obstructive conduct directed at federal courts, federal agencies, and the United States Trustee Program. These four guides explain how each statute reaches into the bankruptcy system.

Last modified 2026-05-23.

Home/Obstruction Statutes

About the obstruction toolkit

The four statutes catalogued here are the federal prosecutor's general-purpose obstruction toolkit. Each operates on a different jurisdictional axis. Section 1001 reaches false statements made in any matter within the jurisdiction of the executive, legislative, or judicial branch - a sweep that covers communications with the United States Trustee, with the Office of the United States Attorney, and with federal investigative agencies. Section 1503 (the so-called omnibus clause) reaches corrupt endeavors to influence, obstruct, or impede the due administration of justice in pending federal judicial proceedings, which includes pending bankruptcy cases. Section 1505 reaches obstruction directed at pending federal agency proceedings, including United States Trustee inquiries and EOUST oversight reviews. Section 1623 criminalizes false statements made under oath in any proceeding before or ancillary to a federal court or grand jury, including 341 meetings and Rule 2004 examinations.

None of these statutes requires proof of an underlying bankruptcy violation. Each is independently chargeable, and each carries substantial maximum sentences - typically five to twenty years per count. The mental-state requirements vary: section 1001 and section 1623 require knowingly making a materially false statement; section 1503 and section 1505 require corruptly endeavoring to obstruct. Materiality and corrupt intent are the most frequently litigated elements.

The deep-dives below examine each statute in turn, surveying the elements, the Supreme Court and circuit case law, the materiality doctrine, and the practical considerations that govern when these statutes are charged alongside the bankruptcy-specific fraud provisions.

Section-by-section deep-dives

18 U.S.C. Section 1001 - False StatementsThe general federal false-statements statute reaching any materially false statement, concealment, or fraudulent representation in a matter within the jurisdiction of the executive, legislative, or judicial branch.

18 U.S.C. Section 1503 - Omnibus ObstructionThe omnibus obstruction-of-justice clause reaching corrupt endeavors to influence, obstruct, or impede the due administration of justice in pending federal judicial proceedings.

18 U.S.C. Section 1505 - Agency ObstructionThe companion provision reaching obstruction directed at pending proceedings before federal departments, agencies, and committees, including United States Trustee inquiries.

18 U.S.C. Section 1623 - False Statements Before AgencyKnowingly false statements made under oath in proceedings before or ancillary to a federal court or grand jury, including 341 meetings and Rule 2004 examinations.

Procedural note: The general five-year statute of limitations of 18 U.S.C. section 3282 governs each of these offenses. Materiality is an element of every charge under section 1001 and section 1623 (United States v. Gaudin, 515 U.S. 506 (1995)) and is decided by the jury, not the court.

18 U.S.C. Section 1001 - False Statements to the Federal Government

Doctrinal overview of the federal false-statements statute. Three statutory categories, the materiality element, the holding of Brogan v. United States, and the five-year statutory maximum.

Home › Obstruction Statutes › 18 U.S.C. Section 1001 - False Statements

What Is Section 1001?

18 U.S.C. Section 1001 is the principal federal false-statements statute. It criminalizes the knowing and willful submission of materially false information to the federal government within any matter within the jurisdiction of the executive, legislative, or judicial branch of the United States. The provision is one of the most broadly applicable criminal statutes in the federal code and is regularly charged in matters ranging from federal-program fraud to false statements made during the course of a federal investigation.

The statute's reach is unusual in two respects. First, it covers statements made outside any formal judicial proceeding, including informal interviews with federal agents. Second, it reaches concealment by trick, scheme, or device as well as affirmative misstatements and the use of false writings. Each of these categories operates independently, and a single course of conduct may satisfy more than one.

Official citation: 18 U.S.C. § 1001

Three Statutory Categories: Section 1001(a)(1)-(3)

Section 1001(a) enumerates three discrete categories of prohibited conduct. Each is independently chargeable, and the elements of each differ in subtle but consequential ways.

Section 1001(a)(1) - Concealment

Subsection (a)(1) criminalizes "falsif[ying], conceal[ing], or cover[ing] up by any trick, scheme, or device a material fact." Liability under this branch requires proof of an affirmative act of concealment together with a legal duty to disclose the concealed fact. Mere passive nondisclosure, in the absence of a duty arising by statute, regulation, contract, or the nature of the proceeding, is generally not chargeable under (a)(1).

Section 1001(a)(2) - False Statements and Representations

Subsection (a)(2) is the most frequently charged branch. It reaches "any materially false, fictitious, or fraudulent statement or representation." It applies to oral statements, written statements, and statements made through any other medium. There is no requirement that the statement be made under oath, and there is no requirement that the person to whom the statement is made be a law-enforcement officer.

Section 1001(a)(3) - False Writings and Documents

Subsection (a)(3) reaches the act of "mak[ing] or us[ing] any false writing or document knowing the same to contain any materially false, fictitious, or fraudulent statement or entry." This branch is commonly charged in matters involving forged or altered documents submitted to federal agencies, false certifications on federal forms, and the submission of falsified records to support claims for federal benefits or program funds.

The Materiality Element

All three branches of Section 1001(a) require that the false statement, concealment, or writing concern a "material" fact. The Supreme Court has defined materiality in this context as a statement having "a natural tendency to influence, or [be] capable of influencing, the decision of the decisionmaking body to which it was addressed." See United States v. Gaudin, 515 U.S. 506 (1995). Materiality is determined as an objective matter; whether the statement actually influenced the decision is not the test.

Importantly, materiality is an element of the offense and must be submitted to the jury, not decided by the court as a matter of law. Gaudin held that the Sixth Amendment requires jury determination of materiality in a Section 1001 prosecution. Statements that are trivial, immaterial to the agency function at issue, or wholly outside the scope of the matter under inquiry do not satisfy the materiality element.

Brogan v. United States and the "Exculpatory No" Doctrine

For several decades, a number of federal circuits recognized an "exculpatory no" doctrine under which a simple, unelaborated denial of wrongdoing to a federal investigator was held outside the reach of Section 1001. The Supreme Court abolished the doctrine in Brogan v. United States, 522 U.S. 398 (1998). The Court held that the text of Section 1001 contains no exception for exculpatory denials and that courts have no authority to engraft one. After Brogan, a knowing and willful false denial made to a federal agent in response to a question about a material matter is a chargeable offense under (a)(2), without regard to whether the denial was offered to avoid self-incrimination.

Brogan did not displace the Fifth Amendment privilege against self-incrimination. A person questioned by a federal agent retains the right to remain silent. The holding is narrower: silence is protected; an affirmative false denial is not.

Jurisdictional Element: "Any Matter Within the Jurisdiction"

Section 1001(a) requires that the false statement, concealment, or writing be made "in any matter within the jurisdiction of the executive, legislative, or judicial branch of the Government of the United States." This jurisdictional element is interpreted broadly. The statement need not be made directly to a federal agency; statements made to state or private entities that are administering federal programs or that are required to report to federal authorities can satisfy the jurisdictional element. See United States v. Rodgers, 466 U.S. 475 (1984).

Section 1001(b) carves out a narrow exception for statements, representations, writings, or documents submitted by a party or counsel to a judge or magistrate in a judicial proceeding. This carve-out does not extend to ancillary submissions, court-required filings outside the immediate adjudication, or statements made to court personnel other than the judge.

Section 1001(c) addresses statements within the jurisdiction of the legislative branch, including statements made in matters within the jurisdiction of congressional committees and offices, with specific definitions of administrative matters and investigations or reviews.

Mens Rea: Knowingly and Willfully

Section 1001(a) requires that the defendant act "knowingly and willfully." Federal courts have generally interpreted "knowingly" to mean that the defendant was aware of the falsity of the statement, and "willfully" to mean that the defendant acted deliberately and with knowledge that the conduct was unlawful, although the precise formulation of the willfulness instruction varies among circuits. The government need not prove that the defendant knew of the specific statute or the specific federal jurisdiction implicated.

Penalty Structure

The base statutory maximum under Section 1001(a) is five years of imprisonment, a fine under Title 18, or both. The maximum is enhanced to eight years for offenses involving international or domestic terrorism (as defined in 18 U.S.C. Section 2331) and for certain offenses involving human trafficking, sex offenses against minors, and related enumerated conduct. The statute also authorizes the imposition of a fine in accordance with the general fine provisions of 18 U.S.C. Section 3571.

Section 1001 is regularly applied in conjunction with United States Sentencing Guidelines Section 2B1.1 (for false statements that cause loss to the government or a victim) and Section 2J1.3 (for perjury-like conduct under certain circumstances).

Relationship to Other Federal Statutes

Section 1001 overlaps substantially with several other federal criminal statutes, and prosecutors frequently choose among them based on the specific factual setting:

18 U.S.C. Section 1621 - General perjury statute, requiring an oath before a competent tribunal, officer, or person.

18 U.S.C. Section 1623 - False declarations before a grand jury or court, narrower in setting but offering procedural advantages including a relaxed two-witness rule.

18 U.S.C. Section 1505 - Obstruction of agency and congressional proceedings.

18 U.S.C. Section 1519 - Destruction, alteration, or falsification of records in federal investigations and bankruptcy.

18 U.S.C. Section 287 - False, fictitious, or fraudulent claims against the United States.

Section 1001's breadth - reaching unsworn statements outside formal proceedings - makes it the default federal false-statement charge in many investigative settings, while sister statutes apply where the procedural context (oath, grand jury, agency proceeding, document destruction) calls for a more specific provision.

Related Statutory Provisions

This section operates in the same enforcement architecture as several other provisions covered on this site:

18 U.S.C. Section 1503 - Omnibus obstruction of court proceedings

18 U.S.C. Section 1505 - Obstruction of agency proceedings

18 U.S.C. Section 1623 - False declarations before grand jury or court

18 U.S.C. Section 1503 - Omnibus Obstruction of Court Proceedings

Doctrinal overview of the omnibus clause: the pending-judicial-proceeding requirement, the corrupt-endeavor standard, the juror and officer protections, and the line between Section 1503 and Sections 1505 and 1512.

Home › Obstruction Statutes › 18 U.S.C. Section 1503 - Omnibus Obstruction

What Is Section 1503?

18 U.S.C. Section 1503 is the historic federal obstruction-of-justice statute, tracing its roots to the Act of March 2, 1831. It protects the integrity of pending judicial proceedings by criminalizing interference with grand or petit jurors, court officers, and - through its omnibus clause - any "corrupt" endeavor to influence, obstruct, or impede the due administration of justice. The statute carries a statutory maximum of ten years of imprisonment, with elevated maximums for offenses involving killing or attempted killing.

Official citation: 18 U.S.C. § 1503

Statutory Structure

Section 1503(a) contains two operative components. The first half enumerates specific protected persons and prohibited acts: corrupt or threatening conduct directed at a grand or petit juror, an officer in or of any court of the United States, a magistrate judge, or a commissioner; and retaliation against any such person on account of the performance of official duties. The second half - the omnibus clause - reaches anyone who "corruptly or by threats or force, or by any threatening letter or communication, influences, obstructs, or impedes, or endeavors to influence, obstruct, or impede, the due administration of justice." Section 1503(b) supplies the penalty schedule, with enhanced maximums where killing or attempted killing is involved.

The Pending-Judicial-Proceeding Requirement

The omnibus clause of Section 1503 reaches conduct affecting the "due administration of justice." Federal courts have consistently held that this language requires the existence of a pending federal judicial proceeding at the time of the obstructive conduct. A merely contemplated investigation, an inchoate matter that has not yet generated court process, or an executive-branch inquiry that is not itself a judicial proceeding does not satisfy the pending-proceeding element. See Pettibone v. United States, 148 U.S. 197 (1893), and modern circuit applications.

The pendency requirement is important because it marks the dividing line between Section 1503 and other obstruction statutes. Conduct affecting an executive-branch agency proceeding - for example, a regulatory inquiry, an SEC investigation, or other administrative adjudication - is generally outside Section 1503 and is instead governed by Section 1505. Conduct directed specifically at a witness, victim, or informant - whether or not a proceeding is pending - is generally governed by Section 1512.

The Nexus Element: United States v. Aguilar

In United States v. Aguilar, 515 U.S. 593 (1995), the Supreme Court held that the omnibus clause requires a "nexus" between the defendant's conduct and the pending judicial proceeding. The act must have "a relationship in time, causation, or logic with the judicial proceedings" such that it has the "natural and probable effect" of interfering with the due administration of justice. A defendant's conduct must be such that he or she knew, or had reason to know, that the conduct was likely to affect the proceeding.

The nexus requirement filters out conduct that is too attenuated from the pending matter to be considered an obstruction. Statements made to an investigator who may or may not later testify before a grand jury, without more, do not satisfy the nexus requirement. The defendant must contemplate the particular proceeding the conduct will affect.

"Corruptly" and the Mens Rea Inquiry

The omnibus clause requires that the defendant act "corruptly." Courts have generally defined this as acting "with an improper purpose, personally or by influencing another, including making a false or misleading statement, or withholding, concealing, altering, or destroying a document or other information." See model jury instructions in several circuits drawing on Section 1515(b), which defines "corruptly" for purposes of Section 1512.

Although Section 1515(b)'s definition applies textually to Section 1512, federal courts have frequently looked to it as a guide in the Section 1503 setting. The Supreme Court in Arthur Andersen LLP v. United States, 544 U.S. 696 (2005), emphasized that "knowingly... corruptly persuade" requires "consciousness of wrongdoing," and lower courts have applied similar reasoning to the "corruptly" element of Section 1503. The endeavor must be undertaken with the conscious purpose of obstructing justice; ordinary advocacy, the legitimate assertion of legal rights, and good-faith argumentation are not within the statute's reach.

"Endeavor" Verb: Inchoate Liability

Section 1503 reaches not only completed obstruction but also any "endeavor" to obstruct. The "endeavor" verb makes the statute an inchoate offense: the government need not prove that the defendant's conduct actually impeded the proceeding, only that it was undertaken with the purpose, and had the natural and probable effect, of obstruction. United States v. Russell, 255 U.S. 138 (1921), is the classic articulation. This feature distinguishes Section 1503 from many other federal offenses, which require completed acts.

Juror-Protection Clause

The first portion of Section 1503(a) provides specific protection for grand and petit jurors. It criminalizes corrupt or threatening attempts to influence, intimidate, or impede any grand or petit juror, as well as retaliation against any juror on account of any verdict or indictment assented to. The juror-protection clause has independent operative force; conduct directed at a juror need not also satisfy the broader nexus and pending-proceeding requirements of the omnibus clause to be chargeable under the specific-juror branch.

The clause likewise protects officers of the court and magistrate judges from corrupt or threatening efforts to influence their official conduct. The protection extends to retaliation undertaken after the fact, recognizing that the threat of post-decision retribution can chill the independent exercise of judicial and quasi-judicial functions.

Distinguishing Section 1503 from Section 1512

The most frequently litigated boundary in this corner of Title 18 is between Section 1503's omnibus clause and 18 U.S.C. Section 1512, the witness-tampering statute. Section 1512 was enacted as part of the Victim and Witness Protection Act of 1982 and was substantially expanded by the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002. It contains comprehensive prohibitions on tampering with witnesses, victims, or informants, including conduct that occurs before any proceeding has commenced and conduct that involves official proceedings as defined in Section 1515.

Federal courts are divided on whether Section 1503 retains independent reach over witness-related conduct in light of Section 1512's coverage. The majority view is that Section 1503's omnibus clause continues to reach witness-related obstruction outside the specific procedures Section 1512 governs, but the precise allocation varies by circuit.

Distinguishing Section 1503 from Section 1505

The Section 1503 / Section 1505 line is set by the type of proceeding. Section 1503 reaches obstruction of pending federal judicial proceedings. Section 1505 reaches obstruction of pending proceedings before a federal department or agency and obstruction of certain congressional inquiries. The two statutes do not overlap; conduct affecting an administrative proceeding is generally not chargeable under Section 1503, and conduct affecting a judicial proceeding is generally not chargeable under Section 1505. The choice of statute is dictated by the forum in which the obstructed proceeding is pending.

Penalty Structure

Section 1503(b) sets the maximum term of imprisonment at ten years for most violations. Where the offense results in killing or attempted killing of a person, the maximum is the term provided for first-degree or second-degree murder or for the offense of attempted murder, as the case may be. Fines are imposed under 18 U.S.C. Section 3571.

Related Statutory Provisions

This section operates within a network of federal statutes addressing obstruction and related conduct:

18 U.S.C. Section 1001 - False statements to the federal government

18 U.S.C. Section 1505 - Obstruction of agency and congressional proceedings

18 U.S.C. Section 1623 - False declarations before grand jury or court

## 18 USC 1505 - Obstruction of Federal Agency Proceedings [2026]
