18 U.S.C. Section 1505 - Obstruction of Federal Agency Proceedings

Doctrinal overview of obstruction directed at pending proceedings before federal departments, agencies, and congressional inquiries. The Department-or-Agency definition, the corrupt-endeavor element, and the line between Section 1505 and the Sarbanes-Oxley anti-shredding statute.

Home › Obstruction Statutes › 18 U.S.C. Section 1505 - Agency Obstruction

What Is Section 1505?

18 U.S.C. Section 1505 criminalizes corrupt interference with pending proceedings before federal departments, agencies, and congressional committees. The statute fills the gap left by Section 1503, which is limited to obstruction of judicial proceedings. Where the proceeding is administrative or legislative rather than judicial, Section 1505 supplies the operative federal obstruction prohibition. The base statutory maximum is five years of imprisonment, enhanced to eight years for offenses involving domestic or international terrorism.

Official citation: 18 U.S.C. § 1505

Statutory Structure

Section 1505 has two operative paragraphs. The first paragraph addresses obstruction of proceedings arising under the Antitrust Civil Process Act, prohibiting the withholding, falsification, removal, or destruction of documentary material required to be produced under that Act. The second paragraph is the principal operative provision and reaches anyone who "corruptly, or by threats or force, or by any threatening letter or communication influences, obstructs, or impedes or endeavors to influence, obstruct, or impede the due and proper administration of the law under which any pending proceeding is being had before any department or agency of the United States, or the due and proper exercise of the power of inquiry under which any inquiry or investigation is being had by either House, or any committee of either House or any joint committee of the Congress."

"Department or Agency": Defining the Forum

The term "department or agency of the United States" is broadly construed. It encompasses the executive departments enumerated in 5 U.S.C. Section 101 (Treasury, Justice, Defense, and the other principal departments), independent regulatory agencies, and the wide range of federal administrative bodies that conduct adjudicatory or investigative proceedings under federal law. The Securities and Exchange Commission, the Internal Revenue Service, the Federal Trade Commission, the Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General, and similar entities all routinely conduct proceedings within the meaning of Section 1505.

Federal bankruptcy proceedings present a question of statutory taxonomy. The bankruptcy courts are units of the federal district courts under 28 U.S.C. Section 151, and proceedings before a bankruptcy judge are judicial proceedings within the meaning of Section 1503. However, certain adjudicative and oversight functions discharged by other components of the bankruptcy system - including the offices of the United States Trustee under 28 U.S.C. Section 581 et seq., which exercise executive-branch oversight under the Attorney General - are agency functions and may fall within Section 1505 where the conduct targets those functions rather than the court itself. The precise allocation depends on the specific forum and function targeted; the same factual conduct may implicate Section 1503, Section 1505, or both depending on the obstructed proceeding.

The Pending-Proceeding Requirement

Like Section 1503, Section 1505 requires that the proceeding be "pending" at the time of the obstructive conduct. The statute is forward-looking only in the sense that the obstruction need not have succeeded; the proceeding itself must already exist. Federal courts have held that an investigation that has not yet produced any official agency action - no formal order of investigation, no subpoena, no notice of hearing - is generally not "pending" within the meaning of Section 1505. The dividing line is often technical, and circuits differ on the precise moment at which an agency's information-gathering crosses into a "pending proceeding."

The pending-proceeding requirement is one of the principal reasons Congress enacted 18 U.S.C. Section 1519 as part of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002. Section 1519 reaches the destruction, alteration, or falsification of records in any matter "in relation to or contemplation of" any federal investigation, agency administration, or bankruptcy case - language that does not require a pending proceeding and extends to inchoate investigations.

The "Corruptly" Element and the Section 1515(b) Definition

The corrupt-endeavor element of Section 1505 was the subject of one of the more consequential statutory amendments in this area of federal law. After the D.C. Circuit's decision in United States v. Poindexter, 951 F.2d 369 (D.C. Cir. 1991), which held that "corruptly" was unconstitutionally vague as applied to the defendant's congressional testimony, Congress enacted 18 U.S.C. Section 1515(b) as part of the False Statements Accountability Act of 1996. Section 1515(b) defines "corruptly" as used in Section 1505 to mean "acting with an improper purpose, personally or by influencing another, including making a false or misleading statement, or withholding, concealing, altering, or destroying a document or other information."

The statutory definition cured the vagueness problem identified in Poindexter by tying the corrupt-purpose element to enumerated categories of conduct. Most courts now treat the Section 1515(b) definition as the operative standard for Section 1505 prosecutions.

"Endeavor" and Inchoate Reach

Section 1505 reaches "endeavors" to obstruct as well as completed obstruction. As in Section 1503, the endeavor verb makes the statute an inchoate offense: the government need not prove that the obstructive act actually impeded the proceeding, only that it was undertaken with the requisite corrupt purpose and had the natural and probable effect of obstruction. Conduct that is too remote from the proceeding to have any realistic effect generally does not satisfy the endeavor element.

Congressional-Inquiry Branch

Section 1505 also reaches corrupt obstruction of "the due and proper exercise of the power of inquiry" by either house of Congress, any committee of either house, or any joint committee. The provision is the principal federal vehicle for prosecuting interference with congressional oversight, investigations, and committee proceedings. The congressional-inquiry branch is structurally parallel to the agency-proceeding branch and incorporates the same corrupt-endeavor standard and pending-proceeding requirement.

Distinction from Section 1519

18 U.S.C. Section 1519, the anti-shredding statute enacted as part of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002, is closely related to Section 1505 but materially different in scope. Section 1519 criminalizes the knowing destruction, alteration, falsification, mutilation, or concealment of any record, document, or tangible object "with the intent to impede, obstruct, or influence the investigation or proper administration of any matter within the jurisdiction of any department or agency of the United States or any case filed under title 11, or in relation to or contemplation of any such matter or case."

Three differences are important. First, Section 1519 does not require a pending proceeding; it reaches conduct undertaken in "contemplation of" a federal matter. Second, Section 1519 explicitly covers bankruptcy cases filed under Title 11 by its own terms. Third, Section 1519 is limited to document-related conduct - destruction, alteration, falsification, concealment - while Section 1505 reaches a broader range of obstructive acts including threats and influence-peddling. Section 1519 carries a higher statutory maximum (twenty years versus five years for Section 1505).

Prosecutors frequently charge both statutes in document-destruction cases, with Section 1519 supplying the broader temporal reach and higher penalty and Section 1505 supplying the more general obstruction theory tied to specific pending proceedings.

Penalty Structure

The base maximum under Section 1505 is five years of imprisonment, a fine under Title 18, or both. Offenses involving international or domestic terrorism (as defined in 18 U.S.C. Section 2331) carry an enhanced maximum of eight years. Fines are imposed under 18 U.S.C. Section 3571.

Related Statutory Provisions

18 U.S.C. Section 1001 - False statements to the federal government

18 U.S.C. Section 1503 - Omnibus obstruction of court proceedings

18 U.S.C. Section 1623 - False declarations before grand jury or court

18 U.S.C. Section 1623 - False Declarations Before Grand Jury or Court

Doctrinal overview of false declarations under oath in federal court and grand jury settings. Narrower setting than Section 1001, the Section 1623(c) inconsistent-declarations theory, abolition of the two-witness rule, and the five-year statutory maximum.

Home › Obstruction Statutes › 18 U.S.C. Section 1623 - False Declarations

What Is Section 1623?

18 U.S.C. Section 1623 is the modern federal false-declarations statute applicable to testimony, declarations, and depositions given under oath in proceedings before or ancillary to any court or grand jury of the United States. Enacted as part of the Organized Crime Control Act of 1970, Section 1623 was designed to address proof problems that limited the practical reach of the older perjury statute, 18 U.S.C. Section 1621. Section 1623 carries a five-year statutory maximum.

Official citation: 18 U.S.C. § 1623

Setting: Narrower than Section 1001

Section 1623 differs from 18 U.S.C. Section 1001 in two structural ways. First, Section 1623 applies only to declarations made "before or ancillary to any court or grand jury of the United States" - a narrower set of forums than the executive, legislative, and judicial sweep of Section 1001. Second, Section 1623 requires that the declaration be made under oath (or under the equivalent declaration permitted by 28 U.S.C. Section 1746). Section 1001 has no oath requirement and reaches unsworn statements made to federal officers in informal settings.

The narrower setting of Section 1623 comes with procedural advantages discussed below. The trade-off is that Section 1623 is unavailable for the broad range of unsworn false statements that arise in federal investigations and administrative matters; for those settings, Section 1001 remains the operative provision.

Elements: Section 1623(a)

Section 1623(a) provides that "[w]hoever under oath (or in any declaration, certificate, verification, or statement under penalty of perjury as permitted under section 1746 of title 28, United States Code) in any proceeding before or ancillary to any court or grand jury of the United States knowingly makes any false material declaration or makes or uses any other information... knowing the same to contain any false material declaration, shall be fined under this title or imprisoned not more than five years, or both."

The elements are: (1) testimony, declaration, or other information given under oath or pursuant to Section 1746; (2) in a proceeding before or ancillary to a federal court or grand jury; (3) that contains a material false declaration; (4) that the defendant knew was false. The materiality element is governed by the same "natural tendency to influence" standard articulated by the Supreme Court in United States v. Gaudin, 515 U.S. 506 (1995), and is a jury question.

The Inconsistent-Declarations Theory: Section 1623(c)

Section 1623(c) is the provision's most distinctive feature. It permits the government to obtain a conviction by proving that the defendant made two or more declarations under oath in federal proceedings that are "irreconcilably inconsistent" to such a degree that "one of them is necessarily false." The government does not have to specify which declaration is the false one or prove the truth or falsity of either declaration independently.

Section 1623(c) was a direct response to one of the proof difficulties the government faced under Section 1621. Under the older perjury statute, the prosecution had to prove the actual falsity of the specific statement charged. A witness who told one story before the grand jury and a different story at trial could be charged with perjury for one of the statements, but the government had to identify which one was false and prove it false to the standard required by the two-witness rule. Section 1623(c) dispenses with both requirements where the inconsistency itself establishes that perjury occurred. The government may simply prove the two declarations and their irreconcilable inconsistency.

Abolition of the Two-Witness Rule: Section 1623(e)

Section 1623(e) expressly provides that "[p]roof beyond a reasonable doubt under this section is sufficient for conviction. It shall not be necessary that such proof be made by any particular number of witnesses or by documentary or other type of evidence." This provision abolishes the common-law two-witness rule for prosecutions brought under Section 1623.

At common law and under Section 1621, a perjury conviction could not rest on the testimony of a single witness contradicting the defendant's sworn statement; corroboration was required. The two-witness rule was a relic of the heightened evidentiary suspicion historically applied to perjury allegations. Section 1623(e) removed it for prosecutions under the new statute, putting Section 1623 on the same evidentiary footing as ordinary federal criminal offenses. The two-witness rule continues to apply, in modified form, in prosecutions under Section 1621.

Recantation Defense: Section 1623(d)

Section 1623(d) provides a limited recantation defense. Where the defendant, in the same continuous court or grand jury proceeding in which the false declaration was made, admits the falsity of the declaration, the prosecution is barred if (1) the recantation occurred before the falsity has substantially affected the proceeding, and (2) before it has become manifest that the falsity has been or will be exposed.

The recantation defense is conjunctive in most circuits: both conditions must be satisfied. A recantation that occurs only after the falsity has affected the proceeding or after the falsity is likely to be exposed does not qualify. Section 1623(d) is an important procedural protection for witnesses who realize they have testified falsely and wish to correct the record before the prosecution becomes irreversible.

"Ancillary to" Any Court or Grand Jury

Section 1623 reaches declarations made in proceedings "before or ancillary to" a federal court or grand jury. The "ancillary" language extends the statute beyond live testimony in open court to depositions, affidavits, declarations submitted in connection with motion practice, and similar quasi-judicial submissions. The Supreme Court in Dunn v. United States, 442 U.S. 100 (1979), held that an unsworn statement to a private attorney in a setting wholly unconnected to any pending federal proceeding is not "ancillary" to a court or grand jury, but ordinary deposition testimony and affidavits filed in federal proceedings clearly qualify.

Section 1623 versus Section 1621

The relationship between Section 1623 and the older perjury statute, 18 U.S.C. Section 1621, is one of overlapping rather than exclusive coverage. Section 1621 retains broader applicability - it covers any "competent tribunal, officer, or person" empowered to administer oaths, not just federal courts and grand juries - while Section 1623 offers the procedural advantages of the inconsistent-declarations theory and the abolition of the two-witness rule.

Prosecutors typically choose between the two statutes based on the proof posture of the case. Where the false statement was made before a federal court or grand jury and either contradicts another sworn statement or can be proved false through evidence that would not satisfy the two-witness rule, Section 1623 is generally preferred. Where the statement was made before a non-court tribunal authorized to administer oaths or where the prosecution proceeds on a single false statement provable through traditional corroborating evidence, Section 1621 may be used.

Penalty Structure

Section 1623 carries a maximum sentence of five years of imprisonment, a fine under Title 18, or both. There is no enhanced penalty schedule comparable to those in some other Title 18 provisions. Fines are imposed under 18 U.S.C. Section 3571.

Related Statutory Provisions

18 U.S.C. Section 1001 - False statements to the federal government

18 U.S.C. Section 1503 - Omnibus obstruction of court proceedings

18 U.S.C. Section 1505 - Obstruction of agency and congressional proceedings

Confirming a Plan of Reorganization

Plan Confirmation

Plan confirmation is the gateway through which a reorganizing debtor exits bankruptcy with a discharge and a binding compromise of pre-petition obligations. Each of the four reorganization chapters has its own confirmation standard, voting rules, and creditor-protection tests. These four deep-dives unpack the framework for chapter 11, chapter 12, chapter 13, and Subchapter V of chapter 11.

Last modified 2026-05-22.

Home/Plan Confirmation

About the confirmation process

Plan confirmation in bankruptcy serves two functions simultaneously: it binds creditors to a compromise of their pre-petition rights, and it triggers the discharge that gives the debtor a fresh start. The Bankruptcy Code prescribes detailed substantive and procedural standards to ensure that the compromise is fair and that creditors had meaningful opportunity to vote and object.

The confirmation framework is built on a shared scaffolding of feasibility, good faith, best-interests-of-creditors, and (in chapter 11 and Subchapter V) absolute-priority or fair-and-equitable rules. But each chapter has its own statutory section enumerating the confirmation requirements: section 1129 for chapter 11, section 1225 for chapter 12, section 1325 for chapter 13, and the cross-referenced sections 1191 and 1129(a) for Subchapter V. The differences across chapters are not cosmetic - they reflect Congress's judgment that different debtor types warrant different protections for different creditor classes.

The mechanics of confirmation also differ. Chapter 11 typically requires a disclosure statement under section 1125, solicitation of votes from impaired classes under section 1126, and a confirmation hearing that may be contested by any party in interest. Chapter 12 and chapter 13 do not require a disclosure statement (the plan itself plus the section 341 meeting serves the disclosure function), and confirmation is heard before the chapter 12/13 trustee and the bankruptcy judge on a streamlined timeline. Subchapter V eliminates the disclosure statement and the creditors' committee while preserving most other chapter 11 confirmation standards in modified form.

Chapter-by-chapter confirmation deep-dives

Chapter 11 Plan ConfirmationThe sixteen section 1129(a) confirmation requirements, the section 1129(b) cramdown alternative, absolute-priority and new-value, and the impaired-accepting-class requirement.

Chapter 12 Plan ConfirmationThe section 1225(a) confirmation requirements for family-farmer and family-fisherman reorganizations, the section 1222(b)(9) cramdown of secured creditors over collateral value, and the standing-trustee role.

Chapter 13 Plan ConfirmationThe section 1325(a) confirmation requirements, the section 1325(b) disposable-income test, the applicable-commitment-period rules, and the section 1322(b)(2) anti-modification restriction for principal-residence mortgages.

Subchapter V Plan ConfirmationSections 1181-1195 and the cross-referenced sections 1129(a) requirements, the section 1191(b) cramdown without an impaired-accepting class, the section 1191(c) fair-and-equitable test, and the SBRA-modified absolute-priority rule.

Voting note: Under section 1126(c), a class of claims accepts the plan if it is accepted by holders of at least two-thirds in amount and more than one-half in number of the allowed claims actually voting. Non-voters do not count for or against acceptance. Vote solicitation must comply with the section 1125 disclosure-statement requirements in chapter 11.

Chapter 11 Plan Confirmation: Disclosure, Voting, and Cramdown

A complete walk-through of how a Chapter 11 plan moves from filing to confirmation: disclosure statement under Section 1125, solicitation and voting under Section 1126, the sixteen confirmation requirements of Section 1129(a), nonconsensual cramdown under Section 1129(b), and the absolute priority rule.

Home › Plan Confirmation › Chapter 11 Plan

Empirical research on Chapter 11 confirmation

For docket-level data on how district courts apply the Section 1129 confirmation standards, including outcome rates for contested confirmation and cramdown rulings, see openbankruptcyproject.org/cases/. All datasets licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

Quick Answer

A Chapter 11 plan is confirmed in a sequence of statutorily defined steps. The debtor (or another plan proponent) files a written plan together with a court-approved disclosure statement under Section 1125. Creditors and interest holders then vote by class under Section 1126. At the confirmation hearing the court applies the sixteen requirements of Section 1129(a), including the best-interests test, feasibility, and good faith. If every impaired class accepts, the plan is confirmed consensually. If at least one impaired class rejects, the proponent may still obtain confirmation by cramdown under Section 1129(b), but only if the plan is "fair and equitable" and "does not discriminate unfairly," and at least one impaired class of non-insiders has accepted.

Governing provisions: 11 U.S.C. §§ 1121–1129.

The Disclosure Statement: Section 1125

Before a plan proponent may solicit votes on a Chapter 11 plan, the court must approve a written disclosure statement containing "adequate information" sufficient to enable a hypothetical reasonable investor in a particular class to make an informed judgment about the plan. 11 U.S.C. § 1125(a)(1). The disclosure statement is the bridge between the plan as a legal instrument and the creditors and equity holders who must evaluate it as an economic proposition.

Adequate information is a fact-specific standard. Courts evaluate the size and complexity of the case, the nature of the debtor's business, the sophistication of the creditor body, and the cost and feasibility of producing additional disclosure. A small-trade-creditor case will warrant a different level of detail than a publicly held debtor whose creditors include institutional bondholders.

Typical disclosure-statement contents include:

A description of the debtor's pre-petition business and the circumstances that led to bankruptcy.

Historical financial statements and projected post-confirmation operating results.

A liquidation analysis comparing creditor recoveries under the plan with what those creditors would receive in a hypothetical Chapter 7 liquidation.

A description of the classification and treatment of claims and interests under the plan.

The identity and compensation of officers and directors expected to serve after confirmation.

Identification of insiders, related-party transactions, and known litigation.

A risk-factor discussion analogous to securities-law disclosure.

The disclosure statement is itself approved at a noticed hearing. Objections at that stage typically focus on factual completeness, not on the legal merits of the plan itself. A common refrain in chambers is that disclosure-statement objections that are really plan-confirmation objections should be reserved for the confirmation hearing.

Solicitation and Voting: Section 1126

Once the disclosure statement is approved, the plan proponent transmits the plan, the disclosure statement, and ballots to all holders of claims and interests in impaired classes. Under Section 1126(c), a class of claims accepts the plan if creditors holding at least two-thirds in dollar amount and more than one-half in number of allowed claims actually voting in the class vote to accept. A class of interests accepts under Section 1126(d) if holders of at least two-thirds in amount of allowed interests actually voting accept.

An unimpaired class is "conclusively presumed" to have accepted the plan and does not vote. 11 U.S.C. § 1126(f). Conversely, a class that receives or retains nothing under the plan is "deemed not to have accepted." 11 U.S.C. § 1126(g). The deemed-rejection rule is significant: a wipe-out class need not be solicited at all, but its deemed rejection is what forces the proponent into cramdown.

Section 1126(e) permits the court to designate (disqualify) a vote that was not solicited or procured in good faith or in accordance with the Code. Designation is an extraordinary remedy and requires a showing that the voter acted with an ulterior motive untethered from a legitimate creditor interest, such as voting strategically to obtain a blocking position for a competitor.

The Sixteen Requirements of Section 1129(a)

Section 1129(a) lists sixteen separate confirmation requirements. The court must find that each applicable requirement is satisfied; the proponent bears the burden of proof by a preponderance of the evidence. The most contested provisions are described below.

1129(a)(3) — Good faith

The plan must be "proposed in good faith and not by any means forbidden by law." Good faith is measured against the totality of the circumstances and the fundamental purposes of Chapter 11 (rehabilitation and fair distribution to creditors).

1129(a)(7) — Best-interests test

Each holder of an impaired claim or interest that has not accepted the plan must receive property of a value, as of the effective date, that is "not less than" what the holder would receive in a Chapter 7 liquidation. This makes the liquidation analysis indispensable to the confirmation record.

1129(a)(8) — Class acceptance

Each class of claims or interests must either accept the plan or be unimpaired. Failure of this requirement is what makes cramdown necessary.

1129(a)(10) — At least one accepting impaired class

If any class is impaired, at least one impaired class (determined without including the acceptance of any insider) must accept the plan. This is the so-called "impaired-acceptance" requirement and operates as a structural gating mechanism for cramdown.

1129(a)(11) — Feasibility

Confirmation must not be likely to be followed by liquidation or further reorganization unless such liquidation or reorganization is itself proposed in the plan. Feasibility is proven through cash-flow projections, capital-structure analysis, and (in larger cases) expert testimony.

Cramdown: Section 1129(b)

When at least one impaired class has accepted, the court may still confirm a plan over the rejection of one or more dissenting impaired classes. Section 1129(b) requires that the plan "does not discriminate unfairly" and is "fair and equitable" with respect to each dissenting class.

Fair-and-equitable for secured claims

For a dissenting class of secured claims, the plan must (i) retain the lien and provide deferred cash payments equal to the present value of the collateral, (ii) sell the collateral free and clear with the lien attaching to proceeds, or (iii) provide the "indubitable equivalent." The Supreme Court's decision in Till v. SCS Credit Corp., 541 U.S. 465 (2004), provides the prevailing framework for computing the appropriate interest rate to discount deferred payments (the formula approach), and Associates Commercial Corp. v. Rash, 520 U.S. 953 (1997), establishes that collateral is valued at replacement value when the debtor proposes to retain it.

Fair-and-equitable for unsecured claims — the absolute priority rule

For a dissenting class of unsecured claims, the plan must either pay the class in full or ensure that no holder of a junior claim or interest receives or retains property "on account of" the junior claim or interest. This is the absolute priority rule, codified at Section 1129(b)(2)(B)(ii).

The Supreme Court in Bank of America National Trust & Savings Ass'n v. 203 North LaSalle Street Partnership, 526 U.S. 434 (1999), held that the absolute priority rule prohibits a plan that gives existing equity an exclusive right to acquire new equity for a contribution of new value, without market exposure. Earlier, in Norwest Bank Worthington v. Ahlers, 485 U.S. 197 (1988), the Court held that promises of future "sweat equity" do not satisfy the new-value exception. The boundaries of any new-value exception remain narrow and litigation-intensive.

Classification and the One-Class-One-Vote Architecture

The plan's classification scheme under Section 1122 sits upstream of the entire confirmation analysis. Section 1122(a) permits classification of claims or interests in a particular class only if the claims or interests are "substantially similar." Section 1122(b) authorizes a separate class for unsecured claims under a stated dollar amount for administrative convenience. The proponent's classification decisions shape which classes are impaired, how votes are tallied, whether the at-least-one-accepting-impaired-class requirement of Section 1129(a)(10) is met, and the contours of any cramdown.

Classification gerrymandering — placing similar creditors into different classes to manufacture an accepting class — is one of the most frequently litigated confirmation issues. Courts apply a "business reason" test that focuses on whether the separate treatment is supported by a legitimate, non-strategic justification. Common approved bases for separate classification include differences in legal rights, in collateral position, in subordination posture, and in pre-petition contractual terms. Separating identical unsecured trade claims from identical unsecured tort claims solely to obtain a vote is generally rejected.

Impairment under Section 1124

A class of claims or interests is impaired unless the plan "leaves unaltered the legal, equitable, and contractual rights" to which the holder is entitled. Even a plan that pays a creditor in full in cash on the effective date can leave the class impaired if it alters the legal terms of the underlying obligation. Unimpaired classes are conclusively presumed to accept under Section 1126(f) and do not vote.

Effect of Confirmation and Appellate Posture

Confirmation discharges the debtor (with the exceptions in Section 1141(d)) and vests property of the estate in the reorganized debtor free and clear of claims and interests except as provided in the plan. The Supreme Court in Bullard v. Blue Hills Bank, 575 U.S. 496 (2015), held in the Chapter 13 context that an order denying plan confirmation is not a final, appealable order; courts have applied analogous reasoning to Chapter 11 denials, though confirmation orders themselves are routinely treated as final and reviewable.

Once confirmed, a plan binds all creditors and equity holders whether or not they voted to accept and whether or not their claims are impaired, subject only to the limited grounds for revocation under Section 1144 (fraud, brought within 180 days) and the narrow due-process exceptions recognized in United Student Aid Funds, Inc. v. Espinosa, 559 U.S. 260 (2010).

Related Bankruptcy Code Sections

Section 1125 — Disclosure statement

Section 1126 — Acceptance of plan

Section 1129 — Confirmation requirements

Section 1141 — Effect of confirmation

Subchapter V Plan — Small business reorganization variant

## Chapter 12 Plan Confirmation: Family Farmer and Fisherman [2026]

Chapter 12 Plan Confirmation: Family Farmer and Family Fisherman

A complete walk-through of the Chapter 12 plan: family-farmer and family-fisherman eligibility, plan contents under Section 1222, confirmation requirements under Section 1225, and the distinctive Chapter 12 cramdown standards for secured agricultural debt.

Home › Plan Confirmation › Chapter 12 Plan

Empirical research on Chapter 12

Chapter 12 filings are small in number relative to the consumer chapters but concentrate in agricultural districts where seasonal income, land collateral, and federal farm-loan programs interact in distinctive ways. See openbankruptcyproject.org/cases/ for docket-level analysis. All datasets licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

Quick Answer

Chapter 12 is the bankruptcy chapter purpose-built for the family farmer and the family fisherman. It combines the rehabilitative structure of Chapter 13 (a wage-earner-style three-to-five-year plan administered by a standing trustee) with the more permissive cramdown rules of Chapter 11, all calibrated to the realities of agricultural cash flow. The plan must satisfy the content requirements of Section 1222 and the confirmation requirements of Section 1225. Chapter 12 also includes a distinctive feature: secured creditors can be crammed down on present-value terms without the impaired-class-acceptance requirement that constrains Chapter 11.

Governing provisions: 11 U.S.C. §§ 1201–1232.

Who Can File: Family Farmer and Family Fisherman

Eligibility is the gateway question. The Code defines "family farmer" and "family fisherman" in Section 101(18) and Section 101(19A), respectively. Both definitions impose four interrelated tests on individuals (and on closely held corporations or partnerships in parallel form):

Engagement in farming or commercial fishing — the debtor must be actually engaged in the relevant operation.

Aggregate debt cap — total debt cannot exceed the inflation-adjusted statutory ceiling (the cap is materially higher for farmers than for fishermen and has been adjusted multiple times since 1986).

Debt-composition test — a specified percentage of aggregate non-contingent, liquidated debt (excluding debt secured by the principal residence, with carve-outs for residences used in farming) must arise from the farming or fishing operation.

Income-composition test — for individuals, more than a specified percentage of gross income for the relevant tax year (or, alternatively, in each of the second and third preceding tax years) must come from farming or fishing.

These tests filter out hobby farms, gentleman estates, and integrated agribusinesses whose scale is more suited to Chapter 11. The chapter is intentionally limited to the operator whose livelihood is in the land or on the water.

Contents of the Plan: Section 1222

Section 1222(a) sets out the mandatory plan contents. Every Chapter 12 plan must:

Provide for submission of all or such portion of the debtor's future earnings or other future income to the trustee's supervision and control as is necessary to execute the plan.

Provide for the full payment, in deferred cash payments, of all claims entitled to priority under Section 507, unless the holder agrees otherwise (with a special carve-out, discussed below, for certain tax claims arising from disposition of farm assets).

Provide the same treatment for each claim within a class.

Section 1222(b) lists permitted provisions. Among the most operationally important:

Modification of the rights of secured creditors (with no exception for residential-mortgage holders — a striking contrast to Chapter 13's anti-modification rule for principal residences).

Cure of defaults within a reasonable time.

Payments on long-term secured debt extending beyond the plan period (the "long-term obligation" provision, parallel to Section 1322(b)(5)).

Sale of property of the estate or distribution of property to satisfy claims.

Designation of certain tax claims arising from sale of farm assets used in the farming operation as unsecured claims that are not entitled to priority — an important loophole opened by the 2005 amendments and interpreted by the Supreme Court in Hall v. United States, 566 U.S. 506 (2012), which held that post-petition capital-gains taxes do not qualify for that treatment in an individual Chapter 12 case.

Section 1222(c) sets the plan period: the plan may not exceed three years unless the court, for cause, approves a longer period; the period may not in any case exceed five years.

Confirmation Requirements: Section 1225

Section 1225(a) sets the confirmation standard. The court "shall confirm" a plan if six conditions are met:

The plan complies with the provisions of Chapter 12 and other applicable provisions of the Code.

The required filing fees have been paid.

The plan has been proposed in good faith and not by any means forbidden by law.

The plan satisfies the best-interests-of-creditors test — each unsecured claim holder receives at least the Chapter 7 liquidation value.

With respect to each allowed secured claim provided for by the plan, one of three things is true: (a) the secured creditor has accepted the plan; (b) the plan provides retention of the lien and distribution of property of a value, as of the effective date, not less than the allowed amount of the secured claim; or (c) the plan surrenders the collateral.

The debtor will be able to make all payments and otherwise comply with the plan (feasibility).

The structural advantage of Chapter 12 is what is not on the list: there is no requirement of class acceptance and no absolute-priority rule. A secured creditor's rejection cannot block confirmation if the plan satisfies Section 1225(a)(5)(B) by retaining the lien and paying present value.

The Section 1225(b) Disposable-Income Test

If the trustee or an unsecured creditor objects to confirmation, Section 1225(b) requires that the plan either pay unsecured claims in full or commit all of the debtor's "projected disposable income" for the duration of the plan to payments under the plan. Disposable income under Section 1225(b)(2) is income received by the debtor that is not reasonably necessary for the maintenance or support of the debtor or a dependent, or for payment of expenses necessary for the continuation, preservation, and operation of the debtor's farming or fishing business.

The business-expense carve-out mirrors the language later imported into Subchapter V. This is the practical mechanism by which Chapter 12 preserves an operating margin for the next planting season, the next vessel-maintenance cycle, or the next equipment-replacement event.

Cramdown of Secured Agricultural Debt

The Chapter 12 cramdown standard under Section 1225(a)(5)(B) requires the plan to provide the secured creditor with deferred cash payments of a value, as of the effective date, "not less than the allowed amount of such claim." Computing that present value requires the application of an appropriate discount rate. The Supreme Court's reasoning in Till v. SCS Credit Corp., 541 U.S. 465 (2004), arose under Chapter 13 but has been widely applied to Chapter 12 cramdown as well: courts begin with the national prime rate and adjust upward to reflect the risk of nonpayment. The size and basis of the upward adjustment is the most common evidentiary battleground.

Collateral valuation follows the principles articulated in Associates Commercial Corp. v. Rash, 520 U.S. 953 (1997): when the debtor proposes to retain and use the collateral, valuation looks to replacement value rather than foreclosure value. For specialized agricultural equipment, that distinction can be the difference between feasibility and surrender.

A distinctive Chapter 12 feature, recognized in early appellate decisions interpreting the chapter's secured-creditor cramdown, is that the long-term-obligation provision of Section 1222(b)(5) permits secured payments to extend beyond the three-to-five-year plan period. A real-estate mortgage with a thirty-year amortization may be reinstated and cured on its original terms, with deferred-cash present-value treatment confined to any deficiency or modified principal balance. This combination of long-amortization preservation with present-value cramdown of the modified portion is what allows operating farms and fishing operations to right-size secured debt without forcing surrender of the underlying asset.

The Chapter 12 Trustee and Plan Administration

Chapter 12 cases are administered by a standing trustee appointed under Section 1202, modeled in significant respects on the Chapter 13 standing-trustee system but with adjustments reflecting the chapter's operating-business orientation. The trustee receives plan payments, distributes funds to creditors, monitors compliance with the plan, and serves as a check on the debtor's continued performance.

Unlike the Chapter 11 estate, the Chapter 12 debtor remains in possession of property of the estate under Section 1203 and continues to operate the farm or fishing business. The trustee is not a debtor-in-possession's adversary in the day-to-day operation but functions as a distribution agent and a fiduciary check at moments of plan modification, default, and conversion. The standing-trustee model spreads administrative cost across the chapter's caseload, an essential feature given Chapter 12's relatively low filing volume in most districts.

Plan modification under Section 1229

Section 1229 permits the debtor, the trustee, or an unsecured creditor to seek post-confirmation modification of the plan at any time before completion. Modifications commonly respond to harvest variability, market price moves, weather and disease events affecting livestock or crops, and gains or losses from the sale of equipment or land. The flexibility of the modification mechanism is one of the chapter's most important practical features: a rigid plan that cannot survive an off-year is no rehabilitation plan at all.

Effect of Confirmation and Discharge

Under Section 1227, confirmation binds the debtor and each creditor, secured or unsecured, whether or not the creditor objected to or accepted the plan. Property of the estate vests in the debtor on confirmation, free and clear of any claim or interest of any creditor provided for by the plan. The Chapter 12 discharge under Section 1228 is entered after the debtor completes all payments under the plan, with the broader hardship-discharge alternative in Section 1228(b) available where circumstances beyond the debtor's control (drought, flood, market collapse, vessel loss) make completion impracticable.

Related Bankruptcy Code Sections

Section 1221 — Filing of the plan

Section 1222 — Contents of the plan

Section 1225 — Confirmation

Section 1228 — Discharge

Chapter 13 Plan Confirmation: Plan Contents, Confirmation, and the Disposable-Income Test

A complete walk-through of how a Chapter 13 plan is confirmed: mandatory and permissive plan contents under Section 1322, the confirmation requirements of Section 1325, the applicable commitment period, projected disposable income after Hamilton v. Lanning, and the doctrine of lien stripping in Chapter 13.

Home › Plan Confirmation › Chapter 13 Plan

Empirical research on Chapter 13 confirmation

Chapter 13 confirmation outcomes vary enormously by district, by trustee, and by judge. Confirmation timelines, completion rates, and conversion rates are all available at openbankruptcyproject.org/cases/. All datasets licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

Quick Answer

A Chapter 13 plan is the centerpiece of an individual debtor's reorganization. The debtor files the plan within fourteen days of the petition (Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 3015(b)), and the contents of the plan are governed by Section 1322. The court applies the confirmation requirements of Section 1325, including the best-interests test, the good-faith test, the secured-creditor cramdown standard, and (for above-median-income debtors) the projected-disposable-income test. The plan must run for the applicable commitment period — three or five years — determined by the debtor's income relative to the state median.

Governing provisions: 11 U.S.C. §§ 1321–1330.

Contents of the Plan: Section 1322

Section 1322(a) lists four mandatory provisions. The plan must:

Provide for the submission of all or such portion of future earnings or other future income as is necessary for execution of the plan.

Provide for full payment, in deferred cash payments, of all priority claims under Section 507 (subject to limited exceptions for domestic-support obligations assigned to a governmental unit and certain tax priorities).

Provide the same treatment for each claim within a particular class.

Provide for the payment of post-petition interest on nondischargeable unsecured claims (added by BAPCPA in 2005, to the extent the debtor has projected disposable income to fund it).

Section 1322(b) lists twelve permissive provisions. Several are case-defining in practice:

1322(b)(2): The plan may modify the rights of holders of secured claims, other than a claim secured only by a security interest in real property that is the debtor's principal residence. The anti-modification clause for primary residences is the source of decades of "lien-stripping" litigation discussed below.

1322(b)(3): The plan may cure or waive any default.

1322(b)(5): Notwithstanding 1322(b)(2), the plan may provide for cure of any default within a reasonable time and maintenance of payments while the case is pending on any claim — including a home mortgage — on which the last payment is due after the plan period. This is the principal mechanism for saving a home from foreclosure in Chapter 13.

Section 1322(d) caps the plan period at five years, and at three years for below-median-income debtors absent cause to extend.

Confirmation Requirements: Section 1325(a)

Section 1325(a) lists nine confirmation requirements that always apply. The court "shall confirm" the plan if:

The plan complies with Chapter 13 and other applicable provisions of the Code.

Filing fees have been paid.

The plan has been proposed in good faith and not by any means forbidden by law.

Best-interests test: the value, as of the effective date, of property distributed to each unsecured claim holder is not less than what the holder would receive in Chapter 7.

For each secured claim provided for by the plan: (i) the secured creditor has accepted; (ii) the plan retains the lien and provides distribution of present value not less than the allowed secured amount; or (iii) the debtor surrenders the collateral.

The debtor will be able to make all payments and otherwise comply with the plan (feasibility).

The petition was filed in good faith.

The debtor has paid post-petition domestic-support obligations as they came due.

The debtor has filed all required tax returns under Section 1308.

The Supreme Court's decision in United Student Aid Funds, Inc. v. Espinosa, 559 U.S. 260 (2010), held that even a confirmation order that improperly discharged a student loan without an adversary proceeding was not "void" under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 60(b)(4), but only "voidable," and could not be collaterally attacked years later. The opinion is a strong endorsement of confirmation finality and a cautionary lesson for creditors who fail to object at the right time.

Cramdown of Secured Claims and the Till Rate

Section 1325(a)(5)(B) permits cramdown of a non-residential secured claim by retaining the lien and distributing present value equal to the allowed secured amount. In Till v. SCS Credit Corp., 541 U.S. 465 (2004), a plurality of the Supreme Court adopted the "formula" or "prime-plus" approach: start with the national prime rate and adjust upward to reflect the risk of nonpayment. Lower courts have largely converged on a one-to-three-percent upward adjustment in routine cases, with greater adjustments available on a fact-specific showing.

For valuation of the collateral, Associates Commercial Corp. v. Rash, 520 U.S. 953 (1997), requires replacement value — "the price a willing buyer in the debtor's trade, business, or situation would pay to obtain like property from a willing seller" — when the debtor retains and uses the collateral. The 2005 amendments added the "hanging paragraph" after Section 1325(a)(9), eliminating cramdown for purchase-money car loans on vehicles acquired for personal use within 910 days of filing.

Section 1325(b): Applicable Commitment Period and Projected Disposable Income

If the trustee or an allowed unsecured creditor objects to confirmation, Section 1325(b) requires the plan to commit either (i) the value of property distributed under the plan to be not less than the allowed amount of each unsecured claim, or (ii) all of the debtor's projected disposable income for the applicable commitment period to payments under the plan.

Applicable commitment period

Section 1325(b)(4) sets the applicable commitment period at three years for below-median-income debtors and five years for above-median-income debtors. The Supreme Court in Hamilton v. Lanning, 560 U.S. 505 (2010), endorsed a "forward-looking" approach to projected disposable income: courts begin with the historical Form 122C calculation but may adjust for known or virtually certain changes in the debtor's income or expenses.

Projected disposable income

The mechanical calculation begins with current monthly income (the six-month average) and subtracts the expense allowances permitted by Section 707(b)(2) for above-median-income debtors or reasonably necessary expenses for below-median-income debtors. The forward-looking adjustments approved in Lanning — loss of a job, end of a temporary side income, retirement of a major debt — can move the calculation substantially in either direction.

Lien Stripping in Chapter 13

The Supreme Court in Nobelman v. American Savings Bank, 508 U.S. 324 (1993), held that Section 1322(b)(2)'s anti-modification clause prevents stripping down a partially secured residential mortgage to the value of the collateral, even where the collateral is worth less than the claim. A junior mortgage that is wholly unsecured (the senior debt exceeds the value of the home), however, is generally treated by lower courts as not "secured" within the meaning of 1322(b)(2) and may be stripped off entirely. That distinction — partial undersecuring versus complete undersecuring — is the operational dividing line.

For non-residential secured claims, valuation under Section 506(a) permits the plan to strip the claim down to the value of the collateral. Excess unsecured deficiency is then paid on the same terms as other general unsecured claims.

Post-Confirmation Modification: Section 1329

Section 1329 permits the debtor, the trustee, or an allowed unsecured creditor to seek modification of a confirmed plan to increase or reduce payments, extend or reduce the time for payments, or alter the amount of distribution to a particular creditor whose claim is paid other than under the plan. The modification must continue to satisfy the Section 1325(a) confirmation requirements, but the plan period may not be extended past five years from the date the first payment was due under the original plan.

The Supreme Court in Bullard v. Blue Hills Bank, 575 U.S. 496 (2015), held that an order denying confirmation of a Chapter 13 plan is not a final, appealable order — the debtor's remedy is to file a modified plan and pursue confirmation again. The opinion narrows the appellate routes available to a debtor whose original plan is rejected and reinforces the iterative nature of Chapter 13 plan confirmation.

Effect of Confirmation and Discharge

Under Section 1327(a), the provisions of a confirmed Chapter 13 plan bind the debtor and each creditor, whether or not the creditor objected to or accepted the plan. Property of the estate vests in the debtor on confirmation under Section 1327(b), free and clear of any claim or interest of any creditor provided for by the plan. The Section 1328(a) discharge follows completion of all payments and is broader than the Chapter 7 discharge in important respects (no Section 727(a)(8) eight-year bar applies to the underlying chapter, and certain non-priority unsecured claims that would survive in Chapter 7 can be discharged in Chapter 13).

The Supreme Court's enforcement-of-finality holding in United Student Aid Funds, Inc. v. Espinosa, 559 U.S. 260 (2010), is particularly important in Chapter 13 because the long plan period invites creditor inattention. A creditor that fails to object at confirmation generally cannot collaterally attack the order years later, even where the plan provision is legally questionable. The corollary for debtors is that confirmation provisions designed to bind a particular creditor must be drafted with conspicuous clarity and supported by adequate notice.

Related Bankruptcy Code Sections

Section 1325 — Confirmation of plan

Section 1328 — Discharge

Section 1329 — Modification of plan after confirmation

Subchapter V Plan: Disposable Income, 1191(b) Cramdown, and Plan Modification

A practitioner-level deep dive into the Subchapter V plan: how projected disposable income is calculated under Section 1191(d), how nonconsensual confirmation under Section 1191(b) modifies the traditional fair-and-equitable test, and how Sections 1193 and 1329 govern pre- and post-confirmation modification.

Home › Plan Confirmation › Subchapter V Plan

Empirical research on Subchapter V

Subchapter V has rapidly become the dominant small-business reorganization vehicle since the 2020 effective date of the SBRA. Filing volumes, confirmation rates, and outcome patterns are tracked at openbankruptcyproject.org/cases/. For an overview of related confirmation strategy, see Subchapter V plan-confirmation strategy. All datasets licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

Quick Answer

Subchapter V is the Small Business Reorganization Act regime, codified at 11 U.S.C. §§ 1181–1195. The plan, filed by the debtor under Section 1189 within ninety days of the order for relief, is confirmed either consensually under Section 1191(a) (the standard Section 1129(a) requirements apply, except for paragraph 15) or nonconsensually by cramdown under Section 1191(b). The cramdown path dispenses with the absolute priority rule and the impaired-acceptance requirement and substitutes a modified "fair and equitable" standard whose centerpiece is the commitment of projected disposable income for a three-to-five-year period. Section 1193 governs modification; Section 1329 (as cross-applied) governs certain post-confirmation modifications in the deferred-discharge regime.

Governing provisions: 11 U.S.C. §§ 1181–1195; cross-applied to selected Chapter 11 sections by Section 1181(a).

Mechanics of the Disposable-Income Calculation

The most operationally significant innovation of the Subchapter V cramdown regime is the disposable-income definition in Section 1191(d). Disposable income is income received by the debtor that is not reasonably necessary for:

The maintenance or support of the debtor or a dependent of the debtor;

A domestic-support obligation that first becomes payable after the date of the filing of the petition; or

The payment of expenditures necessary for the continuation, preservation, or operation of the business of the debtor.

The third prong — the business-expense deduction — is the structural feature that distinguishes Subchapter V from consumer Chapter 13. A Subchapter V debtor running an operating business can deduct payroll, rent, inventory, equipment leases, insurance, utilities, professional fees, and tax obligations before computing the income that must be committed to unsecured creditors. Capital reserves necessary to preserve operations are generally treated as deductible; aggressive owner compensation, by contrast, draws scrutiny on the "reasonably necessary for support" prong.

Projection mechanics

The statute speaks of projected disposable income, which courts have generally interpreted by reference to the forward-looking framework of Hamilton v. Lanning, 560 U.S. 505 (2010). Although Lanning arose in Chapter 13, its instruction that courts may depart from a mechanical historical calculation in light of known or virtually certain changes in income or expenses is widely applied in Subchapter V. The result is that the debtor's projection model becomes a contested issue at confirmation:

Revenue projections must be supported by a reasonable forecasting methodology (typically a baseline tied to historical performance, with documented adjustments).

Expense projections should distinguish fixed and variable costs and capture seasonal patterns.

The debtor should explain capital-expenditure assumptions, equipment-replacement cycles, and any planned changes in the scale of operations.

An owner-compensation policy should be articulated and tied to comparable-business benchmarks where available.

A useful sanity check is whether the projected disposable-income line is consistent with the cash-flow line in the same plan's feasibility analysis. Inconsistencies between these two numbers are a common confirmation-objection target.

Nonconsensual Confirmation: Section 1191(b)

If all consensual confirmation requirements are met except for Section 1129(a)(8) (class acceptance), Section 1129(a)(10) (the impaired-acceptance requirement), and Section 1129(b) (the standard cramdown / absolute-priority regime), Section 1191(b) provides that the court "shall… confirm the plan notwithstanding the requirements of such paragraphs" if the plan does not discriminate unfairly and is fair and equitable.

Three structural consequences follow from this provision:

No impaired-acceptance gating requirement. Unlike standard Chapter 11, a Subchapter V plan can be confirmed without at least one consenting impaired class of non-insiders.

No absolute priority rule. Existing equity may retain its interest even if unsecured creditors are not paid in full, provided the disposable-income commitment is satisfied. This eliminates the LaSalle (Bank of America National Trust & Savings Ass'n v. 203 North LaSalle Street Partnership, 526 U.S. 434 (1999)) and Ahlers (Norwest Bank Worthington v. Ahlers, 485 U.S. 197 (1988)) obstacles that have historically constrained small-business Chapter 11 cases.

Deferred discharge. Under Section 1192, when confirmation is nonconsensual, the discharge is not entered until the debtor completes all payments due within the first three to five years of the plan. This creates a strong incentive to negotiate toward consensual confirmation under 1191(a), where discharge is immediate.

The Modified Fair-and-Equitable Test: Section 1191(c)

Section 1191(c) modifies the "fair and equitable" standard for Subchapter V cramdown. Three components matter at confirmation:

Secured claims

Subsection 1191(c)(1) incorporates Section 1129(b)(2)(A) for secured claims. The plan must provide retention of the lien with deferred payments equal to the present value of the collateral (the Till v. SCS Credit Corp., 541 U.S. 465 (2004), framework controls the rate calculation), sale subject to credit-bidding, or the indubitable equivalent. Collateral is valued at replacement value under Associates Commercial Corp. v. Rash, 520 U.S. 953 (1997), when the debtor proposes to retain it.

Unsecured claims — disposable-income commitment

For unsecured claims, in lieu of the absolute priority rule, Section 1191(c)(2) requires either:

1191(c)(2)(A): the plan provides that all of the debtor's projected disposable income to be received in the three-to-five-year period beginning on the date of the first payment under the plan will be applied to make payments under the plan; or

1191(c)(2)(B): the plan distributes property of a value, as of the effective date, equal to the projected disposable income of the debtor for that period.

The (A)/(B) choice is consequential. Under (A), the debtor commits a stream of future income subject to performance risk; under (B), the debtor commits a present-value lump sum, often funded by a third-party contribution or sale proceeds, with no performance risk in the income stream.

Reasonable likelihood and protective remedies

Subsection 1191(c)(3) imposes two further requirements: a reasonable likelihood that the debtor will be able to make all payments, and appropriate remedies (which may include the liquidation of nonexempt assets) to protect creditors if the payments are not made. These are bridges between feasibility and enforcement; a thoughtful plan addresses both with reserves, milestone reporting, and default triggers.

Pre-Confirmation Modification: Section 1193(a)

Section 1193(a) permits the debtor to modify the plan at any time before confirmation, subject only to the underlying plan-content requirements of Sections 1122 and 1123. Practical use cases include refining the disposable-income calculation in response to trustee or creditor objections, adjusting the treatment of a particular class to capture a swing vote, or substituting (A) for (B) under Section 1191(c)(2) after the financial picture changes.

Post-Confirmation Modification: Section 1193(b)–(d) and the Section 1329 Interface

Section 1193(b) governs post-confirmation modification of a plan confirmed consensually under 1191(a). The debtor (and only the debtor) may modify the plan at any time after confirmation but before substantial consummation. The modified plan must continue to meet Section 1122 and 1123 requirements; the court may confirm the modification if the circumstances warrant.

Section 1193(c) governs post-confirmation modification of a plan confirmed nonconsensually under 1191(b). Here the debtor may modify the plan at any time within the three-to-five-year period and on the same circumstances-warranted standard. The longer modification window in the cramdown regime reflects the longer payment period and the deferred-discharge structure.

Section 1193(d) provides for binding effect of confirmed modifications on all creditors, again subject to the underlying confirmation standards. The Subchapter V trustee, where one remains in office, plays a continuing role in evaluating and recommending action on modifications.

The Section 1329 interface

Section 1329 of the Code governs Chapter 13 plan modification and is not, strictly, applied within Subchapter V; Section 1181(a) does not list 1329 among the Chapter 11 provisions made inapplicable, but the statutory home for Subchapter V modification is 1193 itself. The relevant cross-reference for practitioners is conceptual: courts comparing the deferred-discharge Subchapter V regime to Chapter 13 frequently borrow Section 1329 reasoning on issues such as substantial change in circumstances and the appropriate standard for trustee-initiated modification. The Supreme Court's interpretation of the analogous Chapter 13 framework in Hamilton v. Lanning, supra, and the appellate finality teaching of Bullard v. Blue Hills Bank, 575 U.S. 496 (2015), inform how lower courts evaluate the timing and reviewability of modification orders in Subchapter V as well.

Discharge Finality and the Espinosa Lesson

Once a Subchapter V plan is confirmed, the binding effect of confirmation on creditors is broad. The Supreme Court's holding in United Student Aid Funds, Inc. v. Espinosa, 559 U.S. 260 (2010), that even a confirmation order that improperly granted relief was not "void" but only "voidable" applies with full force in the Subchapter V context. Creditors who fail to object to a plan provision on a known basis — including disposable-income mathematics, a defective remedies clause, or an aggressive owner-compensation policy — will generally find the issue foreclosed once confirmation becomes final and non-appealable.

## Post-Petition Transfer Rules - Section 549 Avoidance [2026] - Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/post-petition-transfer-rules/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Home/Post-Petition Transfer Rules

11 U.S.C. Section 549
Avoidance

Post-Petition Transfer Rules

Section 549 avoidance of unauthorized post-petition transfers, the two-year limitations period, the trustee's burden, and good-faith transferee defenses.

The doctrinal distinction from pre-petition avoidance

The Bankruptcy Code's avoidance arsenal divides into two broad categories. Pre-petition avoidance powers - the trustee's avoidance of preferences (Section 547), fraudulent transfers (Section 548), and unperfected statutory liens (Section 545) - reach transfers made before the petition date and require proof of insolvency, fraudulent intent, or other substantive elements. Post-petition avoidance under Section 549 reaches transfers made after the petition date and operates on a different logic entirely: the property of the estate is owned by the estate and may not be transferred without authorization.

Section 549(a) - the basic rule

Section 549(a) provides that the trustee may avoid a transfer of property of the estate that (1) is made after the commencement of the case, and (2)(A) is authorized only under Section 303(f) or Section 542(c) (involuntary-case gap-period transactions and good-faith pre-notice transfers to the debtor), or (2)(B) is not authorized under the Code or by the court.

The structure is starkly simple. The trustee establishes (i) that the transfer occurred after the petition date, (ii) that the property transferred was property of the estate at the time of transfer, and (iii) that the transfer was not authorized by either the Code or by court order. No proof of insolvency, fraudulent intent, or value-for-value exchange is required. The doctrinal anchor is that estate property may not leave the estate without permission; permission must come from the Code itself, from a court order, or (in narrow circumstances) from the operating-business authority that Section 363(c) confers on a Chapter 11 debtor-in-possession or Chapter 12 or 13 trustee.

What counts as property of the estate

The reach of Section 549 depends on what constitutes property of the estate at the time of transfer. Section 541 defines the estate as comprising "all legal or equitable interests of the debtor in property as of the commencement of the case," plus certain post-petition acquisitions (proceeds of estate property, post-petition earnings of an individual Chapter 11 debtor, and others). In Chapter 13, post-petition earnings of the debtor become property of the estate under Section 1306(a); in Chapter 7, post-petition earnings of an individual debtor generally do not.

The chapter-specific scope of the estate determines whether a particular post-petition asset transfer is reachable under Section 549. A wage payment to a Chapter 13 debtor that the debtor then transfers to a friend may be avoidable under Section 549; the same wage transfer by a Chapter 7 debtor generally is not, because the post-petition wages are not estate property.

Authorization paths

Post-petition transfers are commonly authorized through one of several paths:

Section 363(b) ordinary motion authority: a trustee or debtor-in-possession may use, sell, or lease property of the estate other than in the ordinary course of business after notice and a hearing

Section 363(c) ordinary-course authority: a trustee or debtor-in-possession may use, sell, or lease property of the estate in the ordinary course of business without prior court approval, provided the debtor is authorized to operate the business under Sections 1108, 1183, 1204, or 1304

Section 364 financing authority: post-petition borrowing with court approval may include the use of estate property as collateral

Specific court orders: cash collateral orders under Section 363(c)(2), wage motion orders, critical-vendor orders, and other targeted approvals

A post-petition transfer outside of any of these authorizations is presumptively avoidable. The trustee's burden under Section 549 is met by demonstrating the absence of authorization; the transferee bears the burden of identifying the authorization on which it relied.

Section 549(c) - the real-property good-faith transferee defense

Section 549(c) provides a narrow safe harbor for good-faith purchasers of real property. The transfer of an interest in real property to a good-faith purchaser without knowledge of the bankruptcy case is not avoidable if the transfer was made for present fair equivalent value and before the filing of a notice of the petition in the real estate records of the county where the property is located.

The defense has four elements: (1) the transfer must be of real property; (2) the transferee must be a good-faith purchaser; (3) the transferee must lack knowledge of the case; and (4) the transferee must have given present fair equivalent value. The defense does not extend to personal property or to transfers made after a notice of the petition was filed in the local real-estate records. The notice-filing prong is the principal practical safeguard for the estate: counsel for the trustee (or for the debtor-in-possession) should file a notice of the bankruptcy case in the recording office of every county in which the debtor owns real property promptly after the petition.

Section 549(d) - the two-year statute of limitations

Section 549(d) imposes a two-year statute of limitations on Section 549 actions: an action under Section 549 may not be commenced after the earlier of (1) two years after the date of the transfer sought to be avoided, or (2) the time the case is closed or dismissed. The two-year period runs from the date of the transfer, not from the date the trustee discovered it.

The limitations rule is jurisdictionally rigid. Courts have generally declined to apply equitable tolling, even where the trustee can show that the transferee actively concealed the transfer, except in narrow cases that fit traditional fraudulent-concealment doctrine.

Section 550 - recovery from the transferee

An avoided transfer's recovery is governed by Section 550. The trustee may recover the property transferred or its value from (1) the initial transferee, (2) the entity for whose benefit the transfer was made, or (3) any immediate or mediate transferee of the initial transferee. Section 550(b) provides a good-faith defense for subsequent transferees - the trustee may not recover from a transferee who took for value, in good faith, and without knowledge of the voidability of the transfer.

The initial transferee defense is narrower. The initial transferee has no analog to the Section 550(b) good-faith defense; the only good-faith defense available to an initial transferee is the Section 549(c) real-property defense. The distinction between initial and subsequent transferees often controls the recovery outcome; the line is drawn by reference to control over the transferred funds, not by formal title.

Common Section 549 scenarios

Continued sale of business inventory after Chapter 7 conversion

A debtor whose Chapter 11 case is converted to Chapter 7 may continue to make ordinary-course sales for some period. Sales made after the Chapter 7 trustee's appointment, without the Chapter 7 trustee's authorization, are avoidable. The trustee may recover from the customers (as initial transferees) or from the debtor's bank account (as the recipient of the proceeds).

Bank-account funds paid by the debtor's bank to creditors

A bank may continue to honor the debtor's pre-petition checks or to execute pre-petition automatic-payment authorizations after the petition. The payments are post-petition transfers of estate property (the debtor's bank-account balance) and are generally avoidable unless authorized by court order (such as a wage-or-utility motion order).

Recordation of a security interest after the petition

The recordation of a security interest in real property after the petition is itself a post-petition transfer subject to Section 549 (unless it qualifies under Section 362(b)(3) as completing the perfection of a prior security interest). Section 549 dovetails with Section 362(a)(4), under which the recordation may also be a stay violation.

Real-property sale by the debtor

A Chapter 7 debtor's post-petition sale of a personal residence is avoidable unless authorized. The good-faith purchaser may invoke the Section 549(c) defense if the trustee did not file a notice of the petition in the real-estate records before the sale - one of the principal practical reasons trustees promptly record such notices.

Section 549 is strict-liability avoidance with narrow defenses. Unlike pre-petition fraudulent-transfer avoidance, Section 549 does not require proof of intent, insolvency, or absence of value. A transferee receiving estate property after the petition date assumes the risk of avoidance unless it can identify the specific authorization on which it relied. The Section 549(c) real-property defense and the Section 550(b) subsequent-transferee defense are the principal protections.

## Filing Bankruptcy Pro Se (Without an Attorney) - Procedural Guide

Research Guide

Filing Bankruptcy Without an Attorney

A natural person may file an individual bankruptcy case without an attorney - "pro se." Corporate debtors generally cannot, under Rowland v. California Men's Colony. This page outlines the procedural framework for pro se filers: who's eligible, which Official Forms are required, and what free resources exist from the federal courts and other nonprofits.

Data updated 2026-04-21. See methodology & sources.

Written and maintained by Open Bankruptcy Project staff. Last updated 2026-09-18. Editorial policy.

Home/Pro Se

Who can proceed pro se

Under 28 U.S.C. § 1654, parties in federal court may appear and conduct their own cases. In bankruptcy, this right applies fully to individual debtors in their own Chapter 7, 13, or 11 cases. Corporate debtors (including LLCs and partnerships) are generally barred from proceeding pro se on case-level and plan-level matters under the rule from Rowland v. California Men's Colony, Inc., 506 U.S. 194 (1993).

Required filings to open a case

Every bankruptcy petition filing requires a core set of Official Forms, available free at uscourts.gov/forms/bankruptcy-forms. The exact set varies by chapter but core items include:

Form 101 - Voluntary Petition for Individuals Filing for Bankruptcy

Form 106 Summary and Schedules A/B through J - assets, debts, income, expenses

Form 107 - Statement of Financial Affairs for Individuals

Form 121 - Statement About Your Social Security Numbers (filed separately under Rule 9037, not part of the public record)

Form 122A-1 (Chapter 7) or Form 122C-1 (Chapter 13) - means test / current monthly income

Certificate of Credit Counseling (pre-filing requirement under 11 U.S.C. § 109(h))

Filing fee, installment application (Form 103A), or Chapter 7 fee waiver application (Form 103B)

Pre-filing credit counseling and post-filing debtor education

Section 109(h) requires individual debtors to complete an approved credit-counseling course within 180 days before filing. Section 727(a)(11) requires an approved debtor-education course before discharge can be entered. Both courses are offered by agencies on the US Trustee Program's approved list at justice.gov/ust/list-credit-counseling-agencies.

The 341 meeting

Every bankruptcy case includes a meeting of creditors under 11 U.S.C. § 341, typically held 21–50 days after filing. The case trustee conducts the meeting; the debtor answers questions under oath. Pro se debtors are expected to attend in person or by video (local practice varies) and to provide any documents requested by the trustee.

Common pitfalls for pro se filers

Incomplete exemption claims. State and federal exemption schedules determine which property is protected. Missing or inaccurate claims expose assets. See the exemptions overview.

Unredacted personal information. Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 9037 requires redaction of Social Security Numbers, dates of birth, financial account numbers, and minor-child identifiers in filed documents. Form 121 is an exception - it is explicitly not part of the public case file.

Missed deadlines. Statements of Intention (Form 108) for secured debt, reaffirmation agreements, and amendments all have strict windows.

Credit-counseling timing errors. The course must be completed within 180 days before filing.

Incorrect means-test calculation. Errors in current-monthly-income or expense deductions can delay or derail the case. See the means test guide.

Free resources

Federal bankruptcy courts publish local rules and pro se filer guides on their websites - each court's page is linked from the national district index.

Many law schools operate free consumer-bankruptcy clinics for qualifying low-income filers.

The RECAP Archive provides free access to federal court documents that would otherwise require paid PACER access.

Chapter 7 and Chapter 13 forms and instructions are free at uscourts.gov/forms/bankruptcy-forms.

The Open Bankruptcy Project's free discharge-eligibility screener checks § 1328(f) and § 727(a) timing bars based on a user-supplied filing history.

Frequently asked questions
Can I file bankruptcy without a lawyer?
An individual may file a bankruptcy case pro se under 28 U.S.C. § 1654. Corporate debtors (including LLCs and partnerships) generally cannot proceed pro se on case-level matters under Rowland v. California Men's Colony, 506 U.S. 194 (1993).
Where are the bankruptcy forms?
Official federal bankruptcy forms are free at uscourts.gov/forms/bankruptcy-forms. Each US bankruptcy court also publishes local forms and instructions on its website, linked from the national district index.
Do I need to take a credit counseling course before filing?
Yes. 11 U.S.C. § 109(h) requires an approved credit-counseling course within the 180 days before filing. A second course (debtor education under § 727(a)(11)) is required before discharge can be entered. Approved agencies are listed at justice.gov/ust/list-credit-counseling-agencies.
What is the 341 meeting?
The § 341 "meeting of creditors" is a post-filing examination of the debtor under oath, conducted by the case trustee and typically held 21–50 days after the petition is filed. Pro se debtors are expected to attend and bring any documents the trustee has requested.
Can I avoid unredacted Social Security Number exposure in my filing?
Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 9037 requires redaction of Social Security Numbers, dates of birth, financial account numbers, and minor-child identifiers in filed documents. Form 121 - the Statement About Your Social Security Numbers - is filed separately and is explicitly not part of the public case file.

## Chapter 7 Bankruptcy: How It Works, Who Qualifies, Step by Step [2026]
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/chapter-7-guide/

Open Bankruptcy Project
