## FRBP Rule 1014 - Dismissal and Change of Venue [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/rule-1014-venue/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure
1014

Rule 1014: Dismissal and Change of Venue

The 1014(a) discretionary transfer standard, mandatory action under 1014(b) when venue is improper, and the four-factor Commonwealth Oil framework.

Verbatim text of Rule 1014(a)

(1) Cases Filed in Proper District. If a petition is filed in the proper district, the court, on the timely motion of a party in interest or on its own motion, and after hearing on notice to the petitioners, the United States trustee, and other entities as directed by the court, may transfer the case to any other district if the court determines that the transfer is in the interest of justice or for the convenience of the parties.

(2) Cases Filed in Improper District. If a petition is filed in an improper district, the court, on the timely motion of a party in interest or on its own motion, and after hearing on notice to the petitioners, the United States trustee, and other entities as directed by the court, may dismiss the case or transfer it to any other district if the court determines that transfer is in the interest of justice or for the convenience of the parties. Fed. R. Bankr. P. 1014(a).

The structure of Rule 1014

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 1014 implements the venue statutes for bankruptcy cases - 28 U.S.C. Section 1408 (proper venue for cases under title 11) and 28 U.S.C. Section 1412 (change of venue). The rule has two operative subdivisions:

1014(a)(1) - Discretionary transfer when the case was filed in the proper district. The court may transfer "in the interest of justice or for the convenience of the parties."

1014(a)(2) - When the case was filed in an improper district, the court may either dismiss the case or transfer it to a proper district.

1014(b) - When petitions are filed against the same debtor or related debtors in different districts, the court in the district where the first petition was filed determines, on motion filed within the period prescribed by the court, the district in which the cases should proceed.

Proper venue under 28 U.S.C. Section 1408

Section 1408 establishes that a bankruptcy case may be commenced in any district in which, for the 180 days immediately preceding the commencement of the case (or for the longer portion of that 180-day period than in any other district), the debtor's:

Domicile,

Residence,

Principal place of business in the United States, or

Principal assets in the United States

were located. Section 1408(2) also permits filing in any district where there is a pending case under title 11 concerning an affiliate, general partner, or partnership of the debtor. The 180-day lookback prevents debtors from establishing token contacts with a preferred forum immediately before filing.

The Commonwealth Oil four-factor analysis

The leading framework for evaluating a discretionary transfer motion under Rule 1014(a)(1) is the four-factor analysis articulated in In re Commonwealth Oil Refining Co., 596 F.2d 1239 (5th Cir. 1979). Although decided under the predecessor statute, the framework remains the principal analytical tool used by courts evaluating bankruptcy venue transfer in the interest of justice or for the convenience of parties:

(1) Proximity of creditors of every kind to the court

The court considers where the creditors are physically located. A heavy concentration of creditors in a single district favors administration in that district. The presence of trade creditors, secured creditors, and significant unsecured creditors in the proposed transferee district is weighed against the convenience of the debtor's chosen forum.

(2) Proximity of the debtor to the court

Where is the debtor's headquarters, principal place of business, and management? Where are the debtor's books, records, and operating personnel? A debtor whose operational center is geographically remote from the chosen filing district is more readily transferred than one filing in its operational home.

(3) Proximity of witnesses necessary to administration of the estate

The court considers where the witnesses likely to be called in adversary proceedings, contested matters, and plan confirmation hearings reside. Witness convenience is one component of the broader convenience analysis but is given substantial weight when significant litigation is anticipated.

(4) Location of the assets

The physical location of the estate's principal assets is weighed. Real estate, operating facilities, inventory, and equipment that must be inspected, valued, marketed, or sold weigh in favor of the district where they are located, particularly in liquidating proceedings.

Some courts add a fifth factor - the economic and efficient administration of the estate - as a synthesizing consideration that overlays the four enumerated factors. The party moving for transfer bears the burden of demonstrating by a preponderance of the evidence that transfer is warranted.

Mandatory dismissal or transfer under Rule 1014(a)(2)

When a petition is filed in a district that is not a proper district under 28 U.S.C. Section 1408, the rule directs the court, on timely motion or sua sponte, to either dismiss the case or transfer it to a proper district. The court's choice between dismissal and transfer is governed by the same "interest of justice or convenience of the parties" standard that applies to discretionary transfer.

Some authorities read the rule as effectively requiring transfer rather than dismissal when transfer is feasible, on the theory that dismissal of an improperly venued case typically harms the estate (loss of the automatic stay, risk of preferential transfers becoming unrecoverable, dissipation of assets between dismissal and re-filing) without serving any countervailing interest. Other authorities preserve dismissal as a meaningful option, particularly where the improper venue reflects bad-faith forum shopping.

Timeliness of the venue objection

A motion to transfer or dismiss for improper venue must be "timely" under Rule 1014. Courts construe timeliness in light of when the moving party knew or should have known of the venue defect, the stage of the case at the time of the motion, and the prejudice to the estate from a late-stage transfer. A party that participates substantively in case administration for an extended period without raising venue may be deemed to have waived the objection.

Choice-of-venue concerns and forum shopping

Bankruptcy venue law has long been the subject of academic and policy debate concerning forum shopping. Large corporate debtors have, historically, exhibited a pronounced preference for a small number of districts - notably the District of Delaware and the Southern District of New York - based on perceptions of judicial expertise, favorable case law, and predictable administration. Section 1408(2) permits filing in any district where an affiliate case is pending, which has been used to establish venue in a preferred district by first filing a small affiliate case there.

Rule 1014(a) supplies the principal procedural check on forum shopping in cases that satisfy Section 1408 formally but raise convenience concerns. Courts considering Rule 1014(a)(1) transfer motions have, with varying frequency, transferred large cases away from chosen forums when the Commonwealth Oil factors weighed decisively in favor of a different district, particularly when an affiliate-venue mechanism was used to establish formal compliance with Section 1408.

Common procedural posture

Creditor motion to transfer

A creditor located in a district remote from the filing district moves under Rule 1014(a)(1) to transfer the case to the district where the debtor's operations, assets, and majority of creditors are located. The creditor presents evidence on each of the four Commonwealth Oil factors and argues that the debtor's chosen forum reflects forum shopping rather than operational convenience.

Sua sponte review of venue

On reviewing the petition and supporting documents, the court raises venue on its own motion under Rule 1014(a)(2), sets a hearing on notice to the United States trustee and parties in interest, and requires the debtor to demonstrate that venue is proper under one of the four Section 1408 bases.

Related rules and authority

28 U.S.C. Section 1408 - Venue of cases under title 11

28 U.S.C. Section 1409 - Venue of proceedings arising under title 11

28 U.S.C. Section 1412 - Change of venue

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 1015 - Consolidation or joint administration of related cases

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 1017 - Dismissal or conversion of case; suspension

Practical impact

A successful Rule 1014 transfer motion realigns the entire administrative architecture of a case: a different judge, a different United States trustee region, different local rules, and often a different bar of bankruptcy practitioners. Once a transfer order is entered, the case is administered as if it had originally been filed in the transferee district, and all prior orders remain in effect unless modified by the transferee court. The strategic stakes are high enough that contested venue motions in large cases often involve substantial evidentiary records and multiple days of hearing.

Venue is procedural, not jurisdictional. A bankruptcy court has subject-matter jurisdiction over title 11 cases regardless of venue, and venue objections that are not timely raised are waived. The remedy for improper venue is transfer or dismissal under Rule 1014, not the collateral attack on the validity of orders entered in the improperly venued case.

Rule 1017 (Dismissal)
Rule 1019 (Conversion)

## FRBP Rule 1015 - Consolidation or Joint Administration of Cases [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/rule-1015-joint-administration/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure
1015

Rule 1015: Consolidation or Joint Administration of Cases

The distinction between joint procedural administration and substantive consolidation, the Eagle-Picher factors, and the limits joint administration places on creditor rights.

Verbatim text of Rule 1015(a) and (b)

(a) Cases Involving Same Debtor. If two or more petitions are pending in the same court by or against the same debtor, the court may order consolidation of the cases.

(b) Cases Involving Two or More Related Debtors. If a joint petition or two or more petitions are pending in the same court by or against (1) a husband and wife, or (2) a partnership and one or more of its general partners, or (3) two or more general partners, or (4) a debtor and an affiliate, the court may order a joint administration of the estates. Fed. R. Bankr. P. 1015(a)-(b).

The two concepts are different

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 1015 contains two operative provisions that practitioners frequently elide but that have very different legal consequences:

Rule 1015(a) - Consolidation of cases involving the same debtor. When duplicate petitions are filed by or against a single debtor in the same court, the court may consolidate them into a single case. This is administratively unremarkable.

Rule 1015(b) - Joint administration of related debtors. When separate petitions are filed by related debtors (spouses, partnership and general partners, multiple general partners, or a debtor and an affiliate), the court may order that the cases be administered jointly. The estates remain legally separate.

Neither subdivision authorizes the much more powerful equitable remedy of substantive consolidation, which actually merges the estates and pools their assets and liabilities. Substantive consolidation is not a creature of Rule 1015. It is an equitable remedy derived from the bankruptcy court's general equitable powers under 11 U.S.C. Section 105(a), governed by independent case-law standards, and requires an evidentiary showing of specific factors quite different from the routine showing required for joint administration.

Joint administration under Rule 1015(b)

Joint administration is a procedural mechanism that authorizes the court and parties to administer related cases together for efficiency. The hallmarks of joint administration are:

A single docket or interlinked docket for the related cases

Joint hearings on common matters

Combined notices to creditors when the matter is common to multiple estates

A single set of professionals (subject to retention orders in each case) where appropriate

One captioned filing serving multiple estates

Joint administration does not do any of the following:

Pool the assets of the related estates

Make the creditors of one estate creditors of another

Subject one estate's assets to the claims of another estate's creditors

Permit cross-estate setoff that would not otherwise be available

Eliminate the separate corporate or legal identity of the related debtors

Rule 1015(c) - Joint administration procedures

Rule 1015(c) authorizes the court to enter orders as necessary to carry out the joint administration. These commonly include orders permitting the use of combined captions, authorizing combined service lists, designating a lead case for docketing purposes, and addressing the maintenance of separate accounting and tax records sufficient to permit later disentanglement of the estates.

Substantive consolidation - the Eagle-Picher factors

Substantive consolidation is fundamentally different from joint administration. It is the merger of two or more estates into a single estate, treating the consolidated debtors as one entity for all purposes of the bankruptcy case. Inter-debtor claims are extinguished; assets are pooled; creditors share in the pool without regard to which debtor was originally obligated.

Because substantive consolidation can dramatically affect creditor recoveries (creditors of an asset-rich entity may see their recoveries diluted by claims against an asset-poor affiliate), courts require a substantial evidentiary showing. The factors articulated in In re Eagle-Picher Industries, Inc., 192 B.R. 903 (Bankr. S.D. Ohio 1996), have been widely adopted or paralleled by other courts:

The seven Eagle-Picher factors

The presence or absence of consolidated financial statements

The unity of interests and ownership between the various corporate entities

The existence of parent and intercorporate guarantees on loans

The degree of difficulty in segregating and ascertaining individual assets and liabilities

The transfer of assets without observance of corporate formalities

The commingling of assets and business functions

The profitability of consolidation at a single physical location

Other courts apply different formulations. The Second Circuit's framework, articulated in Union Sav. Bank v. Augie/Restivo Baking Co. (In re Augie/Restivo), 860 F.2d 515 (2d Cir. 1988), reduces the analysis to two principal inquiries: (i) whether creditors dealt with the entities as a single economic unit and did not rely on their separate identity in extending credit, or (ii) whether the affairs of the debtors are so entangled that consolidation will benefit all creditors.

The Third Circuit's articulation in In re Owens Corning, 419 F.3d 195 (3d Cir. 2005), emphasized that substantive consolidation should be used "sparingly," recognized the doctrine's potential to override the corporate separateness on which creditors relied when extending credit, and disapproved a broad-brush "deemed consolidation" approach used in some prior cases.

Joint-administration limitations on creditor rights

Even after joint administration is ordered, creditors retain the rights they would have had in a stand-alone case against the particular debtor on whose obligations they are creditors. Specifically:

Voting on plans

In a plan context, each debtor's classes vote separately on plans applicable to that debtor. A creditor of debtor A does not vote on a plan applicable to debtor B unless the creditor also holds a claim against B (e.g., through a guarantee).

Distribution priority

Distributions from each estate are made from that estate's assets to that estate's creditors in accordance with the priority scheme of 11 U.S.C. Section 507 and the absolute-priority rule. A creditor of debtor A does not share in distributions from debtor B's assets unless the creditor also holds a claim against B.

Setoff and recoupment

Setoff under 11 U.S.C. Section 553 requires mutuality - the obligations being set off must be between the same parties in the same capacity. Joint administration does not create mutuality where it did not exist before; a debt owed to debtor A cannot be set off against a debt that the creditor owes to debtor B.

Avoidance actions

Avoidance actions under 11 U.S.C. Sections 547, 548, and 544 are brought on behalf of the particular estate that received the transfer. The trustee for jointly administered estates must allocate any recoveries to the proper estate.

Common procedural posture

Affiliated corporate group filing

A parent corporation and its operating subsidiaries each file separate Chapter 11 petitions on the same day. The lead case typically files a motion for joint administration under Rule 1015(b)(4) (debtor and affiliates) on the first day. The motion proposes the lead case, sets out the proposed combined caption, and recites that joint administration is sought for procedural convenience only and does not constitute or seek substantive consolidation.

Spousal joint case

Spouses file a joint petition under 11 U.S.C. Section 302. Although a joint petition is technically a single filing, Rule 1015(b)(1) provides the analytical framework for treating the joint case as two estates jointly administered. The trustee or court may, on a particularized showing, order substantive consolidation of the spousal estates if the equitable factors are met.

Related rules and authority

11 U.S.C. Section 302 - Joint cases (spouses)

11 U.S.C. Section 105 - Equitable power (substantive consolidation authority)

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 1014 - Dismissal and change of venue

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 1019 - Conversion procedures

Practical impact

The joint-administration order is among the most routine first-day orders in a corporate Chapter 11 case. It is, however, frequently confused with substantive consolidation by parties who assume that "joint administration" pools the estates. Counsel and creditors must understand that the routine first-day joint-administration order is procedural only, and that any subsequent attempt at substantive consolidation will require a separate motion, evidentiary record, and application of the Eagle-Picher (or analogous circuit) factors.

Joint administration is administrative; substantive consolidation is substantive. The standard joint-administration order entered in the first days of a related-debtor case does nothing to affect the legal separation of the estates. A creditor who wants the protection of separate estates need not object to joint administration; a creditor who wants the benefits of pooling must move for substantive consolidation under the Eagle-Picher factors.

Rule 1019 (Conversion)
Rule 2014 (Retention)
Rule 3015 (Ch 13 Plan)
Rule 9014 (Contested Matters)

In re Owens Corning, 419 F.3d 195 (3d Cir. 2005) - Third Circuit limiting articulation

## FRBP Rule 1017 - Dismissal or Conversion of Case; Suspension [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/rule-1017/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure
1017

Rule 1017: Dismissal or Conversion of Case; Suspension

Procedures for voluntary dismissal, dismissal for cause, conversion between chapters, and suspension of a bankruptcy case.

Verbatim text of Rule 1017(a)

Except as provided in Sections 707(a)(3), 707(b), 1208(b), and 1307(b) of the Code, and in Rule 1017(b), (c), and (e), a case shall not be dismissed on motion of the petitioner, for want of prosecution or other cause, or by consent of the parties, before a hearing on notice as provided in Rule 2002. Fed. R. Bankr. P. 1017(a).

What Rule 1017 governs

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 1017 establishes the procedural framework for ending or pausing a bankruptcy case before the entry of a discharge or other final adjudication. The rule encompasses four substantively distinct case-disposition pathways:

Dismissal - termination of the case without a discharge or plan confirmation, on motion by the debtor, a party in interest, the United States Trustee, or the court

Conversion - change of the case's operative chapter, governed procedurally by Rule 1017 (with post-conversion procedures under Rule 1019)

Suspension - temporary pause in the case under Section 305 abstention or related authority

Means-test dismissal - the special procedure under Section 707(b) for consumer Chapter 7 cases that fail the means test

Voluntary dismissal by the debtor

The debtor's right to dismiss varies by chapter:

Chapter 7 - A debtor may not voluntarily dismiss a Chapter 7 case as of right; dismissal requires court approval after notice and a hearing, on a showing of cause under Section 707(a)

Chapter 11 - Voluntary conversion to Chapter 7 is available as of right under Section 1112(a) in most circumstances; voluntary dismissal requires court approval after notice and a hearing

Chapter 12 - A debtor may dismiss as of right under Section 1208(b) if the case was not previously converted

Chapter 13 - A debtor has an absolute right to dismiss under Section 1307(b) if the case was not previously converted to Chapter 13

The asymmetry reflects the substantive design of each chapter: Chapter 7 is involuntary in significant respects once filed (the trustee has the right to administer assets), while Chapter 13 is designed to permit the debtor to retain control and to exit if circumstances change.

Dismissal for cause

A creditor, the trustee, or the United States Trustee may move to dismiss a case for cause under the chapter-specific authority:

Section 707(a) - Chapter 7: cause, including unreasonable delay prejudicial to creditors, nonpayment of fees, failure to file required information

Section 1112(b) - Chapter 11: extensive enumerated list of grounds including continuing loss to the estate without reasonable likelihood of rehabilitation, gross mismanagement, failure to maintain insurance, unauthorized use of cash collateral, failure to comply with court orders

Section 1208(c) - Chapter 12: cause

Section 1307(c) - Chapter 13: cause, including failure to file plan, failure to make plan payments, denial of confirmation

Rule 1017(f) provides that motions to dismiss for cause shall be governed by Rule 9014 (contested matters), with notice and a hearing required before dismissal.

Means-test dismissal (Rule 1017(e))

Rule 1017(e) implements the special procedure for dismissal of a Chapter 7 case as an abuse under Section 707(b). A motion to dismiss under Section 707(b) must be filed within 60 days after the first date set for the meeting of creditors. The 60-day deadline is firm; only the court may extend it on motion filed before expiration.

The Section 707(b) means-test procedure includes three pathways for finding abuse:

Section 707(b)(2) presumption - mechanical income-vs-expense calculation under the means test triggers a presumption of abuse

Section 707(b)(3) totality of circumstances - the court considers the totality of the debtor's financial situation

Section 707(b)(3) bad faith - the case may be dismissed for bad-faith filing independent of means-test mechanics

The United States Trustee is required to file a statement within 10 days after the first date set for the meeting of creditors indicating whether the presumption of abuse arises. A creditor may also file a motion under Section 707(b)(1) within the 60-day deadline.

Conversion procedure

Rule 1017(d) provides that conversion of a case to another chapter is also governed by Rule 9014 (contested matter procedure), except in the case of an unconditional right of conversion (e.g., Section 1112(a) Chapter 11 voluntary conversion to Chapter 7 by the debtor). Conversion changes the operative chapter without commencing a new case; post-conversion procedures are then governed by Rule 1019.

Suspension under Section 305

Section 305 of the Code authorizes the court to dismiss or suspend a bankruptcy case if the interests of creditors and the debtor would be better served by such dismissal or suspension, or in specific circumstances involving foreign main proceedings under Section 1515. Section 305 abstention is narrow and uncommon; reviewing courts treat it as an extraordinary remedy. The procedural framework is set out in Rule 1017(a), with notice and a hearing required.

Common procedural posture

Chapter 13 voluntary dismissal

A Chapter 13 debtor whose case has not previously been converted decides to dismiss the case to pursue an out-of-court workout. The debtor files a notice of dismissal under Section 1307(b). The Chapter 13 trustee acknowledges the filing, and the court enters an order dismissing the case. The dismissal is essentially as of right; no creditor objection or court evaluation is required.

Chapter 7 means-test dismissal

The United States Trustee files a statement within 10 days after the Section 341 meeting indicating that the presumption of abuse arises based on the debtor's means-test calculation. The United States Trustee then files a motion under Section 707(b)(2) within the 60-day deadline. The court holds a hearing on the means-test calculation and any rebuttal evidence and rules on the motion.

Related rules and authority

11 U.S.C. Section 305 - Abstention

11 U.S.C. Section 707 - Dismissal of a Chapter 7 case

11 U.S.C. Section 1112 - Conversion or dismissal of a Chapter 11 case

11 U.S.C. Section 1208 - Conversion or dismissal of a Chapter 12 case

11 U.S.C. Section 1307 - Conversion or dismissal of a Chapter 13 case

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 1019 - Conversion to Chapter 7 (post-conversion procedures)

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 9014 - Contested matters

Practical impact

Rule 1017 is the procedural rulebook for case exit short of completion. Every bankruptcy case ultimately concludes through one of three pathways: discharge or plan confirmation (the successful endings), dismissal under Rule 1017, or conversion under Rule 1017 followed by Rule 1019 to a different chapter that then has its own ending. The rule's structure - with chapter-specific cross-references and the special Section 707(b) deadline - reflects the substantive distinctions among the chapters.

The interaction between Rule 1017 and the United States Trustee's role is particularly important in consumer cases. The United States Trustee's mandatory Section 707(b) statement and the 60-day Section 707(b) motion deadline shape the practical pace of every consumer Chapter 7 case.

Dismissal is not always a return to the status quo ante. Dismissal of a bankruptcy case terminates the automatic stay and most procedural protections, but a debtor who refiles within 180 days after dismissal under certain circumstances may be subject to the limitations of Section 109(g) and the modified automatic-stay provisions of Section 362(c)(3) and (4). Dismissal has substantive consequences beyond mere termination.

Rule 2007.1 (Trustee)
Rule 4001 (Stay Relief)

Section 707 Dismissal

## FRBP Rule 1019 - Conversion Procedures from Chapter 11, 12, or 13 to Chapter 7 [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/rule-1019-conversion-procedures/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure
1019

Rule 1019: Conversion Procedures from Chapter 11, 12, or 13 to Chapter 7

The post-conversion procedural cascade: new Section 341 meeting, new schedules, restarted claim bar dates, and administrative treatment of post-petition pre-conversion claims.

What Rule 1019 does

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 1019 governs the procedural steps that follow when a case originally filed under Chapter 11, 12, or 13 is converted to Chapter 7. Conversion is not a re-filing; the case retains its original case number, original petition date, and original automatic stay. But the change from a reorganization-or-repayment regime to a liquidation regime triggers a substantial procedural reset that Rule 1019 implements in eight numbered paragraphs.

The eight Rule 1019 directives in summary

Lists, inventories, schedules, and statements already on file are deemed filed in the converted case unless the court directs otherwise (Rule 1019(1)(A)).

The debtor must file a schedule of unpaid debts incurred after the original petition but before conversion (Rule 1019(5)(A)). This is the foundation for administrative-claim treatment of post-petition pre-conversion liabilities.

The trustee or debtor in possession from the prior chapter must turn over records and file a final report and account (Rule 1019(2), (5)(B)).

A new Section 341 meeting of creditors is convened by the United States trustee under the Chapter 7 calendar.

New claim bar dates are established running from the date of conversion for purposes of Rule 3002(c) (Rule 1019(2)).

Post-petition pre-conversion claims receive administrative-expense priority under 11 U.S.C. Section 503(b) and are scheduled and noticed accordingly.

The clerk gives notice to entities listed on the schedules of conversion and of the new bar dates.

The Chapter 7 trustee assumes administration of the estate as it exists on the conversion date.

Section 348 - the substantive companion

Rule 1019 is the procedural implementation of 11 U.S.C. Section 348, which is the substantive provision governing the effect of conversion. Section 348(a) preserves the original commencement date for purposes of automatic stay, claim allowance, and avoidance powers, with specific exceptions. Section 348(b) and (c) carve out exceptions for which the "order for relief" date is the conversion date rather than the original petition date. Section 348(d) provides that post-petition, pre-conversion claims are treated as if they arose immediately before the date of the filing of the petition - meaning they are general unsecured claims rather than administrative-expense claims - except for claims that would have been administrative under Section 503(b) in the original chapter, which retain that priority.

The new Section 341 meeting

The United States trustee, upon entry of the order of conversion, schedules a new meeting of creditors under 11 U.S.C. Section 341. The Chapter 7 trustee - typically newly appointed from the panel for the district - presides. The debtor is required to attend, to be sworn, and to be examined under oath. Topics typically covered include:

Changes in the debtor's financial circumstances since the original petition

Post-petition pre-conversion income and expenses

Disposition of estate property between the original petition and conversion

Existence and location of non-exempt assets that may be liquidated for distribution

Operation of any post-petition business (in a former Chapter 11 or 12 case)

Pre-conversion plan payments (in a former Chapter 13 case) and the source of those payments

The new schedules - the conversion schedule

Rule 1019(5)(A) requires the debtor to file, within 14 days of the conversion order, a schedule of unpaid debts incurred after the original petition but before conversion (post-petition pre-conversion debts). This schedule is in addition to the original schedules and is the basis on which the clerk gives notice to those creditors of the converted case and of the new bar dates. Rule 1019(5) also requires the debtor to file:

A schedule of property of the estate acquired after the original petition

A schedule of executory contracts entered into or assumed after the original petition

Any amendments to the original schedules to reflect changes

Local rules in many districts supply forms or templates for the conversion schedule and prescribe additional content (e.g., a post-conversion statement of financial affairs).

Claim bar dates restart

One of the most important practical consequences of Rule 1019 is the restart of the claim bar dates. Under Rule 3002(c), the bar date in a Chapter 7 case is 70 days after the order for relief. For a converted case, the bar date runs from the date of conversion rather than from the original petition. The clerk's notice of conversion must inform creditors of the new bar date and of the need to file proofs of claim if they have not already done so.

Creditors who filed proofs of claim in the prior chapter need not refile; their claims remain on the docket. But creditors whose claims arose after the original petition and before conversion - or who were added to the schedule of post-petition debts - must file claims by the new bar date to participate in distribution.

Post-petition pre-conversion claims as administrative expenses

Section 348(d) preserves administrative-expense status for claims that, in the prior chapter, would have qualified under Section 503(b) - typically claims for actual, necessary costs and expenses of preserving the estate, post-petition trade debt incurred in the ordinary course of operating a Chapter 11 or 12 business, and compensation for services rendered to the estate. These claims are paid out of the Chapter 7 estate in the priority order of Section 507(a)(2) before any distribution to general unsecured creditors.

The interplay between Section 348(d) and the absolute-priority scheme of Section 507 is one of the most procedurally important features of conversion. A creditor who supplied goods or services to a Chapter 11 debtor in possession during the reorganization phase has a strong claim to administrative priority in the Chapter 7 case - but only if the claim is timely filed and properly characterized as a Section 503(b) claim.

Common procedural posture

Chapter 13 conversion to Chapter 7

A debtor whose Chapter 13 plan has failed (missed payments, loss of employment, material change in circumstances) moves to convert to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. Section 1307(a). Upon conversion, the Chapter 13 trustee files a final report. The Chapter 7 trustee is appointed; a new Section 341 meeting is convened; new bar dates run from conversion; and the trustee evaluates the post-petition pre-conversion period for any non-exempt assets acquired during that period that are now property of the Chapter 7 estate under Section 348(f)(2) (in bad-faith conversion) or excluded under Section 348(f)(1) (in good-faith conversion).

Chapter 11 conversion to Chapter 7

A Chapter 11 reorganization fails after substantial post-petition operations. On conversion, the debtor-in-possession's records are turned over to the Chapter 7 trustee. Post-petition trade creditors who supplied the operating business hold Section 503(b) administrative claims that, under Section 348(d), retain administrative priority in the Chapter 7. The trustee evaluates these claims, files a final report, and proposes distribution that pays the administrative class before any distribution to general unsecured creditors.

Related rules and authority

11 U.S.C. Section 348 - Effect of conversion

11 U.S.C. Section 503 - Administrative expenses

11 U.S.C. Section 1307 - Conversion or dismissal (Chapter 13)

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 1007 - Lists, schedules, statements

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 2003 - Meeting of creditors

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 3002 - Filing proof of claim

Practical impact

Conversion to Chapter 7 is a procedural reset that affects every active party. Creditors who relaxed proof-of-claim diligence during the reorganization phase must promptly attend to the new bar date or risk forfeiture of their position. Debtor's counsel must prepare and file the conversion schedule and prepare the debtor for the new Section 341 meeting. The newly appointed Chapter 7 trustee assumes responsibility for any estate property acquired or disposed of during the prior-chapter administration and must rapidly assess what assets remain available for liquidation.

Conversion is not a re-filing. The case retains its original petition date, original automatic stay, and original look-back periods for avoidance purposes. But the procedural reset triggered by Rule 1019 - new Section 341 meeting, new bar date, conversion schedule, administrative treatment of post-petition pre-conversion claims - is substantial enough that practitioners often refer informally to "the converted case" as a distinct procedural entity within the unified case file.

## FRBP Rule 1019 - Conversion of Chapter 11, 12, or 13 to Chapter 7 [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/rule-1019/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure
1019

Rule 1019: Conversion of Chapter 11, 12, or 13 to Chapter 7

Post-conversion procedures including supplemental schedules, new claims bar dates, administrative claim treatment, and trustee transition.

Verbatim text of Rule 1019 (introductory paragraph)

When a chapter 11, chapter 12, or chapter 13 case has been converted or reconverted to a chapter 7 case:

(1) Filing of lists, inventories, schedules, statements. Lists, inventories, schedules, and statements of financial affairs theretofore filed shall be deemed to be filed in the chapter 7 case, unless the court directs otherwise. If they have not been filed, the debtor shall comply with Rule 1007 as if an order for relief had been entered on an involuntary petition on the date of the entry of the order directing that the case continue under chapter 7. Fed. R. Bankr. P. 1019(1).

Scope of Rule 1019

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 1019 establishes the procedural framework that applies when a Chapter 11, 12, or 13 case is converted to Chapter 7. Conversion changes the operative chapter of the case but does not commence a new case: the original petition date controls for most substantive purposes under 11 U.S.C. Section 348. Rule 1019 governs the bridge from the prior chapter's procedural posture to the Chapter 7 procedural framework.

The rule contains seven numbered subdivisions addressing schedules, claims bar dates, the new meeting of creditors, statements of intent, post-petition transactions, administrative claim treatment, and claim allowance.

Schedules and statements (Rule 1019(1))

Schedules and statements of financial affairs filed in the prior chapter case carry forward into the Chapter 7 case unless the court directs otherwise. The debtor is not required to refile the schedules already on file. If schedules were not filed (e.g., conversion before the debtor's filing deadline expired in a Chapter 13 case), the debtor must file them as if the case were newly opened under Rule 1007.

Schedule of post-petition debts (Rule 1019(5))

Rule 1019(5) requires the debtor to file, within 14 days of the conversion order, a schedule of unpaid debts incurred after the commencement of the original case and before conversion to Chapter 7, and a statement of executory contracts entered into or assumed during the same period. These post-petition debts are eligible for administrative claim treatment to the extent they were authorized by the prior chapter case.

New claims bar date (Rule 1019(2))

Rule 1019(2) provides for a new time to file claims in the Chapter 7 case for claims that arose before the conversion order and were not filed in the prior chapter case. This addresses the situation where the conversion makes claims that would not have shared in a Chapter 13 plan (e.g., late-arising unsecured claims) potentially recoverable in a Chapter 7 liquidation.

The new bar date is set by the court and operates under the framework of Rule 3002 as if the Chapter 7 case were newly commenced. Notice of the new bar date is given through the standard Rule 2002 notice mechanism.

New meeting of creditors (Rule 1019(2))

Rule 1019(2) also provides for a new meeting of creditors under 11 U.S.C. Section 341(a) in the converted Chapter 7 case. The meeting is conducted by the newly-appointed Chapter 7 trustee. The new Section 341 meeting is the operational reset point for the Chapter 7 case: the trustee examines the debtor on the record, parties in interest may question the debtor, and the trustee identifies estate assets and claims.

Trustee transition

Conversion to Chapter 7 results in the appointment of a Chapter 7 trustee under Section 701. The transition issues include:

Transfer of estate property from the debtor in possession (in former Chapter 11 cases) or Chapter 13 trustee to the Chapter 7 trustee

Substitution of the Chapter 7 trustee for the debtor in possession or prior trustee in pending adversary proceedings and contested matters

Resolution of pending professional retention applications and fee applications

Determination of which post-petition contracts and leases will be assumed or rejected under the Chapter 7 trustee's authority

Administrative claim treatment

Administrative claims incurred during the prior chapter case generally retain their administrative status under Section 348(d), but they are subordinated to Chapter 7 administrative claims under the priority scheme of Section 726(b). This "Chapter 7 first" priority recognizes that the Chapter 7 trustee and counsel must be willing to administer the converted estate; without priority, they would be reluctant to take on a case with substantial pre-conversion administrative debt.

The practical effect is that Chapter 11 professionals whose fees were not paid before conversion often face substantially diminished recovery in the converted Chapter 7 case. This priority structure influences professional retention and fee planning in Chapter 11 cases that are at risk of conversion.

Section 348 and the "date of the order for relief"

For most purposes under the Code, the date of the original order for relief - not the conversion date - controls. Section 348(a) provides that conversion does not change the date of the order for relief. Several exceptions apply, however:

Section 348(c) - The date of conversion controls for certain Section 365 (executory contract) deadlines

Section 348(d) - Pre-conversion claims (other than administrative) are treated as if they arose before the order for relief in the converted case

Section 348(f) - In conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7, property of the estate consists of property of the estate as of the original petition date that remains in the debtor's possession or control on the conversion date

Common procedural posture

Chapter 13 conversion to Chapter 7

A Chapter 13 debtor fails to maintain plan payments and the trustee moves to convert under Section 1307(c). The court enters an order converting the case to Chapter 7. A Chapter 7 trustee is appointed and conducts a new Section 341 meeting. Schedules from the Chapter 13 case carry forward. A new bar date is set for post-petition claims under Rule 1019(5). The Chapter 7 trustee identifies non-exempt assets and administers them for distribution under Section 726.

Chapter 11 conversion after failed reorganization

A Chapter 11 debtor in possession fails to confirm a plan within the deadlines under Section 1121, and a creditor moves to convert under Section 1112(b). The court grants the motion. A Chapter 7 trustee is appointed; estate property transfers from the DIP to the trustee. Chapter 11 administrative claims are subordinated to Chapter 7 administrative claims under Section 726(b). The trustee evaluates estate assets, including pending causes of action, for liquidation.

Related rules and authority

11 U.S.C. Section 348 - Effect of conversion

11 U.S.C. Section 701 - Interim trustee in Chapter 7

11 U.S.C. Section 726 - Distribution of estate property (administrative priority structure)

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 1017 - Dismissal or conversion of case

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 3002 - Filing proof of claim or interest

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 1007 - Lists, schedules, statements, and other documents

Practical impact

Rule 1019 is the procedural rulebook for one of the more common transitions in bankruptcy practice: the conversion of a reorganization case to liquidation. Conversion is a substantive change in the case's posture, but Rule 1019's design preserves continuity where possible - schedules and statements carry forward; previously-filed claims remain - while triggering the procedural resets necessary to align the case with Chapter 7's substantive framework.

The administrative-priority subordination under Section 726(b) is one of the most significant practical consequences of conversion. Professionals in distressed Chapter 11 cases routinely structure fee arrangements and interim compensation requests with conversion risk in mind, recognizing that pre-conversion administrative claims may be substantially impaired if the case converts.

Conversion does not commence a new case. The original petition date controls for most Code purposes - the operation of the automatic stay, the relation-back of avoidance powers, the calculation of look-back periods. Rule 1019's procedural resets address claim deadlines, schedules, and the meeting of creditors, but the substantive case remains the same case under a different chapter.

## FRBP Rule 2002 - Notice Mechanics Deep-Dive [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/rule-2002-notice-deep-dive/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure
2002

Rule 2002: Notice Mechanics Deep-Dive

The 21-day baseline under Rule 2002(a), abbreviated-notice carve-outs under 2002(b), the section 341 meeting notice under 2002(d), interaction with Rule 7004 service, and mailing-list maintenance under 2002(g).

The architecture of Rule 2002

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 2002 governs the notice mechanics that move a bankruptcy case from filing to confirmation, sale, or dismissal. Where Rule 7004 governs service in adversary proceedings and contested matters, Rule 2002 governs the broader category of notice to creditors, equity holders, the United States trustee, and other parties in interest. The two regimes interact: a paper served in a contested matter under Rule 7004 frequently also requires Rule 2002 notice to the broader case constituency, and one regime does not substitute for the other.

The rule is long and subsection-dense. The operative architecture, however, is straightforward: Rule 2002(a) sets the 21-day baseline; Rule 2002(b) requires longer notice for plan and disclosure-statement matters; Rule 2002(c) carves abbreviated notice for routine motions; Rule 2002(d) addresses equity-security-holder notice; Rule 2002(f) lists the specific events that trigger notice to all creditors; and Rule 2002(g) governs the address used for notice and the maintenance of the case mailing matrix.

The 21-day notice baseline under Rule 2002(a)

Rule 2002(a) requires the clerk - or, in some districts, the moving party - to give the debtor, the trustee, all creditors, and indenture trustees at least 21 days' notice by mail of the following events:

The meeting of creditors under 11 U.S.C. Section 341

A proposed use, sale, or lease of property of the estate other than in the ordinary course of business, unless the court for cause shown shortens the time or directs another method of giving notice

The hearing on approval of a compromise or settlement of a controversy other than approval of an agreement under Rule 4001(d)

The hearing on the dismissal of the case or the conversion of the case to another chapter

The time fixed to accept or reject a proposed modification of a plan

The hearing on a proposed modification of a Chapter 12 or Chapter 13 plan

The time fixed for filing proofs of claim under Rule 3003(c)

The time fixed for objection to a debtor's claim of exemptions

The 21-day period runs from the date of mailing, not the date of receipt. The mailing must be addressed to the address specified in the mailing-matrix rules of Rule 2002(g).

Abbreviated notice under Rule 2002(b) and (c)

Rule 2002(b) requires 28 days' notice to all creditors of the time fixed for filing objections to and the hearing on approval of a disclosure statement under 11 U.S.C. Section 1125 and confirmation of a Chapter 9, 11, or 12 plan. The 28-day window reflects the higher stakes and the need for creditors to evaluate a complex disclosure statement before objecting.

Rule 2002(c) provides important carve-outs from the 21-day baseline. Notice need not be sent to all creditors of every motion; instead, Rule 2002(c)(1) limits the notice obligation for routine matters - employment of professionals, certain fee applications, and stay-relief motions - to the entities the rule specifies (the debtor, trustee, U.S. trustee, and committee). Rule 2002(c)(2) authorizes the court to limit notice further "for cause shown" - the procedural device that supports "limited notice" motions in larger cases where mailing to every creditor would be prohibitively expensive and largely useless.

Practitioners should resist the assumption that Rule 2002(c) authorizes general truncation of notice. The carve-out is narrow and event-specific; matters affecting creditor distributions generally remain subject to the 21-day baseline notwithstanding 2002(c).

The section 341 meeting notice under Rule 2002(d)

Rule 2002(d) governs notice to equity security holders. In Chapter 11 cases involving a corporate or limited-liability debtor, equity holders are entitled to the same notice as creditors of the section 341 meeting, the time for filing objections to and the hearing on approval of a disclosure statement, the time for filing acceptances or rejections of a plan, and the hearing on confirmation.

The section 341 meeting notice itself - typically issued by the United States trustee or the clerk on Official Form 309 (with variants for each chapter) - communicates the meeting date, the deadline for filing proofs of claim, the deadline for objecting to discharge, and the deadline for objecting to claims of exemption. Each of those deadlines is independently load-bearing; an error in the 309 notice can become a due-process problem if a creditor later argues that the notice was insufficient to bar a late claim or a late discharge objection.

Interaction with Rule 7004 service

Rule 7004 governs service of summons and process in adversary proceedings, and Rule 9014 imports much of Rule 7004 into contested matters. Rule 2002, by contrast, governs notice in administrative contexts that do not require summons-and-complaint formality.

The interaction matters because a single event may trigger both regimes. A motion for sale free and clear under 11 U.S.C. Section 363(f), for example, is a contested matter; the motion must be served on the parties whose interests are to be extinguished under the Rule 7004 service rules incorporated by Rule 9014, and the broader case constituency is entitled to Rule 2002(a)(2) notice of the proposed sale. Substituting one for the other is procedurally defective. A movant who serves only by Rule 2002 mailing on a secured creditor whose lien is to be stripped fails the Rule 7004 service requirement; a movant who serves the secured creditor under Rule 7004 but omits the Rule 2002 mailing fails the broader notice requirement.

Mailing-list maintenance under Rule 2002(g)

Rule 2002(g) is the rule that determines where Rule 2002 notice is sent. The provision is structured around a hierarchy:

Rule 2002(g)(1) directs that notice be sent to the address listed by a creditor or indenture trustee on a request filed with the court, designating where notices should be sent

Rule 2002(g)(2) directs that, absent such a request, notice be sent to the address in the proof of claim filed by the creditor

Rule 2002(g)(3) directs that, absent both a request and a proof of claim, notice be sent to the address shown on the list of creditors or schedules

Rule 2002(g)(4) requires that, with respect to a notice of the section 341 meeting, notice be sent to the address shown on the list of creditors or schedules, regardless of any later-filed request or proof of claim

Rule 2002(g)(5) addresses the "preferred address" mechanism for certain large institutional creditors that file a notice of preferred address under 11 U.S.C. Section 342(f) - a creditor that registers a preferred address is entitled to notice at that address rather than the address shown on the schedules.

The mailing matrix is the operational substrate of Rule 2002. If the matrix is incomplete or out-of-date, the notice that issues under Rule 2002(a) is not effective, and the deadlines triggered by that notice may be unenforceable against a creditor who did not receive the notice the rule requires.

Notice to the United States trustee

Rule 2002(k) requires that the United States trustee receive copies of all notices sent under Rule 2002(a)(2) through (a)(8), (b), (f)(1), (f)(2), (f)(4), (f)(6), (f)(7), (q), and (p). The provision exists to preserve the U.S. trustee's monitoring role under 28 U.S.C. Section 586; a movant who serves creditors but omits the U.S. trustee creates a procedural defect that is independently raisable.

Notice by publication and equivalents

Rule 2002(l) authorizes the court, on motion or sua sponte, to direct notice by publication if it finds that notice by mail is impracticable or that it is desirable to supplement the notice. Publication is not a default; it is a court-authorized supplement triggered by a particularized showing. Service by electronic means is governed by Rule 9036 and is increasingly the operational reality - the National Creditor Registration Service operated by the federal bankruptcy courts is the principal mechanism by which sophisticated institutional creditors elect to receive Rule 2002 notice electronically.

Common procedural posture

Section 363 sale notice

A trustee proposes to sell estate property outside the ordinary course. Rule 2002(a)(2) requires 21 days' notice to all creditors. The trustee must mail the notice to every address on the Rule 2002(g) matrix and serve any creditor whose lien is to be extinguished under the Rule 7004 service rules. The notice must describe the property, the proposed price, and the deadline for objections.

Plan confirmation notice

A Chapter 11 debtor seeks confirmation of a plan. Rule 2002(b) requires 28 days' notice to all creditors of the disclosure-statement hearing and the confirmation hearing. The notice must specify the deadlines for filing objections, the deadlines for casting ballots, and the date and time of the hearing. Omission of any of these elements is correctable only by an amended notice that restarts the 28-day clock.

Related rules and authority

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 7004 - Service in adversary proceedings

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 9014 - Contested matters and incorporation of Rule 7004

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 9036 - Notice by electronic transmission

11 U.S.C. Section 342 - Notice (statutory framework)

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 2003 - Meeting of creditors and equity holders

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 9014 - Contested-matter procedure

Practical impact

Rule 2002 is the rule most often violated unintentionally, because its requirements are dispersed across two dozen subsections and because the Rule 2002(g) mailing-matrix obligation is administrative rather than substantive. Defects in Rule 2002 notice rarely surface during the case; they surface when a creditor argues post-confirmation that the discharge or the sale order does not bind it because notice was insufficient. The remedy is reopening, a costly and time-consuming process that the precise compliance the rule requires at the front end would have avoided.

Notice and service are different regimes. Rule 2002 governs notice; Rule 7004 governs service. Compliance with one does not establish compliance with the other. A motion in a contested matter typically requires both, and the failure to satisfy either is independently fatal.

Rule 9014 (Contested)

## FRBP Rule 2003 - Meeting of Creditors Under Section 341 [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/rule-2003-section-341-meeting/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Home › Federal Rules of Bankruptcy Procedure › Rule 2003

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure
2003

Rule 2003: Meeting of Creditors Under Section 341

Scheduling, presiding officer, examination scope, USTP-required questions, and transcript availability at the meeting of creditors.

Statutory foundation

11 U.S.C. Section 341(a) requires that, in every case under Chapter 7, 11, 12, or 13, the United States Trustee convene and preside at a meeting of creditors within a reasonable time after the order for relief. Section 341(c) prohibits the judge from presiding at or attending the meeting. Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 2003 implements Section 341 by specifying the timing of the meeting, the procedures for conducting it, the scope of permissible examination, and the record-keeping requirements.

Timing of the meeting

Rule 2003(a) provides timing windows that vary by chapter:

Chapter 7 individual case: 21 to 40 days after the order for relief

Chapter 7 non-individual case: 21 to 40 days

Chapter 11 case: 21 to 40 days (Chapter 11 individual cases) or as ordered by the United States Trustee in Subchapter V and other Chapter 11 cases

Chapter 12 case: 21 to 35 days

Chapter 13 case: 21 to 50 days

The meeting may be held at a location designated by the United States Trustee. Since 2020, many districts have continued post-pandemic procedures permitting or requiring telephonic or video appearance for routine consumer cases; the U.S. Trustee Program has issued guidance on remote-appearance procedures, and individual district practice varies.

Who presides

The presiding officer at the Section 341 meeting depends on the chapter:

Chapter 7: The interim trustee (who normally becomes the permanent trustee under 11 U.S.C. Section 702(d) when no permanent trustee is elected) presides.

Chapter 13: The standing Chapter 13 trustee for the district presides.

Chapter 12: The standing Chapter 12 trustee presides.

Chapter 11 (non-Subchapter V): The United States Trustee or a designee presides. There is no estate-administering trustee unless one is appointed under Section 1104.

Chapter 11 Subchapter V: The Subchapter V trustee presides (28 U.S.C. Section 586(b); 11 U.S.C. Section 1183).

Section 341(c) prohibits the bankruptcy judge from presiding at or attending the meeting. The exclusion preserves the judge's neutrality on factual disputes that may emerge from the meeting and that may later require judicial resolution.

Identification, oath, and the USTP-required questions

The Handbook for Chapter 7 Trustees and the Handbook for Chapter 13 Standing Trustees, both issued by the Executive Office for United States Trustees, require trustees to begin the examination of each debtor with a uniform set of identification, identity-verification, and substantive questions. The "USTP-required questions" cover, at minimum:

Verification of the debtor's full name, address, and Social Security number against photo identification (driver's license, state identification card, or U.S. passport) and an original Social Security card or other acceptable evidence of the SSN

Confirmation that the debtor reviewed and signed the petition, schedules, and Statement of Financial Affairs and that the documents are true and correct to the best of the debtor's knowledge

Confirmation of completion of the pre-petition credit-counseling briefing required by 11 U.S.C. Section 109(h)

Whether the debtor has filed a prior bankruptcy case within the time periods that affect discharge eligibility under Section 727(a)(8)-(9) (Chapter 7) or that limit access to the automatic stay under Section 362(c)(3)-(4)

Whether the debtor has disclosed all assets, all transfers within the lookback windows, and all sources of income

Whether the debtor has any pending claims, lawsuits, or other potential causes of action that may belong to the estate

Whether the debtor expects any inheritance, life-insurance proceeds, or property-settlement payments within 180 days after the petition date (relevant to 11 U.S.C. Section 541(a)(5))

The trustee then proceeds to chapter-specific questions: in Chapter 7, focus on liquidation assets and dischargeability indicators; in Chapter 13, focus on feasibility of the proposed plan, the debtor's budget, and treatment of secured creditors.

Examination by creditors and the United States Trustee

After the presiding officer's examination concludes, creditors and the United States Trustee may examine the debtor. The scope of examination is governed by Section 343, which requires the debtor to appear and submit to examination under oath at the meeting. The examination scope under Section 343 is broad and includes the operation of the debtor's business, the debtor's financial affairs, and any matter that may affect administration of the estate or the debtor's right to discharge.

Although the scope is broad, creditor examination is not unlimited. The presiding officer has authority to control the orderly conduct of the meeting and may limit cumulative, harassing, or off-topic examination. Rule 2003 does not provide for cross-examination in the trial-procedure sense; the meeting is an examination, not an adversary hearing.

Record of the meeting

Rule 2003(c) requires the presiding officer to make a record of the meeting that includes the time and place, the trustee's report of the examination, and any matters that the parties or the presiding officer specifically request to be recorded. In practice, Section 341 meetings are recorded by audio (or, in some districts, by stenographic reporter) and the recording is preserved by the office of the United States Trustee.

An audio recording or transcript of the meeting is generally available on written request to the U.S. Trustee field office or the trustee's office that conducted the meeting. The U.S. Trustee Program publishes a uniform request procedure; requesters typically pay a duplication fee. The 341 transcript is frequently used as an evidentiary record in later contested matters - for example, a debtor's testimony at the 341 meeting may be used as a prior inconsistent statement under Federal Rule of Evidence 613 if the debtor takes a different position at a later contested-matter hearing.

Adjournment and continuation

Rule 2003(e) authorizes the presiding officer to adjourn the meeting from time to time by oral announcement at the meeting without further written notice. An adjournment may be necessary when:

The debtor fails to appear, requiring rescheduling and a renewed appearance demand

The debtor's identification or other verification documents are not available

Significant amendments to the schedules or SOFA are required and the trustee defers examination until the amendments are filed

The debtor's responses suggest the need for production of additional documents

Sub V or Chapter 11 cases involve substantial creditor questioning that cannot be completed in the original time slot

A continued 341 meeting restarts the clock for various deadlines tied to the "conclusion" of the meeting - most importantly, the deadline for filing a complaint objecting to discharge or to determine dischargeability under Rule 4004 and Rule 4007 runs from the first date set for the meeting, but the deadline for filing objections to claimed exemptions under Rule 4003(b)(1) runs from the conclusion of the meeting.

Common procedural posture

Asset case discovered at the meeting

A Chapter 7 case initially designated "no asset" becomes an asset case when the trustee's examination reveals an undisclosed account, a pre-petition transfer, or a non-exempt asset. The trustee adjourns the meeting, files a notice of assets with the bankruptcy court, and proceeds with administration. Creditors then receive a Section 341(d) notice to file proofs of claim.

Debtor non-appearance

The debtor fails to appear at the scheduled meeting. The trustee continues the meeting and notifies the debtor. A second non-appearance is grounds for the trustee to recommend dismissal under 11 U.S.C. Section 707(a)(1) (Chapter 7) or Section 1307(c)(1) (Chapter 13) for unreasonable delay. In Chapter 13, the standing trustee will typically move to dismiss for failure to appear.

Subchapter V status conference under Section 1188

For Subchapter V cases, the Section 341 meeting is supplemented by the status conference required by 11 U.S.C. Section 1188, held within 60 days after the order for relief, at which the debtor must report on the efforts to obtain a consensual plan and the court enters scheduling orders. The Section 341 meeting and the Section 1188 conference are distinct events: the 341 meeting is creditor-facing and conducted by the Subchapter V trustee; the 1188 conference is court-facing and conducted by the bankruptcy judge.

Related rules and authority

11 U.S.C. Section 341 - Meetings of creditors and equity security holders (statutory foundation)

11 U.S.C. Section 343 - Examination of the debtor

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 2004 - Examination (broader examination tool not limited to the 341 meeting)

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 1007 - Schedules and Statement of Financial Affairs

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 4007 - Determination of dischargeability of a debt

The 341 transcript is a public-record evidentiary anchor. Testimony at the meeting is under oath and is recorded. A party who later takes a position inconsistent with that testimony in a contested matter may be impeached with the recording, and material false statements at the meeting may be prosecuted under 18 U.S.C. Section 152(2) or referred for denial of discharge under 11 U.S.C. Section 727(a)(4).

Rule 3001 (Claims)
Rule 3007 (Objections)
Rule 3015 (Plan)
Rule 4007 (Dischargeability)
Rule 9014 (Contested)

## FRBP Rule 2007.1 - Election of Trustee in Subchapter V Case [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/rule-2007-1/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure
2007.1

Rule 2007.1: Appointment of Trustee or Examiner in a Chapter 11 Reorganization Case

Procedures for the United States Trustee's appointment of a Chapter 11 trustee or examiner, the creditor election under Section 1104(b), and the Subchapter V trustee under Section 1183.

Verbatim text of Rule 2007.1(a) and (b)(1)

(a) Appointment of trustee or examiner. Except in a case governed by subchapter V of chapter 11, an order approving the appointment of a trustee or an examiner under Section 1104(d) of the Code shall be made on application of the United States trustee. The application shall state the name of the person appointed and, to the best of the applicant's knowledge, all the person's connections with the debtor, creditors, any other party in interest, their respective attorneys and accountants, the United States trustee, or persons employed in the office of the United States trustee. The application shall state the names of the parties in interest with whom the United States trustee consulted regarding the appointment. The application shall be accompanied by a verified statement of the person appointed setting forth the person's connections with the debtor, creditors, any other party in interest, their respective attorneys and accountants, the United States trustee, or persons employed in the office of the United States trustee.

(b)(1) Election of trustee. On the timely request of a party in interest made not later than 30 days after the court orders the appointment of a trustee, the United States trustee shall convene a meeting of creditors for the purpose of electing one disinterested person to serve as trustee in the case. Fed. R. Bankr. P. 2007.1(a) and (b)(1).

The two trustee tracks in Chapter 11

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 2007.1 addresses the appointment of a trustee in a Chapter 11 case. The rule encompasses two distinct trustee tracks that share the rule's procedural framework but operate under different substantive standards:

Standard Chapter 11 trustee under 11 U.S.C. Section 1104, appointed by the United States Trustee on order of the court after a finding of cause (fraud, dishonesty, incompetence, gross mismanagement) or in the interests of creditors, equity holders, and the estate

Subchapter V trustee under 11 U.S.C. Section 1183, appointed by the United States Trustee in every Subchapter V small-business reorganization case as a standard feature of the subchapter

The two trustees serve fundamentally different functions. The Section 1104 trustee replaces the debtor in possession as the estate's operating officer. The Section 1183 Subchapter V trustee does not displace the debtor in possession; the Subchapter V trustee operates alongside the debtor in possession as a facilitator of consensual plan negotiation, monitor of estate operations, and (in some circumstances) disbursing agent for plan payments.

Standard Chapter 11 trustee (Rule 2007.1(a))

Under Section 1104(a), the court may order the appointment of a Chapter 11 trustee at any time after the commencement of the case and before confirmation of a plan, on request of a party in interest or the United States Trustee, after notice and a hearing. The grounds are:

Cause, including fraud, dishonesty, incompetence, or gross mismanagement of the affairs of the debtor by current management, either before or after the commencement of the case, or similar cause

The interests of creditors, any equity security holders, and other interests of the estate

Once the court orders the appointment, the United States Trustee selects the trustee under Rule 2007.1(a), consults with parties in interest, and files an application identifying the proposed trustee and disclosing the proposed trustee's connections. The court then enters an order approving the appointment.

The creditor election option (Rule 2007.1(b))

Within 30 days after the court orders the appointment of a trustee, a party in interest may request that the United States Trustee convene a meeting of creditors to elect a trustee under Section 1104(b). The election is conducted under the procedure of Section 702 (the Chapter 7 trustee election procedure), incorporated by reference.

The election requires (i) a request by holders of at least 20% in amount of allowed unsecured claims, (ii) a quorum of holders of at least 20% in amount of allowed unsecured claims, and (iii) election by holders of a majority in amount of allowed unsecured claims represented at the meeting. The elected trustee replaces the trustee initially selected by the United States Trustee. In practice, Section 1104(b) elections are rare; the appointed trustee usually continues to serve.

Subchapter V trustee (Section 1183 framework)

Subchapter V of Chapter 11, added by the Small Business Reorganization Act of 2019, requires the appointment of a trustee in every Subchapter V case. The Section 1183 Subchapter V trustee:

Investigates the acts, conduct, assets, liabilities, and financial condition of the debtor

Facilitates the development of a consensual plan of reorganization

Appears and is heard at status conferences and certain hearings

May be authorized by the court to operate the business under specified circumstances (e.g., after removal of the debtor in possession)

Serves as disbursing agent for plan payments in cases where the plan is not consensual

The Subchapter V trustee is appointed by the United States Trustee from a panel maintained for that purpose. The rule's procedural requirements for verified statements of disinterestedness and disclosure of connections apply to Subchapter V trustees in the same manner they apply to standard Chapter 11 trustees.

Disinterestedness and connections disclosure

Rule 2007.1(a) requires that the United States Trustee's application identify the proposed trustee and disclose, to the best of the United States Trustee's knowledge, the proposed trustee's connections with the debtor, creditors, other parties in interest, their attorneys and accountants, and personnel of the United States Trustee's office. The application must be accompanied by a verified statement by the proposed trustee personally disclosing the same categories of connections.

The disclosure obligation mirrors the structure of Rule 2014 (employment of professional persons): a two-track disclosure (by the proposing party and by the proposed appointee) with a verified statement under oath that must disclose all connections regardless of materiality. The court determines materiality on the disclosed record.

Common procedural posture

Section 1104(a) trustee appointment

A creditors' committee files a motion under Section 1104(a) alleging that current management has engaged in self-dealing transactions inconsistent with fiduciary duties to the estate. After an evidentiary hearing, the court grants the motion and orders the appointment of a trustee. The United States Trustee files an application under Rule 2007.1(a) identifying a proposed trustee from the regional panel and disclosing connections. After 14 days for objection (and possible election within 30 days), the court enters an order approving the appointment.

Subchapter V trustee in small-business case

A small business files a voluntary Chapter 11 petition with an election to proceed under Subchapter V. Promptly after filing, the United States Trustee files an application under Rule 2007.1(a) identifying the proposed Subchapter V trustee from the panel and providing the verified statement. The court enters an order approving the appointment. The Subchapter V trustee thereafter participates in the case alongside the debtor in possession.

Related rules and authority

11 U.S.C. Section 1104 - Appointment of trustee or examiner

11 U.S.C. Section 1183 - Subchapter V trustee

11 U.S.C. Section 1184 - Rights and powers of debtor in possession in Subchapter V

11 U.S.C. Section 702 - Election of trustee (incorporated by reference)

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 2014 - Employment of professional persons (parallel disclosure structure)

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 9011 - Signature, representations to the court, sanctions

Practical impact

Rule 2007.1 governs the procedural mechanics of trustee appointment in a population of cases that has expanded substantially since the Small Business Reorganization Act took effect in 2020. Every Subchapter V case requires a trustee appointment under the rule. The rule's disclosure requirements - the verified statement of connections - are the procedural backbone of trustee accountability, just as Rule 2014's verified-statement requirement is the procedural backbone of professional accountability.

The election procedure under Rule 2007.1(b) and Section 1104(b) is rarely invoked but remains an important creditor-protection mechanism. In a standard Chapter 11 case in which the United States Trustee selects a trustee, creditors retain the right to convene a Section 702-style election if they prefer a different candidate and can muster the statutory thresholds.

The Subchapter V trustee is not a substitute for the debtor in possession. Unlike a Section 1104 standard Chapter 11 trustee, the Subchapter V trustee does not displace the debtor in possession. The two operate alongside each other, with the Subchapter V trustee functioning as a monitor and consensual-plan facilitator rather than as the estate's operating officer.

Rule 9020 (Contempt)
