## FRBP Rule 2014 - Employment of Professional Persons (Application and Disclosure) [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/rule-2014-employment-application/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure
2014

Rule 2014: Employment of Professional Persons

The verified statement of connections, the no-adverse-interest finding, and the BH&P and Granite Partners adequacy-of-disclosure standards.

Verbatim text of Rule 2014(a)

An order approving the employment of attorneys, accountants, appraisers, auctioneers, agents, or other professionals pursuant to Section 327, Section 1103, or Section 1114 of the Code shall be made only on application of the trustee or committee. The application shall be filed and, unless the case is a chapter 9 municipality case, a copy of the application shall be transmitted by the applicant to the United States trustee. The application shall state the specific facts showing the necessity for the employment, the name of the person to be employed, the reasons for the selection, the professional services to be rendered, any proposed arrangement for compensation, and, to the best of the applicant's knowledge, all of the person's connections with the debtor, creditors, any other party in interest, their respective attorneys and accountants, the United States trustee, or any person employed in the office of the United States trustee. The application shall be accompanied by a verified statement of the person to be employed setting forth the person's connections with the debtor, creditors, any other party in interest, their respective attorneys and accountants, the United States trustee, or any person employed in the office of the United States trustee. Fed. R. Bankr. P. 2014(a).

The two-document architecture

Rule 2014 requires two documents to support an order approving employment of a professional:

The application filed by the trustee (or debtor in possession, or committee). The application explains why the professional is needed, identifies the professional, recites the proposed compensation arrangement, and itself states the applicant's understanding of the professional's connections.

The verified statement from the professional itself, separately disclosing the professional's own connections with the debtor, creditors, other parties in interest, their counsel and accountants, and the United States trustee's office.

The verified statement is the procedural mechanism by which the bankruptcy court evaluates whether the proposed professional satisfies the "disinterested person" and "no adverse interest" requirements of 11 U.S.C. Section 327(a).

The substantive standard - Section 327(a)

11 U.S.C. Section 327(a) permits the trustee, with court approval, to employ professionals "that do not hold or represent an interest adverse to the estate, and that are disinterested persons." The two prongs are independent:

No adverse interest. The professional must not hold or represent any interest that is adverse to the estate with respect to the matter for which the professional is to be retained.

Disinterested person. The professional must be a "disinterested person" within the meaning of 11 U.S.C. Section 101(14), which excludes creditors, equity security holders, insiders, certain former insiders, and any person with a materially adverse interest by reason of any direct or indirect relationship with the debtor.

For Chapter 11 cases, Section 327(c) provides that representation of a creditor is not, in and of itself, a basis for disqualification, but an objection by a creditor or the United States trustee can require the court to disapprove the employment if there is an actual conflict of interest.

The duty to disclose - "all connections"

The verified statement must disclose "all of the person's connections" with the listed categories. The duty is broad and is interpreted with reference to the purpose of the rule: to give the court and the United States trustee the information necessary to evaluate disinterestedness and adverse interest. The leading cases on adequacy of disclosure are In re BH&P, Inc., 949 F.2d 1300 (3d Cir. 1991), and In re Granite Partners, L.P., 219 B.R. 22 (Bankr. S.D.N.Y. 1998).

The BH&P standard

In BH&P, the Third Circuit emphasized that the disclosure duty under Rule 2014 is "ongoing" and is not satisfied by a single application at the time of retention. Connections that arise or that become apparent after the initial retention must be supplementally disclosed. The court rejected the argument that only connections the professional believes to be material need be disclosed: the determination of materiality is for the court, not for the professional. The professional's task is to disclose; the court's task is to evaluate.

The Granite Partners standard

In Granite Partners, the bankruptcy court for the Southern District of New York elaborated the BH&P duty and articulated the standard that has been widely adopted: the professional must disclose any "connection" - the term is read broadly - and is not permitted to engage in "self-screening" by deciding for itself which connections are sufficiently material to warrant disclosure. The court explained that a "connection" includes any relationship that, viewed objectively, could give rise to a reasonable question about the professional's disinterestedness or potential for adverse interest, even if the professional believes (subjectively) that no actual conflict exists.

What "connections" means in practice

The verified statement typically discloses, at a minimum:

Present and former representations of any creditor, equity holder, or party in interest, even in unrelated matters

Family, social, and business relationships of attorneys at the firm with any party in interest

Financial holdings of the firm or its partners in any party in interest

Prior representations of the debtor (which may be permissible or disqualifying depending on context)

Relationships with the United States trustee's office or members of its staff

Relationships with the bankruptcy judge or chambers personnel

Connections through any database or affiliate relationship that the firm has searched in preparing the disclosure

Large firms typically run conflict-check databases against the case parties list (creditors, equity holders, professionals, etc.) and disclose the results in the verified statement. The disclosure should describe the search methodology, the parties searched, and any matches identified, along with an explanation of why each match (if any) does or does not constitute an adverse interest.

The continuing duty to supplement

The Rule 2014 duty is not satisfied by the initial verified statement. Both BH&P and Granite Partners establish that the professional has a continuing duty to supplement the disclosure as new connections become known. Common triggers for supplemental disclosure include:

Acquisition of a new client whose interests intersect with the case

Hiring of a new attorney whose prior representations or relationships intersect with the case

Disclosure by the debtor of previously undisclosed creditor or transaction parties

Filing of new schedules or amended schedules adding parties

Discovery of a prior connection that was missed in the original conflict search

Sanctions for nondisclosure

The consequences of inadequate Rule 2014 disclosure can be severe and have been the subject of substantial published case law. Available sanctions and remedies include:

Disgorgement of all fees paid or payable to the professional, even if the underlying services were properly performed and the estate benefited from them. Courts have repeatedly held that the loss of fees is the appropriate response to a Rule 2014 violation even absent actual harm.

Disqualification from continued representation

Denial of compensation under 11 U.S.C. Section 328(c) (employment of a professional who is not disinterested may be terminated and compensation denied)

Referral to the United States trustee for further investigation or recommendation

Referral to the appropriate state disciplinary authority under the local rules of professional conduct

Sanctions under Rule 9011 for the verified statement, which is a court filing subject to the 9011(b) representations

Common procedural posture

First-day retention application

On the first or second day of a Chapter 11 case, the debtor in possession files an application to retain bankruptcy counsel under Section 327(a), accompanied by counsel's verified statement disclosing the results of a comprehensive conflict check against the parties listed on the petition, top-20 creditor list, and initial schedules. The application proposes compensation under Section 330 and Section 331, and seeks an order approving the employment.

Supplemental disclosure mid-case

After filing of the amended schedules and the addition of previously unlisted creditors, counsel files a supplemental verified statement disclosing newly identified connections with creditors added in the amendment, explaining why each connection does or does not constitute an adverse interest, and confirming continuing eligibility under Section 327(a).

Related rules and authority

11 U.S.C. Section 327 - Employment of professional persons

11 U.S.C. Section 328 - Limitation on compensation of professional persons

11 U.S.C. Section 330 - Compensation of officers

11 U.S.C. Section 101(14) - Definition of "disinterested person"

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 2016 - Compensation for services rendered

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 9011 - Signature, representations, sanctions

Practical impact

Rule 2014 is the single most important procedural rule governing professional employment in bankruptcy cases. The verified statement is the document on which the court relies to authorize employment; its accuracy and completeness are the foundation of every fee award that follows. Practitioners who treat Rule 2014 disclosure as a clerical exercise rather than as a substantive professional-responsibility obligation expose themselves to disgorgement, disqualification, and disciplinary referral - outcomes that have been imposed even in cases where the underlying conflict was, in retrospect, immaterial to the case outcome.

Disclose first; characterize second. The professional's job under Rule 2014 is to disclose every "connection" within the rule's broad definition. The job of the court (and the United States trustee, who reviews retention applications as part of the office's standard practice) is to evaluate whether the disclosed connections amount to a disqualifying adverse interest. A professional who "self-screens" connections out of the verified statement has substituted its own judgment for the court's and violated the rule even if no actual conflict existed.

Rule 1019 (Conversion)

In re Granite Partners, L.P., 219 B.R. 22 (Bankr. S.D.N.Y. 1998) - prohibition on professional self-screening of connections

## FRBP Rule 2014 - Employment of Professional Persons in Bankruptcy [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/rule-2014/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure
2014

Rule 2014: Employment of Professional Persons

Application requirements, verified statement of disinterestedness, and the continuing duty to supplement.

Verbatim text of Rule 2014(a)

An order approving the employment of attorneys, accountants, appraisers, auctioneers, agents, or other professionals pursuant to 11 U.S.C. Section 327, Section 1103, or Section 1114 shall be made only on application of the trustee or committee. The application shall be filed and, unless the case is a chapter 9 municipality case, a copy of the application shall be transmitted by the applicant to the United States trustee. The application shall state the specific facts showing the necessity for the employment, the name of the person to be employed, the reasons for the selection, the professional services to be rendered, any proposed arrangement for compensation, and, to the best of the applicant's knowledge, all of the person's connections with the debtor, creditors, any other party in interest, their respective attorneys and accountants, the United States trustee, or any person employed in the office of the United States trustee. The application shall be accompanied by a verified statement of the person to be employed setting forth the person's connections with the debtor, creditors, any other party in interest, their respective attorneys and accountants, the United States trustee, or any person employed in the office of the United States trustee. Fed. R. Bankr. P. 2014(a).

What Rule 2014 requires

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 2014 prescribes the procedure by which professional persons are employed in a bankruptcy case under 11 U.S.C. Section 327 (trustee employment of attorneys and other professionals), Section 1103 (committee employment), and Section 1114 (retiree-committee employment). The rule operates as the procedural mechanism that gives effect to the substantive disinterestedness standard set out in Section 327(a).

The rule contemplates two coordinated documents: (1) the application itself, prepared by the trustee, debtor in possession, or committee, identifying the professional, the services to be rendered, the proposed compensation arrangement, and the professional's connections as known to the applicant; and (2) a verified statement signed by the professional disclosing the professional's own connections with the debtor, creditors, parties in interest, their attorneys and accountants, the United States Trustee, and personnel of the United States Trustee's office.

The verified statement of disinterestedness

The verified statement is the operative disclosure document. It is signed under oath by the professional and must enumerate "connections" comprehensively. Courts have repeatedly held that the disclosure obligation is broader than the disqualification standard: the professional must disclose all connections and let the court determine which connections require disqualification, recusal, or limitation. Connections that are arguably innocuous still must be disclosed; the determination of materiality belongs to the court, not the disclosing professional.

The verified statement typically addresses, at minimum:

Prior representations of the debtor or its principals

Representations of creditors of the debtor in unrelated matters

Co-counsel relationships with other professionals in the case

Financial interests in any party in interest

Family and personal relationships that could affect impartial judgment

Receipt of any retainer or transfer from the debtor in the period before filing

The continuing duty to supplement

Rule 2014's disclosure duty is not satisfied at retention and frozen thereafter. The duty is continuing: when new connections become known or new relationships are formed during the case, the professional must supplement the verified statement. Courts have characterized the rule as imposing an "affirmative and ongoing" disclosure obligation. A connection that is discovered post-retention, or a relationship that newly arises post-retention, generates a supplemental disclosure obligation that operates on the same standard as the initial verified statement.

Failure to supplement when supplementation is required has been treated by reviewing courts as a basis for denial of compensation under Section 328(c), disgorgement of fees already paid, vacatur of the retention order, and in some circuits referral for disciplinary investigation.

Common procedural posture

Chapter 7 trustee retention

The Chapter 7 trustee files an application to employ general counsel, special counsel, or an accountant. The application is served on the United States Trustee. The verified statement is filed concurrently. The court may approve the employment ex parte if the United States Trustee does not object within the statutory comment period set by local rule.

Chapter 11 debtor in possession

The debtor in possession files an application to employ general bankruptcy counsel, ordinary-course professionals under Section 327(e), special litigation counsel, financial advisors, investment bankers, and claims agents. Each retention typically requires its own application and verified statement, though some jurisdictions permit aggregate retention orders for ordinary-course professionals.

Related rules and authority

11 U.S.C. Section 327 - Employment of professional persons (substantive disinterestedness standard)

11 U.S.C. Section 328 - Compensation and limitations on compensation; Section 328(c) denial for adverse interest

11 U.S.C. Section 330 - Compensation of officers

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 2016 - Compensation for services rendered and reimbursement of expenses

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 6003 - Interim and final relief immediately following commencement

Practical impact

Rule 2014 is the gatekeeping rule for compensation in a bankruptcy case. A professional who is not employed under a court order entered on a Rule 2014 application cannot recover compensation from the estate under Section 330, with limited exceptions for nunc pro tunc retention in extraordinary circumstances and for professionals retained under Section 327(e) on a limited basis. The verified statement is therefore the first document the United States Trustee, the court, and reviewing parties examine when assessing the professional's eligibility to be compensated from estate funds.

The continuing duty to supplement is the second compliance pressure point. A retention that was clean at the time of approval can become problematic mid-case if a new connection is formed and not promptly disclosed. Reviewing courts treat the omission, not merely the underlying connection, as the violation.

Disclosure is broader than disqualification. The standard taught in published opinions across multiple circuits is that the disclosure obligation under Rule 2014 is broader than the disqualification standard under Section 327. Marginal connections that may not require disqualification still must be disclosed so the court can make the disqualification determination on a complete record.

## FRBP Rule 2016 - Compensation for Services and Disclosure of Fees [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/rule-2016/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure
2016

Rule 2016: Compensation for Services Rendered and Reimbursement of Expenses

Fee applications under 2016(a), the Form B2030 attorney disclosure under 2016(b), and post-confirmation services.

Verbatim text of Rule 2016(a)

An entity seeking interim or final compensation for services, or reimbursement of necessary expenses, from the estate shall file an application setting forth a detailed statement of (1) the services rendered, time expended and expenses incurred, and (2) the amounts requested. An application for compensation shall include a statement as to what payments have theretofore been made or promised to the applicant for services rendered or to be rendered in any capacity whatsoever in connection with the case, the source of the compensation so paid or promised, whether any compensation previously received has been shared and whether an agreement or understanding exists between the applicant and any other entity for the sharing of compensation received or to be received for services rendered in or in connection with the case, and the particulars of any sharing of compensation or agreement or understanding therefor. Fed. R. Bankr. P. 2016(a).

Verbatim text of Rule 2016(b)

Every attorney for a debtor, whether or not the attorney applies for compensation, shall file and transmit to the United States trustee within 14 days after the order for relief, or at another time as the court may direct, the statement required by Section 329 of the Code including whether the attorney has shared or agreed to share the compensation with any other entity. The statement shall include the particulars of any such sharing or agreement to share by the attorney, but the details of any agreement for the sharing of the compensation with a member or regular associate of the attorney's law firm shall not be required. A supplemental statement shall be filed and transmitted to the United States trustee within 14 days after any payment or agreement not previously disclosed. Fed. R. Bankr. P. 2016(b).

Two distinct disclosures

Rule 2016 operates as two related but distinct disclosure regimes. Subdivision (a) governs compensation applications filed by any professional seeking payment from the estate. Subdivision (b) governs the statement of attorney compensation that every debtor's attorney must file, regardless of whether the attorney intends to seek compensation from the estate. The Section 329 statement is filed on Official Form B2030.

Rule 2016(a) - Compensation applications

A fee application under Rule 2016(a) must show, with particularity, the services rendered, the time expended, the expenses incurred, and the amounts requested. The application is the operational vehicle for compensation under 11 U.S.C. Section 330. Courts evaluate fee applications under the lodestar method or the alternative reasonableness factors enumerated in Section 330(a)(3). Time entries are expected to identify the timekeeper, the task, the duration, and enough detail that the United States Trustee and the court can evaluate necessity, benefit to the estate, and reasonableness.

Many districts have adopted local guidelines that prescribe time-entry formats, billing-increment conventions, prohibited entries (block billing, vague descriptions, clerical tasks billed at attorney rates), and disclosure of fee-sharing or referral arrangements. The United States Trustee Program publishes national fee-application guidelines for Chapter 11 cases of substantial size.

Rule 2016(b) - Form B2030 disclosure

The Section 329 statement on Form B2030 is the attorney's verified disclosure of:

The total amount agreed for legal services to be rendered in connection with the case

Amounts paid prior to filing and the source of those payments

Balance due, if any

The services covered by the agreement (and equally important, the services not covered)

Whether the attorney has shared or agreed to share compensation with any entity outside the attorney's firm

The form's prepopulated language enumerates services typically included in a flat fee (analysis of financial situation, preparation of petition and schedules, representation at the Section 341 meeting) and services typically excluded (representation in adversary proceedings, reaffirmation negotiations beyond the initial review). The attorney edits the form to reflect the actual scope of the engagement.

The 14-day timing rule and supplements

The initial Rule 2016(b) statement is due within 14 days after the order for relief. A supplemental statement is required within 14 days after any payment or fee agreement not previously disclosed. The supplemental obligation is continuing throughout the pendency of the case; an attorney who receives an additional payment from the debtor mid-case has a 14-day window to file a supplemental Form B2030 disclosing that payment.

The post-confirmation services question

A recurring practical issue is whether services rendered after plan confirmation are "in connection with the case" for Section 329 purposes, and therefore require Rule 2016(b) disclosure. Local rules in many jurisdictions address this directly. Local Rule 2016-1(E), where adopted, typically provides that compensation for services rendered after confirmation on matters within the scope of the original retention requires either a supplemental Rule 2016(b) statement or a separate fee application, depending on the source of the payment.

The general principle drawn from published decisions: payments to the debtor's attorney that arise from the engagement memorialized on the original Form B2030 are within the disclosure obligation regardless of whether the services are rendered pre- or post-confirmation. Payments for matters entirely outside the scope of the original engagement are not. The distinction is fact-dependent and the burden of demonstrating that a payment falls outside the disclosure obligation rests on the attorney.

Common procedural posture

Chapter 7 consumer case

Counsel files Form B2030 with the petition disclosing the flat fee and the scope of services. If counsel agrees post-petition to handle a reaffirmation, an adversary proceeding, or a Section 522(f) motion outside the original flat fee, a supplemental Form B2030 disclosing the additional fee is filed within 14 days of the supplemental engagement.

Chapter 11 Subchapter V

Debtor's counsel typically files both the Rule 2014 retention application and a Rule 2016(b) Section 329 statement. Subsequent compensation flows through periodic Rule 2016(a) interim fee applications, with a final fee application at or near confirmation. Post-confirmation work generally requires either a supplemental Form B2030 or a separate fee application depending on local practice.

Consequences of non-disclosure

Section 329(b) authorizes the court to "cancel any such agreement, or order the return of any such payment" to the extent the compensation "exceeds the reasonable value of any such services." Where the underlying defect is non-disclosure rather than excess, courts routinely order disgorgement of undisclosed payments without a separate reasonableness inquiry on the theory that an undisclosed payment cannot be approved as reasonable on a record that does not contain it. The remedy reaches both pre-petition and post-petition payments that should have been disclosed.

Disclosure precedes reasonableness. The threshold question in any Rule 2016 review is whether the payment was disclosed at all. A payment that was not disclosed is not eligible for reasonableness analysis on its merits; the typical remedy is disgorgement, with subsequent application available if the attorney wishes to seek approval of compensation actually earned.

Related rules and authority

11 U.S.C. Section 329 - Debtor's transactions with attorneys

11 U.S.C. Section 330 - Compensation of officers

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 2014 - Employment of professional persons

Official Form B2030 - Disclosure of Compensation of Attorney for Debtor

USTP Guidelines for Reviewing Fee Applications

## FRBP Rule 2017 - Court Review of Debtor Counsel Transactions [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/rule-2017-attorney-fee-review/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure
2017

Rule 2017: Court Review of Debtor Counsel Transactions

Pre-petition fee review under Rule 2017(a), post-petition transactions under 2017(b), the section 329 statutory framework, and the disgorgement remedy.

Verbatim text of Rule 2017

(a) Payment or transfer to attorney before order for relief. On motion by any party in interest or on the court's own initiative, the court after notice and a hearing may determine whether any payment of money or any transfer of property by the debtor, made directly or indirectly and in contemplation of the filing of a petition under the Code by or against the debtor or before entry of the order for relief in an involuntary case, to an attorney for services rendered or to be rendered is excessive.

(b) Payment or transfer to attorney after order for relief. On motion by the debtor, the United States trustee, or on the court's own initiative, the court after notice and a hearing may determine whether any payment of money or any transfer of property, or any agreement therefor, by the debtor to an attorney after entry of an order for relief in a case under the Code is excessive, whether the payment or transfer is made or is to be made directly or indirectly, if the payment, transfer, or agreement therefor is for services in any way related to the case. Fed. R. Bankr. P. 2017.

The statutory anchor: 11 U.S.C. Section 329

Rule 2017 is the procedural mechanism for the substantive authority granted by 11 U.S.C. Section 329. Section 329(a) requires debtor counsel to file a statement of the compensation paid or agreed to be paid for services rendered or to be rendered in contemplation of or in connection with the case. Section 329(b) authorizes the court to cancel any agreement or order the return of any payment "to the extent excessive."

Section 329 is one of the few statutory provisions in the Bankruptcy Code that grants the court roving authority over transactions in which the court itself is not directly a party. The premise is that debtor counsel occupies a position of trust relative to a debtor whose financial distress impairs ordinary arm's-length bargaining. The court is the disinterested check on that bargain.

The structure of Rule 2017

Rule 2017 has two operative subdivisions corresponding to the two temporal phases of the attorney-debtor relationship:

Rule 2017(a) governs pre-petition transactions - any payment or transfer made "in contemplation of" the filing of a petition or before the order for relief in an involuntary case. The standard is whether the payment is excessive.

Rule 2017(b) governs post-petition transactions - any payment, transfer, or agreement made after the order for relief that is "in any way related to the case." The standard is again whether the payment is excessive.

The two subdivisions differ in the parties authorized to initiate review. Rule 2017(a) permits initiation by "any party in interest" or by the court. Rule 2017(b) limits party initiation to the debtor and the United States trustee, but preserves the court's sua sponte authority. The distinction reflects the different constituency interests implicated: pre-petition fees affect the size of the estate available to all creditors, while post-petition fees come from the estate itself and are subject to other oversight regimes.

The "excessive" standard

Neither Section 329 nor Rule 2017 defines "excessive." Courts have developed a multi-factor analysis substantially overlapping the lodestar framework applied to professional fee applications under Section 330. Typical factors include:

The nature and complexity of the services rendered

The time reasonably required for the services

The customary fee charged in the local market for comparable services

The experience and skill of the attorney

The results achieved

Whether the fee was the product of arm's-length negotiation under conditions permitting informed consent

The "excessive" standard is not coextensive with the Section 330 "reasonable" standard, however. Section 329 review reaches transactions that may not be reviewable under Section 330 at all - notably, pre-petition retainer agreements with consumer debtors who were not yet debtors when the agreement was made.

Sua sponte review

One of the structural features of Rule 2017 that distinguishes it from most procedural rules is the express grant of sua sponte authority to the court. The court need not wait for a motion; it may set fees for review on its own initiative after notice and a hearing.

The practical implication is significant. A debtor who has paid fees to counsel pre-petition often has no incentive to challenge those fees - the debtor has already paid and may continue to depend on counsel. A creditor with standing to challenge under Rule 2017(a) may lack the information to identify a problem. The court's sua sponte authority closes the gap. A judge who observes an unusual fee disclosure, a sudden lawsuit by counsel against a former client, or an unexplained absence of post-petition representation may set the fee for review without any motion from the parties.

Disgorgement remedy

The remedy under Section 329(b) is structured in the alternative: the court may "cancel" the agreement (preventing future enforcement) or order the return of any payment "to the extent excessive." The two remedies are not mutually exclusive. A court may cancel a contingent or installment-fee agreement going forward and order disgorgement of payments already received that exceed the value of services actually rendered.

Disgorgement under Section 329(b) is mandatory once the court finds excessiveness; the statute provides that the court "may" cancel and order return, but the consistent case law treats the discretion as one over the scope of disgorgement rather than over whether to disgorge at all. A finding that a fee is excessive without a corresponding disgorgement order is rare.

The destination of disgorged funds depends on the circumstances. Where the fee was paid from estate property, return is to the estate (with redistribution to creditors through ordinary distribution mechanisms). Where the fee was paid from non-estate property (a relative's contribution, for example), return is typically to the source of the payment.

Interaction with the Rule 2016 disclosure

Rule 2017 review is operationally dependent on the disclosure required by Section 329(a) and Rule 2016(b). Section 329(a) requires debtor counsel to file a statement of compensation within 14 days after the order for relief. The Rule 2016(b) disclosure - filed on Official Form 2030 - identifies the source of compensation, the amount, the services covered, and any agreement for further payment.

An incomplete or inaccurate Section 329(a) / Rule 2016(b) disclosure has two consequences. First, it deprives the court and parties in interest of the information needed to evaluate whether to seek Rule 2017 review. Second, it is itself an independently sanctionable defect: a knowing failure to disclose is a basis for denial of all compensation under the "fiduciary disclosure" doctrine that pre-dates the Bankruptcy Code and has been consistently applied under it.

Common procedural posture

Pre-petition retainer review

A consumer debtor pays a flat-fee retainer to counsel before filing a Chapter 7 petition. A creditor or the U.S. trustee believes the fee was excessive in light of the simplicity of the case. The challenger files a Rule 2017(a) motion. The court reviews the fee against the local-market customary fee, the work actually performed, and any unusual circumstances justifying departure. If the court finds the fee excessive, it orders disgorgement of the excess.

Post-petition installment-fee review

Debtor counsel enters into a post-petition installment-payment agreement for services rendered in the bankruptcy. The U.S. trustee believes the agreement was not disclosed under Rule 2016(b) and that the installment structure operates as an undisclosed contingent fee. The U.S. trustee files a Rule 2017(b) motion. The court may cancel the agreement going forward and order disgorgement of installments already received.

Related rules and authority

11 U.S.C. Section 329 - Debtor's transactions with attorneys

11 U.S.C. Section 330 - Compensation of officers and professionals

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 2014 - Employment of professional persons

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 2016 - Compensation for services rendered (disclosure)

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 9011 - Signature and representations to the court

Practical impact

Rule 2017 is the procedural rule that most directly enforces the substantive principle that debtor counsel does not have unconstrained pricing authority over a financially distressed client. The rule operates at three time horizons: pre-petition (subdivision (a)), post-petition (subdivision (b)), and post-confirmation - because Section 329 review remains available, by the consistent case law, even after the case is closed, when an excessive fee was concealed at the time of disclosure.

The court's sua sponte authority is the load-bearing feature. A debtor who has paid counsel and remains dependent on counsel for representation has little incentive to challenge the fee; a creditor without access to the underlying engagement information cannot identify a problem. Sua sponte review under Rule 2017 closes the gap that party-driven review would otherwise leave open.

## FRBP Rule 3001 - Proof of Claim and Supporting Documentation [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/rule-3001-proof-of-claim/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Home › Federal Rules of Bankruptcy Procedure › Rule 3001 (Proof of Claim)

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure
3001

Rule 3001: Proof of Claim and Supporting Documentation

Official Form 410, Rule 3001(c) writing requirement, Rule 3001(f) prima facie validity, and the circuit split on stale collection-statute claims.

What Rule 3001 does

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 3001 specifies the form a proof of claim must take, the supporting documentation a claimant must attach, the evidentiary effect of a properly filed proof of claim, and supplemental disclosure obligations for consumer claims and claims secured by an interest in the debtor's principal residence. A proof of claim that complies with Rule 3001 is the principal vehicle by which a creditor asserts a right to payment from the bankruptcy estate.

Official Form 410

Rule 3001(a) requires that a proof of claim "conform substantially" to the appropriate Official Form. Official Form 410 is the standard proof-of-claim form used in all chapters and is structured into discrete fields covering creditor identification, the basis of the claim, the amount claimed, secured-claim disclosures, priority-claim disclosures, and the claimant's signature under Section 152 false-claim warnings. The Form 410 series includes:

Form 410 - Proof of claim (the principal form)

Form 410A - Mortgage proof of claim attachment (required for any claim secured by the debtor's principal residence under Rule 3001(c)(2)(C))

Form 410S1 - Notice of mortgage payment change (required for ongoing changes in a residential mortgage under Rule 3002.1(b))

Form 410S2 - Notice of post-petition mortgage fees, expenses, and charges (required under Rule 3002.1(c))

Rule 3001(c) - the writing-attachment requirement

Rule 3001(c) requires that a claim "based on a writing" be supported by a copy of the writing filed with the proof of claim. The requirement applies to the underlying contract, note, security agreement, judgment, or other instrument that establishes the claim. Rule 3001(c)(2), added in 2011 and amended thereafter, imposes additional disclosure for claims by individual debtors:

(c)(2)(A) Itemization. If the claim includes interest, fees, expenses, or other charges incurred before the petition date, an itemized statement of the interest, fees, expenses, or charges must accompany the proof of claim.

(c)(2)(B) Escrow. If a security interest is claimed in the debtor's property, a statement of the amount necessary to cure any default as of the petition date must accompany the claim.

(c)(2)(C) Principal residence. If the claim is secured by a security interest in the debtor's principal residence, the proof of claim must include Form 410A (the mortgage proof of claim attachment), which itemizes the principal balance, accrued and unpaid interest, prepetition fees, escrow balance, and the loan-history information sufficient to demonstrate how the claim amount was calculated.

(c)(2)(D) Sanctions for noncompliance. If the claimant fails to provide the required information, the court may, after notice and hearing, preclude the claimant from presenting the omitted information as evidence in any contested matter or adversary proceeding and may award expenses (including attorney's fees) to the prevailing party.

Rule 3001(f) - prima facie validity

Rule 3001(f) provides:

A proof of claim executed and filed in accordance with these rules shall constitute prima facie evidence of the validity and amount of the claim. Fed. R. Bankr. P. 3001(f).

The prima facie validity rule is a procedural burden-shifting mechanism. When a proof of claim is filed in compliance with Rule 3001 (i.e., on the correct form, with required attachments, with required supplemental disclosures, and signed under penalty of perjury), the claim is presumed valid and the burden of going forward shifts to the party objecting to the claim. The objector must present evidence "equal in force to the prima facie case" to overcome the presumption; once the objector does so, the burden of persuasion remains with the claimant by a preponderance of the evidence.

A proof of claim that does not comply with Rule 3001 - for example, a claim that omits required attachments, omits required Rule 3001(c)(2) itemization, or is signed by an unauthorized representative - is not entitled to the prima facie validity presumption. Such a claim may still be allowed if the claimant proves it by a preponderance of evidence at a contested-matter hearing, but the claimant carries the initial burden of going forward.

The In re Heath line and the stale-claim circuit split

One of the most-litigated questions under Rule 3001 has been whether a creditor (typically a debt buyer) violates the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act by filing a proof of claim on a debt as to which the applicable state-law statute of limitations has expired. The leading early decision is In re Heath, 331 B.R. 424 (B.A.P. 9th Cir. 2005), which addressed (in a different posture) the documentation a claimant must attach to support a credit-card claim.

The stale-claim FDCPA controversy reached the Supreme Court in Midland Funding, LLC v. Johnson, 137 S. Ct. 1407 (2017). The Court held 5-3 that filing a proof of claim on a debt that is "obviously time-barred" by the applicable state statute of limitations is not a violation of the FDCPA, reasoning that the proof of claim is a "claim" within the Bankruptcy Code's definition (a right to payment, whether or not enforceable) and that the bankruptcy claims-allowance process provides the trustee and the debtor adequate procedural protection. Midland Funding resolved the FDCPA question but left intact the procedural rule under 11 U.S.C. Section 502(b)(1) that an objection asserting the statute of limitations is a valid ground for disallowance.

The practical effect of Midland Funding is that a debt buyer may file a proof of claim on a time-barred debt without FDCPA exposure, but the trustee or debtor may object and the bankruptcy court must disallow the claim if the applicable statute of limitations has run. Several circuits had previously held (before Midland Funding) that the FDCPA prohibited such filings; the Court's decision unified the rule in favor of permissible filing-subject-to-objection.

Filing and amendment of proofs of claim

Rule 3002(c) sets the deadline for filing a proof of claim in voluntary Chapter 7, Chapter 12, and Chapter 13 cases: 70 days after the order for relief (with longer windows for governmental units under Section 502(b)(9)). In Chapter 11 cases, the court sets the bar date by order. A proof of claim filed after the bar date is generally disallowed unless an exception applies (excusable neglect, late-filed government claim within the statutory window, etc.).

Amendment of a proof of claim is permitted as a matter of right at any time before the bar date and may be permitted after the bar date when the amendment relates back to a timely-filed claim and does not assert a wholly new ground of recovery. Courts apply a discretionary standard to post-bar-date amendments, weighing prejudice to other creditors against the equities supporting amendment.

Transfer of claim (Rule 3001(e))

Rule 3001(e) governs the transfer of a claim. When a claim is transferred after the proof of claim is filed, the transferee files a notice of transfer with the clerk; the clerk gives notice to the alleged transferor, who has 21 days to object. If no objection is timely filed, the transferee is substituted for the transferor as the holder of the claim. The transfer-of-claim procedure is the principal vehicle by which debt buyers acquire and prosecute consumer claims in active bankruptcy cases.

Common procedural posture

Credit-card claim without itemization

A debt buyer files a proof of claim on a charged-off credit-card account but does not attach an account statement or itemize the interest and fees accrued before the charge-off date. The debtor objects under 11 U.S.C. Section 502(b)(1) and asserts the Rule 3001(c)(2)(A) itemization failure. The claim is not entitled to prima facie validity; the claimant must produce the underlying account documentation to carry its burden of proof.

Mortgage claim missing Form 410A

A mortgage servicer files a proof of claim on a residential mortgage without attaching the required Form 410A. The Chapter 13 trustee objects. The court treats the noncompliant filing as failing the Rule 3001(c)(2)(C) requirement, denies the claim prima facie validity, and may, under Rule 3001(c)(2)(D), preclude the servicer from later introducing the omitted loan-history evidence in any contested matter.

Related rules and authority

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 3002 - Filing proof of claim or interest (bar dates)

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 3007 - Objections to claims

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 3002.1 - Notice relating to claims secured by debtor's principal residence

11 U.S.C. Section 502 - Allowance of claims or interests

Midland Funding, LLC v. Johnson, 137 S. Ct. 1407 (2017)

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 9011 - Signature, representations, sanctions

Form compliance is not optional for prima facie validity. Filing a proof of claim on the correct form, with required attachments and required supplemental disclosures, is the procedural predicate for the Rule 3001(f) presumption. A claim that skips the required Rule 3001(c)(2) disclosures may still be allowed, but the claimant carries the burden of going forward and may face Rule 3001(c)(2)(D) preclusion sanctions.

## FRBP Rule 3001 - Proof of Claim, Form and Supporting Documents [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/rule-3001/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure
3001

Rule 3001: Proof of Claim

Form, content, attachments, evidentiary effect, and supplemental disclosures for claims filed in a bankruptcy case.

Verbatim text of Rule 3001(a) and (f)

(a) Form and content. A proof of claim is a written statement setting forth a creditor's claim. A proof of claim shall conform substantially to the appropriate Official Form.

(f) Evidentiary effect. A proof of claim executed and filed in accordance with these rules shall constitute prima facie evidence of the validity and amount of the claim. Fed. R. Bankr. P. 3001(a) and (f).

What Rule 3001 establishes

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 3001 governs the form, content, and evidentiary effect of a proof of claim. A "claim" is defined in 11 U.S.C. Section 101(5) as a right to payment, whether or not the right is reduced to judgment, liquidated, unliquidated, fixed, contingent, matured, unmatured, disputed, undisputed, legal, equitable, secured, or unsecured. Rule 3001 specifies how a creditor asserts and documents that right in the bankruptcy case.

The rule operates in coordination with Rule 3002 (filing deadlines for proofs of claim in Chapter 7, 12, and 13 cases) and Rule 3003 (Chapter 9 and 11 cases). Rule 3001 addresses how a claim is presented; Rules 3002 and 3003 address when it must be filed.

Form and signature (Rule 3001(a) and (b))

A proof of claim must conform substantially to Official Form 410 (the unified Proof of Claim form). The form must be signed by the creditor or by the creditor's authorized agent. The Advisory Committee Notes establish that the signature serves the same gatekeeping function as a signature under Rule 9011: it certifies that the information provided has a reasonable factual basis after inquiry reasonable under the circumstances.

Supporting documentation (Rule 3001(c))

If a claim is based on a writing - a promissory note, a contract, a lease, an account agreement - the original or a duplicate of the writing must be filed with the proof of claim. If the writing has been lost or destroyed, a statement of the circumstances of the loss or destruction must be filed with the proof of claim.

Open-end or revolving consumer credit (Rule 3001(c)(3))

For claims based on an open-end or revolving consumer credit agreement, Rule 3001(c)(3) requires a statement that includes:

The name of the entity from whom the creditor purchased the account

The name of the entity to whom the debt was owed at the time of the account holder's last transaction

The date of the account holder's last transaction

The date of the last payment on the account

The date on which the account was charged to profit and loss

The 3001(c)(3) statement is the procedural mechanism by which Congress addressed the proliferation of stale and inadequately documented consumer credit claims in Chapter 13 cases. The information required is the documentary backbone of a consumer credit claim and is the threshold for prima facie validity under Rule 3001(f).

Itemized statement of interest, fees, expenses (Rule 3001(c)(2))

For claims that include charges in addition to principal, the proof of claim must include an itemized statement of the interest, fees, expenses, or other charges incurred before the petition was filed. Aggregate amounts unsupported by itemization do not satisfy Rule 3001(c)(2) and are not entitled to prima facie effect.

Evidence of perfection of security interest (Rule 3001(d))

If a claim is secured by a security interest in property of the debtor, evidence that the security interest has been perfected must accompany the proof of claim. The evidence depends on the collateral: a UCC-1 financing statement for personal property, a recorded mortgage or deed of trust for real property, a certificate of title for a motor vehicle. A secured claim filed without evidence of perfection is not entitled to be treated as secured for purposes of Rule 3001(f) prima facie validity.

Transfer of claim (Rule 3001(e))

Rule 3001(e) governs the procedure for transferring a claim after a proof of claim has been filed. The transferee files a statement of the transfer; the clerk gives notice to the alleged transferor, who has twenty-one days to object. If no objection is filed, the transferee is substituted as the holder of the claim. The procedure exists to ensure that the docket accurately reflects the current holder of each claim, particularly relevant in cases with active secondary trading.

Prima facie validity (Rule 3001(f))

A proof of claim that complies with the form, signature, and attachment requirements of Rule 3001 constitutes prima facie evidence of the validity and amount of the claim. Prima facie validity does not mean the claim is conclusively allowed; it means the claim is allowed unless an objecting party comes forward with evidence sufficient to overcome the presumption.

If the proof of claim is not compliant - if a required attachment is missing, if the 3001(c)(3) consumer statement is incomplete, if itemization is absent - the claim does not enjoy prima facie validity. The objecting party still must overcome the underlying claim, but the burden of going forward shifts.

Sanctions for non-compliance (Rule 3001(c)(2)(D))

Rule 3001(c)(2)(D) authorizes the court, after notice and a hearing, to preclude a creditor that fails to provide the information required by Rule 3001(c) from presenting the omitted information in any contested matter or adversary proceeding in the case, and to award other appropriate relief including reasonable expenses and attorney's fees caused by the failure. This provision gives Rule 3001(c) operational teeth beyond mere loss of prima facie validity.

Common procedural posture

Trade creditor claim in Chapter 11

A vendor files a proof of claim for the unpaid balance on an open trade account. The proof of claim attaches the most recent invoice, the account statement, and a summary of payment history. The debtor in possession reviews the claim against its books and either accepts the claim or files an objection under Rule 3007 setting forth the basis for the objection.

Credit-card debt purchaser in Chapter 13

A debt buyer files a proof of claim on a purchased consumer credit account. The proof must include the Rule 3001(c)(3) statement: the original creditor, the entity holding the debt at the last transaction, the date of last transaction, the date of last payment, and the charge-off date. If the statement is incomplete or the chain of assignment is not documented, the claim is subject to objection under Rule 3007.

Related rules and authority

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 3002 - Filing proof of claim or interest (deadlines)

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 3003 - Claims and equity security interests in Chapter 9 and 11 cases

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 3007 - Objections to claims

11 U.S.C. Section 501 - Filing of proofs of claims and interests

11 U.S.C. Section 502 - Allowance of claims or interests

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 9011 - Signature, representations to the court, sanctions

Practical impact

Rule 3001 is the gatekeeping rule for participation in any distribution from the estate. A claim that is not properly filed under Rule 3001 (and timely filed under Rule 3002 or 3003) is at risk of disallowance for non-compliance. The prima facie validity provision in Rule 3001(f) creates a meaningful procedural advantage for compliant claims: the objecting party bears the burden of going forward with evidence to overcome the presumption.

The 2011 and 2017 amendments to Rule 3001 - particularly the 3001(c)(2) itemization requirement and the 3001(c)(3) consumer-credit disclosure requirement - reflected Advisory Committee findings that proofs of claim filed by high-volume creditors and debt buyers often lacked the documentary foundation necessary for meaningful objection practice. The amendments shifted the burden of documentary precision onto the claim filer.

Prima facie validity is rebuttable, not conclusive. A compliant proof of claim shifts the burden of going forward to the objecting party, but the burden of persuasion on the underlying claim remains with the creditor. An objection that comes forward with sufficient evidence to neutralize the presumption returns the burden to the creditor to prove the claim by a preponderance.

## FRBP Rule 3002 - Filing Proof of Claim Deadlines and Extensions [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/rule-3002/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure
3002

Rule 3002: Filing Proof of Claim or Interest

The 70-day general claims bar date, the 180-day government unit deadline, and the limited grounds for extension.

Verbatim text of Rule 3002(c)

In a voluntary chapter 7 case, chapter 12 case, or chapter 13 case, a proof of claim is timely filed if it is filed not later than 70 days after the order for relief under that chapter or the date of the order of conversion to a case under chapter 12 or chapter 13. In an involuntary chapter 7 case, a proof of claim is timely filed if it is filed not later than 90 days after the order for relief under that chapter is entered. But in all these cases, the following exceptions apply: ... Fed. R. Bankr. P. 3002(c).

What Rule 3002 establishes

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 3002 establishes the deadlines by which a proof of claim must be filed in a Chapter 7, 12, or 13 case in order to be timely. The rule operates in coordination with Rule 3001 (the form and content of a proof of claim) and with Rule 3003 (which governs deadlines in Chapter 9 and Chapter 11 cases). Rule 3002 controls when a claim must be filed; Rule 3001 controls how.

The general 70-day bar date

The 2017 amendment to Rule 3002(c) replaced the previous 90-day post-meeting-of-creditors deadline with a uniform 70-day deadline measured from the order for relief in a voluntary case. The change was intended to make the deadline more predictable and easier to calculate without reference to the date of the Section 341 meeting of creditors. In an involuntary Chapter 7 case, the deadline is 90 days after the order for relief is entered.

The deadline applies generally to all creditors with notice of the case. A creditor who fails to file within the deadline is at risk of disallowance under 11 U.S.C. Section 502(b)(9), which provides that a claim shall be disallowed to the extent that proof of the claim is not timely filed.

Special deadlines for government units

A government unit (federal, state, or local taxing authority, or other governmental claimant) is entitled to the later of (i) the 70-day general deadline or (ii) 180 days after the date of the order for relief. The 180-day government-unit deadline is grounded in 11 U.S.C. Section 502(b)(9) and reflects the additional time often needed by government units to identify the debtor in their internal records and to calculate the amount of any tax claim.

Limited grounds for extension (Rule 3002(c))

Rule 3002(c) enumerates several specific exceptions under which a claim may be filed after the general deadline:

3002(c)(1) - The court may extend the time for filing for a government unit on motion filed before the expiration of the 180-day deadline

3002(c)(2) - An infant or incompetent person may file at any time before five years after the order for relief

3002(c)(3) - An unsecured claim arising from a judgment in a pre-petition action may be filed within 30 days after the judgment becomes final

3002(c)(4) - A claim arising from the rejection of an executory contract or unexpired lease may be filed within such time as the court may direct

3002(c)(5) - In a previously no-asset Chapter 7 case in which a notice of possible dividend is later sent, claims may be filed within 90 days of that notice

3002(c)(6) - A creditor who was not given timely notice of the claims bar date may file within 60 days after the date of mailing of the notice of the time to file claims

3002(c)(7) - A claim secured by a security interest in the debtor's principal residence may be filed within a period set by the court

Outside of the enumerated exceptions, Rule 3002(c) does not authorize extension of the general bar date. The 2017 amendment to Rule 3002(c)(6) - permitting late-filed claims by creditors who did not receive timely notice - addressed a recurring fairness concern but did not generalize the extension authority.

The Section 502(b)(9) disallowance pathway

A late-filed claim is not automatically disallowed; disallowance under Section 502(b)(9) requires an objection. In practice, the Chapter 13 trustee often objects to late-filed claims as part of routine case administration. In Chapter 7 cases, the trustee may not bother to object to a late-filed claim if the case is a no-asset case, since the claim will not receive distribution in any event.

The Supreme Court has confirmed that the bar date operates as a substantive deadline: a creditor with notice of the case who fails to file within the deadline forfeits the right to a distribution from the estate. The narrow Rule 3002(c) exceptions are the exclusive procedural avenue for filing a late claim that will share in the distribution.

Tardy claims in Chapter 7 (Section 726(a)(3))

In a Chapter 7 case, a tardily filed claim that is not allowed under Section 502(b)(9) (because the creditor did not have actual notice or actual knowledge of the case in time to file timely) may still receive a distribution under 11 U.S.C. Section 726(a)(3), after timely filed unsecured claims have been paid in full. The Section 726(a)(3) tardy-claim distribution is a separate pathway that operates only after timely-filed claims are paid.

Common procedural posture

Chapter 13 unsecured creditor

A credit-card creditor receives notice of the debtor's Chapter 13 case on the date of filing. The 70-day deadline runs from the order for relief. The creditor files a proof of claim within the deadline through the court's electronic claims filing system. If the deadline passes without filing, the trustee will likely object to any later-filed claim under Section 502(b)(9).

Government tax claim

A state taxing authority receives notice of the case but requires time to identify the debtor in its records and calculate the tax owed. The authority files within 180 days of the order for relief - within the extended deadline available to government units under Rule 3002(c)(1) and Section 502(b)(9).

Related rules and authority

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 3001 - Proof of claim (form and content)

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 3003 - Claims in Chapter 9 and 11 cases

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 3007 - Objections to claims

11 U.S.C. Section 501 - Filing of proofs of claims and interests

11 U.S.C. Section 502 - Allowance of claims (Section 502(b)(9) disallowance for late filing)

11 U.S.C. Section 726 - Distribution of property of the estate (Section 726(a)(3) tardy claims)

Practical impact

Rule 3002 is the bright-line procedural threshold that separates a participating creditor from a barred one. Unlike many bankruptcy procedural deadlines that can be extended for cause, the Rule 3002 claims bar date is extended only on the narrow grounds enumerated in subdivision (c). A claim that misses the deadline without falling within an enumerated exception is at risk of disallowance even if the underlying claim is meritorious and undisputed.

The 2017 amendment that established a uniform 70-day deadline measured from the order for relief - rather than from the meeting of creditors - simplified deadline calculation but did not change the substantive consequence of missing the deadline. Practitioners should calendar the bar date from the order-for-relief date and verify the date against the Notice of Bankruptcy Filing issued by the clerk.

Lack of notice is a narrow exception, not a general extension ground. Rule 3002(c)(6) permits late filing only by a creditor who did not receive timely notice of the bar date. A creditor who received the notice but failed to file is not within the exception, regardless of internal docketing failures or other operational excuses.

Rule 9011 (Sanctions)
Rule 4007 (Dischargeability)
Rule 1019 (Conversion)
Rule 1017 (Dismissal)

## FRBP Rule 3007 - Objections to Claims [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/rule-3007-claim-objections/

Open Bankruptcy Project

Home › Federal Rules of Bankruptcy Procedure › Rule 3007

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure
3007

Rule 3007: Objections to Claims

Procedure for objecting to a proof of claim, the 30-day notice requirement, contested matter status, omnibus objections, and the evidentiary burden-shift framework.

What Rule 3007 does

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 3007 prescribes the procedure for objecting to a proof of claim filed in a bankruptcy case. The rule covers (1) the form, content, and service of a claim objection, (2) the 30-day notice period before a claim objection may be heard, (3) the conversion of a claim objection to a contested matter under Rule 9014, and (4) the use of omnibus objections to multiple claims under Rule 3007(d). The rule operates in tandem with 11 U.S.C. Section 502 (the substantive grounds for disallowance) and Rule 3001(f) (the prima facie validity presumption that the objection must overcome).

The basic objection procedure - Rule 3007(a)

Rule 3007(a) provides that an objection to a claim "shall be in writing and filed." A copy of the objection, with notice of the hearing on the objection, must be served on the claimant, the debtor or debtor in possession, and the trustee at least 30 days before the scheduled hearing.

The 30-day notice requirement is procedural. A claim objection set for hearing on less than 30 days' notice is procedurally defective and is normally continued by the court to a date satisfying the rule. Some districts have local rules that provide for a "negative-notice" or "no-response-required-if-no-objection" procedure: the objector serves the objection with notice that the court will consider the objection without hearing if no response is filed within a stated period; this local procedure is supplementary to and does not displace the Rule 3007 requirements.

Contested-matter status under Rule 9014

An objection to a claim is a contested matter governed by Rule 9014. Rule 9014 makes certain Part VII (adversary-proceeding) rules applicable to contested matters, including Rules 7026 through 7037 (discovery), Rule 7052 (findings of fact and conclusions of law), and Rule 7054 (judgment). Rule 9014(c) also gives the court discretion to apply other Part VII rules at any stage of the proceeding.

Treating a claim objection as a contested matter has practical consequences:

Discovery is available under Rules 7026-7037 (with court approval where the rules require it)

Motion practice (summary judgment, motions in limine) is available under the Part VII rules

The court enters findings of fact and conclusions of law on the record under Rule 7052

The court's order disallowing or allowing the claim is a final, appealable order

What the objection must contain

Although Rule 3007 does not prescribe the content of the objection itself, established practice requires that the objection:

Identify the claim being objected to by claimant name and claim number on the claims register

State the amount of the claim as filed and the amount, if any, the objector believes should be allowed

State the legal and factual grounds for the objection with specificity

Identify the statutory or rule-based basis for the objection (e.g., 11 U.S.C. Section 502(b)(1) - claim unenforceable under applicable nonbankruptcy law; Section 502(b)(2) - unmatured interest; Section 502(b)(4) - excessive insider compensation; etc.)

Be supported by exhibits, declarations, or other evidence sufficient to overcome the prima facie validity of the claim under Rule 3001(f)

Include a notice of hearing or, in negative-notice districts, the notice prescribed by local rule

A bare or conclusory objection that recites "lack of documentation" or "amount is disputed" without specifying the basis for the dispute may be insufficient to shift the evidentiary burden, even when the underlying claim is questionable. The objector's burden of going forward is satisfied only when the objection (and any supporting evidence) is sufficient to "equal the prima facie case" of the claim.

The evidentiary burden-shift framework

The burden-shift framework operating in claim-objection practice is well settled:

Claimant's initial burden: The claimant files a proof of claim that complies with Rule 3001. If the claim is "executed and filed in accordance with these rules," Rule 3001(f) gives the claim "prima facie evidence of the validity and amount of the claim."

Objector's burden of going forward: The objector must produce evidence sufficient to rebut the prima facie validity of the claim - evidence "equal in force" to the prima facie case. A bare denial does not suffice.

Claimant's burden of persuasion: Once the objector rebuts the prima facie validity, the claimant carries the ultimate burden of proving the claim by a preponderance of the evidence. The claimant must produce the underlying documentation and any other evidence necessary to establish entitlement to the claim amount.

When a proof of claim does not comply with Rule 3001 (e.g., a credit-card claim lacking the Rule 3001(c)(2)(A) itemization, or a residential-mortgage claim lacking Form 410A), the claim is not entitled to prima facie validity. In that situation, the objector's burden of going forward is satisfied by pointing to the procedural deficiency, and the claimant must produce evidence supporting the claim from the outset.

Omnibus objections - Rule 3007(d)

Rule 3007(d) authorizes a single objection to more than one claim - an "omnibus objection" - but only on enumerated procedural grounds. The grounds permitted for an omnibus objection are limited:

Duplicate claims - the claims duplicate other claims

Amended or superseded claims - the claims have been amended by subsequently filed proofs of claim

Wrong claimant - the claims were not filed by the correct entity

Late-filed claims - the claims were not timely filed

Satisfied or released claims - the claims have been satisfied or released during the case

Incorrect classification - the claims were presented in a form that does not comply with applicable rules and the failure rendered the claim defective

Insufficient documentation - the claims are unsupported by the documentation required by Rule 3001

Amount disclosed on the schedules - the claims, as filed, are inconsistent with the amounts on the debtor's schedules

An omnibus objection asserting substantive (rather than procedural) grounds is procedurally defective; each substantive objection requires a separate filing. The rule also requires that an omnibus objection list the claims by claimant name and claim number, state the basis for the objection as to each claim, and be limited to no more than 100 claims unless the court orders otherwise.

Effect of a successful objection

If the court sustains the objection, the claim is disallowed (in whole or in part). The disallowance is binding for purposes of distribution and discharge: a disallowed claim receives no distribution from the estate, but a discharge under 11 U.S.C. Section 727 (Chapter 7) or Section 1328 (Chapter 13) generally extinguishes personal liability for the underlying debt to the same extent as an allowed claim, subject to Section 523 nondischargeability exceptions.

If the court overrules the objection, the claim is allowed in the amount stated (or in an amount the court determines after evidentiary hearing) and receives the distribution provided by the plan or trustee's final report.

Common procedural posture

Insufficient-documentation objection

The trustee objects to a credit-card debt-buyer claim that lacks the Rule 3001(c)(2)(A) itemization and any underlying account statement. The objection asserts the procedural ground (Rule 3001 noncompliance) and the substantive ground (insufficient evidence to establish the claim amount). The claimant fails to produce account-history evidence in response; the court disallows the claim under Section 502(b)(1) for failure to prove entitlement.

Omnibus objection to duplicate claims

The Chapter 13 trustee files an omnibus objection to 47 claims that duplicate other claims (commonly, a debt buyer filing a claim on a debt also asserted by the original creditor). The omnibus objection is properly limited to the Rule 3007(d) procedural ground of duplication, lists each duplicate by claimant and claim number, and is supported by a spreadsheet reconciling the duplicates. The court sustains the omnibus objection without individual hearings.

Related rules and authority

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 3001 - Proof of claim and supporting documentation

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 3002 - Filing proof of claim or interest (bar dates)

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 9014 - Contested matters

11 U.S.C. Section 502 - Allowance of claims or interests (substantive grounds for disallowance)

11 U.S.C. Section 506 - Determination of secured status

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 9011 - Signature, representations, sanctions

The 30-day service window is a hard procedural floor. A claim objection set for hearing on less than 30 days' notice to the claimant, the debtor, and the trustee is procedurally defective. Courts will not adjudicate the merits of an under-served objection; the matter will be continued to a date that satisfies Rule 3007(a). The 30-day window is the claimant's notice-and-opportunity-to-be-heard protection.
