## FRBP Rule 3008 - Reconsideration of Allowed and Disallowed Claims [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/rule-3008-reconsideration-of-claims/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure
3008

Rule 3008: Reconsideration of Allowed and Disallowed Claims

The for-cause reconsideration standard, the equitable-factors framework, and interplay with Rule 9024 / FRCP 60 for time-bar relief.

Verbatim text of Rule 3008

A party in interest may move for reconsideration of an order allowing or disallowing a claim against the estate. The court after a hearing on notice shall enter an appropriate order. Fed. R. Bankr. P. 3008.

The two-sentence rule and what it does not say

Rule 3008 is one of the shortest rules in the Federal Rules of Bankruptcy Procedure, and what the rule does not say is more important than what it does. The rule does not specify a deadline. It does not specify a standard. It does not specify who counts as a "party in interest" for reconsideration purposes. It does not address whether reconsideration is available after the case is closed, after a plan is confirmed, or after distribution has begun.

The case law has filled each of these gaps. The standard - drawn from the Advisory Committee Note to the 1983 rule and from the parallel statute, 11 U.S.C. Section 502(j) - is "cause." Reconsideration is committed to the discretion of the bankruptcy court, exercised in light of equitable considerations. The exact contours of "cause" depend on whether the reconsideration motion is filed within the time fixed for an appeal (in which case the standard is essentially that of FRCP 59) or after that time has expired (in which case the standard is essentially that of FRCP 60, imported through Rule 9024).

The Section 502(j) statutory hook

Section 502(j) provides that "a claim that has been allowed or disallowed may be reconsidered for cause." The statute and Rule 3008 are coextensive; together they create a regime that distinguishes claim-allowance orders from other orders in the case. Most orders are final when entered and subject to amendment only under the limited grounds of FRCP 59 and 60 (incorporated through Rule 9023 and Rule 9024). Claim-allowance orders are different: they remain reconsiderable "for cause" without the temporal and substantive constraints of the civil-procedure rules.

The structural justification for the distinction is the ongoing nature of the bankruptcy claim-administration process. A claim allowance entered early in a case may turn out to be erroneous as later evidence emerges; new information may surface during the section 341 meeting, during plan negotiations, or during distribution. The reconsideration regime exists to allow the claim allowance to track the actual entitlement rather than to lock in an early error.

The "for cause" standard

"Cause" under Rule 3008 has been articulated through a multi-factor analysis in most circuits. Typical factors include:

Whether new evidence has come to light that was not reasonably available at the time of the original allowance

Whether the original allowance was based on a mistake of fact or law

Whether the movant exercised diligence in seeking reconsideration after the basis for reconsideration became known

The extent to which other parties or the estate would be prejudiced by reconsideration

Whether distributions have already been made on the basis of the original allowance

The amount in controversy relative to the cost of further litigation

The factors are weighed equitably; no single factor is dispositive. The closer the motion is filed to the original allowance, and the less reliance has accrued on that allowance, the more readily reconsideration is granted. The further the motion is from the original allowance, and the more substantial the reliance, the more demanding the showing.

Interaction with Rule 9024 and FRCP 60

Rule 9024 imports FRCP 60 into bankruptcy proceedings, but with a critical exception: "a motion to reopen a case under the Code or for the reconsideration of an order allowing or disallowing a claim against the estate entered without a contest is not subject to the one year limitation prescribed in Rule 60(c)." The carve-out is structural: Rule 3008 reconsideration is not subject to the one-year deadline that ordinarily limits Rule 60(b) motions based on mistake, inadvertence, surprise, or newly discovered evidence.

The interaction matters most where the reconsideration motion is filed after the appeal period has expired. Within the appeal period (14 days under Rule 8002), the motion functions essentially as a motion to alter or amend under FRCP 59, suspending the appeal clock under Rule 8002(b). After the appeal period, the motion must satisfy the Rule 3008 "cause" standard - and where the original allowance was contested, must also satisfy the substantive grounds of FRCP 60(b) (subject to the equitable considerations the case law overlays on the rule).

The Supreme Court's decision in Pioneer Investment Services Co. v. Brunswick Associates Limited Partnership, 507 U.S. 380 (1993), supplies the equitable framework that bankruptcy courts apply to "excusable neglect" determinations under Rule 9006(b) and, by extension, to the equitable analysis under Rule 3008. The Pioneer factors - the danger of prejudice, the length of the delay and its potential impact on judicial proceedings, the reason for the delay (including whether it was within the reasonable control of the movant), and whether the movant acted in good faith - are the standard analytic framework for late-filed reconsideration motions.

Contested versus uncontested original allowance

The distinction between contested and uncontested original allowances drives much of the practical operation of Rule 3008. An allowance entered by default - because no objection was filed within the time fixed under Rule 3007 - is reviewed under a more lenient standard on reconsideration than an allowance entered after a contested hearing.

The justification is the absence of a prior adjudication. An uncontested allowance reflects the default rule of Section 502(a) (claims are deemed allowed unless objected to); it does not reflect a judicial determination of the merits. Reconsideration of an uncontested allowance is therefore less disturbing to the integrity of prior adjudication and to the reliance interests of the parties.

A contested allowance, by contrast, reflects an actual judicial determination. The reconsidering court is being asked to undo not a default but a decision. The showing required is correspondingly more demanding. The case law characterizes this distinction as one between "reconsideration" properly so-called (of contested allowances, requiring something like the Rule 60(b) standard) and "review" (of uncontested allowances, requiring only the Rule 3008 "cause" standard).

Reopening and post-confirmation reconsideration

Rule 3008 reconsideration is not limited to the pendency of the case. Where new information surfaces after the case has been closed, the path is typically (a) a motion to reopen under 11 U.S.C. Section 350(b) and Rule 5010, followed by (b) a Rule 3008 motion in the reopened case. The reopening motion must satisfy its own "cause" standard - typically requiring a showing that reconsideration would affect distributions or alter the rights of parties in a way that justifies the administrative cost of reopening.

Post-confirmation reconsideration in Chapter 11, 12, and 13 is procedurally more difficult. Confirmation orders are subject to the finality protection of Bullard v. Blue Hills Bank, 575 U.S. 496 (2015), which holds that a confirmation order is a final, appealable order; the reciprocal proposition is that confirmation triggers reliance interests that weigh heavily against later disturbance. Where a claim allowance is bound up with confirmation - because the allowance was a predicate to the plan's treatment of the claim - reconsideration may face the additional hurdle of demonstrating that the requested change does not collide with the binding effect of the confirmed plan.

Common procedural posture

Default allowance, newly discovered defense

A claim is deemed allowed because no objection was filed within the Rule 3007 window. The debtor or trustee subsequently discovers that the claim is barred by a statute of limitations or an exemption. A Rule 3008 motion is filed; because the allowance was uncontested, the standard is the more lenient "cause" standard. The court grants reconsideration if the equitable factors favor disturbing the allowance.

Contested allowance, intervening authority

A contested claim is allowed after a hearing. The appeal period expires without an appeal. An intervening decision of the controlling circuit overturns the rule of law on which the allowance was based. A party in interest files a Rule 3008 motion; because the allowance was contested, the court applies the equivalent of Rule 60(b)(6) - exceptional circumstances - subject to the Rule 3008 equitable analysis.

Related rules and authority

11 U.S.C. Section 502(j) - Allowance of claims (reconsideration)

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 9024 - Relief from judgment or order

Fed. R. Civ. P. 60 - Relief from a judgment or order

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 3007 - Objections to claims

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 3001 - Proof of claim

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 8001 - Appellate procedure framework

Practical impact

Rule 3008 is the procedural escape hatch that prevents claim-allowance error from becoming permanent simply because the appeal clock has expired. The rule's brevity is deceptive: the entire weight of doctrine - the contested/uncontested distinction, the equitable-factors framework, the Pioneer analysis, the Rule 9024 / FRCP 60 interaction, the Rule 5010 reopening interplay - sits on two sentences. Practitioners moving for or against reconsideration should expect that the court will not apply the rule mechanically; the court will apply equitable judgment to the totality of circumstances.

Reconsideration is discretionary, not corrective. Rule 3008 does not give the court a mandate to correct every claim-allowance error; it gives the court discretion to do so when equity supports it. A movant who treats Rule 3008 as a routine appeal-substitute will find the discretion exercised against the motion. A movant who frames the motion around concrete equitable factors - reliance, prejudice, diligence, new evidence - will find the discretion more receptive.

Rule 3007 (Objections)
Rule 8001 (Appeals)
Rule 9014 (Contested)
Rule 2002 (Notice)
Rule 9011 (Signature)

## FRBP Rule 3015 - Chapter 13 Plan Filing and Modification [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/rule-3015-chapter-13-plan/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Home › Federal Rules of Bankruptcy Procedure › Rule 3015

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure
3015

Rule 3015: Chapter 13 Plan Filing and Modification

Filing the Chapter 13 plan, Official Form 113 national plan and local-form alternatives, pre-confirmation and post-confirmation modification, and confirmation timing under 11 U.S.C. Section 1324.

What Rule 3015 does

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 3015 governs the filing, service, modification, and confirmation procedure for plans under Chapter 12 (subdivisions (a) and (b)) and Chapter 13 (subdivisions (b) through (h)). For Chapter 13 cases, Rule 3015 specifies the filing deadline for the plan, the official form on which the plan must be presented, the procedure for pre-confirmation modification, the procedure for post-confirmation modification under 11 U.S.C. Section 1329, and the service requirements that ensure creditors receive the plan with sufficient time to evaluate and respond.

Filing deadline - Rule 3015(b)

Rule 3015(b) provides:

The debtor may file a chapter 13 plan with the petition. If a plan is not filed with the petition, it shall be filed within 14 days thereafter, and such time may not be further extended except for cause shown and on notice as the court may direct. Fed. R. Bankr. P. 3015(b).

The 14-day deadline is procedural; failure to file the plan within the deadline is grounds for dismissal under 11 U.S.C. Section 1307(c)(1) for unreasonable delay prejudicial to creditors. Many districts have implemented automatic dismissal procedures that mirror the Rule 1007 schedules-default procedure: the clerk issues a deficiency notice when the plan is not timely filed and the case is dismissed if the deficiency is not cured within a stated period.

Official Form 113 - the national Chapter 13 plan

Effective December 1, 2017, the Judicial Conference adopted Official Form 113 as a national, uniform Chapter 13 plan form. Form 113 is a structured plan that addresses the principal categories of plan treatment in a standardized format:

Part 1 - Notice to interested parties (the "warning section" identifying nonstandard provisions and limit-on-creditor-objection deadlines)

Part 2 - Plan payments and length, including monthly payment amount, payment source (employer payroll deduction order or direct payment), and plan length (36-60 months depending on above-median or below-median status)

Part 3 - Treatment of secured claims (cure-and-maintain on home mortgages, lien strip on wholly underwater junior mortgages, valuation and modification of non-home secured claims under Section 506(a), and treatment of 910-day auto claims)

Part 4 - Treatment of priority claims (domestic-support obligations, tax claims, and other Section 507 priorities)

Part 5 - Treatment of nonpriority unsecured claims and the proposed dividend

Part 6 - Executory contracts and unexpired leases (assumption or rejection)

Part 7 - Vesting of estate property (at confirmation or at discharge)

Part 8 - Nonstandard plan provisions (must be itemized in Part 1 and set forth in Part 8 to be effective)

Local-form variation under Rule 3015.1

Rule 3015.1, also effective December 1, 2017, permits districts to opt out of Official Form 113 and adopt a local form upon certification by the district's judges that the local form complies with the rule's substantive requirements. Rule 3015.1 requires that any local form:

Have its title and content in substantial conformity with Official Form 113

Adequately address the same matters as Official Form 113

Include a section for nonstandard plan provisions that mirrors Form 113 Part 8

Be approved by the district's judges and adopted by local rule following the public-comment procedure required for local rules

Approximately half the federal judicial districts use Official Form 113; the remaining districts use locally adopted plans certified under Rule 3015.1. The Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts publishes a current list of districts using local forms. A practitioner appearing in an unfamiliar district must determine at the outset which plan form applies.

Service and notice of the plan

Rule 3015(d) requires the debtor or the proponent of a plan to give service to creditors and other parties in interest. The plan must be served on the trustee and all creditors not later than the date the plan is filed. The notice of confirmation hearing required by Section 1324 (sent by the clerk or the proponent depending on local practice) must include the proposed plan or a summary sufficient to apprise creditors of the proposed treatment.

Confirmation hearing under Section 1324

11 U.S.C. Section 1324(b) provides that the confirmation hearing "may be held not earlier than 20 days and not later than 45 days after the date of the meeting of creditors under section 341(a), unless the court determines that it would be in the best interests of the creditors and the estate to hold such hearing at an earlier date." The statutory timing window converts the Chapter 13 case into a comparatively fast-moving proceeding: in most districts, the confirmation hearing follows the 341 meeting by 30-45 days, and the trustee's confirmation recommendation is filed shortly after the meeting.

At the confirmation hearing, the court determines whether the plan satisfies the confirmation requirements of Section 1325(a), which include:

The plan complies with the provisions of Chapter 13 and other applicable provisions of the Code

The required fees have been paid

The plan is proposed in good faith

The plan satisfies the "best-interests-of-creditors" test (unsecured creditors receive at least what they would receive in a hypothetical Chapter 7)

The plan is feasible (the debtor can make the payments and comply with the plan)

Secured claims are treated as provided in Section 1325(a)(5) (surrender, cure-and-maintain, or pay in full with interest under the Till v. SCS Credit Corp. rate methodology)

The debtor has filed all required tax returns under Section 1308

Pre-confirmation modification - Rule 3015(c)

Before confirmation, the debtor may modify the plan as a matter of right under 11 U.S.C. Section 1323. Rule 3015(c) requires that a modified plan be filed and served on the trustee and any other entity affected by the modification. The court will not confirm the original plan if a modified plan has been filed; the modified plan supersedes the original.

Pre-confirmation modification is common: the debtor may modify in response to trustee objections, creditor objections, valuation determinations, or amended proofs of claim that materially change the plan's feasibility or distribution structure. The modified plan typically follows the same Official Form 113 (or local-form equivalent) and goes through a renewed service process.

Post-confirmation modification - Rule 3015(g) and (h)

After confirmation, the plan may be modified under 11 U.S.C. Section 1329 to (1) increase or decrease the amount of payments on claims of a particular class, (2) extend or reduce the time for payments, (3) alter the amount of distribution to a creditor whose claim is provided for by the plan, or (4) reduce the amount of payments required by the plan to the extent of payments made by the debtor's employer.

Rule 3015(g) specifies the procedure for the debtor's, trustee's, or unsecured-claim-holder's motion to modify the plan after confirmation. The motion must be filed, served on the trustee and any other entity affected, and set for hearing on 21 days' notice. Rule 3015(h) provides a streamlined procedure when the modification is unopposed and the proposed modification has no material adverse effect on the debtor or creditors.

Post-confirmation modification is the principal vehicle for accommodating changed circumstances during the plan term: job loss, medical emergency, vehicle loss, divorce, or any other event that changes the debtor's ability to pay or the case's feasibility. The Supreme Court's decision in Hamilton v. Lanning, 560 U.S. 505 (2010), addressing the projected-disposable-income test for plan confirmation, also informs the analysis of post-confirmation modification when the debtor's actual income diverges from the projected income calculated at confirmation.

Common procedural posture

Mortgage modification mid-plan

The debtor obtains a loan modification on the home mortgage after confirmation. The debtor files a Rule 3015(g) post-confirmation modification motion to conform the plan to the modified mortgage payment and to discontinue conduit payments (if the plan provided for them). The motion is served on the trustee and the mortgage servicer with 21 days' notice and is granted on negative notice if no objection is filed.

Plan defeasibility for income drop

The debtor loses employment in plan month 28 and finds new employment at lower pay. The debtor files a Section 1329 motion to reduce the monthly plan payment. The trustee evaluates the reduced payment against the projected-disposable-income test and the best-interests-of-creditors test as of the modification effective date and either consents or contests. If contested, the court holds an evidentiary hearing on feasibility under the modified terms.

Related rules and authority

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 3015.1 - Requirements for a local-form Chapter 13 plan

11 U.S.C. Section 1322 - Contents of plan

11 U.S.C. Section 1324 - Confirmation hearing

11 U.S.C. Section 1325 - Confirmation of plan

11 U.S.C. Section 1329 - Modification of plan after confirmation

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 1007 - Schedules and Statement of Financial Affairs

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 2003 - 341 meeting

Nonstandard plan provisions must be in Part 8 to be effective. Official Form 113 Part 1 contains a notice that nonstandard provisions buried elsewhere in the plan are not effective. A plan that purports to alter standard treatment (e.g., a vesting provision different from the form's default, a non-cure default-cure structure, a special interest rate on a secured claim) must place the nonstandard provision in Part 8 and identify it in Part 1. The structural rule prevents creditor surprise from buried nonstandard terms.

## FRBP Rule 4001 - Relief from Stay, Cash Collateral, DIP Financing [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/rule-4001/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure
4001

Rule 4001: Relief from Stay; Use of Cash Collateral; Obtaining Credit; Agreements

Procedural requirements for stay relief motions, cash-collateral use, post-petition financing, and adequate-protection stipulations.

Verbatim text of Rule 4001(a)(1)

A motion for relief from an automatic stay provided by the Code or a motion to prohibit or condition the use, sale, or lease of property pursuant to Section 363(e) shall be made in accordance with Rule 9014 and shall be served on any committee elected pursuant to Section 705 or appointed pursuant to Section 1102 of the Code or its authorized agent, or, if the case is a chapter 9 municipality case or a chapter 11 reorganization case and no committee of unsecured creditors has been appointed pursuant to Section 1102, on the creditors included on the list filed pursuant to Rule 1007(d), and on such other entities as the court may direct. Fed. R. Bankr. P. 4001(a)(1).

The four subjects of Rule 4001

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 4001 consolidates the procedural framework for four substantively distinct categories of motion that share a common feature: each affects the rights of secured creditors, the use of encumbered estate property, or the priority of post-petition financing. The four categories are:

4001(a) - Relief from the automatic stay under 11 U.S.C. Section 362(d)

4001(b) - Use of cash collateral under Section 363(c)(2)

4001(c) - Post-petition credit under Section 364

4001(d) - Agreements relating to relief from stay, cash collateral, adequate protection, or credit

Each subdivision specifies the parties on whom the motion must be served, the contents of the motion, and where applicable the bifurcated interim-and-final hearing structure that allows a debtor to obtain emergency relief at the outset of a case without prejudging the rights of parties who have not yet had time to respond.

Relief from the automatic stay (Rule 4001(a))

A motion for relief from the automatic stay is the procedural vehicle by which a secured creditor, lessor, or other party in interest seeks an order permitting the movant to enforce remedies against estate property notwithstanding the operation of Section 362(a). The substantive grounds are set out in Section 362(d): cause (including lack of adequate protection), absence of equity in the property coupled with absence of necessity to an effective reorganization, and bad-faith filing in certain single-asset real-estate cases.

Rule 4001(a)(3) imposes a 14-day stay of the order granting stay relief unless the court orders otherwise. The 14-day stay gives the debtor an opportunity to seek a stay pending appeal, refinance, or otherwise respond before the secured creditor proceeds with foreclosure, repossession, or eviction.

The thirty-day default rule under Section 362(e)

Under Section 362(e), the automatic stay terminates automatically thirty days after a request for stay relief is made unless the court, after notice and a hearing, orders the stay continued in effect. This default-termination provision creates the procedural pressure for prompt hearings on stay-relief motions and is one of the operational reasons that stay-relief motions are routinely calendared on expedited tracks in many districts.

Use of cash collateral (Rule 4001(b))

"Cash collateral" is defined in Section 363(a) as cash, negotiable instruments, securities, deposit accounts, and other cash equivalents in which the estate and an entity other than the estate have an interest. A debtor in possession or trustee may not use cash collateral without either the consent of each entity with an interest or court authorization after notice and a hearing.

Rule 4001(b)(1) sets out the contents of a motion for authorization to use cash collateral. The motion must describe the amount of cash collateral sought to be used, the purposes of the use, the duration of the requested authorization, and the material terms of any proposed adequate protection. Rule 4001(b)(2) requires that the motion be accompanied by a proposed budget setting forth projected receipts and disbursements.

Interim and final hearings

Rule 4001(b)(2) authorizes the court to conduct a preliminary hearing on a cash-collateral motion within fourteen days of filing and to enter an interim order authorizing use only to the extent necessary to avoid immediate and irreparable harm to the estate pending a final hearing. The final hearing must be conducted on notice that satisfies the rule's service requirements, including service on the parties identified in Rule 4001(a)(1).

Post-petition credit (Rule 4001(c))

A motion to obtain post-petition credit, including debtor-in-possession financing, is governed by Rule 4001(c). The motion must be accompanied by a copy of the proposed credit agreement and a proposed form of order, and must contain a concise statement of the material provisions of the proposed agreement, including any provision for cross-collateralization, waivers of rights against pre-petition collateral, adequate-protection provisions, deadlines for filing a plan, provisions affecting the validity of pre-petition liens, indemnification of the lender, releases, milestones, and any default or termination provisions.

The disclosure of these material provisions in the motion itself is a substantive procedural protection: it requires the debtor to surface in the motion the provisions of a financing facility that might otherwise be embedded only in the underlying credit documents.

Agreements (Rule 4001(d))

Rule 4001(d) governs agreements relating to relief from stay, use of cash collateral, providing adequate protection, or obtaining credit. The motion to approve the agreement must include a copy of the agreement, a summary of the agreement's material provisions, and notice to the parties identified in the rule. The court may set a hearing on no less than fourteen days' notice unless an emergency justifies shorter notice.

Common procedural posture

Chapter 13 stay relief on a mortgage

A mortgage creditor moves for relief from the automatic stay under Section 362(d)(1) for cause based on post-petition payment default. The motion is served on the debtor, debtor's counsel, the Chapter 13 trustee, and parties on the notice list. A hearing is held, the order entering stay relief is subject to the 14-day stay under Rule 4001(a)(3) unless the court orders otherwise, and the secured creditor may thereafter proceed with state-law foreclosure remedies.

Chapter 11 cash collateral and DIP financing

On day one of a Chapter 11 case, the debtor in possession files a motion under Rule 4001(b) for use of cash collateral and a motion under Rule 4001(c) for approval of a debtor-in-possession credit facility. An interim hearing is held within fourteen days; an interim order authorizes use and borrowing to the extent of immediate and irreparable harm. A final hearing is held on full notice, and the final order incorporates the negotiated adequate-protection and financing terms.

Related rules and authority

11 U.S.C. Section 362 - Automatic stay (substantive grounds for relief)

11 U.S.C. Section 363 - Use, sale, or lease of property (cash-collateral standards)

11 U.S.C. Section 364 - Obtaining credit (post-petition financing standards)

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 9014 - Contested matters (general procedure for motions)

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 9019 - Compromise and settlement (related stipulation procedure)

Practical impact

Rule 4001 is the procedural backbone of the first-day motion practice that defines the opening days of large Chapter 11 cases and of the routine stay-relief practice that occupies a substantial portion of the docket in consumer Chapter 13 cases. The rule's interim-and-final structure for cash-collateral and credit motions reflects a deliberate balance: it allows a debtor to obtain operational liquidity at the outset of a case without prejudging the rights of creditors who require time to evaluate the financing structure.

The disclosure requirements in Rule 4001(c)(1)(B) - the enumerated list of material provisions that must be highlighted in the motion - operate as a procedural antidote to embedded credit-agreement terms that might otherwise pass without focused attention from the court or other parties in interest.

The 14-day stay under Rule 4001(a)(3) is a default, not an entitlement. An order granting relief from the automatic stay is stayed for 14 days unless the court orders otherwise. A movant who needs immediate enforcement should request that the 14-day stay be waived as part of the proposed order, and should be prepared to articulate the cause for waiver.

## FRBP Rule 4002 - Duties of the Debtor [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/rule-4002-debtor-duties/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure
4002

Rule 4002: Duties of the Debtor

The Rule 4002(a) general duties and the Rule 4002(b) specific document and identification requirements at the Section 341 meeting.

Verbatim text of Rule 4002(a)

In addition to performing other duties prescribed by the Code and rules, the debtor shall (1) attend and submit to an examination at the times ordered by the court; (2) attend the hearing on a complaint objecting to discharge and testify, if called as a witness; (3) inform the trustee immediately in writing as to the location of real property in which the debtor has an interest and the name and address of every person holding money or property subject to the debtor's withdrawal or order if a schedule of property has not yet been filed pursuant to Rule 1007; (4) cooperate with the trustee in the preparation of an inventory, the examination of proofs of claim, and the administration of the estate; and (5) file a statement of any change of the debtor's address. Fed. R. Bankr. P. 4002(a).

The structure of Rule 4002

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 4002 is the procedural codification of the debtor's affirmative duties in a bankruptcy case. The rule has two principal subdivisions:

Rule 4002(a) sets out five general categories of duty: attendance at examinations, attendance and testimony at discharge hearings, immediate disclosure of real property and asset-holders, cooperation with the trustee, and notice of address changes.

Rule 4002(b) specifies the documents and identification the debtor must provide at the Section 341 meeting of creditors, including the personal-photo-ID requirement.

Rule 4002 supplements - but does not replace - the substantive debtor duties prescribed by 11 U.S.C. Section 521(a), which establishes the underlying statutory obligations.

The five general duties under Rule 4002(a)

(1) Attendance at examinations

The debtor must attend and submit to examination at any time ordered by the court. This includes the Section 341 meeting of creditors, any Rule 2004 examination (the bankruptcy equivalent of a free-ranging deposition), and any other examination ordered in the case. Failure to attend is grounds for dismissal of the case under 11 U.S.C. Section 707(a) (Chapter 7) or denial of discharge under Section 727(a)(6) (refusal to obey a lawful order of the court).

(2) Attendance and testimony at discharge hearings

If a complaint objecting to discharge is filed (under Section 727 in Chapter 7 or Section 1328 in Chapter 13), the debtor must attend the hearing and testify if called as a witness. The debtor's failure to attend may result in the objection being sustained.

(3) Immediate disclosure of real property and asset-holders

If the debtor has not yet filed schedules under Rule 1007, the debtor must, immediately upon the appointment of the trustee, inform the trustee in writing of:

The location of all real property in which the debtor has an interest

The name and address of every person holding money or property subject to the debtor's withdrawal or order

This is a pre-schedule disclosure obligation - it applies in the gap between commencement of the case and the filing of the formal schedules. Its purpose is to ensure that the trustee can secure assets before they can be transferred or dissipated.

(4) Cooperation with the trustee

The debtor must cooperate with the trustee in the preparation of an inventory, the examination of proofs of claim, and the administration of the estate. This is a broad and ongoing duty. Specific manifestations include:

Producing the debtor's books, records, and documents on request

Appearing for examination on request

Providing access to real property and physical premises for inspection or marketing

Answering inquiries from the trustee and the United States trustee regarding the debtor's financial affairs

Executing documents necessary to perfect the trustee's title to estate property

(5) Notice of address changes

The debtor must file a statement of any change in the debtor's address. This is essential to ensure that notices required by the rules reach the debtor and to permit the trustee to maintain communication.

Rule 4002(b) - documents and identification at the Section 341 meeting

Rule 4002(b) addresses what the debtor must bring to and produce at the Section 341 meeting of creditors. The subdivision was added in part to standardize practice across districts and in part to implement the more rigorous documentation requirements that emerged from the 2005 amendments to the Bankruptcy Code (BAPCPA).

(1) Personal identification

The debtor must bring to the Section 341 meeting:

A photo identification issued by a governmental unit, sufficient to permit the trustee to verify that the debtor is the person who signed the petition. The standard form is a state driver's license or a state-issued identification card. A U.S. passport is also accepted. Some districts accept additional forms by local rule.

Evidence of the debtor's social security number, or a written statement that no such evidence exists. The standard form is the original social security card; a W-2 form or a tax return showing the number is typically accepted as a substitute when the card is unavailable.

The two-document identification protocol is universal. A debtor who appears without acceptable identification will typically be continued to a later meeting date, with the trustee or the United States trustee noting on the record the failure to appear with proper identification.

(2) Financial information

Rule 4002(b)(2) requires the debtor to bring to the Section 341 meeting and produce on request:

Evidence of current income (typically pay stubs or an equivalent), unless previously produced

Statements for each depository and investment account in which the debtor has an interest, for the period including the petition date

Documentation of monthly expenses claimed on Schedule J if the trustee requests verification

(3) Tax returns

Rule 4002(b)(3) implements the BAPCPA tax-return production requirements. The debtor must produce, at the request of the trustee or the United States trustee:

The most recently filed federal income tax return (or, if no return was filed, a written statement to that effect)

Federal income tax returns for the period before the petition, as required by other rules and orders

Tax returns must also be made available to a requesting creditor under 11 U.S.C. Section 521(e)(2), subject to confidentiality safeguards.

The Section 521(a) statutory backbone

Rule 4002 implements the broader statutory duties of 11 U.S.C. Section 521(a). The rule's document-production and cooperation requirements track the statutory text. Section 521(a) requires the debtor to:

File a list of creditors, schedules of assets and liabilities, a schedule of current income and expenditures, a schedule of executory contracts and unexpired leases, and a statement of financial affairs

If an individual debtor's debts are primarily consumer debts, file a statement of intention with respect to property securing those debts

Cooperate with the trustee as necessary to enable the trustee to perform the trustee's duties

Surrender to the trustee all property of the estate and any recorded information relating to property of the estate

Appear at the meeting required by Section 343

The Rule 4002 cooperation duty (4002(a)(4)) is the procedural counterpart of the Section 521(a)(3) statutory cooperation duty. The two operate together.

Consequences of noncompliance

Failure to comply with Rule 4002 or Section 521 has direct and substantial consequences. Available responses include:

Dismissal of the case

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 707(a) (Chapter 7) or Section 1307(c) (Chapter 13), dismissal "for cause" includes failure of the debtor to perform the duties required by the Code and rules. The standard for dismissal varies by circuit; some require notice and hearing, and a graduated response (e.g., a deadline to cure before dismissal).

Denial of discharge

Section 727(a)(6) authorizes denial of discharge in Chapter 7 for refusal to obey a lawful order of the court. Section 1328(a) conditions discharge in Chapter 13 on completion of plan payments and compliance with the rules.

Conversion or other relief

In Chapter 13, repeated failure to cooperate or to produce required documents is grounds for the trustee's motion to dismiss or convert under Section 1307(c).

Adverse evidentiary inferences

A debtor who refuses to produce documents or to answer questions at the Section 341 meeting may be subject to adverse evidentiary inferences in any related contested matter (e.g., claim objection, motion for relief from stay, complaint to determine dischargeability).

Common procedural posture

Section 341 meeting attendance

The debtor appears at the Section 341 meeting with photo ID, social security card, the most recently filed tax return, and pay stubs for the 60 days before the petition. The trustee verifies identification on the record, reviews the schedules with the debtor under oath, and may ask questions about specific transactions, asset values, and income sources. The meeting typically lasts five to fifteen minutes in a routine Chapter 7 case.

Trustee document request

Following the Section 341 meeting, the Chapter 7 trustee identifies a potential asset (e.g., a personal-injury claim, an account receivable, a non-exempt vehicle) and requests additional documents under Rule 4002(a)(4) cooperation. The debtor produces the documents through counsel within the deadline set by the trustee. Failure to produce may prompt a motion under Section 707(a) for dismissal for cause.

Related rules and authority

11 U.S.C. Section 521 - Debtor's duties (statutory backbone)

11 U.S.C. Section 343 - Examination of the debtor at the Section 341 meeting

11 U.S.C. Section 727 - Denial of discharge in Chapter 7

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 1007 - Lists, schedules, statements

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 2003 - Section 341 meeting of creditors

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 1019 - Conversion to Chapter 7 (new Section 341 meeting)

Practical impact

Rule 4002 is the procedural floor of the debtor's relationship with the trustee and the court. Every Chapter 7 and Chapter 13 case implicates the rule from the date of filing through the date of discharge. Debtor's counsel typically prepares the debtor for the Section 341 meeting by reviewing the schedules in detail, confirming that the photo ID and social security documentation are in order, and rehearsing the trustee's standard line of questions. Trustees, in turn, build their case-administration practice around the cooperation and document-production requirements - much of what a Chapter 7 trustee does in the first 30 days of a case is enforcement of Rule 4002 and Section 521(a).

Bring the photo ID and the social security card. The most common Section 341 problem is a debtor who appears without acceptable identification. The trustee will continue the meeting; the case clock effectively pauses; and creditors receive renewed notice. The simplest way to avoid the problem is for counsel to confirm, in writing and by reminder the day before, that the debtor will bring both documents.

## FRBP Rule 4007 - Determination of Dischargeability of a Debt [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/rule-4007/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure
4007

Rule 4007: Determination of Dischargeability of a Debt

Adversary complaints to determine the dischargeability of a debt under Section 523, with the 60-day filing deadline measured from the first date set for the meeting of creditors.

Verbatim text of Rule 4007(c)

Except as otherwise provided in subdivision (d), a complaint to determine the dischargeability of a debt under Section 523(c) shall be filed no later than 60 days after the first date set for the meeting of creditors under Section 341(a). The court shall give all creditors no less than 30 days' notice of the time so fixed in the manner provided in Rule 2002. On motion of a party in interest, after hearing on notice, the court may for cause extend the time fixed under this subdivision. The motion shall be filed before the time has expired. Fed. R. Bankr. P. 4007(c).

The substantive backdrop: Section 523

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 4007 is the procedural rule that gives effect to 11 U.S.C. Section 523. Section 523(a) enumerates twenty-one categories of debts that are excepted from the bankruptcy discharge. Some categories are "self-executing" - a debt is nondischargeable as a matter of law regardless of whether any party files an adversary proceeding (e.g., most tax debts under Section 523(a)(1), domestic support obligations under Section 523(a)(5), certain criminal restitution under Section 523(a)(7), and most student loans under Section 523(a)(8)).

Three categories are not self-executing and instead require an affirmative adversary proceeding to determine nondischargeability:

Section 523(a)(2) - Debts incurred by fraud, false pretenses, or false representations

Section 523(a)(4) - Debts arising from fraud or defalcation in a fiduciary capacity, embezzlement, or larceny

Section 523(a)(6) - Debts for willful and malicious injury to person or property

These three categories - identified collectively as "Section 523(c) debts" - require a creditor to file a Rule 4007 adversary complaint within the 60-day deadline. If no complaint is filed, the debt is discharged.

The 60-day deadline (Rule 4007(c))

For Section 523(c) categories, the deadline to file a dischargeability complaint is 60 days after the first date set for the meeting of creditors under Section 341(a). The "first date set" controls; rescheduling of the meeting does not restart the deadline. The clerk of the bankruptcy court issues a notice that includes the bar date as part of the initial notice of the case.

Extension of the 60-day deadline is available only on motion filed before the deadline expires, and only for cause. The cause standard is strict; mere oversight or inadvertence is insufficient. Reviewing courts have routinely refused extensions where the motion was filed after the deadline, even by a single day.

Who may file

A complaint to determine dischargeability of a debt under Section 523(c) may be filed by:

The creditor to whom the debt is owed

The debtor (defensively, seeking a declaration that the debt is dischargeable)

The trustee in some circumstances

The creditor-plaintiff is the typical posture. A debtor-plaintiff may file defensively to obtain a binding declaration of dischargeability before a creditor pursues post-discharge collection.

Non-Section 523(c) categories (Rule 4007(b))

For Section 523 categories that are not within Section 523(c) - the self-executing categories - Rule 4007(b) provides that a complaint to determine dischargeability may be filed at any time. There is no deadline for, e.g., a complaint to determine the dischargeability of a tax debt under Section 523(a)(1) or a student loan under Section 523(a)(8). The absence of a deadline reflects the substantive design: these debts are nondischargeable by operation of law, and the proceeding under Rule 4007(b) functions to obtain a binding court declaration where one is needed.

Chapter 13 dischargeability differences

Chapter 13 has a narrower set of nondischargeable debts than Chapter 7. The Section 523(a) exceptions that apply in Chapter 13 are listed in Section 1328(a). Notably, the Section 523(a)(2) fraud exception, the Section 523(a)(4) defalcation exception, and the Section 523(a)(6) willful injury exception do not bar discharge under a standard Section 1328(a) Chapter 13 completion discharge - only under the "hardship discharge" available where the debtor cannot complete the plan, under Section 1328(b)-(c).

This Chapter 13 design is a substantial substantive consequence: a creditor with a colorable Section 523(a)(2), (4), or (6) claim against a Chapter 7 debtor must file a Rule 4007 adversary complaint within 60 days or lose the right. The same creditor against a Chapter 13 debtor who completes a plan has no equivalent procedural option.

Notice requirements

Rule 4007(c) requires the court to give all creditors at least 30 days' notice of the deadline to file a Rule 4007(c) complaint. The notice is typically incorporated in the initial notice of the case mailed by the clerk under Rule 2002. A creditor who was not given the required notice may have an argument that the deadline does not bar a later-filed complaint, but the precise contours of the lack-of-notice exception vary by circuit.

Common procedural posture

Fraud complaint by trade creditor

A trade creditor extended credit based on a financial statement that materially misstated the debtor's financial condition. After the bankruptcy filing, the creditor identifies the misstatement and files an adversary complaint within 60 days alleging nondischargeability under Section 523(a)(2)(B) (use of materially false written financial statement). The proceeding moves through the standard adversary procedure of Part VII.

Willful injury complaint by tort victim

A tort plaintiff with an unliquidated personal-injury claim files an adversary complaint within 60 days alleging that the debtor's conduct constituted willful and malicious injury under Section 523(a)(6). Because the underlying tort liability has not been adjudicated, the bankruptcy court may bifurcate liability from damages and determine only the dischargeability question.

Related rules and authority

11 U.S.C. Section 523 - Exceptions to discharge

11 U.S.C. Section 727 - Discharge in Chapter 7

11 U.S.C. Section 1328 - Discharge in Chapter 13

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 7001 - Scope of Part VII (dischargeability proceeding listed in 7001(6))

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 4004 - Grant or denial of discharge (parallel deadline for Section 727 objections)

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 2002 - Notice to creditors (the vehicle for the 30-day deadline notice)

Practical impact

Rule 4007 is one of the bright-line deadline rules in bankruptcy procedure: the 60-day deadline for Section 523(c) complaints is strictly enforced, and a creditor who fails to file is effectively barred from challenging dischargeability on fraud, defalcation, or willful-injury grounds. The Advisory Committee Notes and successive Supreme Court decisions have emphasized the importance of the deadline in providing finality to the discharge.

For practitioners, the deadline begins running from the first date set for the meeting of creditors - not from the date of the meeting itself, which may be continued or rescheduled. A creditor evaluating a possible dischargeability action should calendar the deadline immediately upon receipt of the case notice and should file a motion for extension well before the deadline if additional time is needed for pre-suit investigation.

Extension motions must be filed before the deadline expires. Rule 4007(c) authorizes extension "on motion filed before the time has expired." A motion filed after the deadline is procedurally barred from extending it. The rule does not contain a "excusable neglect" provision comparable to other procedural deadlines.

Rule 3002 (Claim Deadlines)
Rule 9019 (Settlement)
Rule 1017 (Dismissal)
Rule 1019 (Conversion)

11 U.S.C. Section 523 - Cornell LII

11 U.S.C. Section 1328 - Cornell LII

Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts - Bankruptcy Procedural Resources

## FRBP Rule 4008 - Discharge and Reaffirmation Hearing [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/rule-4008-reaffirmation-procedure/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure
4008

Rule 4008: Discharge and Reaffirmation Hearing

The Rule 4008(a) filing requirement, the 4008(b) attorney certification, the 4008(c) undue-hardship affidavit, and the 60-day post-discharge default rule.

What reaffirmation does

A reaffirmation agreement under 11 U.S.C. Section 524(c) permits an individual debtor to agree, post-petition and before discharge, to remain personally liable on a debt that the discharge would otherwise extinguish. Reaffirmation is most commonly used in Chapter 7 to preserve secured-creditor relationships on vehicles, mortgages, and other collateral the debtor wishes to retain, by maintaining the personal-liability layer above the secured creditor's in rem rights against the collateral.

Because reaffirmation has the substantial consequence of preserving a personal-liability obligation that the bankruptcy would otherwise discharge, Section 524(c) and its implementing rule, Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 4008, impose a tight set of procedural and substantive requirements.

The substantive Section 524(c) framework

Before turning to the procedural rule, the substantive prerequisites of Section 524(c) must be understood. A reaffirmation agreement is enforceable only if:

(1) The agreement was made before the granting of the discharge under Section 727, Section 1141, Section 1228, or Section 1328

(2) The debtor received the disclosures described in Section 524(k) at or before the time the debtor signed the agreement

(3) The agreement was filed with the court

(4) If the debtor was represented by an attorney during the negotiation, the agreement was accompanied by a declaration or affidavit of the attorney stating that the agreement (i) represents a fully informed and voluntary agreement of the debtor, (ii) does not impose an undue hardship on the debtor or any dependent of the debtor, and (iii) the attorney has fully advised the debtor of the legal effect and consequences of the agreement and any default under the agreement

(5) The debtor did not, before the granting of the discharge, exercise the right to rescind the agreement

(6) For a debtor not represented by an attorney, the court approves the agreement after a hearing, finding that it does not impose an undue hardship and is in the best interest of the debtor (subject to certain consumer-debt exceptions)

Rule 4008(a) - filing the agreement

Rule 4008(a) requires that a reaffirmation agreement be filed no later than 60 days after the first date set for the meeting of creditors under Section 341(a). The court may, for cause, extend the time at any time before expiration of the period. The 60-day filing window aligns the reaffirmation deadline with the typical Chapter 7 discharge timeline, ensuring that reaffirmation agreements come before the court before the discharge enters.

The filed agreement must include the disclosure documents required by Section 524(k) and any required attorney declaration or affidavit. The agreement is submitted on Official Form 2400 (or its current numerical equivalent), which embeds the statutorily required disclosures and the structured presentation of debtor income, expenses, and any presumption of undue hardship.

Rule 4008(b) - attorney certification

When the debtor is represented by counsel during the reaffirmation negotiation, Rule 4008(b) requires the agreement to be accompanied by the attorney's declaration or affidavit certifying:

That the agreement represents a fully informed and voluntary agreement of the debtor

That the agreement does not impose an undue hardship on the debtor or any dependent of the debtor

That the attorney has fully advised the debtor of the legal effect and consequences of the agreement, including any default under the agreement

The attorney certification is a substantive professional-responsibility undertaking. The attorney who signs the certification is representing to the court that the attorney has, in fact, conducted the analysis required to make the three findings - not that the debtor wants to sign, not that the creditor has offered the agreement, but that the attorney has independently evaluated and concluded that the reaffirmation does not impose undue hardship on the debtor.

Rule 4008(c) - undue-hardship presumption and affidavit

Rule 4008(c) implements the Section 524(m) statutory framework governing the presumption of undue hardship. Where the debtor's monthly income on Schedule I (less monthly expenses on Schedule J) is less than the scheduled payment under the reaffirmation agreement, a presumption of undue hardship arises.

The presumption may be rebutted by a written statement, filed with the court, identifying additional sources of funds to make the agreed payments. The statement must:

Identify the additional sources of funds with reasonable specificity

Explain why the additional funds were not reflected on Schedules I or J

State that the additional funds are reasonably anticipated to be available throughout the term of the agreement

If the presumption arises and is not rebutted, the court must review the agreement and may decline to approve it. In the case of a represented debtor, the attorney's Rule 4008(b) certification - particularly the no-undue-hardship prong - is a separate evaluative checkpoint that does not depend on the mechanical calculation that triggers the Section 524(m) presumption.

Pro se debtors and the court hearing

When the debtor is not represented by counsel during the reaffirmation negotiation, Section 524(c)(6) and Rule 4008 require the court to hold a hearing and make findings before the agreement is enforceable. At the hearing, the court inquires of the debtor whether the reaffirmation is fully informed and voluntary, whether the debtor understands the legal effect, and whether the agreement imposes undue hardship. The court must approve the agreement on the record for the reaffirmation to be enforceable. The hearing is sometimes consolidated with the discharge hearing under Section 524(d).

Exceptions: For consumer debt secured by real property, the Section 524(c)(6) court-approval requirement does not apply. For other consumer debt of an unrepresented debtor, the court-approval requirement is the default.

The Section 524(d) discharge hearing

Section 524(d) authorizes the court to hold a discharge hearing for the purpose of informing the debtor of the granting of the discharge, the general effect of the discharge, the legal effect of any pending reaffirmation agreement, and the right to rescind such an agreement. The discharge hearing is a discretionary mechanism that the court may use, particularly in cases involving pro se reaffirmation negotiations. Rule 4008 governs the procedural posture of the hearing.

The right to rescind

Section 524(c)(4) permits the debtor to rescind a reaffirmation agreement at any time before discharge or within 60 days after the agreement is filed with the court, whichever is later. The rescission must be effective notice to the creditor of the debtor's intent to rescind. After rescission, the personal-liability discharge takes its ordinary effect, and the creditor's remaining rights are limited to its in rem rights against the collateral.

The 60-day post-discharge default rule

The interaction of the Rule 4008(a) filing window (60 days from the first Section 341 date) and the Section 524(c)(4) rescission window (60 days from filing) typically positions the reaffirmation decision before discharge. The discharge in a routine Chapter 7 case is granted shortly after the close of the rescission period, leaving the debtor a clean choice between reaffirmation (preservation of personal liability) and non-reaffirmation (personal liability discharged, in rem rights of the secured creditor preserved).

If the reaffirmation is not filed within the Rule 4008(a) deadline (and no extension is granted), the agreement is not enforceable under Section 524(c)(1). The debtor's personal liability on the debt is discharged. The secured creditor retains its in rem rights against the collateral and may pursue collateral recovery through nonbankruptcy remedies, subject to any "ride-through" practices recognized in the particular district.

Common procedural posture

Vehicle reaffirmation in Chapter 7

A Chapter 7 debtor wishes to retain a vehicle subject to a purchase-money security interest. The vehicle lender prepares a reaffirmation agreement on Official Form 2400 and transmits it to debtor's counsel. Counsel reviews the agreement, performs the Section 524(m) hardship analysis using Schedules I and J, makes the Rule 4008(b) certification, and files the agreement within the 60-day Rule 4008(a) window. The debtor may rescind within the 60-day rescission period; if no rescission, the personal-liability obligation survives discharge.

Pro se reaffirmation hearing

An unrepresented debtor files a reaffirmation agreement on Official Form 2400. Because no attorney certification can be made under Rule 4008(b), and because the debtor is not represented, the court schedules a hearing under Section 524(c)(6). At the hearing, the court inquires of the debtor, makes findings on the record regarding voluntariness, understanding, and absence of undue hardship, and either approves or declines to approve the agreement.

Related rules and authority

11 U.S.C. Section 524 - Effect of discharge and reaffirmation

11 U.S.C. Section 727 - Discharge in Chapter 7

11 U.S.C. Section 521 - Statement of intention

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 4002 - Duties of the debtor

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 4007 - Determination of dischargeability of a debt

Official Form 2400 (Reaffirmation Agreement)

Practical impact

Reaffirmation is a tightly regulated procedural moment in the Chapter 7 case. The decision to reaffirm a debt that the bankruptcy would otherwise discharge is one of the few moments in the case where the debtor knowingly takes on a forward-looking liability. The procedural infrastructure of Rule 4008 - the 60-day filing deadline, the attorney certification, the undue-hardship affidavit, the rescission window, and (for pro se debtors) the court hearing - is designed to ensure that the decision is informed, voluntary, and not financially destructive.

Attorneys who routinely make Rule 4008(b) certifications carry substantial professional-responsibility exposure. The certification that the agreement "does not impose an undue hardship" is a substantive opinion grounded in the debtor's actual budget; an attorney who certifies in disregard of a debtor's evident inability to perform may be subject to sanctions under Rule 9011 and to disciplinary referral under the state rules of professional conduct.

Reaffirmation is the personal-liability decision; surrender and redemption are the in rem decisions. The debtor's choices for secured collateral in Chapter 7 are: (i) reaffirm (preserve personal liability + retain collateral), (ii) redeem under Section 722 (pay lump-sum value, discharge personal liability, retain collateral), (iii) surrender (discharge personal liability, surrender collateral to the secured creditor), or (iv) in some districts, ride-through (discharge personal liability, retain collateral, continue payments without contractual obligation). Rule 4008 governs only option (i).

Rule 4007 (Dischargeability)
Rule 2003 (341 Meeting)
Rule 1019 (Conversion)
Rule 9011 (Sanctions)

## FRBP Rule 6004 - Sale Procedure (363 Sales) [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/rule-6004-sale-procedure/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure
6004

Rule 6004: Sale Procedure (363 Sales)

21-day notice, free-and-clear sales under 6004(c), stalking-horse and bidding procedures under 6004(f), good-faith findings under section 363(m), and the credit-bid framework under section 363(k).

The architecture of Rule 6004

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 6004 is the procedural rulebook for sales, uses, and leases of estate property under 11 U.S.C. Section 363. The rule operates downstream of the substantive Section 363 framework: Section 363 authorizes the trustee (or debtor in possession) to sell estate property outside the ordinary course of business with court approval, and Rule 6004 specifies the procedure by which that approval is sought and granted.

The rule has seven operative subdivisions. Rule 6004(a) ties notice into Rule 2002. Rule 6004(b) provides the procedure for objections. Rule 6004(c) governs the free-and-clear sale mechanism keyed to Section 363(f). Rule 6004(d) addresses sales of personally identifiable information. Rule 6004(e) addresses sales of property under $2,500. Rule 6004(f) provides the procedure for the sale itself, including bidding procedures. Rule 6004(g) governs documentation of the sale.

The 21-day notice baseline under Rule 6004(a)

Rule 6004(a) cross-references Rule 2002(a)(2), (c)(1), (i), and (k) for notice of a proposed use, sale, or lease of property other than in the ordinary course of business. The baseline is 21 days' notice to all creditors. The notice must describe the property to be sold, the proposed terms, and the deadline for objections. Where the sale is "private" rather than public, Rule 6004(c) requires that the notice describe the terms of the proposed sale with sufficient particularity to allow informed objection.

The 21-day window can be shortened only "for cause shown." The "for cause" determination is fact-specific; courts have shortened the period for emergencies (perishable inventory, rapidly depreciating assets, time-sensitive transactions), but routine sales are expected to proceed on the standard window.

Free-and-clear sales under Rule 6004(c)

Section 363(f) authorizes the sale of estate property "free and clear" of interests held by third parties - typically liens, security interests, and other encumbrances - if one of five statutory grounds is satisfied:

Applicable nonbankruptcy law permits sale of the property free and clear of the interest

The holder of the interest consents

The interest is a lien and the price at which the property is to be sold is greater than the aggregate value of all liens on the property

The interest is in bona fide dispute

The holder of the interest could be compelled, in a legal or equitable proceeding, to accept a money satisfaction of the interest

Rule 6004(c) is the procedural rule for invoking Section 363(f). The rule requires that the motion to sell free and clear be served on the parties whose interests are to be extinguished, with notice of the time fixed for filing objections. The interests, once extinguished, attach to the proceeds of sale - the "interests follow proceeds" principle that protects the substantive entitlement while permitting the transactional clearing of title.

Service on lienholders is service, not notice. A motion to sell free and clear of a lien must be served on the lienholder under Rule 9014's incorporation of Rule 7004; mere Rule 2002 mailing to the creditor matrix is insufficient. A free-and-clear sale order entered without proper Rule 7004 service on a lienholder is vulnerable to collateral attack.

Stalking-horse bidder and bidding procedures under Rule 6004(f)

Rule 6004(f) governs the procedure for the sale itself. Most non-trivial bankruptcy sales proceed through a two-step process. First, the trustee or debtor in possession identifies a "stalking-horse" bidder - a buyer who has negotiated terms with the seller and is prepared to bind itself to the sale subject to higher and better offers from other bidders. Second, the court approves "bidding procedures" - typically including a minimum overbid increment, a deadline for competing bids, a deposit requirement, and conditions on the form of competing bids - and conducts an auction.

Bidding procedures are typically approved by a separate order entered before the sale-approval hearing itself. The two-step structure protects all participants: the stalking-horse bidder receives the certainty of going-forward bidding procedures and (often) a break-up fee in the event of overbid; competing bidders receive notice and a defined process for submitting bids; the estate receives the benefit of competitive pricing.

Break-up fees - payments to the stalking-horse bidder if the asset is ultimately sold to a competing bidder - are themselves subject to bankruptcy-court approval. The case law evaluates break-up fees against an "actual and necessary" standard under 11 U.S.C. Section 503(b), with consideration of whether the fee was the inducement that secured the stalking-horse commitment and whether the fee is reasonable in relation to the value the stalking-horse provided.

The good-faith finding under Section 363(m)

Section 363(m) provides that "the reversal or modification on appeal of an authorization under [Section 363(b) or (c)] does not affect the validity of a sale or lease under such authorization to an entity that purchased or leased such property in good faith, whether or not such entity knew of the pendency of the appeal, unless such authorization and such sale or lease were stayed pending appeal."

The Section 363(m) "good-faith" finding is the structural feature that gives 363 sales their commercial finality. Once a sale is consummated to a good-faith purchaser and is not stayed pending appeal, the sale stands even if the underlying authorization is later overturned. This finality is what permits sophisticated buyers to participate in bankruptcy sales without the discount that residual reversal risk would otherwise impose.

The "good-faith" finding is not automatic. The case law requires the bankruptcy court to make a particularized finding on the record, typically addressing whether the purchase was at arm's length, whether the purchaser had knowledge of any defects in the sale process, whether the purchase price was the result of competitive bidding, and whether any insider relationships affected the transaction. A sale order that omits a Section 363(m) finding - or that recites the finding in conclusory terms unsupported by record evidence - is vulnerable.

The credit-bid framework under Section 363(k)

Section 363(k) authorizes a secured creditor whose claim is secured by a lien on the property being sold to "bid at such sale, and, if such holder of such claim purchases such property, [to] offset such claim against the purchase price of such property." The mechanism - "credit bidding" - allows the secured creditor to bid up to the full amount of its allowed claim without putting cash on the table.

The credit bid serves two functions. First, it protects the secured creditor against a sale that would dilute its collateral position by allowing the creditor to set a floor at the full amount of its lien. Second, it creates a market-discipline mechanism: a credit-bidding secured creditor that does not believe the property is worth at least its claim amount will not credit-bid, and the willingness of a credit-bidding secured creditor to bid the full claim provides a signal of value.

Section 363(k) credit-bidding may be limited or denied "for cause." The case law characterizes "cause" narrowly; allegations of inequitable conduct by the secured creditor or substantial uncertainty about the validity of the underlying lien are typical bases. The Supreme Court's decision in RadLAX Gateway Hotel, LLC v. Amalgamated Bank, 566 U.S. 639 (2012), confirms that the credit-bid right also constrains the structure of confirmation in Chapter 11: a plan that purports to sell collateral free and clear without permitting the secured creditor to credit bid does not satisfy the "fair and equitable" requirement of Section 1129(b)(2)(A).

Common procedural posture

Chapter 7 trustee asset sale

A Chapter 7 trustee identifies estate equipment subject to a perfected lien held by a secured creditor. The trustee files a motion under Rule 6004 to sell free and clear under Section 363(f)(3) (price exceeds aggregate liens). The motion is served on the secured creditor under Rule 7004 and noticed to all creditors under Rule 2002. The court holds the hearing, makes a Section 363(m) good-faith finding, and enters the sale order. Liens attach to proceeds.

Chapter 11 going-concern sale

A Chapter 11 debtor proposes to sell its business as a going concern. The debtor files a motion to approve bidding procedures, identifies a stalking-horse bidder with a break-up fee, and proposes an auction schedule. The court approves the bidding procedures by a first-day order, the auction proceeds on the scheduled date, and the court enters a sale order with a Section 363(m) finding approving the sale to the winning bidder.

Related rules and authority

11 U.S.C. Section 363 - Use, sale, or lease of property

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 2002 - Notice to creditors and other parties in interest

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 9014 - Contested matters (incorporating Rule 7004 service)

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 6003 - Interim and final relief in first-day matters

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 9019 - Compromise and settlement

Practical impact

Rule 6004 governs one of the most consequential transactions in any bankruptcy case. A sale order entered without satisfying the Rule 6004 procedural requirements - 21-day notice, proper service on lienholders, supported Section 363(m) finding - is vulnerable to collateral attack. A sale order entered with full procedural compliance is largely bulletproof, even on appeal, because the Section 363(m) finality protection insulates the consummated transaction.

The Section 363(m) finding is the load-bearing element. Without an articulated good-faith finding on the record, the sale lacks the appellate finality that gives 363 sales their commercial value. Practitioners drafting sale orders should ensure that the Section 363(m) finding is supported by specific record evidence - not merely recited as a conclusion.

Rule 9014 (Contested)
Rule 9019 (Compromise)
