## FRBP Rule 7001 - Scope of Adversary Proceedings in Bankruptcy [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/rule-7001/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure
7001

Rule 7001: Scope of Rules of Part VII

The ten categories of disputes that must proceed as adversary proceedings rather than as contested matters.

Verbatim text of Rule 7001

An adversary proceeding is governed by the rules of this Part VII. The following are adversary proceedings:

(1) a proceeding to recover money or property, other than a proceeding to compel the debtor to deliver property to the trustee, or a proceeding under Rule 2017, Rule 6002, or Rule 6009;

(2) a proceeding to determine the validity, priority, or extent of a lien or other interest in property, other than a proceeding under Rule 3012 or Rule 4003(d);

(3) a proceeding to obtain approval under Section 363(h) for the sale of both the interest of the estate and of a co-owner in property;

(4) a proceeding to object to or revoke a discharge, other than an objection to discharge under Sections 727(a)(8), (a)(9), or 1328(f);

(5) a proceeding to revoke an order of confirmation of a chapter 11, chapter 12, or chapter 13 plan;

(6) a proceeding to determine the dischargeability of a debt;

(7) a proceeding to obtain an injunction or other equitable relief, except when a chapter 9, chapter 11, chapter 12, or chapter 13 plan provides for the relief;

(8) a proceeding to subordinate any allowed claim or interest, except when a chapter 9, chapter 11, chapter 12, or chapter 13 plan provides for subordination;

(9) a proceeding to obtain a declaratory judgment relating to any of the foregoing; or

(10) a proceeding to determine a claim or cause of action removed under 28 U.S.C. Section 1452. Fed. R. Bankr. P. 7001.

The adversary-proceeding / contested-matter distinction

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 7001 is the threshold rule that defines what kinds of disputes within a bankruptcy case must be brought as adversary proceedings. An adversary proceeding is a separate civil action filed within the bankruptcy case, initiated by complaint, served by summons, assigned its own adversary proceeding number, and governed by the full procedural framework of Part VII of the rules (which incorporates many of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure).

A "contested matter" is a dispute that arises within a bankruptcy case but is not enumerated in Rule 7001. Contested matters are governed by Rule 9014 and are initiated by motion rather than complaint. They generally have shorter response periods, simpler discovery, and faster resolution than adversary proceedings.

Why the distinction matters

The choice between adversary proceeding and contested matter is not merely procedural housekeeping. The categories enumerated in Rule 7001 are matters in which the substantive stakes - dischargeability, lien validity, recovery of property, denial of discharge, injunctive relief - warrant the heightened procedural protections of full Part VII practice. Each Rule 7001 category corresponds to a substantive right that the rule drafters considered too consequential to be decided on motion practice alone.

Bringing a matter as a motion when Rule 7001 requires an adversary complaint is procedurally defective. Courts have routinely dismissed contested-matter motions that should have been adversary complaints, requiring the party to refile by complaint and to satisfy the procedural requirements of Part VII (including Rule 7004 service of summons).

The ten categories explained

(1) Recovery of money or property

An action to recover money or property of the estate must be brought as an adversary proceeding. This category covers trustee avoidance actions under Sections 544, 547, 548, and 550, turnover actions under Section 542 against non-debtor third parties, and recovery actions on accounts receivable.

(2) Lien validity, priority, or extent

An action to determine the validity, priority, or extent of a lien or other interest in property must be brought as an adversary proceeding. Lien-stripping in Chapter 13 under Rule 3012 and exemption-related lien-avoidance actions under Rule 4003(d) are excluded; those are contested matters.

(3) Section 363(h) co-owner sales

A sale of both the estate's interest and a co-owner's interest in property under Section 363(h) requires an adversary proceeding so that the co-owner receives full procedural protections.

(4) Objection to or revocation of discharge

An objection to discharge under Section 727(a) (other than the specifically excluded prior-discharge provisions) or revocation of a granted discharge must be brought as an adversary proceeding.

(5) Revocation of plan confirmation

An action to revoke confirmation of a Chapter 11, 12, or 13 plan must be brought as an adversary proceeding under Sections 1144, 1230, or 1330.

(6) Dischargeability of a debt

An action to determine the dischargeability of a debt under Section 523 must be brought as an adversary proceeding under Rule 4007. The 60-day deadline runs from the first date set for the meeting of creditors and is generally not extendable except for cause shown by motion filed before the deadline.

(7) Injunctive or equitable relief

A proceeding to obtain injunctive or other equitable relief - other than such relief provided in a confirmed plan - must be brought as an adversary proceeding. This category includes actions for declaratory injunctions against creditor conduct, third-party releases sought outside a confirmed plan, and similar equitable applications.

(8) Subordination of claim or interest

An action under Section 510(c) to subordinate a claim or interest must be brought as an adversary proceeding, unless the subordination is provided in a confirmed plan.

(9) Declaratory judgment

An action for a declaratory judgment relating to any of the categories in (1)-(8) must be brought as an adversary proceeding. This catchall ensures that declaratory framing does not provide an end-run around the adversary-procedure requirement for the underlying substantive subject.

(10) Removed civil actions

A claim or cause of action removed to the bankruptcy court under 28 U.S.C. Section 1452 proceeds as an adversary proceeding from the date of removal, with the full procedural framework of Part VII.

Common procedural posture

Trustee preference action

A Chapter 7 trustee identifies a pre-petition transfer that appears recoverable as a preference under Section 547. The trustee files an adversary complaint within the two-year statute of limitations of Section 546, serves a summons under Rule 7004, and the matter proceeds with answer, discovery, dispositive motion practice, and trial as in a federal civil action.

Nondischargeability complaint under Section 523

A creditor alleges that a debt was incurred by fraud actionable under Section 523(a)(2)(A). The creditor files an adversary complaint within the 60-day deadline under Rule 4007(c), serves a summons, and the matter proceeds as an adversary proceeding through answer, discovery, and trial. The bankruptcy court's judgment of nondischargeability is appealable on the same basis as any other adversary judgment.

Related rules and authority

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 7003 - Commencement of adversary proceeding

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 7004 - Process; service of summons, complaint

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 9014 - Contested matters (the alternative procedural track)

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 4007 - Determination of dischargeability of a debt

28 U.S.C. Section 1452 - Removal of claims related to bankruptcy cases

Practical impact

Rule 7001 is the procedural classification rule that determines the entire shape of dispute resolution within a bankruptcy case. A practitioner contemplating an action within a bankruptcy case must first determine whether the contemplated action falls within one of the ten Rule 7001 categories. If it does, the action must be filed as an adversary complaint; if not, it proceeds as a contested-matter motion under Rule 9014.

Procedurally defective filings - a motion where a complaint is required - are routinely dismissed or held in abeyance pending refiling as an adversary complaint. The dismissal may, in some circumstances, result in loss of a substantive right if the applicable statute of limitations (e.g., the Rule 4007(c) sixty-day dischargeability deadline) has expired in the interim.

Declaratory framing does not avoid Rule 7001. Rule 7001(9) ensures that a request for declaratory judgment relating to a matter within categories (1) through (8) must still be brought as an adversary proceeding. A motion seeking declaratory relief on a Rule 7001 subject is no less defective than a motion seeking the underlying substantive relief itself.

Rule 9019 (Settlement)
Rule 9020 (Contempt)
Rule 9011 (Sanctions)
Rule 2014 (Retention)

Further reading

Federal Rules of Bankruptcy Procedure Part VII - Cornell LII Index

28 U.S.C. Section 1452 - Cornell LII

Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts - Bankruptcy Procedure Resources

## FRBP Rule 7012 - Motion to Dismiss in Adversary Proceedings [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/rule-7012-motion-to-dismiss/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure
7012

Rule 7012: Motion to Dismiss in Adversary Proceedings

FRCP 12(b)(1)/(2)/(3)/(6) incorporation, the Stern v. Marshall jurisdictional motion framework, abstention-grounds motions, and the responsive-pleading choice between answer and motion.

The structure of Rule 7012

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 7012 governs the responsive pleading in an adversary proceeding. The rule has two operative subdivisions. Rule 7012(a) sets the time within which a defendant must serve an answer (30 days after issuance of the summons, with extensions for service on the United States and its agencies). Rule 7012(b) incorporates Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b) through (i) and adds the bankruptcy-specific Stern-v.-Marshall consent requirement: "A responsive pleading shall admit or deny an allegation that the proceeding is core or non-core. If the response is that the proceeding is non-core, it shall include a statement that the party does or does not consent to entry of final orders or judgment by the bankruptcy judge."

The incorporation of FRCP 12 is comprehensive. Every motion available under the civil-procedure rule - lack of subject-matter jurisdiction (12(b)(1)), lack of personal jurisdiction (12(b)(2)), improper venue (12(b)(3)), insufficient process (12(b)(4)), insufficient service of process (12(b)(5)), failure to state a claim (12(b)(6)), and failure to join an indispensable party (12(b)(7)) - is available in a bankruptcy adversary proceeding.

The FRCP 12(b)(1) motion: subject-matter jurisdiction

The 12(b)(1) motion is the standard mechanism for raising the threshold question whether the bankruptcy court has subject-matter jurisdiction over the claims pled in the complaint. Bankruptcy-court subject-matter jurisdiction is conferred by 28 U.S.C. Section 1334, which gives the district court original and exclusive jurisdiction over Title 11 cases and original (but not exclusive) jurisdiction over civil proceedings "arising under" Title 11, "arising in" a Title 11 case, or "related to" a Title 11 case.

The "arising under," "arising in," and "related to" distinctions are jurisdictionally consequential. "Arising under" proceedings invoke substantive rights created by Title 11 (avoidance actions, exemption disputes, dischargeability proceedings). "Arising in" proceedings are those that could not exist outside a bankruptcy case (motions to assume executory contracts, plan confirmation). "Related to" proceedings have a more attenuated connection - the test, as articulated in Pacor, Inc. v. Higgins, 743 F.2d 984 (3d Cir. 1984) and adopted in most circuits, is whether the outcome of the proceeding could conceivably have any effect on the estate being administered in bankruptcy.

A 12(b)(1) motion may challenge the jurisdictional predicate at any of these levels. The challenge is non-waivable - subject-matter jurisdiction may be raised at any time, including for the first time on appeal.

The Stern v. Marshall jurisdictional framework

The Supreme Court's decision in Stern v. Marshall, 564 U.S. 462 (2011), introduced a constitutional layer to bankruptcy-court adjudicatory authority that operates separately from the statutory jurisdictional grant. Stern holds that even where a proceeding is statutorily "core" under 28 U.S.C. Section 157(b)(2), the bankruptcy court lacks constitutional authority under Article III to enter a final judgment on certain state-law counterclaims if the counterclaim is not necessarily resolved in the process of ruling on the creditor's proof of claim.

The practical operation of Stern is that the responsive-pleading determination required by Rule 7012(b) carries constitutional weight. A defendant in an adversary proceeding must affirmatively address whether the proceeding is "core" or "non-core" - and, if non-core, whether the defendant consents to entry of final orders by the bankruptcy judge. The Supreme Court's decision in Wellness International Network, Ltd. v. Sharif, 575 U.S. 665 (2015), confirmed that a litigant may consent to bankruptcy-court adjudication of a Stern claim, but the consent must be knowing and voluntary. Silence on consent is interpreted under the case law to be inconsistent with adjudication.

Stern v. Marshall is a constitutional, not statutory, issue. The Rule 7012(b) consent statement is not a procedural courtesy; it is the mechanism by which the defendant either accepts or preserves objection to bankruptcy-court entry of final judgment. A defendant who fails to address consent in the answer risks being held to have waived the constitutional objection.

The FRCP 12(b)(6) motion: failure to state a claim

The 12(b)(6) motion challenges the sufficiency of the complaint to state a claim upon which relief can be granted. The motion is governed by the plausibility standard articulated in Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007), and Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009): the complaint must contain factual allegations that, accepted as true, state a claim that is plausible on its face. Conclusory allegations and bare recitations of the elements of a cause of action are insufficient.

In the bankruptcy context, 12(b)(6) motions are most commonly directed at avoidance-action complaints (preference, fraudulent-transfer, equitable-subordination), at non-dischargeability complaints under Section 523, and at adversary complaints seeking declarations of property rights. Each context applies the plausibility standard against the substantive elements of the specific claim. A preference complaint, for example, must allege facts that plausibly support each element of 11 U.S.C. Section 547(b); a non-dischargeability complaint under Section 523(a)(2)(A) must plead with the particularity required by FRCP 9(b) (incorporated by Rule 7009) the facts constituting the alleged fraud.

The 12(b)(2) and 12(b)(3) motions: personal jurisdiction and venue

Personal jurisdiction in bankruptcy adversary proceedings benefits from the nationwide service provision of Rule 7004(d), which authorizes service of summons anywhere in the United States. Nationwide service generally satisfies the personal-jurisdiction inquiry against U.S. defendants, subject to the constitutional minimum-contacts analysis required by the Due Process Clause.

Venue is governed by 28 U.S.C. Section 1409. The general rule is that a proceeding arising in or related to a bankruptcy case may be commenced in the district where the case is pending. Section 1409(b) provides a "small-dollar" carve-out: trustee suits to recover a money judgment of less than approximately $1,500 (or to recover a consumer debt of less than approximately $23,000, with periodic dollar-amount adjustments) must be brought in the district where the defendant resides.

Abstention as a basis for dismissal

Although abstention is not expressly listed in FRCP 12(b), bankruptcy courts routinely entertain abstention motions in the same procedural posture as a motion to dismiss. The statutory authority is 28 U.S.C. Section 1334(c), which provides two abstention regimes:

Mandatory abstention under Section 1334(c)(2) - applies if the proceeding is based on a state-law claim, is "related to" a bankruptcy case but not "arising under" or "arising in" the case, an action is pending in a state forum of appropriate jurisdiction, and the action can be timely adjudicated. All four conditions must be satisfied.

Permissive abstention under Section 1334(c)(1) - applies "in the interest of justice, or in the interest of comity with State courts or respect for State law." The multi-factor analysis varies by circuit but typically considers the effect on bankruptcy administration, the extent of state-law issues, the relative expertise of the forum, and the prejudice to non-debtor parties.

A motion invoking abstention is typically framed as a motion to abstain and dismiss (or, in some circuits, to abstain and remand if the proceeding was removed). The procedural mechanics align with the 12(b) motion practice.

The answer-versus-motion choice

FRCP 12(b) permits the assertion of the listed defenses either in the responsive pleading (the answer) or by motion before the responsive pleading. The choice is consequential. A defense raised by 12(b) motion must be decided before the answer is due; the time to answer is suspended pending disposition. A defense raised in the answer must be litigated on a more compressed schedule, typically without the focused pre-discovery treatment that a 12(b) motion permits.

The 12(b)(6) "failure to state a claim" defense and the 12(b)(1) "lack of subject-matter jurisdiction" defense are typically raised by motion when the defendant believes the issue can be resolved on the face of the pleadings. Personal-jurisdiction and venue defenses are usually raised by motion because they are waived under Rule 12(h)(1) if not raised in the first responsive pleading or motion.

Common procedural posture

Stern-implicated counterclaim

A trustee files an adversary proceeding seeking to recover a fraudulent transfer. The defendant files a counterclaim asserting state-law tort claims unrelated to the bankruptcy. The defendant files a Rule 7012(b) answer expressly declining consent to entry of final judgment on the counterclaim. The bankruptcy court must then enter proposed findings and conclusions for de novo review by the district court rather than a final judgment.

Mandatory abstention motion

A debtor files an adversary proceeding asserting state-law breach-of-contract claims against a non-debtor defendant. The defendant moves to dismiss under Rule 7012(b) on mandatory-abstention grounds, identifying a pending state-court action between the parties. The bankruptcy court evaluates the four Section 1334(c)(2) conditions; if satisfied, it abstains and dismisses the proceeding.

Related rules and authority

Fed. R. Civ. P. 12 - Defenses and objections (incorporated by Rule 7012)

28 U.S.C. Section 157 - Procedures for bankruptcy proceedings (core/non-core)

28 U.S.C. Section 1334 - Bankruptcy jurisdiction and abstention

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 7001 - Scope of adversary proceedings

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 9011 - Signature and representations to the court

Practical impact

Rule 7012 is the procedural gateway between the filing of an adversary complaint and the substantive litigation of the dispute. Beyond the standard FRCP 12 incorporation, the bankruptcy-specific Stern-consent requirement places constitutional weight on a step that civil-procedure practitioners are accustomed to treating as routine. The responsive pleading is no longer a perfunctory document; it is the instrument by which the defendant either accepts bankruptcy-court adjudicative authority or preserves the right to Article III review.

The core/non-core determination is the structural pivot. Where the proceeding is core and the court has constitutional authority under Stern, the bankruptcy court enters final judgment subject to ordinary appellate review. Where the proceeding is non-core, or core but Stern-implicated, the bankruptcy court enters proposed findings for de novo review by the district court. The Rule 7012(b) consent statement is the procedural mechanism by which this choice is made.

## FRBP Rule 8001 - Appellate Procedure Framework [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/rule-8001-appellate-procedure/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure
8001

Rule 8001: Appellate Procedure Framework

The Part VIII appellate framework, the interlocutory vs. final order distinction under 28 USC Section 158(a)(1)/(2)/(3), and the bankruptcy court to district court / BAP appellate routing.

The structure of Part VIII

Part VIII of the Federal Rules of Bankruptcy Procedure - comprising Rules 8001 through 8028 - governs the procedure for appeals from a bankruptcy court. Part VIII was substantially rewritten effective December 1, 2014, to model its structure on the Federal Rules of Appellate Procedure and to recognize the increasing use of electronic filing in bankruptcy appellate practice.

Rule 8001 is the framing rule. It introduces the scope of Part VIII, identifies the appellate courts that may hear bankruptcy appeals (the district court and the bankruptcy appellate panel), and ties Part VIII to the statutory appellate authority in 28 U.S.C. Section 158. The remaining rules in Part VIII govern specific procedural elements: Rule 8002 (time for appeal), Rule 8003 (notice of appeal), Rule 8004 (leave to appeal interlocutory orders), Rule 8005 (election to district court), and so on through the briefing, record, and disposition rules.

The statutory framework: 28 U.S.C. Section 158

Section 158(a) authorizes the district court to hear appeals from a bankruptcy judge:

Section 158(a)(1) - from final judgments, orders, and decrees

Section 158(a)(2) - from interlocutory orders and decrees issued under Section 1121(d) (extending or reducing the exclusivity periods in Chapter 11)

Section 158(a)(3) - with leave of the court, from other interlocutory orders and decrees

Section 158(b) authorizes the establishment of bankruptcy appellate panels in each circuit, comprising bankruptcy judges from the districts within the circuit, to hear appeals that would otherwise be heard by the district court. Section 158(c) governs the appellate jurisdiction of the bankruptcy appellate panel and provides the election mechanism by which a party may opt for district-court review rather than panel review.

Section 158(d) governs appeals to the courts of appeals from the district court or the bankruptcy appellate panel. Section 158(d)(2), added by the 2005 BAPCPA amendments, creates the direct-appeal mechanism by which the bankruptcy court, the district court, or the bankruptcy appellate panel may certify an order for direct appeal to the court of appeals, bypassing the intermediate appellate court.

Interlocutory versus final orders

The interlocutory/final distinction is the most consequential jurisdictional fork in the appellate framework. A final order is appealable as of right under Section 158(a)(1); an interlocutory order is appealable only with leave under Section 158(a)(3).

The general rule of finality in federal civil practice - that an order is final when it ends the litigation on the merits and leaves nothing for the court to do but execute the judgment - applies in bankruptcy with substantial modification. Bankruptcy cases involve numerous discrete proceedings (claim objections, dischargeability complaints, sale motions, plan confirmation), each of which may be functionally "final" with respect to a particular controversy even though the larger case continues. The Supreme Court's decision in Bullard v. Blue Hills Bank, 575 U.S. 496 (2015), addressed the finality question in the context of plan confirmation: the denial of plan confirmation, in itself, does not constitute a final order if the debtor remains free to propose an amended plan. Confirmation of a plan, by contrast, is a final, appealable order.

The case law has settled on a flexible standard for bankruptcy finality. The order disposes of a discrete dispute within the larger bankruptcy case; the order resolves the rights of one or more parties; the order is sufficiently distinct that delayed appellate review would impose meaningful prejudice. A sale order, a stay-relief order, a confirmation order, an order granting or denying discharge, and a dischargeability order are typically final. An order denying confirmation (following Bullard), an order denying summary judgment, and an order on a discovery motion are typically interlocutory.

Leave to appeal interlocutory orders under Rule 8004

Rule 8004 governs the procedure for seeking leave to appeal an interlocutory order under Section 158(a)(3). A party seeking leave must file a notice of appeal accompanied by a motion for leave to appeal. The motion must state the facts necessary to understand the question presented, identify the question itself, address the relief sought, and explain why an appeal is warranted under the standard the district court applies.

Most circuits apply the standard articulated in 28 U.S.C. Section 1292(b) (the analogous interlocutory-appeal provision in the district-court context) by analogy: a controlling question of law, substantial ground for difference of opinion, and an immediate appeal that would materially advance the ultimate termination of the litigation. The standard is exacting; leave is granted sparingly.

District court versus bankruptcy appellate panel

Section 158 creates two parallel intermediate appellate forums for bankruptcy appeals. Where a circuit has established a bankruptcy appellate panel under Section 158(b), the default is panel review unless a party elects district-court review under Section 158(c)(1). The election must be made under Rule 8005 within the time fixed by the rule (typically at the time of filing the notice of appeal or within 30 days after entry of the order being appealed).

The bankruptcy appellate panel is composed of bankruptcy judges from the districts within the circuit, selected on a rotating basis. The panel typically sits in three-judge configurations. The choice between district-court review and panel review carries practical consequences. The bankruptcy appellate panel is composed of judges with subject-matter expertise in bankruptcy law and tends to dispose of appeals more rapidly. District courts hear bankruptcy appeals along with their general civil and criminal docket and typically lack the subject-matter specialization the panel provides, but generate decisions that are sometimes given greater weight by parties evaluating future positions.

Not every circuit has a bankruptcy appellate panel. The First, Sixth, Eighth, Ninth, and Tenth Circuits have established panels; the others rely on district-court review as the default. Within a circuit that has a panel, the election mechanism preserves the parties' choice.

Direct appeal under Section 158(d)(2)

Section 158(d)(2) authorizes direct appeal to the court of appeals - bypassing the district court or the bankruptcy appellate panel - if the bankruptcy court, the district court, or the bankruptcy appellate panel, or all parties jointly, certify that one of three conditions is satisfied:

The order involves a question of law as to which there is no controlling decision of the court of appeals or of the Supreme Court, or involves a matter of public importance

The order involves a question of law requiring resolution of conflicting decisions

An immediate appeal from the order may materially advance the progress of the case or proceeding in which the appeal is taken

Even with certification, the court of appeals may decline to authorize the direct appeal. Section 158(d)(2)(A) makes the direct appeal subject to the court of appeals' authorization.

The time-for-appeal regime under Rule 8002

Rule 8002 sets the time for filing the notice of appeal. The general rule is 14 days after entry of the judgment, order, or decree being appealed. The 14-day window is jurisdictional in nature - a late notice of appeal deprives the appellate court of authority to entertain the appeal except where the rule itself provides for an extension.

Rule 8002(b) provides that the time for appeal is suspended by the filing of any of several specified motions, including motions for new trial, motions to alter or amend judgment under Rule 9023 (incorporating FRCP 59), and motions for relief from judgment under Rule 9024 (incorporating FRCP 60) if filed within the appeal period. The suspension runs from the filing of the motion until entry of the order disposing of the last such motion outstanding.

Rule 8002(d) authorizes the bankruptcy court to extend the time for appeal upon a showing of excusable neglect. The extension may not exceed 21 days from the original deadline, and the motion must be filed within the original 14-day window or within the 21-day extension period. The case law applies the Pioneer equitable-factors framework to the excusable-neglect inquiry.

Common procedural posture

Final-order appeal from sale order

A bankruptcy court enters a sale order approving the sale of estate property under Section 363. A party in interest believes the order is improper and files a notice of appeal within 14 days under Rule 8002. The sale is a final order; the appeal proceeds as of right under Section 158(a)(1). Unless the appellant obtains a stay pending appeal under Rule 8007, the Section 363(m) good-faith finding will likely render the appeal moot upon closing.

Leave-required appeal from denial of summary judgment

The bankruptcy court denies a motion for summary judgment in a dischargeability adversary proceeding. The denial is interlocutory - it does not dispose of the dispute. A party seeking immediate appellate review must file a notice of appeal accompanied by a motion for leave to appeal under Rule 8004, demonstrating the Section 1292(b) factors. Leave is granted sparingly.

Related rules and authority

28 U.S.C. Section 158 - Appeals (statutory framework)

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 8002 - Time for filing notice of appeal

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 8003 - Appeal as of right

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 8004 - Appeal by leave

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 3008 - Reconsideration of claims

BAP vs. District Court Appeals - Selection of intermediate appellate forum

Practical impact

Rule 8001 and the broader Part VIII framework operate as the formal interface between the trial-level bankruptcy court and the appellate system. The most common errors at this interface are timing errors (missed 14-day deadlines) and characterization errors (treating an interlocutory order as final or vice versa). Both errors are typically fatal to appellate review: a missed deadline forecloses appeal entirely, and an attempted appeal of an interlocutory order without leave is subject to dismissal.

Finality in bankruptcy is functional, not formal. The question is not whether the bankruptcy case has ended, but whether the specific order disposes of a discrete dispute within the case. A sale order, a confirmation order, a discharge order, and an order in an adversary proceeding can each be final even though the larger bankruptcy case continues. The Bullard v. Blue Hills Bank framework distinguishes orders that conclusively resolve from orders that leave room for further litigation.

## FRBP Rule 9010 - Representation and Appearances in Bankruptcy [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/rule-9010/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure
9010

Rule 9010: Representation and Appearances; Powers of Attorney

Who may appear in a bankruptcy case, the Notice of Appearance, and the local-rule pathway for withdrawal.

Verbatim text of Rule 9010(a) and (b)

(a) Authority to act personally or by attorney. A debtor, creditor, equity security holder, indenture trustee, committee or other party may (1) appear in a case under the Code and act either in the entity's own behalf or by an attorney authorized to practice in the court, and (2) perform any act not constituting the practice of law, by an authorized agent, attorney in fact, or proxy.

(b) Notice of appearance. An attorney appearing for a party in a case under the Code shall file a notice of appearance with the attorney's name, office address and telephone number, unless the attorney's appearance is otherwise noted in the record. Fed. R. Bankr. P. 9010(a)-(b).

What Rule 9010 governs

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 9010 establishes who may appear in a bankruptcy case and how appearances are noted in the court's record. The rule operates in two coordinated parts: subdivision (a) authorizes appearances by parties themselves or through counsel admitted to practice in the bankruptcy court, and subdivision (b) requires attorneys appearing for a party to file a notice of appearance unless the appearance is otherwise noted of record.

The phrase "otherwise noted in the record" is significant. An attorney whose appearance is reflected on the docket through the act of filing a petition, schedules, or other initiating documents is generally treated as having entered an appearance for that party without needing to file a separate notice. Subsequent counsel joining a case, or counsel for a creditor or other party in interest appearing for the first time, files a Notice of Appearance.

Who may appear personally

Individuals may appear pro se on their own behalf. The Bankruptcy Code and Rules permit an individual debtor, creditor, or party in interest to file documents, attend hearings, and prosecute or defend matters without counsel. The right is qualified by the requirement that legal services for any other person constitute the unauthorized practice of law if performed by a non-attorney.

Corporate debtors, partnerships, and other artificial entities cannot appear pro se. A long line of federal authority - including binding Supreme Court precedent in Rowland v. California Men's Colony, 506 U.S. 194 (1993) - holds that artificial entities must appear in federal court through counsel admitted to practice. A corporate Chapter 11 petition signed by an officer who is not an attorney is procedurally defective and may be subject to dismissal.

The Notice of Appearance

A Notice of Appearance under Rule 9010(b) identifies counsel of record for a particular party and provides the attorney's office address and telephone number. The Notice typically also requests notice under Rule 2002 on behalf of the represented party. Most districts have integrated the Notice of Appearance with the ECF docket-entry system; the act of filing a Notice through ECF adds the attorney to the case's electronic notice list automatically.

Appearance creates duties

An attorney who files a Notice of Appearance becomes counsel of record. Counsel of record receive electronic notice of filings, are responsible for receipt and acknowledgment of court orders, and remain counsel of record until either substituted out or formally withdrawn under the local rule governing withdrawal. The mere fact that a representation has practically ended - because a discrete matter is resolved, because the attorney-client relationship has ruptured, or because the client has retained substitute counsel - does not by itself remove counsel from the court's record.

Powers of attorney

Rule 9010(c) governs the filing of evidence of authority for appearances and acts taken through agents, attorneys in fact, or proxies. The requirements differ across contexts: a proxy used to vote a claim at a Section 341 meeting is governed by specific provisions of Rule 2006; an agent acting on behalf of a creditor in filing a proof of claim is generally permitted under Rule 9010(c) on filing of evidence of the agent's authority, which can be a written authorization signed by the principal.

Withdrawal of counsel

Rule 9010 itself does not prescribe a uniform withdrawal procedure. Withdrawal of counsel of record in a bankruptcy case is governed by the local rules of each bankruptcy court, typically a local rule numbered in the 9010 series or in the 2090 series of attorney-admission rules. The substantive standards generally track the rules of professional conduct adopted by the bankruptcy court (the state-court rules of the forum state, sometimes supplemented by the ABA Model Rules).

Common local-rule requirements for withdrawal

Application or motion

Most districts require counsel seeking to withdraw to file a written application or motion identifying the case, the client, the basis for withdrawal, and successor counsel if any. Some districts permit an unopposed substitution by stipulation signed by withdrawing counsel, successor counsel, and the client; absent stipulation, a motion with notice is the standard pathway.

Notice to client and parties

The withdrawal motion is typically served on the client at the client's last known address and on all parties entitled to notice in the case. Many local rules require the motion to certify that the client has been advised of pending deadlines and hearings, and to identify any matters that are then pending and time-sensitive.

Court order is what terminates representation on the record

A withdrawal motion does not by itself remove counsel from the record. Counsel remains counsel of record - and therefore continues to receive notice and bears the obligations attached to that status - until the court enters an order granting withdrawal. Some districts permit ex parte orders on uncontested motions; others require notice and the opportunity for hearing. The form of relief (order versus stipulation) and the timing differ by local rule.

A second consequence flows from the same principle: counsel of record for a party in interest who claims to have withdrawn but has not obtained a court order remains, as a matter of the court's record, counsel of record. The substantive question whether a fee-paying engagement has ended is distinct from the procedural question whether the docket reflects that termination.

Related rules and authority

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 2002 - Notice to creditors and other interested parties

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 2006 - Solicitation and voting of proxies in chapter 7 liquidation cases

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 2014 - Employment of professional persons

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 2016 - Compensation for services rendered

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 9011 - Signature, representations, sanctions

KRPC 1.16 / MRPC 4-1.16 - Declining or terminating representation

Practical impact

Rule 9010 is the procedural foundation for the entire architecture of representation in a bankruptcy case. Three practical pressure points recur:

Pro se artificial entities. A corporate petition signed without counsel is procedurally defective. Cases are routinely dismissed on this ground, often with leave to refile through counsel.

Counsel of record persists until court order. An attorney whose substantive representation has ended remains counsel of record - with associated notice obligations and obligations to act when court orders are received - until a withdrawal motion is filed and granted.

Coordination with state ethics rules. The court order granting withdrawal is the procedural endpoint; the state rule of professional conduct (KRPC 1.16, MRPC 4-1.16, or its analog) governs the substantive duties on termination - including the duty to take reasonable steps to protect the client's interests and to surrender papers and property.

Two records, two endpoints. Termination of an attorney-client representation has both a substantive endpoint (governed by state rules of professional conduct) and a procedural endpoint (governed by Rule 9010 and the local rule for withdrawal). The substantive engagement can end before the procedural appearance is terminated; until both endpoints are reached, counsel of record remains accountable on the docket.

## FRBP Rule 9011 - Signature, Representations to the Court, Sanctions [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/rule-9011/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure
9011

Rule 9011: Signature, Representations to the Court, Sanctions

The 9011(b) representations made by signing a filing, the 9011(c) sanctions procedure, and the safe-harbor letter.

Verbatim text of Rule 9011(b)

By presenting to the court (whether by signing, filing, submitting, or later advocating) a petition, pleading, written motion, or other paper, an attorney or unrepresented party is certifying that to the best of the person's knowledge, information, and belief, formed after an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances,

(1) it is not being presented for any improper purpose, such as to harass or to cause unnecessary delay or needless increase in the cost of litigation;

(2) the claims, defenses, and other legal contentions therein are warranted by existing law or by a nonfrivolous argument for the extension, modification, or reversal of existing law or the establishment of new law;

(3) the allegations and other factual contentions have evidentiary support or, if specifically so identified, are likely to have evidentiary support after a reasonable opportunity for further investigation or discovery; and

(4) the denials of factual contentions are warranted on the evidence or, if specifically so identified, are reasonably based on a lack of information or belief. Fed. R. Bankr. P. 9011(b).

The structure of Rule 9011

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 9011 is the bankruptcy analog of Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 11. The two rules are substantively parallel; case law construing Rule 11 is routinely applied to Rule 9011, subject to bankruptcy-specific considerations. Rule 9011 has four operative subdivisions:

9011(a) requires every paper filed with the court (other than a list, schedule, or statement) to be signed by an attorney of record or by the party if unrepresented.

9011(b) identifies four representations the signer makes by presenting the paper to the court.

9011(c) establishes the procedure for imposing sanctions for violations of subdivision (b), including the 21-day safe harbor.

9011(d) exempts certain bankruptcy-specific filings (lists, schedules, statements, amendments) from the operation of the rule.

The four Rule 9011(b) representations

Every paper filed with a bankruptcy court carries four implicit certifications by the signing attorney or unrepresented party:

(1) No improper purpose

The paper is not presented for harassment, unnecessary delay, or needless increase in litigation cost. The standard is objective; subjective good faith is not a defense to a filing whose effect a reasonable attorney would have foreseen as harassment or as an attempt to delay or to increase costs. Courts examine the timing of the filing, its relationship to prior filings, and its substantive effect.

(2) Legal contentions warranted by existing law

Legal contentions must be warranted by existing law or by a nonfrivolous argument for extension, modification, or reversal of existing law. The rule expressly accommodates good-faith efforts to change the law. A contention that has been rejected by binding authority in the circuit, advanced without acknowledgment of the controlling adverse authority and without a nonfrivolous argument for departure, is sanctionable.

(3) Factual contentions have evidentiary support

Allegations and other factual contentions must have evidentiary support, or - if specifically so identified - are likely to have evidentiary support after a reasonable opportunity for further investigation or discovery. The signing attorney certifies a pre-filing inquiry reasonable under the circumstances. The reasonableness of the inquiry is evaluated in light of the time available, the resources of the attorney, and the accessibility of the relevant information.

(4) Denials warranted on the evidence

Denials of factual contentions must be warranted on the evidence or - if specifically so identified - are reasonably based on a lack of information or belief. A denial of a fact known to the denying party to be true is sanctionable.

The Rule 9011(c) sanctions procedure

Sanctions for Rule 9011(b) violations may be initiated either by motion of a party or sua sponte by the court. The two pathways have different procedural requirements.

Motion by a party - the 21-day safe harbor

A motion for sanctions filed by a party must be served on the alleged offender at least 21 days before it is filed with the court. The 21-day window - the "safe harbor" - allows the alleged offender to withdraw or correct the challenged filing without exposure to sanctions. The safe-harbor letter accompanying the motion typically:

Identifies the specific filing or filings that allegedly violate Rule 9011(b)

Identifies the specific representation(s) under 9011(b)(1)-(4) the filing is alleged to violate

Explains the basis for the alleged violation with sufficient particularity to allow informed assessment

Demands withdrawal or correction within 21 days

States that the motion will be filed with the court if the safe harbor expires without compliance

If the challenged paper is withdrawn or corrected within the 21-day window, the motion may not be filed. The safe harbor is not optional; a sanctions motion filed without compliance with the safe-harbor requirement is procedurally defective.

Court-initiated sanctions

The court may, sua sponte, enter an order describing specific conduct that appears to violate Rule 9011(b) and directing the attorney or party to show cause why sanctions should not be imposed. Court-initiated sanctions are not subject to the safe-harbor requirement, but the show-cause procedure provides comparable notice and opportunity to respond.

Available sanctions

The sanction imposed under Rule 9011(c)(2) must be limited to what is "sufficient to deter repetition of such conduct or comparable conduct by others similarly situated." Available sanctions include:

Nonmonetary directives (e.g., training, supervision, additional certifications on future filings)

A penalty payable into court

An order directing payment of some or all of the reasonable attorney's fees and other expenses incurred as a direct result of the violation, payable to the movant

Striking the offending paper

Monetary sanctions may not be awarded against a represented party for a violation of subdivision (b)(2) (frivolous legal contentions). Monetary sanctions may not be awarded on the court's initiative unless the show-cause order issued before voluntary dismissal or settlement of the claims made by or against the party that would be sanctioned.

Common procedural posture

Disputed proof of claim

A creditor files a proof of claim that the debtor believes is unsupported by competent evidence. The debtor sends a safe-harbor letter identifying the specific deficiencies (e.g., absence of contract documentation, calculations not reconcilable with the underlying account history) and demanding withdrawal within 21 days. If the claim is not withdrawn or amended, the debtor may file the Rule 9011 motion concurrently with or after the claim objection.

Repeat petition without good-faith basis

A debtor files a serial Chapter 13 petition that lacks evidentiary support for the ability to fund a plan. The trustee or a creditor may move for sanctions under Rule 9011 against the petitioning attorney for failure to conduct a reasonable inquiry into the debtor's ability to satisfy 11 U.S.C. Section 1325 confirmation requirements.

The "later advocating" clause

The 1997 amendment to FRCP Rule 11 - mirrored in Rule 9011 - expanded the certification to cover not only the original presentation of a paper but also "later advocating" of it. An attorney who continues to advocate a factual or legal contention after learning that the contention lacks evidentiary or legal support may be sanctioned even if the original filing satisfied Rule 9011(b) when made. The duty is not frozen at signing; it is renewed each time the attorney advocates the position to the court.

Related rules and authority

Fed. R. Civ. P. 11 - The civil-procedure analog; case law is largely interchangeable

28 U.S.C. Section 1927 - Counsel's liability for excessive costs (alternative sanctions authority)

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 2014 - Employment of professional persons (disclosure duty)

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 2016 - Compensation for services rendered

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 9010 - Representation and appearances

KRPC 3.3 / MRPC 4-3.3 - Candor toward the tribunal

Practical impact

Rule 9011 sits at the intersection of procedural law and professional responsibility. A violation of 9011(b)(3) - filing a contention without evidentiary support - is also typically a violation of KRPC 3.3(a)(1) / MRPC 4-3.3(a)(1) (false statement of fact to a tribunal) and may trigger reporting obligations under KRPC 8.3 / MRPC 4-8.3. Counsel evaluating a possible Rule 9011 violation should expect parallel exposure under the state rules of professional conduct that bind the attorney in the forum and home jurisdictions.

The safe harbor is procedural, not optional. A motion for sanctions filed by a party without compliance with the 21-day service requirement is subject to denial on that ground alone, regardless of the merits of the underlying allegation. The safe-harbor letter is the necessary procedural predicate.

## FRBP Rule 9014 - Contested Matters [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/rule-9014-contested-matters/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure
9014

Rule 9014: Contested Matters

Motion practice in bankruptcy, the Rule 7001 line that separates contested matters from adversary proceedings, and the Part VII rules applied under Rule 9014(c).

Verbatim text of Rule 9014(a)

In a contested matter not otherwise governed by these rules, relief shall be requested by motion, and reasonable notice and opportunity for hearing shall be afforded the party against whom relief is sought. No response is required under this rule unless the court directs otherwise. Fed. R. Bankr. P. 9014(a).

The contested-matter / adversary-proceeding distinction

The Federal Rules of Bankruptcy Procedure divide disputes that arise in a bankruptcy case into two procedural tracks. The dividing line is drawn by Rule 7001, which enumerates ten categories of disputes that must be brought as adversary proceedings - separately captioned lawsuits filed with their own docket within the main bankruptcy case, governed by the Part VII rules that closely track the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure.

Any dispute that is not within one of the ten Rule 7001 categories is a "contested matter" governed by Rule 9014. Contested matters are initiated by motion within the main bankruptcy case, without a separate complaint, summons, or adversary docket.

The ten Rule 7001 adversary-proceeding categories

Rule 7001 requires an adversary proceeding for:

Actions to recover money or property (with specified exceptions)

Actions to determine the validity, priority, or extent of a lien or other interest in property

Actions to obtain approval of the sale of both the interest of the estate and a co-owner's interest in property

Actions to object to or revoke a discharge

Actions to revoke an order of confirmation of a Chapter 11, Chapter 12, or Chapter 13 plan

Actions to determine the dischargeability of a debt

Actions to obtain an injunction or other equitable relief (with specified exceptions)

Actions to subordinate any allowed claim or interest (with specified exceptions)

Actions to obtain a declaratory judgment relating to any of the foregoing

Actions to determine a claim or cause of action removed under 28 U.S.C. Section 1452

Common contested-matter examples

Disputes that are not within Rule 7001 and therefore proceed by motion under Rule 9014 include:

Motions for relief from the automatic stay under 11 U.S.C. Section 362(d)

Objections to proofs of claim (unless the objection is combined with an affirmative claim against the claimant, which converts it into an adversary)

Motions to assume, assume and assign, or reject executory contracts under Section 365

Motions to sell estate property under Section 363

Motions to approve compromises and settlements under Rule 9019

Motions to convert or dismiss a case under Sections 1112, 1208, or 1307

Applications for compensation under Section 330

Motions for sanctions under Rule 9011

Motions to use cash collateral or obtain post-petition financing under Sections 363 and 364

Rule 9014(b) - service of the motion

Rule 9014(b) requires that the motion be served on the party against whom relief is sought in the same manner as a summons and complaint under Rule 7004 - the Part VII service rule. Service by ordinary mail to counsel is generally insufficient; service must be made on the party in the manner specified by Rule 7004 for the type of party involved (individual, corporation, partnership, governmental unit, insured depository institution, etc.). The 2017 amendment to Rule 9014(b) eliminated the prior cross-reference to Rule 7005 and clarified that subsequent papers may be served as provided in Rule 7005.

Rule 9014(c) - applicable Part VII rules

Rule 9014(c) imports several Part VII rules into contested matters as if the matter were an adversary proceeding. The rules made applicable by Rule 9014(c) include:

Rule 7009 (pleadings)

Rule 7017 (parties)

Rule 7021 (misjoinder and non-joinder)

Rule 7025 (substitution of parties)

Rule 7026 (discovery)

Rule 7028 through Rule 7037 (the discovery rules - depositions, interrogatories, production, admissions, sanctions)

Rule 7041 (dismissal of actions)

Rule 7042 (consolidation and separate trials)

Rule 7052 (findings by the court)

Rule 7054 through Rule 7056 (judgments, costs, summary judgment)

Rule 7064 (seizures)

Rule 7069 (execution)

Rule 7071 (process in behalf of and against persons not parties)

The court may, at any stage of a particular contested matter, direct that one or more of the other Part VII rules apply. This discretion is most commonly exercised to import the pleading or amendment rules (Rules 7008, 7012, 7015) when the complexity of the dispute warrants it.

Discovery in contested matters

Because Rule 9014(c) imports the discovery rules (Rules 7026 through 7037), discovery in contested matters proceeds substantially as it does in adversary proceedings - depositions, interrogatories, requests for production, requests for admission, and the corresponding scope, protective-order, and sanctions framework all apply. The principal practical differences are:

Discovery in a contested matter is typically conducted on an expedited timeline reflecting the often-urgent nature of the underlying motion (stay relief, cash collateral, cure dispute, sale objection)

Rule 7026(f) initial-disclosure procedure is often modified or waived by local rule or court order in routine contested matters

Pretrial scheduling under Rule 7016 is incorporated only at the court's direction

Evidentiary standards

Contested-matter hearings are evidentiary unless the parties and the court agree otherwise. The Federal Rules of Evidence apply (made applicable to bankruptcy proceedings by 28 U.S.C. Section 2075 and Federal Rule of Evidence 1101). The court receives testimony, admits exhibits, and makes findings of fact and conclusions of law under Rule 7052 (made applicable to contested matters by Rule 9014(c)).

The burden of proof is allocated by the underlying substantive law. For example:

In a motion for relief from the automatic stay under Section 362(d), the moving party bears the burden of showing cause or lack of equity; the party opposing relief bears the burden on all other issues, including adequate protection, per Section 362(g)

In a claim objection (a contested matter unless combined with affirmative relief), a properly filed proof of claim is prima facie evidence of validity and amount under Rule 3001(f); the objector bears the burden of producing evidence to overcome the presumption

In a motion to approve a sale under Section 363(b), the trustee or debtor in possession bears the burden of showing a sound business justification

Conversion of a contested matter to an adversary proceeding

When a contested matter is filed but the relief actually sought falls within Rule 7001, the court may order that the matter proceed as an adversary proceeding. The procedural posture must be corrected because Rule 7001 categories carry due-process protections - particularly summons service and a formal complaint-and-answer pleading regime - that contested-matter motion practice does not replicate. A claim objection that asks the court not only to disallow a claim but also to recover prepetition transfers from the claimant must be filed as an adversary proceeding because the affirmative recovery falls within Rule 7001(1).

Common procedural posture

Stay-relief contested matter

A secured creditor files a motion for relief from the automatic stay. Service is made on the debtor under Rule 7004. The debtor responds with a written objection. The court holds a preliminary hearing within 30 days (per Section 362(e)) and, if cause is shown, conducts an evidentiary final hearing with witnesses and exhibits. The court issues findings of fact and conclusions of law under Rule 7052.

Claim objection

The debtor or trustee files an objection to a proof of claim. The objection is a contested matter. Discovery proceeds under the Part VII rules. The court holds an evidentiary hearing. If the debtor wishes to recover money from the claimant in addition to disallowing the claim, the matter must be brought as an adversary proceeding under Rule 7001(1).

Rule 9014(d) - testimony of witnesses

Rule 9014(d) provides that, in a contested matter, the court may direct that testimony of witnesses with respect to disputed material factual issues be taken in the same manner as testimony in an adversary proceeding. In practice, this means live testimony at the hearing rather than submission on declarations or affidavits. The court's discretion under Rule 9014(d) is broad; many contested matters involving disputed facts proceed on live testimony as a matter of course.

The Rule 7001 line is jurisdictional in effect. A motion filed as a contested matter that seeks relief properly classified under Rule 7001 may be procedurally defective even if the merits are sound. Counsel should evaluate the Rule 7001 enumeration before selecting the procedural vehicle; the choice of motion versus complaint is not discretionary.

Related rules and authority

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 7001 - Scope of adversary proceedings

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 7004 - Service of summons; service of process

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 7026 - Discovery; general provisions

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 7052 - Findings by the court

Fed. R. Evid. 1101 - Applicability of the Federal Rules of Evidence

Rule 9011 (Sanctions)

## Rule 9018 Sealed Records - Categories, Standards, and Common-Law Right of Access | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/rule-9018-sealed-records/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure
9018
Section 107

Rule 9018: Sealed Records in Federal Bankruptcy Cases

The statutory anchor, the categories of sealable matter, and the access doctrines that limit when a court can close the file.

Sealing in bankruptcy is exceptional, not routine.

Federal bankruptcy filings are presumptively public. Rule 9018 and its statutory anchor at 11 U.S.C. Section 107 define narrow categories in which a court may seal, protect, or restrict access. Outside those categories the common-law right of access recognized in Nixon v. Warner Communications, Inc., 435 U.S. 589 (1978), and the First Amendment access doctrine, control.

The statutory and rule framework

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 9018 is the procedural vehicle for sealing or protecting matter filed in a bankruptcy case. The rule itself does not define what may be sealed. It implements 11 U.S.C. Section 107, which establishes that papers filed in a case under the Bankruptcy Code and the dockets of a bankruptcy court are public records and open to examination by an entity at reasonable times without charge.

Section 107(b) and Section 107(c) carve out the exceptions. Subsection (b) authorizes the court to issue an order to protect an entity with respect to (1) a trade secret or confidential research, development, or commercial information, or (2) scandalous or defamatory matter contained in any paper filed in a case under the Code. Subsection (c) addresses personal-identification information that would create undue risk of identity theft or other unlawful injury if disclosed.

Rule 9018 supplies the procedure: on motion, or on its own initiative, with or without notice, the court may make any order permitted by Section 107.

The sealable categories under Section 107(b) and (c)

Trade secret or confidential research, development, or commercial information. The category covers business information whose disclosure would cause competitive harm. Courts apply a definitional gate. Generic embarrassment about financial difficulty does not qualify. The Second Circuit's analysis in In re Orion Pictures Corp., 21 F.3d 24 (2d Cir. 1994), is the leading authority and reads Section 107(b)(1) as a directive: if the matter fits the category, the court is required to protect, without the discretionary balancing that governs sealing under the common law.

Scandalous or defamatory matter. The category protects parties and non-parties from gratuitous reputational injury embedded in court filings. Courts distinguish material that is merely embarrassing or unfavorable from material whose only function is to defame. The leading framework derives from In re Gitto Global Corp., 422 F.3d 1 (1st Cir. 2005), which treats matter as scandalous if it would cause a reasonable person to alter their opinion of the affected party based on potentially untrue information.

Personal-identification information creating undue risk of identity theft or other unlawful injury. Section 107(c) is the separate sealing pathway for identifiers that go beyond the redaction floor of Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 9037(a). The undue-risk standard requires a showing that goes beyond the routine privacy interest already covered by mandatory redaction.

Means of access to the names of governmental matters. Section 107(b)(1) extends protection to confidential commercial information held by governmental units in narrow circumstances. The protection is rare in consumer cases and arises principally in complex Chapter 11 matters involving governmental contracts or regulatory information.

What sealing does and does not cover

Covers

Specific documents, specific exhibits, specific lines or paragraphs within a document. Courts often order sealing of an exhibit attached to a public motion while the motion itself remains on the docket with the exhibit replaced by a placeholder.

Does not cover

The fact of the filing, the existence of the case, the identity of the parties, the docket itself, or the general subject matter of a motion. Section 107(a) protects all of these as presumptively public.

The common-law right of access - Nixon v. Warner Communications

The Supreme Court in Nixon v. Warner Communications, Inc., 435 U.S. 589 (1978), recognized a federal common-law right of access to judicial records. The right is not absolute, and the Court declined to specify a single test, but it framed the inquiry as a sound-discretion balancing in which the trial court must weigh the relevant facts and circumstances of the particular case.

The circuits have since elaborated the framework. In bankruptcy, the common-law right operates alongside Section 107(a)'s express public-record declaration, which several courts read as a stronger statutory statement than the general common-law presumption. The practical consequence is that movants seeking to seal bear a heavy burden, and the court's reasoned analysis must appear on the record. See, for example, Father M v. Various Tort Claimants (In re Roman Catholic Archbishop of Portland in Or.), 661 F.3d 417 (9th Cir. 2011) (collecting authorities and holding that Section 107 is a clear statutory exception to the general presumption).

The First Amendment overlay - Globe Newspaper and the experience-and-logic test

Where the common-law right is grounded in the historical practice of public access to court records, the First Amendment right of access derives from Richmond Newspapers, Inc. v. Virginia, 448 U.S. 555 (1980), and was elaborated for press access in Globe Newspaper Co. v. Superior Court, 457 U.S. 596 (1982). The Court's analytical framework, often called the experience-and-logic test, asks (1) whether the place and process have historically been open to the press and the general public, and (2) whether public access plays a significant positive role in the functioning of the particular process in question.

Most circuits hold that the First Amendment access right applies to civil judicial proceedings, including bankruptcy, with respect to documents that play a meaningful role in the adjudicative process. Where the right applies, sealing requires a higher showing: the order must be supported by specific, on-the-record findings demonstrating that closure is essential to preserve higher values and is narrowly tailored to serve that interest.

Standard for issuing a Rule 9018 order

The court considering a motion to seal under Rule 9018 generally proceeds through a layered inquiry. First, does the matter fall within one of the Section 107(b) or 107(c) categories. Second, even within a covered category, is the proposed sealing the least restrictive means of protecting the interest. Third, has the movant carried the burden with specific evidence rather than conclusory assertions.

If the matter falls within Section 107(b), the Orion Pictures line of authority treats the protection as required rather than discretionary. The court still must verify the categorical fit. Conclusory assertions that information is a trade secret will not suffice; the movant typically must describe what the information is, why it qualifies as a trade secret or confidential commercial information, and what specific competitive harm would result from disclosure.

Procedure

Motion or sua sponte. Rule 9018 permits the court to act on its own initiative, but in practice sealing arises by motion of a party or affected non-party.

Notice. The rule allows the court to proceed with or without notice. In practice, motions affecting public access are routinely served on the United States Trustee and other parties in interest. Press intervention to challenge sealing is procedurally available and not uncommon in high-profile cases.

Provisional sealing. Many courts permit provisional sealing while the motion is pending so that the matter does not enter the public record before the court rules.

On-the-record findings. Where the First Amendment access right applies, the court must articulate specific findings supporting closure. Boilerplate is not sufficient.

Narrow tailoring. Even when sealing is appropriate, the order should reach only the matter that satisfies the statutory category. Redaction of specific lines is preferred over wholesale sealing of an exhibit where the affected portion is severable.

Sealing is not a remedy for inadvertent Rule 9037(a) violations. When a personal identifier has been publicly filed in violation of the mandatory redaction floor, the appropriate remedy is a motion to redact under Rule 9037 paired with clerk notification and, where warranted, an auxiliary Section 107(c) order for the underlying record. Sealing an entire filing to suppress an identifier already on PACER does not cure prior disclosure and may obscure the procedural record needed for downstream remediation.

Press and public intervention

News organizations and members of the public have standing to challenge sealing orders. The procedural posture is typically a motion to intervene for the limited purpose of unsealing, followed by a motion to unseal that frames the challenge under both the common-law and First Amendment access doctrines. The intervenor need not be a party in interest in the bankruptcy case itself.

Courts evaluating intervention have generally favored access where the sealed material has been considered by the court in connection with a substantive ruling. The rationale is that documents that informed an adjudication should be available to the public so the basis for the ruling can be understood.

## FRBP Rule 9019 - Compromise and Settlement Approval [2026] | Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/rule-9019-compromise/

Open Bankruptcy Project
Home
Tools

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure
9019

Rule 9019: Compromise and Settlement

Court approval of compromises of estate claims, the Iridium fair-and-equitable test, and the TMT Trailer factors.

Verbatim text of Rule 9019(a)

On motion by the trustee and after notice and a hearing, the court may approve a compromise or settlement. Notice shall be given to creditors, the United States trustee, the debtor, and indenture trustees as provided in Rule 2002 and to any other entity as the court may direct. Fed. R. Bankr. P. 9019(a).

The structure of Rule 9019

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 9019 governs court approval of compromises and settlements of claims by and against the bankruptcy estate. The rule has three subdivisions:

9019(a) requires court approval of any compromise or settlement after notice and a hearing.

9019(b) permits the court, after notice and a hearing, to authorize the trustee to compromise and settle controversies of a particular class without further hearing or notice.

9019(c) authorizes the court to require parties to participate in a settlement conference or other alternative dispute resolution proceeding.

Rule 9019(a) applies to virtually every consensual resolution of a contested matter, adversary proceeding, or claim dispute in which the estate has an interest. Settlements presented for approval typically include resolutions of avoidance actions, insurance coverage disputes, lien priority controversies, fraudulent transfer claims, breach-of-contract claims held by the estate, and contested proofs of claim.

The TMT Trailer Ferry standard

The Supreme Court's decision in Protective Committee for Independent Stockholders of TMT Trailer Ferry, Inc. v. Anderson, 390 U.S. 414 (1968), establishes the foundational rule that a bankruptcy court may not approve a compromise of estate claims unless the settlement is "fair and equitable." The Court emphasized that the bankruptcy judge must apprise himself or herself of the relevant facts and law so that an informed and intelligent judgment can be reached. A perfunctory approval, or approval based solely on the recommendation of the trustee, is insufficient.

The TMT Trailer Ferry standard requires the court to consider:

The probability of success in the underlying litigation

The complexity, expense, and likely duration of the litigation

The difficulties to be encountered in collecting any judgment obtained

The paramount interest of the creditors and a proper deference to their reasonable views

These four factors are the canonical TMT Trailer factors, applied in some formulation by every circuit. Courts have elaborated on the standard with additional considerations including the extent to which the settlement is the product of arm's-length bargaining, whether the settlement is supported by competent counsel, and whether the settlement is in the public interest.

The Iridium fair-and-equitable refinement

The Second Circuit's decision in In re Iridium Operating LLC, 478 F.3d 452 (2d Cir. 2007), refined the application of the fair-and-equitable test in the specific context of settlements that distribute estate assets in a manner inconsistent with the absolute priority rule. The Iridium court held that, in evaluating whether a proposed settlement of avoidance claims may bypass the statutory priority scheme of the Bankruptcy Code, the bankruptcy court must consider:

Whether the settlement complies with the priority rules of the Bankruptcy Code

If not, whether a sufficient reason exists to deviate from those rules

Iridium signals a strong preference for settlements that distribute consideration in priority order. A settlement that pays unsecured creditors out of consideration that would otherwise reach administrative claimants, secured creditors, or priority claimants requires articulated justification. The Iridium standard is most often invoked in Chapter 11 cases where the proposed settlement is part of a plan or a structured dismissal.

Notice under Rule 2002(a)(3)

Rule 9019(a) requires notice "as provided in Rule 2002." Under Rule 2002(a)(3), the clerk or other person directed by the court shall give the debtor, the trustee, all creditors, and indenture trustees at least 21 days' notice by mail of the hearing on approval of a compromise or settlement, unless the court orders otherwise.

The notice must include:

The date, time, and place of the hearing

A summary of the proposed compromise or settlement sufficient to permit informed evaluation

The deadline for filing objections, if any is set

Identification of the claim or controversy being compromised

The consideration to be received by the estate, if any, and the consideration to be released or paid by the estate

A compromise approved without the notice required by Rule 2002(a)(3) is vulnerable to collateral attack and may be set aside if the failure to give notice prejudiced a party in interest. The 21-day notice requirement may be shortened by the court for cause, but the cause must be apparent on the record.

The Rule 9019(a) motion

The motion to approve a compromise or settlement typically includes:

A description of the underlying claim or controversy

A summary of the proposed compromise, including the consideration to be received by and paid by the estate

An analysis of each TMT Trailer factor applied to the specific controversy

A statement of the relationship of the settlement to the priority scheme of the Bankruptcy Code, where Iridium applies

Identification of the parties whose consent has been obtained and the parties from whom objections are anticipated

The proposed form of order

The settlement agreement itself is typically attached as an exhibit. A settlement that includes mutual releases, confidentiality provisions, or non-disparagement clauses must disclose those terms in the motion; the court is unlikely to approve undisclosed settlement terms.

Objections and the hearing

Any party in interest may object to a proposed compromise. The most common objectors are:

Unsecured creditors who believe the settlement undercompensates the estate for valuable claims

Secured creditors whose collateral is implicated by the settlement

The United States Trustee, where the settlement raises questions about administrative-claim treatment, fee structure, or compliance with the priority scheme

Other holders of estate claims that may be affected by the proposed release

The objector bears the burden of identifying specific deficiencies in the settlement under the TMT Trailer factors. A general objection that "the estate could do better" without identifying the basis for that belief is unlikely to succeed. The proponent of the settlement carries the ultimate burden of demonstrating that the compromise is fair and equitable and in the best interests of the estate.

Common settlement contexts

Avoidance action settlements

The trustee compromises a preference or fraudulent transfer action against a creditor for a percentage of the alleged transfer amount. The court evaluates the probability of success on the merits of the avoidance theory, the defendant's defenses (ordinary course, new value, contemporaneous exchange), the cost of trial, and collection risk.

Insurance coverage settlements

The estate settles with an insurer over coverage of a pre-petition mass-tort or environmental claim. The settlement typically includes a buyback of the policy. Notice must reach claimants whose recoveries depend on the policy proceeds; courts often require supplemental notice to such claimants under Rule 9019(a)'s "any other entity as the court may direct" clause.

Rule 9019(b) class compromises

Rule 9019(b) permits the court to authorize the trustee to settle controversies of a defined class - typically small-dollar preference claims, repetitive contract claims, or routine clean-up matters - without separate motion practice for each. The order authorizing class compromise establishes parameters (dollar thresholds, factual criteria, reporting requirements) within which the trustee may settle without further court approval. The trustee files periodic reports identifying the settlements made under the class authority.

Rule 9019(c) settlement conferences

Rule 9019(c) authorizes the court to direct the parties to participate in a settlement conference or other alternative dispute resolution proceeding. Many districts have implemented mediation programs by local rule that operate within the Rule 9019(c) framework. See the companion page on court-annexed bankruptcy mediation.

The "fair and equitable" standard requires informed judgment, not deference. The bankruptcy court must apprise itself of the facts and law; mere reliance on the trustee's recommendation is insufficient under TMT Trailer Ferry. The proponent of the settlement should expect the court to engage substantively with the TMT Trailer factors and, where applicable, the Iridium priority analysis.

Related rules and authority

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 2002 - Notice to creditors and other parties in interest

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 9014 - Contested matters (the procedural vehicle for most Rule 9019 motions)

Fed. R. Bankr. P. 7016 - Pretrial procedures, including settlement procedures, in adversary proceedings

Rule 9014 (Contested Matters) - Procedural framework for compromise motions

Bankruptcy Mediation - Court-annexed ADR under Rule 9019(c)
