Credit Bid Mechanics Under Section 363(k)

The secured creditor's right to credit bid; modification for cause; debt as bid currency; the RadLAX rule.

Home › Section 363 › Credit Bid Mechanics

What a Credit Bid Is

A credit bid is the secured creditor's right to offset its allowed secured claim against the purchase price at a Section 363 sale of its collateral. Instead of paying cash and then receiving cash back as distribution on its claim, the secured creditor simply tenders its debt — up to the full amount of the allowed claim — as currency for the asset. The mechanic is grounded in Section 363(k), one of the most consequential single sentences in Chapter 11 practice.

Statutory text — 11 U.S.C. § 363(k): "At a sale under subsection (b) of this section of property that is subject to a lien that secures an allowed claim, unless the court for cause orders otherwise the holder of such claim may bid at such sale, and, if the holder of such claim purchases such property, such holder may offset such claim against the purchase price of such property."

The text establishes three propositions: (1) the secured creditor has a presumptive right to bid; (2) the right may be denied only "for cause"; and (3) where the secured creditor is the successful bidder, it may offset its claim against the purchase price — the credit bid mechanic itself.

The Economic Logic

The credit-bid right exists because the secured creditor already owns the economic value of its collateral up to the amount of its allowed secured claim under Section 506(a). Requiring the creditor to bid cash and then receive cash distributions would impose a wasteful round-trip. More importantly, credit bidding protects the secured creditor against sale at a price that does not reflect the asset's intrinsic value. If the auction process produces a low cash bid, the secured creditor can take the asset itself rather than be cashed out at the depressed price.

This protection is what makes secured lending in distressed contexts viable. Without credit-bid rights, a debtor or junior stakeholder could orchestrate a sale at a fire-sale price, distribute the proceeds, and leave the secured creditor with a depressed recovery even though the underlying asset value supported a fuller payment. Credit bidding gives the secured creditor an inside option: accept the cash bid (and the implied valuation) or take the asset and find its own buyer at a price the creditor believes is fair.

The RadLAX Rule

The Supreme Court's 2012 decision in RadLAX Gateway Hotel, LLC v. Amalgamated Bank, 566 U.S. 639 (2012), resolved a circuit split over whether a Chapter 11 plan could be confirmed under the cramdown provisions of Section 1129(b)(2)(A)(iii) by selling the secured creditor's collateral free and clear of liens without permitting the secured creditor to credit bid. The Court held unanimously that it could not.

The Court reasoned that Section 1129(b)(2)(A) sets out three alternatives for cramming down a secured creditor: (i) leaving the lien in place and providing deferred cash payments with present value at least equal to the secured claim; (ii) selling the collateral free and clear with the lien attaching to the proceeds, subject to Section 363(k); or (iii) providing the "indubitable equivalent." The debtors in RadLAX attempted to use clause (iii) — the indubitable-equivalent route — to sell collateral without permitting credit bidding, on the theory that all-cash proceeds were the indubitable equivalent. The Court rejected this as an end-run around clause (ii)'s explicit cross-reference to Section 363(k).

The doctrinal holding: When a Chapter 11 plan proposes to sell encumbered collateral free and clear of the secured creditor's lien, the plan must permit the secured creditor to credit bid under Section 363(k). The "indubitable equivalent" alternative cannot be used to circumvent this requirement. RadLAX establishes that the credit-bid right is a structural feature of secured-creditor protection that cannot be drafted around in plan formulation.

Modification "For Cause"

Section 363(k)'s "unless the court for cause orders otherwise" clause permits modification or denial of credit-bid rights in appropriate cases. Courts have identified a non-exhaustive list of circumstances in which "cause" may exist:

Disputed claim or lien validity: Where the secured creditor's claim or lien is in bona fide dispute and a credit bid would prejudice the estate by foreclosing resolution of the dispute.

Chilling effect on the auction: Where the credit-bid right would deter other bidders from participating, depressing the price the estate ultimately realizes.

Inequitable conduct: Where the secured creditor has engaged in conduct that would warrant equitable subordination or other relief.

Strategic acquisition for non-bona-fide purpose: Where the credit bid is being used to acquire collateral for an improper purpose unrelated to maximizing recovery on the secured claim.

Lender-debtor misconduct: Where the secured creditor has acted in concert with insiders to undermine the sale process.

The leading articulation of the chilling-effect rationale appears in In re Fisker Automotive Holdings, Inc., 510 B.R. 55 (Bankr. D. Del. 2014), where the court capped the secured creditor's credit-bid right at the price the creditor had paid for the underlying debt — finding that an uncapped credit bid would chill the auction and frustrate the sale process. The decision remains controversial but is widely cited in cause-based modification disputes.

The burden of proof: Cause to deny or modify credit-bid rights is on the party seeking modification. The default under Section 363(k) is that credit bidding is permitted; the proponent of modification must establish cause by competent evidence, not mere conjecture about possible chilling effects.

Mechanics of Tendering a Credit Bid

Court-approved bidding procedures typically address credit-bid mechanics explicitly. Standard provisions include:

Bid increment treatment: Whether the secured creditor is required to credit bid only in cash-equivalent overbid increments, or whether the credit bid can be matched cent-for-cent against a cash overbid.

Cash component for non-collateral assets: Where the sale includes both collateral and non-collateral assets, the secured creditor is generally required to bid cash for the value attributable to non-collateral assets.

Cash component for administrative claims: Many sale orders require the secured creditor to fund administrative claims, cure costs for assumed contracts, and other estate expenses in cash, regardless of credit-bid rights against the asset value.

Allocation of credit bid against multiple assets: In multi-asset sales, the secured creditor's credit bid may be allocated among the assets, with overbids permitted on individual lots.

Stalking horse credit bids: Secured creditors increasingly serve as stalking-horse bidders with credit-bid components, entitled to a break-up fee if outbid in cash.

The Allowed-Claim Limitation

Section 363(k) speaks of "an allowed claim." Where the allowance of the underlying secured claim is disputed — whether on validity, priority, extent, or amount — a credit bid cannot exceed the amount of the claim ultimately allowed. Practitioners often address this by requiring the credit bidder to post a cash reserve in the amount of the disputed portion, or by structuring the bid as contingent on subsequent allowance.

The allowed-claim limitation also caps the credit bid at the allowed secured amount under Section 506(a). A claim that is undersecured produces a bifurcated treatment: the secured portion may be credit-bid; the unsecured deficiency portion cannot. In single-asset cases, this distinction usually does not matter (because the asset value sets the secured amount), but in multi-asset sales the allocation is consequential.

Related Provisions and Deep Dives

Section 506 — secured status and valuation, which determines credit-bid cap.

Free-and-Clear Sales Under Section 363(f)

The five alternative bases for clearing liens and competing interests; lienholder consent; post-sale attachment of liens to proceeds.

Home › Section 363 › Free-and-Clear Sales

The Power to Sell Free and Clear

Section 363(f) is the engine that makes 363 sales valuable to purchasers. Outside bankruptcy, a buyer of distressed assets inherits every recorded lien, mortgage, judgment, mechanic's claim, and adverse interest of record — and faces the risk of unrecorded claims surfacing post-closing. Section 363(f) authorizes the trustee or debtor in possession to sell estate property free and clear of any interest in such property of an entity other than the estate, provided one of five disjunctive conditions is satisfied.

Statutory text — 11 U.S.C. § 363(f): "The trustee may sell property under subsection (b) or (c) of this section free and clear of any interest in such property of an entity other than the estate, only if — (1) applicable nonbankruptcy law permits sale of such property free and clear of such interest; (2) such entity consents; (3) such interest is a lien and the price at which such property is to be sold is greater than the aggregate value of all liens on such property; (4) such interest is in bona fide dispute; or (5) such entity could be compelled, in a legal or equitable proceeding, to accept a money satisfaction of such interest."

The conditions are alternatives, not cumulative. Satisfying any one of the five subsections is sufficient. This pleading flexibility is what allows 363(f) to clear title across virtually every distressed-asset transaction, no matter how complicated the lien stack.

Subsection (f)(1) — Applicable Nonbankruptcy Law

The first basis permits a free-and-clear sale where applicable nonbankruptcy law would itself authorize sale free of the interest. Examples include sales under state foreclosure statutes that strip junior liens, tax sales that extinguish other claims under state law, and Article 9 dispositions of personal-property collateral after notice. In practice (f)(1) is invoked less frequently than the other subsections because the trustee usually has more efficient alternatives within bankruptcy itself.

Subsection (f)(2) — Lienholder Consent

The second basis is consent. If the holder of the interest consents to the sale free of its interest, the court may approve. Consent is the most common path in negotiated sales: the secured creditor with the largest economic stake typically negotiates the terms of its consent — including the price floor, distribution waterfall, expense allocations, and release language — well before the sale motion is filed.

The "Deemed Consent" Doctrine

Many courts have held that a lienholder's failure to object after proper notice of a 363(f) sale constitutes implied consent under (f)(2). This is not universal — some courts require affirmative consent and reject the deemed-consent theory — but the majority view is that silence in the face of a clear notice satisfies the statute. Practitioners drafting sale notices should highlight the free-and-clear request prominently and identify (f)(2) deemed consent as a basis being relied on, so as to maximize the deemed-consent argument later.

Practice point: The deemed-consent doctrine puts the burden squarely on lienholders. A creditor that does not object before the objection deadline may find itself bound by the free-and-clear order even if it never affirmatively agreed. Court-approved bidding procedures often include an express finding that non-objecting lienholders are deemed to have consented.

Subsection (f)(3) — Price Exceeds Aggregate Lien Value

The third basis authorizes a free-and-clear sale where the sale price is greater than the aggregate value of all liens on the property. The aggregate-value question has produced a substantial split among bankruptcy courts. The majority view interprets "aggregate value" as the face amount of allowed secured claims — meaning a sale must exceed the total dollar value of all liens to satisfy (f)(3). The minority view interprets the phrase to mean the economic value of the liens, calculated under Section 506(a), which can be substantially less than the face amount when collateral is underwater.

Under the strict majority view, (f)(3) is rarely available in distressed sales — almost by definition, a distressed asset is selling below the aggregate face amount of liens encumbering it. The economic-value reading expands (f)(3)'s utility but is rejected by influential courts. Practitioners typically plead (f)(3) in the alternative alongside (f)(2) or (f)(5) rather than relying on it as the principal basis.

Subsection (f)(4) — Bona Fide Dispute

The fourth basis applies where the interest is in bona fide dispute. The bona-fide-dispute standard is met where there is an objective basis for either a factual or a legal dispute as to the validity of the asserted interest. The court need not resolve the dispute — only determine that one genuinely exists. The disputed interest does not vanish; it attaches to the sale proceeds and is resolved later, either by stipulation or by an adversary proceeding to determine the validity, priority, or extent of the lien under Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 7001(2).

(f)(4) is particularly useful for sales where mechanic's liens, judgment liens of uncertain validity, or contested security interests cloud title. Rather than litigating the validity of each disputed interest before closing — which would destroy the sale's economic value — the court can authorize the sale free of the disputed interests with the proceeds held in escrow.

Subsection (f)(5) — Compellable Money Satisfaction

The fifth basis applies where the interest holder could be compelled, in a legal or equitable proceeding, to accept a money satisfaction of the interest. This catch-all has become one of the most heavily-litigated provisions in 363(f) practice, particularly in the context of nondebtor third-party interests such as long-term leases, easements, covenants running with the land, successor-liability claims, and unexpired contracts.

The "Money Satisfaction" Question

Courts have divided on whether (f)(5) requires that the claimant could be compelled to accept a money satisfaction in lieu of its full interest (the broad view) or whether the claimant must be compellable to accept money satisfaction under existing nonbankruptcy law (the narrow view). The broad view treats (f)(5) as a flexible equitable mechanism; the narrow view limits it to interests already subject to monetization remedies such as foreclosure or condemnation. The majority of circuits now require some existing legal or equitable mechanism — the bankruptcy court's general equitable powers alone are insufficient.

Strategic use of (f)(5): Where the interest is a lien that could be satisfied through judicial foreclosure (legal proceeding) or specific performance damages (equitable proceeding), (f)(5) is usually available. Where the interest is a covenant, easement, or property-law servitude that nonbankruptcy law does not authorize to be extinguished by money payment, (f)(5) is contested.

Attachment of Liens to Proceeds

Section 363(f) extinguishes the lien against the sold property, but it does not extinguish the underlying claim. Under longstanding bankruptcy doctrine, liens that are stripped from property by a 363(f) sale attach to the sale proceeds with the same priority, validity, and extent as they had against the original property. The proceeds substitute for the collateral. Sale orders typically include express findings to this effect, often coupled with directions on segregation, escrow, and distribution.

For purchasers, this means clean title at closing. For secured creditors, it means the loss of in rem rights against the specific asset but preservation of priority in the cash proceeds — subject to adequate protection and any further litigation over priority, validity, or extent.

What Section 363(f) Does Not Reach

Several categories of interests sit at the contested edge of (f)'s reach:

Successor liability: Whether 363(f) can extinguish successor-liability claims — particularly tort claims by future or unknown claimants — has produced significant circuit-level litigation, with influential decisions taking restrictive views.

Collective bargaining agreements: Section 1113 procedures govern rejection of CBAs in Chapter 11; the interplay between 1113 and 363(f) is complex and disputed.

Environmental liabilities: CERCLA and state-law environmental claims of regulatory authorities are often held to be outside the reach of 363(f).

In personam claims: 363(f) addresses interests in property; pure in personam claims against the debtor are addressed through plan discharge under Section 1141, not through sale orders.

Stalking Horse and Auction Procedure

Stalking horse selection, break-up fees, expense reimbursement, overbid increments, and court-approved bidding procedures.

Home › Section 363 › Stalking Horse and Auction Procedure

The Stalking Horse Concept

A stalking horse bidder is a pre-selected purchaser whose offer becomes the floor for a Section 363 auction. The stalking horse signs a definitive asset purchase agreement (APA) before the auction, agreeing to consummate the transaction at a stated price and on stated terms unless a higher and better offer emerges. The stalking horse arrangement gives the estate three benefits: a guaranteed minimum sale price, a fully-negotiated set of transaction terms that other bidders must match or improve, and a measurable benchmark against which competing offers can be evaluated.

For the stalking horse, the trade-off is asymmetric. The stalking horse commits to a transaction, incurs diligence and negotiation costs, and exposes its valuation thinking to the market — only to risk being outbid by a competitor who free-rides on the floor it has established. The compensating benefits the stalking horse typically negotiates are commonly known as bid protections.

Break-Up Fees

A break-up fee is a cash payment to the stalking horse if the debtor consummates an alternative transaction with a different buyer. The fee compensates the stalking horse for the time, expense, and opportunity cost of serving as the floor-setter. Break-up fees are paid from the proceeds of the alternative transaction, typically as a closing-mechanics expense.

Courts in the Third Circuit historically applied the O'Brien standard from Calpine Corp. v. O'Brien Environmental Energy, Inc. (In re O'Brien Environmental Energy, Inc.), 181 F.3d 527 (3d Cir. 1999), which requires the proponent to demonstrate that the break-up fee is "actually necessary to preserve the value of the estate." Other circuits apply a more lenient business-judgment review focused on whether the fee induced participation that would not otherwise have occurred.

Typical Range

Break-up fees commonly fall in the range of 1% to 3% of the purchase price, though distressed sales of difficult-to-value or specialized assets sometimes warrant higher fees. Courts often scrutinize fees above 3% closely; fees above 5% face significant approval risk in most jurisdictions.

Practice point: The break-up fee is generally an administrative expense of the estate and paid at closing of the alternative transaction. Where the stalking horse arrangement collapses without an alternative transaction (e.g., the case converts to Chapter 7), recovery of the break-up fee depends on the specific terms of the bidding procedures order.

Expense Reimbursement

In addition to or in lieu of a break-up fee, the stalking horse often negotiates reimbursement of out-of-pocket expenses incurred in connection with the transaction. Reimbursable expenses typically include legal fees, financial-advisor fees, diligence costs, environmental consultants, and travel expenses. Expense reimbursement is usually capped at a stated dollar amount.

Courts approve expense reimbursement on a similar standard to break-up fees: necessary to induce participation, reasonable in amount, and not so generous as to chill competing bids. The combination of break-up fee plus expense reimbursement is generally evaluated as a single package against the overall purchase price and the estate's interest in maximizing recovery.

Overbid Increments

Bidding procedures typically specify the minimum overbid required to start the auction and the minimum subsequent overbid increment. The initial overbid is usually structured to exceed the stalking horse bid by an amount at least equal to the break-up fee plus expense reimbursement, plus a stated minimum incremental amount. The logic: any competing bid must beat the stalking horse on a net basis after accounting for the bid protections the estate must pay.

Sample Overbid Construction

Stalking horse bid: $50,000,000 cash purchase price.

Break-up fee: $1,500,000 (3% of purchase price).

Expense reimbursement cap: $500,000.

Minimum initial overbid: $52,250,000 ($50M + $1.5M + $500K + $250K incremental).

Subsequent bid increments: $250,000.

This construction ensures the estate is no worse off accepting an overbid than accepting the stalking horse bid. The exact incremental structure varies; some sales use percentage-based increments rather than fixed dollar amounts, and some allow flexibility for the debtor's financial advisor to negotiate down increments in the auction room to encourage bidding.

Court-Approved Bidding Procedures

Bidding procedures must be approved by the court before the auction is held. The motion to approve bidding procedures is typically filed near the start of the case (or shortly after the stalking horse APA is signed) and addresses topics including:

Qualification requirements for competing bidders (financial wherewithal, good-faith deposit, executed-APA submission deadline).

Bid deposit requirements (typically 10% of the purchase price, held in escrow).

The deadline for submitting qualifying competing bids.

The auction date, time, and location (often the debtor's counsel's offices).

Auction procedures, including round structure, time limits per round, and minimum overbid increments.

Bid evaluation criteria, including credit-bid treatment and valuation of non-cash consideration.

Designation of the successful bidder and back-up bidder.

The sale hearing date and notice requirements.

Bid protections for the stalking horse (break-up fee, expense reimbursement).

Court oversight: The bidding procedures order is the procedural backbone of the sale. Once entered, parties' rights and obligations are largely fixed: bidders know the rules, the stalking horse knows its protections, and the estate knows the schedule. Mid-process changes require court approval and create appellate risk.

The Auction

Most Chapter 11 363 auctions are conducted in person, with bidders, their counsel, financial advisors, the debtor, the creditors' committee, the secured-lender group, and the U.S. Trustee in attendance. The debtor (typically through its investment banker) acts as auctioneer. Each round invites the qualified bidders to improve their bids by at least the minimum overbid increment; rounds continue until no qualified bidder is willing to improve.

The debtor designates the highest and best bid as the successful bid and the next-highest bid as the back-up bid. Both are presented to the court at the sale hearing. If the successful bidder fails to close, the back-up bid becomes the deal — without the need for a second auction — though typically the back-up obligation has a sunset date (often 30 to 60 days after the sale hearing).

Special Topics

"Highest and Best" vs "Highest"

Bidding procedures and sale orders consistently use the phrase "highest and best" rather than simply "highest." The distinction allows the debtor to consider qualitative factors — certainty of closing, regulatory approval risk, employee-retention commitments, financing contingencies — in addition to nominal price. A nominally-lower bid with cleaner closing conditions can be selected over a nominally-higher bid with significant execution risk.

Naked No-Shop and Match-Right Provisions

Stalking horse APAs sometimes include provisions that prevent the debtor from soliciting alternative bids ("no-shops") or that give the stalking horse the right to match any superior proposal. Both are scrutinized in bankruptcy: a strict no-shop is generally incompatible with the estate's fiduciary duty to maximize value, and a match right that chills bidding may be denied or modified. Most modern stalking horse APAs include a fiduciary-out and limit match rights to a single matching round.

Post-Petition Operating Capital

Section 364 DIP Financing

Section 364 authorizes the trustee or debtor-in-possession to obtain credit post-petition. The escalating subsections create a four-rung ladder, from unsecured ordinary-course trade credit at the bottom to senior priming liens at the top. These five deep-dives explain each rung and the inter-creditor mechanics that make DIP financing the single most consequential motion in many chapter 11 cases.

Last modified 2026-05-22.

Home/Section 364 DIP Financing

About section 364

Section 364 is built as a hierarchy of escalating remedies. Section 364(a) authorizes ordinary-course unsecured credit without court approval. Section 364(b) authorizes non-ordinary-course unsecured credit on notice and a hearing. Section 364(c) authorizes credit secured by liens on unencumbered property, junior liens on encumbered property, or super-priority administrative-claim status under section 364(c)(1) - but only if the debtor cannot obtain unsecured credit under section 364(b). Section 364(d) authorizes priming liens - senior liens on already-encumbered property - but only if the holder of the primed lien receives adequate protection.

The procedural protection at each rung is the burden on the debtor to demonstrate that financing on more favorable terms was unavailable. In practice, this burden is met through a marketing affidavit from an investment banker or financial advisor describing the unsuccessful search for alternative financing. The court must also find that the credit is necessary to preserve the estate.

DIP financing motions typically arrive at the court on an emergency basis at the case-commencement first-day hearing, with interim approval of a portion of the financing followed by a final hearing within thirty days. The DIP credit agreement is frequently a complex multi-hundred-page document with covenants, milestones, fees, and remedies that effectively control the trajectory of the case. The associated cash-collateral order (governed by section 363(c)(2) and (e)) is usually negotiated and approved in tandem.

Section 364 deep-dives

DIP Financing Types OverviewThe four section 364 rungs (unsecured ordinary, unsecured non-ordinary, secured/super-priority, priming) and when each is used.

Priming LiensSection 364(d) priming, the adequate-protection requirement, the equity-cushion analysis, and the typical inter-creditor dynamics when an existing senior secured lender is primed.

Cross-CollateralizationThe controversial practice of granting pre-petition lender additional security as part of the DIP package; the Saybrook/Vanguard split; and the use of "roll-up" features to convert pre-petition exposure to post-petition status.

Administrative PrioritySection 364(c)(1) super-priority administrative claims, the section 507(b) adequate-protection super-priority, and the ranking of competing super-priority claims.

Financing HierarchyThe escalating-burden structure of section 364, the requirement to show alternative financing was unavailable, and the typical first-day/final hearing two-step approval process.

Practitioner note: The DIP order routinely contains "milestone" covenants tying continued financing to plan-filing, sale-closing, or confirmation deadlines. These milestones often become the de facto schedule of the case. Counsel for the creditors' committee should scrutinize milestone language at the interim hearing.

## Section 364(c) Administrative-Priority and Super-Priority Claims [2026]

11 U.S.C. Section 364(c) Administrative-Priority and Super-Priority

How Section 364(c) authorizes credit secured by super-priority administrative status, by liens on unencumbered property, and by junior liens on encumbered property — and how it connects with the ordinary administrative-expense regime of Section 503(b)(1).

Home › Statutes › Section 364 › Administrative-Priority

Empirical research on this section

For case-pattern analysis on how federal bankruptcy courts apply Section 364(c), including district-level patterns and primary-source dockets, see openbankruptcyproject.org/cases/. All datasets licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

From Ordinary Admin Expense to Section 364(c)(1) Super-Priority

Section 503(b)(1) creates the ordinary administrative-expense category that covers post-petition costs of preserving the estate, wages and benefits for post-petition services, and similar charges. Administrative expenses are entitled to first priority under Section 507(a)(2) and must be paid in full on the effective date of a confirmed Chapter 11 plan unless their holders agree to different treatment.

Official citation: 11 U.S.C. § 364(c)

For a small post-petition trade obligation, ordinary Section 503(b)(1) administrative status is usually sufficient. For a meaningful DIP loan, it is almost never enough. The lender wants assurance that even in a downside scenario (conversion to Chapter 7, attempted sale at a value insufficient to pay accrued professionals' fees and other administrative claims), the DIP loan will be paid first. Section 364(c)(1) is the mechanism that delivers that assurance.

Section 364(c)(1): Super-Priority Over All Other Admin Expenses

Section 364(c)(1) authorizes the court to approve credit "with priority over any or all administrative expenses of the kind specified in section 503(b) or 507(b) of this title." A claim granted Section 364(c)(1) priority sits above every other administrative expense, including:

Section 503(b)(1) post-petition operating costs and wages;

Section 503(b)(2) professional-fee awards for debtor and committee counsel and financial advisors;

Section 503(b)(3) and (4) substantial-contribution claims and their related fees;

Section 503(b)(9) twenty-day pre-petition goods claims;

Section 507(b) failed-adequate-protection claims arising from depletion of secured-creditor collateral.

The Section 364(c)(1) priority is itself junior, by statute and by negotiation, to any "carve-out" the DIP order may create. A typical carve-out reserves a defined dollar amount for accrued and unpaid professional fees and U.S. Trustee fees so that the estate can fund its own wind-down even in a default scenario. The size of the carve-out is one of the most heavily-negotiated terms in any DIP order.

Section 364(c)(2): Liens on Unencumbered Property

Section 364(c)(2) authorizes a lien on property of the estate that is not otherwise subject to a lien. This is the standard mechanism for granting the DIP lender a first-priority lien on previously unencumbered assets: free-and-clear accounts receivable, free-and-clear intellectual property, cash and deposit accounts not subject to pre-petition liens, equity interests in non-debtor subsidiaries (subject to applicable restrictions), and similar property. Because no existing lienholder is being displaced, Section 364(c)(2) does not require adequate protection.

Section 364(c)(3): Junior Liens on Encumbered Property

Section 364(c)(3) authorizes a junior lien on property of the estate that is already subject to a lien. This option is used when the debtor's collateral pool is largely encumbered and there is no unencumbered property of meaningful value. The DIP lender takes a second-out or third-out position behind the existing secured creditors and is repaid only after the senior liens are satisfied. Because the existing lienholder's position is unchanged, Section 364(c)(3) does not require adequate protection.

In practice, Section 364(c)(3) is the least common of the three Section 364(c) tiers because the economics are usually unattractive: a lender that is willing to take a junior lien on encumbered property is often also willing to take a Section 364(c)(1) super-priority claim, and the combination of both is the standard structure of a modern DIP facility.

The Threshold Showing: "Unable to Obtain Credit Otherwise"

Section 364(c) is unavailable unless the trustee is "unable to obtain unsecured credit allowable under Section 503(b)(1)." Courts have construed this requirement flexibly: the debtor does not need to canvass the entire credit market exhaustively but must demonstrate a good-faith effort to obtain less-aggressive financing and a credible explanation of why such financing is not available on commercially reasonable terms. A typical first-day declaration from the debtor's chief financial officer or investment banker recites the financing efforts undertaken, the responses received, and the reasons why a Section 364(a) or (b) facility is not feasible.

The threshold showing is generally easier to make in cases where the debtor's principal pre-petition secured lender is the only realistic source of DIP financing, because pre-petition lenders typically condition any DIP facility on Section 364(c) and (d) protections that no third-party lender would forgo.

Section 364(e): Good-Faith Lender Protection

Section 364(e) is the doctrinal back-stop that gives DIP lenders confidence in court-approved priority and lien grants. It provides that the reversal or modification on appeal of an authorization to obtain credit or incur debt, or of a grant of priority or a lien, does not affect the validity of any debt incurred or any priority or lien granted, to an entity that extended credit in good faith. The lender's good-faith reliance on the bankruptcy court order is protected even if the order is later vacated, provided the appeal was not stayed pending review.

Section 364(e) is the reason that interim DIP orders are functionally final: a party objecting to a DIP order generally must obtain a stay pending appeal to preserve any meaningful appellate remedy. Without a stay, the lender will fund the loan and acquire valid liens and priority that cannot be undone by appellate reversal.

Risks to Section 364(c)(1) Priority: Section 507(b) and the Carve-Out

Two principal risks dilute Section 364(c)(1) super-priority. First, Section 507(b) creates a competing super-priority for adequate-protection failures by secured creditors who consented to use of cash collateral or were primed under Section 364(d). The DIP order must specify the relative priority of the Section 364(c)(1) claim and any Section 507(b) claim; many orders rank the DIP super-priority above 507(b), but careful drafting and disclosure are required.

Second, the carve-out for professional fees and U.S. Trustee fees creates an explicit, statutorily-permitted senior claim against the DIP-lender collateral and super-priority. The carve-out is often structured as a "trigger" amount (unlimited fees accrued and unpaid before a default notice, plus a capped amount after the trigger). The interplay between the trigger, the funding mechanism, and the success-fee provisions of professional retention orders is a frequent source of post-effective-date disputes and should be negotiated with care at the DIP-approval stage.

Related Bankruptcy Code Sections

Section 507(a)(2) and (b) — administrative priority and adequate-protection failure

Section 361 — adequate-protection forms

Cross-Collateralization in DIP Financing — Saybrook and the Circuit Split

When a DIP lender's pre-petition unsecured exposure piggybacks on the post-petition financing collateral: the Eleventh Circuit per se ban, the case-by-case balancing test, and the Second Circuit's interim-relief constraint.

Home › Statutes › Section 364 › Cross-Collateralization

Empirical research on this section

For case-pattern analysis on how federal bankruptcy courts treat cross-collateralization provisions, including district-level patterns and primary-source dockets, see openbankruptcyproject.org/cases/. All datasets licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

What Is Cross-Collateralization?

Cross-collateralization in DIP financing refers to a provision in the post-petition loan documents that grants the DIP lender liens on the debtor's property to secure not only the new post-petition advances but also the lender's pre-petition claim against the debtor. In its most aggressive form, sometimes called "Texlon-style" cross-collateralization, the pre-petition portion of the lender's exposure is given a lien (or an upgraded lien) on collateral that would otherwise have been available to the general unsecured creditor body.

Underlying provision: 11 U.S.C. § 364(c), (d)

The practical effect is that the DIP lender exits bankruptcy with an enhanced pre-petition position relative to what it had on the petition date, paid for by the bankruptcy estate. The lender argues that this is the price of extending new credit to a distressed borrower. Other constituencies argue that this is exactly the kind of preference-style elevation of one pre-petition unsecured claim over equally-situated others that the Code is designed to prevent.

The Eleventh Circuit Per Se Ban: In re Saybrook Manufacturing Co.

In In re Saybrook Manufacturing Co., 963 F.2d 1490 (11th Cir. 1992), the Eleventh Circuit held that cross-collateralization is per se impermissible under Section 364. The court reasoned that Section 364 authorizes the use of collateral to secure post-petition credit, not to secure pre-petition claims. Allowing a DIP lender to leverage post-petition collateral for the benefit of its pre-petition exposure improperly elevates one unsecured creditor ahead of others outside the strictures of Section 507's priority scheme and the Chapter 11 plan-confirmation process.

The Eleventh Circuit acknowledged that some courts had previously approved cross-collateralization under their general equitable powers, but rejected that rationale, holding that Section 364's specific provisions on post-petition financing displaced any general equitable authority that might otherwise support the practice. The opinion treated cross-collateralization as a form of improper preference and refused to find authority for it anywhere in the Code.

The Pre-Saybrook Balancing Approach

Before Saybrook, several courts had approved cross-collateralization under a multi-factor test sometimes traced to the bankruptcy court opinion in In re Vanguard Diversified, Inc., 31 B.R. 364 (Bankr. E.D.N.Y. 1983), and elaborated in subsequent decisions. The factors typically included:

Whether absent the proposed financing the debtor's business would not survive;

Whether the debtor is unable to obtain alternative financing on acceptable terms;

Whether the proposed lender will not accept less preferential terms;

Whether the proposed financing is in the best interest of the estate.

Some courts continue to apply versions of this balancing test outside the Eleventh Circuit, particularly where the cross-collateralization is bounded in scope (for example, limited to the existing under-secured portion of the pre-petition claim), where the DIP loan delivers substantial new value, and where the official unsecured creditors' committee has affirmatively consented. The legality of cross-collateralization is therefore genuinely jurisdiction-dependent.

The Texlon Constraint on Interim Cross-Collateralization

The Second Circuit's earlier decision in In re Texlon Corp., 596 F.2d 1092 (2d Cir. 1979), is the foundational case on cross-collateralization. Texlon did not impose a per se rule, but it sharply criticized the entry of a cross-collateralization order ex parte and without adequate notice or a contested hearing. The case is frequently cited for the proposition that cross-collateralization, if it is to be approved at all, may not be approved at the first-day interim hearing and must instead await a final hearing with full notice to the creditor body.

This is the source of the standard practice that "first-day" interim DIP orders do not grant cross-collateralization or roll-up relief; those features are deferred to the final order. Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 4001(c)(1)(B) reinforces the constraint by requiring that motions to obtain credit specifically identify any cross-collateralization provision and that interim relief be limited to what is necessary to avoid immediate and irreparable harm.

Roll-Ups as Functional Cross-Collateralization

A modern "roll-up" structure achieves much of the same economic result as cross-collateralization without facing the formal Saybrook prohibition. In a roll-up, the new DIP advances are used (in whole or part) to pay down the lender's pre-petition exposure dollar-for-dollar, after which the previously-pre-petition exposure has been converted into a Section 364 post-petition secured claim. Roll-ups have been approved in many jurisdictions, including some within the Eleventh Circuit, where the new-money component is significant relative to the rolled-up amount and where other creditor constituencies have consented or received adequate concessions.

The distinction between cross-collateralization and a roll-up is one of mechanics rather than economics, and several commentators have noted that the doctrinal gap is increasingly artificial. Courts and creditor committees scrutinize roll-ups for many of the same concerns that animate the cross-collateralization doctrine: disparate treatment of similarly-situated unsecured creditors, foreclosure of plan-confirmation oversight, and entrenchment of the DIP lender as the only viable buyer at any subsequent sale.

Practical Posture: Disclosure and Objection

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 4001(c)(1)(B) requires motions to obtain credit to specifically identify cross-collateralization provisions, roll-ups, Section 506(c) waivers, liens on avoidance actions, and other "extraordinary" provisions. The United States Trustee Program's guidelines for DIP-financing motions list these provisions as items meriting heightened review. An official committee of unsecured creditors, where appointed, will routinely negotiate carve-outs, investigation budgets, and challenge periods to mitigate the impact of cross-collateralization or roll-up relief.

In jurisdictions following Saybrook, the answer to a cross-collateralization request is straightforward: the court will not approve it. In other jurisdictions, the practical question becomes whether the financing is sufficiently necessary, the new money sufficiently substantial, and the creditor-body concessions sufficiently meaningful to justify the deviation from ordinary unsecured-creditor parity.

11 U.S.C. Section 364 Financing Hierarchy and Approval Procedure

The Section 364(b)/(c)/(d) ladder of escalation, Rule 4001(c) notice and disclosure requirements, the interim/final two-step, and the standard components of a contemporary DIP financing order.

Home › Statutes › Section 364 › Hierarchy and Approval Procedure

Empirical research on this section

For case-pattern analysis on Section 364 hierarchy and DIP-order patterns, including district-level practices and primary-source dockets, see openbankruptcyproject.org/cases/. All datasets licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

The Statutory Ladder of Escalation

Section 364 is structured as a ladder. Each rung represents a stronger lender protection — and, correspondingly, a greater level of court scrutiny and procedural protection for other creditors. A debtor must show that the rung below is genuinely unavailable before climbing higher. The four-rung framework is:

Official citation: 11 U.S.C. § 364

Section 364(a) — Ordinary-course unsecured credit. No motion, no hearing.

Section 364(b) — Non-ordinary-course unsecured credit. Notice and a hearing; result is Section 503(b)(1) administrative claim.

Section 364(c) — Super-priority claim, lien on unencumbered property, or junior lien on encumbered property. Notice and a hearing; debtor must show inability to obtain Section 503(b)(1)-level credit.

Section 364(d) — Senior or equal (priming) lien on already-encumbered property. Notice and a hearing; debtor must show inability to obtain credit otherwise and adequate protection of the existing lienholder.

Each successive rung incorporates the protections of the rung below and adds new ones. A modern DIP order routinely invokes multiple rungs of the ladder simultaneously: liens on unencumbered property under Section 364(c)(2), junior liens on already-encumbered property under Section 364(c)(3), super-priority administrative claims under Section 364(c)(1), and priming liens on selected categories of collateral under Section 364(d).

Rule 4001(c): Notice and Disclosure

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 4001(c) governs motions to obtain credit. The rule requires:

Service: Service on the United States Trustee, any committee elected under Section 705 or appointed under Section 1102, the twenty largest unsecured creditors if no committee has been appointed, and any other party the court directs.

Concise statement: The motion must contain a concise statement of the relief requested, with the proposed form of order attached.

Disclosure of significant provisions: The motion must specifically identify any provision of the type listed in Rule 4001(c)(1)(B), including: grant of priority or a lien on property of the estate under Section 364(c) or (d); adequate-protection or priority of pre-petition claims; determination of validity, enforceability, priority, or amount of a pre-petition claim or lien; waiver or modification of the automatic stay; waiver or modification of any entity's authority to file a plan, seek extensions of exclusivity, or request use of cash collateral; establishment of deadlines for filing a plan of reorganization or for confirmation; waiver or modification of the applicability of nonbankruptcy law relating to perfection of liens; release, waiver, or limitation of any claim or right against any entity; indemnification of any entity; release, waiver, or limitation of any right under Section 506(c); grant of a lien on any claim or cause of action arising under Sections 544-553; and cross-collateralization.

Final hearing: A final hearing may not be commenced earlier than 14 days after service of the motion.

Interim relief: The court may conduct a preliminary hearing before the 14-day period expires, but may only authorize the obtaining of credit to the extent necessary to avoid immediate and irreparable harm to the estate.

The Interim/Final Two-Step

Nearly every meaningfully-sized DIP facility is approved through a two-step process. On or shortly after the petition date, the debtor files a motion for entry of an interim order and a final order. The interim order, entered at a first-day hearing typically held within one to four business days of the petition, authorizes a limited tranche of borrowing (the amount necessary to fund operations until the final hearing) and grants the interim liens and priority on a limited basis. The final order, entered after the 14-day notice period and a contested final hearing, authorizes the full facility, including any extraordinary provisions deferred from the interim stage.

The interim period is critical for committee formation and creditor diligence. The official committee of unsecured creditors, if appointed, will use the interim period to investigate the proposed financing, negotiate carve-outs, investigation budgets, and challenge periods, and prepare any objections to the final order. The interim/final cadence is the principal mechanism by which Rule 4001(c)'s notice-and-disclosure protections are operationalized.

Standard Components of a Final DIP Order

A typical modern final DIP order runs many pages and contains a recurring set of provisions. The components below are not exhaustive but represent the standard taxonomy:

Findings of fact: Good faith of the lender (for Section 364(e) protection), the debtor's inability to obtain alternative financing, the necessity of the financing to avoid immediate and irreparable harm and (in due course) to maximize the value of the estate.

Authorization: The debtor is authorized to borrow up to the committed amount and to execute the DIP loan documents.

Liens and priorities: Specific Section 364(c)(1), 364(c)(2), 364(c)(3), and (where applicable) 364(d) grants, with descriptions of the affected collateral and the rank of the resulting liens.

Adequate protection for primed lenders: Replacement liens, Section 507(b) super-priority, periodic cash payments, and reporting rights for any existing lienholder being primed under Section 364(d) or whose cash collateral is being used.

Budget and variance covenants: The approved budget that governs use of the DIP proceeds, the permitted variance, and the rights of the lender if variances are exceeded.

Carve-out: The reservation of a portion of the DIP collateral and proceeds for accrued and unpaid professional fees, U.S. Trustee fees, and (sometimes) wind-down expenses, with specified pre- and post-default caps.

Milestones: Sale, plan, or restructuring milestones tied to the case timeline; default upon missed milestone.

Stipulations and challenge period: Stipulations as to the validity, priority, and amount of the lender's pre-petition claims and liens, subject to a defined challenge period (typically 60-75 days) during which the committee or other parties may bring adversary proceedings to challenge.

Section 506(c) and 552(b) waivers: Waiver of the estate's surcharge rights under Section 506(c) and of the equities-of-the-case exception under Section 552(b), subject to Rule 4001(c) disclosure.

Investigation budget: A small carve-out (often $25,000 to $250,000) available to the committee for investigation of pre-petition lender claims.

Events of default and remedies: A defined cure period for non-payment defaults, notice obligations to the U.S. Trustee and committee before exercising remedies, and the lender's rights upon a continuing default.

Section 364(e) good-faith finding: An express finding that the lender extended credit in good faith and is entitled to the protections of Section 364(e).

U.S. Trustee Guidelines and Local Practice

The United States Trustee Program has published guidelines for DIP-financing motions that flag specific provisions as warranting heightened review, including roll-ups, cross-collateralization, milestones perceived as overly aggressive, and short challenge periods. Many districts have local rules or general orders that supplement Rule 4001(c) with district-specific disclosure requirements (for example, a standard form of side-by-side comparison of "extraordinary" DIP provisions). Practitioners should consult both the U.S. Trustee guidelines and applicable local rules in any new district to ensure that the disclosure requirements are satisfied.

Related Bankruptcy Code Sections

Section 102 — "after notice and a hearing" defined

Section 105 — general equitable powers

Section 506(c) — surcharge against collateral

Section 552(b) — equities-of-the-case exception

Priming Liens under 11 U.S.C. Section 364(d) and Adequate Protection

When a DIP lender can leapfrog an existing secured creditor: the consent path, the contested adequate-protection path, and the Section 361 menu of protections the existing lienholder must receive.

Home › Statutes › Section 364 › Priming Liens

Empirical research on this section

For case-pattern analysis on how federal bankruptcy courts apply Section 364(d), including district-level patterns and primary-source dockets, see openbankruptcyproject.org/cases/. All datasets licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

What Is a Priming Lien?

A priming lien is a lien granted to a post-petition DIP lender that ranks senior to, or pari passu with, an already-existing lien on the same collateral. The new lender "primes" the existing secured creditor: when the collateral is later sold or liquidated, the DIP lender is paid first, even though the existing lien predates the DIP loan. In a sense, priming reorders the secured creditor waterfall by judicial decree rather than by consensual intercreditor agreement.

Official citation: 11 U.S.C. § 364(d)

Because priming radically alters the property rights of the existing lienholder, Section 364(d) is hedged with two threshold requirements. The court may approve priming credit only if (i) the trustee is unable to obtain such credit otherwise and (ii) there is adequate protection of the interest of the holder of the lien on the property on which the senior or equal lien is proposed to be granted.

The Two Paths: Consent or Adequate Protection

In practice, priming-lien approvals come in two flavors. The far more common is the consensual priming, where the existing lienholder agrees to subordinate its position in exchange for negotiated concessions. Consent is often documented in the DIP order itself and is sometimes purchased through a paydown of the existing facility, a roll-up of the existing facility into the new DIP, expansion of the existing lender's collateral pool, or other intercreditor accommodations.

The contested path is the non-consensual priming under Section 364(d). Here the debtor must affirmatively prove, by a preponderance of the evidence, both the inability-to-obtain-otherwise prong and the adequate-protection prong. The burden of proof on adequate protection is on the debtor under Section 364(d)(2). Contested primings are rare but consequential: a wrongly-decided priming can wipe out millions of dollars of secured value with no recourse for the displaced lienholder.

The Inability-to-Obtain-Otherwise Prong

The debtor must show that less aggressive financing is unavailable. Courts generally require evidence of a good-faith canvass of the financing market and proof that no lender will extend a Section 364(c) facility (junior liens, super-priority claim) on commercially reasonable terms. A single declined term sheet is not enough; courts typically expect multiple solicitations and a credible explanation of why each was unavailable or unsuitable. The standard does not require the debtor to find the worst possible terms before resorting to priming, but it does require a genuine inability to secure equivalent value through subordinated post-petition credit.

Section 361 Adequate Protection: The Three Statutory Forms

Section 361 sets the menu of adequate-protection devices. In a priming context, the same menu applies:

Section 361(1) — Cash payments: Periodic cash payments to the existing lienholder equal to the decrease in the value of its interest caused by the priming or by the use of collateral.

Section 361(2) — Additional or replacement liens: A lien on additional or replacement collateral sufficient to compensate for the decrease in value. In a typical priming order, the existing lienholder receives a replacement lien junior to the new DIP lien but senior to other estate property of equivalent value.

Section 361(3) — The "indubitable equivalent": Any other relief, other than an administrative-priority claim under Section 503(b)(1), that will result in the realization by the holder of the indubitable equivalent of its interest in the property.

Section 361 expressly forbids the use of a Section 503(b)(1) administrative priority as adequate protection. This is a recognition that an administrative claim against a fragile estate is no substitute for a recorded lien on identifiable collateral.

Equity Cushion as Adequate Protection

The most common adequate-protection theory in contested priming hearings is the equity cushion: if the collateral is worth materially more than the priming and existing debts combined, the existing lienholder is protected by the cushion of unencumbered value. Courts have generally accepted equity cushions in the range of 20 percent or more as sufficient adequate protection, with cushions below 10 percent generally inadequate and the intermediate band requiring a fact-intensive analysis. The valuation of the collateral and the size of the existing and proposed debts are typically the most heavily litigated facts at a contested priming hearing.

An undersecured lienholder cannot be primed without genuine new value flowing back to it; the only "cushion" available in an undersecured posture is whatever new collateral, cash payments, or other consideration the priming arrangement is willing to deliver.

Risk of Failed Adequate Protection: Section 507(b)

If adequate protection later proves inadequate (for example, because the collateral declines in value beyond the cushion or replacement-lien valuation), Section 507(b) gives the existing lienholder a super-priority administrative claim for the shortfall. This claim outranks all other administrative expenses, including the DIP lender's own Section 364(c)(1) super-priority unless specifically subordinated in the DIP order. Section 507(b) is, in effect, the back-stop guarantee that adequate protection will deliver real economic value, not just a paper recital.

DIP orders often include carefully-negotiated waterfalls that govern the relative priority of the DIP super-priority claim and the Section 507(b) claim. Existing lienholders should pay close attention to these provisions before consenting to a priming arrangement.

Evidentiary Burden and Hearing Posture

The debtor bears the burden of proof on adequate protection. Evidence typically takes the form of an appraisal, a financial-advisor declaration on alternative financing efforts, and a budget showing the use of the new financing. The existing lienholder will frequently offer competing valuation evidence. Courts often require live testimony at contested final-DIP hearings and will not rubber-stamp a contested priming on declarations alone.

Where the priming is sought on interim relief, courts limit the interim priming to the amount reasonably necessary to avoid immediate and irreparable harm pending the final hearing, consistent with Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 4001(c)(2).

Related Bankruptcy Code Sections

Section 361 — forms of adequate protection

Section 362 — automatic stay and stay-relief on lack of adequate protection

Section 506 — valuation of secured claims

Section 507(b) — super-priority for failed adequate protection

DIP Financing Types Overview — 11 U.S.C. Section 364

Plain-English overview of the four tiers of post-petition credit available to a debtor in possession: ordinary-course unsecured, court-approved unsecured, administrative-priority and super-priority secured, and priming liens.

Home › Statutes › Section 364 › Types Overview

Empirical research on this section

For case-pattern analysis on how federal bankruptcy courts apply Section 364, including district-level patterns and primary-source dockets, see openbankruptcyproject.org/cases/. All datasets licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

What Is Section 364?

Section 364 of the Bankruptcy Code is the gateway through which a debtor in possession (or a Chapter 11 trustee) obtains post-petition credit. Without Section 364, a debtor could not borrow money or buy goods on credit after the petition date, because the automatic stay and the rules of administrative priority would make any new lender's claim subordinate to a host of pre-petition obligations and existing liens. Section 364 solves that problem by creating a tiered system: the more aggressive the financing terms a debtor needs, the higher the level of court scrutiny required.

Official citation: 11 U.S.C. § 364

The four tiers reflect a deliberate ladder of escalation. Each tier responds to the practical reality that a debtor's credit profile in bankruptcy is severely compromised and that lenders will demand progressively stronger protections before extending new money to an insolvent enterprise.

Section 364(a): Ordinary-Course Unsecured Credit

Section 364(a) authorizes a trustee or debtor in possession operating the business under Section 1108 to obtain unsecured credit and incur unsecured debt in the ordinary course of business without notice or a hearing. The resulting claim is treated as an administrative expense under Section 503(b)(1).

This subsection is the workhorse provision that lets an operating debtor buy inventory on net-30 trade terms, accept utility services, and incur day-to-day operating liabilities without running to the bankruptcy court for each transaction. The "ordinary course" limit is fact-bound and turns on both the horizontal test (consistent with industry norms) and the vertical test (consistent with the debtor's own pre-petition practice).

Section 364(b): Court-Approved Unsecured Credit

Section 364(b) covers unsecured credit outside the ordinary course. The court, after notice and a hearing, may authorize the trustee to obtain unsecured credit or to incur unsecured debt other than under Section 364(a). The claim is again treated as a Section 503(b)(1) administrative expense.

This tier is invoked when the debtor needs unsecured credit that does not fit the trade-credit pattern (for example, a large unsecured loan from a parent entity or a strategic partner). The hearing requirement gives creditors and the United States Trustee a chance to object before the obligation is incurred.

Section 364(c): Administrative-Priority and Super-Priority Secured Credit

When the debtor cannot obtain unsecured credit allowable as an ordinary administrative expense, Section 364(c) allows the court, after notice and a hearing, to authorize new credit secured by one or more of three escalating protections:

Section 364(c)(1): A super-priority administrative expense having priority over any or all administrative expenses of the kind specified in Sections 503(b) or 507(b);

Section 364(c)(2): A lien on property of the estate that is not otherwise subject to a lien; or

Section 364(c)(3): A junior lien on property of the estate already subject to a lien.

The hallmark of Section 364(c) is that it gives the new lender a security interest in unencumbered property, or a junior lien on already-encumbered property, without disturbing the position of existing secured creditors. The threshold finding that the debtor could not obtain credit on better terms is essential.

Section 364(d): Priming Liens

Section 364(d) is the most aggressive of the tiers. It authorizes the court to approve credit secured by a senior or equal lien on property already subject to a lien (a "priming" lien) only if (i) the debtor cannot obtain credit otherwise and (ii) there is adequate protection of the interest of the existing lienholder being primed.

Priming a non-consenting secured lender is one of the most consequential remedies available in a bankruptcy case. The existing lienholder's collateral position is subordinated to a new loan, and unless adequate protection (typically a replacement lien, cash payments, or a sufficient equity cushion) is provided, that subordination violates the takings principle that runs through the secured-creditor protections of the Code. The priming-liens deep-dive page covers the adequate-protection mechanics in detail.

Roll-Ups and Cross-Collateralization

Two recurring features of modern DIP facilities sit on top of the basic Section 364 framework and have generated extensive doctrinal controversy:

Roll-ups are provisions in a DIP loan that use new-money advances to pay down a pre-petition claim held by the same lender, converting an unsecured or under-secured pre-petition position into a fully-secured post-petition position. Courts have approved roll-ups where the new money is substantial relative to the rolled-up amount, where unsecured creditors receive meaningful concessions, and where the alternative is liquidation. They are scrutinized closely under the Section 364(c) and (d) standards.

Cross-collateralization is the practice of granting the DIP lender a lien on the debtor's assets to secure not only the new post-petition advances but also the lender's pre-petition claim. The Eleventh Circuit's In re Saybrook Manufacturing Co., 963 F.2d 1490 (11th Cir. 1992) treats cross-collateralization as per se impermissible under Section 364, on the rationale that it improperly elevates a pre-petition unsecured claim ahead of other unsecured creditors. Other circuits apply a balancing test. The cross-collateralization deep-dive page traces the circuit split.

Procedure and Approval Standards

Section 364(b), (c), and (d) all require "notice and a hearing" within the meaning of Section 102(1). Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 4001(c) lays out the specific notice requirements for motions to obtain credit, including a 14-day notice period and detailed disclosure of significant terms (cross-collateralization, roll-ups, waivers of Section 506(c), liens on avoidance actions, and so forth).

Courts routinely enter an interim DIP order on a short turnaround (often within a few days of the petition) and then schedule a final hearing roughly three weeks later. The interim order is constrained to the financing reasonably necessary to avoid immediate and irreparable harm. The final order resolves all objections and approves the full facility. The financing-hierarchy deep-dive page walks through the standard procedural cadence and the components of a typical final DIP order.

## Section 365 Executory Contracts - Open Bankruptcy Project

Assumption and Rejection

Section 365 Executory Contracts

Section 365 gives the trustee or debtor-in-possession a powerful triage tool: the ability to assume contracts and leases that benefit the estate, reject those that burden it, and (subject to limits) assign assumed contracts to third parties. The framework rests on the half-century-old Countryman definition of an executory contract and has spawned specialized rules for real estate, intellectual property, collective bargaining, and retiree benefits.

Last modified 2026-05-22.

Home/Section 365 Executory Contracts

About section 365

The Bankruptcy Code does not define "executory contract." The accepted working definition comes from Vern Countryman's 1973 article: an executory contract is one under which the obligations of both parties are so far unperformed that the failure of either to complete performance would constitute a material breach excusing the performance of the other. The functional test is what matters: a contract is executory if rejection would relieve the estate of material unperformed obligations.

Assumption requires the estate to cure existing defaults (with limited exceptions for ipso facto and "non-monetary historical" defaults under section 365(b)(2)), to compensate for actual pecuniary loss, and to provide adequate assurance of future performance. Rejection is treated as a breach immediately before the petition date, generating a general unsecured rejection-damages claim under section 502(g). Rejection of certain contracts triggers special treatment: real-property leases are subject to the section 502(b)(6) cap on landlord damages; intellectual-property licenses are subject to the section 365(n) preservation right for licensees; and personal-property leases of motor vehicles are subject to the section 365(p) special rule.

The Code carves out four categories from the general assumption-rejection rules: section 365(c)(1) anti-assignment for personal-services contracts and non-delegable rights; section 365(c)(2) for financial accommodations; section 1113 for collective bargaining agreements (requiring negotiated modification before rejection); and section 1114 for retiree benefits (requiring a similar negotiation track for post-employment health and welfare benefits).

Section 365 deep-dives

Section 365 FrameworkThe Countryman definition of executory contract, the assumption requirements (cure, compensation, adequate assurance), the rejection-as-breach rule, and the rejection-damages claim under section 502(g).

Commercial Real Estate LeasesThe section 365(d)(4) 120-day assumption-or-rejection deadline for non-residential real estate, the section 502(b)(6) landlord-damages cap, and the assignment of shopping-center leases under section 365(b)(3).

Intellectual Property LicensesThe section 365(n) preservation right that protects non-debtor licensees on rejection, the Mission Product Holdings v. Tempnology trademark rule, and the assumption of executive software and patent licenses.

Section 1113 Collective Bargaining AgreementsThe pre-rejection procedural prerequisites under section 1113, the nine-factor Bildisco-superseded standard, and the timeline for negotiation, proposal, and court hearing.

Section 1114 Retiree BenefitsThe parallel section 1114 framework for modifying retiree health and welfare benefits in chapter 11, including the authorized representative requirement and the modification standard.

Deadline trap: Section 365(d)(4) gives the trustee or debtor-in-possession 120 days from the order for relief to assume or reject a non-residential real-property lease. The court can extend the deadline by 90 days for cause on motion filed before the original deadline. Further extensions require landlord consent. Missing the deadline operates as automatic rejection.

## Collective Bargaining Agreement Rejection Under Section 1113: NLRB v. Bildisco, 1113(c) Test, Wheeling-Pittsburgh
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/section-365-executory-contracts/collective-bargaining-1113/

openbankruptcyproject.org
☰

Collective Bargaining Agreements (Section 1113)

NLRB v. Bildisco origins, the codified Bildisco standard, the nine-element Section 1113(c) test, and the Wheeling-Pittsburgh Steel circuit split on what "necessary" modifications require.

Home › Section 365 › Collective Bargaining (Section 1113)

Why Section 1113 instead of Section 365

Collective bargaining agreements are technically executory contracts. Before 1984 they were rejectable under the ordinary § 365 business-judgment standard. The Supreme Court confirmed that authority in NLRB v. Bildisco & Bildisco, 465 U.S. 513 (1984), but also held that a Chapter 11 debtor that unilaterally modified a CBA after filing did not commit an unfair labor practice under the NLRA — the bankruptcy filing changed the analytic baseline.

Organized labor reacted strongly. Within months Congress enacted § 1113 (1984), pulling CBA rejection out of § 365 entirely and substituting a much more demanding procedure. The objective was to ensure that the Bankruptcy Code did not become a quiet route around the National Labor Relations Act and the duty to bargain in good faith. Section 1113 is now the exclusive vehicle for rejection or modification of a CBA in a Chapter 11 case.

Official citation: 11 U.S.C. § 1113 (rejection of collective bargaining agreements).

The codified Bildisco standard

Section 1113 codifies the substantive standard the Supreme Court articulated in Bildisco — that a CBA may be rejected only if it "burdens the estate" and the "equities balance in favor" of rejection — but layers on top of that substantive test a strict procedural pre-rejection process designed to force the debtor to genuinely bargain before going to the court.

The two key procedural pieces are § 1113(b) (the proposal-and-bargaining process the debtor must complete before it can even file a rejection motion) and § 1113(c) (the nine-element showing the debtor must make to obtain a rejection order). Section 1113(e) provides a separate procedure for interim relief during the negotiation period.

Section 1113(b): the pre-rejection bargaining process

Before a debtor can move to reject a CBA, § 1113(b)(1) requires the debtor to:

Make a proposal to the authorized representative of the employees (the union) that is "based on the most complete and reliable information available at the time of such proposal" and that "provides for those necessary modifications in the employees benefits and protections that are necessary to permit the reorganization of the debtor and assures that all creditors, the debtor and all of the affected parties are treated fairly and equitably";

Provide the authorized representative with "such relevant information as is necessary to evaluate the proposal."

Section 1113(b)(2) then requires the debtor to "meet, at reasonable times, with the authorized representative to confer in good faith in attempting to reach mutually satisfactory modifications" of the CBA. The bargaining is to take place between the date of the proposal and the rejection hearing.

Procedural shortcuts fail. Courts have rejected motions where the debtor's "proposal" was made simultaneously with or only days before the rejection motion, where the debtor refused to share underlying financial information sufficient for the union to evaluate the proposal, or where the debtor's bargaining behavior amounted to a take-it-or-leave-it ultimatum. Section 1113(b) is not satisfied by going through the motions.

The nine-element Section 1113(c) test

If the bargaining process under § 1113(b) does not produce agreement, the debtor may move to reject. Section 1113(c) provides that the court "shall approve" rejection only if it finds three things, each of which is typically broken down further to produce a nine-element checklist:

The debtor made a proposal that fulfilled the requirements of subsection (b)(1). Courts typically break this down into four sub-elements:

(a) The debtor made a proposal to the authorized representative;

(b) The proposal was based on the most complete and reliable information available at the time;

(c) The proposed modifications were "necessary" to permit reorganization;

(d) The proposal assured that all creditors, the debtor, and all affected parties were treated fairly and equitably.

The authorized representative refused to accept the proposal without good cause. Two sub-elements:

(e) The representative actually refused; and

(f) The refusal lacked good cause — i.e., the proposal was reasonable in light of the debtor's circumstances and the union had no legitimate basis to reject it.

The balance of the equities clearly favors rejection. Three sub-elements:

(g) The likelihood and consequences of reorganization failure if relief is not granted;

(h) The likely effect on creditors, employees, and the public if rejection is or is not granted;

(i) The "good faith" efforts the debtor undertook to negotiate a voluntary modification with the union.

Each of the nine elements must be carried by the debtor by a preponderance of the evidence. The failure of any one element defeats the motion. In practice, the litigation almost always centers on element (c) — whether the proposed modifications are "necessary" — and that is where the circuit split lives.

Wheeling-Pittsburgh Steel and the “necessary” circuit split

The Third Circuit's decision in In re Wheeling-Pittsburgh Steel Corp., 791 F.2d 1074 (3d Cir. 1986), construes "necessary" narrowly. Under Wheeling-Pittsburgh, the debtor's proposal must include only those modifications strictly necessary to permit the debtor's reorganization — meaning the minimum bargained-for concessions that will keep the debtor afloat. Modifications that go beyond bare necessity to provide a margin of safety, to give the post-confirmation entity competitive labor costs, or to align with industry benchmarks are not "necessary" within the meaning of the statute. The Third Circuit explicitly disclaimed reading "necessary" as a synonym for "useful," "desirable," or "important to long-term viability."

The Second Circuit, in Truck Drivers Local 807 v. Carey Transportation, Inc., 816 F.2d 82 (2d Cir. 1987), took the opposite view. Under the Carey Transportation approach, "necessary" includes modifications that contribute to the debtor's long-term viability, not just modifications strictly required to avoid immediate liquidation. The debtor need not propose the minimum — it need only propose modifications that are necessary in the broader sense of being needed for the reorganization to succeed.

Why the split matters operationally. Debtors in the Third Circuit face a real risk that an "ambitious" CBA-modification proposal will be denied because it goes beyond bare necessity, even where the modifications would clearly help the post-confirmation entity. Debtors in the Second Circuit have more room to propose modifications keyed to long-term competitive labor cost. Other circuits have aligned variously with one approach or the other, and the venue choice for major labor-dependent Chapter 11 cases routinely turns on this distinction.

Section 1113(e): interim relief

If the debtor can show that, during the § 1113(b) bargaining period, "interim changes in the terms, conditions, wages, benefits, or work rules provided by a collective bargaining agreement are essential to the continuation of the debtor's business, or in order to avoid irreparable damage to the estate," § 1113(e) permits the court to enter an interim order authorizing those changes. The standard is high — "essential" rather than merely useful — but it gives a debtor in genuine cash crisis a mechanism to obtain immediate relief without waiting out the entire pre-rejection bargaining process.

## Commercial Real Estate Leases Under Section 365: 365(d)(3), 365(d)(4), 365(b)(3)

openbankruptcyproject.org
☰
