11 U.S.C. Section 510 - Subordination of Claims and Interests

Three regimes for ranking claims behind others: contractual subordination agreements, mandatory subordination of securities-rescission claims, and the equitable subordination doctrine.

Home › Statutes › 11 U.S.C. Section 510 - Subordination

Empirical research on this section

For case-pattern analysis on how federal bankruptcy courts apply this provision, including district-level patterns and primary-source dockets, see openbankruptcyproject.org/cases/. All datasets licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

What Is Section 510?

Section 510 is the principal Bankruptcy Code provision authorizing the demotion of one claim or interest behind others in the distribution priority. It contains three independent regimes: (a) enforcement of pre-petition contractual subordination agreements; (b) mandatory subordination of claims arising from the purchase or sale of securities of the debtor or an affiliate; and (c) equitable subordination of allowed claims and interests based on misconduct.

Subordination is a powerful remedy: a subordinated claim retains its allowed status but is paid only after the senior class (or specified senior creditor) is paid in full. In an insolvent estate, subordination commonly means the subordinated creditor receives nothing.

Official citation: 11 U.S.C. § 510

Contractual Subordination: Section 510(a)

Section 510(a) provides: "A subordination agreement is enforceable in a case under this title to the same extent that such agreement is enforceable under applicable nonbankruptcy law." The Code thus respects intercreditor agreements rather than overriding them. A bondholder who has contractually agreed to be paid only after senior bondholders is held to that bargain in bankruptcy.

Common forms include intercreditor agreements between senior and subordinated lenders, subordinated indenture provisions in publicly issued debt, and turnover provisions requiring junior creditors to deliver any received distributions to senior creditors until the senior debt is paid in full. Disputes typically center on the scope of the senior debt, the trigger for payment turnover, and the enforceability of voting waivers under Section 1126.

Securities Subordination: Section 510(b)

Section 510(b) imposes mandatory subordination of claims arising from "the rescission of a purchase or sale of a security of the debtor or of an affiliate of the debtor, for damages arising from the purchase or sale of such a security, or for reimbursement or contribution allowed under section 502 on account of such a claim." Such claims are subordinated to all claims or interests senior to or equal to the claim or interest represented by the security; if the security is common stock, the subordinated claim has the same priority as common stock (i.e., last).

The policy rationale is that equity investors should not be able to convert their risk-bearing investment into a creditor claim through securities-fraud or rescission theories. Allowing pari passu treatment would let shareholders share in the recovery pool ahead of creditors who never bore the equity risk in the first place. The leading appellate authority (most often cited from In re Telegroup, Inc., 281 F.3d 133 (3d Cir. 2002)) construes 510(b) broadly to capture indirect damages claims and breach-of-contract claims tied to the issuance.

Equitable Subordination: Section 510(c)

Section 510(c) codifies the equitable-subordination doctrine: "Notwithstanding subsections (a) and (b) of this section, after notice and a hearing, the court may - (1) under principles of equitable subordination, subordinate for purposes of distribution all or part of an allowed claim to all or part of another allowed claim or all or part of an allowed interest to all or part of another allowed interest; or (2) order that any lien securing such a subordinated claim be transferred to the estate."

The classic articulation, from In re Mobile Steel Co., 563 F.2d 692 (5th Cir. 1977) - widely followed in other circuits - requires three findings:

The claimant must have engaged in some type of inequitable conduct;

The misconduct must have resulted in injury to the creditors of the bankrupt or conferred an unfair advantage on the claimant; and

Equitable subordination of the claim must not be inconsistent with the provisions of the Bankruptcy Code.

For insiders (officers, directors, controlling shareholders, affiliates), courts apply heightened scrutiny to their dealings with the debtor. For non-insiders, the standard is significantly more demanding, generally requiring proof of gross misconduct akin to fraud, spoliation, or moral turpitude.

Recharacterization Distinguished

Equitable subordination should not be confused with recharacterization. Recharacterization treats what is labeled "debt" as equity from its inception - meaning the claim is not a claim at all, but an equity interest. Subordination, by contrast, accepts the claim as a claim but pushes it back in the priority queue. Recharacterization rests on factors developed in tax and corporate-law cases (capitalization, intent of the parties, source of repayment, identity of interests between lender and borrower, etc.), while subordination focuses on post-loan misconduct and resulting harm.

Some circuits authorize recharacterization under Section 105(a), others under Section 502(b)'s incorporation of state law. The Supreme Court has not resolved the split, and practitioners frequently plead recharacterization and equitable subordination as alternative or successive theories.

Common Procedural Postures

Subordination disputes typically arise in adversary proceedings under Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 7001(8) (proceedings to subordinate claims). Standing to seek equitable subordination is most clearly held by the trustee or debtor in possession; whether individual creditors have standing to assert derivative subordination claims depends on the jurisdiction and on whether the trustee has refused to act. Common factual settings include:

Insider loans made when the debtor was undercapitalized;

Insider claims arising from self-dealing transactions, dividend recapitalizations, or below-market guarantees;

Lender liability claims where the senior lender exercised excessive control over the debtor's operations;

Fraudulent-transfer-related claims where the recipient of a voidable transfer also holds a contract claim against the estate;

Rescission claims by recent purchasers of stock or notes alleging issuance fraud.

Related Bankruptcy Code Sections

Section 502 - Allowance of claims (a claim must first be allowed before it can be subordinated)

Section 509(c) - Mandatory subordination of subrogation claims behind original creditor

Section 105 - Equitable powers (recharacterization, in some circuits)

Section 548 - Fraudulent transfers (often paired with subordination claims)

Section 1129(b) - Absolute priority rule (subordination changes the priority ladder for cramdown)

Topical deep-dive on Section 510

11 USC 510 - subordination of claims (deep dive) — contractual subordination, mandatory subordination of securities-rescission claims, equitable subordination under the Mobile Steel three-prong test, and the AutoStyle recharacterization framework.

## 11 USC 510 - Subordination [2026]
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/section-510-subordination/

11 U.S.C. Section 510 - Subordination

How and why a claim can be moved down the priority ladder: contractual subordination agreements, the mandatory subordination of securities-rescission claims, equitable subordination under the Mobile Steel three-prong test, and the doctrinal cousin of recharacterizing debt as equity.

Home › Statutes › 11 U.S.C. Section 510 - Subordination

Empirical research on this section

For case-pattern analysis on how federal bankruptcy courts apply this provision, including district-level patterns and primary-source dockets, see openbankruptcyproject.org/cases/. All datasets licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

What Section 510 Does

Section 510 governs the subordination of claims and interests in bankruptcy. Subordination moves a claim down the distribution waterfall: instead of sharing pro rata with claims of the same nominal priority, a subordinated claim is paid only after the senior claims to which it is subordinated have been paid in full. The provision recognizes three distinct subordination doctrines: contractual (510(a)), mandatory by statute (510(b)), and equitable (510(c)).

Official citation: 11 U.S.C. § 510

Section 510(a): Contractual Subordination

Section 510(a) provides that a subordination agreement is "enforceable in a case under this title to the same extent that such agreement is enforceable under applicable nonbankruptcy law." The provision is a one-line statutory codification of the common-law principle that parties may contract for relative priority among themselves and that the bankruptcy court will honor those contracts.

The most common application is in syndicated and tiered debt structures. A senior credit facility will require junior debt to execute an intercreditor agreement under which the junior lender agrees that, until the senior debt is paid in full, it will turn over to the senior lender any distribution it receives on account of its junior claim. In bankruptcy, Section 510(a) tells the court to enforce that turnover obligation according to its terms.

Contractual subordination is generally enforced even when it produces outcomes that look harsh, because Section 510(a) does not give the bankruptcy court authority to rewrite the agreement on equity grounds. The bankruptcy court can refuse to enforce a subordination agreement only on the same grounds that would defeat it outside bankruptcy: lack of consideration, fraud in the inducement, unconscionability under applicable state contract law, and so on.

X-clause litigation: intercreditor agreements often contain "X-clauses" that carve out certain payments (most commonly distributions of reorganized-debtor equity in a plan of reorganization) from the turnover obligation. Whether a specific plan distribution falls inside or outside the X-clause has become a recurrent confirmation-stage fight in large Chapter 11 cases.

Section 510(b): Mandatory Subordination of Securities-Rescission Claims

Section 510(b) is a statutorily mandated subordination rule that applies regardless of contract. It provides that "a claim arising from rescission of a purchase or sale of a security of the debtor or of an affiliate of the debtor, for damages arising from the purchase or sale of such a security, or for reimbursement or contribution allowed under section 502 on account of such a claim, shall be subordinated to all claims or interests that are senior to or equal the claim or interest represented by such security."

The provision implements the policy judgment that investors who bought equity (or debt that has been recharacterized as equity) accepted the risk that the company would fail; allowing them to recover ahead of trade creditors on a fraud-on-the-market or rescission theory would shift that investment risk onto the trade creditors who never priced for it. The Third Circuit's In re Telegroup, Inc., 281 F.3d 133 (3d Cir. 2002), and the Ninth Circuit's In re Betacom of Phoenix, Inc., 240 F.3d 823 (9th Cir. 2001), are leading constructions of the provision's scope.

Section 510(b) is broad. A federal securities fraud claim against an issuer based on misrepresentations in a registration statement is subordinated. A contract claim for breach of a stock purchase agreement is subordinated. A claim for contribution from a third party whose primary liability arose from a securities-fraud claim is subordinated. The investor's claim is treated, for distribution purposes, as if it occupied the same level as the security it relates to: equity subordinated to all debt, debt securities subordinated to claims senior to or equal to that debt class.

Section 510(c): Equitable Subordination

Section 510(c) codifies the bankruptcy court's equitable subordination power. It provides that the court may "under principles of equitable subordination, subordinate for purposes of distribution all or part of an allowed claim to all or part of another allowed claim" or "order that any lien securing such a subordinated claim be transferred to the estate."

The provision codifies an equitable doctrine developed by the federal courts under prior bankruptcy regimes. The seminal articulation comes from the Fifth Circuit's In re Mobile Steel Co., 563 F.2d 692 (5th Cir. 1977), which established the three-prong test still applied across the circuits.

The Mobile Steel Three-Prong Test

The claimant must have engaged in some type of inequitable conduct;

The misconduct must have resulted in injury to the creditors of the bankrupt or conferred an unfair advantage on the claimant; and

Equitable subordination of the claim must not be inconsistent with the provisions of the Bankruptcy Code.

The Supreme Court endorsed the Mobile Steel framework in United States v. Noland, 517 U.S. 535 (1996), and clarified that equitable subordination requires individualized misconduct, not category-wide subordination of an entire class of claims. The Court reaffirmed in United States v. Reorganized CF&I Fabricators, 518 U.S. 213 (1996), that a bankruptcy court cannot use Section 510(c) to recategorize a statutory tax priority on policy grounds alone.

The misconduct showing is more demanding when the claimant is an arms-length lender or trade creditor than when the claimant is an insider. The leading articulation of the insider-versus-outsider distinction is the Third Circuit's In re Citicorp Venture Capital, Ltd. v. Committee of Creditors Holding Unsecured Claims, 160 F.3d 982 (3d Cir. 1998): for insiders, "egregious conduct" is not required, and "breach of fiduciary duty" or "unfair advantage" suffices; for non-insiders, the conduct must be "very substantial" and approach actual fraud or moral turpitude.

Remedy is calibrated: equitable subordination is meant to undo the injury, not to punish. A court that finds inequitable conduct typically subordinates the claim only to the extent necessary to neutralize the injury or unfair advantage; full subordination of an otherwise-valid secured claim is reserved for the most serious cases.

Recharacterization Versus Equitable Subordination

Recharacterization is a doctrinally distinct cousin of equitable subordination. Where Section 510(c) subordinates a valid claim because of misconduct, recharacterization holds that the asserted claim was never debt at all but rather a disguised equity contribution, which is subordinated by Section 510(b) and Section 726(a) to all true debt claims.

The Sixth Circuit's In re AutoStyle Plastics, Inc., 269 F.3d 726 (6th Cir. 2001), is the leading treatment. AutoStyle adopted a thirteen-factor test originally developed in the Eleventh Circuit's In re Roth American, Inc. (and traceable to the Tax Court's Estate of Mixon), grouped into three core inquiries:

Form of the instrument: Is there a written promissory note? Fixed maturity date? Fixed interest rate? Right to enforce repayment? Status as a creditor in event of liquidation?

Intent of the parties: Did the parties intend the transaction as debt or equity? Was the loan secured? Was there a sinking fund? Did the corporation make payments on schedule? Was the lender treated as a creditor in the corporation's books and tax filings?

Reasonableness of the transaction: Was the corporation adequately capitalized? Was the loan made when no disinterested third party would have lent? Was the contribution proportional to the lender's equity ownership? Was repayment dependent on the success of the business?

The test is fact-intensive and contextual. No single factor is dispositive; courts weigh the totality. The Fourth Circuit's In re Dornier Aviation (North America), Inc., 453 F.3d 225 (4th Cir. 2006), and the Tenth Circuit's In re Hedged-Investments Associates, 380 F.3d 1292 (10th Cir. 2004), follow comparable approaches.

Doctrinal Significance

The distinction matters because the elements are different. To recharacterize, the proponent must show the instrument was always equity in substance, regardless of how it was labeled. No misconduct is required. To equitably subordinate, the proponent must show conduct meeting the Mobile Steel test; even an obviously real debt can be subordinated if the lender behaved badly. A claim that survives recharacterization (it is debt) can still be subordinated under Section 510(c) (the lender's conduct was inequitable). A claim that is recharacterized never reaches the Section 510(c) inquiry, because it has been moved into the equity priority tier outright.

Subordination in Plan Distributions

Subordination determinations made under Section 510 carry through to plan-distribution allocation under Sections 1129 and 1191. A claim that has been equitably subordinated to general unsecured claims is paid only after general unsecureds are paid in full. A claim subordinated under Section 510(b) is treated as occupying the priority tier of the underlying security, which in most cases means it is paid only after all true debt has been satisfied. Subordination is a powerful tool because it reorders the waterfall without changing the allowed amount of the claim; the claim still exists, it just has to wait.

Related Bankruptcy Code Sections

Section 507 - Priorities in distribution

Section 726 - Distribution in Chapter 7

Section 502 - Allowance of claims and interests

Section 1129 - Chapter 11 confirmation requirements

Section 105 - General powers of the court

## 11 USC 511 - Interest Rate on Tax Claims in Bankruptcy [2026]

11 U.S.C. Section 511 - Rate of Interest on Tax Claims

The BAPCPA rule fixing the interest rate on tax claims at the rate determined under applicable nonbankruptcy law - displacing the Till prime-plus-risk methodology for tax obligations.

Home › Statutes › 11 U.S.C. Section 511 - Interest on Tax Claims

Empirical research on this section

For case-pattern analysis on how federal bankruptcy courts apply this provision, including district-level patterns and primary-source dockets, see openbankruptcyproject.org/cases/. All datasets licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

What Is Section 511?

Section 511, added by the Bankruptcy Abuse Prevention and Consumer Protection Act of 2005 (BAPCPA), prescribes the interest rate to be paid on tax claims in any case under Title 11. It overrides the case-by-case interest analysis required by Till v. SCS Credit Corp., 541 U.S. 465 (2004), for tax claims specifically. For tax claims, courts no longer apply a prime-plus-risk-adjustment methodology; the applicable rate is whatever rate applicable nonbankruptcy law - typically the Internal Revenue Code's underpayment rate, or the analogous state-tax rate - prescribes.

Official citation: 11 U.S.C. § 511

The Statutory Text

Section 511(a) provides: "If any provision of this title requires the payment of interest on a tax claim or on an administrative expense tax, or the payment of interest to enable a creditor to receive the present value of the allowed amount of a tax claim, the rate of interest shall be the rate determined under applicable nonbankruptcy law."

Section 511(b) adds a timing rule for non-assessed taxes: "In the case of taxes paid under a confirmed plan under this title, the rate of interest shall be determined as of the calendar month in which the plan is confirmed."

The IRS Underpayment Rate

For federal tax claims, the applicable nonbankruptcy law is Internal Revenue Code § 6621, which sets the underpayment rate at the federal short-term rate plus three percentage points (plus an additional two points for large corporate underpayments above $100,000). The rate is determined quarterly by the IRS and published in revenue rulings. For state and local tax claims, the rate is set by the analogous statute of the taxing authority - many states track the federal rate, others apply fixed statutory percentages.

The practical effect: tax claimants in bankruptcy receive a non-negotiable, statutorily fixed rate, not a Till-style market rate. This is generally favorable to taxing authorities because the IRS underpayment rate frequently exceeds the prime rate in low-interest-rate environments and approximates or slightly exceeds prime in moderate-rate environments.

Claims to Which Section 511 Applies

Section 511 applies wherever Title 11 calls for interest on a tax claim, including:

Priority unsecured tax claims under Section 507(a)(8): When a Chapter 13 plan or a Chapter 11 plan pays the priority tax claim in installments under Section 1129(a)(9)(C) or Section 1322(a)(2), the present-value interest component is computed at the Section 511 rate;

Secured tax claims (tax liens): When a plan provides for cramdown of a secured tax claim under Section 1129(b)(2)(A) or Section 1325(a)(5)(B), the present-value interest is computed at the Section 511 rate, not the Till rate;

Administrative expense tax claims under Section 503(b)(1)(B): Post-petition taxes incurred by the estate, where Title 11 requires interest, accrue at the Section 511 rate;

Cures under Section 1322(b)(5) or 1123(a)(5)(G): Where a tax obligation is cured under a plan, the cure interest, if any, is determined under Section 511.

The Till Backdrop

In Till v. SCS Credit Corp., the Supreme Court adopted a "formula approach" for determining the cramdown interest rate under Section 1325(a)(5)(B)(ii) - prime rate plus a risk adjustment (typically 1-3%) tailored to the debtor's circumstances. Till applies to general secured-creditor cramdown, but Section 511 carves taxes out: for tax claims, Congress directed the use of the nonbankruptcy rate, which in many cases is materially higher than a Till rate.

The carve-out reflects a policy judgment that taxing authorities are involuntary creditors entitled to the same interest treatment they would receive outside bankruptcy, rather than a court-derived market rate. The Internal Revenue Manual and the U.S. Trustee Program's tax-claim guidance reflect this position.

Variable Rates Under Section 511(b)

Section 511(b) fixes the rate as of the calendar month of confirmation. Because the IRS underpayment rate changes quarterly, a confirmation in (for example) March 2026 locks in the Q1 2026 rate for the life of the plan, even if rates later rise or fall. Some courts and commentators have debated whether 511(b) creates a true fixed rate or whether it merely sets the initial rate, with subsequent adjustments tracking quarterly changes. The majority view treats 511(b) as fixing the rate at confirmation, providing certainty for plan feasibility analysis under Section 1129(a)(11) and Section 1325(a)(6).

Common Procedural Postures

Section 511 issues typically arise in the following contexts:

Chapter 13 plan confirmation where the IRS or state tax authority objects to the interest rate proposed in the plan;

Chapter 11 plan confirmation involving priority tax claims paid over up to five years from the petition date under Section 1129(a)(9)(C);

Cramdown of a secured tax lien claim (real-property tax lien, federal tax lien) where the debtor proposes to retain the encumbered property and pay the secured portion with interest;

Determining whether a plan is feasible when the required Section 511 interest pushes payments above the debtor's projected disposable income.

Related Bankruptcy Code Sections

Section 507(a)(8) - Priority of unsecured tax claims

Section 1129(a)(9)(C) - Chapter 11 treatment of priority tax claims

Section 1322(a)(2) - Chapter 13 treatment of priority tax claims

Section 1325(a)(5) - Cramdown of secured claims (Till context)

Section 505 - Determination of tax liability by the bankruptcy court

Section 523(a)(1) - Nondischargeability of certain tax debts

## 11 USC 521 - Debtor Duties Enumerated [2026]
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/section-521-debtor-duties/

openbankruptcyproject.org
☰

Home
Tools

Impact
Legal Aid

11 U.S.C. Section 521 - Debtor Duties Enumerated

A deep-dive guide to the affirmative duties imposed on every bankruptcy debtor: schedules and SOFA, statement of intention, document production, tax returns, and the post-petition financial-management course.

Home › Statutes › 11 U.S.C. Section 521 - Debtor Duties

Empirical research on this section

For case-pattern analysis on how federal bankruptcy courts enforce Section 521 duties and what happens when they are missed, see openbankruptcyproject.org/cases/. All datasets licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

What Is Section 521?

Section 521 is the master debtor-duty provision of the Bankruptcy Code. It catalogs the affirmative obligations every debtor undertakes by filing a petition. These duties run from the moment of filing through (in Chapters 13 and 11) the completion of plan payments and the entry of discharge.

The 2005 BAPCPA amendments substantially expanded Section 521, particularly with respect to document production, tax-return delivery, and consequences of noncompliance. Failure to comply with several of these duties triggers automatic case dismissal under Section 521(i), automatic stay termination under Section 362(h), or denial of discharge under Sections 727(a)(11) or 1328(g).

Official citation: 11 U.S.C. § 521

Schedules and Statement of Financial Affairs: Section 521(a)(1)

Section 521(a)(1) requires the debtor to file a list of creditors, a schedule of assets and liabilities, a schedule of current income and current expenditures, a statement of the debtor's financial affairs, copies of all payment advices received from any employer within 60 days before the petition date, a statement of the amount of monthly net income, and a statement disclosing any reasonably anticipated increase in income or expenditures over the 12 months following the petition date.

Bankruptcy Rule 1007 implements these requirements through specific Official Forms: Schedules A/B through J, the Statement of Financial Affairs (SOFA), and the means-test Forms 122A, 122B, or 122C as applicable. The filings are signed under penalty of perjury, with criminal exposure under 18 U.S.C. Sections 152 and 157 for knowingly false statements.

Under Section 521(i)(1), if an individual Chapter 7 or Chapter 13 debtor does not file all of the required information within 45 days after the petition date, the case is "automatically dismissed effective on the 46th day after the date of the filing of the petition," subject to limited extension or excusal provisions.

Statement of Intention: Section 521(a)(2)

Individual Chapter 7 debtors must file a statement of intention with respect to property securing consumer debts. The debtor must indicate whether the property will be retained or surrendered and, if retained, whether it will be claimed exempt, redeemed under Section 722, or reaffirmed under Section 524(c). The statement is due within 30 days after the petition date or by the date of the meeting of creditors, whichever is earlier, and the stated intention must be performed within 30 days after the first date set for the meeting of creditors.

Section 521(a)(6) provides a powerful enforcement mechanism: if the debtor fails to timely take the stated action with respect to personal property securing a purchase-money debt, the automatic stay terminates with respect to that property, and the property is no longer property of the estate.

Document Production: Section 521(a)(3)-(4) and 521(e)

The debtor must cooperate with the trustee as necessary to enable the trustee to perform the trustee's duties, must surrender to the trustee all property of the estate and any recorded information relating to property of the estate, and must provide documents that the trustee or U.S. Trustee requests.

Section 521(e)(2) requires the individual debtor to provide a copy of the federal income tax return for the most recent year for which a return was filed to the trustee not later than 7 days before the first date set for the meeting of creditors. Failure to comply, absent circumstances beyond the debtor's control, results in dismissal under Section 521(e)(2)(B).

A creditor may also request a copy of the return at any time, and the debtor must file the requested return with the court or provide a copy to the requesting creditor.

Tax Return Obligations: Section 521(f)-(g)

Section 521(f) imposes a continuing tax-return-delivery obligation through the life of an individual Chapter 7, 11, or 13 case. At the request of the court, U.S. Trustee, or any party in interest, the debtor must file with the court a copy of each federal income tax return required by the IRS and a copy of each amendment of any such return, plus any statement of income and expenditures during the tax year that the court requires.

Section 521(g) applies specifically to Chapter 13 debtors and Chapter 11 individual debtors and requires the filing of pre-petition tax returns. The debtor must file with the appropriate tax authorities all tax returns for taxable periods ending in the 4-year period before the petition date that have not been filed as of the petition date. Section 1308 imposes a related requirement specific to Chapter 13.

Post-Petition Financial-Management Course: Section 521(b) and the 727(a)(11) Bar

Section 521(b) requires the individual Chapter 7 debtor to file a certificate of credit counseling completion from the pre-petition briefing required by Section 109(h). Distinct from that pre-petition counseling, BAPCPA imposed a post-petition financial-management course as a discharge prerequisite.

Section 727(a)(11) provides that the court "shall grant the debtor a discharge, unless . . . after filing the petition, the debtor failed to complete an instructional course concerning personal financial management." The parallel Chapter 13 provision is Section 1328(g). Bankruptcy Rule 1007(b)(7) operationalizes the requirement by requiring the debtor to file a statement of completion (Official Form 423) within 60 days after the first date set for the meeting of creditors in a Chapter 7 case, or before the last plan payment in Chapter 13.

Failure to file the completion certificate is one of the most common reasons individual Chapter 7 cases close without discharge. The remedy is typically a motion to reopen the case under Section 350(b) and pay the reopening fee, file the certificate, and obtain entry of the previously withheld discharge.

Means-Test Information: Section 521(a)(1)(B)(iv)-(v)

Individual debtors must include with their schedules a statement of the amount of monthly net income, itemized to show how the amount is calculated, and a statement disclosing any reasonably anticipated increase in income or expenditures over the 12 months following the petition date. These figures feed into the Section 707(b) means-test calculation in Chapter 7 and into the projected-disposable-income analysis in Chapter 13.

Consequences of Noncompliance

The Code calibrates penalty to duty:

Automatic dismissal: Section 521(i)(1) for missing schedules within 45 days; Section 521(e)(2)(B) for missing tax return.

Automatic stay termination: Section 362(h) for failure to timely file statement of intention or perform stated intention as to consumer-debt collateral.

Discharge denial or withholding: Section 727(a)(11) / 1328(g) for missing financial-management course; Section 727(a)(3)-(5) for concealment, destruction of records, false statements, or failure to explain loss of assets.

Criminal exposure: 18 U.S.C. Sections 152 and 157 for knowingly false statements in schedules, SOFA, or related disclosures.

Related Bankruptcy Code Sections

Section 109 - Debtor eligibility, including pre-petition credit counseling

Section 341 - Meeting of creditors at which debtor testifies under oath

Section 707 - Means test and dismissal of Chapter 7 case

Section 727 - Chapter 7 discharge, including Section 727(a)(11) financial-management bar

Section 1308 - Chapter 13 tax-return filing requirement

Section 1328 - Chapter 13 discharge, including Section 1328(g) financial-management bar

## 11 USC 521(i) - Automatic Dismissal for Missing Documents [2026]
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/section-521i-automatic-dismissal/

openbankruptcyproject.org
☰

Home
Tools

Impact
Legal Aid

11 U.S.C. Section 521(i) - Automatic Dismissal for Failure to File Documents

Plain-English guide to the 45-day automatic-dismissal rule for individual Chapter 7 and Chapter 13 debtors, the Section 521(i)(3) extension safety valve, and the unresolved statutory-construction split on whether the dismissal is truly automatic.

Home › Statutes › 11 U.S.C. Section 521(i) - Automatic Dismissal

Empirical research on this section

For case-pattern analysis on how federal bankruptcy courts apply Section 521(i), including district-level patterns and primary-source dockets, see openbankruptcyproject.org/cases/. All datasets licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

What Is Section 521(i)?

Section 521(i) is the BAPCPA-era enforcement mechanism for the document-filing duties imposed on individual debtors by Section 521(a)(1). Added in 2005, it provides that if an individual debtor in a voluntary Chapter 7 or Chapter 13 case fails to file all of the information required by Section 521(a)(1) within 45 days after the date of the filing of the petition, the case "shall be automatically dismissed effective on the 46th day after the date of the filing of the petition."

The required documents under Section 521(a)(1) include the list of creditors, schedules of assets and liabilities, statement of the debtor's financial affairs, copies of pay stubs received from any employer within 60 days before the petition, statement of monthly net income, and a statement disclosing any reasonably anticipated increase in income or expenditures over the 12 months following the petition.

Official citation: 11 U.S.C. § 521(i)

The 45-Day Clock and the Safety Valve

The 45-day deadline is calculated from the petition date under the Federal Rules of Bankruptcy Procedure governing time computation. Section 521(i)(3) provides the safety valve: on request of the debtor made within the 45-day period, and after notice and a hearing, the court may allow the debtor an additional period of not to exceed 45 days to file the required information if the court finds justification for extending the period for the filing.

The structure produces a hard 45-day baseline with a one-time 45-day extension available only if the debtor moves before the original deadline expires and only on a showing of justification. There is no provision for nunc pro tunc extensions filed after the 45 days have run, and most courts read the statute as foreclosing that possibility.

The Statutory-Construction Split: How "Automatic" Is Automatic?

The literal language of Section 521(i)(1) - "shall be automatically dismissed" - has produced a long-running interpretive disagreement. Two strands of authority have emerged.

The Acosta-Rivera Strand: Self-Executing Dismissal

The First Circuit in In re Acosta-Rivera, 557 F.3d 8 (1st Cir. 2009), and a substantial group of bankruptcy courts have read 521(i) literally. On this view, if the 45 days expire and the required documents are not on file (and no timely extension was granted), the case is dismissed as a matter of law on the 46th day. No order is required. The clerk should note the dismissal; a creditor or party in interest may file a motion to confirm dismissal under Section 521(i)(2), but the motion confirms an event that has already happened rather than creating it.

This reading produces sharp consequences. The automatic stay terminates on the 46th day. A trustee may not validly administer the estate after that point. Acts by the debtor or others after the deemed-dismissed date are evaluated as if no bankruptcy case were pending. Courts adopting this strand have sometimes been required to unwind transactions that occurred after the technical dismissal date.

The In re Wirum Strand: Judicial Discretion Preserved

The countervailing line, exemplified by In re Wirum, 308 B.R. 918 (Bankr. N.D. Cal. 2004) and its successors (and informed by some appellate dicta in other circuits), holds that the dismissal is not truly automatic. On this view, "shall be automatically dismissed" must be read against the background of the court's longstanding authority to manage its own cases under Section 105(a) and the court's continuing jurisdiction to determine its own jurisdiction. A court entertaining a substantial-compliance argument, an equitable-tolling argument, or a question whether the missing item was actually required under 521(a)(1) is not bound to treat the case as dismissed before deciding those questions.

This strand stresses anomalous outcomes that flow from a literal reading - dismissals that occur silently while the case continues to be administered, transactions vulnerable to attack months later, creditor reliance interests upended retroactively - and treats the dismissal as effective only after the court enters a confirming order.

The Section 521(i)(4) Trustee Veto

Section 521(i)(4) supplies a partial reconciliation. It allows the trustee, with the consent of the debtor, to request the court to decline to dismiss the case if the trustee determines that the missing information would not materially impair administration of the estate. The court "may decline to dismiss the case" on that motion. This statutory grant of discretion is one of the textual hooks the Wirum strand uses to argue that "automatic" cannot mean fully self-executing - if the trustee can ask the court to keep the case alive, the dismissal cannot have already happened in any final sense before that motion is decided.

Practically, 521(i)(4) is most often invoked when the missing item is a pay stub or similar peripheral document and the trustee has already gathered the necessary information through the meeting of creditors or other means.

Practical Workflow for Debtors and Counsel

Calendar discipline matters. Section 521(i) is unusual in the Code because it sets a fixed deadline that can trigger dismissal regardless of judicial action. Counsel cannot rely on a court "getting around to" entering a dismissal order; the statutory clock runs in the background.

The standard workflow for individual cases is to confirm at the time of filing that every 521(a)(1) document is either filed contemporaneously or scheduled for filing well within the 45-day window. Pay stubs and statements of net income are common late-filed items because they require coordination with employers and payroll processors; missing these is the most frequent trigger for 521(i) dismissals.

If the debtor anticipates inability to meet the deadline, the 521(i)(3) extension motion should be filed before day 45 with a specific showing of justification - illness, employer non-responsiveness, document destruction, or similar concrete obstacles. The motion must be set for hearing or otherwise resolved within the 45-day window unless local practice permits ex parte relief.

Documents Subject to the 45-Day Rule

Not every filing obligation in Section 521 is policed by the 521(i) automatic-dismissal mechanism. By its terms, 521(i)(1) applies to "the information required by paragraph (1) of subsection (a)." Items required by other subsections - the Section 521(a)(2) statement of intention, the Section 521(a)(6) duty to surrender or redeem secured personal property, or the Section 521(e)(2) tax-return delivery to the trustee - are enforced through different mechanisms (typically Section 707 dismissal motions, Section 362(h) termination of stay, or denial of confirmation in Chapter 13).

The distinction matters in practice. A debtor who has filed all 521(a)(1) documents but failed to provide tax returns under 521(e)(2) is not subject to automatic dismissal under 521(i) - but the case may still be vulnerable to discretionary dismissal on motion of the trustee or US Trustee.

Related Bankruptcy Code Sections

Section 521(i) operates in concert with several other provisions of the Bankruptcy Code:

Section 521(a) - The underlying debtor document-filing duties

Section 105(a) - The court's general equitable authority

Section 707 - Chapter 7 dismissal for cause

Section 362 - The automatic stay (terminates on dismissal)

Section 349 - Effect of dismissal

Understanding how these sections interact is important for debtors, creditors, trustees, and counsel navigating an individual bankruptcy case during its critical first 45 days.

## 11 USC 522 - Exemptions Framework [2026]

☰

11 U.S.C. Section 522 - Exemptions

How the Bankruptcy Code lets a debtor keep certain property out of the estate, when state versus federal exemption schedules apply, the 730-day domicile rule for choosing which state's law governs, and the limits the Supreme Court has placed on courts to surcharge those exemptions.

Home › Statutes › 11 U.S.C. Section 522 - Exemptions

Empirical research on this section

For case-pattern analysis on how federal bankruptcy courts apply this provision, including district-level patterns and primary-source dockets, see openbankruptcyproject.org/cases/. All datasets licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

What Section 522 Does

Section 522 is the exemption statute. Exemptions are the mechanism by which a debtor keeps property out of the bankruptcy estate, beyond the reach of unsecured creditors. Without exemptions, every dollar of a Chapter 7 debtor's assets would be available for liquidation; the exemption schedule is what makes Chapter 7 a workable fresh-start tool rather than a forced surrender of everything the debtor owns.

Official citation: 11 U.S.C. § 522

The section also contains the procedural rules for objecting to claimed exemptions, the federal exemption schedule in subsection (d), the lien-avoidance powers of subsection (f), the homestead caps and reductions in subsections (o), (p), and (q), and the protection of retirement funds in subsection (n).

Section 522(b): Federal Versus State Election

Section 522(b)(1) gives the debtor the option to claim the federal exemptions listed in subsection (d) or the exemptions allowed under applicable nonbankruptcy law (state exemptions plus federal nonbankruptcy exemptions). Section 522(b)(2) authorizes any state to "opt out" and force its residents to use only the state exemption schedule. About two-thirds of states have opted out; the rest permit the debtor to choose.

The choice between federal and state schedules is binary; a debtor in a permissive state cannot mix and match. For married couples filing jointly, both spouses must elect the same schedule (Section 522(b)(1)).

Opt-out states include large jurisdictions like Florida, Texas, Tennessee, North Carolina, and Ohio. Permissive states include Massachusetts, Pennsylvania, New York (with restrictions), and Washington. The list moves; check current state law before electing.

Section 522(b)(3): State-Domicile Rule and the 730-Day Lookback

Before BAPCPA, a debtor could move from a low-exemption state to a high-exemption state shortly before filing and claim the new state's more generous exemptions. BAPCPA added a domicile-lookback rule in Section 522(b)(3)(A) to discourage that maneuver.

Under current law, the debtor must use the exemptions of the state where the debtor was domiciled "for the 730 days immediately preceding the date of the filing of the petition." If the debtor has lived in the current state for less than 730 days, the debtor uses the exemptions of the state where the debtor was domiciled "for the 180-day period immediately preceding such 730-day period, or for a longer portion of such 180-day period than in any other place."

If application of the lookback rule "renders the debtor ineligible for any exemption," the debtor may use the federal exemptions in Section 522(d). This savings clause prevents a debtor from being trapped between two states where, for example, the prior state restricts its exemptions to current residents.

Worked example: debtor moves from State A to State B 18 months before filing. Because the debtor has not been domiciled in State B for the full 730 days, the lookback turns to the 180 days before that 730-day window. If the debtor was in State A throughout that earlier 180-day window, State A's exemptions apply, even though the debtor now lives in State B.

Section 522(d): The Federal Exemption Schedule

For debtors who elect or default into the federal schedule, Section 522(d) lists the federally allowed exemptions, with dollar amounts that are adjusted every three years for inflation under Section 104. The major categories include a homestead exemption, motor vehicle exemption, household goods exemption with a per-item cap, jewelry exemption, "wildcard" exemption (the unused portion of the homestead allowance plus an additional fixed amount that can be applied to any property), tools-of-the-trade exemption, life insurance, professionally prescribed health aids, retirement funds, alimony and support, and personal-injury and wrongful-death recoveries.

The federal homestead is materially less generous than several state homesteads. Debtors in opt-in states with significant home equity routinely elect state law for the homestead reason alone. The federal wildcard, by contrast, is often more flexible than state wildcards and can be load-bearing for a debtor with a checking-account balance or other property that does not fit a category-specific exemption.

Section 522(f): Lien Avoidance

Section 522(f) gives the debtor a powerful tool: the right to avoid (strip off) two kinds of liens that impair an exemption to which the debtor would otherwise be entitled.

Section 522(f)(1)(A) allows avoidance of "a judicial lien" that impairs an exemption, with limited carve-outs for domestic-support obligations. A judgment creditor who has recorded a judgment lien against the debtor's home can have that lien avoided to the extent it impairs the debtor's homestead exemption. The calculation formula in Section 522(f)(2) is mathematical: the lien impairs the exemption to the extent that the sum of the lien, all other liens, and the exemption exceeds the value the debtor's interest in the property would have absent any liens.

Section 522(f)(1)(B) allows avoidance of "a nonpossessory, nonpurchase-money security interest" in certain categories of consumer goods: household furnishings, household goods, wearing apparel, appliances, books, animals, crops, musical instruments, jewelry held primarily for personal use, professionally prescribed health aids, and tools of the trade. The classic application is the "consolidation loan" lender that took a blanket security interest in everything in the debtor's house as nonpurchase-money collateral; Section 522(f)(1)(B) eliminates the security interest and converts the lender to general unsecured status.

Section 522(o) and (p): Homestead Reduction

BAPCPA added two homestead caps targeting pre-filing equity manipulation.

Section 522(o) reduces a debtor's homestead claim by the value of any nonexempt property the debtor "disposed of in the 10-year period ending on the date of the filing of the petition" with intent to hinder, delay, or defraud creditors, if that nonexempt value was converted into the homestead. This addresses the abuse of liquidating nonexempt assets and pouring the proceeds into an unlimited-homestead-state residence shortly before filing.

Section 522(p) imposes an absolute cap on homestead exemptions claimed for residences acquired within 1,215 days (about 3 years and 4 months) before filing. The cap is adjusted for inflation under Section 104. The provision applies regardless of intent: even an honest move into a high-exemption state and an honest purchase of a primary residence is subject to the cap if it falls within the 1,215-day window. Section 522(p) does not cover transfers between in-state principal residences (the "rollover" carve-out).

Section 522(q) imposes a similar absolute cap when the debtor has been convicted of a felony demonstrating abuse of the bankruptcy laws, has been found liable for certain securities-law violations, or owes a debt arising from intentional misconduct that caused serious physical injury or death.

Law v. Siegel: Limits on Equitable Surcharge

The Supreme Court held in Law v. Siegel, 571 U.S. 415 (2014), that a bankruptcy court may not "surcharge" a debtor's homestead exemption to compensate a trustee for fees incurred in unwinding the debtor's fraud. The trustee had argued that the debtor's misconduct in fabricating a fake second mortgage to defeat the trustee's nonexempt-equity recovery justified using the court's equitable powers under Section 105(a) to allow recovery from the otherwise-exempt homestead. The Court unanimously rejected that approach.

The opinion holds that Section 105(a) cannot be used to override the express provisions of the Bankruptcy Code. Section 522 sets out specific grounds on which an exemption may be denied or reduced, and bad-faith litigation conduct is not among them. The fact that the debtor's behavior was "egregious" did not give the bankruptcy court free-floating equitable authority to penalize him by stripping his statutory exemption. Other tools (denial of discharge under Section 727(a), criminal referral, sanctions under nonbankruptcy law) remained available, but reaching into a properly claimed homestead was not.

Doctrinal effect: Law v. Siegel locks the four corners of Section 522 as the only basis for limiting exemptions. A trustee who believes the debtor has obtained an exemption through misconduct must work within the statute (timely objection under Rule 4003, denial of discharge under Section 727) rather than asking the court to forge a remedy from Section 105.

Procedure: Objections Under Rule 4003

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 4003(b) requires a party objecting to a claimed exemption to file the objection within 30 days after the conclusion of the meeting of creditors (or within 30 days of an amendment to the exemption schedule). The Supreme Court held in Taylor v. Freeland & Kronz, 503 U.S. 638 (1992), that the failure to object within the deadline forecloses challenges to even patently improper exemption claims. Trustees and creditors must act quickly or lose the right entirely.

Related Bankruptcy Code Sections

Section 541 - Property of the estate

Section 727 - Chapter 7 discharge and denial grounds

Section 105 - General powers of the court

Section 704 - Chapter 7 trustee duties

Section 104 - Dollar amount adjustments

11 U.S.C. Section 522 - Exemptions

Plain-English guide to bankruptcy exemptions: federal versus state systems, the homestead exemption, the wildcard, lien avoidance under 522(f), and the BAPCPA caps.

Home › Statutes › 11 U.S.C. Section 522 - Exemptions in Bankruptcy

Empirical research on this section

For case-pattern analysis on how federal bankruptcy courts apply this provision, including district-level patterns and primary-source dockets, see openbankruptcyproject.org/cases/. All datasets licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

Exemptions under 11 U.S.C. 522 are the rules that let you keep property in bankruptcy: home equity, a car, household goods, tools of your trade, and retirement accounts up to set dollar limits. You use either the federal exemption set or your state's, depending on where you have lived under the domicile rule, and many states require their own. Property covered by an exemption is protected from both the trustee and your creditors.

What Is Section 522?

Section 522 governs what property an individual debtor may exempt from the bankruptcy estate. Exempt property is removed from the trustee's reach and remains with the debtor after the case, even though it is initially property of the estate under Section 541. Exemptions are central to the fresh-start policy of consumer bankruptcy, ensuring that debtors retain a minimum baseline of property necessary for ongoing life.

Official citation: 11 U.S.C. § 522

Federal Versus State Exemptions: Section 522(b)

Section 522(b)(1) gives individual debtors the option to elect either the federal exemptions listed in Section 522(d) or the exemptions provided by applicable state law plus federal nonbankruptcy exemptions, "unless the State law that is applicable to the debtor under paragraph (3)(A) specifically does not so authorize." This "opt-out" provision allows states to require their residents to use state exemptions exclusively. Approximately two-thirds of states have opted out, leaving residents with no choice but state exemptions.

Section 522(b)(3) defines applicable state law by reference to the debtor's domicile during the 730 days preceding the petition. Where the debtor has moved between states during the look-back period, the applicable state is determined by where the debtor was domiciled for the greater portion of the 180-day period preceding the 730-day look-back. The complex domicile rules are an anti-forum-shopping measure adopted by BAPCPA in 2005.

Federal Exemptions: Section 522(d)

The federal exemptions of Section 522(d), available in non-opt-out states, include (with dollar amounts subject to triennial inflation adjustment under Section 104):

522(d)(1): Homestead exemption in residence used as a residence by the debtor or a dependent.

522(d)(2): Motor vehicle exemption.

522(d)(3): Household furnishings, clothing, appliances, books, animals, crops, or musical instruments, up to per-item and aggregate caps.

522(d)(4): Jewelry held primarily for personal use.

522(d)(5): The "wildcard" exemption, allowing the debtor to exempt additional value in any property, including unused portions of the homestead exemption.

522(d)(6): Tools of the trade.

522(d)(7): Life-insurance contracts (other than credit life).

522(d)(8): Life-insurance dividends and interest, up to a cap.

522(d)(10): Various social-security, public-assistance, alimony, retirement, and similar benefits to the extent reasonably necessary.

522(d)(11): Right to receive certain personal-injury, wrongful-death, lost-future-earnings, and other awards.

522(d)(12): Retirement funds in tax-exempt accounts (added in 2005).

Homestead Cap: Section 522(p) and 522(q)

BAPCPA imposed federal limits on state-law homestead exemptions to combat forum shopping. Section 522(p) caps the homestead exemption at a specified amount (subject to inflation adjustment) for interests acquired by the debtor within 1,215 days before the petition. Section 522(q) imposes an additional cap on debtors with certain pre-petition misconduct (securities-law violations, intentional torts causing serious physical injury or death within 5 years preceding the petition, racketeering convictions).

These provisions limit, but do not eliminate, the ability of debtors to use favorable state homestead exemptions (such as Florida or Texas). The 1,215-day look-back is roughly 40 months, meaning a debtor can fully claim a generous state homestead exemption only if the property was acquired more than three years before filing.

Lien Avoidance: Section 522(f)

Section 522(f) allows the debtor to avoid certain liens that impair an exemption. The two categories of avoidable liens are:

522(f)(1)(A): Judicial liens (other than judicial liens securing a domestic-support obligation).

522(f)(1)(B): Nonpossessory, non-purchase-money security interests in certain household goods, tools of the trade, and similar property.

The arithmetic test for impairment is set out in Section 522(f)(2)(A): the lien impairs an exemption to the extent the sum of the lien, all other liens on the property, and the amount of the exemption that could be claimed if there were no liens exceeds the value of the debtor's interest in the property absent any liens. Section 522(f) is one of the few avoidance powers vested in the debtor (rather than the trustee), reflecting its purpose of protecting the fresh start.

Procedure for Claiming Exemptions

The debtor claims exemptions on Schedule C, filed with the petition or shortly thereafter under Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 1007. Parties in interest may object to claimed exemptions under Rule 4003(b), generally within 30 days after the conclusion of the meeting of creditors under Section 341. Failure to object timely results in the exemption being allowed as claimed, even if invalid, under Taylor v. Freeland & Kronz, 503 U.S. 638 (1992).

Related Bankruptcy Code Sections

This section operates in concert with several other provisions of the Bankruptcy Code:

Section 541 - Property of the estate from which exemptions are drawn

Section 521 - Debtor duty to file a list of exempt property

Section 727 - Discharge in Chapter 7 protecting exempt-property recovery

Section 524 - Discharge injunction protecting exempt property post-discharge

Understanding how these sections interact is important for debtors, creditors, trustees, and counsel navigating a bankruptcy case.

Topical deep-dive on Section 522

11 USC 522 - exemptions framework (deep dive) — federal versus state election, the 730-day domicile rule, lien avoidance under 522(f), homestead reduction under 522(o) and 522(p), and Law v. Siegel.

## 11 USC 524 - The Discharge Injunction [2026]
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/section-524-discharge-injunction.html

openbankruptcyproject.org

11 U.S.C. Section 524 - The Discharge Injunction

Plain-English guide to the permanent injunction against collection of discharged debts, reaffirmation procedures, and the boundary between dischargeable and non-dischargeable obligations.

Home › Statutes › 11 U.S.C. Section 524 - The Discharge Injunction

Empirical research on this section

For case-pattern analysis on how federal bankruptcy courts apply this provision, including district-level patterns and primary-source dockets, see openbankruptcyproject.org/cases/. All datasets licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

The discharge injunction under 11 U.S.C. 524 is the permanent court order that replaces your discharged debts: once a debt is discharged, creditors are barred forever from trying to collect it. Unlike the automatic stay, which is temporary, the 524 injunction never expires. A creditor who knowingly tries to collect a discharged debt can be held in civil contempt and ordered to pay your damages and attorney's fees.

What Is Section 524?

Section 524 of Title 11 establishes the discharge injunction, the permanent successor to the automatic stay of Section 362. Once a discharge is entered under Section 727 (Chapter 7), 1141 (Chapter 11), 1192 (Subchapter V), 1228 (Chapter 12), or 1328 (Chapter 13), Section 524(a) operates as a court-ordered injunction against any act to collect, recover, or offset a discharged debt as a personal liability of the debtor.

The injunction is in rem with respect to the debtor's personal liability: it does not extinguish the debt itself, but it permanently bars the creditor from pursuing the debtor personally. Valid liens on property survive the discharge unless avoided.

Official citation: 11 U.S.C. § 524

Scope of the Injunction: Section 524(a)

Section 524(a) operates in three ways:

524(a)(1): Voids any judgment, at any time obtained, to the extent it is a determination of personal liability of the debtor on a discharged debt.

524(a)(2): Operates as an injunction against the commencement or continuation of any action, the employment of process, or any act to collect, recover, or offset any such debt as a personal liability of the debtor.

524(a)(3): Operates as an injunction against acts to collect community property acquired after the petition that would be property of the estate if the spouse had been a debtor.

The injunction reaches collection letters, phone calls, lawsuits, credit-reporting inaccuracies that imply continued personal liability, and any other conduct designed to coerce repayment of a discharged debt.

Reaffirmation Agreements: Section 524(c) and (d)

A debtor may voluntarily agree to remain personally liable on a discharged debt through a reaffirmation agreement under Section 524(c). To be enforceable, the agreement must satisfy stringent requirements:

The agreement must be made before discharge is granted.

The debtor must receive the disclosures required by Section 524(k).

The agreement must be filed with the court.

If the debtor was represented by counsel during negotiation, counsel must file the declaration required by Section 524(c)(3) attesting to the voluntariness of the agreement and that it does not impose an undue hardship.

If the debtor was not represented by counsel, court approval is required after a hearing under Section 524(d), with a finding that the agreement is in the debtor's best interest and does not impose an undue hardship.

The agreement is subject to a rescission period running until the later of discharge or 60 days after filing with the court (Section 524(c)(4)).

Caution: A reaffirmation agreement that is not properly disclosed, executed, or supported by counsel's declaration is unenforceable. Courts scrutinize reaffirmations involving real estate, vehicles in good repair, and other high-value collateral closely.

Liens Survive the Discharge

The discharge eliminates the debtor's personal liability but does not, on its own, eliminate liens. As the Supreme Court has consistently observed, a valid security interest "rides through" the bankruptcy unless the lien is avoided under Sections 506, 522(f), 544, 547, 548, or another avoidance provision. A secured creditor may not pursue the debtor for a personal deficiency on a discharged debt, but it retains its in rem rights against the collateral.

Where a debtor wishes to keep collateral free of a lien securing a discharged consumer debt, the debtor may invoke redemption under Section 722 (lump-sum payment of the present value of the collateral) or negotiate a voluntary reaffirmation under Section 524(c).

Remedies for Violations

Section 524 does not contain its own damages provision. Most courts enforce violations of the discharge injunction through civil contempt under Section 105(a). The Supreme Court clarified the standard in Taggart v. Lorenzen, 587 U.S. 554 (2019), holding that a creditor may be held in civil contempt for violating a discharge order if "there is no fair ground of doubt as to whether the order barred the creditor's conduct." This is an objective standard; subjective good faith is not a complete defense where there is no reasonable basis for the creditor's view.

Available remedies include actual damages, attorneys' fees, and in egregious cases, coercive sanctions. Punitive damages are available in some circuits but are not uniformly recognized under the contempt framework.

Exceptions to the Injunction

The injunction reaches only debts that are discharged. Debts excepted from discharge under Section 523 (such as certain taxes, domestic-support obligations, student loans absent undue hardship, debts obtained by fraud, and willful and malicious injury) remain collectible after discharge. Whether a debt is excepted may itself require litigation through an adversary proceeding under Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 7001.

Section 524(e) further clarifies that the discharge of the debtor does not affect the liability of any other entity (co-debtors, guarantors, sureties). Creditors may continue to pursue non-debtor obligors even after the debtor's discharge, subject to the codebtor stays of Sections 1201 and 1301 while the case is pending.

Related Bankruptcy Code Sections

This section operates in concert with several other provisions of the Bankruptcy Code:

Section 362 - Automatic stay, the temporal predecessor to the discharge injunction

Section 523 - Exceptions to discharge

Section 727 - Chapter 7 discharge

Section 1192 - Subchapter V discharge

Section 522 - Exemptions and lien avoidance under 522(f)

Understanding how these sections interact is important for debtors, creditors, trustees, and counsel navigating a bankruptcy case.

Topical deep-dives on Section 524

Section 524 discharge injunction deep dive — scope of the injunction under 524(a)(2), the reaffirmation framework under 524(c) and (d), and the Taggart v. Lorenzen willful-violation standard.

11 U.S.C. Section 524(j) - Mortgage Statements and Reaffirmation Specifics

The narrow BAPCPA-era safe harbor permitting home-mortgage holders to send ordinary periodic statements and accept voluntary payments after discharge - and what falls outside the safe harbor.

Home › Statutes › 11 U.S.C. Section 524(j) - Mortgage Safe Harbor

Empirical research on this section

For case-pattern analysis on how federal bankruptcy courts apply this provision, including district-level patterns and primary-source dockets, see openbankruptcyproject.org/cases/. All datasets licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

What Is Section 524(j)?

Section 524(j) is a narrow safe harbor inside the discharge-injunction structure of Section 524. It permits a holder of a claim secured by the debtor's principal residence to communicate with the discharged debtor about the mortgage and accept voluntary payments, without violating the Section 524(a)(2) discharge injunction, provided certain conditions are met. The provision was added to address the practical reality that many Chapter 7 debtors choose to retain their home and continue making payments without formally reaffirming the mortgage.

Outside of 524(j), the discharge injunction prohibits any "act, to collect, recover or offset any such debt as a personal liability of the debtor." Sending account statements, late notices, or arrearage demands to a discharged debtor would ordinarily be presumptively coercive and sanctionable. Section 524(j) carves out a defined zone where such ordinary servicing communications are permitted.

Official citation: 11 U.S.C. § 524(j)

The Three Statutory Conditions

Section 524(j) requires all three of the following:

(j)(1): The creditor holds a security interest in the principal residence of the debtor;

(j)(2): The creditor (or its assignee) seeks "periodic payments associated with a valid security interest" in lieu of pursuit of in rem relief to enforce the lien; and

(j)(3): The creditor's communication is "in the ordinary course of business between the creditor and the debtor" and is not an attempt to collect the debt as a personal liability of the debtor.

If any of these conditions is missing, the communication falls outside the safe harbor and is governed by the general 524(a)(2) injunction.

What the Safe Harbor Permits

Under Section 524(j), a home-mortgage holder may, after discharge, send:

Periodic billing statements showing current payment amount, escrow figures, payment due date, and outstanding principal balance;

Notices of escrow adjustments, including annual escrow analyses required by RESPA;

Year-end mortgage-interest statements (IRS Form 1098);

Insurance and tax notices showing flood insurance, hazard insurance, and property tax obligations;

Routine servicing communications such as transfer-of-servicing notices, change-of-address notifications, and customer-service correspondence.

The creditor may also accept voluntary payments from the discharged debtor and apply them to the loan account. The CFPB has issued guidance and amended Regulation X periodic-statement rules to align with the Section 524(j) framework, recognizing that most discharged debtors who retain their home expect and benefit from continued statements.

What the Safe Harbor Does Not Permit

Section 524(j) does not protect:

Demand letters, collection calls, or threats of personal-liability collection;

Late notices or default notices that imply personal liability beyond the in rem remedy;

Suit, judgment, or wage-garnishment efforts seeking personal recovery on the discharged debt;

Negative credit reporting that misrepresents the debt as a personal obligation (the underlying personal liability is discharged; only the in rem lien survives);

Statements that omit required bankruptcy-discharge disclosures where Regulation X / Regulation Z requires them.

A creditor that strays beyond ordinary-course servicing into collection-coercive conduct loses 524(j) protection and exposes itself to contempt sanctions under Taggart v. Lorenzen, 587 U.S. 554 (2019), which establishes that a contempt sanction for violating a discharge injunction requires "no fair ground of doubt" that the conduct was unlawful.

"Ride-Through" and the Practical Reality

Although the Code formally requires either reaffirmation or redemption to retain personal liability on a secured debt, courts have long recognized a "ride-through" or "fourth option": continue to make payments without reaffirming, and the creditor's lien survives but the personal liability is discharged. Section 524(j) effectively codifies the servicing dimension of ride-through for mortgages, allowing the loan to continue functioning operationally even though personal liability has been wiped out. BAPCPA's 2005 amendments tightened ride-through for personal property (see Section 521(a)(2) and (a)(6)), but the home-mortgage ride-through remains common practice.

Reaffirmation Distinguished: Section 524(c) and (d)

Section 524(c) provides the procedure for an enforceable reaffirmation agreement: written agreement, attorney certification (or, if pro se, court approval after a hearing), disclosures required under 524(k), and timely filing. A properly reaffirmed debt remains personally enforceable after discharge. Section 524(j) is fundamentally different: it does not create or revive any personal liability. The discharged debt remains discharged; 524(j) simply permits routine post-discharge servicing communications about the surviving lien.

The distinction matters in default scenarios: if the debtor reaffirmed, the creditor may sue for any deficiency after foreclosure; if the debtor merely rode through with 524(j) servicing, the creditor is limited to foreclosure proceeds and cannot pursue a deficiency judgment.

Common Procedural Postures

Section 524(j) issues typically arise in the following contexts:

Post-discharge contempt motions where a homeowner alleges the mortgage servicer's statements crossed into collection coercion;

Class-action discharge-injunction litigation against national servicers over statement formatting and disclosure language;

CFPB or state-AG enforcement actions under the FDCPA or state UDAP statutes targeting servicer communications with discharged debtors;

Loss-mitigation disputes where servicer post-discharge documentation requirements implicate ordinary-course-servicing analysis;

Credit-reporting disputes about how discharged mortgage debt should be coded with the consumer reporting agencies.

Related Bankruptcy Code Sections

Section 524(a) - General discharge injunction

Section 524(c), (d), (k) - Reaffirmation agreements and disclosures

Section 521(a)(2) - Statement of intention for secured debts

Section 722 - Redemption of personal property

Section 1322(b)(5) - Cure and maintenance of home mortgages in Chapter 13

Section 727 - Chapter 7 discharge

## 11 USC 525 - Anti-Discrimination Protections [2026]
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/section-525-anti-discrimination/

11 U.S.C. Section 525 - Anti-Discrimination Protections

A deep-dive guide to the protections that bar governmental units, private employers, and certain student-loan lenders from discriminating against bankruptcy debtors.

Home › Statutes › 11 U.S.C. Section 525 - Anti-Discrimination

Empirical research on this section

For case-pattern analysis of how courts apply Section 525 to professional licensing, public employment, and student-loan contexts, see openbankruptcyproject.org/cases/. All datasets licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

What Is Section 525?

Section 525 is the bankruptcy anti-discrimination statute. It supplements the Section 524 discharge injunction by prohibiting certain types of post-bankruptcy retaliation that fall outside the literal collection conduct that Section 524 covers. Where Section 524 stops creditors from collecting discharged debts, Section 525 stops governmental units, employers, and student-loan creditors from punishing the debtor for having filed bankruptcy or for having discharged a debt.

Section 525 was enacted in response to Perez v. Campbell, 402 U.S. 637 (1971), in which the Supreme Court struck down an Arizona statute that suspended driver's licenses of discharged debtors who had not paid pre-bankruptcy judgment debts. Congress codified Perez and extended its rule to a broader set of governmental and employment contexts.

Official citation: 11 U.S.C. § 525

Section 525(a): Governmental Unit Discrimination

Section 525(a) prohibits a governmental unit from denying, revoking, suspending, or refusing to renew a license, permit, charter, franchise, or "other similar grant" to, condition such a grant to, discriminate with respect to such a grant against, or deny employment to, terminate the employment of, or discriminate with respect to employment against, a person that is or has been a debtor under this title, solely because the debtor is or has been a debtor under this title, has been insolvent before commencement of the case or during the case but before discharge, or has not paid a debt that is dischargeable or has been discharged.

The "solely because" qualifier matters. A governmental licensor can refuse a license for any reason unrelated to the bankruptcy filing or the discharged debt, but it cannot impose conditions specifically tied to those facts.

In re Stoltz, 315 F.3d 80 (2d Cir. 2002), held that a public housing authority's eviction of a Chapter 7 debtor for nonpayment of discharged rent violated Section 525(a). The court treated continued occupancy in public housing as a "similar grant" within the statute's reach, extending Section 525(a) beyond conventional licenses and permits.

Section 525(b): Private Employer Discrimination

Section 525(b) extends a narrower set of anti-discrimination protections to private employment. A private employer may not terminate the employment of, or discriminate with respect to employment against, an individual who is or has been a debtor under this title, has been insolvent before commencement of the case or during the case but before discharge, or has not paid a debt that is dischargeable or has been discharged.

The key textual difference from Section 525(a) is the absence of any protection against initial hiring discrimination. The leading case, In re Burnett, 635 F.3d 169 (5th Cir. 2011), and several other circuits have held that Section 525(b) does not prohibit a private employer from refusing to hire a person because of a prior bankruptcy filing. The protection runs only to existing employees, not applicants.

Section 525(b)'s "solely because" trigger applies identically, requiring causation tracing to the bankruptcy filing or the unpaid discharged debt.

Section 525(c): Student Loan Discrimination

Section 525(c), added in 1994, prohibits a governmental unit that operates a student grant or loan program, and a person engaged in a business that includes the making of loans guaranteed or insured under a student loan program, from denying a grant, loan, loan guarantee, or loan insurance to a person that is or has been a debtor under this title or a bankrupt or debtor under the Bankruptcy Act, or another person with whom the debtor or bankrupt has been associated, because the debtor or bankrupt is or has been a debtor under this title or a bankrupt or debtor under the Bankruptcy Act, has been insolvent before the commencement of a case under this title or during the pendency of the case but before the debtor is granted or denied a discharge, or has not paid a debt that is dischargeable in the case under this title or that was discharged under the Bankruptcy Act.

Section 525(c) does not prohibit denial based on standard creditworthiness factors that are independent of the bankruptcy event. It does prohibit denial that is causally traceable to the bankruptcy filing or to the underlying discharged debt.

Interplay with the Section 524 Discharge Injunction

Section 524 and Section 525 work in tandem. Section 524(a)(2) operates as a permanent injunction against any act to collect, recover, or offset any discharged debt as a personal liability of the debtor. Section 525 picks up where Section 524 leaves off, prohibiting collateral retaliation that does not technically constitute collection conduct.

The two provisions can be violated by a single act. A governmental agency that refuses to renew a contractor's license unless the contractor pays a discharged pre-petition tax debt is simultaneously attempting to coerce payment of a discharged debt (Section 524(a)(2)) and conditioning a license on payment of a discharged debt (Section 525(a)). Remedies overlap but are not identical, and litigants typically plead both provisions.

Remedies and Enforcement

Section 525 does not contain its own express damages provision. Courts have generally relied on Section 105(a), which authorizes the bankruptcy court to "issue any order, process, or judgment that is necessary or appropriate to carry out the provisions of this title," as the basis for compensatory damages, attorney fees, and injunctive relief for Section 525 violations.

In re Bracewell, 454 F.3d 1234 (11th Cir. 2006), illustrates the procedural framework. The court treated a creditor's improper offset against farm program payments as both a Section 525 and a Section 524 violation and confirmed that Section 105 supports a money remedy for noncompliance.

Punitive damages remain controversial. Some courts require willful and egregious conduct; others have declined to award them absent an express Section 525 punitive provision. Sovereign immunity issues under Section 106 must be navigated when the defendant is a governmental unit.

In re Doser, 412 F.3d 1056 (9th Cir. 2005), addresses ancillary remedy questions in the discharge-related context. The general rule is that Section 525 supports actual damages, attorney fees, and equitable relief, with punitive damages available in narrower circumstances depending on circuit.

Related Bankruptcy Code Sections

Section 105 - Equitable powers supporting Section 525 remedies

Section 106 - Abrogation of governmental sovereign immunity

Section 362 - Automatic stay during pendency of case

Section 524 - Discharge injunction operating in tandem with Section 525

Section 727 - Chapter 7 discharge

Section 1328 - Chapter 13 discharge

## 11 USC 526 - Restrictions on Debt Relief Agencies [2026]
