Home
›
RECAP and PACER
›
Should I Register on PACER?

Should I register myself on PACER as a debtor?

Will your attorney do it for you? Almost never. Should you do it yourself? Yes — on day one, before anything else moves in your case. Here is the short version, the long version, and the five-minute registration playbook.

Published by the Open Bankruptcy Project. Updated 2026-05-21. Educational information only; not legal advice.

The Short Answer

No, your attorney will probably not register you. Yes, you should register yourself.

Most bankruptcy attorneys use PACER under their own credentials and send their clients paper or PDF copies of the major filings. That is the default. It is not malpractice; it is the way most firms have always done it. But it leaves you dependent on the firm for visibility into your own case, and that is a posture an informed debtor does not need to accept.

Registering yourself takes about five minutes. It costs nothing at signup. For the typical debtor who checks their own docket once or twice a month, it stays free indefinitely. You will see exactly what the court, the trustee, your attorney, and every opposing party sees — the complete, unfiltered, chronological record of your case.

Why Your Attorney Probably Won't

The default in most firms is that clients do not have PACER accounts

This is worth saying plainly because it is the part most debtors find surprising. When you sign a representation agreement, the firm registers itself with the court as your counsel of record. The firm gets electronic notice of filings through its own CM/ECF system. It does not, as a matter of course, set up a separate PACER account for you.

There are a few reasons this is the norm:

It saves the firm a step

Registering a client requires the client's personal information, a credit card, and a few minutes of staff time. Multiply by hundreds of clients per year and it is a workflow many firms have simply never built.

The firm has the information it needs without it

Once an attorney is counsel of record, the firm receives every electronic notice the court generates. The firm does not need the client to have a PACER account to do its job.

Some attorneys prefer the simpler relationship

An informed client asks better questions, which is good for the case but means a longer phone call. A firm that operates at high volume may default to summarizing rather than copying the client on every filing.

None of these are bad reasons. But none of them are reasons you should not register. Your account costs the firm nothing, requires nothing from them, and changes nothing about how they do their work. It only changes what you can see.

Why You Should Register Yourself

Five things you can see with PACER that you might not otherwise

The point of registering is not distrust of your attorney. It is independent visibility into a public record about you. Here is what that visibility actually buys you:

1. The complete docket in date order

Every filing in your case, by every party, in the sequence the court received it. Your attorney is likely to forward you the major ones. PACER shows you every one, including the routine notices, scheduling orders, and short procedural entries that are easy to skip in summary.

2. The claims register

Every creditor who filed a proof of claim against you, the date filed, the amount claimed, and the supporting documentation. Some claims will be ones you expected. Others may be from creditors you forgot about, were unaware of, or believe were already paid. If a claim is inflated or duplicative, you will not know to flag it for your attorney unless you see it.

3. Filings by parties who are not your attorney

The trustee files status reports and statements. Creditors file motions for relief from stay, objections to discharge, and adversary complaints. The U.S. Trustee files notices and inquiries. These are all yours to read. They show what is happening around your case, not just what your side is doing.

4. The exact timing of every entry

Filings are date-stamped to the minute. If something happens late on a Friday, you can see it Friday night. You do not have to wait for the firm to flag it on Monday. For time-sensitive responses, the timestamp matters.

5. Fee applications

If your attorney files a fee application (most Chapter 13 and Chapter 11 cases require one), it lists the time entries, hourly rates, and total billed. You should know what is being charged to your estate. The fee application is on the docket whether or not anyone forwards it to you.

None of these are exotic. They are the ordinary contents of a bankruptcy file. Independent docket monitoring is the difference between knowing what is in your own case and being told a summary.

What It Actually Costs

For a typical debtor: almost certainly nothing

PACER's fee structure looks complicated but is unusually friendly to low-volume users.

$0.10 per page, with a $3.00 cap per document. A 50-page motion costs $3.00, not $5.00.

If your total fees in a calendar quarter (Jan-Mar, Apr-Jun, Jul-Sep, Oct-Dec) stay under $30.00, the bill is waived. You owe nothing.

Account creation is free. The card on file is for billing only and is not charged at signup.

341 meeting audio recordings are a flat $2.40 each and do not count against the $3.00 document cap.

A debtor checking their own docket once or twice a month, pulling a handful of documents over the life of the case, will almost never reach the $30 quarterly threshold. The most common bill a casual user sees is $0.00.

If you do come close to the threshold — for example, because you want to read every filing in a complex Chapter 11 — install the free RECAP browser extension. Every document you pull is automatically mirrored to the free RECAP Archive. Future readers (including you) get it for free.

Common Objections (And the Honest Answer)

The things debtors hesitate over — and why they shouldn't

"Won't my attorney be offended?"

No. Reading your own court file is not a vote of no confidence; it is the normal posture of an informed client. Good attorneys welcome it because it means fewer basic questions over the phone. A firm that actively discourages you from looking at the public record of your own case is telling you something about how they operate, and it is worth knowing.

"Will my attorney know I'm checking?"

No. PACER does not notify any party when a user views a docket. Your reads are recorded in your own billing log only.

"I don't understand most of what's on a docket."

That is normal at the start. Most debtors find that after a few visits they can recognize the major entry types: motions, orders, notices, status reports, claims. You do not have to read every page. You just have to be able to scan the docket and notice when something unexpected appears. If something looks wrong, send your attorney the entry number and the date and ask.

"I'm worried about giving my credit card."

The card is held for billing only. It is not charged at signup. If you never cross the $30 quarterly threshold, it is never charged at all. PACER is a federal court system; the card-on-file requirement is standard, and the system is not in the habit of surprise charges.

"What if I find something I don't understand or that worries me?"

Ask your attorney. That is what they are there for. Independent docket monitoring is not a substitute for legal advice. It is the visibility that lets you ask better questions.

When to Register

The right time is day one

If you have not filed yet, you can register before your case is even on the docket. There is no waiting period and no requirement that you be a party to a case. PACER is open to the public.

If you have already filed, the right time to register is now. The longer you wait, the more of the early case record (petition, schedules, statement of financial affairs, first creditor notices) you are reading second-hand.

Registration takes about five minutes. The system issues credentials immediately. We have a separate step-by-step walkthrough that covers the registration form, picking the right court, and pulling your first document:

› How to Use PACER (Step-by-Step Walkthrough)

FAQ

Frequently asked questions

Will my attorney register me on PACER?

Usually no. Most bankruptcy attorneys do not register their clients on PACER. They use the system through their own credentials, send the client paper or PDF copies of the major filings, and assume the client will rely on the firm for case visibility. This is the default in most firms, but it is not a rule. You can register yourself at any time, and most experienced debtors do.

Do I need PACER if I have a lawyer?

You do not strictly need it. Your case will function whether or not you have an account. But an independent PACER account gives you the same view of your own case that your lawyer, the trustee, the court, and any opposing party already have. Most debtors who register say it took five minutes to set up and gave them confidence they did not have before.

Is it rude to my attorney if I look at my own docket?

No. The bankruptcy docket is a public record. Reading your own case is not a vote of no confidence in your attorney; it is the normal posture of an informed client. Good attorneys welcome it because it reduces the number of basic questions they have to field by phone.

How much does it cost a debtor to monitor their own case on PACER?

Almost always nothing. PACER charges $0.10 per page with a $3.00 cap per document. If your total fees for a calendar quarter stay under $30.00, the bill is waived. A typical debtor checking their own docket once or twice a month will not come close. Many never see a bill.

What can I see on PACER about my own case that I would not otherwise see?

The complete docket: every filing in the case, in date order, with the underlying PDF. That includes things your attorney may not forward you proactively: trustee status reports, creditor proofs of claim with attached documentation, U.S. Trustee inquiries, fee applications, motions filed by other parties, and the timing of every entry. You see the case the way the court sees it, not a filtered summary.

Can I register on PACER the same day my case is filed?

Yes. There is no waiting period. Registration takes about five minutes, and the system issues credentials immediately. You can do it the same day your petition is filed, or even before.

Will my attorney know if I check my own docket?

No. PACER does not notify any party when another user views a docket. Your activity is recorded in your own account billing log only. Your attorney has no visibility into your reads.

If I find something on PACER I do not understand, what should I do?

Ask your attorney. That is exactly what they are there for. The point of independent docket monitoring is not to substitute for legal advice; it is to make sure nothing important is happening in your case without your awareness. If something looks wrong, send your attorney the entry number and the date and ask.

Can I get PACER access without giving a credit card?

Not for an individual account. PACER requires a card on file at registration, but it is not charged at signup. The card is only billed if your quarterly activity exceeds $30.00. Many users never see a charge. If the card-on-file requirement is a hard stop, the free RECAP Archive at CourtListener is the best alternative; many bankruptcy dockets are mirrored there in full and require no registration at all.

What if my attorney tells me I don't need PACER?

They are right that the case will function without it. They are wrong if they suggest you should not have it. The bankruptcy docket is your own court record; reading it is normal and recommended. If a firm pushes back on a client setting up their own PACER account, that is a question worth raising directly: why?

Where to go from here

Less-Common Bankruptcy Vehicles

Specialty Chapters

Most bankruptcy practice involves Chapter 7, Chapter 11, or Chapter 13. But the Bankruptcy Code reserves several chapters and sub-chapters for specialized debtor types - municipalities, family farmers and fishermen, healthcare businesses, single-asset real-estate entities, and stockbroker/commodity-broker liquidations. These five deep-dives explain when each specialty vehicle applies and how its rules differ from the general framework.

Last modified 2026-05-22.

Home/Specialty Chapters

About the specialty chapters

The Bankruptcy Code's specialty chapters exist because the standard reorganization or liquidation machinery does not fit every debtor type. Chapter 9 covers municipalities and other governmental units; it is far more limited than chapter 11 because state sovereignty constraints prevent the federal court from interfering with the political or governmental powers of the debtor. Chapter 12 covers family farmers and fishermen with regular annual income; it offers a more debtor-friendly cramdown framework than chapter 11 or chapter 13, reflecting the seasonal nature of agricultural income.

Within chapter 7 and chapter 11, the Code further differentiates by industry. Subchapter III of chapter 7 contains the special rules for stockbroker liquidations under SIPA-coordinated framework, and subchapter IV covers commodity-broker liquidations. Chapter 11 contains streamlined provisions for single-asset real-estate cases (the so-called SARE provisions in sections 101(51B) and 362(d)(3)) and special provisions for healthcare businesses (sections 333, 351, and 1170-1174) that recognize the regulatory and patient-care complications of healthcare reorganizations.

Each specialty regime modifies the standard framework in ways that can be load-bearing for case strategy. Practitioners moving from a general chapter 11 practice into a specialty chapter must reorient to the modified deadlines, the specialized officers (patient-care ombudsmen, stockbroker liquidation trustees), and the substantive carve-outs.

Specialty-chapter deep-dives

Chapter 9 Municipal BankruptcyEligibility under section 109(c) including the state-authorization requirement, the limited scope of judicial intervention under section 904, and the plan-confirmation standards adapted for governmental debtors.

Chapter 12 Family Farmer and Family FishermanEligibility ceilings, the section 1222(b)(9) cramdown of secured creditors over the value of the collateral, and the simplified plan-confirmation framework relative to chapter 11.

Healthcare Business BankruptcyThe patient-care ombudsman required by section 333, transfer of patients under section 704(a)(12) and section 1106(a)(1), and the disposal of patient records under section 351.

Single Asset Real Estate (SARE)SARE eligibility under section 101(51B), the section 362(d)(3) accelerated relief-from-stay timeline (90 days to file a plan or commence monthly interest payments), and the litigation strategy for the secured lender.

Stockbroker and Commodity Broker LiquidationSubchapter III of chapter 7 (stockbrokers) and subchapter IV (commodity brokers), the priority of customer claims under sections 752 and 766, and the relationship with SIPA proceedings.

Eligibility note: Each specialty chapter has strict eligibility requirements policed by the United States Trustee and challenged by parties in interest. A case filed under the wrong chapter can be dismissed or converted, with significant loss of debtor-friendly procedural advantages.

## Chapter 12 Family Farmer and Fisherman Bankruptcy - Eligibility, Cramdown, and Reorganization [2026]
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/specialty-chapters/chapter-12-family-farmer/

openbankruptcyproject.org
☰

Chapter 12 Family Farmer and Fisherman

A purpose-built reorganization chapter for family farms and family fishing operations: who qualifies under Sections 101(18) and 101(19A), how the debt limits work, and how the Section 1225 secured-claim cramdown can rewrite a farm-loan balance to the value of the collateral.

Home › Specialty Chapters › Chapter 12 Family Farmer and Fisherman Bankruptcy

Empirical research on this chapter

For case-pattern analysis on Chapter 12 filings, including district-level patterns and primary-source dockets, see openbankruptcyproject.org/cases/. All datasets licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

Why Chapter 12 Exists

Chapter 12 was enacted in response to the 1980s farm crisis, when collapsing land values, high interest rates, and weak commodity prices put tens of thousands of American family farms into default. Existing Chapter 11 was too expensive and procedurally heavy for most operating farms, while Chapter 13's debt limits were too low to capture realistic farm balance sheets. Congress created Chapter 12 in 1986 as a temporary measure, repeatedly extended it, and made it permanent in 2005. In 2005 it was also expanded to cover "family fishermen," recognizing that commercial fishing operations faced structurally similar problems: heavy secured debt against specialized depreciating equipment, seasonal cash flow, and limited collateral substitutes.

The structural innovations of Chapter 12 - aggressive secured-debt cramdown, generous plan length, treatment of capital-gains taxes on farm-asset sales as unsecured claims, and a streamlined trustee - all reflect the same underlying judgment: that working farms and fishing operations whose only realistic chance to repay creditors is to keep operating need a procedural environment that lets them keep operating.

Official citation: 11 U.S.C. Chapter 12 (Sections 1201-1232); eligibility definitions at 11 U.S.C. Section 101(18) and 101(19A).

Who Is a "Family Farmer"? Section 101(18)

Section 101(18) defines "family farmer" with two parallel sub-definitions: one for individuals (and spouses) and one for corporations and partnerships. Both versions require (in their current statutory form) that the debtor be engaged in a farming operation, that the debtor's aggregate debts not exceed the statutory cap, that at least 50 percent of the debt (excluding the debt on the principal residence, unless that debt arises from the farming operation) arises out of the farming operation, and that more than 50 percent of the debtor's gross income for the applicable look-back period came from the farming operation.

The aggregate-debt limit is set in the Code at a dollar figure that has been raised multiple times by amendment and is further adjusted for inflation under Section 104. Practitioners should always confirm the current cap against the most recent Section 104 adjustment, because the figure has changed materially over the past decade. Individuals must also be U.S. residents and must satisfy the gross-income and percentage tests on a personal basis; corporate and partnership filers must satisfy parallel structural tests, including that more than 50 percent of the equity be held by one family (and relatives of that family) conducting the farming operation, and that more than 80 percent of the value of corporate or partnership assets be related to the farming operation.

Who Is a "Family Fisherman"? Section 101(19A)

Section 101(19A) defines "family fisherman" using the same architectural template as Section 101(18) but tuned to commercial fishing operations. The definition was added in 2005 to extend Chapter 12 to commercial fishing families that had been ineligible under the original 1986 statute despite facing structurally identical reorganization problems. The aggregate-debt cap for family fishermen has historically been lower than the family-farmer cap; both are subject to Section 104 inflation adjustments. The 50-percent-of-debt-from-fishing-operation test and the 50-percent-of-gross-income-from-fishing-operation test mirror the family-farmer structure.

What "Farming Operation" Covers

Section 101(21) defines "farming operation" inclusively: "farming, tillage of the soil, dairy farming, ranching, production or raising of crops, poultry, or livestock, and production of poultry or livestock products in an unmanufactured state." Courts have repeatedly grappled with edge cases - vertically integrated operations, custom-feeding contracts, hobby farms, large industrial agribusiness operations, and similar - and the case law tends to focus on whether the debtor bears the risks inherent in farming (weather, market, biological cycle) as opposed to operating in an essentially industrial or service capacity. In re Hayes and similar cases illustrate how courts apply the test functionally rather than by reference to formal labels.

The Section 1225 Cramdown - The Signature Tool

The most consequential single provision in Chapter 12 is the secured-claim cramdown under Section 1225(a)(5). It allows the debtor to keep secured collateral over the secured creditor's objection by paying the secured creditor, through the plan, the present value of the allowed secured claim. The "allowed secured claim" is determined by valuing the collateral under Section 506(a). If the collateral is worth less than the contract balance - the typical scenario when land or equipment values have fallen - the contract is bifurcated: the secured portion equals collateral value; the deficiency is an unsecured claim treated alongside other unsecured claims under the plan.

The Section 1225(a)(5)(B) "cramdown" path requires that the secured creditor retain its lien and that the plan provide for payments of a value (as of the effective date of the plan) of not less than the allowed amount of the secured claim. Through this mechanism a $1,200,000 farm-loan balance on land worth $800,000 can be effectively rewritten to an $800,000 secured obligation plus a $400,000 unsecured claim. The unsecured deficiency is paid (if at all) only out of disposable income over the plan term.

The applicable interest rate on the rewritten secured claim is determined under Till v. SCS Credit Corp., 541 U.S. 465 (2004), which adopted a formula-rate approach (the prime rate plus a risk premium). The cramdown plus the Till rate together make Chapter 12 a powerful tool for over-leveraged operations that have a credible operating future.

Plan Length and Disposable Income

A Chapter 12 plan is generally a three-year plan but may extend to five years "for cause." The "disposable income" commitment under Section 1225(b) requires that all of the debtor's projected disposable income to be received during the plan period, after deducting amounts reasonably necessary for the maintenance or support of the debtor or a dependent and amounts reasonably necessary for the continuation, preservation, and operation of the debtor's farming or fishing operation, be applied to make payments to unsecured creditors. As with Subchapter V, the business-expense deduction is critical: the disposable-income computation runs after legitimate operating expenses, not before.

Treatment of Capital-Gains Tax on Farm Asset Sales

One of the more specialized features of Chapter 12 is Section 1232 (added in 2005, amended in 2017), which treats federal, state, and local capital-gains-tax claims arising from the sale of farm assets used in the debtor's farming operation as unsecured claims that are not entitled to priority under Section 507(a)(8) and are dischargeable. The Supreme Court resolved a circuit split on a related question in Hall v. United States, 566 U.S. 506 (2012), and Congress responded by enacting the Family Farmer Bankruptcy Clarification Act of 2017. The practical effect is that a Chapter 12 debtor can sell appreciated farm assets during the case (for example, to right-size the operation or to satisfy a secured creditor) without the resulting capital-gains tax becoming a non-dischargeable priority obligation.

The Chapter 12 Trustee

The Chapter 12 standing trustee has a narrower role than a Chapter 11 trustee. The debtor remains in possession and continues to operate the farm or fishing business. The trustee distributes plan payments, monitors compliance, and may object to claims and plans, but does not displace management. This light-touch structure mirrors Chapter 13 and reflects the same underlying judgment that an operating business reorganizing under tight cash-flow conditions needs continuity of operations.

Discharge in Chapter 12

Section 1228 governs the Chapter 12 discharge. The default discharge under Section 1228(a) is granted after the debtor completes all payments under the plan. The "hardship discharge" under Section 1228(b) is available where the debtor's failure to complete plan payments is due to circumstances for which the debtor should not justly be held accountable, modification of the plan under Section 1229 is not practicable, and unsecured creditors have already received at least as much as they would have received in a hypothetical Chapter 7. As with Subchapter V cramdown discharges, the timing of discharge in Chapter 12 differs materially from immediate-discharge regimes - the debtor must complete the plan term to receive the full discharge benefit.

The scope of the Chapter 12 discharge is broad. It excepts the same categories of debt that are excepted from a Chapter 13 discharge under Section 523(a), but the Chapter 12 discharge is otherwise general. Long-term secured debts paid through a plan but maturing after the plan term remain enforceable on their contract terms; the discharge does not extinguish the underlying lien or accelerate the maturity.

Chapter 12 Compared to Chapter 11 and Chapter 13

Versus Chapter 11: Chapter 12 is materially cheaper, faster, and procedurally simpler. There is no creditors' committee, no disclosure-statement requirement, and no absolute-priority rule. Chapter 11 (including Subchapter V) is available to family farmers and fishermen as an alternative when the debt cap is exceeded or when other structural reasons argue against Chapter 12.

Versus Chapter 13: Chapter 12's debt caps are much higher than Chapter 13's, and Chapter 12's cramdown of secured claims on principal residence is unconstrained by the Section 1322(b)(2) anti-modification rule that protects home mortgages in Chapter 13. Chapter 13 is generally available only to wage-earning individuals; Chapter 12 is purpose-built for farming and fishing operations whose income is seasonal and tied to commodity cycles.

Related Bankruptcy Code Sections

Section 101(18) - Definition of family farmer

Section 101(19A) - Definition of family fisherman

Section 101(21) - Definition of farming operation

Section 506 - Determination of secured status (basis for the bifurcation that drives cramdown)

Section 1222 - Contents of plan

Section 1225 - Confirmation of plan (including the cramdown standard)

Section 1228 - Discharge

Section 1232 - Treatment of capital-gains tax on farm-asset sales

## Chapter 9 Municipal Bankruptcy - Eligibility, State Authorization, and Tenth Amendment Limits [2026]
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/specialty-chapters/chapter-9-municipal/

openbankruptcyproject.org
☰

Chapter 9 Municipal Bankruptcy

Eligibility under Section 109(c), the state-authorization gatekeeper, why municipalities cannot be liquidated, the Tenth Amendment ceiling on judicial power, and the modern case framework from Detroit through Puerto Rico.

Home › Specialty Chapters › Chapter 9 Municipal Bankruptcy

Empirical research on this chapter

For case-pattern analysis on Chapter 9 filings, including district-level patterns and primary-source dockets, see openbankruptcyproject.org/cases/. All datasets licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

What Is Chapter 9?

Chapter 9 of the Bankruptcy Code provides a specialized reorganization path for an insolvent "municipality." It is one of the smallest chapters by filing volume but among the most legally consequential: every Chapter 9 case touches deep questions about federalism, public services, public pensions, and the limits of federal judicial power over a state's political subdivisions. There were only a few hundred Chapter 9 filings in the entire modern era of the Bankruptcy Code, and many of those were small special-purpose districts rather than cities. The headline cases that the public remembers - Detroit (2013), Stockton (2012), San Bernardino (2012), Jefferson County, Alabama (2011), Vallejo (2008), and Orange County (1994) - are statistical outliers.

The defining structural feature is that Chapter 9 is a reorganization-only chapter. There is no liquidation analogue. A municipality cannot be sold, dissolved by a federal court, or have its assets distributed to creditors the way a Chapter 7 debtor's property is liquidated by a trustee. This is not a drafting oversight; it is constitutional architecture. The federal courts cannot dismantle a state's political subdivision because the Tenth Amendment reserves to the states the power to define and organize their own governments.

Official citation: 11 U.S.C. Chapter 9 (Sections 901-946); eligibility at 11 U.S.C. Section 109(c).

Who Is a "Municipality"? Section 101(40)

Section 101(40) defines "municipality" as a "political subdivision or public agency or instrumentality of a State." That phrase reaches farther than the everyday meaning of "city." Counties, towns, villages, school districts, sewer authorities, water districts, hospital districts, transit authorities, and similar bodies have all qualified at one time or another. What it excludes is also important. A state itself is not a municipality and cannot file Chapter 9. Federal entities cannot file. A private nonprofit hospital that happens to receive public funding is not a municipality. The State of Puerto Rico's debt restructuring proceeded under a different federal statute (PROMESA, 48 U.S.C. Chapter 20) rather than Chapter 9 precisely because the Commonwealth was not, on the better reading of the statute, a "State" for Chapter 9 purposes and so could not authorize its own Chapter 9 filing.

The Five-Part Section 109(c) Eligibility Test

Section 109(c) is the gatekeeper. A would-be Chapter 9 debtor must satisfy all five of the following:

Section 109(c)(1) - Municipality: The debtor must be a municipality as defined by Section 101(40).

Section 109(c)(2) - State authorization: The debtor must be "specifically authorized, in its capacity as a municipality or by name, to be a debtor under such chapter by State law, or by a governmental officer or organization empowered by State law to authorize such entity to be a debtor under such chapter." This is the single most contested element in modern Chapter 9 litigation.

Section 109(c)(3) - Insolvent: The debtor must be "insolvent" as defined in Section 101(32)(C), meaning generally unable to pay debts as they become due or unable to pay debts as they become due within the meaning of cash-flow insolvency.

Section 109(c)(4) - Desire to effect a plan: The debtor must desire to effect a plan to adjust its debts.

Section 109(c)(5) - Pre-petition negotiation or impracticability: The debtor must have either (A) obtained creditor agreement, (B) negotiated in good faith and failed, (C) been unable to negotiate because negotiation was impracticable, or (D) reasonably believed a creditor was about to obtain an avoidable preference.

Each prong is an independent hurdle. A petition that satisfies four out of five fails. Eligibility is typically litigated at the outset, and the burden is on the petitioning municipality to prove each element by a preponderance of the evidence.

The State-Authorization Requirement

The Section 109(c)(2) state-authorization requirement is what most clearly distinguishes Chapter 9 from every other chapter. The default rule across the United States is that a municipality is not authorized to file Chapter 9 unless its home state has affirmatively said so. States fall into roughly four categories: (1) states that broadly authorize municipal filings without precondition; (2) states that authorize filings subject to a state oversight process or gubernatorial approval; (3) states that have specific case-by-case authorization mechanisms; and (4) states that prohibit municipal bankruptcy outright. As a result, the same financially distressed city would have very different options depending on which state line it sits on.

When the City of Detroit filed in 2013, the constitutionality and procedure of Michigan's emergency-manager statute and the governor's authorization were among the central litigated issues. When the City of Stockton, California filed in 2012, California's pre-bankruptcy mediation process under AB 506 was the threshold question. When Bridgeport, Connecticut tried to file in the early 1990s, the absence of state authorization defeated the petition. The state-authorization step is therefore not a formality but the substantive choke point of Chapter 9 access.

No Liquidation, No Sale, No Dissolution

A Chapter 9 case can have only one possible terminus: a confirmed plan of adjustment, dismissal, or conversion (and conversion is not available for Chapter 9). The case cannot end with the court liquidating the municipality's assets. Federal courts cannot abolish, dissolve, or restructure the municipality's governance. They cannot order the sale of public assets without the municipality's consent. They cannot appoint a receiver to run the city. They cannot order tax increases or budget changes.

This is in part a constitutional limit and in part written into the Code. Section 904 ("Limitation on jurisdiction and powers of court") expressly prohibits the bankruptcy court from interfering, by any stay, order, or decree, with: (1) any of the political or governmental powers of the debtor; (2) any of the property or revenues of the debtor; or (3) the debtor's use or enjoyment of any income-producing property, unless the debtor consents. The municipality holds far more practical leverage than a corporate Chapter 11 debtor because the court's powers over it are dramatically narrower.

The Tenth Amendment Backdrop

The constitutional question that runs underneath Chapter 9 is whether the federal bankruptcy power, granted in Article I, Section 8, Clause 4, can reach a state's own political subdivisions at all. The Supreme Court answered yes, but with substantial limits, in United States v. Bekins, 304 U.S. 27 (1938), which upheld a redesigned municipal bankruptcy statute after an earlier version had been struck down in Ashton v. Cameron County Water Improvement District No. One, 298 U.S. 513 (1936). The compromise the Court accepted - and that survives in the modern statute - is that the federal government can give a willing municipality a forum to restructure its debts, but it cannot impose the regime over the objection of the state or the municipality, and the federal court cannot displace the municipality's governmental functions.

Every modern Chapter 9 case operates within that compromise. The state-authorization requirement, the Section 904 limitations on court power, the absence of a trustee with management authority, and the inability to liquidate are all expressions of the same underlying constitutional balance.

Treatment of Public Pensions

One of the most heavily litigated questions in modern Chapter 9 has been whether and how public-employee pension obligations can be modified in a plan of adjustment. The orthodoxy before Detroit was that state constitutional or statutory protections for public pensions placed them outside the reach of federal bankruptcy. The Eastern District of Michigan held in 2013 that pension obligations are contract rights for federal supremacy purposes, that contract rights can be impaired in a federal bankruptcy, and that state constitutional pension protections do not bind the federal bankruptcy court. The Detroit plan ultimately reduced pension benefits through negotiated adjustment, though by less than initial proposals.

Other Chapter 9 cases have reached different practical outcomes through negotiation rather than litigation. The Stockton plan preserved its CalPERS pension obligations while imposing larger haircuts on bond debt; bondholders objected, and the question of whether CalPERS could have been impaired was litigated but not definitively answered on appeal because the parties settled. The legal landscape therefore offers no single bright-line rule about pensions in Chapter 9; the answer turns on the state-law characterization of the pension, the contractual structure, and the negotiation dynamics in the particular case.

The Puerto Rico Framework: PROMESA

Puerto Rico is not a state for Chapter 9 purposes and could not authorize its own Chapter 9 filing under the statute as written. After the Commonwealth's debt crisis escalated, Congress enacted the Puerto Rico Oversight, Management, and Economic Stability Act (PROMESA) in 2016. PROMESA Title III created a separate federal-court debt-adjustment proceeding modeled on Chapter 9 but adapted for a non-state territory, with oversight by the Financial Oversight and Management Board. The Commonwealth and several instrumentalities, including the Puerto Rico Electric Power Authority, restructured tens of billions of dollars of debt under PROMESA between 2017 and 2022.

PROMESA is not a part of the Bankruptcy Code, but a Chapter 9 reader needs to understand it because the doctrines, case law, and many of the practitioners overlap. The eligibility, plan-confirmation, and creditor-protection rules in PROMESA Title III incorporate Chapter 9 provisions by cross-reference.

Plan Confirmation in Chapter 9

The Chapter 9 plan-confirmation standards in Section 943 borrow heavily from Chapter 11 but include several Chapter 9-specific requirements: the plan must comply with the provisions of title 11 made applicable by Section 901; the plan must be in the "best interests of creditors"; the plan must be feasible; the debtor cannot be prohibited by law from taking any action necessary to carry out the plan; and any regulatory or electoral approval necessary under non-bankruptcy law has been obtained or the plan is expressly conditional on such approval. The "best interests" test in Chapter 9 is qualitatively different from its Chapter 7 counterpart because there is no liquidation comparator; courts have applied a "more than the creditors would otherwise receive" standard tied to realistic non-bankruptcy alternatives.

Section 904 - Limitation on jurisdiction and powers of court

Section 943 - Confirmation of a plan of adjustment

## Healthcare Business Bankruptcy - Patient-Care Ombudsman, Patient Transfers, and Records Disposal [2026]
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/specialty-chapters/healthcare-business-bankruptcy/

openbankruptcyproject.org
☰

Home
Tools
Research
Impact
Legal Aid
About
Contact

Healthcare Business Bankruptcy

When a hospital, nursing home, hospice, or other "health care business" files bankruptcy, three sections do most of the special work: the Section 333 patient-care ombudsman, the Section 704(a)(12) duty to transfer patients, and the Section 351 protocol for disposal of patient records.

Home › Specialty Chapters › Healthcare Business Bankruptcy

Empirical research on this area

For case-pattern analysis on healthcare-business bankruptcies, including district-level patterns and primary-source dockets, see openbankruptcyproject.org/cases/. All datasets licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

What Makes a Health Care Business Different

A bankruptcy proceeding involving a hospital, nursing home, hospice, ambulatory surgical center, or other healthcare provider is not procedurally different from any other Chapter 7 or Chapter 11 in its broad strokes - the automatic stay, the property of the estate, the priority and claims rules, the plan-confirmation framework all apply identically. What is different is the overlay of patient-protection provisions that Congress added in the 2005 amendments. Those provisions exist because the property of the estate in a healthcare-business case includes operating clinical capacity (admitted patients, ongoing treatment plans, custody of vulnerable individuals) and informational assets (medical records subject to federal and state privacy law) whose mishandling can cause clinical harm or violate other federal statutes.

Three statutory tools carry most of the load: (1) Section 333, which authorizes appointment of a patient-care ombudsman; (2) Section 704(a)(12), which imposes a transfer duty on a trustee or debtor in possession when patients can no longer be cared for in the existing facility; and (3) Section 351, which prescribes how patient records must be handled if the estate's assets are insufficient to pay for indefinite storage.

Official citations: 11 U.S.C. Section 333; 11 U.S.C. Section 351; 11 U.S.C. 704(a)(12); definition at 11 U.S.C. 101(27A).

Who Is a "Health Care Business"? Section 101(27A)

Section 101(27A) defines "health care business" as a public or private entity that is primarily engaged in offering to the general public facilities and services for the diagnosis or treatment of injury, deformity, or disease, or for surgical, drug-treatment, psychiatric, or obstetric care, and includes (among other things) any general or specialized hospital, ancillary ambulatory, emergency, or surgical treatment facility, hospice, home health agency, and other health care institution that is similar to those entities. The definition also expressly includes long-term-care facilities, including skilled nursing facilities, intermediate-care facilities, and assisted-living facilities.

The definition is functional rather than formal. A debtor's status as a health care business does not turn on its tax classification, ownership structure, or whether it accepts Medicare. It turns on whether the debtor is primarily engaged in offering diagnostic or treatment services to the public. A medical-equipment manufacturer is not a health care business under Section 101(27A); a pharmacy that simply fills prescriptions is generally not; a physical-therapy clinic open to the public generally is.

The Patient-Care Ombudsman: Section 333

Section 333(a)(1) provides that if the debtor is a health care business, the court "shall order, not later than 30 days after the commencement of the case, the appointment of an ombudsman to monitor the quality of patient care and to represent the interests of the patients of the health care business unless the court finds that the appointment of such ombudsman is not necessary for the protection of patients under the specific facts of the case." Appointment is the default; non-appointment is the exception that must be affirmatively found.

The ombudsman is appointed by the United States Trustee (subject to court approval) and is typically a person experienced in long-term-care ombudsman work, healthcare administration, or healthcare law. The ombudsman is not a trustee and does not displace management. The ombudsman's role is to monitor the quality of patient care, interview patients and staff, review records, and report findings to the court no less than every 60 days. If the ombudsman determines that the quality of patient care is declining significantly or is otherwise being materially compromised, the ombudsman must file a motion or written report with the court immediately.

Section 333(c) protects the confidentiality of patient information accessed by the ombudsman; the ombudsman may not review confidential patient records without court approval and authorization consistent with applicable non-bankruptcy privacy law (including HIPAA where applicable). The compensation and expense reimbursement of the ombudsman are administrative-priority expenses of the estate under Section 503(b).

Patient Transfers: Section 704(a)(12)

Section 704(a)(12), made applicable in Chapter 11 by Section 1106(a)(1), imposes a transfer duty on the trustee (or debtor in possession) "if the debtor is a health care business, [to] use all reasonable and best efforts to transfer patients from a health care business that is in the process of being closed to an appropriate health care business that - (A) is in the vicinity of the health care business that is closing; (B) provides the patient with services that are substantially similar to those provided by the health care business that is in the process of being closed; and (C) maintains a reasonable quality of care."

The duty is triggered by closure of the health care business or any unit within it that admits patients. The transferee facility must be in the vicinity, must provide substantially similar services, and must maintain a reasonable quality of care. "Vicinity" is judged practically - a 200-mile transfer of an elderly nursing-home resident is generally not a transfer to a vicinity facility; a transfer across town generally is. Substantially similar services means the receiving facility must be capable of providing the same level of clinical care, not merely a different healthcare service of any kind.

Disposal of Patient Records: Section 351

Section 351 governs what happens to patient records when a healthcare-business case ends and the estate cannot afford indefinite storage. The procedure is sequenced.

First, the trustee (or debtor in possession) must publish notice in one or more appropriate newspapers that the records will be destroyed unless claimed within 365 days. The notice must give patients and insurance providers the opportunity to claim their records.

Second, during the 365-day notice period, the trustee must attempt to provide individual notice by certified mail to each patient (and to the patient's most recent insurance carrier) at the last known address.

Third, if the records are not claimed within the 365-day period, the trustee may dispose of them. The disposal protocol depends on the format. Electronic records must be created in a manner that prevents disclosure of confidential patient information (deletion with overwriting, destruction of storage media, or equivalent). Paper records must be destroyed by burning, shredding, or other physical-destruction means designed to prevent reconstruction.

The statute is designed to thread a narrow needle: estates of failed healthcare businesses often have no funds to pay for permanent records-retention contracts, but federal and state law require that medical records not be casually disposed of. Section 351 supplies a federally compliant safe-harbor procedure that satisfies the privacy and records-retention requirements while liberating the estate from open-ended storage obligations.

When the Ombudsman Is Not Necessary

Section 333(a)(1) creates a default of appointment but allows the court to find that "the appointment of such ombudsman is not necessary for the protection of patients under the specific facts of the case." The factor list that has emerged from the case law is generally non-exclusive but commonly includes: the cause of the bankruptcy filing (financial vs. clinical); whether the case is a reorganization or a liquidation; the number of patients served; whether the facility is subject to ongoing oversight by state or federal regulators (a CMS-certified facility, for example, already has the federal survey-and-certification apparatus watching it); whether the debtor has its own internal quality-of-care and compliance program; whether there is any history of patient-care complaints; and whether the debtor is small enough that the cost of an ombudsman would materially erode the estate.

The decision is typically litigated at the outset of the case on the debtor's motion to forgo ombudsman appointment. The U.S. Trustee usually takes a position; if the court denies the motion the ombudsman is appointed within the 30-day default window. Most operating-hospital cases see an ombudsman appointed; small non-clinical providers (for example, a billing service that meets a narrow reading of the definition) more often obtain the no-ombudsman finding.

Operating Issues Specific to Healthcare Bankruptcies

Medicare and Medicaid receivables and claims: Provider-agreement obligations, recoupment rights, and program-integrity audits all sit alongside the bankruptcy case. The federal government's setoff and recoupment rights against pending Medicare receivables can materially affect available estate liquidity.

State licensure: A state hospital or long-term-care license is generally not transferable as a matter of property of the estate. A sale of substantially all assets typically requires the buyer to obtain its own state license, which can introduce timing risk into a Section 363 sale.

Critical-vendor and emergency-services issues: Pharmaceuticals, blood products, dialysis supplies, and the like cannot be interrupted; first-day motions in healthcare cases typically include broader critical-vendor relief than in non-healthcare Chapter 11s.

EMTALA and similar federal obligations: The federal Emergency Medical Treatment and Active Labor Act and related obligations continue to apply through the bankruptcy; they are not stayed.

Related Bankruptcy Code Sections

Section 101(27A) - Definition of health care business

Section 333 - Appointment of patient-care ombudsman

Section 351 - Disposal of patient records

Section 503(b) - Allowance of administrative expenses (including ombudsman compensation)

Section 704(a)(12) - Duty to transfer patients

Section 1106(a)(1) - Chapter 11 trustee/DIP duties (incorporating Section 704)

## Single Asset Real Estate (SARE) Bankruptcy - Definition, the 90-Day Deadline, and Section 362(d)(3) [2026]
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/specialty-chapters/single-asset-real-estate/

openbankruptcyproject.org
☰

Single Asset Real Estate (SARE)

When a Chapter 11 debtor's only meaningful asset is a single piece of income-producing real property, Section 101(51B) reclassifies the case as SARE and the 90-day adequate-protection deadline of Section 362(d)(3) starts running on day one.

Home › Specialty Chapters › Single Asset Real Estate (SARE)

Empirical research on this area

For case-pattern analysis on SARE filings, including district-level patterns and primary-source dockets, see openbankruptcyproject.org/cases/. All datasets licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

The SARE Designation Matters

Single Asset Real Estate is not a separate chapter of the Bankruptcy Code. SARE is a designation applied to a Chapter 11 case whose debtor satisfies the Section 101(51B) definition. Once the designation attaches, a special creditor-protective deadline kicks in: under Section 362(d)(3), a creditor with a security interest in the SARE real property can obtain stay relief unless, by the later of 90 days after the order for relief or 30 days after the court determines the SARE status, the debtor either (1) files a plan of reorganization that has a reasonable possibility of being confirmed within a reasonable time or (2) begins making monthly payments to the secured creditor at the contract or non-default rate on the value of the creditor's interest.

The original 1994 enactment of SARE applied only to small projects (those with secured debt of $4 million or less). The 2005 amendments removed the debt cap, expanding SARE coverage to large commercial real estate projects. Today the typical SARE case is an office building, a strip-center landlord, a hotel-property single-asset SPE, a multifamily-residential SPE, or a development-land holder. Excluded by statutory definition is real estate that is also being used in an active business by the debtor that goes beyond the operation of the real property itself - most prominently, hotels (which the case law generally treats as not SARE because the hotel operation is itself a substantial business beyond mere real estate operation) and family-farm operations (which are statutorily excluded).

Official citations: 11 U.S.C. Section 101(51B); 11 U.S.C. Section 362(d)(3).

The Section 101(51B) Definition

Section 101(51B) defines "single asset real estate" as "real property constituting a single property or project, other than residential real property with fewer than 4 residential units, which generates substantially all of the gross income of a debtor who is not a family farmer and on which no substantial business is being conducted by a debtor other than the business of operating the real property and activities incidental thereto."

The definition has four operative elements: (1) a single property or project, (2) excluding small (under four-unit) residential real property, (3) generating substantially all of the debtor's gross income, and (4) no substantial business is conducted on the property other than operating the real property itself and incidental activities. The fourth element is the most heavily litigated. The hotel-versus-not question turns on it; so does the question whether an assisted-living facility, a self-storage facility, or a parking-garage operation is SARE. The case law is fact-specific. A debtor that is simply collecting rent from tenants is generally SARE; a debtor whose income depends on operating a substantial service business that happens to be conducted on real property it owns is generally not SARE.

"Project" is broader than "property" - the definition permits a "single project" to include multiple parcels that function as an integrated whole (for example, a master-planned development with several adjacent parcels under common ownership and a single development plan). Conversely, a debtor that owns multiple unrelated properties is generally not SARE even if each property would qualify on its own.

The Section 362(d)(3) Deadline

Section 362(d)(3) is the operative consequence of SARE classification. On a creditor's motion, the court "shall grant relief from the stay" for cause to a creditor whose claim is secured by an interest in SARE real property unless, not later than the date that is the later of (A) 90 days after the entry of the order for relief or (B) 30 days after the court determines that the debtor is subject to Section 362(d)(3), one of the following has occurred:

Plan path: The debtor has filed a plan of reorganization that has a reasonable possibility of being confirmed within a reasonable time, or

Payment path: The debtor has commenced monthly payments that may, in the debtor's sole discretion, be made from rents or other income generated before, on, or after the date of the commencement of the case by or from the property to each creditor whose claim is secured by the real estate (other than a claim secured by a judgment lien or by an unmatured statutory lien), in an amount equal to interest at the then applicable non-default contract rate of interest on the value of the creditor's interest in the real estate.

The 90-day clock is short by the standards of complex Chapter 11. A SARE debtor has roughly three months to either file a plan or begin paying contract-rate interest on the secured value of the property. Failure to satisfy one of the two paths is independent grounds for stay relief.

What the Two Paths Look Like in Practice

The plan path requires more than filing any plan. The plan must have "a reasonable possibility of being confirmed within a reasonable time." Courts have read this requirement strictly. A plan that depends on speculative future financing, a contingent equity infusion, or refinancing in a market that does not exist is generally not a plan with a reasonable possibility of confirmation. The standard is meaningfully tighter than the general feasibility standard at confirmation; the SARE plan must look plausibly confirmable from the moment it is filed.

The payment path requires the debtor to begin paying monthly contract-rate interest on the value of the secured creditor's interest. The value of the secured creditor's interest is determined under Section 506(a) by reference to the value of the collateral - so if the property has fallen in value, the debtor's interest-payment obligation is correspondingly reduced. The interest rate is the non-default contract rate. The payments can come from any source, including rents subject to a cash-collateral order. This is sometimes the more attractive path because it preserves all of the debtor's confirmation optionality.

The Pre-1994 Two-Party Dispute Problem

Before the SARE provisions were enacted in 1994, single-asset real-estate Chapter 11 filings were a perennial complaint of secured creditors. The case typically involved one piece of real estate, one principal secured lender, and a debtor-borrower whose only realistic business was holding that property. There were essentially no unsecured creditors of consequence and no operating business to reorganize. Chapter 11 was used (the creditor complaint went) primarily as a delay device to extract better terms from the lender in what was substantively a two-party dispute. Congress's SARE provisions, refined in 2005, were designed to compress the time available for that kind of use without categorically prohibiting the filing. The 90-day deadline and the two-path safe harbor are the compromise structure.

Strategic Considerations for SARE Debtors

SARE designation is not optional: A debtor cannot opt out of SARE classification by declining to identify the case as SARE on its petition. A secured creditor can move for a determination of SARE status, and if the debtor fits Section 101(51B) the designation attaches and the deadline starts running.

Valuation is the central battleground: Both paths under Section 362(d)(3) turn on the value of the property. A low valuation makes the interest payment small and reduces the secured creditor's leverage on stay relief; a high valuation does the opposite. SARE debtors and their creditors often litigate valuation early in the case.

The plan need not propose a sale: A reorganization-only plan that contemplates a refinance, a new equity infusion, or a workout of the mortgage is permissible if it meets the "reasonable possibility" standard. Many SARE plans propose a sale of the property within the plan because a sale is often the cleanest realistic exit.

Subchapter V interaction: A small commercial real estate debtor that satisfies the Subchapter V debt threshold may be both SARE and a Subchapter V debtor. The Section 362(d)(3) deadline runs in either case; Subchapter V's expedited 90-day plan-filing requirement under Section 1189 maps closely to the SARE timeline.

SARE and the Absolute Priority Rule

Outside of Subchapter V, a SARE Chapter 11 confirmation still has to navigate the absolute-priority rule of Section 1129(b)(2)(B)(ii). Because the typical SARE debtor has a single secured creditor, one or two impaired classes, and limited unsecured creditor body, the practical question is whether the equity holders can retain their interests over the dissent of a secured creditor whose claim exceeds the property's value. The "new value corollary" - the doctrine that equity may retain its interest if it contributes "new value" that is substantial, necessary, in money or money's worth, and proportionate to the retained interest - is frequently litigated in SARE cases. The Supreme Court left the new-value corollary's vitality unresolved in Bank of America v. 203 North LaSalle Street Partnership, 526 U.S. 434 (1999), but held that any retention of equity in exchange for new value must be subject to a market test (typically through competitive bidding or some equivalent mechanism). For SARE debtors with equity-holder restructuring proposals, the LaSalle market-test requirement is a regular procedural hurdle.

Related Bankruptcy Code Sections

Section 101(51B) - Definition of single asset real estate

Section 362(d)(3) - Stay relief in SARE cases

Section 506(a) - Determination of secured status (drives the value of the creditor's interest)

Section 1129 - Standard Chapter 11 confirmation requirements

Section 1189 - Subchapter V plan-filing deadline (parallel structure)

## Stockbroker and Commodity Broker Liquidation - Subchapters III and IV, SIPA Interplay, and Customer-Property Priority [2026]
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/specialty-chapters/stockbroker-commodity-broker-liquidation/

openbankruptcyproject.org

Stockbroker and Commodity Broker Liquidation

Subchapters III and IV of Chapter 7 carve out specialized liquidation regimes for failed brokerage firms. Customer property is segregated from the general estate, customers' net equity claims have priority over general unsecured claims, and the SIPA framework runs in parallel for securities firms.

Home › Specialty Chapters › Stockbroker and Commodity Broker Liquidation

Empirical research on this area

For case-pattern analysis on stockbroker and commodity-broker liquidations, including district-level patterns and primary-source dockets, see openbankruptcyproject.org/cases/. All datasets licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

Why Brokerage Failures Need Special Rules

The standard Chapter 7 distribution model - collect all assets of the debtor into the estate, pay administrative expenses, then pay priority claims, then pay general unsecured claims pro rata - is the wrong model for a failed brokerage. Customers of a broker-dealer typically have assets that they consider theirs: cash held in customer accounts, securities held in street name, margin collateral, and the like. Treating those assets as part of a general bankruptcy estate, available pro rata to all creditors, would convert customer property into general estate funds and produce ruinous outcomes for retail investors. The Bankruptcy Code recognizes this by carving out two specialized subchapters of Chapter 7: Subchapter III for stockbroker liquidation (Sections 741 through 753) and Subchapter IV for commodity broker liquidation (Sections 761 through 767).

The common architecture of both subchapters is to define a category of "customer property," segregate it from the general estate, distribute it first to customers in satisfaction of their "net equity" claims, and only then turn what remains over to general estate distribution. Layered on top, for securities firms, is the Securities Investor Protection Act of 1970 (SIPA), 15 U.S.C. Sections 78aaa et seq., which establishes the Securities Investor Protection Corporation (SIPC) and authorizes a SIPA liquidation proceeding that incorporates large portions of Subchapter III but is administered by SIPC rather than the U.S. Trustee system.

Official citations: 11 U.S.C. Sections 741-753 (stockbroker); 11 U.S.C. Sections 761-767 (commodity broker); 15 U.S.C. 78aaa et seq. (SIPA).

Subchapter III: Stockbroker Liquidation

Subchapter III applies to a "stockbroker" as defined in Section 101(53A) - generally, a person engaged in the business of effecting transactions in securities for the account of others or for its own account. A stockbroker can be a debtor only in Chapter 7; Sections 109(d) and 109(e) preclude a stockbroker from filing Chapter 11 or Chapter 13. The reasoning is that a failed brokerage's only realistic path is an orderly wind-down designed to maximize customer recovery, not a reorganization that contemplates continued operation.

The mechanics in Subchapter III are: the trustee collects "customer property" (Section 741(4)) into a separate distribution pool; the trustee determines each customer's "net equity" claim (Section 741(6)) - the dollar value of the customer's account had the firm liquidated all positions on the filing date; the trustee distributes customer property to customers ratably in satisfaction of net equity claims (Section 752(a)); only after customer claims are paid does any remaining customer property revert to the general estate (Section 752(c)); general unsecured creditors of the broker share in the general estate but not in customer property.

Section 745 governs the treatment of customers whose securities are held in margin accounts and whose accounts are subject to setoff. Section 746 governs how securities of customers may be liquidated and what protections customers have. Section 748 deals with the disposition of property of customers who cannot be identified. Section 749 addresses voidable transfers received by customers. Section 750 prohibits Chapter 11 reorganization for stockbrokers (subject to Section 109's eligibility rules).

SIPA Interplay

For securities firms that are SIPC members - which include virtually all registered broker-dealers that hold customer property - a SIPA liquidation under 15 U.S.C. Section 78eee is the default pathway when the firm fails. SIPA proceedings are filed by SIPC in district court; the court appoints a SIPA trustee; the trustee administers the case under SIPA, which incorporates Bankruptcy Code provisions by reference (with SIPA overlays). The SIPA trustee determines customer claims, distributes customer property, and pays out SIPC-funded "advances" of up to specified caps per customer to cover shortfalls in customer-property distributions.

The SIPA framework is the dominant liquidation regime for retail broker failures. Pure-Chapter-7 Subchapter III liquidations of broker-dealers are unusual because SIPA preempts in nearly every case where customer property is at issue. Subchapter III remains relevant doctrinally: it supplies definitions that SIPA incorporates, it governs cases where SIPA does not apply, and the conceptual model of customer-property segregation and net-equity distribution is identical.

The Bernard L. Madoff Investment Securities (BLMIS) SIPA liquidation, commenced in 2008, is the most prominent modern application of the framework. The trustee's calculation of "net equity" - and specifically the decision to value each customer's claim as the net amount of cash deposited minus cash withdrawn, rather than the fictitious balance shown on the customer's last statement - was litigated to the Second Circuit and beyond. The Second Circuit's decision in In re Bernard L. Madoff Investment Securities LLC, 654 F.3d 229 (2d Cir. 2011), affirmed the trustee's "cash-in, cash-out" approach, holding that customers' net-equity claims were properly measured by their actual contributions and withdrawals rather than by the fabricated account statements they had received. That holding has shaped every subsequent Ponzi-driven SIPA liquidation.

Subchapter IV: Commodity Broker Liquidation

Subchapter IV applies to a "commodity broker" as defined in Section 101(6) - generally, a futures commission merchant, foreign futures commission merchant, clearing organization, leverage transaction merchant, or commodity options dealer. As with stockbrokers, a commodity broker can only be a Chapter 7 debtor; Chapter 11 reorganization is not available.

The structural design parallels Subchapter III but is tuned to the realities of the commodity-futures markets. Section 761(10) defines "customer," Section 761(11) defines "customer property," and Section 761(17) defines "net equity." Section 766 governs the distribution of customer property and contains the central priority scheme: customer property is distributed ratably to customers based on the net equity of customer claims, with subordinate distribution to non-public customers, and any remaining customer property reverts to the general estate.

Two features of commodity broker liquidation deserve highlighting. First, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission's segregation rules under the Commodity Exchange Act (7 U.S.C. Section 6d) require commodity brokers to hold customer funds in segregated accounts before any bankruptcy is contemplated; segregation is therefore a pre-existing regulatory protection that interacts with Section 766's bankruptcy-side distribution priority. Second, Section 766(h) permits the trustee to make prompt distributions of "specifically identifiable" customer property without waiting for the full liquidation, which is particularly important for open commodity positions that must be transferred or liquidated within tight market windows.

The Net Equity Calculation

"Net equity" is the centerpiece concept in both subchapters. In essence, net equity is what the customer's account would have been worth if the broker had liquidated all positions and settled all open transactions as of the filing date. The statutory definitions in Section 741(6) (stockbroker) and Section 761(17) (commodity broker) work through the same conceptual steps: identify the customer's positive balance (the value of securities, cash, or commodity contracts in the account); subtract amounts the customer owes the broker (margin loans, debit balances, contract obligations); the resulting figure is net equity. Customers with positive net equity have claims against customer property; customers with negative net equity have no customer claim and are general creditors (or debtors) of the estate.

In a Ponzi-scheme failure, net equity calculation becomes contentious because account statements may be fictitious. The Madoff/BLMIS litigation established that "cash-in, cash-out" is the appropriate net-equity measure in such cases. Customers who deposited more than they withdrew are net winners with allowable customer claims; customers who withdrew more than they deposited (often early Ponzi participants who received their original investment back plus fictitious "profits") are net losers from the estate's perspective and may face fraudulent-transfer clawback under Sections 548 and 550.

Safe-Harbor Provisions: Sections 546(e), 555, and 559

Brokerage failures interact with a series of "safe harbor" provisions scattered through the Bankruptcy Code that protect certain financial transactions from the avoidance and unwinding tools available in an ordinary bankruptcy. Section 546(e) protects margin payments, settlement payments, and transfers made to or by stockbrokers, financial institutions, financial participants, and securities clearing agencies from preference and constructive-fraudulent-transfer avoidance (with an actual-fraud carve-out under Section 548(a)(1)(A)). Section 555 protects a securities-contract counterparty's right to liquidate, terminate, or accelerate a securities contract notwithstanding the automatic stay. Section 559 provides analogous protection for repurchase agreements. The combined effect is to insulate the securities settlement system from cascading bankruptcy unwinds that could destabilize markets. These safe harbors are particularly consequential in stockbroker liquidations because most of the broker's pre-petition transactions are likely to fall within their protected categories.

Customer-Property Priority Over General Estate Claims

The decisive structural fact about both subchapters is that customer-property distribution is prior to general estate distribution. A general unsecured creditor of a failed broker-dealer - a landlord, a vendor, a trade creditor - does not share in customer property at all. The general creditor recovers only from the general estate (the broker's own assets, after segregation of customer property). Because customer property typically dwarfs the broker's own assets, the general estate in a broker-dealer liquidation is often modest, and the recovery ratio for general unsecured creditors is correspondingly low. This is the opposite of the standard Chapter 7 dynamic, where the estate is the universal source of recovery for all unsecured creditors.

Related Bankruptcy Code Sections

Section 101(6) - Definition of commodity broker

Section 101(53A) - Definition of stockbroker

Section 109(d) - Stockbroker and commodity broker may only be Chapter 7 debtors

Section 741 - Definitions for Subchapter III (including net equity and customer property)

Section 752 - Distribution of customer property in stockbroker liquidation

Section 761 - Definitions for Subchapter IV

Section 766 - Distribution of customer property in commodity broker liquidation

15 U.S.C. Sections 78aaa et seq. - SIPA (parallel statutory framework for securities firms)

Small Business Reorganization Act

Subchapter V Statutes

Subchapter V of Chapter 11 - added by the Small Business Reorganization Act of 2019 and codified at 11 U.S.C. sections 1181 through 1195 - provides a streamlined reorganization track for small business debtors. It eliminates the disclosure-statement requirement, compresses the plan-filing deadline, appoints a standing trustee in every case, and modifies the cramdown rules so that an individual small-business debtor can confirm a plan without unsecured-creditor approval. These six guides walk through the core provisions.

Last modified 2026-05-23.

Home/Subchapter V Statutes

About Subchapter V

Subchapter V is the most consequential reorganization reform Congress has enacted since the Bankruptcy Reform Act of 1978. Before the Small Business Reorganization Act took effect in February 2020, most small businesses that filed Chapter 11 either failed to confirm a plan or converted to Chapter 7. The combination of expensive disclosure-statement litigation, the absolute priority rule, and the cost of professional fees made traditional Chapter 11 functionally inaccessible to firms with revenues below roughly ten million dollars.

Subchapter V solves these problems through three structural changes. First, the eligibility cap (currently set at the inflation-adjusted version of the section 1182(1) threshold) restricts the procedure to true small businesses. Second, the appointment of a standing trustee in every case shifts oversight responsibility from the United States Trustee Program to a private trustee paid from the estate, who reports to the court on plan feasibility and post-confirmation compliance. Third, section 1191(b) cramdown replaces the absolute priority rule with a fair-and-equitable test that turns on the debtor's projected disposable income over a three-to-five year period, allowing an owner-operator to retain equity without paying unsecured creditors in full.

The deep-dives below treat the six core provisions that drive almost every Subchapter V case: eligibility (section 1182), debtor duties (section 1184), trustee authority to remove the debtor-in-possession (section 1185), plan-filing deadlines (section 1189), required plan contents (section 1190), and post-confirmation plan modification (section 1193).

Section-by-section deep-dives

Section 1182 - Small Business Debtor DefinitionThe eligibility definition, the noncontingent-liquidated debt cap (currently the inflation-adjusted threshold), the single-asset real estate exclusion, and the engaged-in-commercial-or-business-activities requirement.

Section 1184 - Debtor-in-Possession DutiesThe Subchapter V debtor-in-possession's fiduciary duties, the section 1116 reporting requirements imported by reference, and the limits on operating the business in the ordinary course.

Section 1185 - Trustee Removal of DebtorThe standard for removing the debtor-in-possession for fraud, dishonesty, incompetence, gross mismanagement, or material default, and the consequences for the standing trustee's role.

Section 1189 - Plan Filing DeadlineThe 90-day plan-filing deadline, the circumstances-beyond-control extension standard, and the consequences of failing to meet the deadline.

Section 1190 - Plan ContentsRequired and permissive plan contents, the section 1190(3) modification of section 1123(b)(5) permitting modification of mortgages secured by the debtor's principal residence in limited circumstances, and the section 1190(1) historical operating disclosures.

Section 1193 - Plan ModificationPre-confirmation and post-confirmation plan modification, the distinct rules for consensual (section 1191(a)) and nonconsensual (section 1191(b)) plans, and the substantial-consummation cutoff.

Procedural note: Subchapter V election is made by checking the appropriate box on the voluntary petition (Official Form 201) at the time of filing. The election can be made later by motion under Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 1020, but doing so resets neither the section 1189 plan-filing deadline nor the standing trustee's appointment date.

## 11 USC 1182 - Subchapter V Small Business Debtor Definition [2026]
