Subchapter V: Plan Confirmation Strategy

Consensual confirmation under Section 1191(a) versus nonconsensual cramdown under Section 1191(b). The modified fair-and-equitable test. The disposable-income commitment over the 3-to-5 year period.

Home › Subchapter V › Plan Confirmation Strategy

Empirical research on Subchapter V confirmation

For case-pattern analysis on Sub V confirmation outcomes, disposable-income disputes, and cramdown decisions by district, see openbankruptcyproject.org/cases/. All datasets licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

The Confirmation Decision Tree

Every Subchapter V plan reaches confirmation through one of two paths. Section 1191(a) provides consensual confirmation; Section 1191(b) provides nonconsensual confirmation, commonly referred to as cramdown. The choice between them is not always elective — if every impaired class accepts, the plan is necessarily a 1191(a) plan; if any impaired non-insider class rejects, the only remaining path is 1191(b). But the negotiation leading up to confirmation is shaped by which path is realistically available, because the discharge timing and post-confirmation oversight regime differ materially between them.

Citation: 11 U.S.C. § 1191(a)-(d); see In re Cleary Packaging, LLC, 36 F.4th 509 (4th Cir. 2022); 11 U.S.C. § 1129(a).

Consensual Confirmation under Section 1191(a)

Section 1191(a) provides that the court shall confirm a plan only if all of the requirements of Section 1129(a), other than paragraph (15), are met. The Section 1129(a)(15) carve-out matters only for individual debtors and addresses the projected disposable income test in standard Chapter 11; it is excluded from Sub V because the disposable-income concept is captured separately under Section 1191(c)(2) and Section 1191(d).

The practical Section 1129(a) checklist for a consensual Sub V plan includes:

1129(a)(1): Plan complies with applicable provisions of the Code (classification under Section 1122, content requirements under Section 1123 as modified by Section 1181(b) and Section 1190).

1129(a)(2): Plan proponent complied with the Code, including disclosure requirements (modified by Section 1181(b) to eliminate the Section 1125 disclosure statement absent court order).

1129(a)(3): Plan proposed in good faith.

1129(a)(4): All payments to professionals and other administrative parties have been approved or are subject to court approval as reasonable.

1129(a)(5): Identity and affiliations of post-confirmation officers and directors disclosed.

1129(a)(6): Rate changes subject to regulatory approval have been obtained.

1129(a)(7): Best interests of creditors test — each holder of an impaired claim either accepted the plan or will receive at least as much as it would in a Chapter 7 liquidation.

1129(a)(8): Each impaired class accepted the plan.

1129(a)(9): Treatment of priority claims complies with subsections (A), (B), and (C).

1129(a)(10): At least one impaired non-insider class accepted.

1129(a)(11): Plan is feasible — not likely to be followed by liquidation or further reorganization.

1129(a)(12): All fees under Section 1930 of Title 28 have been paid.

1129(a)(13): Continued payment of retiree benefits.

1129(a)(14): Domestic support obligations current (individual debtors).

1129(a)(16): Transfers of property by nonprofit debtors compliant with non-bankruptcy law.

The signature consequence of consensual confirmation is immediate discharge under Section 1192. The discharge enters on the effective date of the plan, not on completion of payments. See Subchapter V discharge mechanics.

Nonconsensual Cramdown under Section 1191(b)

Section 1191(b) provides that if a plan meets all requirements of Section 1129(a) other than (a)(8), (a)(10), and (b), the court shall confirm the plan over creditor objection if the plan does not discriminate unfairly and is fair and equitable. Three Section 1129 requirements are dropped:

1129(a)(8): The requirement that each impaired class accept the plan.

1129(a)(10): The requirement that at least one impaired non-insider class accept the plan.

1129(b): The cramdown provisions, including the absolute-priority rule of Section 1129(b)(2)(B)(ii).

What replaces them is the Section 1191(b) standard: no unfair discrimination and fair and equitable, with the latter defined separately in Section 1191(c). Under standard Chapter 11, the fair-and-equitable test forces equity holders to either pay unsecured creditors in full or contribute new value commensurate with the equity retained. Under Sub V, that test is replaced by the disposable-income commitment of Section 1191(c)(2).

The Modified Fair-and-Equitable Standard: Section 1191(c)

Section 1191(c) defines "fair and equitable" for Sub V cramdown purposes. The standard has two components, one for secured claims and one for unsecured claims:

Secured claims — Section 1191(c)(1)

For secured claims, the Sub V standard tracks the standard Chapter 11 standard under Section 1129(b)(2)(A). The plan must provide one of:

Retention of the lien securing the claim and deferred cash payments totaling at least the allowed amount of the claim, with a present value as of the effective date equal to the value of the collateral;

Sale of the collateral subject to the holder’s right to credit bid under Section 363(k); or

The "indubitable equivalent" of the claim.

Unsecured claims — Section 1191(c)(2) and (c)(3)

For unsecured claims, the standard is unique to Sub V. The plan must provide either:

1191(c)(2)(A): All of the debtor’s projected disposable income (Section 1191(d)) for a period of not less than 3 nor more than 5 years, beginning on the date of the first plan payment, will be applied to plan payments; or

1191(c)(2)(B): The value of property to be distributed under the plan in the 3-to-5 year period is not less than the projected disposable income of the debtor.

The plan must also satisfy Section 1191(c)(3): reasonable likelihood that the debtor will be able to make all payments under the plan, and appropriate remedies (which may include liquidation of nonexempt assets) to protect creditors if payments are not made.

The leading appellate decision applying these standards is In re Cleary Packaging, LLC, 36 F.4th 509 (4th Cir. 2022), which addressed the scope of Section 523(a) discharge exceptions in Sub V cramdown but in dicta touched on the broader operational architecture of Section 1191(b). The fair-and-equitable analysis under Section 1191(c) is still being developed at the circuit-court level; most cases addressing the standard remain bankruptcy-court and district-court opinions.

Projected Disposable Income: Section 1191(d)

Section 1191(d) defines disposable income as income received by the debtor that is not reasonably necessary for one of three purposes:

The maintenance or support of the debtor or a dependent;

A domestic-support obligation that first becomes payable after the petition; or

The payment of expenditures necessary for the continuation, preservation, or operation of the debtor’s business.

The third item — the business-expense carve-out — is the most consequential. A Sub V debtor projects future revenue and future operating expenses, and the net is the disposable income subject to the Section 1191(c)(2) commitment. Disputes routinely arise over (a) the realism of revenue projections, (b) the necessity of disputed expense categories (owner compensation is frequently contested), (c) the appropriate period over which to average historical results, and (d) treatment of capital expenditures versus operating expenses.

Compared to the consumer Chapter 13 disposable-income test of Section 1325(b), the Sub V test is more permissive. There is no means-test integration, no statutory schedule of allowed expenses, and explicit recognition that business operating costs come off the top before disposable income is computed. The trade-off is heavier litigation over what counts as a "necessary" business expense.

The 3-to-5 Year Commitment Period

Section 1191(c)(2)(A) sets the commitment period at "not less than 3 years . . . nor more than 5 years." The court has discretion within that range, with most confirmed plans setting the period at 3 years (the statutory minimum) unless cause exists to extend.

The factors considered for extending beyond 3 years include the magnitude of unsecured-claim recovery at the 3-year mark, the debtor’s recovery trajectory, and any creditor-specific equities. A 5-year commitment substantially increases total recovery in cases with growing revenue projections; a 3-year commitment closes the plan faster and accelerates discharge under Section 1192. Practitioners typically propose 3 years and accept extension only on creditor objection or trustee recommendation.

Practitioner note: The 3-to-5 year period runs from the date of the first plan payment, not from the petition date or the confirmation date. Plans that backload payments into a deferred ramp-up structure should anchor the commitment period to the actual first-payment date and not assume confirmation triggers the clock.

Discharge Timing Compared

Confirmation pathDischarge timingSub V trustee durationTypical post-conf. oversight

Section 1191(a) consensualEffective date of the planOften terminates at/near effective dateLimited; plan may specify retention

Section 1191(b) cramdownAfter completion of payments due in the first 3-5 yearsTypically continues through commitment periodActive; trustee often acts as paying agent

The discharge-timing differential is the single most important reason debtors and counsel work hard to achieve consensual confirmation even when the disposable-income economics would support cramdown. Immediate discharge eliminates exposure on dischargeable pre-petition claims and accelerates re-engagement with the credit markets. Deferred discharge keeps the debtor under the jurisdiction of the bankruptcy court for the entire commitment period and exposes the debtor to potential conversion or dismissal under Section 1112 if performance lags.

Strategic Negotiation Sequence

Successful Sub V confirmation typically follows a sequenced negotiation pattern from petition to plan filing:

Days 1-30: Initial Sub V trustee call. Identify the largest creditors and disputed claims. File monthly operating reports promptly and accurately.

Days 30-60: Status conference under Section 1188. Plan term sheet circulated to major creditors. Disposable-income projections in working draft.

Days 60-90: Final plan negotiation. Lock-up agreements with key creditors where possible. File plan under Section 1189(b) within the 90-day window.

Days 90-150: Solicitation period. Ballot deadlines set by court. Address objections at confirmation hearing.

Days 150-180: Confirmation hearing. Trustee report. Court enters confirmation order under Section 1191(a) or (b).

Cases that miss the 90-day plan-filing deadline trigger Section 1189(b)’s "circumstances . . . for which the debtor should not justly be held accountable" standard for extension. Courts are generally accommodating of first extension requests for cause, less so of repeated extensions absent unusual circumstances.

Best practice: Treat the consensual-versus-nonconsensual question as a negotiation outcome, not a binary choice made at filing. The Sub V trustee’s facilitation function (Section 1183(b)(3)) exists precisely to convert prospective 1191(b) cases into 1191(a) consensual confirmations through pre-filing creditor engagement.

Subchapter V: SBRA Overview

The Small Business Reorganization Act of 2019 created a streamlined Chapter 11 path for small-business debtors. History, purpose, key innovations, and contrast with the BAPCPA-era small-business framework.

Home › Subchapter V › SBRA Overview

Empirical research on Subchapter V

For case-pattern analysis on how federal bankruptcy courts apply Subchapter V, including district-level patterns and primary-source dockets, see openbankruptcyproject.org/cases/. All datasets licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

What the SBRA Did

The Small Business Reorganization Act of 2019, Public Law 116-54, was signed into law on August 23, 2019, and took effect on February 19, 2020. It added a new Subchapter V to Chapter 11 of the Bankruptcy Code, codified at 11 U.S.C. §§ 1181-1195. The Act provides a streamlined reorganization track exclusively for small-business debtors.

The legislation arose from years of consensus that traditional Chapter 11 was structurally hostile to small businesses. Reorganization cases routinely cost more than the going-concern value of the business itself, and the absolute-priority rule of Section 1129(b) effectively prevented closely held businesses from confirming a plan over unsecured-creditor opposition unless the owners contributed substantial new value.

Citation: Small Business Reorganization Act of 2019, Pub. L. No. 116-54, 133 Stat. 1079 (codified at 11 U.S.C. §§ 1181-1195).

Legislative History and Purpose

The SBRA was the product of a multi-year drafting process led by the American Bankruptcy Institute Commission to Study the Reform of Chapter 11 and the National Bankruptcy Conference. Both groups concluded that small businesses needed a procedural framework distinct from the one designed for publicly held corporations and large privately held enterprises.

The Senate Judiciary Committee report identified three principal goals: (1) reduce the cost of small-business reorganization; (2) accelerate the timeline to confirmation; and (3) allow owners of viable small businesses to retain their equity stake while restructuring debt. Those goals are reflected directly in the statutory architecture — no creditors’ committee unless ordered, no disclosure statement unless ordered, a 90-day plan-filing deadline, and the elimination of the absolute-priority rule in nonconsensual confirmation.

Subchapter V is an opt-in track. A small-business debtor must affirmatively elect Subchapter V on the bankruptcy petition under Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 1020. The election controls procedure throughout the case unless modified by court order.

Key Innovations

Subchapter V introduced six structural changes that mark it as a separate reorganization framework rather than a procedural shortcut within standard Chapter 11:

Mandatory Subchapter V trustee. Under Section 1183, the United States Trustee appoints a private trustee in every case to facilitate reorganization, monitor financial reporting, and appear at hearings. The trustee does not displace management.

No creditors’ committee absent court order. Section 1181(b) makes the appointment of a creditors’ committee under Section 1102 inapplicable unless the court orders otherwise for cause. This eliminates one of the most expensive overhead categories of standard Chapter 11.

No disclosure statement absent court order. Section 1181(b) likewise makes Section 1125 inapplicable. The plan itself functions as the principal disclosure document.

Debtor-only plan filing. Section 1189 grants exclusivity to the debtor throughout the case. There is no competing-plan period as in standard Chapter 11.

Nonconsensual cramdown without absolute priority. Section 1191(b) allows confirmation over creditor objection if the plan commits all projected disposable income for 3 to 5 years to creditors. The absolute-priority rule of Section 1129(b)(2)(B)(ii) is replaced by the disposable-income commitment.

Status conference. Section 1188 requires a status conference within 60 days of the order for relief, with the debtor required to file a status report 14 days in advance. The conference sets the procedural posture early and keeps the case moving.

Contrast with BAPCPA-Era Small Business Practice

Before the SBRA, small-business debtors elected the "small business case" track under 11 U.S.C. § 101(51D), added by the Bankruptcy Abuse Prevention and Consumer Protection Act of 2005 (BAPCPA). The BAPCPA small-business framework was widely viewed as a failure. It imposed additional reporting and oversight obligations on small-business debtors but did not relax the substantive confirmation rules that made small-business reorganization economically infeasible.

FeatureBAPCPA Small Business (2005)Subchapter V (SBRA 2019)

TrusteeNone — debtor in possessionPrivate Sub V trustee in every case

Creditors’ committeeRequired unless waivedNone unless court orders

Disclosure statementRequired (with simplified procedures)None unless court orders

Plan deadline300 days for plan + 45 days for confirmation90 days for plan

Absolute priority ruleApplies fullyReplaced by disposable-income commitment

Owner equity retentionRequires new value or full creditor paymentPermitted via disposable-income plan

Competing plansPermitted after exclusivity expiresDebtor only

The empirical record since 2020 confirms the design intent. Sub V confirmation rates are substantially higher than BAPCPA small-business confirmation rates, average professional fees are materially lower, and median case duration is roughly half that of comparable standard Chapter 11 cases.

The COVID-Era Debt Ceiling Adjustment

The SBRA as enacted set the eligibility debt ceiling at $2,725,625 (an inflation-adjusted figure tied to Section 101(51D)). One month after Subchapter V took effect, Congress passed the CARES Act (March 27, 2020), which temporarily raised the debt ceiling to $7,500,000 in response to the pandemic. The CARES adjustment was extended twice, first by the COVID-19 Bankruptcy Relief Extension Act of 2021 and again by the Bankruptcy Threshold Adjustment and Technical Corrections Act of 2022.

The expanded ceiling lapsed on June 21, 2024. Eligibility reverted to the inflation-adjusted statutory figure, then $3,024,725. The April 1, 2025 adjustment raised it to $3,424,000 for cases filed through March 31, 2028. Bills to restore the $7.5 million ceiling have been introduced in subsequent Congresses but had not been enacted as of the date of this publication. See Subchapter V eligibility under Section 1182 for the current operative number and the practical effect on debtors near the ceiling.

Practitioner note: The shifting debt ceiling has produced a population of cases filed during the elevated-ceiling window with debts above $3,424,000 that would no longer qualify if refiled today. Pending cases retain Sub V status if eligibility was satisfied at the petition date; subsequent debt increases through scheduling amendments do not retroactively disqualify a case absent court order.

Doctrinal Development to Date

The leading appellate decision on nonconsensual Subchapter V confirmation is In re Cleary Packaging, LLC, 36 F.4th 509 (4th Cir. 2022), which addressed the application of Section 523(a) discharge exceptions to corporate Subchapter V debtors confirming under Section 1191(b). The Fourth Circuit held that Section 1192(2) incorporates the Section 523(a) exceptions for all Subchapter V debtors confirming nonconsensually, including corporate debtors. The decision created an active circuit split that remains unresolved; the contrary position is represented by district-court decisions following the bankruptcy court’s view in In re Lapeer Aviation, 2022 WL 1110072 (Bankr. E.D. Mich. Apr. 13, 2022). See Subchapter V discharge mechanics for the full analysis.

Other significant doctrinal developments include the recurring litigation over the “single asset real estate” exclusion in Section 1182(1)(B)(i), the treatment of affiliated-debtor aggregation under Section 1182(1)(B)(iii), and the standards for converting a standard Chapter 11 to Subchapter V mid-case.

Practical Impact

The SBRA has measurably broadened access to reorganization for the small-business sector. Cases that would historically have gone straight to Chapter 7 liquidation, or been settled in state-court receivership at a discount, are now reorganized under Subchapter V. Typical professional fees in confirmed cases range from $15,000 to $40,000, against $50,000 to $200,000-plus for comparable standard Chapter 11 cases. Median time to confirmation runs four to eight months, against twelve to twenty-four months for standard Chapter 11.

The trade-offs are real. The debt ceiling sharply limits eligibility. The disposable-income commitment locks debtors into a multi-year payment plan with limited room for modification. The Subchapter V trustee role adds an oversight layer that did not exist under prior small-business practice. And the unresolved circuit split on Section 523(a) discharge exceptions creates significant uncertainty for individual Sub V debtors with potentially nondischargeable claims.

The SBRA represents the most significant restructuring of small-business bankruptcy practice since the 1978 Bankruptcy Reform Act. Six years in, it has matured into the default reorganization path for small businesses below the debt ceiling and continues to generate doctrinal development at the circuit-court level.

Subchapter V: Trustee Role Expanded

Statutory duties under Section 1183. The facilitation function. Plan oversight, monitoring, and reporting. How the Sub V trustee differs from a Chapter 7 or Chapter 13 trustee, and from a Chapter 11 examiner.

Home › Subchapter V › Trustee Role Expanded

Empirical research on Subchapter V trustees

For case-pattern analysis of Sub V trustee appointments, fee applications, and post-confirmation distributions by district, see openbankruptcyproject.org/cases/. All datasets licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

The Statutory Framework

The Subchapter V trustee is created by 11 U.S.C. § 1183. The United States Trustee, acting under the supervisory authority of the Attorney General through the Executive Office for United States Trustees (EOUST), appoints a Subchapter V trustee in every case promptly after the order for relief. Section 1183(a) makes the appointment mandatory; there is no discretionary path under which a Sub V case proceeds without a trustee.

Sub V trustees are private trustees, typically attorneys, accountants, or financial professionals selected from a standing district panel maintained by the United States Trustee for each judicial district. Some districts also maintain a standing trustee model (analogous to the Chapter 13 standing trustee structure), particularly in high-volume jurisdictions.

Citation: 11 U.S.C. § 1183(a)-(c); 28 U.S.C. § 586(b) (USTP supervisory authority over Sub V panels).

Statutory Duties under Section 1183(b)

Section 1183(b) enumerates the Sub V trustee’s duties. The list is denser than the duty list for Chapter 7 or Chapter 13 trustees and reflects the SBRA’s dual posture of leaving the debtor in possession while ensuring meaningful neutral oversight:

1183(b)(1) — Perform the duties specified in Section 704(a)(2), (5), (6), (7), and (9), which include investigating the debtor’s financial affairs, examining proofs of claim, opposing the debtor’s discharge if appropriate, and providing information to parties in interest.

1183(b)(2) — Perform the duties specified in Section 1106(a)(3) and (4) if the court orders the debtor removed from possession, including investigating and reporting on the operation of the business.

1183(b)(3) — Facilitate the development of a consensual plan of reorganization. This is the signature duty and distinguishes the Sub V trustee from every other trustee role in the Code.

1183(b)(4) — Appear and be heard at the status conference under Section 1188 and at hearings on disposition of property of the estate, plan confirmation, and modification, sale, post-confirmation modification, and motions for trustee removal of the debtor in possession.

1183(b)(5) — Ensure the debtor commences making timely payments required by a confirmed plan.

1183(b)(6) — If the debtor ceases to be a debtor in possession, perform the duties of a Chapter 11 trustee under Section 1106(a)(1), (2), and (6) and operate the business of the debtor.

1183(b)(7) — In a case in which the debtor is an individual, perform certain Section 1106 duties relating to property of the estate and the debtor’s post-petition earnings.

The Facilitation Function

Section 1183(b)(3) is the heart of the Sub V trustee role. The trustee is statutorily charged with facilitating the development of a consensual plan. This is an active mediation-style role: convening creditor calls, brokering plan terms, surfacing structural issues that would impair confirmation, and shuttling proposals between debtor and significant creditors.

Facilitation is not adjudication. The Sub V trustee does not bind the parties, does not order anyone to do anything, and has no power to impose plan terms. The trustee’s leverage is informational and reputational: the trustee will appear at the confirmation hearing under Section 1183(b)(4) and the court will hear the trustee’s assessment of the case. Debtors and creditors negotiate against the backdrop of a known third-party voice at confirmation.

Best-practice facilitation is sequenced and time-pressured against the Section 1189(b) 90-day plan deadline:

Within the first 30 days, the trustee typically conducts an introductory call with debtor’s counsel and the largest creditors, reviews monthly operating reports as filed, and identifies known disputed claims.

By the Section 1188 status conference (within 60 days of the order for relief), the trustee should have formed a view on feasibility and the realistic confirmation path (consensual versus nonconsensual cramdown).

Between the status conference and the plan-filing deadline, the trustee shuttles between the debtor and major creditor groups on plan terms, attempts to resolve objections in advance, and where possible negotiates lock-up agreements that secure accepting votes before the plan is filed.

Successful facilitation converts what would otherwise be a 1191(b) cramdown into a 1191(a) consensual confirmation. The payoff for the debtor is immediate discharge on the effective date under Section 1192, rather than discharge deferred until completion of the 3-to-5-year disposable-income period.

Plan Oversight and Monitoring

Under Section 1183(b)(5), the trustee’s post-confirmation responsibilities focus on ensuring that the debtor commences and continues making payments under the confirmed plan. In nonconsensual confirmation cases under Section 1191(b), the trustee typically remains in place throughout the 3-to-5-year payment period, acting as paying agent and reviewing the debtor’s ongoing financial reporting.

In consensual confirmation cases under Section 1191(a), the trustee’s role often terminates at or shortly after the effective date. The statute and the United States Trustee Program have generally favored prompt termination of consensual-case trusteeships to avoid unnecessary administrative cost. Confirmed plans should specify whether the trustee continues after the effective date and, if so, the trustee’s post-effective-date duties and compensation arrangement.

Monthly Operating Reports (MORs) under the U.S. Trustee Program’s Operating Guidelines and Section 1107(a) remain the central financial-reporting vehicle. The Sub V trustee reviews MORs for completeness, internal consistency, and compliance with the confirmed plan’s financial projections.

Reporting Function

Section 1183(b)(4) requires the Sub V trustee to appear and be heard at confirmation and certain other hearings. The trustee’s appearance is typically accompanied by a written report or recommendation, although the form varies by district and judge. Common content includes:

A statement of the trustee’s investigation into the debtor’s financial affairs;

An assessment of plan feasibility under Section 1129(a)(11);

An analysis of disposable income under Section 1191(d) where applicable;

Any identified issues with classification, treatment of claims, or the absolute-priority-rule substitute under Section 1191(c)(2);

The trustee’s position on consensual versus nonconsensual confirmation and discharge timing implications.

Trustee reports are not formal findings of fact and do not bind the court, but in practice they carry significant weight. A trustee report that flags feasibility concerns or unresolved claim objections often results in a continued confirmation hearing or denial of confirmation pending plan amendment.

How the Sub V Trustee Differs from Other Trustee Roles

RolePossession of estatePlan facilitationInvestigation dutyPayment processing

Chapter 7 trusteeTakes possession; liquidatesNone — no planYes (Section 704(a)(4))Final distribution only

Chapter 13 trusteeDebtor retains; trustee disbursesNone — plan filed by debtorLimited (Section 1302)Monthly disbursing agent

Standard Chapter 11 trusteeDisplaces debtor in possessionMay file plan (Section 1121(c))Yes (Section 1106)Operates business

Chapter 11 examinerNone — investigatory onlyNone unless court expandsYes — the core dutyNone

Subchapter V trusteeDebtor remains in possessionMandatory (Section 1183(b)(3))Yes (Section 1183(b)(1))Often, in 1191(b) cases

The closest analog to the Sub V trustee is the Chapter 13 trustee, which also leaves the debtor in possession and acts as paying agent. The key differences are scale and discretion: Chapter 13 trustees handle thousands of consumer cases with standardized plans, while Sub V trustees handle a smaller volume of more complex small-business reorganizations requiring individualized facilitation. The Sub V trustee also has a clearer investigation duty than the Chapter 13 trustee.

Trustee Compensation and Fee Applications

Sub V trustee compensation is governed by Section 330(a) and is paid as an administrative expense. Trustees file fee applications under Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 2016 and Section 330. Routine engagements typically generate trustee fees in the range of $5,000 to $25,000 through confirmation, with post-confirmation monitoring billed separately if the case calls for continuing trustee involvement.

Fee applications are subject to Section 330 reasonableness review and the same lodestar standards that apply to debtor’s counsel. Routine objections from the United States Trustee or creditors are infrequent but not unheard of, particularly where the trustee has not produced a written facilitation product, where billing entries lack the specificity required by Section 330(a)(3), or where the time billed appears disproportionate to the case’s complexity. The Tenth Circuit’s disclosure-violation jurisprudence in In re Stewart, 970 F.3d 1255 (10th Cir. 2020), informs fee review by analogy where Sub V trustees fail to disclose disinterestedness or conflicts.

Removal of the Debtor in Possession

Section 1185 (not Section 1183) authorizes the court to remove the debtor in possession for cause, including fraud, dishonesty, incompetence, or gross mismanagement. On removal, the Sub V trustee assumes the duties of a standard Chapter 11 trustee under Section 1183(b)(6) and operates the business pending plan confirmation. Removal is rare in practice; most Sub V cases reach confirmation or conversion without expansion of the trustee’s role beyond facilitation and oversight.

Jurisdictional Architecture

Title 28 Jurisdiction

The bankruptcy courts are creatures of statute, not of Article III. Their jurisdiction, the scope of their authority to enter final judgments, the avenues of appellate review, the venue rules for adversary proceedings, and the removal and remand mechanism for state-court actions all flow from a small cluster of provisions in Title 28 of the United States Code. These five guides walk through the jurisdictional architecture section by section.

Last modified 2026-05-23.

Home/Title 28 Jurisdiction

About the Title 28 framework

The Bankruptcy Amendments and Federal Judgeship Act of 1984 (often called the Marathon fix, after the Supreme Court's decision in Northern Pipeline Construction Co. v. Marathon Pipe Line Co., 458 U.S. 50 (1982)) restructured the relationship between the Article III district courts and the non-Article III bankruptcy courts. Under that framework, 28 U.S.C. section 1334 vests bankruptcy jurisdiction in the district courts, which then refer all bankruptcy cases and proceedings to the bankruptcy judges of their district by standing order under 28 U.S.C. section 157(a). Section 157(b) authorizes bankruptcy judges to enter final orders in core proceedings, while section 157(c) restricts them to proposed findings in non-core proceedings that are merely related to a bankruptcy case.

This architecture has been the subject of repeated Supreme Court litigation. Stern v. Marshall, 564 U.S. 462 (2011), held that some statutorily core proceedings - specifically certain counterclaims under section 157(b)(2)(C) - could not constitutionally be finally adjudicated by a bankruptcy judge. Wellness International Network, Ltd. v. Sharif, 575 U.S. 665 (2015), held that the parties may consent to bankruptcy-court adjudication of Stern-affected matters.

The deep-dives below take each Title 28 provision in turn, explaining the reference mechanism (section 157), the appellate pathway (section 158), the underlying jurisdictional grant (section 1334), the venue rules for the case and for adversary proceedings (section 1409), and the unique bankruptcy removal and remand statute (section 1452).

Section-by-section deep-dives

28 U.S.C. Section 157 - Bankruptcy Court JurisdictionThe reference of bankruptcy cases and proceedings from the district court to the bankruptcy judges, the core/non-core distinction, and the constitutional limits established by Stern v. Marshall.

28 U.S.C. Section 158 - Appellate JurisdictionAppeals to the district court, the optional Bankruptcy Appellate Panel, the section 158(d)(2) direct certification to the court of appeals, and the interlocutory leave-to-appeal standard.

28 U.S.C. Section 1334 - Federal Court JurisdictionThe original and exclusive jurisdiction over the bankruptcy case itself, jurisdiction over civil proceedings arising under, arising in, or related to the case, and the mandatory and permissive abstention provisions.

28 U.S.C. Section 1409 - VenueThe home-court venue for proceedings against the estate, the small-dollar exception for preference and other claims against non-insiders, and the related venue-transfer mechanism of section 1412.

28 U.S.C. Section 1452 - Removal and RemandThe bankruptcy-specific removal statute reaching any related-to claim or cause of action in a state-court civil action, and the equitable-grounds remand standard that displaces the ordinary 28 U.S.C. section 1447 framework.

Procedural note: Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 9027 governs the procedure for removal under 28 U.S.C. section 1452. The deadline for filing a notice of removal in a pending state-court action is, in general, the longer of 90 days after the order for relief or 30 days after the claim arose post-petition.

28 U.S.C. Section 1334 - District Court Jurisdiction Over Bankruptcy

Plain-English guide to the original-jurisdiction grant for bankruptcy: exclusive jurisdiction over Title 11 cases, non-exclusive jurisdiction over arising-under, arising-in, and related-to proceedings, mandatory and permissive abstention, and in rem authority over estate property.

Home › Title 28 Jurisdiction › 28 U.S.C. Section 1334

Empirical research on this section

For case-pattern analysis on how federal bankruptcy courts apply this provision, including district-level patterns and primary-source dockets, see openbankruptcyproject.org/cases/. All datasets licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

What Is Section 1334?

Section 1334 is the original-jurisdiction grant for the federal bankruptcy system. It vests jurisdiction in the United States district courts; 28 U.S.C. § 157 then provides the mechanism by which the district courts refer that jurisdiction to bankruptcy judges. Without Section 1334, there would be no federal subject-matter jurisdiction over bankruptcy at all, because the Constitution's Bankruptcy Clause (Article I, Section 8, Clause 4) authorizes Congress to create uniform bankruptcy laws but does not by itself confer jurisdiction.

The statute draws three categorical distinctions that drive jurisdictional analysis in every contested matter: (i) "cases under Title 11" (the bankruptcy case itself), (ii) "civil proceedings arising under, arising in, or related to" a Title 11 case, and (iii) property of the estate. Each receives a different jurisdictional treatment.

Official citation: 28 U.S.C. § 1334

Section 1334(a) - Exclusive Jurisdiction Over Title 11 Cases

Section 1334(a) provides that "the district courts shall have original and exclusive jurisdiction of all cases under title 11." The "case under Title 11" refers to the umbrella bankruptcy proceeding initiated by the filing of a petition. State courts have no jurisdiction to entertain a bankruptcy petition; only federal district courts (acting through their bankruptcy units) may administer the case itself.

The exclusivity is narrow but important. Many disputes that arise during a bankruptcy case are not themselves "cases under Title 11" - they are proceedings within the case - and those receive the non-exclusive treatment of Section 1334(b).

Section 1334(b) - Non-Exclusive Jurisdiction Over Civil Proceedings

Section 1334(b) gives the district courts "original but not exclusive jurisdiction of all civil proceedings arising under title 11, or arising in or related to cases under title 11." The three categories embedded in this single sentence drive the practical scope of bankruptcy jurisdiction:

Arising Under Title 11

These are proceedings whose cause of action is created by the Bankruptcy Code itself - for example, a trustee's avoidance action under Section 547 (preferences) or Section 548 (fraudulent transfers), a complaint objecting to discharge under Section 727, or a turnover action under Section 542.

Arising In a Title 11 Case

These are proceedings that, by their nature, can arise only in a bankruptcy case - administrative matters such as claim allowance, plan confirmation, sale approvals, and stay-relief motions. They are not created by the Bankruptcy Code in the cause-of-action sense, but they have no existence outside of bankruptcy.

Related To a Title 11 Case

The "related to" category is the broadest and most litigated. The leading test, articulated by the Third Circuit in Pacor, Inc. v. Higgins, 743 F.2d 984 (3d Cir. 1984), and adopted by the Supreme Court in Celotex Corp. v. Edwards, 514 U.S. 300 (1995), asks whether the outcome of the proceeding "could conceivably have any effect on the estate being administered in bankruptcy." Conceivability is a generous threshold, but it has limits. After confirmation of a plan, "related-to" jurisdiction generally contracts to matters affecting plan implementation, consistent with In re Resorts International, Inc., 372 F.3d 154 (3d Cir. 2004).

Section 1334(c) - Abstention

Even where Section 1334(b) jurisdiction exists, Section 1334(c) provides for abstention - the district court may, and sometimes must, decline to exercise its jurisdiction.

Section 1334(c)(1) - Permissive Abstention

The district court may abstain "in the interest of justice, or in the interest of comity with State courts or respect for State law." Permissive abstention is discretionary and is analyzed under a multi-factor balancing test that includes the effect on bankruptcy administration, the predominance of state-law issues, the difficulty or unsettled nature of the applicable law, the presence of a related state-court proceeding, the substance rather than form of an asserted "core" proceeding, the feasibility of severing state claims, the burden on the bankruptcy court's docket, the likelihood of forum shopping, and the right to a jury trial.

Section 1334(c)(2) - Mandatory Abstention

The district court "shall abstain" from hearing a non-core, related-to state-law claim if (i) the claim could not have been commenced in federal court absent bankruptcy jurisdiction, (ii) the action was commenced in state court, (iii) the action can be timely adjudicated in state court, and (iv) timely motion is made. Mandatory abstention applies only to "related-to" proceedings; it does not reach claims arising under or arising in Title 11. The mandatory-abstention requirement reflects Congress's intent that bankruptcy not become a vehicle for federalizing routine state-law disputes that merely happen to share a party with a bankruptcy estate.

Section 1334(d) - Immediate Effect of Abstention Orders

Section 1334(d) provides that any decision to abstain or not to abstain "is not reviewable by appeal or otherwise by the court of appeals" under Section 158(d), Section 1291, or Section 1292. The provision does not preclude review of related orders (such as remand orders or jurisdictional determinations) on appropriate grounds, but it does shield the core abstention decision from ordinary appellate review. Combined with the non-appealability of remand orders under 28 U.S.C. § 1452(b), the abstention regime gives bankruptcy and district courts substantial latitude to manage their dockets without prolonged appellate intervention.

Section 1334(e) - In Rem Jurisdiction Over Estate Property

Section 1334(e)(1) provides that the district court in which a Title 11 case is commenced has "exclusive jurisdiction" over "all of the property, wherever located, of the debtor as of the commencement of such case, and of property of the estate." This is the in rem foundation of bankruptcy. It explains why courts in other jurisdictions cannot adjudicate competing claims to estate property without leave of the bankruptcy court, and why the automatic stay under 11 U.S.C. § 362 is enforceable against actors in any jurisdiction.

Section 1334(e)(2), added in 2005, adds exclusive jurisdiction over "all claims or causes of action that involve construction of section 327 of title 11, or rules relating to disclosure requirements under section 327." This was Congress's response to debates over which forum could resolve professional-employment and disclosure disputes.

Constitutional Foundation and Practical Effect

Section 1334 implements the Bankruptcy Clause through the Article III district courts, then permits reference of routine matters to Article I bankruptcy judges under Section 157. The Supreme Court has consistently treated the underlying jurisdiction as residing in the district court. Northern Pipeline Construction Co. v. Marathon Pipe Line Co., 458 U.S. 50 (1982), invalidated the 1978 Code's broader grant of authority to bankruptcy judges; the 1984 amendments responded by retaining jurisdiction in the district courts under Section 1334 and routing it through Section 157 reference.

In practical operation, parties rarely litigate Section 1334 directly. The standing order of reference takes the case to the bankruptcy court; jurisdictional disputes typically appear as withdrawal-of-reference motions under Section 157(d), abstention motions under Section 1334(c), or remand motions under Section 1452(b). Each of those frames a Section 1334 question without naming it.

28 U.S.C. Section 1409 - Venue of Bankruptcy Proceedings

Plain-English guide to where a proceeding arising under or related to a Title 11 case may be brought: the home-court default, the small-claims threshold protecting nonresident defendants, and special venue provisions for trustees and debtors-in-possession.

Home › Title 28 Jurisdiction › 28 U.S.C. Section 1409

Empirical research on this section

For case-pattern analysis on how federal bankruptcy courts apply this provision, including district-level patterns and primary-source dockets, see openbankruptcyproject.org/cases/. All datasets licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

What Is Section 1409?

Section 1409 governs venue for "proceedings" arising under or related to a Title 11 case - the adversary proceedings and contested matters that are litigated within a bankruptcy case. It is the counterpart to 28 U.S.C. § 1408, which addresses venue for the bankruptcy case itself. The fundamental rule is the "home court" preference: most bankruptcy litigation is venued in the district where the bankruptcy case is pending, regardless of where the defendant resides or where the underlying transaction occurred.

The home-court rule serves the efficient administration of the estate. Trustees can pursue avoidance actions, turnover claims, and contract disputes in a single forum, before a judge familiar with the case, without the venue limitations that constrain ordinary civil litigation. But the rule has trade-offs: it concentrates defendants in distant fora, sometimes in cases where the defendant has no other connection to the district. Section 1409(b) addresses this through the small-claims threshold.

Official citation: 28 U.S.C. § 1409

Section 1409(a) - The Home-Court Rule

Section 1409(a) states the general rule: "Except as otherwise provided in subsections (b) and (d), a proceeding arising under title 11 or arising in or related to a case under title 11 may be commenced in the district court in which such case is pending." Three categories are reached: arising-under, arising-in, and related-to proceedings. The covered universe is coextensive with the jurisdictional grant of Section 1334(b).

"May" is the key word. Section 1409 is permissive rather than mandatory. A trustee may file an adversary proceeding in the home court even if the defendant has no contacts with the district; the trustee may also file in another district where venue would be proper under ordinary venue rules. In practice, the home court is the overwhelmingly preferred forum because of efficiency, judicial familiarity, and convenience to the trustee.

Section 1409(b) - The Small-Claims Threshold

Section 1409(b) carves out an important exception for nonresident defendants in small-claims cases. The trustee may not commence a proceeding "arising in or related to" a Title 11 case to recover (i) a money judgment of less than the statutory threshold for a consumer debt, (ii) a money judgment of less than the statutory threshold for a non-consumer debt against a non-insider, or (iii) a money judgment of less than the statutory threshold for a non-consumer debt - in the home court if the defendant is a nonresident.

The thresholds are periodically adjusted for inflation under 11 U.S.C. § 104. Below the applicable threshold, the trustee must sue in the district where the defendant resides or where venue would otherwise be proper. The carve-out is sometimes called the "anti-deadbeat-defendant" provision because, before its enactment, trustees routinely filed small-dollar preference actions in the home court against vendors and contractors across the country - a tactic that often produced default judgments simply because the cost of defending in a distant forum exceeded the amount in dispute.

The threshold applies only to "arising in or related to" proceedings; "arising under" proceedings (such as Bankruptcy-Code avoidance actions) are partially excluded from the carve-out in some courts' reading, though the statutory text and 2005 amendments have narrowed the trustee's home-court advantage in small-dollar preference and fraudulent-transfer claims as well.

Section 1409(c) - Personal-Injury and Wrongful-Death Claims

Section 1409(c) addresses an unusual but important category: a personal-injury or wrongful-death claim that the estate holds as a cause of action. Such a claim may be brought in the district court for the district where the bankruptcy case is pending, or in the district court for the district where the claim arose, "as determined by the applicable rules of venue." The provision recognizes that personal-injury actions implicate trial mechanics and witness availability that often counsel against shoehorning the case into a distant home court.

Section 1409(d) - Post-Petition Claims

Section 1409(d) provides that a proceeding arising under Title 11 or arising in or related to a Title 11 case based on a claim arising after the commencement of the case "from the operation of the business of the debtor" may be commenced only in a district court in which venue would be proper under 28 U.S.C. § 1391 (the general civil-venue statute) - that is, where the defendant resides, where a substantial part of the events occurred, or under the catchall in cases of foreign defendants.

The reason is fairness. Post-petition trade creditors and counterparties who deal with a debtor-in-possession should not be hauled into the home court for routine commercial disputes simply because their counterparty filed bankruptcy. Section 1409(d) restores ordinary civil-venue rules for the post-petition operations of the business.

Special Provisions for Trustees and Debtors-in-Possession

Section 1409(e) addresses claims by the trustee as the representative of the estate against claimants who have filed proofs of claim. Such claims may be commenced in the home court regardless of the amount and regardless of the claimant's residence. The rationale is the claims-allowance principle articulated in Langenkamp v. Culp, 498 U.S. 42 (1990), and its predecessors: a creditor who files a proof of claim subjects itself to the equitable jurisdiction of the bankruptcy court for the resolution of all claims by and against it.

Transfer of Venue and the Venue-of-Convenience Analysis

Where Section 1409 permits venue in the home court, defendants may still seek transfer under 28 U.S.C. § 1412, which authorizes transfer "in the interest of justice or for the convenience of the parties." The analysis tracks the traditional forum-non-conveniens factors: location of witnesses and evidence, the cost of obtaining attendance, the relative ease of access to sources of proof, and the public interest in resolving disputes locally.

Cases such as In re COIR Construction, Inc. illustrate the venue-of-convenience analysis in practice. Where the underlying transactions, the defendant's records, and most witnesses are located outside the home court, transfer is often appropriate even though the trustee's home-court designation is technically permissible. The party seeking transfer bears the burden, and courts generally afford some deference to the trustee's chosen forum, but a well-supported transfer motion can overcome the default home-court preference.

Interaction with Personal Jurisdiction

Venue and personal jurisdiction are distinct inquiries. Bankruptcy Rule 7004(d) authorizes nationwide service of process on parties to adversary proceedings, which solves most personal-jurisdiction questions through the minimum-contacts-with-the-United-States analysis. Venue under Section 1409 is the separate question of which district is the proper forum. A nonresident defendant may be subject to personal jurisdiction nationwide under Rule 7004(d) but still be entitled to a venue ruling in its favor under Section 1409(b) or a transfer under Section 1412.

28 U.S.C. Section 1452 - Removal and Remand of Bankruptcy-Related Claims

Plain-English guide to bankruptcy removal: who may remove, where the claim goes, the discretionary equitable-remand standard, the non-appealability of remand orders, and the practical differences between bankruptcy removal under Section 1452 and ordinary removal under Section 1441.

Home › Title 28 Jurisdiction › 28 U.S.C. Section 1452

Empirical research on this section

For case-pattern analysis on how federal bankruptcy courts apply this provision, including district-level patterns and primary-source dockets, see openbankruptcyproject.org/cases/. All datasets licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

What Is Section 1452?

Section 1452 is the bankruptcy-specific removal statute. It allows a party to a state-court action to remove the action to the federal district court for the district where the state action is pending, provided the action is one over which the district court has jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1334 - meaning it arises under, arises in, or is related to a Title 11 case. Removed actions become part of the federal docket and are typically referred to the bankruptcy court under the district's standing order of reference.

Section 1452 operates separately from the general removal statute, 28 U.S.C. § 1441. The two statutes differ in several important respects: who may remove, which claims are removable, where the case goes, and how remand operates. Understanding the differences is critical because a defective removal under one statute is not automatically curable under the other.

Official citation: 28 U.S.C. § 1452

Section 1452(a) - Removal Authority

Section 1452(a) provides: "A party may remove any claim or cause of action in a civil action other than a proceeding before the United States Tax Court and a civil action by a governmental unit to enforce such governmental unit's police or regulatory power, to the district court for the district where such civil action is pending, if such district court has jurisdiction of such claim or cause of action under section 1334 of this title."

Several features distinguish Section 1452(a) from ordinary removal:

"A party" may remove. Unlike Section 1441, which limits removal to defendants, Section 1452 permits any party to remove - including a plaintiff in some configurations. This is a meaningful expansion. A plaintiff who initially filed in state court and later becomes a debtor in a Title 11 case may want to consolidate the litigation in the bankruptcy court.

Claim-by-claim removal. Section 1452 permits removal of a "claim or cause of action" rather than the entire civil action. A party may remove only the bankruptcy-related claims and leave non-bankruptcy claims in state court, although in practice courts often remand or sever for case-management reasons.

Two statutory exclusions. Tax Court proceedings and police-or-regulatory-power actions by governmental units are categorically nonremovable. The police-power exclusion mirrors the automatic-stay exception in 11 U.S.C. § 362(b)(4) and reflects federalism concerns about federal interference with state regulatory enforcement.

Destination district. Removal is to the district court for the district where the state action is pending - not necessarily where the bankruptcy case is pending. If the state action is in one district and the bankruptcy case is in another, post-removal transfer under 28 U.S.C. § 1412 may be needed to consolidate.

Procedural Mechanics

The procedure for removal under Section 1452 is governed primarily by Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 9027. The notice of removal must be filed in the bankruptcy court for the district in which the state-court action is pending, and a copy must be promptly served on all parties and filed with the state court. The timing rules differ depending on when the claim becomes removable:

If the claim is removable when the state action is commenced, the notice must be filed within 90 days after the order for relief in the bankruptcy case;

If the claim becomes removable later (for example, by amendment or by later filing of the bankruptcy petition), the notice must be filed within 30 days after the event making the claim removable;

In Chapter 11 cases with an entered confirmation order, removal must occur before plan confirmation in most circumstances.

The timing structure differs materially from Section 1441 / Section 1446 removal, where the default window is 30 days from service or 30 days from the receipt of "other paper" rendering the case removable. Practitioners moving between general civil removal and bankruptcy removal must consult the applicable rule and confirm the operative deadline.

Section 1452(b) - Discretionary Equitable Remand

Section 1452(b) gives the receiving court broad discretion to remand: "The court to which such claim or cause of action is removed may remand such claim or cause of action on any equitable ground." This is a far broader standard than the limited remand authority under Section 1447(c) for ordinary removed cases, which permits remand only for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction or for procedural defects timely raised.

Courts addressing equitable-remand motions typically apply a multi-factor analysis that includes:

The effect on the efficient administration of the bankruptcy estate;

The extent to which state-law issues predominate over bankruptcy issues;

The difficulty or unsettled nature of the applicable state law;

The presence of related state-court litigation that argues for consolidation in the state forum;

The jurisdictional basis for retention (core, non-core but related, or arising under);

The feasibility of severing state claims from bankruptcy issues;

The burden on the bankruptcy court's docket;

The likelihood that removal involved forum-shopping;

The right to a jury trial; and

The prejudice to the involuntarily removed parties.

The factors overlap substantially with the permissive-abstention analysis under 28 U.S.C. § 1334(c)(1), and courts often analyze the two doctrines in parallel. The practical effect is that bankruptcy and district courts have considerable freedom to send state-law claims back to state court when the federal interest is attenuated.

Section 1452(b) - Non-Appealability of Remand

The second sentence of Section 1452(b) provides: "An order entered under this subsection remanding a claim or cause of action, or a decision to not remand, is not reviewable by appeal or otherwise by the court of appeals under section 158(d), 1291, or 1292 of this title or by the Supreme Court of the United States under section 1254 of this title." The non-appealability provision is sweeping. Unlike Section 1447(d), which preserves appellate review of certain remand grounds, Section 1452(b) shields the remand decision from ordinary appellate review.

The Supreme Court has interpreted analogous non-appealability provisions narrowly to preserve review of underlying jurisdictional questions where appropriate. But the core remand decision under Section 1452(b) - whether the equitable factors favor returning the case to state court - is effectively unreviewable. This gives the trial-level court enormous practical authority over the federal-state allocation of bankruptcy-related litigation.

Section 1452 Versus Section 1441 - Practical Differences

The two removal statutes can apply to the same dispute, and parties sometimes invoke both. The principal differences are:

Eligible removers. Section 1452 permits any party; Section 1441 limits removal to defendants.

Jurisdictional basis. Section 1452 requires Section 1334 jurisdiction (bankruptcy-related); Section 1441 requires diversity, federal question, or other original jurisdiction.

Scope. Section 1452 permits claim-by-claim removal; Section 1441 generally requires removal of the entire civil action.

Timing. Section 1452 follows Bankruptcy Rule 9027's tiered deadlines; Section 1441 follows the 30-day default in Section 1446.

Remand standard. Section 1452(b) authorizes remand on "any equitable ground"; Section 1447(c) is much more constrained.

Appellate review of remand. Section 1452(b) bars review categorically; Section 1447(d) preserves review for certain grounds.

Categorical exclusions. Section 1452 excludes Tax Court matters and police-power actions; Section 1441 has its own list of statutory exclusions.

Strategic Use of Section 1452

Removal under Section 1452 is most often invoked by debtors-in-possession and trustees seeking to consolidate state-court litigation in a single federal forum that is familiar with the estate's affairs. Creditors with significant exposure to a debtor sometimes remove to position their claims for resolution alongside the broader claim-allowance process. The equitable-remand standard means that aggressive removal often fails - courts routinely return predominantly state-law disputes to state court - but the removal itself produces a procedural pause and forces the opposing party to expend resources defending the federal forum.

The non-appealability of remand under Section 1452(b) makes the receiving court's discretion effectively final. Parties contemplating removal should evaluate not just the removability of the claim but the likelihood that the receiving court will exercise its broad equitable-remand authority to send it back.

28 U.S.C. Section 157 - Bankruptcy Court Jurisdiction and Core Proceedings

Plain-English guide to the bankruptcy referral statute, the sixteen categories of core proceedings, non-core "related-to" matters, withdrawal of the reference, and how Stern v. Marshall reshaped what a bankruptcy judge can finally decide.

Home › Title 28 Jurisdiction › 28 U.S.C. Section 157

Empirical research on this section

For case-pattern analysis on how federal bankruptcy courts apply this provision, including district-level patterns and primary-source dockets, see openbankruptcyproject.org/cases/. All datasets licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

What Is Section 157?

Section 157 is the mechanical heart of the federal bankruptcy system. Title 11 cases and "civil proceedings arising under, arising in, or related to" Title 11 are vested in the district courts by 28 U.S.C. § 1334. Section 157 then authorizes the district courts to refer that business to the bankruptcy judges of their district. Every federal district has adopted a standing order of reference under Section 157(a), so in practice virtually every bankruptcy matter begins in the bankruptcy court rather than the district court.

Section 157 also draws the constitutional line. Because bankruptcy judges are Article I officers serving fourteen-year terms rather than Article III judges with life tenure, Congress had to construct a framework that respected the separation of powers identified by the Supreme Court in Northern Pipeline Construction Co. v. Marathon Pipe Line Co., 458 U.S. 50 (1982). The 1984 Bankruptcy Amendments and Federal Judgeship Act adopted the "core" versus "non-core" distinction in response.

Official citation: 28 U.S.C. § 157

Section 157(a) - The Standing Order of Reference

Section 157(a) authorizes each district court to provide that "any or all" cases under Title 11 and any or all proceedings arising under, in, or related to Title 11 "shall be referred to the bankruptcy judges for the district." Every district in the United States has entered a standing order of reference that automatically refers all bankruptcy business. The reference is administrative, not jurisdictional - the underlying jurisdiction is the district court's under Section 1334, and reference is the routing mechanism.

Section 157(b) - Core Proceedings: The Sixteen Categories

Under Section 157(b)(1), the bankruptcy judge "may hear and determine" core proceedings and enter "appropriate orders and judgments." Section 157(b)(2) provides a non-exhaustive enumeration of sixteen categories of core proceedings:

Matters concerning the administration of the estate

Allowance or disallowance of claims and exemptions

Counterclaims by the estate against persons filing claims

Orders in respect to obtaining credit

Orders to turn over property of the estate

Proceedings to determine, avoid, or recover preferences

Motions to terminate, annul, or modify the automatic stay

Proceedings to determine, avoid, or recover fraudulent conveyances

Determinations as to the dischargeability of particular debts

Objections to discharges

Determinations of the validity, extent, or priority of liens

Confirmations of plans

Orders approving the use or lease of property

Orders approving the sale of property other than ordinary-course

Other proceedings affecting the liquidation of estate assets or the adjustment of the debtor-creditor or equity-security-holder relationship

Recognition of foreign proceedings and other matters under chapter 15

The statutory list reaches almost the entirety of routine bankruptcy work. But the Supreme Court's decision in Stern v. Marshall, 564 U.S. 462 (2011), held that the statutory grant of "core" status is not coextensive with constitutional authority to enter final judgment.

Stern v. Marshall and the Constitutional Overlay

In Stern, the bankruptcy court entered judgment on a state-law tortious-interference counterclaim that was statutorily designated "core" under Section 157(b)(2)(C). The Supreme Court held that Congress could not constitutionally vest a non-Article III bankruptcy judge with authority to finally decide such a state-law claim that is independent of the federal bankruptcy proceeding and not necessarily resolved through the claims-allowance process. The result is a category of proceedings - sometimes called "Stern claims" - that are statutorily core but constitutionally non-core.

The Court in Wellness International Network, Ltd. v. Sharif, 575 U.S. 665 (2015), softened the practical impact by holding that the parties may consent (expressly or by implication) to final adjudication by a bankruptcy judge of a Stern claim. Most districts have implemented procedural rules requiring parties to elect or object in their pleadings.

The Granfinanciera, S.A. v. Nordberg, 492 U.S. 33 (1989), Seventh Amendment line is also pertinent: a defendant who has not filed a proof of claim retains a jury-trial right on a fraudulent-transfer action against it, which constrains the bankruptcy court's authority to enter final judgment without consent.

Section 157(c) - Non-Core "Related-To" Proceedings

Section 157(c)(1) addresses proceedings that are not core but are "otherwise related to a case under title 11." In a non-core proceeding, the bankruptcy judge submits proposed findings of fact and conclusions of law to the district court, which then enters final judgment "after considering the bankruptcy judge's proposed findings and conclusions and after reviewing de novo those matters to which any party has timely and specifically objected."

Section 157(c)(2) provides a consent override: with the consent of all parties, the district court may refer a non-core related-to proceeding to the bankruptcy judge for entry of final orders and judgments, subject to ordinary appellate review under 28 U.S.C. § 158. After Wellness International, this consent mechanism is the workhorse for resolving Stern-affected matters at the bankruptcy court level.

Section 157(d) - Withdrawal of the Reference

Section 157(d) authorizes the district court to withdraw a case or proceeding from the bankruptcy court. The statute creates two distinct paths:

Permissive Withdrawal

The district court may withdraw "in whole or in part, any case or proceeding referred under this section, on its own motion or on timely motion of any party, for cause shown." Courts evaluating "cause" typically weigh factors articulated by the Second Circuit in In re Orion Pictures Corp., 4 F.3d 1095 (2d Cir. 1993): whether the proceeding is core or non-core, judicial economy, uniformity of bankruptcy administration, reduction of forum shopping, conservation of debtor and creditor resources, expediency, and the presence of a jury demand.

Mandatory Withdrawal

The second sentence of Section 157(d) requires withdrawal "if the court determines that resolution of the proceeding requires consideration of both title 11 and other laws of the United States regulating organizations or activities affecting interstate commerce." Most circuits read this narrowly, requiring "substantial and material" consideration of non-bankruptcy federal law rather than routine application. The mandatory-withdrawal provision is most often invoked in cases implicating federal securities, environmental, communications, antitrust, and labor statutes.

Section 157(e) - Jury Trials by Consent

Section 157(e) provides that a bankruptcy judge may conduct a jury trial if specially designated by the district court and if "all the parties" have expressly consented. Without that consent and designation, jury proceedings must be conducted in the district court. The combined effect of Sections 157(d), 157(e), and the Granfinanciera jury right is that jury demands on non-consenting parties typically trigger withdrawal of the reference.

Practical Workflow

The day-to-day operation of Section 157 follows a predictable pattern. A bankruptcy petition is filed; the district's standing order automatically refers the case; the bankruptcy judge presides over all core proceedings and enters final judgments; non-core related-to proceedings either proceed by consent under Section 157(c)(2) or generate proposed findings under Section 157(c)(1); and a motion to withdraw the reference is filed only when a party identifies a substantial non-bankruptcy federal-law question, a constitutional limitation on bankruptcy-court authority, or a jury demand from a non-consenting party.

Even after Stern and Wellness International, the bankruptcy court remains the default federal forum for virtually all matters arising in bankruptcy. The architecture works because reference is automatic, withdrawal is the exception, and consent fills the constitutional gap left by Northern Pipeline.

Related Title 28 Provisions

28 U.S.C. § 158 - Appellate jurisdiction over bankruptcy orders

28 U.S.C. § 1409 - Venue of proceedings arising under or related to Title 11

28 U.S.C. § 1452 - Removal of claims related to bankruptcy cases

28 U.S.C. Section 158 - Appellate Jurisdiction in Bankruptcy

Plain-English guide to bankruptcy appeals: where to appeal, when to elect the Bankruptcy Appellate Panel, what counts as a final order, interlocutory review by leave, and direct certification to the court of appeals.

Home › Title 28 Jurisdiction › 28 U.S.C. Section 158

Empirical research on this section

For case-pattern analysis on how federal bankruptcy courts apply this provision, including district-level patterns and primary-source dockets, see openbankruptcyproject.org/cases/. All datasets licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

What Is Section 158?

Section 158 is the appellate roadmap for bankruptcy cases. While ordinary federal civil litigation has a single appellate path - district court to circuit court of appeals under 28 U.S.C. § 1291 - bankruptcy appeals follow a multi-track structure that gives parties a meaningful choice of first-level appellate forum, while also providing a fast path to the circuit court in cases of unusual importance.

The fundamental architecture: an order entered by the bankruptcy court is appealed first to the district court (or, in circuits that have established one, to a Bankruptcy Appellate Panel), and the second-tier appeal goes to the regional court of appeals. The 2005 BAPCPA amendments added Section 158(d)(2), a direct-certification mechanism that allows certain appeals to leap-frog the first appellate tier and go straight to the court of appeals.

Official citation: 28 U.S.C. § 158

Section 158(a) - District Court Appellate Jurisdiction

Section 158(a) gives the district courts jurisdiction to hear appeals from three categories of bankruptcy court orders:

Final judgments, orders, and decrees - appealable as of right;

Interlocutory orders and decrees issued under Section 1121(d) extending or reducing the exclusivity periods in Chapter 11 - appealable as of right;

Other interlocutory orders and decrees - appealable only with leave of the district court.

The first category is the workhorse. Bankruptcy "finality" is judged more flexibly than in ordinary civil litigation because a bankruptcy case is a collection of many discrete controversies. An order resolving a single adversary proceeding, a contested matter, or even a discrete dispute within a larger contested matter can be final and immediately appealable. The Supreme Court confirmed this in Bullard v. Blue Hills Bank, 575 U.S. 496 (2015), which held that an order denying confirmation of a Chapter 13 plan is not itself final, but emphasized that bankruptcy finality is determined by reference to the discrete proceeding rather than the entire case.

Section 158(b) and (c) - The Bankruptcy Appellate Panel

Section 158(b) authorizes each circuit's judicial council to establish a Bankruptcy Appellate Panel (BAP) composed of bankruptcy judges from districts within the circuit, sitting in three-judge panels. BAPs currently operate in the First, Sixth, Eighth, Ninth, and Tenth Circuits. A BAP appeal proceeds with the same scope of review and the same standards as a district-court appeal.

Section 158(c) - The BAP Election

Where a BAP exists, the appellant has a one-time election under Section 158(c)(1). The default is BAP review unless the appellant timely elects to have the appeal heard by the district court. The election must be made by filing a statement with the bankruptcy clerk at the time the notice of appeal is filed (or within 30 days after service of an opposing appeal). Any other party to the appeal then has 30 days to opt the appeal back to the district court. The opt-out right ensures that no party is forced into BAP review against its will.

Strategic considerations drive the election. BAP panels are composed entirely of bankruptcy judges, which often translates to greater facility with the Bankruptcy Code and faster disposition. District judges hear bankruptcy appeals only occasionally and may bring a fresh perspective; in some districts the additional delay is meaningful. Both BAP and district-court decisions are reviewable in the court of appeals on equal terms.

Section 158(d)(1) - Court of Appeals Jurisdiction

Section 158(d)(1) gives the courts of appeals jurisdiction over appeals from "all final decisions, judgments, orders, and decrees entered" by district courts and BAPs in their appellate capacity. This is the second-tier review. Standard appellate-review principles apply: legal conclusions are reviewed de novo, factual findings for clear error, and discretionary rulings for abuse of discretion.

Section 158(d)(2) - Direct Certification to the Circuit

Section 158(d)(2), added by BAPCPA in 2005, allows the court of appeals to take immediate jurisdiction over an appeal from a bankruptcy court order - bypassing the district court or BAP entirely - if the order is certified for direct review. Certification may issue from:

The bankruptcy court, the district court, or the BAP that entered or is hearing the appeal of the order;

All the appellants and appellees acting jointly; or

A majority of the parties to the appeal acting together.

To support certification, the certifying authority must find that one of three statutory triggers is satisfied: (1) the order involves a question of law as to which there is no controlling decision of the Supreme Court or the relevant circuit, or involves a matter of public importance; (2) the order involves a question of law requiring resolution of conflicting decisions; or (3) immediate appeal "may materially advance the progress of the case or proceeding."

Even after certification, the court of appeals must accept the appeal. Acceptance is discretionary, and the courts of appeals have taken a measured approach, granting direct review in cases of genuine circuit-wide importance and declining in cases that are factbound or that would benefit from a first-tier appellate record.

Finality, Mootness, and Equitable Mootness

Bankruptcy appellate practice has developed a distinctive equitable-mootness doctrine. Where a Chapter 11 plan has been substantially consummated and the relief requested on appeal would unravel the consummated plan, the courts of appeals will often dismiss the appeal as equitably moot even though Article III mootness is not satisfied. The doctrine has been controversial - it is judge-made and turns on a multi-factor balancing test - but it remains influential in large-case Chapter 11 appellate practice. Critics argue it short-circuits review of legally significant confirmation orders; defenders argue it protects the reliance interests of plan participants. The doctrine is uniquely a creature of Section 158 appellate practice and has no direct analog in ordinary civil appellate law.

Procedural Timing

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 8002 generally requires a notice of appeal to be filed within fourteen days of entry of the order being appealed - a significantly shorter window than the thirty-day default in ordinary civil litigation under Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 4. Tolling motions and extensions of time are available but are governed by their own strict deadlines. The compressed timetable reflects the policy preference for prompt resolution of bankruptcy disputes.

Related Title 28 Provisions

28 U.S.C. § 1334 - District court original jurisdiction over Title 11 matters

28 U.S.C. § 1409 - Venue of proceedings arising under or related to Title 11

28 U.S.C. § 1452 - Removal of claims related to bankruptcy cases

## Trustee Economics - Open Bankruptcy Project
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/trustee-economics/

Open Bankruptcy Project
