How the System Pays Itself

Trustee Economics

Trustees, estate professionals, and the United States Trustee Program are paid through interlocking statutory mechanisms that determine who can be retained, how compensation is calculated, and how the system is funded. These four deep-dives cover the trustee-compensation framework of section 326, the professional-fee framework of section 330, the section 327/328 employment retention regime, and the structural and budgetary architecture of the US Trustee Program.

Last modified 2026-05-22.

Home/Trustee Economics

About the compensation framework

The Bankruptcy Code carefully separates the right to be employed (sections 327 and 1103), the right to be compensated (section 330), the cap on trustee compensation (section 326), and the priority of those payments (sections 503 and 507). Each section has its own standard, its own procedure, and its own body of case law. A professional employed in violation of section 327 forfeits the right to compensation under section 330; a fee award that exceeds the section 326 cap is reversible; and an administrative claim must be allowed under section 503 before it can be paid under the section 507(a)(2) priority.

Section 330 codifies the lodestar method for fee awards: the reasonable hourly rate multiplied by the reasonable number of hours. The court must consider the section 330(a)(3) factors including the time spent, the rates charged, the necessity of the services, the results achieved, and whether the services were beneficial to the estate. The court has discretion to reduce fees that fail any of those tests. Detailed time records are required by Local Rules in most districts.

The US Trustee Program, established in the Bankruptcy Reform Act of 1978 and made permanent in 1986, is an executive-branch component of the Department of Justice charged with administrative oversight of the bankruptcy system. The Program is funded through quarterly fees paid by chapter 11 debtors under 28 U.S.C. section 1930(a)(6) - a fee schedule that scales with debtor disbursements and that has been the subject of significant constitutional litigation over the past decade.

Trustee-economics deep-dives

Section 326 Trustee CompensationThe sliding-scale percentage cap on chapter 7 and chapter 11 trustee fees, the special chapter 12 and chapter 13 fee rules, and the interaction with section 330(a)(7) for chapter 13 standing trustees.

Section 330 Professional FeesThe lodestar method, the section 330(a)(3) factors, the section 330(a)(4) duplication and time-on-fee-applications rules, and the standards for interim compensation under section 331.

Section 327 and 328 Professional EmploymentThe disinterested-person and no-adverse-interest requirements of section 327(a), the section 327(c) exception for creditor's counsel, and the difference between section 328(a) pre-approved compensation arrangements and section 330 reasonableness review.

UST Program StructureThe 21-region structure of the United States Trustee Program, the role of the Executive Office for US Trustees (EOUST), the section 586 statutory duties, and the section 1930(a)(6) quarterly-fee funding model.

Disclosure rule: Bankruptcy Rule 2014 requires every professional applying for employment under section 327 to file a verified statement disclosing all connections with the debtor, creditors, and other parties in interest. Incomplete disclosure can result in fee denial, disgorgement, or sanctions even years after the original retention.

11 U.S.C. Section 326 - Trustee Compensation Caps

Plain-English guide to the sliding-scale ceiling on bankruptcy trustee fees, the Pro Forma presumption for Chapter 7 trustees, and the disbursement-method jurisprudence that determines what counts toward the cap.

Home › Trustee Economics › 11 U.S.C. Section 326 - Trustee Compensation

Empirical research on this section

For case-pattern analysis on how federal bankruptcy courts apply this provision, including district-level patterns and primary-source dockets, see openbankruptcyproject.org/cases/. All datasets licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

What Is Section 326?

Section 326 is the statutory ceiling on the compensation a bankruptcy trustee may receive for serving in that role. It does not authorize the compensation. The authorization comes from Section 330. Section 326 instead operates as an upper bound: regardless of what the trustee’s timesheets and lodestar calculation might otherwise support, the court may not award more than the sliding-scale percentages set out in subsection (a). For trustees serving in cases with significant disbursements, the cap rarely binds. For trustees in modest cases, the cap can be the operative number.

The cap exists because Congress chose to compensate trustees primarily out of money that flows through the estate to non-debtor parties. That structural choice creates a built-in alignment between trustee effort and creditor recovery: trustees are paid more when they marshal more money, less when there is little to marshal. It also creates the well-documented problem that no-asset Chapter 7 cases generate almost no compensation, which the statute addresses through a separate fixed-fee mechanism.

Official citation: 11 U.S.C. § 326

The Sliding-Scale Formula: Section 326(a)

In a case under Chapter 7 or Chapter 11 (other than a railroad reorganization), Section 326(a) caps trustee compensation at percentages of "all moneys disbursed or turned over in the case by the trustee to parties in interest, excluding the debtor, but including holders of secured claims." The current scale is:

Disbursement trancheMaximum percentage

First $5,00025%

$5,000.01 to $50,00010%

$50,000.01 to $1,000,0005%

Over $1,000,0003%

The percentages are marginal, not average: a trustee in a case with $200,000 of qualifying disbursements is capped at $1,250 (25% of first $5,000) + $4,500 (10% of next $45,000) + $7,500 (5% of next $150,000) = $13,250, not 5% of $200,000.

The carve-out for "the debtor" is doctrinally significant. Money returned to the debtor (for example, surplus in a rare solvent Chapter 7) is not part of the base. Money to "holders of secured claims" is explicitly included even though secured creditors are not unsecured-creditor distributees in the conventional sense. That inclusion was a Bankruptcy Reform Act amendment intended to recognize trustee work in liquidating collateral.

Disbursed or Turned Over: The In re Mohns Approach

The phrase "moneys disbursed or turned over" has produced substantial litigation about what counts toward the cap. Two competing approaches developed:

Source-of-funds approach. Only funds that physically passed through the trustee’s hands and were disbursed by the trustee count. A direct payoff of a secured lender by a third-party purchaser at closing, for example, would not count because the trustee never held those funds.

Disbursement-method approach. Funds count if the trustee’s administration was the operative mechanism by which a party in interest received payment, even if the funds did not literally flow through a trustee’s account.

The Seventh Circuit’s decision in In re Mohns, Inc., 55 F.3d 1268 (7th Cir. 1995), articulates the disbursement-method approach in the Chapter 11 context. The court held that a trustee’s commission base properly includes funds that the trustee caused to be paid to creditors at closing, even when the funds were wired directly from buyer to creditor and never sat in a trustee account. The court reasoned that the cap is meant to track the trustee’s administrative achievement, not the bookkeeping route taken by the dollars.

Other circuits have aligned with Mohns in result while articulating the test in slightly different terms. Practitioners should check the local circuit’s formulation. The practical effect under the disbursement-method approach is that trustees who structure sales producing direct payoffs at closing are not penalized in their compensation base.

Chapter 7 Trustees and the No-Asset Reality

Section 326(a) is the cap for Chapter 7 trustees handling asset cases. But the majority of Chapter 7 cases produce no nonexempt assets for distribution at all. In those cases, the cap is effectively zero. Congress therefore created a separate fixed compensation mechanism: under Section 330(b)(1), the Chapter 7 trustee receives a flat amount (currently $60) out of the filing fee for each case noticed, win or lose. This is the only compensation a no-asset trustee receives for that case.

The Pro Forma practice that has developed in many districts holds that when a trustee in an asset case files a Trustee’s Final Report seeking compensation at the statutory maximum, the bankruptcy court will ordinarily approve the request without an evidentiary hearing on the trustee’s hours, treating the cap as a presumptively reasonable fee. This Pro Forma presumption is judicially constructed, not statutory. It reflects the recognition that Chapter 7 trustees subsidize no-asset work with asset-case compensation, and that micro-managing hours in asset cases would defeat the cross-subsidy.

The Supreme Court’s decision in Lamie v. United States Trustee, 540 U.S. 526 (2004), addressed a separate but related compensation question (debtor’s attorney compensation in converted cases) and reinforced the principle that Section 330’s text controls, the bankruptcy compensation structure is heavily textual, and courts should not import equitable adjustments not grounded in the statute. Districts that have considered whether the Pro Forma presumption survives Lamie have generally concluded that it does, because the cap itself is a textual ceiling and applying it as a presumptive award is consistent with the statute.

Chapter 11 Trustee Compensation

A Chapter 11 trustee (appointed under Section 1104) is compensated under the same Section 326(a) sliding scale as a Chapter 7 trustee. Because Chapter 11 estates often involve very large disbursements, the cap rarely operates as a binding constraint in those cases. The operative number is usually the lodestar reasonableness analysis under Section 330.

The Chapter 11 trustee’s professional fees (counsel, financial advisors, accountants) are separately authorized under Section 330 and are not part of the trustee’s own cap. A debtor or creditor objecting to a Chapter 11 trustee’s fee application typically attacks the underlying hourly rates or the reasonableness of specific time entries under Section 330; the Section 326 cap is the outer bound that the parties rarely reach.

Chapter 12 Trustee Compensation: Section 326(b)

For a standing Chapter 12 trustee, Section 326(b) does not impose a percentage cap of its own. Instead, the standing trustee’s compensation is governed by the percentage fee set by the Attorney General under 28 U.S.C. § 586(e), capped at the higher of 5% or the amount specified for the relevant judicial district. The same framework controls standing Chapter 13 trustees.

The 28 U.S.C. § 586(e) framework treats standing trustees as quasi-public officials whose compensation is set administratively rather than case-by-case. Each standing trustee operates an office, hires staff, and bears overhead; the percentage fee on plan payments funds the operation. This is materially different from the case-by-case Section 326(a) cap that controls Chapter 7 and Chapter 11 trustees.

Chapter 13 Trustee Compensation

Standing Chapter 13 trustees collect a percentage of every plan payment received from the debtor. The percentage is set by the United States Trustee Program (or the Bankruptcy Administrator in Alabama and North Carolina) for the relevant district, subject to the 10% statutory ceiling in 28 U.S.C. § 586(e)(1)(B). The percentage funds the standing trustee’s entire operation, including disbursement to creditors, staff, and overhead.

Because the Chapter 13 standing trustee operates an ongoing office with predictable case flow, the percentage is calibrated annually based on projected receipts and approved expenses. The U.S. Trustee’s Office reviews each standing trustee’s annual budget and adjusts the percentage to fit. A debtor whose plan payment is $500 per month does not pay a separately-calculated trustee fee; the trustee’s percentage is built into the payment and disbursed to creditors after deduction.

Subchapter V Trustees

A Subchapter V trustee appointed under Section 1183 is compensated under Section 330 (subject to court approval) and is not subject to the Section 326(a) sliding-scale cap. The Subchapter V trustee’s role is intentionally narrower than a Chapter 11 trustee’s, focused on facilitating consensual plan formation, and the compensation framework reflects that narrower role. Subchapter V trustees typically bill at an hourly rate and submit fee applications for court approval.

Related Bankruptcy Code Sections

Section 330 - Authorization of compensation and lodestar reasonableness

Section 327 - Employment of professionals

U.S. Trustee Program Structure - Oversight and panel-trustee appointment under 28 U.S.C. § 586

Section 1183 - Subchapter V trustee

11 U.S.C. Sections 327 and 328 - Employment of Estate Professionals

Plain-English guide to the gatekeeping provisions that govern who a bankruptcy estate can hire: disinterestedness, no adverse interest, the 327(c) creditor-representation safe harbor, the 327(e) limited-purpose exception, and 328 alternative compensation terms with the reasonableness reservation.

Home › Trustee Economics › 11 U.S.C. Sections 327 and 328 - Professional Employment

Empirical research on this section

For case-pattern analysis on how federal bankruptcy courts apply this provision, including district-level patterns and primary-source dockets, see openbankruptcyproject.org/cases/. All datasets licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

What Is Section 327?

Section 327 is the front door for any professional who wants to be paid by a bankruptcy estate. Before a trustee, debtor-in-possession, or official committee can hire an attorney, accountant, auctioneer, appraiser, or other professional and pay them from the estate, the engagement must be approved under Section 327. Without Section 327 approval, Section 330 compensation is unavailable: the work may be excellent, the rates reasonable, the result favorable, and the court still cannot order payment from estate funds.

The gatekeeping function exists because every dollar paid to a professional reduces the pool available for creditors. Congress structured Section 327 to ensure that the professionals taking those dollars have no conflicting loyalties that would skew their judgment away from the estate’s interests.

Official citations: 11 U.S.C. §§ 327, 328

The Two-Part Test of Section 327(a)

Section 327(a) authorizes a trustee, with the court’s approval, to "employ one or more attorneys, accountants, appraisers, auctioneers, or other professional persons" provided the professional:

Does not hold or represent an interest adverse to the estate; and

Is a disinterested person as defined in Section 101(14).

The two requirements operate independently. A professional who is "disinterested" within the technical definition can still hold an adverse interest, and vice versa. Both must be satisfied. The "adverse interest" inquiry is functional: does the professional hold any economic interest that would tend to lessen the value of the estate or create a predisposition under conditions of conflict?

"Disinterested person" is defined in Section 101(14). The core requirement is that the person is not a creditor, equity security holder, or insider; is not and was not within two years before the petition a director, officer, or employee of the debtor; and does not have an interest materially adverse to the estate by reason of any direct or indirect relationship to, connection with, or interest in the debtor.

Disclosure Obligations

Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 2014 requires the proposed professional to file a verified statement disclosing all of the proposed professional’s connections with the debtor, creditors, any other party in interest, their respective attorneys and accountants, the United States trustee, or any person employed in the office of the United States trustee.

The disclosure obligation is comprehensive and ongoing. A professional who later discovers an undisclosed connection must supplement promptly. Failure to disclose is independently sanctionable even if the undisclosed relationship would not have disqualified the professional from employment. Courts routinely deny or disgorge fees for incomplete disclosures, treating Rule 2014 as a strict information-forcing rule.

Section 327(c): The Creditor-Representation Exception

Section 327(c) carves out a limited exception to the disinterestedness requirement. A person is not disqualified for employment under Section 327 "solely because of such person’s employment by or representation of a creditor, unless there is objection by another creditor or the United States trustee, in which case the court shall disapprove such employment if there is an actual conflict of interest."

The provision recognizes that in commercial cases, the universe of qualified professionals is finite, and many of them represent some creditor somewhere. A blanket prohibition on creditor-side connections would shrink the talent pool dramatically. Section 327(c) accordingly treats creditor representation as presumptively allowable, but creates a fast-track objection process: any creditor or the U.S. Trustee can force the court to evaluate whether the representation creates an "actual" (not merely potential) conflict.

Section 327(e): Limited-Purpose Employment of Debtor’s Pre-Petition Counsel

Section 327(e) is a narrower exception that allows the trustee, with court approval, to employ an attorney "for a specified special purpose, other than to represent the trustee in conducting the case," if such employment is in the best interest of the estate, and "if such attorney does not represent or hold any interest adverse to the debtor or to the estate with respect to the matter on which such attorney is to be employed."

The provision is commonly used to continue employment of the debtor’s pre-petition counsel for a discrete, non-bankruptcy task (for example, defending an ongoing patent-infringement suit or completing a real-estate closing). The key distinctions from Section 327(a) are: (1) the employment is for a specified special purpose, not general representation of the estate; (2) the disinterestedness requirement is relaxed; and (3) the no-adverse-interest test is matter-specific rather than estate-wide.

Section 327(e) cannot be used to employ general bankruptcy counsel for the estate. The Fifth Circuit and other courts have emphasized that the "specified special purpose" language is a meaningful limitation; counsel who would be conducting the bankruptcy case itself cannot be employed under 327(e) and must qualify under 327(a) with full disinterestedness.

Section 328 Alternative Compensation Terms

Section 328(a) allows the trustee or debtor-in-possession, "with the court’s approval, [to] employ or authorize the employment of a professional person under section 327 or 1103 of this title, as the case may be, on any reasonable terms and conditions of employment, including on a retainer, on an hourly basis, on a fixed or percentage fee basis, or on a contingent fee basis." This is the textual hook for investment-banker success fees, contingent fee arrangements for litigation counsel, and similar non-lodestar compensation structures.

The critical feature of Section 328 is what comes next: the court may allow compensation "different from the compensation provided under such terms and conditions after the conclusion of such employment, if such terms and conditions prove to have been improvident in light of developments not capable of being anticipated at the time of the fixing of such terms and conditions." This reservation is narrow; it preserves the court’s ability to adjust only if circumstances were genuinely unforeseeable at the time of approval.

A retention application that invokes Section 328 must make the invocation explicit. The Fifth Circuit’s line of cases addressing this point holds that a professional employed under a vague order that does not clearly invoke Section 328 will be evaluated under Section 330’s ordinary reasonableness standard, even if the engagement letter purported to set fixed fees. Practitioners seeking Section 328’s deferential review should ensure the retention order recites Section 328 expressly and identifies the specific terms being approved.

Section 328(c): Denial of Compensation for Adverse Interest

Section 328(c) provides an enforcement teeth: "Except as provided in section 327(c), 327(e), or 1107(b) of this title, the court may deny allowance of compensation for services and reimbursement of expenses of a professional person employed under section 327 or 1103 of this title if, at any time during such professional person’s employment under section 327 or 1103 of this title, such professional person is not a disinterested person, or represents or holds an interest adverse to the interest of the estate with respect to the matter on which such professional person is employed."

The provision authorizes both retroactive denial and disgorgement when an adverse interest or loss of disinterestedness emerges during the engagement. The "at any time" language captures both initial defects and post-employment conflicts. Even a professional approved under Section 327 in good faith faces a fee-denial risk if a disqualifying interest later comes to light.

Nunc Pro Tunc Employment

Professionals who begin work before obtaining a Section 327 employment order historically sought nunc pro tunc (retroactive) approval. The Supreme Court’s 2020 decision in Roman Catholic Archdiocese of San Juan v. Acevedo Feliciano sharply curtailed nunc pro tunc orders generally, holding that federal courts lack equitable authority to alter the historical record. Bankruptcy courts now generally require strict, contemporaneous compliance with Section 327, although some districts have adopted procedures allowing approval of pre-application work upon a showing of extraordinary circumstances.

## 11 USC 330 - Professional Fees, Lodestar, Johnson Factors, ASARCO [2026]

11 U.S.C. Section 330 - Allowance of Compensation

Plain-English guide to the authorizing provision for trustee and professional compensation in bankruptcy: lodestar methodology, the Johnson factors, the benefit-to-the-estate requirement, and the Supreme Court’s fee-defense rule under Baker Botts v. ASARCO.

Home › Trustee Economics › 11 U.S.C. Section 330 - Professional Fees

Empirical research on this section

For case-pattern analysis on how federal bankruptcy courts apply this provision, including district-level patterns and primary-source dockets, see openbankruptcyproject.org/cases/. All datasets licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

What Is Section 330?

Section 330 is the authorizing provision for compensation in bankruptcy cases. Where Section 326 sets the ceiling on trustee compensation, Section 330 sets the framework for awarding compensation in the first instance to trustees, examiners, Subchapter V trustees, and professionals employed under Section 327 or Section 1103. Every dollar paid from a bankruptcy estate to a trustee, attorney, accountant, financial advisor, investment banker, or other professional traces its authority to Section 330.

The statute mandates a "reasonable compensation for actual, necessary services" plus "reimbursement for actual, necessary expenses." Reasonableness is the workhorse standard, and the statute supplies a non-exhaustive list of factors a court must consider. Sections 330(a)(3) and 330(a)(4) supply both the affirmative criteria and the categories of work that are not compensable.

Official citation: 11 U.S.C. § 330

The Reasonableness Factors: Section 330(a)(3)

Section 330(a)(3) directs the bankruptcy court, in determining the amount of reasonable compensation, to consider the nature, extent, and value of the services, taking into account all relevant factors, including:

The time spent on such services;

The rates charged for such services;

Whether the services were necessary to the administration of, or beneficial at the time at which the service was rendered toward the completion of, a case under this title;

Whether the services were performed within a reasonable amount of time commensurate with the complexity, importance, and nature of the problem, issue, or task addressed;

With respect to a professional person, whether the person is board certified or otherwise has demonstrated skill and experience in the bankruptcy field; and

Whether the compensation is reasonable based on the customary compensation charged by comparably skilled practitioners in cases other than cases under this title.

The final factor (comparable-rate analysis) is the textual hook for importing market-rate evidence. A bankruptcy professional cannot ordinarily bill the estate at a premium over what comparably skilled non-bankruptcy practitioners charge for similar work in the same market.

The Lodestar Methodology

Although Section 330 does not by its terms require a lodestar, virtually every circuit applies lodestar analysis as the default starting point: reasonable hours multiplied by a reasonable hourly rate equals the presumptive fee. The lodestar may then be adjusted upward or downward based on case-specific factors.

Lodestar analysis requires contemporaneous, detailed time records. Block-billing (lumping multiple tasks into a single time entry) is disfavored and often reduced. Vague descriptions ("work on case," "review file") are routinely cut. Many districts have local rules or U.S. Trustee guidelines specifying minimum descriptive detail; the U.S. Trustee Program publishes Appendix A and Appendix B guidelines for fee applications in Chapter 11 cases of various sizes.

The Third Circuit’s decision in In re Busy Beaver Building Centers, Inc., 19 F.3d 833 (3d Cir. 1994), is a frequently-cited articulation of the bankruptcy court’s independent duty to review fee applications regardless of whether any party objects. The court emphasized that the bankruptcy judge sits in a quasi-fiduciary posture for the estate, must inspect fee applications for unreasonable entries on its own initiative, and cannot rubber-stamp an unopposed application. The Busy Beaver framework remains the leading articulation of judicial fee-review duty.

The Johnson Factors

The twelve factors articulated in Johnson v. Georgia Highway Express, Inc., 488 F.2d 714 (5th Cir. 1974), predate the current Bankruptcy Code but supply the canonical reasonableness vocabulary that bankruptcy courts continue to use. The Johnson factors are:

The time and labor required;

The novelty and difficulty of the questions;

The skill requisite to perform the legal service properly;

The preclusion of other employment due to acceptance of the case;

The customary fee;

Whether the fee is fixed or contingent;

Time limitations imposed by the client or circumstances;

The amount involved and the results obtained;

The experience, reputation, and ability of the attorneys;

The "undesirability" of the case;

The nature and length of the professional relationship with the client; and

Awards in similar cases.

The Supreme Court’s general fee-shifting jurisprudence (notably Hensley v. Eckerhart and Perdue v. Kenny A.) has constrained the Johnson factors’ role outside the bankruptcy context, generally folding them into the lodestar rather than treating them as independent multipliers. Bankruptcy courts use the Johnson vocabulary primarily to describe the reasonableness adjustments authorized by Section 330(a)(3), not as a separate test.

Benefit to the Estate: Section 330(a)(4)(A)

Section 330(a)(4)(A) excludes from compensation any services that were not "reasonably likely to benefit the debtor’s estate" or "necessary to the administration of the case." This is the textual anchor for the benefit-to-the-estate doctrine that bars fees for work that, judged at the time it was performed, could not reasonably have advanced the estate’s interests.

The doctrine is judged ex ante, not ex post. A professional who pursued a non-frivolous litigation strategy that ultimately failed is not automatically denied fees; the question is whether a reasonable professional would have undertaken the work at the time. Conversely, work that obviously could not benefit the estate (for example, briefing a moot issue, or duplicative work already done by another professional) is not compensable even if it succeeded in some derivative sense.

Section 330(a)(4)(A) also disallows "unnecessary duplication of services." When multiple professionals work on the same matter, the court will scrutinize whether each contribution added value beyond what the others provided. Conferences among multiple billing professionals are a common source of duplication reductions.

The Baker Botts v. ASARCO Fee-Defense Rule

One of the most consequential modern Supreme Court bankruptcy compensation decisions is Baker Botts L.L.P. v. ASARCO LLC, 576 U.S. 121 (2015). The question was whether time spent defending a fee application against objections is itself compensable from the estate under Section 330. The Court held it is not.

Justice Thomas, writing for the majority, applied the American Rule presumption that each party bears its own attorney’s fees absent specific and explicit statutory authorization. Section 330 authorizes compensation for "services rendered" to the estate. The Court reasoned that defending one’s own fee application is a service rendered to the professional, not to the estate, and the statute’s text does not displace the American Rule for this category of work.

The practical effect is that a professional whose fee application is challenged absorbs the cost of the defense. Engagement letters in large Chapter 11 cases sometimes attempt to contract around ASARCO by providing for indemnification, but Section 328 must be invoked at the employment stage with full disclosure for any such provision to be enforceable, and even then courts have been skeptical of fee-defense indemnification clauses post-ASARCO. The decision has materially altered fee-application risk allocation in contested cases.

Debtor’s Attorney Compensation: The Lamie Question

In Lamie v. United States Trustee, 540 U.S. 526 (2004), the Supreme Court held that Section 330(a)(1), as amended in 1994, does not authorize compensation from the estate for a debtor’s attorney in a Chapter 7 case who is not employed under Section 327. The Court applied a strict textual reading: the post-1994 statute lists trustees, examiners, and "professional person[s] employed under section 327 or 1103," and a Chapter 7 debtor’s attorney is not in that list.

The Lamie holding does not bar a Chapter 7 debtor’s attorney from being paid; it simply means the payment must come from the debtor, not from estate funds. In Chapter 13 cases, by contrast, debtor’s attorney fees are routinely paid through the plan because Section 330(a)(4)(B) expressly authorizes compensation to debtor’s counsel in individual Chapter 12 and Chapter 13 cases.

United States Trustee Program - Structure, Funding, and Oversight

Plain-English guide to the USTP’s status as a DOJ component, its 21 regional offices, panel and standing trustee appointments, funding through the US Trustee System Fund under 28 U.S.C. § 589a, and the statutory oversight functions under 28 U.S.C. § 586.

Home › Trustee Economics › United States Trustee Program Structure

Empirical research on this topic

For case-pattern analysis on how the USTP and its panel trustees interact with bankruptcy cases, including district-level patterns and primary-source dockets, see openbankruptcyproject.org/cases/. All datasets licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

What Is the United States Trustee Program?

The United States Trustee Program (USTP) is a component of the U.S. Department of Justice charged with the federal supervision of the administration of bankruptcy cases under Chapters 7, 11, 12, 13, and 15 of the Bankruptcy Code. The Program is the executive-branch arm of bankruptcy administration. Bankruptcy judges decide cases; the USTP supervises the trustees, professionals, and debtors who execute those decisions and ensures that the system functions in accordance with the Bankruptcy Code and Federal Rules of Bankruptcy Procedure.

The USTP was created in pilot form by the Bankruptcy Reform Act of 1978 and expanded nationwide (with the exception of Alabama and North Carolina) by the Bankruptcy Judges, United States Trustees, and Family Farmer Bankruptcy Act of 1986. Alabama and North Carolina districts are instead served by Bankruptcy Administrators, who are appointed by the judiciary and perform parallel functions outside the executive branch.

Official citations: 28 U.S.C. §§ 581-589a; 11 U.S.C. § 307

DOJ Component Status

The USTP sits within the Department of Justice. It is headed by the Director of the Executive Office for United States Trustees (EOUST), appointed by the Attorney General. The Director supervises the regional United States Trustees and sets nationwide policy. The placement matters: as an executive-branch agency, the USTP can appear in bankruptcy cases and be heard on any issue under 11 U.S.C. § 307, but it does not adjudicate. Adjudication remains with the Article I bankruptcy courts and, on appeal, with the Article III district courts, bankruptcy appellate panels, and courts of appeals.

The structural distinction is important for understanding the USTP’s role. The USTP is a watchdog and gatekeeper. It objects, moves, examines, audits, refers, and reports. It does not decide. When the USTP and a debtor disagree, the bankruptcy court resolves the dispute on the merits.

21 Regions and Field Office Structure

The country (excluding Alabama and North Carolina) is divided into 21 USTP regions. Each region is headed by a United States Trustee, appointed by the Attorney General under 28 U.S.C. § 581 for a five-year term, with possible reappointment. Each region contains one or more field offices, and each field office is operated by Assistant United States Trustees who report to the regional U.S. Trustee. Field offices are staffed by trial attorneys, bankruptcy analysts, paralegals, and administrative personnel.

The regional structure tracks judicial districts rather than circuits. A single region may include multiple federal judicial districts; conversely, especially in large states, multiple regions may share state boundaries. Each judicial district’s bankruptcy cases are assigned to one specific regional U.S. Trustee’s jurisdiction.

Panel of Chapter 7 Trustees

Under 28 U.S.C. § 586(a)(1), the United States Trustee for each region "shall establish, maintain, and supervise a panel of private trustees that are eligible and available to serve as trustees in cases under chapter 7 of title 11." When a Chapter 7 case is filed, an interim trustee from the panel is appointed under 11 U.S.C. § 701, and absent election of a successor by creditors at the meeting of creditors, that interim trustee becomes the trustee for the case under Section 702.

Panel-trustee selection is administrative. The regional U.S. Trustee publishes application criteria and reviews applicants for qualifications including legal or accounting background, integrity, and operational capacity. Panel trustees are not federal employees; they are private individuals (typically attorneys, occasionally accountants) who accept appointments case-by-case. The USTP exercises ongoing supervision: it reviews Trustee’s Final Reports, audits no-asset reports, and can remove a panel trustee for cause.

Compensation of panel trustees follows the dual framework discussed at Section 326: a fixed amount (currently $60) out of the filing fee for each case under 28 U.S.C. § 330(b)(1), plus the sliding-scale percentage cap under 11 U.S.C. § 326(a) for asset cases.

Standing Chapter 12 and Chapter 13 Trustees

Under 28 U.S.C. § 586(b), the United States Trustee may appoint one or more individuals to serve as standing trustees for Chapter 12 and Chapter 13 cases in the region. Unlike panel trustees who serve case-by-case, a standing trustee operates an ongoing office that handles all (or a designated geographic share) of the Chapter 12 or Chapter 13 caseload in a district.

Standing trustees are quasi-public officials. They collect plan payments, disburse to creditors, monitor debtor compliance, and bring motions to dismiss or modify when warranted. The standing trustee’s office is funded by a percentage of plan payments (set by the U.S. Trustee under 28 U.S.C. § 586(e), capped at 10% for Chapter 13 and 10% or the actual maximum allowed in Chapter 12 for the relevant district), which covers staff, office overhead, and the trustee’s own compensation.

The standing trustee model achieves administrative economies of scale that the case-by-case panel model cannot: a single office handles thousands of repayment plans simultaneously, with standardized processes, payment portals, and creditor-disbursement infrastructure. The cost is borne by the debtor population through the percentage fee, which functions as a built-in administrative tax on plan payments.

Subchapter V Trustee Appointment

Subchapter V trustees, authorized by the Small Business Reorganization Act of 2019 and codified at 11 U.S.C. § 1183, are appointed by the United States Trustee under 28 U.S.C. § 586(a)(7). Each region maintains a roster of qualified individuals available for appointment. Unlike Chapter 7 panel trustees, Subchapter V trustees are not selected by automated rotation; the regional U.S. Trustee or Assistant U.S. Trustee designates a specific trustee for each Subchapter V case, exercising discretion based on case complexity, trustee availability, and any relevant subject-matter background.

Subchapter V trustees serve a facilitator role focused on consensual plan formation, monitoring debtor performance, and reporting to the court. They are compensated under Section 330, subject to court approval of fee applications, and are not subject to the Section 326(a) sliding-scale cap. The compensation framework reflects the trustee’s narrower role compared to a Chapter 11 trustee appointed under Section 1104.

Oversight Functions Under 28 U.S.C. § 586

Section 586(a) enumerates the United States Trustee’s statutory duties. These include:

Establishing, maintaining, and supervising the Chapter 7 panel;

Serving as and supervising standing Chapter 12 and Chapter 13 trustees;

Supervising the administration of cases and trustees in all chapters by monitoring applications for compensation and reimbursement, monitoring plans and disclosure statements, and monitoring creditors’ committees;

Taking action to ensure that all reports, schedules, and fees required to be filed under the Bankruptcy Code are properly and timely filed;

Monitoring the progress of cases and taking action to prevent undue delay;

Monitoring the appointment and performance of professionals employed by trustees and debtors-in-possession;

Notifying the U.S. Attorney of matters that relate to the occurrence of any action which may constitute a crime under the laws of the United States and assisting the U.S. Attorney in carrying out prosecutions; and

Establishing, maintaining, and supervising a list of Subchapter V trustees.

The criminal-referral function is enumerated by statute and is one of the USTP’s significant accountability tools. Section 586(a)(3)(F) operationalizes the U.S. Trustee’s parallel obligation under 18 U.S.C. § 3057, which requires any judge, receiver, or trustee to report apparent violations of bankruptcy criminal statutes to the appropriate U.S. Attorney.

Funding: The US Trustee System Fund (28 U.S.C. § 589a)

The USTP is funded almost entirely through user fees rather than through general DOJ appropriations. 28 U.S.C. § 589a establishes the United States Trustee System Fund in the U.S. Treasury, into which specified bankruptcy filing fees and Chapter 11 quarterly fees are deposited. The Fund supports the operation of the USTP, including salaries, office expenses, training, and information technology.

The principal revenue source historically has been the Chapter 11 quarterly fee assessed against debtors-in-possession under 28 U.S.C. § 1930(a)(6). Quarterly fees scale with the debtor’s disbursements during the quarter, producing a funding stream that grows with the size and activity of the Chapter 11 caseload. Smaller filing-fee allocations from Chapter 7, 12, and 13 cases supplement the Chapter 11 stream.

The user-fee funding model has policy consequences. Because Chapter 11 quarterly fees are the dominant revenue source, the USTP’s budget is sensitive to fluctuations in large-business bankruptcy filings. Congress has periodically adjusted the Chapter 11 quarterly fee schedule to balance USTP funding against debtor cost burdens, and the Supreme Court’s decision in Siegel v. Fitzgerald, 596 U.S. 464 (2022), addressed constitutional uniformity questions arising from differential fee treatment between USTP and Bankruptcy Administrator districts.

Bankruptcy Administrators in Alabama and North Carolina

Alabama and North Carolina remain outside the USTP. Bankruptcy cases in those states are administered by Bankruptcy Administrators appointed by and reporting to the judiciary rather than the executive branch. The Bankruptcy Administrator program is funded through judicial-branch appropriations rather than user fees. The functional duties largely parallel those of regional U.S. Trustees, and many policies (including the Chapter 7 panel structure and standing Chapter 13 trustee system) are mirrored.

The dual system has produced occasional constitutional and policy frictions, most prominently the fee-uniformity question addressed in Siegel v. Fitzgerald. Subsequent congressional action equalized the Chapter 11 quarterly fee schedule between USTP and Bankruptcy Administrator districts.

The Section 307 Standing Provision

11 U.S.C. § 307 provides that "[t]he United States trustee may raise and may appear and be heard on any issue in any case or proceeding under this title but may not file a plan pursuant to section 1121(c) of this title." This is the USTP’s litigation authority. The U.S. Trustee can object to plan confirmation, professional employment, fee applications, claim allowances, discharge, and virtually any other matter without needing to establish party-in-interest standing under any other provision. The carve-out for filing a Chapter 11 plan preserves the debtor’s and creditors’ primary role in plan formation.

Related Bankruptcy Code Sections

Section 330 - Allowance of compensation

Sections 327 and 328 - Employment of estate professionals

Find out whether a new Chapter 7 or Chapter 13 discharge is available now, the earliest date any timing bar lifts, and which statute controls. Applies the successive-discharge rules (the 2-4-6-8 rule). All math runs in your browser. Nothing is sent or stored.

Home › Discharge Timing Calculator

If you already received a bankruptcy discharge, you must usually wait before a new discharge is available. The waiting period runs from the filing date of your prior case to the filing date of your new case: 2 years (prior Chapter 13 to new Chapter 13), 4 years (prior Chapter 7, 11, or 12 to new Chapter 13), 6 years (prior Chapter 13 to new Chapter 7, with a 100 percent or 70 percent payment exception), or 8 years (prior Chapter 7 or 11 to new Chapter 7). This is the 2-4-6-8 rule.

Enter the chapter and filing date of your prior bankruptcy case and the chapter you intend to file next. The calculator reports whether a discharge is available today, and if not, the exact earliest date the bar lifts and the statute that controls.

The Four Successive-Discharge Bars (the 2-4-6-8 Rule)

Federal law limits how soon you can receive a second bankruptcy discharge after receiving a first one. There are four separate timing bars. Each one is measured from the filing date of the prior case to the filing date of the new case, unless noted. The shorthand is the 2-4-6-8 rule.

Prior caseNew caseWaiting periodStatute

Chapter 13Chapter 132 years11 U.S.C. 1328(f)(2)

Chapter 7, 11, or 12Chapter 134 years11 U.S.C. 1328(f)(1)

Chapter 13Chapter 76 years (with exception)11 U.S.C. 727(a)(9)

Chapter 7 or 11Chapter 78 years11 U.S.C. 727(a)(8)

Prior Chapter 7 or 11 to a new Chapter 7: the 8-year bar

Under 11 U.S.C. 727(a)(8), you cannot receive a Chapter 7 discharge if you already received a discharge in a Chapter 7 or Chapter 11 case that was filed within 8 years before the new Chapter 7 is filed. The 8-year clock runs from the prior filing date to the new filing date. See our guide to Section 727 and the Chapter 7 discharge.

Prior Chapter 13 to a new Chapter 7: the 6-year bar with a payment exception

Under 11 U.S.C. 727(a)(9), if your prior discharge was in a Chapter 13 (or Chapter 12) case filed within 6 years before the new Chapter 7, the new Chapter 7 discharge is generally barred. There is an important exception: the 6-year bar does not apply if payments under the prior plan totaled at least 100 percent of the allowed unsecured claims, or at least 70 percent of those claims under a plan that was proposed in good faith and was your best effort. If either condition is met, a Chapter 7 discharge may be available even inside the 6-year window.

Exception in plain terms: A prior Chapter 13 that paid creditors in full (100 percent), or paid 70 percent or more under a good-faith best-effort plan, can let you obtain a new Chapter 7 discharge before 6 years have passed. Whether your prior plan qualifies is a fact question that turns on what the prior plan actually paid.

Prior Chapter 7, 11, or 12 to a new Chapter 13: the 4-year bar

Under 11 U.S.C. 1328(f)(1), you cannot receive a Chapter 13 discharge if you received a discharge in a Chapter 7, Chapter 11, or Chapter 12 case filed within 4 years before the new Chapter 13. Again, the clock runs filing date to filing date.

Prior Chapter 13 to a new Chapter 13: the 2-year bar

Under 11 U.S.C. 1328(f)(2), you cannot receive a Chapter 13 discharge if you received a prior Chapter 13 discharge in a case filed within 2 years before the new one. Because most Chapter 13 plans run 3 to 5 years, this 2-year bar rarely blocks a later Chapter 13 discharge in practice.

Two Things People Get Wrong

The clock runs from the filing date, not the discharge date. Every one of these bars uses the phrase a case filed under. If your prior Chapter 7 was filed on March 1, 2019, the 8-year bar lifts on March 1, 2027, even if your discharge was not entered until several months after you filed.

These are discharge bars, not filing bars. You can still file a new case during the waiting period. Filing triggers the automatic stay, which can stop a foreclosure, garnishment, or repossession, and a Chapter 13 plan can cure arrears over time. The only thing the timing bar takes away is the discharge of personal liability at the end of the new case. Separate filing limits, such as Section 109(g) after certain dismissals, can also apply.

Dismissed without a discharge? These four bars apply only when you actually received a discharge in the prior case. If the prior case was dismissed without a discharge, the 2-4-6-8 bars do not apply. Other rules may still affect a quick refiling.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the 2-4-6-8 rule in bankruptcy?

The 2-4-6-8 rule is shorthand for the four successive-discharge timing bars. A prior Chapter 13 to a new Chapter 13 is a 2-year bar (Section 1328(f)(2)). A prior Chapter 7, 11, or 12 to a new Chapter 13 is a 4-year bar (Section 1328(f)(1)). A prior Chapter 13 to a new Chapter 7 is a 6-year bar with a payment exception (Section 727(a)(9)). A prior Chapter 7 or 11 to a new Chapter 7 is an 8-year bar (Section 727(a)(8)). Every period is measured from the filing date of the prior case to the filing date of the new case.

Does the clock run from the filing date or the discharge date?

It runs from the filing date of the prior case to the filing date of the new case, not from the discharge date. Each statute uses the phrase a case filed under. So if a prior Chapter 7 was filed on March 1, 2019, the 8-year bar lifts on March 1, 2027, regardless of when the discharge was actually entered.

Can I still file bankruptcy during the bar period?

Yes. These are discharge bars, not filing bars. You may file a new case during the bar period and still receive the automatic stay, stop a foreclosure, and treat debts through a plan. You simply will not receive a discharge of your personal liability at the end if the timing bar applies. Other filing limits, such as Section 109(g) after certain dismissals, are separate.

What is the exception to the 6-year Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 bar?

Under Section 727(a)(9), the 6-year bar after a prior Chapter 13 does not apply if payments under that prior plan totaled at least 100 percent of the allowed unsecured claims, or at least 70 percent of those claims under a plan that was proposed in good faith and was your best effort. If either condition is met, a new Chapter 7 discharge may be available even inside the 6-year window.

Is the relevant date the same in every district?

The statutory periods are federal and uniform, but how a court treats edge cases (such as conversions between chapters, refiled cases, or the precise day-count) can vary. The controlling date in your situation can depend on local rules and case law. Always confirm the exact date with a licensed bankruptcy attorney before relying on it.

This is general information, not legal advice. This calculator applies only the four successive-discharge timing bars and does not account for every eligibility rule. It does not create an attorney-client relationship. Rules have exceptions, the controlling date can vary by jurisdiction and on facts like conversions or refilings, and other requirements (the means test, exemptions, Section 109(g) filing bars, and prior-case payment history) may also apply. Consult a licensed bankruptcy attorney before relying on any date shown here.

What happens to cases like mine?

Real outcomes from 37.9 million federal bankruptcy cases (FJC Integrated Database, 2008–2024). Pick your court and chapter.

Across millions of federal bankruptcy cases (FJC data, 2008–2024): Chapter 7 cases are discharged about 95% of the time; Chapter 13 about 41% of cases that reach a final outcome. Having an attorney matters enormously: Chapter 13 filers with a lawyer are discharged about 42% of the time versus about 2% filing pro se. Median time to discharge is about 3–4 months for Chapter 7 and about 5 years for Chapter 13.

Bankruptcy in Alabama

Complete guide: exemptions, means test income limits, filing costs, and real case outcome data for Alabama.

Important: This page provides educational information about bankruptcy in Alabama. It is not legal advice. Median income figures are approximate (Census/DOJ, effective April 2026). Verify current amounts at the DOJ Means Testing page.

Alabama Exemptions

State Exemptions Only

Alabama requires bankruptcy filers to use state exemptions exclusively. Federal exemptions under 11 U.S.C. Section 522(d) are not available. Research Alabama's homestead, vehicle, personal property, and wildcard exemptions before filing.

Alabama exemption amounts

Federal exemptions: not allowed. Alabama has opted out of the federal exemptions, so filers use the state exemptions below (Ala. Code § 6-10-11).

Married couples filing jointly: each spouse can claim these exemptions (source).

ExemptionAmountStatuteNotes

Homestead$18,800 needs reviewAla. Code § 6-10-2 (as amended by 2026 HB96); § 6-10-12 (CPI adjustment)(CPI-adjusted 4/1/2024; statutory base $15,000); $56,400 if the resident is 62 or older or has a disability (effective 6/1/2026); up to 160 acres

Motor vehicleNot yet verified needs reviewAla. Code § 6-10-6

Retirement accounts also have federal protection. ERISA-qualified plans stay out of the bankruptcy estate under 11 U.S.C. § 541(c)(2), and 11 U.S.C. § 522(b)(3)(C) exempts tax-exempt retirement funds whatever the state law says. IRAs carry a federal dollar cap under § 522(n). Which state's exemptions you use depends on where you lived during the two years before filing (11 U.S.C. § 522(b)(3)(A)).

Last verified September 20, 2026. Amounts change, so check the statute before you rely on a figure. "Needs review" marks a figure we have not yet confirmed against the statute or the court. This is general information, not legal advice.

Homestead Exemption

Protects equity in your primary residence. Amounts vary by state. Check Alabama homestead exemption amounts.

Vehicle Exemption

Protects equity in your car. Most states protect $2,000 to $7,500. See vehicle exemption details.

Retirement Accounts

401(k)s, IRAs, and pensions are generally fully exempt in bankruptcy. See retirement exemptions.

Wildcard Exemption

Applies to any property. Not all states offer this. See wildcard exemptions.

If your household income is at or below these thresholds, you pass Part 1 of the means test and likely qualify for Chapter 7.

Filing Bankruptcy in Alabama

Districts

Alabama has 3 federal bankruptcy districts. The district where you file depends on where you have lived for the greater part of the last 180 days. Each district may have different local rules, no-look fee amounts, and trustee practices.

Filing Costs

Chapter 7 filing fee: $338. Chapter 13: $313. Fee waivers are available for filers below 150% of the poverty line. Installment payments available for all filers. Full cost breakdown.

Before You File

Complete credit counseling from an approved provider (required within 180 days before filing).

Determine your chapter - Chapter 7 vs. Chapter 13 comparison.

Gather income documentation for the last 6 full calendar months.

List all debts, assets, income, and expenses for the bankruptcy schedules.

Research Alabama exemptions to understand what property you can keep.

After You File

The automatic stay takes effect immediately, stopping collections, garnishments, and lawsuits.

Attend the 341 meeting of creditors (usually 30-45 days after filing).

Complete a debtor education course (required before discharge).

Receive your discharge (Chapter 7: ~60-90 days after 341 meeting; Chapter 13: after completing 3-5 year plan).

Step-by-step guides: How Chapter 7 works (liquidation: who qualifies, the process, what you keep) · How Chapter 13 works (the repayment plan: eligibility, how the payment is set, why plans fail). Both are free, plain-English, and not legal advice.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does Alabama use federal or state exemptions?

Alabama uses state exemptions only. The state has opted out of the federal exemptions in 11 U.S.C. § 522(d) (Ala. Code § 6-10-11).

How much does it cost to file bankruptcy in Alabama?

The court filing fee for Chapter 7 is $338 and Chapter 13 is $313. Attorney fees in Alabama typically range from $1,000 to $3,500 for Chapter 7 and $2,500 to $5,000 for Chapter 13. You can also file without an attorney (pro se) and request to pay the filing fee in installments.

What is the income limit for Chapter 7 in Alabama?

The means test compares your household income to Alabama's median. For a single person, the current threshold is approximately $56,050 per year. For a family of four, it is approximately $99,208. If your income is below the median for your household size, you pass Part 1 of the means test.

What property can I keep in Alabama bankruptcy?

Alabama requires filers to use state exemptions only. Key exemptions to research include the homestead exemption (how much home equity you can protect), vehicle exemption, personal property exemption, and any wildcard exemption. Check Alabama statutes for current amounts.

How long does bankruptcy stay on my credit in Alabama?

Chapter 7 stays on your credit report for 10 years from the filing date. Chapter 13 stays for 7 years. However, many people begin rebuilding credit within 1-2 years of discharge and can qualify for a mortgage within 2-4 years.

Can I file bankruptcy again in Alabama?

Yes, but there are waiting periods between discharges. Chapter 7 to Chapter 7: 8 years. Chapter 7 to Chapter 13: 4 years. Chapter 13 to Chapter 13: 2 years. Chapter 13 to Chapter 7: 6 years (unless you paid 100% or 70%+ with good faith). Use the free discharge eligibility screener to check your dates.

Which bankruptcy court do I file in within Alabama?

Alabama has 3 federal bankruptcy districts. You file in the district where you have lived for the greater part of the last 180 days. If you recently moved, the 180-day rule may require filing in your previous district. Check local court websites for county-to-district lookups.

What debts cannot be discharged in bankruptcy?

Most debts are dischargeable, but exceptions include most student loans (unless you prove undue hardship), child support and alimony, recent tax debts (generally last 3 years), debts from fraud or willful injury, DUI-related debts, and criminal fines. See nondischargeable.org for the full list.

## Bankruptcy in Arkansas: Filing Guide, Exemptions, and Statistics [2026]
Source: https://openbankruptcyproject.org/states/arkansas.html

Open Bankruptcy Project›Exemptions by State›Arkansas

Bankruptcy in Arkansas

Complete guide: exemptions, means test income limits, filing costs, and real case outcome data for Arkansas.

Important: This page provides educational information about bankruptcy in Arkansas. It is not legal advice. Median income figures are approximate (Census/DOJ, effective April 2026). Verify current amounts at the DOJ Means Testing page.

2

Bankruptcy Districts

$54,714

Median Income (1 person)

Yes

Federal Exemptions

$338

Ch. 7 Filing Fee

Arkansas Exemptions

Federal Exemptions Available

Filers in Arkansas can choose between state and federal bankruptcy exemptions. Compare both sets carefully - the federal wildcard exemption, $1,675 plus up to $15,800 of any unused homestead exemption for cases filed on or after April 1, 2025, may protect more personal property, while Arkansas state exemptions may offer stronger homestead protection.

Arkansas exemption amounts

Federal exemptions: allowed. Arkansas has not opted out, so filers choose either the state exemptions below or the federal exemptions in 11 U.S.C. § 522(d), not a mix of both (Ark. Code Ann. § 16-66-217 (election of state or federal 11 U.S.C. § 522(d) exemptions)).

Married couples filing jointly: not every exemption here doubles for a joint case; check each statute (source).

ExemptionAmountStatuteNotes

HomesteadNot yet verified needs reviewArk. Const. art. 9, §§ 3-5; Ark. Code Ann. §§ 16-66-210, 16-66-218(a)(1), (b)

Motor vehicle$1,200 needs reviewArk. Code Ann. § 16-66-218(a)(2)In one motor vehicle

Household goodsNot yet verified needs reviewArk. Const. art. 9, §§ 1-2; Ark. Code Ann. § 16-66-218(b)(1)

Wildcard$500 needs reviewArk. Const. art. 9, §§ 1-2; Ark. Code Ann. § 16-66-218(b)(1)Of any personal property (married person or head of family); $200 (unmarried, not head of family); plus wearing apparel

WagesNot yet verified needs reviewArk. Code Ann. § 16-66-208

Tools of the trade$750 needs reviewArk. Code Ann. § 16-66-218(a)(4)Aggregate; implements, professional books and tools of the trade

Retirement accountsNot yet verified needs reviewArk. Code Ann. §§ 16-66-220, 16-66-218(b)(16)

Retirement accounts also have federal protection. ERISA-qualified plans stay out of the bankruptcy estate under 11 U.S.C. § 541(c)(2), and 11 U.S.C. § 522(b)(3)(C) exempts tax-exempt retirement funds whatever the state law says. IRAs carry a federal dollar cap under § 522(n). Which state's exemptions you use depends on where you lived during the two years before filing (11 U.S.C. § 522(b)(3)(A)).

Last verified September 20, 2026. Amounts change, so check the statute before you rely on a figure. "Needs review" marks a figure we have not yet confirmed against the statute or the court. This is general information, not legal advice.

Homestead Exemption

Protects equity in your primary residence. Amounts vary by state. Check Arkansas homestead exemption amounts.

Vehicle Exemption

Protects equity in your car. Most states protect $2,000 to $7,500. See vehicle exemption details.

Retirement Accounts

401(k)s, IRAs, and pensions are generally fully exempt in bankruptcy. See retirement exemptions.

Wildcard Exemption

Applies to any property. Not all states offer this. See wildcard exemptions.

Filing Bankruptcy in Arkansas

Districts

Arkansas has 2 federal bankruptcy districts. The district where you file depends on where you have lived for the greater part of the last 180 days. Each district may have different local rules, no-look fee amounts, and trustee practices.

Filing Costs

Chapter 7 filing fee: $338. Chapter 13: $313. Fee waivers are available for filers below 150% of the poverty line. Installment payments available for all filers. Full cost breakdown.

Before You File

Complete credit counseling from an approved provider (required within 180 days before filing).

Determine your chapter - Chapter 7 vs. Chapter 13 comparison.

Gather income documentation for the last 6 full calendar months.

List all debts, assets, income, and expenses for the bankruptcy schedules.

Research Arkansas exemptions to understand what property you can keep.

After You File

The automatic stay takes effect immediately, stopping collections, garnishments, and lawsuits.

Attend the 341 meeting of creditors (usually 30-45 days after filing).

Complete a debtor education course (required before discharge).

Receive your discharge (Chapter 7: ~60-90 days after 341 meeting; Chapter 13: after completing 3-5 year plan).

Step-by-step guides: How Chapter 7 works (liquidation: who qualifies, the process, what you keep) · How Chapter 13 works (the repayment plan: eligibility, how the payment is set, why plans fail). Both are free, plain-English, and not legal advice.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does Arkansas use federal or state exemptions?

Arkansas lets filers choose. Arkansas has not opted out, so you can use either the Arkansas exemptions or the federal exemptions in 11 U.S.C. § 522(d), but not a mix of both (Ark. Code Ann. § 16-66-217 (election of state or federal 11 U.S.C. § 522(d) exemptions)).

How much does it cost to file bankruptcy in Arkansas?

The court filing fee for Chapter 7 is $338 and Chapter 13 is $313. Attorney fees in Arkansas typically range from $1,000 to $3,500 for Chapter 7 and $2,500 to $5,000 for Chapter 13. You can also file without an attorney (pro se) and request to pay the filing fee in installments.

What is the income limit for Chapter 7 in Arkansas?

The means test compares your household income to Arkansas's median. For a single person, the current threshold is approximately $54,714 per year. For a family of four, it is approximately $96,844. If your income is below the median for your household size, you pass Part 1 of the means test.

Can I use federal exemptions in Arkansas?

Yes. Arkansas allows you to choose between state exemptions and federal bankruptcy exemptions under 11 U.S.C. Section 522(d). You must pick one complete set - you cannot mix individual exemptions from both. Compare homestead, vehicle, and wildcard amounts under each system before deciding.

How long does bankruptcy stay on my credit in Arkansas?

Chapter 7 stays on your credit report for 10 years from the filing date. Chapter 13 stays for 7 years. However, many people begin rebuilding credit within 1-2 years of discharge and can qualify for a mortgage within 2-4 years.

Can I file bankruptcy again in Arkansas?

Yes, but there are waiting periods between discharges. Chapter 7 to Chapter 7: 8 years. Chapter 7 to Chapter 13: 4 years. Chapter 13 to Chapter 13: 2 years. Chapter 13 to Chapter 7: 6 years (unless you paid 100% or 70%+ with good faith). Use the free discharge eligibility screener to check your dates.

Which bankruptcy court do I file in within Arkansas?

Arkansas has 2 federal bankruptcy districts. You file in the district where you have lived for the greater part of the last 180 days. If you recently moved, the 180-day rule may require filing in your previous district. Check local court websites for county-to-district lookups.

What debts cannot be discharged in bankruptcy?

Most debts are dischargeable, but exceptions include most student loans (unless you prove undue hardship), child support and alimony, recent tax debts (generally last 3 years), debts from fraud or willful injury, DUI-related debts, and criminal fines. See nondischargeable.org for the full list.

California Exemptions

State Exemptions Only

California exemption amounts

Married couples filing jointly: not every exemption here doubles for a joint case; check each statute (source).

Retirement accounts also have federal protection. ERISA-qualified plans stay out of the bankruptcy estate under 11 U.S.C. § 541(c)(2), and 11 U.S.C. § 522(b)(3)(C) exempts tax-exempt retirement funds whatever the state law says. IRAs carry a federal dollar cap under § 522(n). Which state's exemptions you use depends on where you lived during the two years before filing (11 U.S.C. § 522(b)(3)(A)).

Filing Bankruptcy in Connecticut

Districts

Connecticut has a single federal bankruptcy district. All cases are filed in this one court, which simplifies the process.

Filing Costs

Chapter 7 filing fee: $338. Chapter 13: $313. Fee waivers are available for filers below 150% of the poverty line. Installment payments available for all filers. Full cost breakdown.

Before You File

Complete credit counseling from an approved provider (required within 180 days before filing).

Determine your chapter - Chapter 7 vs. Chapter 13 comparison.

Gather income documentation for the last 6 full calendar months.

List all debts, assets, income, and expenses for the bankruptcy schedules.

Research Connecticut exemptions to understand what property you can keep.

After You File

The automatic stay takes effect immediately, stopping collections, garnishments, and lawsuits.

Attend the 341 meeting of creditors (usually 30-45 days after filing).

Complete a debtor education course (required before discharge).

Receive your discharge (Chapter 7: ~60-90 days after 341 meeting; Chapter 13: after completing 3-5 year plan).

Step-by-step guides: How Chapter 7 works (liquidation: who qualifies, the process, what you keep) · How Chapter 13 works (the repayment plan: eligibility, how the payment is set, why plans fail). Both are free, plain-English, and not legal advice.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I keep my car in Connecticut bankruptcy?

Connecticut protects $7,000 in a motor vehicle under Conn. Gen. Stat. § 52-352b(10). Details: Aggregate value in up to two motor vehicles (fair market value less liens). Last verified September 20, 2026. Amounts change, so check the statute.

Does Connecticut use federal or state exemptions?

Connecticut lets filers choose. Connecticut has not opted out, so you can use either the Connecticut exemptions or the federal exemptions in 11 U.S.C. § 522(d), but not a mix of both.

How much does it cost to file bankruptcy in Connecticut?

The court filing fee for Chapter 7 is $338 and Chapter 13 is $313. Attorney fees in Connecticut typically range from $1,000 to $3,500 for Chapter 7 and $2,500 to $5,000 for Chapter 13. You can also file without an attorney (pro se) and request to pay the filing fee in installments.

What is the income limit for Chapter 7 in Connecticut?

The means test compares your household income to Connecticut's median. For a single person, the current threshold is approximately $87,411 per year. For a family of four, it is approximately $154,717. If your income is below the median for your household size, you pass Part 1 of the means test.

Can I use federal exemptions in Connecticut?

Yes. Connecticut allows you to choose between state exemptions and federal bankruptcy exemptions under 11 U.S.C. Section 522(d). You must pick one complete set - you cannot mix individual exemptions from both. Compare homestead, vehicle, and wildcard amounts under each system before deciding.

How long does bankruptcy stay on my credit in Connecticut?

Chapter 7 stays on your credit report for 10 years from the filing date. Chapter 13 stays for 7 years. However, many people begin rebuilding credit within 1-2 years of discharge and can qualify for a mortgage within 2-4 years.

Can I file bankruptcy again in Connecticut?

Yes, but there are waiting periods between discharges. Chapter 7 to Chapter 7: 8 years. Chapter 7 to Chapter 13: 4 years. Chapter 13 to Chapter 13: 2 years. Chapter 13 to Chapter 7: 6 years (unless you paid 100% or 70%+ with good faith). Use the free discharge eligibility screener to check your dates.

What debts cannot be discharged in bankruptcy?

Most debts are dischargeable, but exceptions include most student loans (unless you prove undue hardship), child support and alimony, recent tax debts (generally last 3 years), debts from fraud or willful injury, DUI-related debts, and criminal fines. See nondischargeable.org for the full list.

How much does it cost to file bankruptcy in Florida?

The court filing fee for Chapter 7 is $338 and Chapter 13 is $313. Attorney fees in Florida typically range from $1,000 to $3,500 for Chapter 7 and $2,500 to $5,000 for Chapter 13. You can also file without an attorney (pro se) and request to pay the filing fee in installments.

What is the income limit for Chapter 7 in Florida?

The means test compares your household income to Florida's median. For a single person, the current threshold is approximately $69,876 per year. For a family of four, it is approximately $123,681. If your income is below the median for your household size, you pass Part 1 of the means test.

What property can I keep in Florida bankruptcy?

Florida requires filers to use state exemptions only. Key exemptions to research include the homestead exemption (how much home equity you can protect), vehicle exemption, personal property exemption, and any wildcard exemption. Check Florida statutes for current amounts.

How long does bankruptcy stay on my credit in Florida?

Chapter 7 stays on your credit report for 10 years from the filing date. Chapter 13 stays for 7 years. However, many people begin rebuilding credit within 1-2 years of discharge and can qualify for a mortgage within 2-4 years.

Can I file bankruptcy again in Florida?

Yes, but there are waiting periods between discharges. Chapter 7 to Chapter 7: 8 years. Chapter 7 to Chapter 13: 4 years. Chapter 13 to Chapter 13: 2 years. Chapter 13 to Chapter 7: 6 years (unless you paid 100% or 70%+ with good faith). Use the free discharge eligibility screener to check your dates.

Which bankruptcy court do I file in within Florida?

Florida has 3 federal bankruptcy districts. You file in the district where you have lived for the greater part of the last 180 days. If you recently moved, the 180-day rule may require filing in your previous district. Check local court websites for county-to-district lookups.

What debts cannot be discharged in bankruptcy?

Most debts are dischargeable, but exceptions include most student loans (unless you prove undue hardship), child support and alimony, recent tax debts (generally last 3 years), debts from fraud or willful injury, DUI-related debts, and criminal fines. See nondischargeable.org for the full list.

Filing Bankruptcy in Georgia

Districts

Georgia has 3 federal bankruptcy districts. The district where you file depends on where you have lived for the greater part of the last 180 days. Each district may have different local rules, no-look fee amounts, and trustee practices.

Filing Costs

Chapter 7 filing fee: $338. Chapter 13: $313. Fee waivers are available for filers below 150% of the poverty line. Installment payments available for all filers. Full cost breakdown.

Before You File

Complete credit counseling from an approved provider (required within 180 days before filing).

Determine your chapter - Chapter 7 vs. Chapter 13 comparison.

Gather income documentation for the last 6 full calendar months.

List all debts, assets, income, and expenses for the bankruptcy schedules.

Research Georgia exemptions to understand what property you can keep.

After You File

The automatic stay takes effect immediately, stopping collections, garnishments, and lawsuits.

Attend the 341 meeting of creditors (usually 30-45 days after filing).

Complete a debtor education course (required before discharge).

Receive your discharge (Chapter 7: ~60-90 days after 341 meeting; Chapter 13: after completing 3-5 year plan).

Step-by-step guides: How Chapter 7 works (liquidation: who qualifies, the process, what you keep) · How Chapter 13 works (the repayment plan: eligibility, how the payment is set, why plans fail). Both are free, plain-English, and not legal advice.

IRAs carry a federal dollar cap under § 522(n). Which state's exemptions you use depends on where you lived during the two years before filing (11 U.S.C. § 522(b)(3)(A)).

Last verified September 20, 2026. Amounts change, so check the statute before you rely on a figure. "Needs review" marks a figure we have not yet confirmed against the statute or the court. This is general information, not legal advice.

Homestead Exemption

Protects equity in your primary residence. Amounts vary by state. Check Illinois homestead exemption amounts.

Vehicle Exemption

Protects equity in your car. Most states protect $2,000 to $7,500. See vehicle exemption details.

Retirement Accounts

401(k)s, IRAs, and pensions are generally fully exempt in bankruptcy. See retirement exemptions.

Wildcard Exemption

Applies to any property. Not all states offer this. See wildcard exemptions.

Filing Bankruptcy in Illinois

Districts

Illinois has 3 federal bankruptcy districts. The district where you file depends on where you have lived for the greater part of the last 180 days. Each district may have different local rules, no-look fee amounts, and trustee practices.

Filing Costs

Chapter 7 filing fee: $338. Chapter 13: $313. Fee waivers are available for filers below 150% of the poverty line. Installment payments available for all filers. Full cost breakdown.

Before You File

Complete credit counseling from an approved provider (required within 180 days before filing).

Determine your chapter - Chapter 7 vs. Chapter 13 comparison.

Gather income documentation for the last 6 full calendar months.

List all debts, assets, income, and expenses for the bankruptcy schedules.

Research Illinois exemptions to understand what property you can keep.

After You File

The automatic stay takes effect immediately, stopping collections, garnishments, and lawsuits.

Attend the 341 meeting of creditors (usually 30-45 days after filing).

Complete a debtor education course (required before discharge).

Receive your discharge (Chapter 7: ~60-90 days after 341 meeting; Chapter 13: after completing 3-5 year plan).

Step-by-step guides: How Chapter 7 works (liquidation: who qualifies, the process, what you keep) · How Chapter 13 works (the repayment plan: eligibility, how the payment is set, why plans fail). Both are free, plain-English, and not legal advice.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I keep my car in Illinois bankruptcy?

Illinois protects $3,600 in a motor vehicle under 735 ILCS 5/12-1001(c). Last verified September 20, 2026. Amounts change, so check the statute.

Does Illinois use federal or state exemptions?

Illinois uses state exemptions only. The state has opted out of the federal exemptions in 11 U.S.C. § 522(d) (735 ILCS 5/12-1201).

How much does it cost to file bankruptcy in Illinois?

The court filing fee for Chapter 7 is $338 and Chapter 13 is $313. Attorney fees in Illinois typically range from $1,000 to $3,500 for Chapter 7 and $2,500 to $5,000 for Chapter 13. You can also file without an attorney (pro se) and request to pay the filing fee in installments.

What is the income limit for Chapter 7 in Illinois?

The means test compares your household income to Illinois's median. For a single person, the current threshold is approximately $74,430 per year. For a family of four, it is approximately $131,741. If your income is below the median for your household size, you pass Part 1 of the means test.

What property can I keep in Illinois bankruptcy?

Illinois requires filers to use state exemptions only. Key exemptions to research include the homestead exemption (how much home equity you can protect), vehicle exemption, personal property exemption, and any wildcard exemption. Check Illinois statutes for current amounts.

How long does bankruptcy stay on my credit in Illinois?

Chapter 7 stays on your credit report for 10 years from the filing date. Chapter 13 stays for 7 years. However, many people begin rebuilding credit within 1-2 years of discharge and can qualify for a mortgage within 2-4 years.

Can I file bankruptcy again in Illinois?

Yes, but there are waiting periods between discharges. Chapter 7 to Chapter 7: 8 years. Chapter 7 to Chapter 13: 4 years. Chapter 13 to Chapter 13: 2 years. Chapter 13 to Chapter 7: 6 years (unless you paid 100% or 70%+ with good faith). Use the free discharge eligibility screener to check your dates.

Which bankruptcy court do I file in within Illinois?

Illinois has 3 federal bankruptcy districts. You file in the district where you have lived for the greater part of the last 180 days. If you recently moved, the 180-day rule may require filing in your previous district. Check local court websites for county-to-district lookups.

What debts cannot be discharged in bankruptcy?

Most debts are dischargeable, but exceptions include most student loans (unless you prove undue hardship), child support and alimony, recent tax debts (generally last 3 years), debts from fraud or willful injury, DUI-related debts, and criminal fines. See nondischargeable.org for the full list.
