Kansas protects $20,000 in a motor vehicle under K.S.A. 60-2304(c). Details: In one vehicle; no limit for a vehicle designed or equipped for a handicapped person. Last verified September 20, 2026. Amounts change, so check the statute.

Does Kansas use federal or state exemptions?

Kansas uses state exemptions only. The state has opted out of the federal exemptions in 11 U.S.C. § 522(d) (K.S.A. 60-2312(a)).

How much does it cost to file bankruptcy in Kansas?

The court filing fee for Chapter 7 is $338 and Chapter 13 is $313. Attorney fees in Kansas typically range from $1,000 to $3,500 for Chapter 7 and $2,500 to $5,000 for Chapter 13. You can also file without an attorney (pro se) and request to pay the filing fee in installments.

What is the income limit for Chapter 7 in Kansas?

The means test compares your household income to Kansas's median. For a single person, the current threshold is approximately $69,197 per year. For a family of four, it is approximately $122,479. If your income is below the median for your household size, you pass Part 1 of the means test.

What property can I keep in Kansas bankruptcy?

Kansas requires filers to use state exemptions only. Key exemptions to research include the homestead exemption (how much home equity you can protect), vehicle exemption, personal property exemption, and any wildcard exemption. Check Kansas statutes for current amounts.

How long does bankruptcy stay on my credit in Kansas?

Chapter 7 stays on your credit report for 10 years from the filing date. Chapter 13 stays for 7 years. However, many people begin rebuilding credit within 1-2 years of discharge and can qualify for a mortgage within 2-4 years.

Can I file bankruptcy again in Kansas?

Yes, but there are waiting periods between discharges. Chapter 7 to Chapter 7: 8 years. Chapter 7 to Chapter 13: 4 years. Chapter 13 to Chapter 13: 2 years. Chapter 13 to Chapter 7: 6 years (unless you paid 100% or 70%+ with good faith). Use the free discharge eligibility screener to check your dates.

What debts cannot be discharged in bankruptcy?

Most debts are dischargeable, but exceptions include most student loans (unless you prove undue hardship), child support and alimony, recent tax debts (generally last 3 years), debts from fraud or willful injury, DUI-related debts, and criminal fines. See nondischargeable.org for the full list.

Bankruptcy in Kentucky

Complete guide: exemptions, means test income limits, filing costs, and real case outcome data for Kentucky.

Important: This page provides educational information about bankruptcy in Kentucky. It is not legal advice. Median income figures are approximate (Census/DOJ, effective April 2026). Verify current amounts at the DOJ Means Testing page.

Federal Exemptions

Kentucky Exemptions

Federal Exemptions Available

Filers in Kentucky can choose between state and federal bankruptcy exemptions. Compare both sets carefully - the federal wildcard exemption, $1,675 plus up to $15,800 of any unused homestead exemption for cases filed on or after April 1, 2025, may protect more personal property, while Kentucky state exemptions may offer stronger homestead protection.

Kentucky exemption amounts

Federal exemptions: allowed. Kentucky has not opted out, so filers choose either the state exemptions below or the federal exemptions in 11 U.S.C. § 522(d), not a mix of both (source).

Married couples filing jointly: whether these exemptions double is not yet verified.

ExemptionAmountStatuteNotes

Homestead$5,000KRS 427.060

Motor vehicle$2,500KRS 427.010(1)

Household goods$3,000KRS 427.010(1)Aggregate (household furnishings, jewelry, personal clothing and ornaments)

Wildcard$1,000KRS 427.160In any property (bankruptcy only)

WagesGarnishment capped at the lesser of 25% of weekly disposable earnings or the amount by which disposable earnings exceed 30 times the federal minimum hourly wage (i.e., 75% / 30x federal minimum wage protected)KRS 427.010(2)

Tools of the trade$300KRS 427.030; KRS 427.010(1); KRS 427.040Tools of trade; plus $2,500 vehicle for a mechanic/skilled artisan; farmers: $3,000 tools, equipment and livestock; listed professionals: $1,000 library/office equipment plus $2,500 vehicle

Retirement accountsNot yet verified needs reviewKRS 427.150

Retirement accounts also have federal protection. ERISA-qualified plans stay out of the bankruptcy estate under 11 U.S.C. § 541(c)(2), and 11 U.S.C. § 522(b)(3)(C) exempts tax-exempt retirement funds whatever the state law says. IRAs carry a federal dollar cap under § 522(n). Which state's exemptions you use depends on where you lived during the two years before filing (11 U.S.C. § 522(b)(3)(A)).

Last verified September 20, 2026. Amounts change, so check the statute before you rely on a figure. "Needs review" marks a figure we have not yet confirmed against the statute or the court. This is general information, not legal advice.

Protects equity in your primary residence. Amounts vary by state. Check Kentucky homestead exemption amounts.

Vehicle Exemption

Protects equity in your car. Most states protect $2,000 to $7,500. See vehicle exemption details.

Retirement Accounts

401(k)s, IRAs, and pensions are generally fully exempt in bankruptcy. See retirement exemptions.

Wildcard Exemption

Applies to any property. Not all states offer this. See wildcard exemptions.

Filing Bankruptcy in Kentucky

Districts

Kentucky has 2 federal bankruptcy districts. The district where you file depends on where you have lived for the greater part of the last 180 days. Each district may have different local rules, no-look fee amounts, and trustee practices.

Filing Costs

Chapter 7 filing fee: $338. Chapter 13: $313. Fee waivers are available for filers below 150% of the poverty line. Installment payments available for all filers. Full cost breakdown.

Before You File

Complete credit counseling from an approved provider (required within 180 days before filing).

Determine your chapter - Chapter 7 vs. Chapter 13 comparison.

Gather income documentation for the last 6 full calendar months.

List all debts, assets, income, and expenses for the bankruptcy schedules.

Research Kentucky exemptions to understand what property you can keep.

After You File

The automatic stay takes effect immediately, stopping collections, garnishments, and lawsuits.

Attend the 341 meeting of creditors (usually 30-45 days after filing).

Complete a debtor education course (required before discharge).

Receive your discharge (Chapter 7: ~60-90 days after 341 meeting; Chapter 13: after completing 3-5 year plan).

Step-by-step guides: How Chapter 7 works (liquidation: who qualifies, the process, what you keep) · How Chapter 13 works (the repayment plan: eligibility, how the payment is set, why plans fail). Both are free, plain-English, and not legal advice.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I keep my car in Kentucky bankruptcy?

Kentucky protects $2,500 in a motor vehicle under KRS 427.010(1). Last verified September 20, 2026. Amounts change, so check the statute.

Does Kentucky use federal or state exemptions?

Kentucky lets filers choose. Kentucky has not opted out, so you can use either the Kentucky exemptions or the federal exemptions in 11 U.S.C. § 522(d), but not a mix of both.

How much does it cost to file bankruptcy in Kentucky?

The court filing fee for Chapter 7 is $338 and Chapter 13 is $313. Attorney fees in Kentucky typically range from $1,000 to $3,500 for Chapter 7 and $2,500 to $5,000 for Chapter 13. You can also file without an attorney (pro se) and request to pay the filing fee in installments.

What is the income limit for Chapter 7 in Kentucky?

The means test compares your household income to Kentucky's median. For a single person, the current threshold is approximately $58,632 per year. For a family of four, it is approximately $103,779. If your income is below the median for your household size, you pass Part 1 of the means test.

Can I use federal exemptions in Kentucky?

Yes. Kentucky allows you to choose between state exemptions and federal bankruptcy exemptions under 11 U.S.C. Section 522(d). You must pick one complete set - you cannot mix individual exemptions from both. Compare homestead, vehicle, and wildcard amounts under each system before deciding.

How long does bankruptcy stay on my credit in Kentucky?

Chapter 7 stays on your credit report for 10 years from the filing date. Chapter 13 stays for 7 years. However, many people begin rebuilding credit within 1-2 years of discharge and can qualify for a mortgage within 2-4 years.

Can I file bankruptcy again in Kentucky?

Yes, but there are waiting periods between discharges. Chapter 7 to Chapter 7: 8 years. Chapter 7 to Chapter 13: 4 years. Chapter 13 to Chapter 13: 2 years. Chapter 13 to Chapter 7: 6 years (unless you paid 100% or 70%+ with good faith). Use the free discharge eligibility screener to check your dates.

Which bankruptcy court do I file in within Kentucky?

Kentucky has 2 federal bankruptcy districts. You file in the district where you have lived for the greater part of the last 180 days. If you recently moved, the 180-day rule may require filing in your previous district. Check local court websites for county-to-district lookups.

What debts cannot be discharged in bankruptcy?

Most debts are dischargeable, but exceptions include most student loans (unless you prove undue hardship), child support and alimony, recent tax debts (generally last 3 years), debts from fraud or willful injury, DUI-related debts, and criminal fines. See nondischargeable.org for the full list.

Maryland Exemptions

State Exemptions Only

Maryland requires bankruptcy filers to use state exemptions exclusively. Federal exemptions under 11 U.S.C. Section 522(d) are not available. Research Maryland's homestead, vehicle, personal property, and wildcard exemptions before filing.

Maryland exemption amounts

Federal exemptions: not allowed. Maryland has opted out of the federal exemptions, so filers use the state exemptions below (Md. Code, Cts. & Jud. Proc. § 11-504(g)).

Married couples filing jointly: not every exemption here doubles for a joint case; check each statute (source).

Scheduled change (April 1, 2028): The homestead cap re-adjusts automatically with the next triennial § 104 adjustment of § 522(d)(1) (April 1, 2028). Separately, 2026 HB 1520 (Courts - Exemption from Judgment - Alterations and Additions) would raise several § 11-504 amounts effective 10/1/2026; it passed the House 137-0 on 3/23/2026 but the bill page showed it still in the Senate committee; NOT enacted as of the page fetched. Source.

ExemptionAmountStatuteNotes

Homestead$31,575Md. Code, Cts. & Jud. Proc. § 11-504(f)(1)(ii); 11 U.S.C. § 522(d)(1) as adjusted(the federal § 522(d)(1) amount, adjusted 4/1/2025)

Motor vehicleNoneMd. Code, Cts. & Jud. Proc. § 11-504Use the wildcards

Household goods$1,000Md. Code, Cts. & Jud. Proc. § 11-504(b)(4)

Wildcard$11,000Md. Code, Cts. & Jud. Proc. § 11-504(b)(5), (b)(6), (f)(1)(i)$6,000 cash or property of any kind (§ 11-504(b)(6), inclusive of the $500 deposit-account item in (b)(5)) plus $5,000 in personal property in bankruptcy (§ 11-504(f)(1)(i)); $11,000 combined

WagesGreater of 75% of disposable wages or 30 times the Maryland minimum hourly wage per week, plus any medical-insurance deductionMd. Code, Com. Law § 15-601.1(b)

Tools of the trade$5,000Md. Code, Cts. & Jud. Proc. § 11-504(b)(1)

Retirement accountsUnlimited (tax-qualified retirement plans)Md. Code, Cts. & Jud. Proc. § 11-504(h)(1)

Retirement accounts also have federal protection. ERISA-qualified plans stay out of the bankruptcy estate under 11 U.S.C. § 541(c)(2), and 11 U.S.C. § 522(b)(3)(C) exempts tax-exempt retirement funds whatever the state law says. IRAs carry a federal dollar cap under § 522(n). Which state's exemptions you use depends on where you lived during the two years before filing (11 U.S.C. § 522(b)(3)(A)).

Last verified September 20, 2026. Amounts change, so check the statute before you rely on a figure. "Needs review" marks a figure we have not yet confirmed against the statute or the court. This is general information, not legal advice.

Homestead Exemption

Protects equity in your primary residence. Amounts vary by state. Check Maryland homestead exemption amounts.

Vehicle Exemption

Protects equity in your car. Most states protect $2,000 to $7,500. See vehicle exemption details.

Retirement Accounts

401(k)s, IRAs, and pensions are generally fully exempt in bankruptcy. See retirement exemptions.

Wildcard Exemption

Applies to any property. Not all states offer this. See wildcard exemptions.

Filing Bankruptcy in Maryland

Districts

Maryland has a single federal bankruptcy district. All cases are filed in this one court, which simplifies the process.

Filing Costs

Chapter 7 filing fee: $338. Chapter 13: $313. Fee waivers are available for filers below 150% of the poverty line. Installment payments available for all filers. Full cost breakdown.

Before You File

Complete credit counseling from an approved provider (required within 180 days before filing).

Determine your chapter - Chapter 7 vs. Chapter 13 comparison.

Gather income documentation for the last 6 full calendar months.

List all debts, assets, income, and expenses for the bankruptcy schedules.

Research Maryland exemptions to understand what property you can keep.

After You File

The automatic stay takes effect immediately, stopping collections, garnishments, and lawsuits.

Attend the 341 meeting of creditors (usually 30-45 days after filing).

Complete a debtor education course (required before discharge).

Receive your discharge (Chapter 7: ~60-90 days after 341 meeting; Chapter 13: after completing 3-5 year plan).

Step-by-step guides: How Chapter 7 works (liquidation: who qualifies, the process, what you keep) · How Chapter 13 works (the repayment plan: eligibility, how the payment is set, why plans fail). Both are free, plain-English, and not legal advice.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I keep my car in Maryland bankruptcy?

Maryland has no separate motor vehicle exemption under Md. Code, Cts. & Jud. Proc. § 11-504 (use the wildcards). Last verified September 20, 2026. Amounts change, so check the statute.

Does Maryland use federal or state exemptions?

Maryland uses state exemptions only. The state has opted out of the federal exemptions in 11 U.S.C. § 522(d) (Md. Code, Cts. & Jud. Proc. § 11-504(g)).

How much does it cost to file bankruptcy in Maryland?

The court filing fee for Chapter 7 is $338 and Chapter 13 is $313. Attorney fees in Maryland typically range from $1,000 to $3,500 for Chapter 7 and $2,500 to $5,000 for Chapter 13. You can also file without an attorney (pro se) and request to pay the filing fee in installments.

What is the income limit for Chapter 7 in Maryland?

The means test compares your household income to Maryland's median. For a single person, the current threshold is approximately $97,203 per year. For a family of four, it is approximately $172,049. If your income is below the median for your household size, you pass Part 1 of the means test.

What property can I keep in Maryland bankruptcy?

Maryland requires filers to use state exemptions only. Key exemptions to research include the homestead exemption (how much home equity you can protect), vehicle exemption, personal property exemption, and any wildcard exemption. Check Maryland statutes for current amounts.

How long does bankruptcy stay on my credit in Maryland?

Chapter 7 stays on your credit report for 10 years from the filing date. Chapter 13 stays for 7 years. However, many people begin rebuilding credit within 1-2 years of discharge and can qualify for a mortgage within 2-4 years.

Can I file bankruptcy again in Maryland?

Yes, but there are waiting periods between discharges. Chapter 7 to Chapter 7: 8 years. Chapter 7 to Chapter 13: 4 years. Chapter 13 to Chapter 13: 2 years. Chapter 13 to Chapter 7: 6 years (unless you paid 100% or 70%+ with good faith). Use the free discharge eligibility screener to check your dates.

What debts cannot be discharged in bankruptcy?

Most debts are dischargeable, but exceptions include most student loans (unless you prove undue hardship), child support and alimony, recent tax debts (generally last 3 years), debts from fraud or willful injury, DUI-related debts, and criminal fines. See nondischargeable.org for the full list.

Massachusetts Exemptions

Federal Exemptions Available

Filers in Massachusetts can choose between state and federal bankruptcy exemptions. Compare both sets carefully - the federal wildcard exemption, $1,675 plus up to $15,800 of any unused homestead exemption for cases filed on or after April 1, 2025, may protect more personal property, while Massachusetts state exemptions may offer stronger homestead protection.

Massachusetts exemption amounts

Federal exemptions: allowed. Massachusetts has not opted out, so filers choose either the state exemptions below or the federal exemptions in 11 U.S.C. § 522(d), not a mix of both (source).

Married couples filing jointly: not every exemption here doubles for a joint case; check each statute (source).

Wildcard$1,500 needs reviewMinn. Stat. § 550.37 subd. 28In any property, including bank-account funds (bankruptcy only)

WagesGarnishment capped at the lesser of a tiered percentage of disposable earnings (10% if weekly income is over 40x and up to 60x the greater of the Minnesota or federal minimum wage; 15% if over 60x and up to 80x; 25% above 80x) or the amount by which disposable earnings exceed 40x that minimum wage; exempt wages stay exempt for 20 days after depositMinn. Stat. § 571.922; § 550.37 subd. 13

Tools of the trade$13,500 needs reviewMinn. Stat. § 550.37 subds. 5, 6, 7Tools of trade; farm machines and implements $13,000; combined cap $13,000 if both are claimed

Retirement accounts$81,000 needs reviewMinn. Stat. § 550.37 subd. 24Present value in pensions, IRAs, Roth IRAs, SEPs and similar plans, plus additional amounts reasonably necessary for support; ERISA plans unlimited

Retirement accounts also have federal protection. ERISA-qualified plans stay out of the bankruptcy estate under 11 U.S.C. § 541(c)(2), and 11 U.S.C. § 522(b)(3)(C) exempts tax-exempt retirement funds whatever the state law says. IRAs carry a federal dollar cap under § 522(n). Which state's exemptions you use depends on where you lived during the two years before filing (11 U.S.C. § 522(b)(3)(A)).

Last verified September 20, 2026. Amounts change, so check the statute before you rely on a figure. "Needs review" marks a figure we have not yet confirmed against the statute or the court. This is general information, not legal advice.

Homestead Exemption

Protects equity in your primary residence. Amounts vary by state. Check Minnesota homestead exemption amounts.

Vehicle Exemption

Protects equity in your car. Most states protect $2,000 to $7,500. See vehicle exemption details.

Retirement Accounts

401(k)s, IRAs, and pensions are generally fully exempt in bankruptcy. See retirement exemptions.

Wildcard Exemption

Applies to any property. Not all states offer this. See wildcard exemptions.

Filing Bankruptcy in Minnesota

Districts

Minnesota has a single federal bankruptcy district. All cases are filed in this one court, which simplifies the process.

Filing Costs

Chapter 7 filing fee: $338. Chapter 13: $313. Fee waivers are available for filers below 150% of the poverty line. Installment payments available for all filers. Full cost breakdown.

Before You File

Complete credit counseling from an approved provider (required within 180 days before filing).

Determine your chapter - Chapter 7 vs. Chapter 13 comparison.

Gather income documentation for the last 6 full calendar months.

List all debts, assets, income, and expenses for the bankruptcy schedules.

Research Minnesota exemptions to understand what property you can keep.

After You File

The automatic stay takes effect immediately, stopping collections, garnishments, and lawsuits.

Attend the 341 meeting of creditors (usually 30-45 days after filing).

Complete a debtor education course (required before discharge).

Receive your discharge (Chapter 7: ~60-90 days after 341 meeting; Chapter 13: after completing 3-5 year plan).

Step-by-step guides: How Chapter 7 works (liquidation: who qualifies, the process, what you keep) · How Chapter 13 works (the repayment plan: eligibility, how the payment is set, why plans fail). Both are free, plain-English, and not legal advice.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much does it cost to file bankruptcy in Minnesota?

The court filing fee for Chapter 7 is $338 and Chapter 13 is $313. Attorney fees in Minnesota typically range from $1,000 to $3,500 for Chapter 7 and $2,500 to $5,000 for Chapter 13. You can also file without an attorney (pro se) and request to pay the filing fee in installments.

What is the income limit for Chapter 7 in Minnesota?

The means test compares your household income to Minnesota's median. For a single person, the current threshold is approximately $79,161 per year. For a family of four, it is approximately $140,115. If your income is below the median for your household size, you pass Part 1 of the means test.

Can I use federal exemptions in Minnesota?

Yes. Minnesota allows you to choose between state exemptions and federal bankruptcy exemptions under 11 U.S.C. Section 522(d). You must pick one complete set - you cannot mix individual exemptions from both. Compare homestead, vehicle, and wildcard amounts under each system before deciding.

How long does bankruptcy stay on my credit in Minnesota?

Chapter 7 stays on your credit report for 10 years from the filing date. Chapter 13 stays for 7 years. However, many people begin rebuilding credit within 1-2 years of discharge and can qualify for a mortgage within 2-4 years.

Can I file bankruptcy again in Minnesota?

Yes, but there are waiting periods between discharges. Chapter 7 to Chapter 7: 8 years. Chapter 7 to Chapter 13: 4 years. Chapter 13 to Chapter 13: 2 years. Chapter 13 to Chapter 7: 6 years (unless you paid 100% or 70%+ with good faith). Use the free discharge eligibility screener to check your dates.

What debts cannot be discharged in bankruptcy?

Most debts are dischargeable, but exceptions include most student loans (unless you prove undue hardship), child support and alimony, recent tax debts (generally last 3 years), debts from fraud or willful injury, DUI-related debts, and criminal fines. See nondischargeable.org for the full list.

Mississippi Exemptions

State Exemptions Only

Mississippi requires bankruptcy filers to use state exemptions exclusively. Federal exemptions under 11 U.S.C. Section 522(d) are not available. Research Mississippi's homestead, vehicle, personal property, and wildcard exemptions before filing.

Mississippi exemption amounts

Federal exemptions: not allowed. Mississippi has opted out of the federal exemptions, so filers use the state exemptions below (Miss. Code Ann. § 85-3-2).

Married couples filing jointly: whether these exemptions double is not yet verified.

Can I keep my car in Mississippi bankruptcy?

Does Mississippi use federal or state exemptions?

Mississippi uses state exemptions only. The state has opted out of the federal exemptions in 11 U.S.C. § 522(d) (Miss. Code Ann. § 85-3-2).

How much does it cost to file bankruptcy in Mississippi?

The court filing fee for Chapter 7 is $338 and Chapter 13 is $313. Attorney fees in Mississippi typically range from $1,000 to $3,500 for Chapter 7 and $2,500 to $5,000 for Chapter 13. You can also file without an attorney (pro se) and request to pay the filing fee in installments.

What property can I keep in Mississippi bankruptcy?

Mississippi requires filers to use state exemptions only. Key exemptions to research include the homestead exemption (how much home equity you can protect), vehicle exemption, personal property exemption, and any wildcard exemption. Check Mississippi statutes for current amounts.

How long does bankruptcy stay on my credit in Mississippi?

Chapter 7 stays on your credit report for 10 years from the filing date. Chapter 13 stays for 7 years. However, many people begin rebuilding credit within 1-2 years of discharge and can qualify for a mortgage within 2-4 years.

Can I file bankruptcy again in Mississippi?

Most debts are dischargeable, but exceptions include most student loans (unless you prove undue hardship), child support and alimony, recent tax debts (generally last 3 years), debts from fraud or willful injury, DUI-related debts, and criminal fines. See nondischargeable.org for the full list.

Missouri exemption amounts

Married couples filing jointly: not every exemption here doubles for a joint case; check each statute (source).

Scheduled change (January 1, 2027): SS HCS HB 1870 (2026), truly agreed and approved by the Governor 5/6/2026, Section B: the repeal and reenactment of §§ 513.430 and 513.475 and new § 513.423 'shall become effective on January 1, 2027.' New amounts: homestead $15,000 to $40,000 aggregate; household goods $3,000 to $15,000; other jewelry $500 to $1,700 (wedding ring stays $1,500); wildcard ('any other property') $600 to $1,700; motor vehicles $3,000 to $5,000 plus up to $10,000 of unused household-goods exemption; mobile home $5,000 to $12,000; tools of trade unchanged at $3,000; health savings accounts (IRC § 223) added to the retirement-plan exemption. New § 513.423: every §§ 513.430/513.475 dollar amount is CPI-U-adjusted every three years starting April 1, 2029 (revisor publishes the schedule by March 1, 2029); adjustments do not apply to cases commenced before the adjustment date. The revisor site already shows the 1/1/2027 version as the default view of both sections. Source.

Filing Bankruptcy in Montana

Districts

Montana has a single federal bankruptcy district. All cases are filed in this one court, which simplifies the process.

Filing Costs

Chapter 7 filing fee: $338. Chapter 13: $313. Fee waivers are available for filers below 150% of the poverty line. Installment payments available for all filers. Full cost breakdown.

Before You File

Complete credit counseling from an approved provider (required within 180 days before filing).

Determine your chapter - Chapter 7 vs. Chapter 13 comparison.

Gather income documentation for the last 6 full calendar months.

List all debts, assets, income, and expenses for the bankruptcy schedules.

Research Montana exemptions to understand what property you can keep.

After You File

The automatic stay takes effect immediately, stopping collections, garnishments, and lawsuits.

Attend the 341 meeting of creditors (usually 30-45 days after filing).

Complete a debtor education course (required before discharge).

Receive your discharge (Chapter 7: ~60-90 days after 341 meeting; Chapter 13: after completing 3-5 year plan).

Step-by-step guides: How Chapter 7 works (liquidation: who qualifies, the process, what you keep) · How Chapter 13 works (the repayment plan: eligibility, how the payment is set, why plans fail). Both are free, plain-English, and not legal advice.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I keep my car in Montana bankruptcy?

Montana protects $4,000 in a motor vehicle under Mont. Code Ann. § 25-13-609(2). Details: In one motor vehicle. Last verified September 20, 2026. Amounts change, so check the statute.

Does Montana use federal or state exemptions?

Montana uses state exemptions only. The state has opted out of the federal exemptions in 11 U.S.C. § 522(d) (Mont. Code Ann. § 31-2-106).

How much does it cost to file bankruptcy in Montana?

The court filing fee for Chapter 7 is $338 and Chapter 13 is $313. Attorney fees in Montana typically range from $1,000 to $3,500 for Chapter 7 and $2,500 to $5,000 for Chapter 13. You can also file without an attorney (pro se) and request to pay the filing fee in installments.

What is the income limit for Chapter 7 in Montana?

The means test compares your household income to Montana's median. For a single person, the current threshold is approximately $66,501 per year. For a family of four, it is approximately $117,707. If your income is below the median for your household size, you pass Part 1 of the means test.

What property can I keep in Montana bankruptcy?

Montana requires filers to use state exemptions only. Key exemptions to research include the homestead exemption (how much home equity you can protect), vehicle exemption, personal property exemption, and any wildcard exemption. Check Montana statutes for current amounts.

How long does bankruptcy stay on my credit in Montana?

Chapter 7 stays on your credit report for 10 years from the filing date. Chapter 13 stays for 7 years. However, many people begin rebuilding credit within 1-2 years of discharge and can qualify for a mortgage within 2-4 years.

Can I file bankruptcy again in Montana?

Yes, but there are waiting periods between discharges. Chapter 7 to Chapter 7: 8 years. Chapter 7 to Chapter 13: 4 years. Chapter 13 to Chapter 13: 2 years. Chapter 13 to Chapter 7: 6 years (unless you paid 100% or 70%+ with good faith). Use the free discharge eligibility screener to check your dates.

What debts cannot be discharged in bankruptcy?

Most debts are dischargeable, but exceptions include most student loans (unless you prove undue hardship), child support and alimony, recent tax debts (generally last 3 years), debts from fraud or willful injury, DUI-related debts, and criminal fines. See nondischargeable.org for the full list.

Nebraska Exemptions

State Exemptions Only

Nebraska requires bankruptcy filers to use state exemptions exclusively. Federal exemptions under 11 U.S.C. Section 522(d) are not available. Research Nebraska's homestead, vehicle, personal property, and wildcard exemptions before filing.

Nebraska exemption amounts

Federal exemptions: not allowed. Nebraska has opted out of the federal exemptions, so filers use the state exemptions below (Neb. Rev. Stat. § 25-15,105).

Married couples filing jointly: whether these exemptions double is not yet verified.

Scheduled change (January 1, 2028): §§ 25-1552(2) and 25-1556(2): the Department of Revenue adjusts the dollar limits 'every fifth year beginning with the year 2023' by the cumulative 5-year CPI-U change, so the next adjustment is due in 2028 (exact date not stated in the statute). The homestead in § 40-101 is not indexed. Source.

ExemptionAmountStatuteNotes

Homestead$120,000Neb. Rev. Stat. § 40-101Up to 160 acres outside a city or village, or two contiguous lots inside one

Motor vehicle$5,000 needs reviewNeb. Rev. Stat. § 25-1556(1)(e)Statutory base; subject to the Department of Revenue's 2023 CPI adjustment, not located

Household goods$3,000 needs reviewNeb. Rev. Stat. § 25-1556(1)(a)-(c)Aggregate (statutory base; subject to the 2023 CPI adjustment, not located); immediate personal possessions and necessary wearing apparel unlimited

Wildcard$5,000 needs reviewNeb. Rev. Stat. § 25-1552(1)In any personal property except wages (statutory base; subject to the 2023 CPI adjustment, not located)

WagesGarnishment capped at the lesser of 25% of weekly disposable earnings, the amount above 30 times the federal minimum hourly wage, or 15% for a head of familyNeb. Rev. Stat. § 25-1558

Tools of the trade$5,000 needs reviewNeb. Rev. Stat. § 25-1556(1)(d)Aggregate, not including a motor vehicle (statutory base; subject to the 2023 CPI adjustment, not located)

Retirement accountsNot yet verified needs reviewNeb. Rev. Stat. § 25-1563.01

Retirement accounts also have federal protection. ERISA-qualified plans stay out of the bankruptcy estate under 11 U.S.C. § 541(c)(2), and 11 U.S.C. § 522(b)(3)(C) exempts tax-exempt retirement funds whatever the state law says. IRAs carry a federal dollar cap under § 522(n). Which state's exemptions you use depends on where you lived during the two years before filing (11 U.S.C. § 522(b)(3)(A)).

Last verified September 20, 2026. Amounts change, so check the statute before you rely on a figure. "Needs review" marks a figure we have not yet confirmed against the statute or the court. This is general information, not legal advice.

Bankruptcy in New Jersey

Complete guide: exemptions, means test income limits, filing costs, and real case outcome data for New Jersey.

Important: This page provides educational information about bankruptcy in New Jersey. It is not legal advice. Median income figures are approximate (Census/DOJ, effective April 2026). Verify current amounts at the DOJ Means Testing page.

Federal Exemptions

Ch. 7 Filing Fee

New Jersey Exemptions

Federal Exemptions Available

Filers in New Jersey can choose between state and federal bankruptcy exemptions. Compare both sets carefully - the federal wildcard exemption, $1,675 plus up to $15,800 of any unused homestead exemption for cases filed on or after April 1, 2025, may protect more personal property, while New Jersey state exemptions may offer stronger homestead protection.

New Jersey exemption amounts

Federal exemptions: allowed. New Jersey has not opted out, so filers choose either the state exemptions below or the federal exemptions in 11 U.S.C. § 522(d), not a mix of both (source).

Married couples filing jointly: whether these exemptions double is not yet verified.

ExemptionAmountStatuteNotes

HomesteadNot yet verified needs review—

Motor vehicleNot yet verified needs reviewN.J.S.A. 2A:17-19 (general personal property)

Household goods$1,000 needs reviewN.J.S.A. 2A:26-4

Wildcard$1,000 needs reviewN.J.S.A. 2A:17-19In goods, chattels, corporate stock and personal property of every kind (exclusive of wearing apparel; all wearing apparel exempt without limit)

WagesNot yet verified needs reviewN.J.S.A. 2A:17-56

Tools of the tradeNot yet verified needs review—

Retirement accountsNot yet verified needs reviewN.J.S.A. 25:2-1(b) (qualifying trusts) - cite NOT verified; FindLaw URL returned 404

Retirement accounts also have federal protection. ERISA-qualified plans stay out of the bankruptcy estate under 11 U.S.C. § 541(c)(2), and 11 U.S.C. § 522(b)(3)(C) exempts tax-exempt retirement funds whatever the state law says. IRAs carry a federal dollar cap under § 522(n). Which state's exemptions you use depends on where you lived during the two years before filing (11 U.S.C. § 522(b)(3)(A)).

Homestead Exemption

Protects equity in your primary residence. Amounts vary by state. Check New Jersey homestead exemption amounts.

Vehicle Exemption

Protects equity in your car. Most states protect $2,000 to $7,500. See vehicle exemption details.

Retirement Accounts

401(k)s, IRAs, and pensions are generally fully exempt in bankruptcy. See retirement exemptions.

Wildcard Exemption

Applies to any property. Not all states offer this. See wildcard exemptions.

Filing Bankruptcy in New Jersey

Districts

New Jersey has a single federal bankruptcy district. All cases are filed in this one court, which simplifies the process.

Filing Costs

Chapter 7 filing fee: $338. Chapter 13: $313. Fee waivers are available for filers below 150% of the poverty line. Installment payments available for all filers. Full cost breakdown.

Before You File

Complete credit counseling from an approved provider (required within 180 days before filing).

Determine your chapter - Chapter 7 vs. Chapter 13 comparison.

Gather income documentation for the last 6 full calendar months.

List all debts, assets, income, and expenses for the bankruptcy schedules.

Research New Jersey exemptions to understand what property you can keep.

After You File

The automatic stay takes effect immediately, stopping collections, garnishments, and lawsuits.

Attend the 341 meeting of creditors (usually 30-45 days after filing).

Complete a debtor education course (required before discharge).

Receive your discharge (Chapter 7: ~60-90 days after 341 meeting; Chapter 13: after completing 3-5 year plan).

Step-by-step guides: How Chapter 7 works (liquidation: who qualifies, the process, what you keep) · How Chapter 13 works (the repayment plan: eligibility, how the payment is set, why plans fail). Both are free, plain-English, and not legal advice.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does New Jersey use federal or state exemptions?

New Jersey lets filers choose. New Jersey has not opted out, so you can use either the New Jersey exemptions or the federal exemptions in 11 U.S.C. § 522(d), but not a mix of both.

How much does it cost to file bankruptcy in New Jersey?

The court filing fee for Chapter 7 is $338 and Chapter 13 is $313. Attorney fees in New Jersey typically range from $1,000 to $3,500 for Chapter 7 and $2,500 to $5,000 for Chapter 13. You can also file without an attorney (pro se) and request to pay the filing fee in installments.

What is the income limit for Chapter 7 in New Jersey?

The means test compares your household income to New Jersey's median. For a single person, the current threshold is approximately $93,051 per year. For a family of four, it is approximately $164,700. If your income is below the median for your household size, you pass Part 1 of the means test.

Can I use federal exemptions in New Jersey?

Yes. New Jersey allows you to choose between state exemptions and federal bankruptcy exemptions under 11 U.S.C. Section 522(d). You must pick one complete set - you cannot mix individual exemptions from both. Compare homestead, vehicle, and wildcard amounts under each system before deciding.

How long does bankruptcy stay on my credit in New Jersey?

Chapter 7 stays on your credit report for 10 years from the filing date. Chapter 13 stays for 7 years. However, many people begin rebuilding credit within 1-2 years of discharge and can qualify for a mortgage within 2-4 years.

Can I file bankruptcy again in New Jersey?

Yes, but there are waiting periods between discharges. Chapter 7 to Chapter 7: 8 years. Chapter 7 to Chapter 13: 4 years. Chapter 13 to Chapter 13: 2 years. Chapter 13 to Chapter 7: 6 years (unless you paid 100% or 70%+ with good faith). Use the free discharge eligibility screener to check your dates.

What debts cannot be discharged in bankruptcy?

Most debts are dischargeable, but exceptions include most student loans (unless you prove undue hardship), child support and alimony, recent tax debts (generally last 3 years), debts from fraud or willful injury, DUI-related debts, and criminal fines. See nondischargeable.org for the full list.

Retirement accountsUnlimited (IRAs, Roth IRAs, 408(b) annuities, 408(c) trust accounts and inherited IRAs received by direct transfer/rollover; retirement benefits of other states' governmental plans to the extent exempt there)N.C. Gen. Stat. § 1C-1601(a)(9), (a)(11)

Retirement accounts also have federal protection. ERISA-qualified plans stay out of the bankruptcy estate under 11 U.S.C. § 541(c)(2), and 11 U.S.C. § 522(b)(3)(C) exempts tax-exempt retirement funds whatever the state law says. IRAs carry a federal dollar cap under § 522(n). Which state's exemptions you use depends on where you lived during the two years before filing (11 U.S.C. § 522(b)(3)(A)).

Last verified September 20, 2026. Amounts change, so check the statute before you rely on a figure. "Needs review" marks a figure we have not yet confirmed against the statute or the court. This is general information, not legal advice.

Homestead Exemption

Protects equity in your primary residence. Amounts vary by state. Check North Carolina homestead exemption amounts.

Vehicle Exemption

Protects equity in your car. Most states protect $2,000 to $7,500. See vehicle exemption details.

Retirement Accounts

401(k)s, IRAs, and pensions are generally fully exempt in bankruptcy. See retirement exemptions.

Wildcard Exemption

Applies to any property. Not all states offer this. See wildcard exemptions.

Filing Bankruptcy in North Carolina

Districts

North Carolina has 3 federal bankruptcy districts. The district where you file depends on where you have lived for the greater part of the last 180 days. Each district may have different local rules, no-look fee amounts, and trustee practices.

Filing Costs

Chapter 7 filing fee: $338. Chapter 13: $313. Fee waivers are available for filers below 150% of the poverty line. Installment payments available for all filers. Full cost breakdown.

Before You File

Complete credit counseling from an approved provider (required within 180 days before filing).

Determine your chapter - Chapter 7 vs. Chapter 13 comparison.

Gather income documentation for the last 6 full calendar months.

List all debts, assets, income, and expenses for the bankruptcy schedules.

Research North Carolina exemptions to understand what property you can keep.

After You File

The automatic stay takes effect immediately, stopping collections, garnishments, and lawsuits.

Attend the 341 meeting of creditors (usually 30-45 days after filing).

Complete a debtor education course (required before discharge).

Receive your discharge (Chapter 7: ~60-90 days after 341 meeting; Chapter 13: after completing 3-5 year plan).

Step-by-step guides: How Chapter 7 works (liquidation: who qualifies, the process, what you keep) · How Chapter 13 works (the repayment plan: eligibility, how the payment is set, why plans fail). Both are free, plain-English, and not legal advice.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I keep my car in North Carolina bankruptcy?

North Carolina protects $3,500 in a motor vehicle under N.C. Gen. Stat. § 1C-1601(a)(3). Details: In one motor vehicle. Last verified September 20, 2026. Amounts change, so check the statute.

Does North Carolina use federal or state exemptions?

North Carolina uses state exemptions only. The state has opted out of the federal exemptions in 11 U.S.C. § 522(d) (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 1C-1601(f)).

How much does it cost to file bankruptcy in North Carolina?

The court filing fee for Chapter 7 is $338 and Chapter 13 is $313. Attorney fees in North Carolina typically range from $1,000 to $3,500 for Chapter 7 and $2,500 to $5,000 for Chapter 13. You can also file without an attorney (pro se) and request to pay the filing fee in installments.

What is the income limit for Chapter 7 in North Carolina?

The means test compares your household income to North Carolina's median. For a single person, the current threshold is approximately $63,339 per year. For a family of four, it is approximately $112,110. If your income is below the median for your household size, you pass Part 1 of the means test.

What property can I keep in North Carolina bankruptcy?

North Carolina requires filers to use state exemptions only. Key exemptions to research include the homestead exemption (how much home equity you can protect), vehicle exemption, personal property exemption, and any wildcard exemption. Check North Carolina statutes for current amounts.

How long does bankruptcy stay on my credit in North Carolina?

Chapter 7 stays on your credit report for 10 years from the filing date. Chapter 13 stays for 7 years. However, many people begin rebuilding credit within 1-2 years of discharge and can qualify for a mortgage within 2-4 years.

Can I file bankruptcy again in North Carolina?

Yes, but there are waiting periods between discharges. Chapter 7 to Chapter 7: 8 years. Chapter 7 to Chapter 13: 4 years. Chapter 13 to Chapter 13: 2 years. Chapter 13 to Chapter 7: 6 years (unless you paid 100% or 70%+ with good faith). Use the free discharge eligibility screener to check your dates.

Which bankruptcy court do I file in within North Carolina?

North Carolina has 3 federal bankruptcy districts. You file in the district where you have lived for the greater part of the last 180 days. If you recently moved, the 180-day rule may require filing in your previous district. Check local court websites for county-to-district lookups.

What debts cannot be discharged in bankruptcy?

Most debts are dischargeable, but exceptions include most student loans (unless you prove undue hardship), child support and alimony, recent tax debts (generally last 3 years), debts from fraud or willful injury, DUI-related debts, and criminal fines. See nondischargeable.org for the full list.

Filing Bankruptcy in Oklahoma

Districts

Oklahoma has 3 federal bankruptcy districts. The district where you file depends on where you have lived for the greater part of the last 180 days. Each district may have different local rules, no-look fee amounts, and trustee practices.

Filing Costs

Chapter 7 filing fee: $338. Chapter 13: $313. Fee waivers are available for filers below 150% of the poverty line. Installment payments available for all filers. Full cost breakdown.

Before You File

Complete credit counseling from an approved provider (required within 180 days before filing).

Determine your chapter - Chapter 7 vs. Chapter 13 comparison.

Gather income documentation for the last 6 full calendar months.

List all debts, assets, income, and expenses for the bankruptcy schedules.

Research Oklahoma exemptions to understand what property you can keep.

After You File

The automatic stay takes effect immediately, stopping collections, garnishments, and lawsuits.

Attend the 341 meeting of creditors (usually 30-45 days after filing).

Complete a debtor education course (required before discharge).

Receive your discharge (Chapter 7: ~60-90 days after 341 meeting; Chapter 13: after completing 3-5 year plan).

Step-by-step guides: How Chapter 7 works (liquidation: who qualifies, the process, what you keep) · How Chapter 13 works (the repayment plan: eligibility, how the payment is set, why plans fail). Both are free, plain-English, and not legal advice.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I keep my car in Oklahoma bankruptcy?

Oklahoma protects $7,500 in a motor vehicle under 31 O.S. § 1(A)(13). Details: In one motor vehicle. Last verified September 20, 2026. Amounts change, so check the statute.

Does Oklahoma use federal or state exemptions?

Oklahoma uses state exemptions only. The state has opted out of the federal exemptions in 11 U.S.C. § 522(d) (31 O.S. § 1(B)).

How much does it cost to file bankruptcy in Oklahoma?

The court filing fee for Chapter 7 is $338 and Chapter 13 is $313. Attorney fees in Oklahoma typically range from $1,000 to $3,500 for Chapter 7 and $2,500 to $5,000 for Chapter 13. You can also file without an attorney (pro se) and request to pay the filing fee in installments.

What is the income limit for Chapter 7 in Oklahoma?

The means test compares your household income to Oklahoma's median. For a single person, the current threshold is approximately $60,636 per year. For a family of four, it is approximately $107,326. If your income is below the median for your household size, you pass Part 1 of the means test.

What property can I keep in Oklahoma bankruptcy?

Oklahoma requires filers to use state exemptions only. Key exemptions to research include the homestead exemption (how much home equity you can protect), vehicle exemption, personal property exemption, and any wildcard exemption. Check Oklahoma statutes for current amounts.

How long does bankruptcy stay on my credit in Oklahoma?

Chapter 7 stays on your credit report for 10 years from the filing date. Chapter 13 stays for 7 years. However, many people begin rebuilding credit within 1-2 years of discharge and can qualify for a mortgage within 2-4 years.

Can I file bankruptcy again in Oklahoma?

Yes, but there are waiting periods between discharges. Chapter 7 to Chapter 7: 8 years. Chapter 7 to Chapter 13: 4 years. Chapter 13 to Chapter 13: 2 years. Chapter 13 to Chapter 7: 6 years (unless you paid 100% or 70%+ with good faith). Use the free discharge eligibility screener to check your dates.

Which bankruptcy court do I file in within Oklahoma?

Oklahoma has 3 federal bankruptcy districts. You file in the district where you have lived for the greater part of the last 180 days. If you recently moved, the 180-day rule may require filing in your previous district. Check local court websites for county-to-district lookups.

What debts cannot be discharged in bankruptcy?

Most debts are dischargeable, but exceptions include most student loans (unless you prove undue hardship), child support and alimony, recent tax debts (generally last 3 years), debts from fraud or willful injury, DUI-related debts, and criminal fines. See nondischargeable.org for the full list.

Oregon Exemptions

Federal Exemptions Available

Filers in Oregon can choose between state and federal bankruptcy exemptions. Compare both sets carefully - the federal wildcard exemption, $1,675 plus up to $15,800 of any unused homestead exemption for cases filed on or after April 1, 2025, may protect more personal property, while Oregon state exemptions may offer stronger homestead protection.

Oregon exemption amounts

Federal exemptions: allowed. Oregon has not opted out, so filers choose either the state exemptions below or the federal exemptions in 11 U.S.C. § 522(d), not a mix of both (source).

Married couples filing jointly: not every exemption here doubles for a joint case; check each statute (source).

Scheduled change (July 1, 2027): ORS 18.385(2)(a)(E): from 7/1/2027 the weekly wage-exemption floor becomes 30 x the ORS 653.025(1) minimum wage, recomputed yearly by the State Court Administrator (18.385(3)). The homestead amount is also re-indexed each July 1 under ORS 18.395(1)(d). Source.

HomesteadNot yet verified needs reviewORS 18.395(1); ORS 18.402

Motor vehicle$10,000ORS 18.345(1)(d)$3,000 if the debt is child or spousal support or a restitution judgment

Household goods$3,000ORS 18.345(1)(f), (1)(b), (1)(a)Household goods, furniture, radios, a television and utensils; plus $1,800 apparel, jewelry and personal items and $600 books, pictures and musical instruments

Wildcard$400ORS 18.345(1)(p)In any personal property (cannot be used to increase another exemption)

Wages75% of disposable earnings exempt, with a floor: net disposable earnings may not drop below $400 per week for wages payable 7/1/2026 to 6/30/2027 ($832 two-week, $912 half-month, $1,792 monthly); from 7/1/2027 the weekly floor is 30 x the Oregon minimum wageORS 18.385(1), (2)

Retirement accountsUnlimited (tax-qualified retirement plans and IRAs, treated as spendthrift trusts)ORS 18.358

Retirement accounts also have federal protection. ERISA-qualified plans stay out of the bankruptcy estate under 11 U.S.C. § 541(c)(2), and 11 U.S.C. § 522(b)(3)(C) exempts tax-exempt retirement funds whatever the state law says. IRAs carry a federal dollar cap under § 522(n). Which state's exemptions you use depends on where you lived during the two years before filing (11 U.S.C. § 522(b)(3)(A)).

Does Oregon use federal or state exemptions?

Most debts are dischargeable, but exceptions include most student loans (unless you prove undue hardship), child support and alimony, recent tax debts (generally last 3 years), debts from fraud or willful injury, DUI-related debts, and criminal fines. See nondischargeable.org for the full list.

Filing Bankruptcy in South Carolina

Districts

South Carolina has a single federal bankruptcy district. All cases are filed in this one court, which simplifies the process.

Filing Costs

Chapter 7 filing fee: $338. Chapter 13: $313. Fee waivers are available for filers below 150% of the poverty line. Installment payments available for all filers. Full cost breakdown.

Before You File

Complete credit counseling from an approved provider (required within 180 days before filing).

Determine your chapter - Chapter 7 vs. Chapter 13 comparison.

Gather income documentation for the last 6 full calendar months.

List all debts, assets, income, and expenses for the bankruptcy schedules.

Research South Carolina exemptions to understand what property you can keep.

After You File

The automatic stay takes effect immediately, stopping collections, garnishments, and lawsuits.

Attend the 341 meeting of creditors (usually 30-45 days after filing).

Complete a debtor education course (required before discharge).

Receive your discharge (Chapter 7: ~60-90 days after 341 meeting; Chapter 13: after completing 3-5 year plan).

Step-by-step guides: How Chapter 7 works (liquidation: who qualifies, the process, what you keep) · How Chapter 13 works (the repayment plan: eligibility, how the payment is set, why plans fail). Both are free, plain-English, and not legal advice.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I keep my car in South Carolina bankruptcy?

South Carolina protects $8,000 in a motor vehicle under S.C. Code § 15-41-30(A)(2). Details: In one motor vehicle (effective 7/1/2026). Last verified September 20, 2026. Amounts change, so check the statute.

Does South Carolina use federal or state exemptions?

South Carolina uses state exemptions only. The state has opted out of the federal exemptions in 11 U.S.C. § 522(d) (S.C. Code § 15-41-35).

How much does it cost to file bankruptcy in South Carolina?

The court filing fee for Chapter 7 is $338 and Chapter 13 is $313. Attorney fees in South Carolina typically range from $1,000 to $3,500 for Chapter 7 and $2,500 to $5,000 for Chapter 13. You can also file without an attorney (pro se) and request to pay the filing fee in installments.

What is the income limit for Chapter 7 in South Carolina?

The means test compares your household income to South Carolina's median. For a single person, the current threshold is approximately $61,050 per year. For a family of four, it is approximately $108,058. If your income is below the median for your household size, you pass Part 1 of the means test.

What property can I keep in South Carolina bankruptcy?

South Carolina requires filers to use state exemptions only. Key exemptions to research include the homestead exemption (how much home equity you can protect), vehicle exemption, personal property exemption, and any wildcard exemption. Check South Carolina statutes for current amounts.

How long does bankruptcy stay on my credit in South Carolina?

Chapter 7 stays on your credit report for 10 years from the filing date. Chapter 13 stays for 7 years. However, many people begin rebuilding credit within 1-2 years of discharge and can qualify for a mortgage within 2-4 years.

Can I file bankruptcy again in South Carolina?

Yes, but there are waiting periods between discharges. Chapter 7 to Chapter 7: 8 years. Chapter 7 to Chapter 13: 4 years. Chapter 13 to Chapter 13: 2 years. Chapter 13 to Chapter 7: 6 years (unless you paid 100% or 70%+ with good faith). Use the free discharge eligibility screener to check your dates.

What debts cannot be discharged in bankruptcy?

Most debts are dischargeable, but exceptions include most student loans (unless you prove undue hardship), child support and alimony, recent tax debts (generally last 3 years), debts from fraud or willful injury, DUI-related debts, and criminal fines. See nondischargeable.org for the full list.

Federal Exemptions Available

Texas exemption amounts

Motor vehicleOne motor vehicle for each family member or single adult who holds a driver's license (or relies on another to drive for them), within the $100,000 family / $50,000 single aggregateTex. Prop. Code § 42.002(a)(9); § 42.001(a)

Household goods$100,000Tex. Prop. Code §§ 42.001(a), 42.002(a)Aggregate for a family / $50,000 for a single adult, covering home furnishings (incl. heirlooms), provisions, clothing, jewelry (capped at 25% of the aggregate), two firearms, sporting goods, vehicles, tools, listed livestock and pets

WagesCurrent wages for personal services fully exempt (except for court-ordered child support); unpaid commissions exempt up to 25% of the aggregate cap ($25,000 family / $12,500 single) and counted within itTex. Prop. Code § 42.001(b)(1), (d)

Tools of the tradeTools, equipment, books and apparatus (including boats and motor vehicles) used in a trade or profession, plus farming/ranching vehicles and implements, within the $100,000 family / $50,000 single aggregateTex. Prop. Code § 42.002(a)(3), (a)(4)

Retirement accountsUnlimited: qualified savings plans (employer, government and church retirement plans, SEPs, IRAs and Roth IRAs including inherited ones, HSAs, Coverdell, Texas tuition plans, 529 and 529A accounts), in addition to the § 42.001 aggregateTex. Prop. Code § 42.0021

Retirement accounts also have federal protection. ERISA-qualified plans stay out of the bankruptcy estate under 11 U.S.C. § 541(c)(2), and 11 U.S.C. § 522(b)(3)(C) exempts tax-exempt retirement funds whatever the state law says. IRAs carry a federal dollar cap under § 522(n). Which state's exemptions you use depends on where you lived during the two years before filing (11 U.S.C. § 522(b)(3)(A)).

Last verified September 20, 2026. Amounts change, so check the statute before you rely on a figure. "Needs review" marks a figure we have not yet confirmed against the statute or the court. This is general information, not legal advice.

Homestead Exemption

Protects equity in your primary residence. Amounts vary by state. Check Texas homestead exemption amounts.

Vehicle Exemption

Protects equity in your car. Most states protect $2,000 to $7,500. See vehicle exemption details.

Retirement Accounts

401(k)s, IRAs, and pensions are generally fully exempt in bankruptcy. See retirement exemptions.

Wildcard Exemption

Applies to any property. Not all states offer this. See wildcard exemptions.

Filing Bankruptcy in Texas

Districts

Texas has 4 federal bankruptcy districts. The district where you file depends on where you have lived for the greater part of the last 180 days. Each district may have different local rules, no-look fee amounts, and trustee practices.

Filing Costs

Chapter 7 filing fee: $338. Chapter 13: $313. Fee waivers are available for filers below 150% of the poverty line. Installment payments available for all filers. Full cost breakdown.

Before You File

Complete credit counseling from an approved provider (required within 180 days before filing).

Determine your chapter - Chapter 7 vs. Chapter 13 comparison.

Gather income documentation for the last 6 full calendar months.

List all debts, assets, income, and expenses for the bankruptcy schedules.

Research Texas exemptions to understand what property you can keep.

After You File

The automatic stay takes effect immediately, stopping collections, garnishments, and lawsuits.

Attend the 341 meeting of creditors (usually 30-45 days after filing).

Complete a debtor education course (required before discharge).

Receive your discharge (Chapter 7: ~60-90 days after 341 meeting; Chapter 13: after completing 3-5 year plan).

Step-by-step guides: How Chapter 7 works (liquidation: who qualifies, the process, what you keep) · How Chapter 13 works (the repayment plan: eligibility, how the payment is set, why plans fail). Both are free, plain-English, and not legal advice.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much does it cost to file bankruptcy in Texas?

The court filing fee for Chapter 7 is $338 and Chapter 13 is $313. Attorney fees in Texas typically range from $1,000 to $3,500 for Chapter 7 and $2,500 to $5,000 for Chapter 13. You can also file without an attorney (pro se) and request to pay the filing fee in installments.

What is the income limit for Chapter 7 in Texas?

The means test compares your household income to Texas's median. For a single person, the current threshold is approximately $66,837 per year. For a family of four, it is approximately $118,301. If your income is below the median for your household size, you pass Part 1 of the means test.

Can I use federal exemptions in Texas?

Yes. Texas allows you to choose between state exemptions and federal bankruptcy exemptions under 11 U.S.C. Section 522(d). You must pick one complete set - you cannot mix individual exemptions from both. Compare homestead, vehicle, and wildcard amounts under each system before deciding.

How long does bankruptcy stay on my credit in Texas?

Chapter 7 stays on your credit report for 10 years from the filing date. Chapter 13 stays for 7 years. However, many people begin rebuilding credit within 1-2 years of discharge and can qualify for a mortgage within 2-4 years.

Can I file bankruptcy again in Texas?

Yes, but there are waiting periods between discharges. Chapter 7 to Chapter 7: 8 years. Chapter 7 to Chapter 13: 4 years. Chapter 13 to Chapter 13: 2 years. Chapter 13 to Chapter 7: 6 years (unless you paid 100% or 70%+ with good faith). Use the free discharge eligibility screener to check your dates.

Which bankruptcy court do I file in within Texas?

Texas has 4 federal bankruptcy districts. You file in the district where you have lived for the greater part of the last 180 days. If you recently moved, the 180-day rule may require filing in your previous district. Check local court websites for county-to-district lookups.

What debts cannot be discharged in bankruptcy?

Most debts are dischargeable, but exceptions include most student loans (unless you prove undue hardship), child support and alimony, recent tax debts (generally last 3 years), debts from fraud or willful injury, DUI-related debts, and criminal fines. See nondischargeable.org for the full list.

The means test compares your household income to Virginia's median. For a single person, the current threshold is approximately $84,396 per year. For a family of four, it is approximately $149,381. If your income is below the median for your household size, you pass Part 1 of the means test.

What property can I keep in Virginia bankruptcy?

Virginia requires filers to use state exemptions only. Key exemptions to research include the homestead exemption (how much home equity you can protect), vehicle exemption, personal property exemption, and any wildcard exemption. Check Virginia statutes for current amounts.

How long does bankruptcy stay on my credit in Virginia?

Chapter 7 stays on your credit report for 10 years from the filing date. Chapter 13 stays for 7 years. However, many people begin rebuilding credit within 1-2 years of discharge and can qualify for a mortgage within 2-4 years.

Can I file bankruptcy again in Virginia?

Yes, but there are waiting periods between discharges. Chapter 7 to Chapter 7: 8 years. Chapter 7 to Chapter 13: 4 years. Chapter 13 to Chapter 13: 2 years. Chapter 13 to Chapter 7: 6 years (unless you paid 100% or 70%+ with good faith). Use the free discharge eligibility screener to check your dates.

Which bankruptcy court do I file in within Virginia?

Virginia has 2 federal bankruptcy districts. You file in the district where you have lived for the greater part of the last 180 days. If you recently moved, the 180-day rule may require filing in your previous district. Check local court websites for county-to-district lookups.

What debts cannot be discharged in bankruptcy?

Most debts are dischargeable, but exceptions include most student loans (unless you prove undue hardship), child support and alimony, recent tax debts (generally last 3 years), debts from fraud or willful injury, DUI-related debts, and criminal fines. See nondischargeable.org for the full list.

Washington Exemptions

Federal Exemptions Available

Filers in Washington can choose between state and federal bankruptcy exemptions. Compare both sets carefully - the federal wildcard exemption, $1,675 plus up to $15,800 of any unused homestead exemption for cases filed on or after April 1, 2025, may protect more personal property, while Washington state exemptions may offer stronger homestead protection.

Washington exemption amounts

Federal exemptions: allowed. Washington has not opted out, so filers choose either the state exemptions below or the federal exemptions in 11 U.S.C. § 522(d), not a mix of both (source).

Married couples filing jointly: not every exemption here doubles for a joint case; check each statute (source).

ExemptionAmountStatuteNotes

Homestead$125,000RCW 6.13.030Greater of $125,000 or the county median sale price of a single-family home in the preceding calendar year

Motor vehicle$15,000RCW 6.15.010(1)(d)(iv)Aggregate

Household goods$6,500RCW 6.15.010(1)(d)(i), (1)(a)-(c)Household goods, appliances, furniture, home and yard equipment; plus apparel (furs/jewelry capped $3,500), private libraries $3,500, cell phone/computer/printer unlimited

Wildcard$10,000RCW 6.15.010(1)(d)(ii)In a bankruptcy case (any other personal property except personal earnings); $3,000 outside bankruptcy

WagesGreater of 80% of disposable earnings or 35 x state minimum hourly wage (consumer debt); greater of 75% or 35 x federal minimum wage (other debts); private student loans: greater of 85% or 50 x highest state minimum wageRCW 6.27.150

Tools of the trade$15,000RCW 6.15.010(1)(e)

Retirement accountsUnlimited (IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(a)/403(a)/403(b) plans, Keoghs, HSAs/MSAs, retirement bonds)RCW 6.15.020

Retirement accounts also have federal protection. ERISA-qualified plans stay out of the bankruptcy estate under 11 U.S.C. § 541(c)(2), and 11 U.S.C. § 522(b)(3)(C) exempts tax-exempt retirement funds whatever the state law says. IRAs carry a federal dollar cap under § 522(n). Which state's exemptions you use depends on where you lived during the two years before filing (11 U.S.C. § 522(b)(3)(A)).

Last verified September 20, 2026. Amounts change, so check the statute before you rely on a figure. "Needs review" marks a figure we have not yet confirmed against the statute or the court. This is general information, not legal advice.

Filing Bankruptcy in Washington

Districts

Filing Costs

Chapter 7 filing fee: $338. Chapter 13: $313. Fee waivers are available for filers below 150% of the poverty line. Installment payments available for all filers. Full cost breakdown.

Before You File

Complete credit counseling from an approved provider (required within 180 days before filing).

Determine your chapter - Chapter 7 vs. Chapter 13 comparison.

List all debts, assets, income, and expenses for the bankruptcy schedules.

After You File

The automatic stay takes effect immediately, stopping collections, garnishments, and lawsuits.

Complete a debtor education course (required before discharge).

Receive your discharge (Chapter 7: ~60-90 days after 341 meeting; Chapter 13: after completing 3-5 year plan).

Important: This page provides educational information about bankruptcy in Wyoming. It is not legal advice. Median income figures are approximate (Census/DOJ, effective April 2026). Verify current amounts at the DOJ Means Testing page.

Wyoming Exemptions

State Exemptions Only

Wyoming requires bankruptcy filers to use state exemptions exclusively. Federal exemptions under 11 U.S.C. Section 522(d) are not available. Research Wyoming's homestead, vehicle, personal property, and wildcard exemptions before filing.

Wyoming exemption amounts

Federal exemptions: not allowed. Wyoming has opted out of the federal exemptions, so filers use the state exemptions below (Wyo. Stat. § 1-20-109).

Married couples filing jointly: not every exemption here doubles for a joint case; check each statute (source).

ExemptionAmountStatuteNotes

Homestead$100,000Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-20-101, 1-20-102(b)Per resident (each joint owner-occupant)

Motor vehicle$5,000Wyo. Stat. § 1-20-106(a)(iv)

Household goods$4,000Wyo. Stat. § 1-20-106(a)(iii), § 1-20-105Per person occupying the residence (furniture, bedding, provisions, household articles); apparel $2,000 (§ 1-20-105); up to 3 firearms $3,000

WildcardNone needs reviewWyo. Stat. §§ 1-20-101 to 1-20-110

WagesGreater of 75% of weekly disposable earnings or 30 x federal minimum hourly wageWyo. Stat. § 1-15-408(b)

Tools of the trade$4,000Wyo. Stat. § 1-20-106(b)(tools, team, implements or stock in trade), or $4,000 professional library and instruments

Retirement accountsUnlimited (interest in and payments from a retirement plan), except contributions made within 90 days before filingWyo. Stat. § 1-20-110

Retirement accounts also have federal protection. ERISA-qualified plans stay out of the bankruptcy estate under 11 U.S.C. § 541(c)(2), and 11 U.S.C. § 522(b)(3)(C) exempts tax-exempt retirement funds whatever the state law says. IRAs carry a federal dollar cap under § 522(n). Which state's exemptions you use depends on where you lived during the two years before filing (11 U.S.C. § 522(b)(3)(A)).

Last verified September 20, 2026. Amounts change, so check the statute before you rely on a figure. "Needs review" marks a figure we have not yet confirmed against the statute or the court. This is general information, not legal advice.

Homestead Exemption

Protects equity in your primary residence. Amounts vary by state. Check Wyoming homestead exemption amounts.

Vehicle Exemption

Protects equity in your car. Most states protect $2,000 to $7,500. See vehicle exemption details.

Retirement Accounts

401(k)s, IRAs, and pensions are generally fully exempt in bankruptcy. See retirement exemptions.

Wildcard Exemption

Applies to any property. Not all states offer this. See wildcard exemptions.

If your household income is at or below these thresholds, you pass Part 1 of the means test and likely qualify for Chapter 7.

Filing Bankruptcy in Wyoming

Districts

Wyoming has a single federal bankruptcy district. All cases are filed in this one court, which simplifies the process.

Filing Costs

Chapter 7 filing fee: $338. Chapter 13: $313. Fee waivers are available for filers below 150% of the poverty line. Installment payments available for all filers. Full cost breakdown.

Before You File

Complete credit counseling from an approved provider (required within 180 days before filing).

Determine your chapter - Chapter 7 vs. Chapter 13 comparison.

Gather income documentation for the last 6 full calendar months.

List all debts, assets, income, and expenses for the bankruptcy schedules.

Research Wyoming exemptions to understand what property you can keep.

After You File

The automatic stay takes effect immediately, stopping collections, garnishments, and lawsuits.

Attend the 341 meeting of creditors (usually 30-45 days after filing).

Complete a debtor education course (required before discharge).

Receive your discharge (Chapter 7: ~60-90 days after 341 meeting; Chapter 13: after completing 3-5 year plan).

Step-by-step guides: How Chapter 7 works (liquidation: who qualifies, the process, what you keep) · How Chapter 13 works (the repayment plan: eligibility, how the payment is set, why plans fail). Both are free, plain-English, and not legal advice.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I keep my car in Wyoming bankruptcy?

Wyoming protects $5,000 in a motor vehicle under Wyo. Stat. § 1-20-106(a)(iv). Last verified September 20, 2026. Amounts change, so check the statute.

Does Wyoming use federal or state exemptions?

Wyoming uses state exemptions only. The state has opted out of the federal exemptions in 11 U.S.C. § 522(d) (Wyo. Stat. § 1-20-109).

How much does it cost to file bankruptcy in Wyoming?

The court filing fee for Chapter 7 is $338 and Chapter 13 is $313. Attorney fees in Wyoming typically range from $1,000 to $3,500 for Chapter 7 and $2,500 to $5,000 for Chapter 13. You can also file without an attorney (pro se) and request to pay the filing fee in installments.

What is the income limit for Chapter 7 in Wyoming?

The means test compares your household income to Wyoming's median. For a single person, the current threshold is approximately $71,571 per year. For a family of four, it is approximately $126,681. If your income is below the median for your household size, you pass Part 1 of the means test.

What property can I keep in Wyoming bankruptcy?

Wyoming requires filers to use state exemptions only. Key exemptions to research include the homestead exemption (how much home equity you can protect), vehicle exemption, personal property exemption, and any wildcard exemption. Check Wyoming statutes for current amounts.

How long does bankruptcy stay on my credit in Wyoming?

Chapter 7 stays on your credit report for 10 years from the filing date. Chapter 13 stays for 7 years. However, many people begin rebuilding credit within 1-2 years of discharge and can qualify for a mortgage within 2-4 years.

Can I file bankruptcy again in Wyoming?

Yes, but there are waiting periods between discharges. Chapter 7 to Chapter 7: 8 years. Chapter 7 to Chapter 13: 4 years. Chapter 13 to Chapter 13: 2 years. Chapter 13 to Chapter 7: 6 years (unless you paid 100% or 70%+ with good faith). Use the free discharge eligibility screener to check your dates.

What debts cannot be discharged in bankruptcy?

Most debts are dischargeable, but exceptions include most student loans (unless you prove undue hardship), child support and alimony, recent tax debts (generally last 3 years), debts from fraud or willful injury, DUI-related debts, and criminal fines. See nondischargeable.org for the full list.
